\section{Smooth Functions and Smooth Maps}\label{sec:smooth-maps}\label{sub:smooth-maps}

\roadmark{Stage: foundations}{With a smooth structure in hand the chart drops out of the phrase ``smooth'': smooth functions, smooth maps, diffeomorphisms and product manifolds.}

Definition~\ref{def:smooth-in-chart} explains what it means for a function to be smooth \emph{in the sense of one chart}. With a smooth structure in hand the chart can be dropped from the phrase. Throughout, $M$ is a smooth manifold with maximal atlas $\mathcal{A}$.

\begin{defbox}[Smooth Chart]\deflabel{def:smooth-chart-M}
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold with maximal atlas $\mathcal{A}$. A \textbf{smooth chart} of $M$ is a chart belonging to $\mathcal{A}$ --- equivalently, by Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-atlas}, a chart compatible with every chart of some, hence any, atlas generating $\mathcal{A}$.
\leeref{Ch.~1, \emph{Smooth Structures}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[Smooth Function on a Manifold]\deflabel{def:smooth-function}
A function $f : M \to \mathbb{R}$ is \textbf{smooth} if for every $p \in M$ there exists a smooth chart $(U,\varphi)$ with $p \in U$ such that
\[
f_\varphi \;:=\; f|_U \circ \varphi^{-1} : \varphi(U) \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}
\]
is smooth in the sense of analysis. (The function $f_\varphi$ is $f$ written in the coordinates of the chart; it is what Definition~\ref{def:smooth-in-chart} called $h \circ \varphi^{-1}$.)
\leeref{Ch.~2, \emph{Smooth Functions and Smooth Maps}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[Some Chart Suffices --- Every Chart Then Works]\thmlabel{prop:some-any-function}
If $f : M \to \mathbb{R}$ is smooth, then $f_\psi = f|_V \circ \psi^{-1}$ is smooth for \emph{every} smooth chart $(V,\psi)$ of $M$.
\leeref{Ch.~2, \emph{Smooth Functions and Smooth Maps}}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Stated in lecture, with the proof left to the class; filled in.)} Let $(V,\psi)$ be a smooth chart and $q \in V$; we show $f_\psi$ is smooth on a neighborhood of $\psi(q)$. Since smoothness of a function on an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a local property --- all partial derivatives at a point are determined by the values near it --- this suffices. By Definition~\ref{def:smooth-function} there is a smooth chart $(U,\varphi)$ with $q \in U$ and $f_\varphi$ smooth on $\varphi(U)$. Both charts belong to the maximal atlas, so they are compatible (Definition~\ref{def:atlas}): the transition $\varphi \circ \psi^{-1} : \psi(U \cap V) \to \varphi(U \cap V)$ is a diffeomorphism (Definition~\ref{def:compatible}), in particular smooth. The set $\psi(U \cap V)$ is open (Proposition~\ref{prop:transition-homeo}) and contains $\psi(q)$. For $b \in \psi(U \cap V)$ the point $\psi^{-1}(b)$ lies in $U$, so $\varphi^{-1}(\varphi(\psi^{-1}(b))) = \psi^{-1}(b)$, and therefore on the open set $\psi(U \cap V) \ni \psi(q)$,
\[
f_\psi = f \circ \psi^{-1} = \big(f \circ \varphi^{-1}\big) \circ \big(\varphi \circ \psi^{-1}\big) = f_\varphi \circ (\varphi \circ \psi^{-1}),
\]
a composite of the smooth map $f_\varphi$ with the transition function $\varphi \circ \psi^{-1}$, which is smooth by compatibility and takes values in $\varphi(U \cap V) \subseteq \varphi(U)$, where $f_\varphi$ is defined. By the chain rule the composite is smooth. Hence $f_\psi$ is smooth near $\psi(q)$; as $q \in V$ was arbitrary, $f_\psi$ is smooth on $\psi(V)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:smooth-structures-7}
The point of logic: the definition says ``there \emph{exists} a chart,'' and the proposition upgrades it to ``\emph{any} chart.'' Without the proposition, smoothness of $f$ would appear to depend on which charts one happened to test it in. The upgrade costs exactly one use of compatibility --- which is what compatibility was designed to buy (Theorem~\ref{thm:compat-agree}). The proposition was set in lecture as an exercise, not to be collected.
\end{rembox}

To compare two smooth manifolds one needs smooth \emph{maps} between them.

\begin{defbox}[Smooth Map]\deflabel{def:smooth-map}
Let $(M, \mathcal{A}_M)$ and $(N, \mathcal{A}_N)$ be smooth manifolds of dimensions $m$ and $n$. A map $F : M \to N$ is \textbf{smooth} if it is continuous and for every $p \in M$ there are charts $(U,\varphi) \in \mathcal{A}_M$ with $p \in U$ and $(V,\psi) \in \mathcal{A}_N$ with $F(U) \subseteq V$ such that the \textbf{coordinate representation}
\[
\psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1} : \varphi(U) \longrightarrow \psi(V) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n
\]
is smooth.
\leeref{Ch.~2, \emph{Smooth Functions and Smooth Maps}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[Diffeomorphism]\deflabel{def:diffeomorphism}
Let $(M, \mathcal{A}_M)$ and $(N, \mathcal{A}_N)$ be smooth manifolds. A map $F : M \to N$ is a \textbf{diffeomorphism} if it is a smooth bijection with smooth inverse (Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}) --- generalizing Definition~\ref{def:diffeo-euclidean}, with which it agrees on open subsets of Euclidean space (Proposition~\ref{prop:diffeo-agree}).
\leeref{Ch.~2, \emph{Smooth Functions and Smooth Maps}}
\end{defbox}


\begin{propbox}[Smoothness of a Map Does Not Depend on the Charts]\thmlabel{prop:smooth-map-charts}
If $F : M \to N$ is smooth, then for \emph{every} pair of smooth charts $(U',\varphi')$ of $M$ and $(V',\psi')$ of $N$ with $F(U') \subseteq V'$, the coordinate representation $\psi' \circ F \circ \varphi'^{-1} : \varphi'(U') \to \psi'(V')$ is smooth. For $N = \mathbb{R}$ with its standard one-chart atlas, Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map} agrees with Definition~\ref{def:smooth-function}.
\leeref{Proposition 2.5}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} \emph{Every pair of charts.} Let $(U',\varphi')$ and $(V',\psi')$ be smooth charts of $M$ and $N$ with $F(U') \subseteq V'$; we show $\psi' \circ F \circ \varphi'^{-1}$ is smooth on $\varphi'(U')$. Smoothness is local, so it suffices to show it near each point. Fix $a \in \varphi'(U')$ and put $p = \varphi'^{-1}(a)$. Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map} supplies charts $(U,\varphi)$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ at $F(p)$ with $F(U) \subseteq V$ and $\psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}$ smooth. The set $U \cap U'$ is open and contains $p$, so $\varphi'(U \cap U')$ is open and contains $a$. For $b$ in it, $x = \varphi'^{-1}(b)$ lies in $U \cap U'$, so $\varphi^{-1}(\varphi(x)) = x$, and $F(x) \in F(U) \cap F(U') \subseteq V \cap V'$, so $\psi^{-1}(\psi(F(x))) = F(x)$. Hence on the open set $\varphi'(U \cap U') \ni a$,
\[
\psi' \circ F \circ \varphi'^{-1} = (\psi' \circ \psi^{-1}) \circ (\psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}) \circ (\varphi \circ \varphi'^{-1}).
\]
Here $\varphi \circ \varphi'^{-1}$ maps $\varphi'(U \cap U')$ into $\varphi(U \cap U')$, then $F$ maps $U \cap U'$ into $V \cap V'$, and $\psi' \circ \psi^{-1}$ is defined on $\psi(V \cap V')$. The outer factors are transition functions, smooth by compatibility: $(U,\varphi)$ and $(U',\varphi')$ both belong to the maximal atlas of $M$, and $(V,\psi)$ and $(V',\psi')$ to that of $N$, so each pair is compatible (Definitions~\ref{def:atlas} and~\ref{def:compatible}). The middle one is smooth by hypothesis (restricted to the open subset $\varphi(U \cap U')$ of $\varphi(U)$). So the composite is smooth near $a$ by the chain rule, and $a$ was arbitrary.

\emph{The case $N = \mathbb{R}$.} Give $\mathbb{R}$ the structure of its one-chart atlas $\{(\mathbb{R}, \mathrm{id})\}$. For $N = \mathbb{R}$, taking $\psi = \mathrm{id}$ turns Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map} into Definition~\ref{def:smooth-function}; continuity is automatic there, since $f = f_\varphi \circ \varphi$ near each point. In both directions: if $f : M \to \mathbb{R}$ is smooth in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map} and $p \in M$, take any smooth chart $(U,\varphi)$ at $p$; since $f(U) \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, the first part applied to $(U,\varphi)$ and $(\mathbb{R}, \mathrm{id})$ shows that $\mathrm{id} \circ f \circ \varphi^{-1} = f|_U \circ \varphi^{-1} = f_\varphi$ is smooth, which is Definition~\ref{def:smooth-function} at $p$. Conversely, if $f$ satisfies Definition~\ref{def:smooth-function}, then for each $p$ there is a smooth chart $(U,\varphi)$ at $p$ with $f_\varphi$ smooth, and the pair $(U,\varphi)$, $(\mathbb{R}, \mathrm{id})$ has $f(U) \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and coordinate representation $\mathrm{id} \circ f \circ \varphi^{-1} = f_\varphi$, smooth. The remaining condition of Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}, continuity, holds because $f|_U = f_\varphi \circ \varphi$ is a composite of continuous maps on each such open $U$, and these $U$ cover $M$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lembox}[A Chart Mapped into a Given Chart]\thmlabel{lem:charts-around-map}
Let $F : M \to N$ be a continuous map between smooth manifolds (for instance a smooth map), and $p \in M$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item For every smooth chart $(V, \psi)$ of $N$ with $F(p) \in V$ and every smooth chart $(U_0, \varphi_0)$ of $M$ with $p \in U_0$, the set $U = U_0 \cap F^{-1}(V)$ is an open neighbourhood of $p$, $(U, \varphi_0|_U)$ is a smooth chart of $M$, and $F(U) \subseteq V$.
    \item For every open neighbourhood $W$ of $p$ there are smooth charts $(U, \varphi)$ of $M$ with $p \in U \subseteq W$ and $(V, \psi)$ of $N$ with $F(p) \in V$ such that $F(U) \subseteq V$.
    \item If $F$ is smooth, then in the charts of (1) (with $\varphi = \varphi_0|_U$) or of (2) the coordinate representation $\psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1} : \varphi(U) \to \psi(V)$ is smooth.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in --- the shrinking step used, mostly tacitly, whenever charts are chosen on both sides of a map.)}

\emph{(1)} $V$ is open in $N$ and $F$ is continuous, so $F^{-1}(V)$ is open in $M$, and $U = U_0 \cap F^{-1}(V)$ is open as an intersection of two open sets. It contains $p$, since $p \in U_0$ and $F(p) \in V$. As $U$ is an open subset of $U_0$, Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(1) shows that $(U, \varphi_0|_U)$ is a smooth chart of $M$. Finally, every $q \in U$ lies in $F^{-1}(V)$, so $F(q) \in V$; that is, $F(U) \subseteq V$.

\emph{(2)} The domains of the smooth charts cover $M$ and $N$ (the maximal atlases are atlases, Definition~\ref{def:atlas}), so there are a smooth chart $(V, \psi)$ of $N$ with $F(p) \in V$ and a smooth chart $(U_1, \varphi_1)$ of $M$ with $p \in U_1$. The set $U_0 = U_1 \cap W$ is open and contains $p$, and $(U_0, \varphi_1|_{U_0})$ is a smooth chart by Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(1). Part (1), applied to it and to $(V, \psi)$, gives the smooth chart $(U, \varphi) = (U_0 \cap F^{-1}(V), \varphi_1|_U)$ at $p$, with $U \subseteq U_0 \subseteq W$ and $F(U) \subseteq V$.

\emph{(3)} In both cases $(U, \varphi)$ and $(V, \psi)$ are smooth charts with $F(U) \subseteq V$, so Proposition~\ref{prop:smooth-map-charts} applies to them: the coordinate representation $\psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is smooth.
\end{proof}

\begin{defbox}[Diffeomorphic Manifolds]\deflabel{def:diffeomorphic}
Smooth manifolds $M$ and $N$ are \textbf{diffeomorphic} if there is a diffeomorphism $F : M \to N$. Diffeomorphic manifolds are also called \textbf{isomorphic as smooth manifolds}.
\leeref{Ch.~2, \emph{Diffeomorphisms}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:smooth-structures-8}
``Diffeomorphic'' is to smooth manifolds what ``homeomorphic'' is to topological spaces: the notion of sameness, under which every smooth property is preserved. No symbol is introduced for it; $\cong$ is already used in these notes for homeomorphisms and linear isomorphisms, so the word is written out.
\end{rembox}

\begin{propbox}[The Two Notions of Diffeomorphism Agree]\thmlabel{prop:diffeo-agree}
Give open sets $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ and $B \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ their standard smooth structures, determined by the charts $(A, \mathrm{id}_A)$ and $(B, \mathrm{id}_B)$. Then a map $F : A \to B$ is smooth in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map} if and only if it is smooth in the Euclidean sense. Consequently, for $m = n$, $F$ is a diffeomorphism in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:diffeomorphism} if and only if it is one in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:diffeo-euclidean}, and $A$ and $B$ are diffeomorphic in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:diffeomorphic} if and only if they are in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:diffeo-euclidean}.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} \emph{Euclidean-smooth implies smooth.} If $F$ is smooth in the Euclidean sense, it is continuous, and in the charts $(A, \mathrm{id}_A)$ and $(B, \mathrm{id}_B)$ its coordinate representation is $F$ itself, which is smooth: at every $p \in A$ these charts satisfy $p \in A$ and $F(A) \subseteq B$, and $\mathrm{id}_B \circ F \circ \mathrm{id}_A^{-1} = F$. So Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map} holds.

\emph{Smooth implies Euclidean-smooth.} Conversely, suppose $F$ is smooth in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}, and let $p \in A$ with charts $(U, \varphi)$ and $(V, \psi)$ as in that definition: $p \in U$, $F(U) \subseteq V$, and $\psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}$ smooth. These charts belong to the standard structures, so they are compatible with the identity charts (Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-atlas}): $\varphi = \varphi \circ \mathrm{id}_A^{-1}$ and $\psi^{-1} = \mathrm{id}_B \circ \psi^{-1}$ are smooth in the Euclidean sense, by Definition~\ref{def:compatible}. In detail: the transition from $(A, \mathrm{id}_A)$ to $(U,\varphi)$ is $\varphi \circ \mathrm{id}_A^{-1} = \varphi$ on $\mathrm{id}_A(A \cap U) = U$, a diffeomorphism $U \to \varphi(U)$; and the transition from $(V,\psi)$ to $(B, \mathrm{id}_B)$ is $\mathrm{id}_B \circ \psi^{-1} = \psi^{-1}$ on $\psi(V)$, a diffeomorphism $\psi(V) \to V$. Since $\varphi^{-1} \circ \varphi = \mathrm{id}_U$ and $\psi^{-1} \circ \psi = \mathrm{id}_V$ with $F(U) \subseteq V$, on $U$
\[
F = \psi^{-1} \circ \big(\psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}\big) \circ \varphi
\]
is a composite of Euclidean-smooth maps, so $F$ is smooth on the open neighbourhood $U$ of $p$ (chain rule). As $p$ was arbitrary and smoothness is local, $F$ is smooth on $A$.

\emph{Diffeomorphisms.} For diffeomorphisms, apply this to $F$ and to $F^{-1}$. Explicitly, for $m = n$: $F$ is a diffeomorphism in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:diffeomorphism} iff it is a bijection with $F : A \to B$ and $F^{-1} : B \to A$ smooth in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}; by the first two paragraphs (the second time with $A$ and $B$ interchanged) this holds iff $F$ is a bijection with $F$ and $F^{-1}$ smooth in the Euclidean sense, which is Definition~\ref{def:diffeo-euclidean}. Since in both senses ``diffeomorphic'' means that a diffeomorphism $A \to B$ exists, the two notions of being diffeomorphic agree as well.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:smooth-structures-9}
Not stated in lecture. The word is defined twice because the logic needs it twice: Definition~\ref{def:diffeo-euclidean} must exist before smooth manifolds do, since compatibility of charts is phrased with it, and Definition~\ref{def:diffeomorphism} is the general notion. The proposition is what licenses using one word for both. A third notion, the \emph{local} diffeomorphism of \ref{sec:special-maps}, is genuinely different; Corollary~\ref{cor:bijective-local-diffeo} relates it to the other two.
\end{rembox}

\begin{lembox}[Composition of Smooth Maps]\thmlabel{lem:composition-smooth}
If $F : M \to N$ and $G : N \to P$ are smooth maps of smooth manifolds, then $G \circ F : M \to P$ is smooth.
\leeref{Proposition 2.10}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~7, as a routine verification; filled in.)} $G \circ F$ is continuous as a composite of continuous maps. Fix $p \in M$; we must produce charts at $p$ and at $G(F(p))$ satisfying Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}. The order of choices matters.

\emph{Step 1: charts for $G$ at $F(p)$.} Since $G$ is smooth, there are smooth charts $(V, \psi)$ of $N$ with $F(p) \in V$ and $(W, \chi)$ of $P$ with $G(V) \subseteq W$ such that $\chi \circ G \circ \psi^{-1}$ is smooth on $\psi(V)$.

\emph{Step 2: a chart for $F$ at $p$ landing inside $V$.} Since $F$ is smooth, there are smooth charts $(U_0, \varphi)$ of $M$ with $p \in U_0$ and $(V_0, \psi_0)$ of $N$ with $F(U_0) \subseteq V_0$ such that $\psi_0 \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is smooth. The chart $(V_0,\psi_0)$ need not be the $(V,\psi)$ of Step 1, so we adjust. Put $U = U_0 \cap F^{-1}(V)$ and keep the coordinate map $\varphi|_U$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:charts-around-map}(1), applied to the continuous map $F$, the chart $(V, \psi)$ of Step 1 and the chart $(U_0, \varphi)$: $U$ is an open neighborhood of $p$, since $F$ is continuous; $(U, \varphi|_U)$ is still a smooth chart, a restriction of one to an open subset (Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(1)); and $F(U) \subseteq V$. Now $F(U) \subseteq V \cap V_0$: for $a \in \varphi(U)$ the point $y = F(\varphi^{-1}(a))$ lies in $V \cap V_0$, so $\psi_0^{-1}(\psi_0(y)) = y$. Hence on $\varphi(U)$
\[
\psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1} = (\psi \circ \psi_0^{-1}) \circ (\psi_0 \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}),
\]
which is smooth: the first factor is a transition function of the maximal atlas of $N$, smooth on $\psi_0(V \cap V_0)$ by compatibility, the second is smooth by the choice of $(U_0,\varphi)$ and maps $\varphi(U)$ into $\psi_0(V \cap V_0)$; the composite is smooth by the chain rule.

\emph{Step 3: compose.} $G \circ F$ maps $U$ into $W$, because $F(U) \subseteq V$ and $G(V) \subseteq W$. For $a \in \varphi(U)$ the point $F(\varphi^{-1}(a))$ lies in $V$, so $\psi^{-1}(\psi(F(\varphi^{-1}(a)))) = F(\varphi^{-1}(a))$; hence on $\varphi(U)$
\[
\chi \circ (G \circ F) \circ \varphi^{-1} = \big(\chi \circ G \circ \psi^{-1}\big) \circ \big(\psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}\big),
\]
a composite of two smooth maps between open subsets of Euclidean spaces (the inner map takes values in $\psi(V)$ because $F(U) \subseteq V$), smooth by the chain rule. So $(U, \varphi|_U)$ and $(W, \chi)$ witness the smoothness of $G \circ F$ at $p$.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:smooth-structures-11}
That a composite of smooth maps is smooth is a routine verification. The only content is Step 2 --- the middle charts produced by the two hypotheses need not agree, and one must shrink the domain using continuity of $F$ and then pay one transition function to switch. ``Just compose the two'' skips exactly this.
\end{rembox}

\begin{propbox}[Inclusions of and Maps into Open Subsets]\thmlabel{prop:open-inclusion-smooth}
Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds and $S \subseteq M$ open, with the smooth structure of Proposition~\ref{prop:open-smooth}, and let $\iota : S \to M$ be the inclusion.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\iota$ is smooth.
    \item If $F : M \to N$ is smooth, so is its restriction $F|_S = F \circ \iota : S \to N$.
    \item A map $G : P \to S$ from a smooth manifold $P$ is smooth if and only if $\iota \circ G : P \to M$ is smooth.
\end{enumerate}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in --- these are used, mostly tacitly, wherever a map is restricted to, or lands in, an open subset.)} Throughout, the smooth charts of $S$ are the smooth charts of $M$ with domain in $S$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:open-smooth}(2)).

\emph{(1)} $\iota$ is continuous, as the inclusion of a subspace. Let $p \in S$ and let $(U, \varphi)$ be a smooth chart of $M$ at $p$ with $U \subseteq S$ (restrict any chart at $p$ to its intersection with $S$: a smooth chart of $M$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(1), and a chart of $S$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:open-smooth}(1)). It is a chart of $S$ and of $M$, $\iota(U) = U$, and the coordinate representation of $\iota$ in these charts is
\[
\varphi \circ \iota \circ \varphi^{-1} = \mathrm{id}_{\varphi(U)} ,
\]
which is smooth. So $\iota$ is smooth (Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}).

\emph{(2)} $F|_S = F \circ \iota$ is a composite of smooth maps, hence smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}).

\emph{(3)} If $G$ is smooth, so is $\iota \circ G$, by (1) and Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}. Conversely, suppose $\iota \circ G$ is smooth. Then $G$ is continuous into $S$: for $O \subseteq S$ open in $S$, $O$ is open in $M$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:open-in-open}), so $G^{-1}(O) = (\iota \circ G)^{-1}(O)$ is open. Let $x \in P$, and choose a smooth chart $(U, \varphi)$ of $M$ at $G(x)$ with $U \subseteq S$, a chart of $S$ as well, and a smooth chart $(W, \chi)$ of $P$ at $x$ with $G(W) \subseteq U$ (shrink any smooth chart of $P$ at $x$ to its intersection with $G^{-1}(U)$, open by continuity: Lemma~\ref{lem:charts-around-map}(1), applied to the continuous map $G : P \to S$ and the chart $(U, \varphi)$ of $S$). The coordinate representation of $G$ in $\chi$ and $\varphi$ is
\[
\varphi \circ G \circ \chi^{-1} = \varphi \circ (\iota \circ G) \circ \chi^{-1} \quad \text{on } \chi(W),
\]
the coordinate representation of the smooth map $\iota \circ G$ in the same charts, hence smooth. So $G$ is smooth (Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}, Proposition~\ref{prop:smooth-map-charts}).
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[Being Diffeomorphic Is an Equivalence Relation]\thmlabel{prop:diffeomorphic-equivalence}
\begin{enumerate}
    \item Being diffeomorphic is an equivalence relation on smooth manifolds.
    \item Diffeomorphic manifolds are homeomorphic.
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Proposition 2.15}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} (1) We check the three properties of an equivalence relation.

\emph{Reflexive:} $\mathrm{id}_M$ is a diffeomorphism, its coordinate representation in any chart $(U,\varphi)$, taken on both sides, being the identity of $\varphi(U)$. In detail: $\mathrm{id}_M$ is a continuous bijection and its own inverse; at each $p \in M$ choose a smooth chart $(U,\varphi)$ at $p$, so that $\mathrm{id}_M(U) = U \subseteq U$ and $\varphi \circ \mathrm{id}_M \circ \varphi^{-1} = \mathrm{id}_{\varphi(U)}$, which is smooth. So $\mathrm{id}_M$ and its inverse are smooth (Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}), and $M$ is diffeomorphic to itself.

\emph{Symmetric:} if $F$ is a diffeomorphism, so is $F^{-1}$, since the definition is symmetric in $F$ and $F^{-1}$: $F^{-1} : N \to M$ is a bijection, smooth by hypothesis, with inverse $(F^{-1})^{-1} = F$, also smooth (Definition~\ref{def:diffeomorphism}). So if $M$ is diffeomorphic to $N$, then $N$ is diffeomorphic to $M$.

\emph{Transitive:} if $F : M \to N$ and $G : N \to P$ are diffeomorphisms, then $G \circ F$ is smooth by Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}, and so is its inverse $F^{-1} \circ G^{-1}$. Here $G \circ F$ is a bijection with inverse $F^{-1} \circ G^{-1}$, since
\[
(G \circ F) \circ (F^{-1} \circ G^{-1}) = G \circ G^{-1} = \mathrm{id}_P, \qquad (F^{-1} \circ G^{-1}) \circ (G \circ F) = F^{-1} \circ F = \mathrm{id}_M,
\]
and $F^{-1} \circ G^{-1}$ is smooth by the same lemma applied to the smooth maps $G^{-1} : P \to N$ and $F^{-1} : N \to M$. So $M$ is diffeomorphic to $P$.

(2) Smooth maps are continuous by Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}, so a diffeomorphism is a continuous bijection with continuous inverse, that is, a homeomorphism. Hence diffeomorphic manifolds are homeomorphic.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:smooth-structures-10}
The converse of (2) is false: Milnor's exotic $7$-spheres are homeomorphic to $S^7$ but not diffeomorphic to it (see the remark after Example~\ref{ex:two-structures-R}). Two further distinctions are worth keeping apart. \emph{Different smooth structures} on one set may still be \emph{diffeomorphic}: in Example~\ref{ex:two-structures-R}, $\mathbb{R}$ and $\widetilde{\mathbb{R}}$ have different maximal atlases, yet $x \mapsto x^3$ is a diffeomorphism between them. And being diffeomorphic is a property of a \emph{pair} of manifolds, while being a diffeomorphism is a property of a \emph{map}: $\mathrm{id} : \mathbb{R} \to \widetilde{\mathbb{R}}$ is not a diffeomorphism even though the two are diffeomorphic.
\end{rembox}


\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.2em, column sep=3.4em]
U \subseteq M \arrow[r, "F"] \arrow[d, "\varphi"'] & V \subseteq N \arrow[d, "\psi"] \\
\varphi(U) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m \arrow[r, "\psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}"'] & \psi(V) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

The top row is the map one cares about, between spaces where ``smooth'' has no meaning; the bottom row is its coordinate representation, between open subsets of Euclidean spaces where it does. The two vertical arrows are charts, so they are homeomorphisms, and the square commutes by construction. Smoothness of $F$ is \emph{defined} by smoothness of the bottom arrow, and Proposition~\ref{prop:smooth-map-charts} says this does not depend on which charts are used to build it.

\begin{exbox}[Two Smooth Structures on the Real Line]\exlabel{ex:two-structures-R}
Take $M = \mathbb{R}$ as a topological space in both cases, and put
\[
\mathbb{R} = (\mathbb{R}, \{(\mathbb{R}, \varphi)\}), \ \ \varphi = \mathrm{id}; \qquad\qquad
\widetilde{\mathbb{R}} = (\mathbb{R}, \{(\mathbb{R}, \psi)\}), \ \ \psi(p) = \sqrt[3]{p}.
\]
Both $\varphi$ and $\psi$ are homeomorphisms of $\mathbb{R}$ onto $\mathbb{R}$, so each is a legitimate chart (Definition~\ref{def:smooth-chart}), and a one-chart atlas is automatically smooth: the only compatibility to check is of the chart with itself, and the transition function is the identity. By Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-atlas} each therefore determines a smooth structure.
\leeref{Example 1.23}
\end{exbox}

\begin{proof}[Working out the example]
\textit{(Lecture~5 introduced this example --- the two structures are not compatible, but isomorphic --- and Lecture~6 returned to it, naming this kind of isomorphism \emph{diffeomorphism}. Worked out here.)} \emph{Step 1: the formula of a chart is not a legality condition.} One is tempted to object that $\psi$ ``is not smooth.'' On a bare topological manifold that question is not yet posed: ``smooth'' for a function on $M$ has no meaning until a structure is fixed, and here $\psi$ is what supplies the structure. What makes $\sqrt[3]{\,\cdot\,}$ look illegitimate is a silent comparison against the standard structure of $\mathbb{R}$ --- and that comparison is not part of Definition~\ref{def:smooth-chart}; it is the compatibility question of \S\ref{sub:compatibility}, arriving early and in disguise. Any homeomorphism onto an open set is a chart, whatever its formula. The formula is irrelevant to whether the chart may be written down, and decisive for which structure it produces.

\emph{Step 2: each chart is smooth for its own structure.} By Definition~\ref{def:smooth-in-chart}, a function $h : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is smooth in the sense of $\psi$ iff $h \circ \psi^{-1}$ is smooth, where $\psi^{-1}(y) = y^3$. Taking $h = \psi$ gives $\psi \circ \psi^{-1} = \mathrm{id}$, which is smooth. So $\sqrt[3]{\,\cdot\,}$ \emph{is} a smooth function on $\widetilde{\mathbb{R}}$. Nothing is special about this chart: the coordinate representation of any chart in its own coordinates is the identity, so every chart of an atlas is smooth for the structure that atlas generates. In the same way $\psi : \widetilde{\mathbb{R}} \to \mathbb{R}$ is a diffeomorphism --- a chart is exactly an identification of its domain with a piece of Euclidean space, carried out in whichever coordinate the chart names. Explicitly, by Definitions~\ref{def:smooth-map} and~\ref{def:diffeomorphism}: $\psi$ is a homeomorphism, so continuous with continuous inverse $\psi^{-1}(y) = y^3$; in the charts $(\mathbb{R}, \psi)$ of $\widetilde{\mathbb{R}}$ and $(\mathbb{R}, \mathrm{id})$ of $\mathbb{R}$ its coordinate representation is $\mathrm{id} \circ \psi \circ \psi^{-1} = \mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{R}}$, and that of $\psi^{-1}$ is $\psi \circ \psi^{-1} \circ \mathrm{id}^{-1} = \mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{R}}$, both smooth.

\emph{Step 3: the two structures are different.} Compatibility is a condition on a \emph{pair} of charts, and it is here that the two disagree. The two transition functions are
\[
\psi \circ \varphi^{-1}(x) = \sqrt[3]{x}, \qquad\qquad \varphi \circ \psi^{-1}(y) = y^3,
\]
and note the asymmetry: the second is smooth, the first is not, since $\tfrac{d}{dx}\sqrt[3]{x} = \tfrac13 x^{-2/3}$ blows up at $x = 0$. Definition~\ref{def:compatible} demands that the transition function be a diffeomorphism, i.e.\ that \emph{both} directions be smooth --- and this example is why: with only one direction required, compatibility would not even be a symmetric relation. So the charts are not compatible, the atlases are not compatible, and the maximal atlases are distinct. In detail: each atlas has one chart, so the atlases are compatible iff these two charts are (Definition~\ref{def:compatible-atlases}); and by Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-atlas} two atlases lie in the same maximal atlas iff they are compatible. Equivalently, in the language of Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}: the identity map $\mathbb{R} \to \widetilde{\mathbb{R}}$ has coordinate representation $\psi \circ \mathrm{id} \circ \varphi^{-1}(t) = \sqrt[3]{t}$ and is \emph{not} smooth. (If it were smooth, Proposition~\ref{prop:smooth-map-charts} would make its representation in these two charts smooth.)

\emph{Step 4: which functions are smooth in each.} Smooth in the sense of $\varphi$ means $h \circ \varphi^{-1} = h$ is smooth, so $C^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ is the usual class. Smooth in the sense of $\psi$ means $y \mapsto h(y^3)$ is smooth. Every ordinarily smooth $h$ passes this test, being a composite of smooth maps: $y \mapsto h(y^3)$ is $h$ after the polynomial $y \mapsto y^3$, smooth by the chain rule. And $h = \sqrt[3]{\,\cdot\,}$ passes it, since $h(y^3) = \sqrt[3]{y^3} = y$, while failing the first, since it is not differentiable at $0$ (Step 3). Hence
\[
C^\infty(\mathbb{R}) \subsetneq C^\infty(\widetilde{\mathbb{R}}),
\]
a \emph{strict} containment: $\widetilde{\mathbb{R}}$ has more smooth functions than $\mathbb{R}$. The two structures are genuinely different objects, not two names for one.

\emph{Step 5: and yet they are isomorphic.} Define $\Phi : \mathbb{R} \to \widetilde{\mathbb{R}}$, $\Phi(x) = x^3$. It is a bijection, continuous with continuous inverse $\Phi^{-1}(y) = \sqrt[3]{y}$. Its coordinate representation in the charts $(\mathbb{R}, \varphi)$ and $(\mathbb{R}, \psi)$ is $\psi \circ \Phi \circ \varphi^{-1}(t) = \sqrt[3]{t^3} = t$, the identity; the representation of $\Phi^{-1}(y) = \sqrt[3]{y}$ is likewise the identity, namely $\varphi \circ \Phi^{-1} \circ \psi^{-1}(t) = \Phi^{-1}(t^3) = \sqrt[3]{t^3} = t$. So $\Phi$ is a diffeomorphism, and $\mathbb{R}$ and $\widetilde{\mathbb{R}}$ are diffeomorphic. There is no contradiction with Step 4: the isomorphism is not the identity map, and pullback along $\Phi$ carries $C^\infty(\widetilde{\mathbb{R}})$ bijectively onto $C^\infty(\mathbb{R})$, so a strict containment between isomorphic objects is no more paradoxical here than elsewhere in infinite mathematics. (For $k \in C^\infty(\widetilde{\mathbb{R}})$, the function $k \circ \Phi$ is smooth on $\mathbb{R}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}, smooth functions being the smooth maps to $\mathbb{R}$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:smooth-map-charts}; and $g \mapsto g \circ \Phi^{-1}$ is the inverse map, by the same lemma applied to $\Phi^{-1}$.)

The moral is that $x$ is merely a \emph{label} for points of $\mathbb{R}$; the structure decides which functions of that label count as smooth, and the two structures decide differently. The identity map respects labels but not structure, while $x \mapsto x^3$ respects structure and scrambles labels.
\end{proof}

\textbf{Transcription note.} The board reads ``Claim: $\exists\,\Phi : \mathbb{R} \to \widetilde{\mathbb{R}}$ which is $C^\infty$, $\Phi(x) = \sqrt[3]{x}$.'' With $\widetilde{\mathbb{R}}$ carrying the chart $\psi = \sqrt[3]{\ \cdot\ }$, that map has coordinate representation $\sqrt[3]{\sqrt[3]{t}} = t^{1/9}$, which is not smooth at $0$; the domain and the formula have been paired the wrong way. The two correct readings are $\Phi : \mathbb{R} \to \widetilde{\mathbb{R}}$ with $\Phi(x) = x^3$ (used above), or the same map read backwards, $\Phi : \widetilde{\mathbb{R}} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $\Phi(x) = \sqrt[3]{x}$. Either way the coordinate representation is the identity, which is what the lecture meant by ``it looks strange, but rewritten in the differentiable coordinate you just get the identity.''

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=1.25]

\draw[violet!75!black,very thick,domain=-1:1,samples=90,smooth,variable=\t] plot ({\t*\t*\t},{\t});
\draw[orange!80!black,dashed] (0,-1.15) -- (0,1.15);
\node[font=\footnotesize,align=center,anchor=north] at (0,-1.4) {$\psi\circ\varphi^{-1}(t)=\sqrt[3]{t}$\\ vertical tangent at $0$: not smooth};
\begin{scope}[xshift=4.7cm]
\draw[gray!45,->] (-1.25,0)--(1.25,0); \draw[gray!45,->] (0,-1.25)--(0,1.25);
\draw[teal!60!black,very thick] (-1.1,-1.1) -- (1.1,1.1);
\node[font=\footnotesize,align=center,anchor=north] at (0,-1.4) {$\psi\circ\Phi\circ\varphi^{-1}(t)=t$\\ the identity: smooth};

\end{center}

\begin{propbox}[Transport of Smooth Structure]\thmlabel{prop:transport-structure}
Let $N$ be a smooth $n$-manifold, $X$ a topological space, and $h : X \to N$ a homeomorphism. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $X$ is a topological $n$-manifold, and $\mathcal{A}_h = \{\, (h^{-1}(V),\ \psi \circ h) \mid (V,\psi) \text{ a smooth chart of } N \,\}$ is a smooth atlas on $X$;
    \item for the smooth structure it determines, $h$ is a diffeomorphism;
    \item it is the \emph{only} smooth structure on $X$ for which $h$ is a diffeomorphism.
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{cf.\ Problem 1-6}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
(1) \emph{$X$ is a topological $n$-manifold.} Hausdorffness and second countability pass through homeomorphisms. Hausdorff: if $x \neq x'$ in $X$ then $h(x) \neq h(x')$ ($h$ is injective), so they have disjoint open neighbourhoods $O, O'$ in $N$, and $h^{-1}(O)$, $h^{-1}(O')$ are disjoint open neighbourhoods of $x, x'$ ($h$ is continuous). Second countable: if $\mathcal{B}$ is a countable basis of $N$, then $\{h^{-1}(B) \mid B \in \mathcal{B}\}$ is a countable basis of $X$, because every open $W \subseteq X$ has $h(W)$ open in $N$ ($h$ is a homeomorphism), $h(W)$ is a union of members of $\mathcal{B}$, and $W$ is the union of their preimages. Local Euclideanness of dimension $n$ follows from the charts just below (Proposition~\ref{prop:open-charts}).

\emph{The charts.} Each $\psi \circ h$ is a homeomorphism of the open set $h^{-1}(V)$ onto the open set $\psi(V) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$: $h^{-1}(V)$ is open because $h$ is continuous, $h$ restricts to a homeomorphism $h^{-1}(V) \to V$, and $\psi : V \to \psi(V)$ is a homeomorphism onto an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$. These domains cover $X$ because the $V$ cover $N$: for $x \in X$ choose a smooth chart $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ with $h(x) \in V$.

\emph{The transition functions.} For two charts $(h^{-1}(V), \psi \circ h)$ and $(h^{-1}(V'), \psi' \circ h)$ of $\mathcal{A}_h$ the overlap is $h^{-1}(V) \cap h^{-1}(V') = h^{-1}(V \cap V')$, with image $(\psi \circ h)\big(h^{-1}(V \cap V')\big) = \psi(V \cap V')$ (as $h$ is surjective). For $a \in \psi(V \cap V')$,
\[
(\psi' \circ h) \circ (\psi \circ h)^{-1}(a) = \psi'\Big(h\big(h^{-1}(\psi^{-1}(a))\big)\Big) = (\psi' \circ \psi^{-1})(a).
\]
So transition functions are $(\psi' \circ h) \circ (\psi \circ h)^{-1} = \psi' \circ \psi^{-1}$, transition functions of $N$, hence smooth: $(V,\psi)$ and $(V',\psi')$ both lie in the maximal atlas of $N$, so this transition is a diffeomorphism $\psi(V \cap V') \to \psi'(V \cap V')$ (Definitions~\ref{def:atlas} and~\ref{def:compatible}). So $\mathcal{A}_h$ is a smooth atlas (Definition~\ref{def:atlas}).

(2) In the charts $(h^{-1}(V), \psi \circ h)$ of $X$ and $(V, \psi)$ of $N$, the coordinate representation of $h$ is $\psi \circ h \circ (\psi \circ h)^{-1} = \mathrm{id}$, and likewise for $h^{-1}$. Both are continuous, so both are smooth. In detail: for $x \in X$ choose a smooth chart $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at $h(x)$; then $(h^{-1}(V), \psi \circ h) \in \mathcal{A}_h$ is a chart at $x$, $h\big(h^{-1}(V)\big) \subseteq V$, and for $a \in \psi(V)$
\[
\psi \circ h \circ (\psi \circ h)^{-1}(a) = \psi\Big(h\big(h^{-1}(\psi^{-1}(a))\big)\Big) = a,
\]
the identity of $\psi(V)$, which is smooth; so $h$ is smooth (Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}). For $h^{-1} : N \to X$ at $y \in N$ use a chart $(V,\psi)$ at $y$ and $(h^{-1}(V), \psi \circ h)$, which contains $h^{-1}(V)$; the representation is $(\psi \circ h) \circ h^{-1} \circ \psi^{-1} = \mathrm{id}_{\psi(V)}$, smooth. So $h$ is a smooth bijection with smooth inverse, a diffeomorphism (Definition~\ref{def:diffeomorphism}).

(3) Suppose $h$ is a diffeomorphism for some smooth structure $\mathcal{S}$ on $X$, and let $(W, \chi) \in \mathcal{S}$. Then $(\psi \circ h) \circ \chi^{-1} = \psi \circ h \circ \chi^{-1}$ is a coordinate representation of $h$, and $\chi \circ (\psi \circ h)^{-1} = \chi \circ h^{-1} \circ \psi^{-1}$ one of $h^{-1}$; both are smooth by Proposition~\ref{prop:smooth-map-charts}. In detail, fix a chart $(h^{-1}(V), \psi \circ h)$ of $\mathcal{A}_h$; if $W \cap h^{-1}(V) = \emptyset$ the two charts are compatible by Definition~\ref{def:compatible}. Otherwise put $W' = W \cap h^{-1}(V)$, open in $X$, and $V' = V \cap h(W)$, open in $N$ ($h$ is a homeomorphism), so that $h(W') = V'$. The restriction $(W', \chi|_{W'})$ belongs to $\mathcal{S}$ and $(V', \psi|_{V'})$ to the maximal atlas of $N$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(1), applied in the smooth manifold $(X, \mathcal{S})$ to the open subset $W'$ of $W$ and in $N$ to the open subset $V'$ of $V$: the restriction of a chart of a maximal atlas to an open subset has as transition functions the restrictions of the original ones to open sets, so it is compatible with every chart of the atlas and belongs to it by maximality.
\begin{itemize}
    \item The transition $(\psi \circ h) \circ \chi^{-1}$ on $\chi(W')$ is $\psi \circ h \circ (\chi|_{W'})^{-1}$, the coordinate representation of $h$ in the charts $(W', \chi|_{W'})$ of $X$ and $(V, \psi)$ of $N$, which satisfy $h(W') \subseteq V$. Since $h$ is smooth, it is smooth by Proposition~\ref{prop:smooth-map-charts}.
    \item The transition $\chi \circ (\psi \circ h)^{-1} = \chi \circ h^{-1} \circ \psi^{-1}$ on $(\psi \circ h)(W') = \psi(V')$ is the coordinate representation of $h^{-1}$ in the charts $(V', \psi|_{V'})$ of $N$ and $(W, \chi)$ of $X$, which satisfy $h^{-1}(V') = W' \subseteq W$. Since $h^{-1}$ is smooth, it is smooth by Proposition~\ref{prop:smooth-map-charts}.
\end{itemize}
The two transitions are mutually inverse bijections (Proposition~\ref{prop:transition-homeo}) and both smooth, so the charts are compatible (Definition~\ref{def:compatible}). So every chart of $\mathcal{S}$ is compatible with every chart of $\mathcal{A}_h$, i.e.\ $\mathcal{S}$ lies in the maximal atlas generated by $\mathcal{A}_h$, which by Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-atlas} is the set of all charts compatible with every chart of $\mathcal{A}_h$. Since $\mathcal{S}$ is itself maximal, the two coincide (Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-atlas}): $\mathcal{S}$ is contained in the atlas $\overline{\mathcal{A}_h}$, and a maximal atlas is contained in no strictly larger atlas (Definition~\ref{def:maximal-atlas}).
\end{proof}

\begin{defbox}[Transported Smooth Structure]\deflabel{def:transported}
In the situation of Proposition~\ref{prop:transport-structure}, the smooth structure on $X$ generated by $\mathcal{A}_h$ --- the unique one for which $h$ is a diffeomorphism --- is the smooth structure \textbf{transported} along $h$.
\leeref{cf.\ Problem 1-6}
\end{defbox}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:smooth-structures-12}
This is the smooth counterpart of Definition~\ref{def:homogeneous-topology}, where a \emph{topology} was transported along a bijection. Here a smooth structure is transported along a homeomorphism: the charts of $N$, precomposed with $h$, become charts of $X$. The structure on $X$ is then ``$N$'s structure, relabelled by $h$'', which is why $h$ is automatically a diffeomorphism.
\end{rembox}

\begin{corbox}[Single-Chart Structures on $\mathbb{R}^n$]\thmlabel{cor:single-chart-Rn}
Let $h : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be a homeomorphism, and let $M$ be $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the smooth structure determined by the one-chart atlas $\{(\mathbb{R}^n, h)\}$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\{(\mathbb{R}^n, h)\}$ is a smooth atlas.
    \item $h : M \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is a diffeomorphism onto $\mathbb{R}^n$ with its standard structure. So $M$ is diffeomorphic to standard $\mathbb{R}^n$.
    \item The smooth structure of $M$ \emph{equals} the standard one if and only if $h$ is a diffeomorphism of standard $\mathbb{R}^n$.
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Example 1.23 and Problem 1-6}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment 3, Problem 1.)} (1) The single domain $\mathbb{R}^n$ covers $M$; $h$ is a homeomorphism onto $h(\mathbb{R}^n) = \mathbb{R}^n$, which is open; and the only transition function is $h \circ h^{-1} = \mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{R}^n}$, which is smooth. So $\{(\mathbb{R}^n, h)\}$ is an atlas (Definition~\ref{def:atlas}).

(2) The underlying topological spaces of $M$ and of standard $\mathbb{R}^n$ are the same, so $h$ is a homeomorphism $M \to \mathbb{R}^n$, in particular continuous with continuous inverse $h^{-1}$. In the charts $(\mathbb{R}^n, h)$ of $M$ and $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathrm{id})$ of standard $\mathbb{R}^n$, the coordinate representation of $h$ is $\mathrm{id} \circ h \circ h^{-1} = \mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{R}^n}$, and that of $h^{-1}$ is $h \circ h^{-1} \circ \mathrm{id}^{-1} = \mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{R}^n}$. Both are smooth, so $h$ is a smooth bijection with smooth inverse. Equivalently, $M$ carries exactly the structure transported along $h$ from standard $\mathbb{R}^n$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:transport-structure}, with the atlas $\{(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathrm{id})\}$ of the target).

(3) The two one-chart atlases determine the same smooth structure if and only if they are compatible (Definition~\ref{def:compatible-atlases}; Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-atlas}), i.e.\ if and only if $h \circ \mathrm{id}^{-1} = h$ and $\mathrm{id} \circ h^{-1} = h^{-1}$ are both smooth --- that is, if and only if $h$ is a diffeomorphism of standard $\mathbb{R}^n$. In detail: each atlas has one chart, so they are compatible iff $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathrm{id})$ and $(\mathbb{R}^n, h)$ are compatible charts. Their overlap is $\mathbb{R}^n$, and the transition $h \circ \mathrm{id}^{-1} = h : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is a bijection with inverse $\mathrm{id} \circ h^{-1} = h^{-1}$. By Definitions~\ref{def:compatible} and~\ref{def:diffeo-euclidean} the charts are compatible iff $h$ and $h^{-1}$ are both smooth, which is the definition of $h$ being a diffeomorphism of standard $\mathbb{R}^n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=3em, column sep=5em]
M = \big(\mathbb{R}^n, \{h\}\big) \arrow[r, "h"] \arrow[d, "h"'] & \mathbb{R}^n_{\text{standard}} \arrow[d, "\mathrm{id}"] \\
\mathbb{R}^n \arrow[r, "\mathrm{id}"'] & \mathbb{R}^n
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

The proof of (2) in one square. Upstairs, $h$ is the map between the two manifolds; the vertical arrows are their charts, $h$ on the left and $\mathrm{id}$ on the right. The square commutes, so the coordinate representation along the bottom is the identity: $h$ is as smooth as a map can be, even when, as a map of standard $\mathbb{R}^n$, it is not differentiable at all.

\begin{exbox}[The Real Line with the Cube-Root Chart]\exlabel{ex:cube-root-transport}
For $n = 1$ and $h(x) = \sqrt[3]{x}$, the manifold $M$ is the $\widetilde{\mathbb{R}}$ of Example~\ref{ex:two-structures-R}. By Corollary~\ref{cor:single-chart-Rn}(3) its structure differs from the standard one, since $h$ is not differentiable at $0$. By part (2) it is nevertheless diffeomorphic to standard $\mathbb{R}$, via $h : \widetilde{\mathbb{R}} \to \mathbb{R}$ --- equivalently via $h^{-1}(x) = x^3$ in the other direction, the map $\Phi$ of that example.
\leeref{Example 1.23}
\end{exbox}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:smooth-structures-13}
Corollary~\ref{cor:single-chart-Rn} produces, from each homeomorphism of $\mathbb{R}^n$ that is not a diffeomorphism --- there are uncountably many --- a smooth structure on $\mathbb{R}^n$ \emph{different} from the standard one. By (2), every one of them is \emph{diffeomorphic} to the standard one. So ``how many smooth structures'' is the wrong question: the right one is how many up to diffeomorphism. It also shows something about the exotic structures of the next remark: an exotic $\mathbb{R}^4$ cannot admit a single chart whose image is all of $\mathbb{R}^4$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:global-chart-onto-Rn-diffeo}).
\end{rembox}

\begin{rembox}[Distinct Structures versus Non-Diffeomorphic Manifolds]\label{rem:distinct-structures-versus-non-diffeomorphic}
Example~\ref{ex:two-structures-R} shows that one topological manifold can carry distinct smooth structures --- but that alone is cheap, since pulling any structure back along a homeomorphism that is not a diffeomorphism produces another one, and all of these are diffeomorphic to the original (Proposition~\ref{prop:transport-structure}, Corollary~\ref{cor:single-chart-Rn}). The deep question is whether a topological manifold can carry structures that are \emph{not} diffeomorphic to one another. It can: Milnor found smooth structures on $S^7$ not diffeomorphic to the standard one (1956), and $\mathbb{R}^4$ admits uncountably many pairwise non-diffeomorphic structures, the first produced by combining Freedman's topological classification with Donaldson's gauge theory, the uncountable family by Taubes. By contrast $\mathbb{R}^n$ for $n \neq 4$ admits exactly one up to diffeomorphism --- a result of Stallings for $n \ge 5$ and of Rad\'o and Moise for $n \le 3$, not of Donaldson, to whom the lecture attributed it. All of this is far outside the course, but it is why the definitions above are made so carefully.
\end{rembox}

\begin{corbox}[{A Global Chart onto $\mathbb{R}^n$ Is a Diffeomorphism}]\thmlabel{cor:global-chart-onto-Rn-diffeo}
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $(M, \varphi)$ a chart of its smooth structure defined on all of $M$, with image $\varphi(M) = \mathbb{R}^n$. Then $\varphi : M \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is a diffeomorphism onto $\mathbb{R}^n$ with its standard structure. In particular an exotic $\mathbb{R}^4$ --- a smooth structure on $\mathbb{R}^4$ not diffeomorphic to the standard one, as in the remark \emph{Distinct Structures versus Non-Diffeomorphic Manifolds} in \ref{sec:smooth-maps} --- admits no single chart whose image is all of $\mathbb{R}^4$.
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
This is the argument of Corollary~\ref{cor:single-chart-Rn}(2). The chart $\varphi$ is a homeomorphism of $M$ onto $\mathbb{R}^n$ (Definition~\ref{def:smooth-chart}), so it is continuous with continuous inverse. In the charts $(M, \varphi)$ of $M$ and $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathrm{id})$ of standard $\mathbb{R}^n$, the coordinate representation of $\varphi$ is $\mathrm{id} \circ \varphi \circ \varphi^{-1} = \mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{R}^n}$, and that of $\varphi^{-1}$ is $\varphi \circ \varphi^{-1} \circ \mathrm{id}^{-1} = \mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{R}^n}$. Both are smooth, so $\varphi$ and $\varphi^{-1}$ are smooth (Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}) and $\varphi$ is a diffeomorphism (Definition~\ref{def:diffeomorphism}). If an exotic $\mathbb{R}^4$ had a chart defined on all of it with image $\mathbb{R}^4$, it would therefore be diffeomorphic to standard $\mathbb{R}^4$, contrary to its definition.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Product Manifolds}\label{sub:product-manifolds}

\textit{Lecture 11 (Fri Sep 25). The product of two smooth manifolds is a smooth manifold, with the products of charts as an atlas; its tangent spaces are treated in \ref{sub:tangent-products}.}

\begin{defbox}[Product Chart]\deflabel{def:product-chart}
Let $M_1$, $M_2$ be smooth manifolds of dimensions $m_1$, $m_2$, and let $(U_1, \varphi_1)$ be a smooth chart of $M_1$ and $(U_2, \varphi_2)$ a smooth chart of $M_2$. The \textbf{product chart} of the two is the pair
\[
\big(U_1 \times U_2,\ \varphi_1 \times \varphi_2\big), \qquad (\varphi_1 \times \varphi_2)(q_1, q_2) = \big(\varphi_1(q_1), \varphi_2(q_2)\big) \in \mathbb{R}^{m_1} \times \mathbb{R}^{m_2} = \mathbb{R}^{m_1 + m_2},
\]
on the product space $M_1 \times M_2$. That it is a chart is part of Proposition~\ref{prop:product-manifold}.
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[The Product Smooth Structure]\thmlabel{prop:product-manifold}
Let $M_1$, $M_2$ be smooth manifolds of dimensions $m_1$, $m_2$. The product space $M_1 \times M_2$ is a topological manifold of dimension $m_1 + m_2$, and the product charts (Definition~\ref{def:product-chart})
\[
\big(U_1 \times U_2,\ \varphi_1 \times \varphi_2\big), \qquad (\varphi_1 \times \varphi_2)(q_1, q_2) = \big(\varphi_1(q_1), \varphi_2(q_2)\big) \in \mathbb{R}^{m_1} \times \mathbb{R}^{m_2} = \mathbb{R}^{m_1 + m_2},
\]
with $(U_i, \varphi_i)$ a smooth chart of $M_i$, form a smooth atlas on it.
\leeref{Example 1.34}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Point-set conditions.} Hausdorffness and second countability pass to products (Theorem~\ref{thm:product-inherit}), and $M_1$, $M_2$ have both (Definition~\ref{def:manifold}).

\emph{Product charts are charts.} Each $U_1 \times U_2$ is open (a box of open sets), and these sets cover $M_1 \times M_2$: a point $(q_1, q_2)$ lies in $U_1 \times U_2$ for any smooth charts $(U_1,\varphi_1)$ at $q_1$ and $(U_2,\varphi_2)$ at $q_2$. The map $\varphi_1 \times \varphi_2$ is a bijection of $U_1 \times U_2$ onto $\varphi_1(U_1) \times \varphi_2(U_2)$, which is open in $\mathbb{R}^{m_1 + m_2}$ (a product of open sets, and the product topology on $\mathbb{R}^{m_1} \times \mathbb{R}^{m_2}$ is the Euclidean one); it is continuous with continuous inverse $\varphi_1^{-1} \times \varphi_2^{-1}$, because each is continuous in each component (Theorem~\ref{thm:univ-product}): the components of $\varphi_1 \times \varphi_2$ are $\varphi_1 \circ \pi_1$ and $\varphi_2 \circ \pi_2$, where $\pi_i : M_1 \times M_2 \to M_i$ is the projection onto the $i$-th factor, and those of $\varphi_1^{-1} \times \varphi_2^{-1}$ are $\varphi_1^{-1} \circ \mathrm{pr}_1$ and $\varphi_2^{-1} \circ \mathrm{pr}_2$, with $\mathrm{pr}_1(r,s) = r$, $\mathrm{pr}_2(r,s) = s$. So the product charts are charts, and $M_1 \times M_2$ is locally Euclidean of dimension $m_1 + m_2$.

\emph{Transition maps.} Let $(U_1 \times U_2, \varphi_1 \times \varphi_2)$ and $(U_1' \times U_2', \psi_1 \times \psi_2)$ be two product charts. Two product charts overlap in $(U_1 \cap U_1') \times (U_2 \cap U_2')$, whose image under $\varphi_1 \times \varphi_2$ is $\varphi_1(U_1 \cap U_1') \times \varphi_2(U_2 \cap U_2')$. For $(r,s)$ in this set,
\[
(\psi_1 \times \psi_2) \circ (\varphi_1 \times \varphi_2)^{-1}(r,s) = (\psi_1 \times \psi_2)\big(\varphi_1^{-1}(r), \varphi_2^{-1}(s)\big) = \big(\psi_1 \circ \varphi_1^{-1}(r),\ \psi_2 \circ \varphi_2^{-1}(s)\big),
\]
so their transition map is
\[
(\psi_1 \times \psi_2) \circ (\varphi_1 \times \varphi_2)^{-1} = (\psi_1 \circ \varphi_1^{-1}) \times (\psi_2 \circ \varphi_2^{-1}),
\]
smooth because each component is. In detail: its first $m_1$ components are those of $(\psi_1 \circ \varphi_1^{-1}) \circ \mathrm{pr}_1$, a composite of the linear projection $\mathrm{pr}_1$ with the transition $\psi_1 \circ \varphi_1^{-1}$ of $M_1$, smooth by compatibility of the two charts of $M_1$; its last $m_2$ components are those of $(\psi_2 \circ \varphi_2^{-1}) \circ \mathrm{pr}_2$, smooth likewise; and a map into $\mathbb{R}^{m_1 + m_2}$ is smooth iff all its components are. The inverse transition $(\varphi_1 \times \varphi_2) \circ (\psi_1 \times \psi_2)^{-1} = (\varphi_1 \circ \psi_1^{-1}) \times (\varphi_2 \circ \psi_2^{-1})$ is smooth by the same argument with the $\varphi$'s and $\psi$'s interchanged. So every transition is a diffeomorphism (Definition~\ref{def:diffeo-euclidean}), any two product charts are compatible, and the product charts form a smooth atlas (Definition~\ref{def:atlas}).
\end{proof}

\begin{defbox}[Product Manifold]\deflabel{def:product-manifold}
The \textbf{product manifold} $M_1 \times M_2$ is the product space with the smooth structure generated by the product charts (Definition~\ref{def:product-chart}; they form a smooth atlas by Proposition~\ref{prop:product-manifold}). If $\varphi_1 = (x^1, \ldots, x^{m_1})$ and $\varphi_2 = (y^1, \ldots, y^{m_2})$, the coordinate functions of the product chart are $x^i \circ \pi_1$ and $y^j \circ \pi_2$ (with $\pi_1$, $\pi_2$ the projections of $M_1 \times M_2$ onto $M_1$, $M_2$), written again $x^i$, $y^j$: the $x$'s and then the $y$'s.
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[Slice Inclusions]\deflabel{def:slice-inclusions}
For $p_2 \in M_2$ and $p_1 \in M_1$, the \textbf{slice inclusions} into the product manifold $M_1 \times M_2$ (Definition~\ref{def:product-manifold}) are
\[
\iota^{p_2} : M_1 \to M_1 \times M_2, \ q \mapsto (q, p_2), \qquad\qquad \iota^{p_1} : M_2 \to M_1 \times M_2, \ q \mapsto (p_1, q).
\]
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[Projections and Slice Inclusions Are Smooth]\thmlabel{prop:product-maps}
The projections $\pi_1 : M_1 \times M_2 \to M_1$, $\pi_2 : M_1 \times M_2 \to M_2$ and the slice inclusions $\iota^{p_2}$, $\iota^{p_1}$ are smooth. In product charts their coordinate representations are
\[
(r, s) \mapsto r, \qquad (r, s) \mapsto s, \qquad r \mapsto \big(r, \varphi_2(p_2)\big), \qquad s \mapsto \big(\varphi_1(p_1), s\big).
\]
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Continuity.} All four are continuous: the projections by the definition of the product topology, the inclusions because their components are continuous (Theorem~\ref{thm:univ-product}). For the projections, $\pi_1^{-1}(O) = O \times M_2$ and $\pi_2^{-1}(O) = M_1 \times O$ are open for open $O$. For the inclusions, the components of $\iota^{p_2}$ are $\pi_1 \circ \iota^{p_2} = \mathrm{id}_{M_1}$ and the constant map $\pi_2 \circ \iota^{p_2} = p_2$, and those of $\iota^{p_1}$ are the constant $p_1$ and $\mathrm{id}_{M_2}$.

\emph{Coordinate representations.} The coordinate representations are read off from $\varphi_1 \circ \pi_1 \circ (\varphi_1 \times \varphi_2)^{-1}(r, s) = r$ and $(\varphi_1 \times \varphi_2) \circ \iota^{p_2} \circ \varphi_1^{-1}(r) = (r, \varphi_2(p_2))$, and the same for the others. Explicitly, let $(U_1,\varphi_1)$, $(U_2,\varphi_2)$ be smooth charts of $M_1$, $M_2$, and $(r,s) \in \varphi_1(U_1) \times \varphi_2(U_2)$.
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\pi_1$, in the charts $(U_1 \times U_2, \varphi_1 \times \varphi_2)$ and $(U_1, \varphi_1)$, which satisfy $\pi_1(U_1 \times U_2) = U_1$:
    \[
    \varphi_1 \circ \pi_1 \circ (\varphi_1 \times \varphi_2)^{-1}(r,s) = \varphi_1\Big(\pi_1\big(\varphi_1^{-1}(r), \varphi_2^{-1}(s)\big)\Big) = \varphi_1\big(\varphi_1^{-1}(r)\big) = r .
    \]
    \item $\pi_2$, in the charts $(U_1 \times U_2, \varphi_1 \times \varphi_2)$ and $(U_2, \varphi_2)$: the same computation with the second factor gives $\varphi_2 \circ \pi_2 \circ (\varphi_1 \times \varphi_2)^{-1}(r,s) = \varphi_2(\varphi_2^{-1}(s)) = s$.
    \item $\iota^{p_2}$, with $p_2 \in U_2$, in the charts $(U_1, \varphi_1)$ and $(U_1 \times U_2, \varphi_1 \times \varphi_2)$, which satisfy $\iota^{p_2}(U_1) = U_1 \times \{p_2\} \subseteq U_1 \times U_2$:
    \[
    (\varphi_1 \times \varphi_2) \circ \iota^{p_2} \circ \varphi_1^{-1}(r) = (\varphi_1 \times \varphi_2)\big(\varphi_1^{-1}(r), p_2\big) = \big(r, \varphi_2(p_2)\big).
    \]
    \item $\iota^{p_1}$, with $p_1 \in U_1$, in the charts $(U_2, \varphi_2)$ and $(U_1 \times U_2, \varphi_1 \times \varphi_2)$: likewise $(\varphi_1 \times \varphi_2)\big(p_1, \varphi_2^{-1}(s)\big) = \big(\varphi_1(p_1), s\big)$.
\end{itemize}
Each of these is linear or affine (a linear map plus a constant vector), hence smooth. In matrix form, with $r \in \mathbb{R}^{m_1}$ and $s \in \mathbb{R}^{m_2}$, the four linear maps (for the inclusions, the linear parts) are
\[
\begin{pmatrix} I_{m_1} & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
\begin{pmatrix} 0 & I_{m_2} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
\begin{pmatrix} I_{m_1} \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ I_{m_2} \end{pmatrix},
\]
of sizes $m_1 \times (m_1 + m_2)$, $m_2 \times (m_1 + m_2)$, $(m_1 + m_2) \times m_1$ and $(m_1 + m_2) \times m_2$. Since smooth charts cover every manifold involved, every point of each domain lies in such a pair of charts, so all four maps satisfy Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}. They are smooth, so the maps are smooth (Proposition~\ref{prop:smooth-map-charts}), and by that proposition their coordinate representations in any other smooth charts are smooth as well.
\end{proof}

\section{Manifolds in Euclidean Space}\label{sec:euclidean}

\roadmark{Stage: geometric}{The equations thread made smooth: a manifold given inside $\mathbb{R}^N$, and level sets smoothed by graph charts (Proposition~\ref{prop:level-set-smooth}).}

\subsection{Two Descriptions of a Manifold in Euclidean Space}\label{sub:ext-int}

\begin{rembox}[Two Ways to Look at a Manifold in Euclidean Space]\label{rem:closing-remark}
There are two ways to look at a manifold sitting in a big ambient space: either it is defined by the simultaneous zeros of some functions, or it is parametrized. The implicit function theorem says that it does not matter --- they are the same thing.

So one may think of a manifold \emph{internally}, through parametrizations, or \emph{externally}, through the equations that cut it out of the ambient space. The circle shows both: it is cut out by the equation $x^2 + y^2 = 1$, and it is parametrized by the angle $\theta$. The rest of this subsection makes this precise; none of it was proved in lecture.
\end{rembox}

\begin{defbox}[External Description]\deflabel{def:ext-int}
Let $X \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ and $p \in X$. Near $p$, $X$ is described \textbf{externally} if there are an open $W \ni p$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ and a smooth $F : W \to \mathbb{R}^k$ having $\vec 0$ as a regular value, with $X \cap W = F^{-1}(\vec 0)$ --- the level-set or implicit description.
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[Internal Description]\deflabel{def:internal-description}
Let $X \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ and $p \in X$. Near $p$, $X$ is described \textbf{internally} if there are an open $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, an open $W \ni p$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$, and a smooth $\alpha : V \to \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ which is a homeomorphism onto $X \cap W$ and whose Jacobian $D\alpha_q$ has rank $n$ at every $q \in V$ --- the parametric description.
\end{defbox}

\begin{thmbox}[The Two Descriptions Agree]\thmlabel{thm:ext-int}
For $X \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ and $p \in X$, the external and internal descriptions near $p$ are equivalent, and each is equivalent to:
\begin{itemize}
    \item[(G)] \textbf{graph:} after a permutation of the coordinates of $\mathbb{R}^{n+k} = \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}^k$, there are open sets $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, $V' \subseteq \mathbb{R}^k$ with $p \in V \times V'$ and a smooth $h : V \to V'$ such that $X \cap (V \times V') = \{\, (x, h(x)) \mid x \in V \,\}$.
\end{itemize}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}[Proof (not given in lecture)]
\emph{External $\Rightarrow$ (G).} This is Steps 1--3 of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:regular-value}: the rank condition lets one permute coordinates so that $\big(\partial F^i/\partial y^j(p)\big)$ is nonsingular, and Theorem~\ref{thm:ift-general} produces the smooth $h$ with $F(x,y) = \vec 0 \iff y = h(x)$ on a box.

\emph{(G) $\Rightarrow$ external.} Take $W = V \times V'$ and $F(x,y) = y - h(x)$, smooth, with $F^{-1}(\vec 0) = X \cap W$ by hypothesis. Its Jacobian is the $k \times (n+k)$ block matrix $\big(-Dh_x \ \big| \ I_k\big)$, of rank $k$ everywhere because of the identity block; so $\vec 0$ is a regular value. Written out, with $h = (h^1, \ldots, h^k)$,
\[
DF_{(x,y)} = \left(\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}
-\dfrac{\partial h^1}{\partial x^1}(x) & \cdots & -\dfrac{\partial h^1}{\partial x^n}(x) & 1 & & 0 \\[2mm]
\vdots & & \vdots & & \ddots & \\[1mm]
-\dfrac{\partial h^k}{\partial x^1}(x) & \cdots & -\dfrac{\partial h^k}{\partial x^n}(x) & 0 & & 1
\end{array}\right).
\]

\emph{(G) $\Rightarrow$ internal.} Take $\alpha(x) = (x, h(x))$ on $V$. It is smooth, its Jacobian $\big(I_n \, ; \, Dh_x\big)$ has rank $n$, and it is a homeomorphism onto $X \cap (V \times V')$ with inverse the restriction of the projection $(x,y) \mapsto x$. Written out, the $(n+k) \times n$ Jacobian is
\[
D\alpha_x = \left(\begin{array}{ccc}
1 & & 0 \\
& \ddots & \\
0 & & 1 \\[1mm] \hline
\dfrac{\partial h^1}{\partial x^1}(x) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial h^1}{\partial x^n}(x) \\[2mm]
\vdots & & \vdots \\[1mm]
\dfrac{\partial h^k}{\partial x^1}(x) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial h^k}{\partial x^n}(x)
\end{array}\right),
\]
whose top $n \times n$ block is $I_n$.

\emph{Internal $\Rightarrow$ (G).} Let $q = \alpha^{-1}(p)$. Since $D\alpha_q$ has rank $n$, some $n$ of its $n+k$ rows are independent; permute coordinates so these are the first $n$, and write $\alpha = (\alpha_1, \alpha_2)$ with $\alpha_1 : V \to \mathbb{R}^n$, $\alpha_2 : V \to \mathbb{R}^k$. In blocks,
\[
D\alpha_q = \begin{pmatrix} D(\alpha_1)_q \\[1mm] D(\alpha_2)_q \end{pmatrix},
\]
with $D(\alpha_1)_q$ the $n \times n$ block of the $n$ independent rows and $D(\alpha_2)_q$ the remaining $k \times n$ block. Then $D(\alpha_1)_q$ is invertible, so by the inverse function theorem (Lee, Theorem C.34) $\alpha_1$ restricts to a diffeomorphism of a neighborhood $V_1 \ni q$ onto an open $V_2 \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$. Put $h = \alpha_2 \circ (\alpha_1|_{V_1})^{-1} : V_2 \to \mathbb{R}^k$, smooth. Then $\alpha(V_1) = \{(x, h(x)) \mid x \in V_2\}$, and because $\alpha$ is a homeomorphism onto $X \cap W$, the set $\alpha(V_1)$ is open in $X \cap W$: $\alpha(V_1) = X \cap O$ for an open $O \subseteq W$, and $p = \alpha(q) \in O$. The base $V_2$ has to be shrunk as well, because $X$ may have points over $V_2$ that are not in $O$. Write $p = (x_0, h(x_0))$ with $x_0 = \alpha_1(q) \in V_2$, choose open sets $B \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ and $V' \subseteq \mathbb{R}^k$ with $p \in B \times V' \subseteq O$ (open boxes form a basis of $\mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}^k$), and put $V = V_2 \cap B \cap h^{-1}(V')$, an open set containing $x_0$ because $h$ is continuous. Then $h(V) \subseteq V'$, $p \in V \times V' \subseteq O$, and $X \cap (V \times V') = \{(x, h(x)) \mid x \in V\}$: a point $(x,y)$ of the left side lies in $X \cap O = \alpha(V_1)$, so $y = h(x)$, and $x \in V$; conversely, for $x \in V$ the point $(x, h(x))$ lies in $\alpha(V_1) \subseteq X$ and in $V \times V'$. So $V$, $V'$ and $h|_V : V \to V'$ are as (G) requires.
\end{proof}

The circle in its three descriptions is collected in Section~\ref{sec:ex-circle}.

\begin{defbox}[Parametrization]\deflabel{def:parametrization}
Let $(U, \varphi)$ be a chart of a manifold $M$. The inverse $\varphi^{-1} : \varphi(U) \to U$ is the \textbf{parametrization} of $U$ determined by the chart. When $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$, it is also regarded as a map $\varphi(U) \to \mathbb{R}^N$.
\leeref{Ch.~1, \emph{Coordinate Charts} (``local parametrization'')}
\end{defbox}

\begin{rembox}[A Parametrization Is an Inverse Chart]\label{rem:parametrization-inverse-chart}
A parametrization (Definition~\ref{def:parametrization}) is just another name for the inverse of a chart: if $(U, \varphi)$ is a chart then $\varphi^{-1} : \varphi(U) \to U$ is a parametrization, and conversely. The internal description is therefore the chart picture of Chapter 1 with the extra demand that the map be smooth with injective differential; the external one is the level-set picture of \ref{sub:classical-manifolds}. Theorem~\ref{thm:ext-int} says the two carry the same information locally, which is why one may pass freely between solving the equations and drawing the parametrization.
\end{rembox}

% Lecture 6 (Mon Sep 14, 2026)
% SECTION 7.7: SMOOTH STRUCTURES ON REGULAR LEVEL SETS
% ============================================================================
\subsection{Smooth Structures on Regular Level Sets}\label{sub:level-smooth}

\textit{Lecture 6. Theorem~\ref{thm:regular-value} produced a \emph{topological} manifold from a regular level set. The charts it produced were not arbitrary, and the point of this subsection is that they are automatically smoothly compatible --- so the regular value theorem is in fact a machine for manufacturing smooth manifolds.}

Recall the construction in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:regular-value}. Index the coordinates of $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ by $\{1, \ldots, n+k\}$. For $p \in M = F^{-1}(c)$, the hypothesis $\operatorname{rank} F'(p) = k$ says that some $k$ of the $n+k$ columns of $F'(p)$ are linearly independent. Choose such a set of indices $J$, $|J| = k$, and let $I = \{1,\ldots,n+k\} \setminus J$ be the complementary $n$ indices. Write $x_J \in \mathbb{R}^J$ and $x_I \in \mathbb{R}^I$ for the corresponding groups of coordinates. The implicit function theorem then solves for $x_J$ in terms of $x_I$: there are an open box $V_J \times V_J' \ni p$, with $V_J \subseteq \mathbb{R}^I$ and $V_J' \subseteq \mathbb{R}^J$ open, and a smooth $h_J : V_J \to V_J'$ with
\[
F(x) = c \iff x_J = h_J(x_I) \qquad \text{for } x \text{ in the box},
\]
and the chart, with domain $U_J = M \cap (V_J \times V_J')$, is the restriction to $M$ of the linear projection $\pi_I : \mathbb{R}^{n+k} \to \mathbb{R}^I$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\varphi_J &: U_J \to V_J \subseteq \mathbb{R}^I, &\quad \varphi_J &= \pi_I|_{U_J}, \\
\varphi_J^{-1} &: V_J \to \mathbb{R}^{n+k}, &\quad \varphi_J^{-1}(u) &= \text{the point with } x_I = u,\ x_J = h_J(u).
\end{aligned}
\]
The inverse $\varphi_J^{-1}$ is the parametrization of that piece of $M$ determined by the chart $(U_J, \varphi_J)$ (Definition~\ref{def:parametrization}).

\begin{propbox}[Regular Level Sets Are Smooth Manifolds]\thmlabel{prop:level-set-smooth}
Let $W \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ be open, $F : W \to \mathbb{R}^k$ smooth, and $c \in \mathbb{R}^k$ a regular value. Then the charts $\{(U_J, \varphi_J)\}$ above form a $C^\infty$ atlas on $M = F^{-1}(c)$, and $M$ is a smooth manifold of dimension $n$.
\leeref{Example 1.32 and Corollary 5.14}
\end{propbox}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=3em, column sep=1.6em]
& \mathbb{R}^{n+k} \arrow[dr, "\pi_{I'}"] & \\
\varphi_J(U_J \cap U_{J'}) \arrow[ur, "\varphi_J^{-1}"] \arrow[rr, "\varphi_{J'} \circ \varphi_J^{-1}"'] & & \varphi_{J'}(U_J \cap U_{J'})
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

The proof in one picture. The transition function between two graph charts factors through the ambient space: a parametrization up, followed by a linear projection down. Both legs are smooth in the Euclidean sense, so the composite is.



\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture 6 worked the surface of Example~\ref{ex:surface-transition} first, then gave this general argument, which differs from it only in notation.)} What has to be shown: the charts $(U_J, \varphi_J)$ cover $M$ and are pairwise $C^\infty$-compatible, so that they form an atlas (Definition~\ref{def:atlas}) on the topological manifold $M$; the smooth structure is then the maximal atlas containing them.

\emph{$M$ is a topological $n$-manifold, and the $(U_J, \varphi_J)$ are charts.} By Theorem~\ref{thm:regular-value}, in the form of Corollary~\ref{cor:rvt-open} for the open domain $W$ and the value $c$, $M = F^{-1}(c)$ with the subspace topology is a topological manifold of dimension $n$, and Step 3 of that proof shows that each $\varphi_J = \pi_I|_{U_J}$ is a homeomorphism of the open set $U_J \subseteq M$ onto the open set $V_J \subseteq \mathbb{R}^I \cong \mathbb{R}^n$ (with $|I| = n$), i.e.\ a chart (Definition~\ref{def:chart}).

\emph{The domains cover $M$.} Each $p \in M$ lies in some $U_J$: the rank of $F'(p)$ is $k$ because $c$ is a regular value, so a set $J$ of $k$ independent columns exists at $p$, and the construction above produces a chart $(U_J, \varphi_J)$ with $p \in U_J$.

\emph{Compatibility.} Let $(U_J, \varphi_J)$ and $(U_{J'}, \varphi_{J'})$ be two of the charts, with complementary index sets $I$ and $I'$. If $U_J \cap U_{J'} = \emptyset$ there is nothing to check (Definition~\ref{def:compatible}); otherwise, two observations, each valid for every choice of $J$:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\varphi_J^{-1} : V_J \to \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ is smooth \emph{in the Euclidean sense}: its components are either coordinates of $u$ or components of the smooth map $h_J$. Explicitly, for $u \in V_J$ and an index $l \in \{1, \ldots, n+k\}$, the $l$-th coordinate of $\varphi_J^{-1}(u)$ is $u^l$ if $l \in I$, a linear function of $u$, and $h_J^l(u)$ if $l \in J$, a component of the smooth map $h_J$; every component is smooth.
    \item $\varphi_{J'}$ is the restriction of the linear map $\pi_{I'}$, which is smooth on all of $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$: its components are the coordinate functions $x \mapsto x^l$, $l \in I'$.
\end{enumerate}
The domain of the transition function is $\varphi_J(U_J \cap U_{J'})$. It is open in $\mathbb{R}^I$: $U_J \cap U_{J'}$ is open in $U_J$, the homeomorphism $\varphi_J$ carries it onto an open subset of the open set $V_J$, and an open subset of an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^I$ is open in $\mathbb{R}^I$. For $u$ in it, $\varphi_J^{-1}(u) \in U_J \cap U_{J'}$, and on $U_{J'}$ the map $\varphi_{J'}$ is $\pi_{I'}$ (observation 2). So on the open set $\varphi_J(U_J \cap U_{J'}) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^I$,
\[
\varphi_{J'} \circ \varphi_J^{-1} = \pi_{I'} \circ \varphi_J^{-1},
\]
a composite of smooth maps between open subsets of Euclidean spaces, hence smooth (chain rule). In components: for $l \in I'$, the $l$-th component of $\varphi_{J'} \circ \varphi_J^{-1}(u)$ is the $l$-th coordinate of $\varphi_J^{-1}(u)$, which by observation 1 is $u^l$ if $l \in I$ and $h_J^l(u)$ if $l \in J$.

The same argument with $J$ and $J'$ interchanged (a literal renaming, which also interchanges $I$ and $I'$) shows that $\varphi_J \circ \varphi_{J'}^{-1}$ is smooth on $\varphi_{J'}(U_J \cap U_{J'})$. The two maps
\[
\varphi_{J'} \circ \varphi_J^{-1} : \varphi_J(U_J \cap U_{J'}) \to \varphi_{J'}(U_J \cap U_{J'}), \qquad \varphi_J \circ \varphi_{J'}^{-1} : \varphi_{J'}(U_J \cap U_{J'}) \to \varphi_J(U_J \cap U_{J'})
\]
are inverse to each other, since $(\varphi_J \circ \varphi_{J'}^{-1}) \circ (\varphi_{J'} \circ \varphi_J^{-1}) = \varphi_J \circ \varphi_J^{-1} = \mathrm{id}$ and likewise in the other order. So the transition function is a smooth bijection with smooth inverse, a diffeomorphism (Definition~\ref{def:diffeo-euclidean}), and the two charts are $C^\infty$-compatible (Definition~\ref{def:compatible}).

\emph{Conclusion.} The charts $(U_J, \varphi_J)$ cover $M$ and are pairwise compatible, so they form an atlas (Definition~\ref{def:atlas}). By Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-atlas} the atlas lies in a unique maximal atlas, which is a smooth structure on $M$ (Definition~\ref{def:smooth-structure}). Its charts take values in $\mathbb{R}^I \cong \mathbb{R}^n$, so $M$ is a smooth manifold of dimension $n$, the dimension of Theorem~\ref{thm:regular-value}.
\end{proof}
\begin{exbox}[A Surface in $\mathbb{R}^3$]\exlabel{ex:surface-transition}
The case $n = 2$, $k = 1$, where the indices can be written out. Let $F : W \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}$ be smooth with regular value $c$, so $M = F^{-1}(c)$ is a surface and $F'(p) = \nabla F(p) \neq 0$ for $p \in M$. Suppose that at $p$ \emph{two} partial derivatives are nonzero, say $\partial F/\partial z(p) \neq 0$ and $\partial F/\partial y(p) \neq 0$. Written out, the last two entries of the $1 \times 3$ Jacobian
\[
F'(p) = \begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\partial F}{\partial x}(p) & \dfrac{\partial F}{\partial y}(p) & \dfrac{\partial F}{\partial z}(p) \end{pmatrix}
\]
are nonzero. Then $p$ lies in the domains of two charts built from different solved-for variables:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{solving for } z: &\quad z = g(x,y), &\quad \varphi : U \to \mathbb{R}^2, &\quad \varphi(x,y,z) = (x,y);\\
\text{solving for } y: &\quad y = h(x,z), &\quad \psi : V \to \mathbb{R}^2, &\quad \psi(x,y,z) = (x,z).
\end{aligned}
\]
The parametrization inverse to $\varphi$ is $\varphi^{-1}(x,y) = (x,\,y,\,g(x,y))$, and composing with $\psi$ --- which reads off the first and third coordinates --- gives the transition function
\[
\psi \circ \varphi^{-1}(x,y) = \big(x,\; g(x,y)\big),
\]
smooth because $g$ is. In the other direction $\varphi \circ \psi^{-1}(x,z) = \big(x,\, h(x,z)\big)$, smooth because $h$ is. So $(U,\varphi)$ and $(V,\psi)$ are compatible, and the same picture is what Proposition~\ref{prop:level-set-smooth} formalizes: the overlap of two charts is the part of the surface expressible as a graph over two different pairs of variables, and the transition function converts one graph into the other.
\end{exbox}

The same level sets are submanifolds in the sense of Lecture~12, and their graph-chart structure is the induced one (Proposition~\ref{prop:rvt-agree}).

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:euclidean}
The only thing that varies between charts is \emph{which} $k$ coordinates are solved for, and the whole proof is the observation that a projection composed with a parametrization is smooth no matter which choice is made. Note also that the charts are graphs of smooth maps, which is what makes the parametrization smooth --- the topological argument of Theorem~\ref{thm:regular-value} only needed $h_J$ continuous.
\end{rembox}
