The board picture for this example. The patch $M$ is drawn over a rectangle of $(x,y)$, and the two shaded regions are its images under the two charts: straight down onto the $xy$-plane, giving $\varphi(U)$ and presenting $M$ as $z = g(x,y)$; and sideways onto the $xz$-plane, giving $\psi(U)$ and presenting the \emph{same} patch as $y = h(x,z)$. The transition function is the trip up from one shadow and down to the other.

The picture only works because $\partial F/\partial z$ and $\partial F/\partial y$ are \emph{both} nonzero throughout the patch. If $\partial F/\partial y$ vanished anywhere --- if the surface were vertical in the $y$-direction there --- the sideways projection could fold over, and even where $\psi$ stays injective its inverse is not smooth there (for $F = z - y^3$, where $\partial F/\partial y = 0$ along $y = 0$, $\psi$ is injective with inverse $(x,z) \mapsto (x, z^{1/3}, z)$); so $\psi$ would not be a chart of the smooth structure, and there would be no second chart and nothing to compare. Which pairs of variables work is a condition at each point, and in general it changes from point to point; that is the content of the index set $J$ in Proposition~\ref{prop:level-set-smooth}.

\textbf{Transcription note.} The board wrote the parametrization as ``$\psi^{-1}(x,y) = (x,y,g(x,y))$''; it is $\varphi^{-1}$, as the recording confirms. The board also wrote ``$\varphi^{-1}|_{U \cap V} : U \cap V \to \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$'' --- but $\varphi^{-1}$ is defined on $\varphi(U \cap V) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, not on $U \cap V$, which consists of points of the manifold. Two further slips in the statement of the regular value theorem: the value $c$ lies in $\mathbb{R}^k$, not $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$; and the rank condition is on the Jacobian $F'(p)$, not on $F^{-1}(p)$.

\begin{lembox}[Smooth Maps into and out of Regular Level Sets]\thmlabel{lem:level-set-maps}
Let $M = F^{-1}(c)$ be a regular level set in $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$, with the smooth structure of Proposition~\ref{prop:level-set-smooth}.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item If $W' \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ is open and $H : W' \to \mathbb{R}^l$ is smooth, then the restriction $H|_{M \cap W'} : M \cap W' \to \mathbb{R}^l$ is smooth.
    \item If $P$ is a smooth manifold and $G : P \to \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ is smooth with $G(P) \subseteq M$, then $G$ is smooth as a map $P \to M$.
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{cf.\ Ch.~5, \emph{Restricting Maps to Submanifolds}}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
Both parts are checked against Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}: continuity, and at each point one pair of charts in which the coordinate representation is smooth. On the Euclidean side the chart is the identity chart $(\mathbb{R}^l, \mathrm{id})$ or $(\mathbb{R}^{n+k}, \mathrm{id})$ (Example~\ref{ex:atlas-Rn}); on the side of $M$ it is a graph chart $(U_J, \varphi_J)$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:level-set-smooth}, whose parametrization $\varphi_J^{-1} : V_J \to \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ is smooth in the Euclidean sense (observation 1 in that proof) and whose coordinate map is $\varphi_J = \pi_I|_{U_J}$.

\emph{(1)} $M \cap W'$ is open in $M$ (an open set of $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ intersected with $M$, Definition~\ref{def:subspace}), and it is a smooth manifold with the charts of $M$ restricted to it (Proposition~\ref{prop:open-smooth}). \emph{Continuity:} $H|_{M \cap W'}$ is the composite of the inclusion $M \cap W' \hookrightarrow W'$, continuous by Proposition~\ref{prop:univ-subspace}(1), with the continuous map $H$. \emph{Charts:} fix $p \in M \cap W'$ and a graph chart $(U_J, \varphi_J)$ with $p \in U_J$. Its restriction to the open set $U = U_J \cap W'$ is again a smooth chart of $M$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(1)), and $H(U) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^l$, the domain of the identity chart. The coordinate representation is
\[
\mathrm{id} \circ H \circ (\varphi_J|_U)^{-1} = H \circ \varphi_J^{-1} : \varphi_J(U_J \cap W') \to \mathbb{R}^l .
\]
Here $\varphi_J(U_J \cap W')$ is open in $\mathbb{R}^I$ (it is the image of the chart $(U, \varphi_J|_U)$, Lemma~\ref{lem:chart-modify}(1) and Definition~\ref{def:smooth-chart}), $\varphi_J^{-1}$ is smooth on it with values in $U_J \cap W' \subseteq W'$, and $H$ is smooth on the open set $W'$. So the coordinate representation is a composite of smooth maps between open subsets of Euclidean spaces, hence smooth.

\emph{(2)} \emph{Continuity:} $G$ takes values in $M$, and composed with the inclusion $\iota : M \hookrightarrow \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ it is the original map $\iota \circ G = G : P \to \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$, which is continuous because it is smooth (Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}). By Proposition~\ref{prop:univ-subspace}(2), $G$ is continuous into $M$ for the subspace topology. \emph{Charts:} given $q \in P$, take a graph chart $(U_J, \varphi_J)$ of $M$ at $G(q)$ and any chart $(V_0, \chi_0)$ of $P$ at $q$. Put $V = V_0 \cap G^{-1}(U_J)$, open because $G : P \to M$ is continuous and $U_J$ is open in $M$, and $\chi = \chi_0|_V$, a smooth chart of $P$ at $q$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:charts-around-map}(1), applied to the continuous map $G : P \to M$ with the charts $(U_J, \varphi_J)$ and $(V_0, \chi_0)$); now $G(V) \subseteq U_J$. For $a \in \chi(V)$ the point $G(\chi^{-1}(a))$ lies in $U_J$, where $\varphi_J$ is $\pi_I$, so on $\chi(V)$
\[
\varphi_J \circ G \circ \chi^{-1} = \pi_I \circ (G \circ \chi^{-1}) .
\]
The map $G \circ \chi^{-1} = \mathrm{id} \circ G \circ \chi^{-1}$ is the coordinate representation of the smooth map $G : P \to \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ in the charts $(V, \chi)$ and $(\mathbb{R}^{n+k}, \mathrm{id})$, hence smooth by Proposition~\ref{prop:smooth-map-charts}; and $\pi_I$ is linear, hence smooth. So $\varphi_J \circ G \circ \chi^{-1}$, a linear projection of a smooth map, is smooth, and the charts $(V, \chi)$ and $(U_J, \varphi_J)$ witness Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map} at $q$.
\end{proof}

Not stated in lecture; filled in because it is used repeatedly --- tacitly in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:circle-atlases-same}, and explicitly for $S^n \to \mathbb{RP}^n$ in \ref{sec:special-maps}. In words: maps \emph{out of} a level set may be computed by restricting ambient formulas, and maps \emph{into} one may be computed as maps into the ambient space.

That the three circle atlases define one smooth structure is collected in Section~\ref{sec:ex-circle}.

\section{Linear Algebra Toolkit}\label{sec:vector-spaces}

\roadmark{Stage: linear}{The tool both tangent spaces will need: the linear algebra used from here on. The differential of a map between vector spaces (\ref{sec:vs-differential}) and the smooth matrix groups (\ref{sec:on-un-smooth}) follow.}

\label{sub:linalg-toolkit}

\textit{Not from lecture. From here on the course runs on linear algebra --- differentials, bases of tangent spaces, dual spaces --- and this section records, once, the facts used. The first box is imported from linear algebra without proof, as the point-set facts of \ref{sec:review} were imported from 590; everything after it is proved.} Throughout, vector spaces are real.

\begin{propbox}[Standing Facts from Linear Algebra]\thmlabel{fact:linalg}
Let $A : V \to W$ be linear, with $V$ and $W$ finite-dimensional.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \emph{Rank--nullity.} $\dim V = \dim\ker A + \operatorname{rank} A$. Consequently: if $A$ is injective then $\dim V \le \dim W$; if $A$ is surjective then $\dim V \ge \dim W$; and if $\dim V = \dim W$, then $A$ is injective $\iff$ surjective $\iff$ bijective.
    \item \emph{Bases determine linear maps.} A linear map is determined by its values on a basis, and any assignment of values to the vectors of a basis extends uniquely to a linear map. In particular, two linear maps that agree on a basis are equal.
    \item \emph{Matrices.} Given bases $(e_1, \ldots, e_m)$ of $V$ and $(f_1, \ldots, f_n)$ of $W$, the matrix $[A] = (a_{ij})$ of $A$ is defined by $A e_j = \sum_i a_{ij} f_i$: its $j$-th \emph{column} holds the coordinates of $Ae_j$. Written out, $[A]$ is the $n \times m$ matrix
\[
[A] = \begin{pmatrix}
a_{11} & \cdots & a_{1j} & \cdots & a_{1m} \\
\vdots & & \vdots & & \vdots \\
a_{n1} & \cdots & a_{nj} & \cdots & a_{nm}
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
Ae_j = a_{1j} f_1 + \cdots + a_{nj} f_n.
\] Composition corresponds to matrix multiplication, $[AB] = [A][B]$, and $\operatorname{rank} A$ is the rank of $[A]$, which equals the rank of its transpose.
    \item \emph{Change of basis.} If $e'_j = \sum_i P_{ij}\, e_i$ and $f'_l = \sum_k Q_{kl}\, f_k$ are new bases, with $P$ and $Q$ invertible, then the matrix of $A$ in the new bases is $Q^{-1} [A] P$. Here
\[
P = \begin{pmatrix} P_{11} & \cdots & P_{1m} \\ \vdots & & \vdots \\ P_{m1} & \cdots & P_{mm} \end{pmatrix},
\qquad
Q = \begin{pmatrix} Q_{11} & \cdots & Q_{1n} \\ \vdots & & \vdots \\ Q_{n1} & \cdots & Q_{nn} \end{pmatrix},
\]
the $j$-th column of $P$ holding the old coordinates of $e'_j$, and the $l$-th column of $Q$ those of $f'_l$.
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Corollary B.21 and Proposition B.24}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}[Proof (to be filled)]
Imported from linear algebra without proof; proved in Axler, \emph{Linear Algebra Done Right} (see also Lee, Corollary~B.21 and Proposition~B.24). To be filled.
\end{proof}

\begin{defbox}[Dual Space]\deflabel{def:dual}
The \textbf{dual space} of $V$ is $V^* = \{\lambda : V \to \mathbb{R} \mid \lambda \text{ linear}\}$, a vector space under pointwise operations; its elements are \textbf{linear functionals}, or \textbf{covectors}.
\leeref{Proposition 11.1}
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[Dual Basis]\deflabel{def:dual-basis}
If $(e_1, \ldots, e_n)$ is a basis of $V$, the \textbf{dual basis} $(\varepsilon^1, \ldots, \varepsilon^n)$ consists of the covectors (Definition~\ref{def:dual}) with
\[
\varepsilon^i(e_j) = \delta^i_j ,
\]
which exist and are unique by Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(2).
\leeref{Proposition 11.1}
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[The Dual Basis]\thmlabel{prop:dual-basis}
Let $(e_1, \ldots, e_n)$ be a basis of $V$ with dual basis $(\varepsilon^1, \ldots, \varepsilon^n)$. Then $(\varepsilon^i)$ is a basis of $V^*$, so $\dim V^* = \dim V$, and for all $v \in V$ and $\lambda \in V^*$,
\[
v = \sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon^i(v)\, e_i, \qquad\qquad \lambda = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda(e_i)\, \varepsilon^i .
\]
\leeref{Proposition 11.1}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
Three things are to be shown: the two formulas, and that $(\varepsilon^i)$ is a basis of $V^*$. Throughout, the defining property $\varepsilon^i(e_j) = \delta^i_j$ (Definition~\ref{def:dual-basis}) and the pointwise operations of $V^*$ (Definition~\ref{def:dual}) are used.

\emph{First formula.} Let $v \in V$. Since $(e_j)$ is a basis, $v = \sum_j v^j e_j$ for unique numbers $v^j$. Applying the linear map $\varepsilon^i$,
\[
\varepsilon^i(v) = \varepsilon^i\Big(\sum_{j=1}^n v^j e_j\Big) = \sum_{j=1}^n v^j\, \varepsilon^i(e_j) = \sum_{j=1}^n v^j \delta^i_j = v^i ,
\]
which is the first formula: substituting $v^i = \varepsilon^i(v)$ into $v = \sum_i v^i e_i$ gives $v = \sum_i \varepsilon^i(v)\, e_i$. The dual basis \emph{extracts the components} of a vector.

\emph{Second formula.} Let $\lambda \in V^*$ and put $\mu = \sum_i \lambda(e_i)\, \varepsilon^i$, a linear combination of covectors, hence a covector. Both $\lambda$ and $\mu$ are linear maps $V \to \mathbb{R}$, so by Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(2) it suffices that they agree on each $e_j$. Evaluating pointwise,
\[
\mu(e_j) = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda(e_i)\, \varepsilon^i(e_j) = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda(e_i)\, \delta^i_j = \lambda(e_j) .
\]
So $\lambda = \mu = \sum_i \lambda(e_i)\, \varepsilon^i$; hence the $\varepsilon^i$ span $V^*$.

\emph{Independence.} Suppose $\sum_i c_i \varepsilon^i = 0$, the zero covector. Applying it to $e_j$,
\[
0 = \Big(\sum_{i=1}^n c_i \varepsilon^i\Big)(e_j) = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i\, \delta^i_j = c_j ,
\]
for every $j$; so they are independent. Being independent and spanning, the $n$ covectors $\varepsilon^1, \ldots, \varepsilon^n$ form a basis of $V^*$, and $\dim V^* = n = \dim V$.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[The Double Dual]\thmlabel{prop:double-dual}
For a finite-dimensional $V$, the map
\[
\iota : V \to V^{**}, \qquad \iota(v)(\lambda) = \lambda(v),
\]
is a linear isomorphism. It is \textbf{canonical}: its definition involves no choice of basis.
\leeref{Proposition 11.8}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
To be shown: each $\iota(v)$ lies in $V^{**}$, the map $\iota$ is linear, injective, and (by a dimension count) bijective. Canonicity is visible in the formula $\iota(v)(\lambda) = \lambda(v)$, which uses only $v$ and $\lambda$.

\emph{$\iota(v) \in V^{**}$.} For $\lambda, \mu \in V^*$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$, since the operations of $V^*$ are pointwise (Definition~\ref{def:dual}),
\[
\iota(v)(\lambda + c\mu) = (\lambda + c\mu)(v) = \lambda(v) + c\,\mu(v) = \iota(v)(\lambda) + c\,\iota(v)(\mu) ,
\]
so $\iota(v) : V^* \to \mathbb{R}$ is linear.

\emph{$\iota$ is linear}, since each $\lambda$ is: for $v, w \in V$, $c \in \mathbb{R}$ and every $\lambda \in V^*$,
\[
\iota(v + cw)(\lambda) = \lambda(v + cw) = \lambda(v) + c\,\lambda(w) = \iota(v)(\lambda) + c\,\iota(w)(\lambda) = \big(\iota(v) + c\,\iota(w)\big)(\lambda) ,
\]
the last step by the pointwise operations of $V^{**}$. As this holds for every $\lambda$, $\iota(v + cw) = \iota(v) + c\,\iota(w)$.

\emph{$\iota$ is injective.} It suffices that $\iota(v) \ne 0$ whenever $v \ne 0$ (then $\iota(v) = \iota(w)$ gives $\iota(v - w) = 0$, so $v = w$). If $v \ne 0$, the list $(v)$ is linearly independent, so it extends to a basis $(v, e_2, \ldots, e_n)$ of $V$; let $(\varepsilon^1, \ldots, \varepsilon^n)$ be the dual basis (Definition~\ref{def:dual-basis}), whose first covector satisfies $\varepsilon^1(v) = 1$ because $v$ is the first basis vector. Then
\[
\iota(v)(\varepsilon^1) = \varepsilon^1(v) = 1 \ne 0 ,
\]
so $\iota(v) \ne 0$.

\emph{$\iota$ is an isomorphism.} By Proposition~\ref{prop:dual-basis} applied to $V$, $\dim V^* = \dim V$, and applied again to the finite-dimensional space $V^*$, $\dim V^{**} = \dim V^*$. So $\iota : V \to V^{**}$ is an injective linear map between spaces of the same finite dimension, hence bijective by Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1), i.e.\ a linear isomorphism.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:vector-spaces}
A finite-dimensional $V$ is also isomorphic to $V^*$, but only through a choice of basis (Example~\ref{ex:basis-iso-dual-not-canonical}). $V$ and $V^{**}$ are identified \emph{canonically}. This is why tangent vectors and covectors must be kept apart, as Lecture 10 did with $T_pM$ and $T_p^*M$, while the dual of $T_p^*M$ may be silently identified with $T_pM$.
\end{rembox}

\begin{exbox}[{The Basis Isomorphism $V \cong V^*$ Is Not Canonical}]\exlabel{ex:basis-iso-dual-not-canonical}
A finite-dimensional $V$ is isomorphic to $V^*$, for instance by the linear map $e_i \mapsto \varepsilon^i$ sending a basis to its dual basis (Definition~\ref{def:dual-basis}); it is an isomorphism because it carries a basis to a basis (Proposition~\ref{prop:dual-basis}). But that isomorphism depends on the basis: change the basis and it changes. To see this, let $V \neq 0$ have basis $(e_1, \ldots, e_n)$ with dual basis $(\varepsilon^1, \ldots, \varepsilon^n)$, and replace $e_1$ by $e_1' = 2e_1$, keeping $e_i' = e_i$ for $i \ge 2$. The new dual basis is $\varepsilon'^1 = \tfrac12 \varepsilon^1$ and $\varepsilon'^i = \varepsilon^i$ for $i \ge 2$: indeed $\tfrac12 \varepsilon^1(2e_1) = 1$ and $\tfrac12 \varepsilon^1(e_j) = 0$ for $j \ge 2$, while for $i \ge 2$, $\varepsilon^i(2e_1) = 0$ and $\varepsilon^i(e_j) = \delta^i_j$. The first isomorphism sends $e_1 \mapsto \varepsilon^1$. The second sends $e_1' = 2e_1 \mapsto \varepsilon'^1 = \tfrac12 \varepsilon^1$, hence by linearity $e_1 \mapsto \tfrac14 \varepsilon^1$, which differs from $\varepsilon^1$ because $\varepsilon^1 \neq 0$. So the two bases give different isomorphisms $V \to V^*$.
\end{exbox}

\begin{defbox}[Dual Map]\deflabel{def:dual-map}
The \textbf{dual map}, or \textbf{transpose}, of a linear map $A : V \to W$ is
\[
A^* : W^* \to V^*, \qquad A^*(\lambda) = \lambda \circ A .
\]
\leeref{Proposition 11.4}
\end{defbox}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.2em, column sep=4em]
V \arrow[r, "A"] & W & \text{vectors: forward} \\
V^* & W^* \arrow[l, "A^*"'] & \text{covectors: backward}
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

A covector on $W$ becomes a covector on $V$ by first applying $A$; so the dual map runs backwards. This is the linear-algebra shadow of the directions in \S\ref{sub:pushforward}, where germs were pulled back and derivations pushed forward.

\begin{propbox}[Properties of the Dual Map]\thmlabel{prop:dual-map}
Let $A : V \to W$ and $B : W \to Z$ be linear.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $A^*$ is linear, $(\mathrm{id}_V)^* = \mathrm{id}_{V^*}$, and $(B \circ A)^* = A^* \circ B^*$. In particular, if $A$ is an isomorphism, so is $A^*$, with $(A^*)^{-1} = (A^{-1})^*$.
    \item For finite-dimensional $V$ and $W$, the matrix of $A^*$ in the dual bases is the transpose of the matrix of $A$.
    \item For finite-dimensional $V$ and $W$: $A$ is injective $\iff$ $A^*$ is surjective, and $A$ is surjective $\iff$ $A^*$ is injective.
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Proposition 11.4}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
Throughout, two elements of a dual space are equal when they take the same value at every vector, and their operations are pointwise (Definition~\ref{def:dual}).

\emph{(1)} \emph{$A^*\lambda$ is a covector:} $\lambda \circ A$ is a composite of linear maps, hence linear. \emph{$A^*$ is linear:} for $\lambda, \mu \in W^*$, $c \in \mathbb{R}$ and $v \in V$,
\[
A^*(\lambda + c\mu)(v) = (\lambda + c\mu)(Av) = \lambda(Av) + c\,\mu(Av) = (A^*\lambda)(v) + c\,(A^*\mu)(v) = \big(A^*\lambda + c\,A^*\mu\big)(v) ,
\]
so $A^*(\lambda + c\mu) = (\lambda + c\mu) \circ A = A^*\lambda + c\,A^*\mu$. \emph{Identity:} $(\mathrm{id}_V)^*(\lambda) = \lambda \circ \mathrm{id}_V = \lambda$ for every $\lambda \in V^*$. \emph{Composition:} for $\lambda \in Z^*$, by associativity of composition, $(B \circ A)^*(\lambda) = \lambda \circ B \circ A = (\lambda \circ B) \circ A = A^*(B^*\lambda)$. \emph{Isomorphisms:} let $A$ have inverse $A^{-1} : W \to V$. Applying the composition rule to $A^{-1} \circ A = \mathrm{id}_V$ and to $A \circ A^{-1} = \mathrm{id}_W$, and then the identity rule,
\[
A^* \circ (A^{-1})^* = (A^{-1} \circ A)^* = (\mathrm{id}_V)^* = \mathrm{id}_{V^*}, \qquad (A^{-1})^* \circ A^* = (A \circ A^{-1})^* = (\mathrm{id}_W)^* = \mathrm{id}_{W^*} .
\]
So $(A^{-1})^* : V^* \to W^*$ is a two-sided inverse of $A^*$: $A^*$ is an isomorphism with $(A^*)^{-1} = (A^{-1})^*$.

\emph{(2)} Let $(e_j)$ and $(f_i)$ be bases of $V$ and $W$, with dual bases $(\varepsilon^j)$ and $(\varphi^k)$, and $Ae_j = \sum_i a_{ij} f_i$, so that $[A] = (a_{ij})$ (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(3)). Then, by linearity of $\varphi^k$ and $\varphi^k(f_i) = \delta^k_i$,
\[
A^*(\varphi^k)(e_j) = \varphi^k(Ae_j) = \varphi^k\Big(\sum_i a_{ij} f_i\Big) = \sum_i a_{ij}\, \delta^k_i = a_{kj} .
\]
By the second formula of Proposition~\ref{prop:dual-basis}, applied to the covector $A^*(\varphi^k) \in V^*$, $A^*(\varphi^k) = \sum_j A^*(\varphi^k)(e_j)\,\varepsilon^j = \sum_j a_{kj}\,\varepsilon^j$. By Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(3), the $k$-th column of the matrix of $A^*$ (in the bases $(\varphi^k)$ of $W^*$ and $(\varepsilon^j)$ of $V^*$) holds the coordinates of $A^*(\varphi^k)$, namely $a_{k1}, \ldots, a_{km}$. The $k$-th column of the matrix of $A^*$ is therefore the $k$-th row of $[A]$: the matrix of $A^*$ is $[A]^{\mathsf T}$. Written out, as an $m \times n$ matrix,
\[
[A^*] = \begin{pmatrix}
a_{11} & a_{21} & \cdots & a_{n1} \\
\vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\
a_{1m} & a_{2m} & \cdots & a_{nm}
\end{pmatrix} = [A]^{\mathsf T},
\qquad
[A] = \begin{pmatrix}
a_{11} & \cdots & a_{1m} \\
\vdots & & \vdots \\
a_{n1} & \cdots & a_{nm}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

\emph{(3)} By (2) and Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(3), $\operatorname{rank} A^* = \operatorname{rank} [A]^{\mathsf T} = \operatorname{rank} [A] = \operatorname{rank} A$. Also $\dim W^* = \dim W$ and $\dim V^* = \dim V$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:dual-basis}). A linear map is surjective exactly when its rank, the dimension of its image, equals the dimension of its target (a subspace of full dimension is the whole space), and injective exactly when its kernel is $0$, which by rank--nullity (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)) means its rank equals the dimension of its source. Now $A$ is surjective iff $\operatorname{rank} A = \dim W$, iff $\operatorname{rank} A^* = \dim W^*$, which by rank--nullity for $A^* : W^* \to V^*$ means $A^*$ is injective. Likewise $A$ is injective iff $\operatorname{rank} A = \dim V = \dim V^*$, iff $\operatorname{rank} A^* = \dim V^*$, iff $A^*$ is surjective.
\end{proof}

\begin{defbox}[Bilinear Pairing]\deflabel{def:pairing}
A \textbf{bilinear pairing} is a map $B : V \times W \to \mathbb{R}$ that is linear in each argument separately. It induces linear maps
\[
B^\flat : V \to W^*, \ \ v \mapsto B(v, \cdot\,), \qquad\qquad B^\sharp : W \to V^*, \ \ w \mapsto B(\cdot\,, w).
\]
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[Non-Degenerate Pairing]\deflabel{def:non-degenerate-pairing}
A bilinear pairing $B : V \times W \to \mathbb{R}$ (Definition~\ref{def:pairing}) is \textbf{left non-degenerate} if $B(v, w) = 0$ for all $w$ implies $v = 0$, i.e.\ $B^\flat$ is injective; \textbf{right non-degenerate} if $B(v, w) = 0$ for all $v$ implies $w = 0$, i.e.\ $B^\sharp$ is injective; and \textbf{non-degenerate} if both.
\end{defbox}

\begin{thmbox}[Non-Degenerate Pairings]\thmlabel{thm:pairing}
Let $B : V \times W \to \mathbb{R}$ be a non-degenerate bilinear pairing, and suppose $V$ or $W$ is finite-dimensional. Then both are finite-dimensional, $\dim V = \dim W$, and
\[
B^\flat : V \xrightarrow{\ \cong\ } W^*, \qquad\qquad B^\sharp : W \xrightarrow{\ \cong\ } V^*
\]
are isomorphisms.
\leeref{no counterpart}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
Suppose $V$ is finite-dimensional, of dimension $n$; the other case is symmetric, as explained at the end. By Definition~\ref{def:non-degenerate-pairing}, right non-degeneracy means $B^\sharp$ is injective and left non-degeneracy means $B^\flat$ is injective.

\emph{$W$ is finite-dimensional and $\dim W \le n$.} Right non-degeneracy makes $B^\sharp : W \to V^*$ injective, so $B^\sharp$ is a linear isomorphism of $W$ onto the subspace $B^\sharp(W)$ of $V^*$. The space $V^*$ has dimension $n$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:dual-basis}), so its subspace $B^\sharp(W)$ is finite-dimensional of dimension $\le n$, and so is $W$, being isomorphic to it: $W$ is finite-dimensional with $\dim W \le n$.

\emph{$n \le \dim W$.} Now $W$ is finite-dimensional, so $\dim W^* = \dim W$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:dual-basis}). Left non-degeneracy makes $B^\flat : V \to W^*$ injective, so by Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1) (an injective map has source dimension at most target dimension) $n = \dim V \le \dim W^* = \dim W$.

\emph{The isomorphisms.} Hence $\dim V = \dim W = n$, and also $\dim V^* = \dim W^* = n$. So $B^\flat : V \to W^*$ and $B^\sharp : W \to V^*$ are injective maps between spaces of equal finite dimension $n$, hence isomorphisms by Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1).

\emph{The case $W$ finite-dimensional.} This is the case above after the renaming that swaps the two arguments: put $B'(w, v) = B(v, w)$, a bilinear pairing $W \times V \to \mathbb{R}$. Then $B'^\flat(w) = B'(w, \cdot\,) = B(\cdot\,, w) = B^\sharp(w)$ and $B'^\sharp(v) = B'(\cdot\,, v) = B(v, \cdot\,) = B^\flat(v)$, so $B'$ is non-degenerate because $B$ is, and the case already proved, applied to $B'$ with $W$ in the role of $V$, gives $\dim W = \dim V$ and that $B'^\flat = B^\sharp$ and $B'^\sharp = B^\flat$ are isomorphisms.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:vector-spaces-2}
Each half of non-degeneracy gives one inequality of dimensions, and it is the \emph{pair} of inequalities that forces the isomorphisms; neither half suffices alone. The finiteness hypothesis cannot be dropped (Example~\ref{ex:evaluation-pairing-infinite-dim}). Assignment~3, Problem~3 is exactly a pairing $T_pM \times I_p/I_p^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ to which this theorem applies.
\end{rembox}

\begin{exbox}[The Evaluation Pairing in Infinite Dimensions]\exlabel{ex:evaluation-pairing-infinite-dim}
The finiteness hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{thm:pairing} cannot be dropped: for an infinite-dimensional $V$, the evaluation pairing $B : V \times V^* \to \mathbb{R}$, $B(v, \lambda) = \lambda(v)$, is non-degenerate, but its map $B^\flat = \iota : V \to V^{**}$ is injective without being onto. \textit{(Argument filled in; not from lecture. It uses that every linearly independent subset of a vector space extends to a basis, which in infinite dimensions rests on Zorn's lemma.)}
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
\item \emph{$B^\flat = \iota$.} $B^\flat(v) = B(v, \cdot\,)$ is the functional $\lambda \mapsto \lambda(v)$, which is $\iota(v)$ as in Proposition~\ref{prop:double-dual}.
\item \emph{Right non-degenerate.} If $\lambda(v) = 0$ for all $v \in V$, then $\lambda = 0$ as a function on $V$.
\item \emph{Left non-degenerate, i.e.\ $\iota$ injective.} If $v \neq 0$, extend $\{v\}$ to a basis of $V$ and let $\lambda \in V^*$ be the linear functional with $\lambda(v) = 1$ and $\lambda = 0$ on the other basis vectors; then $B(v, \lambda) = 1 \neq 0$.
\item \emph{$\iota$ is not onto.} Choose a basis $(e_\alpha)_{\alpha \in A}$ of $V$; the index set $A$ is infinite. Let $\varepsilon^\alpha \in V^*$ be the coordinate functionals, $\varepsilon^\alpha(e_\beta) = \delta^\alpha_\beta$, and let $\sigma \in V^*$ be the functional with $\sigma(e_\alpha) = 1$ for every $\alpha$. The set $\{\varepsilon^\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A} \cup \{\sigma\}$ is linearly independent: the $\varepsilon^\alpha$ are (applying a vanishing finite combination $\sum_k c_k \varepsilon^{\alpha_k}$ to $e_{\alpha_j}$ gives $c_j = 0$), and $\sigma$ is not in their span, because a finite combination $\sum_{k=1}^m c_k \varepsilon^{\alpha_k}$ vanishes on $e_\beta$ for every $\beta \notin \{\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_m\}$ (such $\beta$ exist since $A$ is infinite), while $\sigma(e_\beta) = 1$. Extend this set to a basis of $V^*$, and let $\Phi \in V^{**}$ be the linear functional with $\Phi(\sigma) = 1$ and $\Phi = 0$ on every other basis vector, in particular $\Phi(\varepsilon^\alpha) = 0$ for all $\alpha$. If $\Phi = \iota(v)$ with $v = \sum_\alpha v_\alpha e_\alpha$ (finitely many $v_\alpha \neq 0$), then $v_\alpha = \varepsilon^\alpha(v) = \Phi(\varepsilon^\alpha) = 0$ for every $\alpha$, so $v = 0$ and $\Phi = \iota(0) = 0$, contradicting $\Phi(\sigma) = 1$.
\end{itemize}
\end{exbox}

\begin{defbox}[Quotient Vector Space]\deflabel{def:quotient-vs}
Let $W \subseteq V$ be a linear subspace. The \textbf{quotient space} $V/W$ is the set of cosets $v + W = \{v + w \mid w \in W\}$, with
\[
(v + W) + (v' + W) = (v + v') + W, \qquad c\,(v + W) = cv + W,
\]
and the \textbf{projection} is $\pi : V \to V/W$, $\pi(v) = v + W$. Two vectors have the same coset iff their difference lies in $W$.
\leeref{App.~B, \emph{Vector Spaces}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[Quotient Spaces and Their Universal Property]\thmlabel{prop:quotient-vs}
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The operations are well defined, $V/W$ is a vector space, and $\pi$ is linear and surjective with $\ker \pi = W$.
    \item \emph{Universal property.} If $A : V \to Z$ is linear with $W \subseteq \ker A$, there is a unique linear $\bar A : V/W \to Z$ with $\bar A \circ \pi = A$, namely $\bar A(v + W) = A(v)$.
    \item If $V$ is finite-dimensional, $\dim V/W = \dim V - \dim W$.
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{App.~B, \emph{Vector Spaces}}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
Throughout, two vectors have the same coset iff their difference lies in $W$ (Definition~\ref{def:quotient-vs}), and $W$, being a subspace, is closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

\emph{(1)} \emph{Well defined.} Suppose $v + W = v' + W$ and $u + W = u' + W$, i.e.\ $v - v' \in W$ and $u - u' \in W$. Then
\[
(v + u) - (v' + u') = (v - v') + (u - u') \in W, \qquad cv - cv' = c\,(v - v') \in W,
\]
so $(v + u) + W = (v' + u') + W$ and $cv + W = cv' + W$: the operations do not depend on representatives. \emph{Vector space.} The vector space axioms are inherited from $V$: each axiom, written out with the defining formulas, becomes the same axiom in $V$ inside a coset; for instance $\big((v+W) + (u+W)\big) + (x+W) = \big((v+u)+x\big) + W = \big(v+(u+x)\big) + W = (v+W) + \big((u+W)+(x+W)\big)$. The zero is $0 + W = W$ and the negative of $v + W$ is $(-v) + W$. \emph{$\pi$ is linear} by the definition of the operations: $\pi(v + cu) = (v + cu) + W = (v + W) + c\,(u + W) = \pi(v) + c\,\pi(u)$. It is \emph{surjective} by construction, every coset $v + W$ being $\pi(v)$. \emph{Kernel:} $\pi(v) = 0 + W$ iff $v - 0 \in W$, i.e.\ iff $v \in W$; so $\ker \pi = W$.

\emph{(2)} \emph{Well defined.} If $v + W = v' + W$, then $v - v' \in W \subseteq \ker A$, so $A(v) - A(v') = A(v - v') = 0$: the value $A(v)$ does not depend on the representative. \emph{Linear}, because $A$ is: $\bar A\big((v + W) + c\,(u + W)\big) = \bar A\big((v + cu) + W\big) = A(v + cu) = A(v) + c\,A(u) = \bar A(v + W) + c\,\bar A(u + W)$. \emph{$\bar A \circ \pi = A$:} $\bar A(\pi(v)) = \bar A(v + W) = A(v)$. \emph{Unique}, because $\pi$ is surjective: if $\bar A'$ is linear with $\bar A' \circ \pi = A$, then every element of $V/W$ is $\pi(v)$ for some $v$, and $\bar A'(\pi(v)) = A(v) = \bar A(\pi(v))$, so $\bar A' = \bar A$.

\emph{(3)} Rank--nullity for $\pi$. The space $V/W$ is finite-dimensional, spanned by the images $\pi(e_i)$ of a basis $(e_i)$ of $V$ since $\pi$ is linear and surjective. By Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1) for $\pi : V \to V/W$, with $\ker \pi = W$ and $\operatorname{rank} \pi = \dim V/W$ (surjectivity) from (1),
\[
\dim V = \dim \ker \pi + \operatorname{rank} \pi = \dim W + \dim V/W .
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.6em, column sep=2.4em]
V \arrow[rr, "A"] \arrow[dr, "\pi"'] & & Z \\
& V/W \arrow[ur, "\bar A"'] &
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

The universal property as a triangle: a linear map that kills $W$ descends to $V/W$. It is the linear counterpart of the universal property of quotient maps, Theorem~\ref{thm:univ-quotient-full}, with ``vanishes on $W$'' in place of ``constant on the fibres'' --- and the proof is the same: define the map on a class by choosing a representative, and check the choice does not matter. Assignment~3, Problem~3(a) is an instance: a derivation kills $I_p^2$, so its restriction to $I_p$ descends to $I_p/I_p^2$.

\begin{defbox}[Direct Sum]\deflabel{def:direct-sum}
The \textbf{direct sum} of vector spaces $V$ and $W$ is $V \oplus W = V \times W$ with the componentwise operations $(v, w) + (v', w') = (v + v', w + w')$ and $c(v, w) = (cv, cw)$. It comes with the \textbf{inclusions} $\iota_V(v) = (v, 0)$, $\iota_W(w) = (0, w)$ and the \textbf{projections} $\pi_V(v, w) = v$, $\pi_W(v, w) = w$, all linear.
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[Internal Direct Sum]\deflabel{def:internal-direct-sum}
A vector space $U$ is the \textbf{internal direct sum} of subspaces $U_1, U_2$, written $U = U_1 \oplus U_2$, if every $u \in U$ is $u_1 + u_2$ for unique $u_1 \in U_1$, $u_2 \in U_2$.
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[Direct Sums]\thmlabel{prop:direct-sum}
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\pi_V \iota_V = \mathrm{id}_V$, $\pi_W \iota_W = \mathrm{id}_W$, $\pi_W \iota_V = 0$ and $\pi_V \iota_W = 0$. So $\iota_V$, $\iota_W$ are injective, and $V \oplus W$ is the internal direct sum of $V \oplus \{0\} = \iota_V(V)$ and $\{0\} \oplus W = \iota_W(W)$.
    \item If $(e_i)$ and $(f_j)$ are bases of $V$ and $W$, then the vectors $(e_i, 0)$ and $(0, f_j)$ together form a basis of $V \oplus W$. In particular $\dim (V \oplus W) = \dim V + \dim W$.
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{App.~B, \emph{Vector Spaces}}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\emph{(1)} Direct from the formulas of Definition~\ref{def:direct-sum}: for $v \in V$ and $w \in W$,
\[
\pi_V \iota_V(v) = \pi_V(v, 0) = v, \quad \pi_W \iota_W(w) = \pi_W(0, w) = w, \quad \pi_W \iota_V(v) = \pi_W(v, 0) = 0, \quad \pi_V \iota_W(w) = \pi_V(0, w) = 0 .
\]
\emph{Injectivity.} If $\iota_V(v) = \iota_V(v')$, apply $\pi_V$: $v = \pi_V\iota_V(v) = \pi_V\iota_V(v') = v'$. Likewise $\iota_W$ is injective, using $\pi_W$ as a left inverse. \emph{Internal direct sum} (Definition~\ref{def:internal-direct-sum}). Existence: by componentwise addition each $(v, w)$ is $(v, 0) + (0, w) = \iota_V(v) + \iota_W(w)$. Uniqueness: suppose $(v, w) = \iota_V(v') + \iota_W(w')$ for some $v' \in V$, $w' \in W$. Applying the linear maps $\pi_V$ and $\pi_W$ and the four identities above,
\[
v = \pi_V(v, w) = \pi_V\iota_V(v') + \pi_V\iota_W(w') = v' + 0, \qquad w = \pi_W(v, w) = \pi_W\iota_V(v') + \pi_W\iota_W(w') = 0 + w' ,
\]
so $v = \pi_V(v, w)$ and $w = \pi_W(v, w)$ are forced, and the summands $\iota_V(v)$, $\iota_W(w)$ are unique.

\emph{(2)} Let $(e_1, \ldots, e_m)$ and $(f_1, \ldots, f_n)$ be the bases. \emph{Spanning.} Given $(v, w)$, write $v = \sum_i v^i e_i$ and $w = \sum_j w^j f_j$ with the coordinates $v^i$, $w^j$ of $v$ and $w$. By the componentwise operations,
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m v^i (e_i, 0) + \sum_{j=1}^n w^j (0, f_j) = \Big(\sum_{i=1}^m v^i e_i,\ 0\Big) + \Big(0,\ \sum_{j=1}^n w^j f_j\Big) = (v, w) .
\]
\emph{Independence.} If $\sum_i a^i (e_i, 0) + \sum_j b^j (0, f_j) = (0, 0)$, the same computation gives $\big(\sum_i a^i e_i,\ \sum_j b^j f_j\big) = (0, 0)$, so $\sum_i a^i e_i = 0$ in $V$ and $\sum_j b^j f_j = 0$ in $W$; by the independence of the two bases all $a^i$ and all $b^j$ vanish. So the $m + n$ vectors form a basis, and $\dim(V \oplus W) = m + n = \dim V + \dim W$.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[Direct Sum and Product]\label{rem:direct-sum-product}
For two summands, or finitely many, the direct sum \emph{is} the Cartesian product with componentwise operations. The two notions differ only for infinitely many summands: the product $\prod_\alpha V_\alpha$ contains all families $(v_\alpha)$, while the direct sum $\bigoplus_\alpha V_\alpha$ contains only those with finitely many nonzero entries.
\end{rembox}

% ============================================================================
% SECTION: THE DIFFERENTIAL OF A MAP BETWEEN VECTOR SPACES
% ============================================================================

\section{The Differential of a Map Between Vector Spaces}\label{sec:vs-differential}\label{sub:vs-differential}

\roadmark{Stage: linear}{The derivative of a map between finite-dimensional vector spaces, without coordinates --- the model for the differential of a smooth map.}

\textit{Lecture 7. The $\Ogp(n)$ argument computed a derivative by differentiating along straight lines and read off surjectivity from the result, without ever writing a Jacobian matrix. This section says exactly what that computes and why it is legitimate. For now it is all linear algebra, but it is also the template for the differential of a map between manifolds, to come.}

Throughout, $X$ and $Y$ are finite-dimensional real vector spaces, of dimensions $m$ and $n$, and $F : X \to Y$ is a map of sets.

\begin{defbox}[Linear Coordinate System]\deflabel{def:linear-coords}
A \textbf{linear coordinate system} on $X$ is a linear isomorphism $L : X \to \mathbb{R}^m$ --- equivalently, a choice of basis, $L$ sending a vector to its coordinate column.
\leeref{Example 1.24}
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[Coordinate Representation]\deflabel{def:vs-coordinate-representation}
Given linear coordinate systems $L$ on $X$ and $K$ on $Y$ (Definition~\ref{def:linear-coords}), the \textbf{coordinate representation} of $F$ is
\[
\widetilde F = K \circ F \circ L^{-1} : \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^n .
\]
\leeref{Example 1.24}
\end{defbox}

Since $L$ and $K$ are bijections, $\widetilde F$ is the unique map making the square commute:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.2em, column sep=3.2em]
X \arrow[r, "F"] \arrow[d, "L"', "\cong"] & Y \arrow[d, "K", "\cong"'] \\
\mathbb{R}^m \arrow[r, "\widetilde F"'] & \mathbb{R}^n
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad\qquad \widetilde F = K \circ F \circ L^{-1}.
\]
Commutativity means: apply $F$ and then take coordinates, or take coordinates and then apply $\widetilde F$; the result is the same: $\widetilde F$ is $F$ expressed in coordinates.

\begin{defbox}[Smooth Map Between Vector Spaces]\deflabel{def:vs-smooth}
$F : X \to Y$ is \textbf{smooth} if $\widetilde F = K \circ F \circ L^{-1} : \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is smooth for any choice of linear coordinates $L, K$ --- equivalently, by Lemma~\ref{lem:vs-smooth-indep}, for some choice.
\end{defbox}

\begin{lembox}[Independence of Coordinates]\thmlabel{lem:vs-smooth-indep}
If the coordinate representation $\widetilde F = K \circ F \circ L^{-1}$ of Definition~\ref{def:vs-coordinate-representation} is smooth for one choice of linear coordinates $L$ on $X$ and $K$ on $Y$, it is smooth for every choice. Hence ``any'' in Definition~\ref{def:vs-smooth} may be replaced by ``some''.
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not proved in lecture; filled in.)} Let $L', K'$ be another choice, with $\widetilde F' = K' F L'^{-1}$; we show $\widetilde F'$ is smooth, given that $\widetilde F = K F L^{-1}$ is. Since $L$ and $K$ are bijections, $F$ can be recovered from $\widetilde F$:
\[
K^{-1} \circ \widetilde F \circ L = K^{-1} \circ K \circ F \circ L^{-1} \circ L = F .
\]
Substituting this expression for $F$ into the definition of $\widetilde F'$ gives
\[
\widetilde F' = K' \circ F \circ L'^{-1} = K' \circ \big(K^{-1} \circ \widetilde F \circ L\big) \circ L'^{-1} = (K' K^{-1}) \circ \widetilde F \circ (L L'^{-1}),
\]
and $K'K^{-1} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$, $LL'^{-1} : \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^m$ are linear isomorphisms, being composites of linear isomorphisms, hence smooth: by Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(3) each component of a linear map $\mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is a linear function $\sum_j a_{ij} r^j$ of the coordinates, a polynomial. A composite of smooth maps between Euclidean spaces is smooth (chain rule), so $\widetilde F'$ is smooth.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[A Vector Space Is a Smooth Manifold]\thmlabel{prop:vs-manifold}
Any two linear coordinate systems $L, L' : X \to \mathbb{R}^m$ on a finite-dimensional real vector space are $C^\infty$-compatible charts. Consequently $X$ carries a canonical smooth structure, the one generated by any single linear chart $(X, L)$, and a map $F : X \to Y$ is smooth in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:vs-smooth} iff it is smooth in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map} for these structures.
\leeref{Example 1.24}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Topology.} Give $X$ the topology transported from $\mathbb{R}^m$ by $L$: $U \subseteq X$ is open iff $L(U)$ is open. It is independent of $L$ since all norms on $\mathbb{R}^m$ are equivalent; concretely, for another linear coordinate system $L'$, $L'(U) = (L'L^{-1})\big(L(U)\big)$, and $L'L^{-1}$ is a linear isomorphism of $\mathbb{R}^m$, continuous with continuous (linear) inverse $LL'^{-1}$, i.e.\ a homeomorphism, so $L(U)$ is open iff $L'(U)$ is. With this topology $L$ is a homeomorphism of $X$ onto the open set $\mathbb{R}^m$, so $X$ is Hausdorff, second countable and locally Euclidean, like $\mathbb{R}^m$ --- a topological $m$-manifold --- and $(X, L)$ is a chart (Definition~\ref{def:chart}).

\emph{Compatibility.} For two linear coordinate systems $L, L'$, the overlap of the charts $(X, L)$ and $(X, L')$ is $X$, and the transition function is $L' \circ L^{-1} : \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^m$, a linear isomorphism with linear inverse $L \circ L'^{-1}$. Linear maps of $\mathbb{R}^m$ are smooth (their components are linear polynomials, Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(3)), so $L' \circ L^{-1}$ is a smooth bijection with smooth inverse, a diffeomorphism (Definition~\ref{def:diffeo-euclidean}), and the two charts are compatible (Definition~\ref{def:compatible}).

\emph{The smooth structure.} A single chart is an atlas (Example~\ref{ex:atlas-Rn}), so by Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-atlas} the one-chart atlas $\{(X,L)\}$ determines a smooth structure, the unique maximal atlas $\overline{\{(X,L)\}}$ of charts compatible with $(X, L)$. It is the same structure for every $L$, by compatibility: $(X, L')$ is compatible with $(X, L)$, so $\overline{\{(X,L)\}}$ is a maximal atlas containing $\{(X, L')\}$, and by the uniqueness in Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-atlas} it equals $\overline{\{(X,L')\}}$.

\emph{Smooth maps.} For the last claim, the coordinate representation of $F$ in the linear charts $L$ and $K$ is precisely $K \circ F \circ L^{-1} = \widetilde F$. If $F$ is smooth in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:vs-smooth}, then $F = K^{-1} \circ \widetilde F \circ L$ is continuous, as a composite of continuous maps, and at every $p \in X$ the charts $(X, L) \ni p$ and $(Y, K)$, with $F(X) \subseteq Y$, have smooth coordinate representation $\widetilde F$; so $F$ is smooth in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}. Conversely, if $F$ is smooth in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}, then by Proposition~\ref{prop:smooth-map-charts}, applied to the smooth charts $(X, L)$ and $(Y, K)$ with $F(X) \subseteq Y$, the coordinate representation $K \circ F \circ L^{-1} = \widetilde F$ is smooth; so $F$ is smooth in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:vs-smooth}.
\end{proof}

\begin{defbox}[The Standard Smooth Structure on a Vector Space]\deflabel{def:vs-structure}
A finite-dimensional real vector space $X$ of dimension $m$ is given the topology for which one, hence every, linear coordinate system $L : X \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is a homeomorphism, and the smooth structure generated by one, hence every, \textbf{linear chart} $(X, L)$ --- ``hence every'' by Proposition~\ref{prop:vs-manifold}. With these, $X$ is a smooth manifold of dimension $m$ whose linear coordinate systems are smooth charts.
\leeref{Example 1.24}
\end{defbox}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:vector-spaces-3}
This is the sense in which $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$, $\Sym(n,\mathbb{R})$, and $\Mat(n,\mathbb{C})$ are smooth manifolds without anyone having chosen coordinates on them. Such a space is an abstract vector space made into a manifold by choosing a linear chart, and it does not matter which linear chart is chosen: they are all smoothly compatible.
\end{rembox}

Now suppose $F$ is smooth and fix $p \in X$. There is a second square, with the same vertical arrows but a \emph{linear} map along the bottom: the linear map $\mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^n$ given by the Jacobian matrix $\widetilde F'(\tilde p)$, where $\tilde p = L(p)$ is the coordinate vector of $p$. Written out, with $\widetilde F = (\widetilde F^1, \ldots, \widetilde F^n)$ and coordinates $(r^1, \ldots, r^m)$ on $\mathbb{R}^m$, it is the $n \times m$ matrix
\[
\widetilde F'(\tilde p) = \begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial \widetilde F^1}{\partial r^1}(\tilde p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial \widetilde F^1}{\partial r^m}(\tilde p) \\[2mm]
\vdots & & \vdots \\[1mm]
\dfrac{\partial \widetilde F^n}{\partial r^1}(\tilde p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial \widetilde F^n}{\partial r^m}(\tilde p)
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

\begin{defbox}[The Differential]\deflabel{def:vs-differential}
Let $F : X \to Y$ be smooth and $p \in X$. Choose linear coordinates $L$ on $X$ and $K$ on $Y$, let $\widetilde F = K \circ F \circ L^{-1}$ be the coordinate representation (Definition~\ref{def:vs-coordinate-representation}), and put $\tilde p = L(p)$. The \textbf{differential} of $F$ at $p$ is the unique linear map $dF_p : X \to Y$ making the square commute:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.2em, column sep=3.6em]
X \arrow[r, "dF_p"] \arrow[d, "L"'] & Y \arrow[d, "K"] \\
\mathbb{R}^m \arrow[r, "\widetilde F'(\tilde p)"'] & \mathbb{R}^n
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad\qquad dF_p = K^{-1} \circ \widetilde F'(\tilde p) \circ L.
\]
\end{defbox}

\begin{thmbox}[Coordinate-Free Formula for the Differential]\thmlabel{thm:vs-differential-curves}
Let $F : X \to Y$ be smooth and $p, v \in X$. Then
\[
dF_p(v) \;=\; \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} F(p + tv) \;=\; \lim_{t \to 0} \frac{1}{t}\big( F(p+tv) - F(p) \big).
\]
In particular $dF_p$ does not depend on the choice of bases used to define it.
\leeref{cf.\ Corollary 3.25}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
Fix linear coordinates $L$ on $X$ and $K$ on $Y$ as in Definition~\ref{def:vs-differential}, and write $\tilde p = L(p)$, $\tilde v = L(v)$. The plan: express the curve $t \mapsto F(p+tv)$ through $\widetilde F$, differentiate in coordinates by the chain rule, and recognise $dF_p(v)$.

\emph{The curve in coordinates.} The curve $t \mapsto p + tv$ in $X$ has coordinate curve $t \mapsto L(p+tv) = L(p) + t\,L(v) = \tilde p + t\,\tilde v$ in $\mathbb{R}^m$, by linearity of $L$. Since $\widetilde F \circ L = K \circ F \circ L^{-1} \circ L = K \circ F$, applying $K^{-1}$ gives
\[
F(p+tv) = K^{-1}\big( \widetilde F(L(p + tv)) \big) = K^{-1}\big( \widetilde F(\tilde p + t \tilde v) \big).
\]

\emph{Differentiating in coordinates.} The map $c(t) = \widetilde F(\tilde p + t\tilde v)$ is a smooth curve in $\mathbb{R}^n$, the composite of the smooth $\widetilde F$ (smoothness of $F$, Definition~\ref{def:vs-smooth}) with the line $\gamma(t) = \tilde p + t\tilde v$, for which $\gamma(0) = \tilde p$ and $\gamma'(0) = \tilde v$. By the chain rule its velocity at $t = 0$ is the Jacobian applied to the direction:
\[
c'(0) = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_0 \widetilde F(\tilde p + t\tilde v) = \widetilde F'(\gamma(0))\,\gamma'(0) = \widetilde F'(\tilde p)\,\tilde v .
\]

\emph{Applying $K^{-1}$.} Since $K^{-1}$ is linear, it commutes with differentiation of curves: it is linear and continuous (a homeomorphism for the topology of Definition~\ref{def:vs-structure}), so
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} K^{-1}(c(t)) = \lim_{t \to 0} \frac{1}{t}\big( K^{-1}c(t) - K^{-1}c(0) \big) = \lim_{t \to 0} K^{-1}\Big( \frac{c(t) - c(0)}{t} \Big) = K^{-1}\big( c'(0) \big) .
\]
Combining the three displays with the formula $dF_p = K^{-1} \circ \widetilde F'(\tilde p) \circ L$ of Definition~\ref{def:vs-differential},
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} F(p+tv) = K^{-1}\Big( \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} \widetilde F(\tilde p + t\tilde v) \Big) = K^{-1}\big( \widetilde F'(\tilde p) L(v) \big) = dF_p(v).
\]
The second expression for $dF_p(v)$ is the definition of the derivative of the $Y$-valued curve $t \mapsto F(p+tv)$ at $t = 0$. The right-hand side of the displayed formula makes no reference to $L$ or $K$, so neither does $dF_p$: two choices of linear coordinates give linear maps with the same value at every $v$, hence the same map.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:vector-spaces-4}
Two things are worth isolating. First, the hypothesis that $F$ is smooth is used: it is what makes $\widetilde F$ differentiable so that the chain rule applies. A map can have all directional derivatives $\frac{d}{dt}\big|_0 F(p+tv)$ at a point without being differentiable there, and for such a map the formula need not define anything linear (Example~\ref{ex:directional-derivative-not-linear}; see also Example~\ref{ex:directional-not-differentiable}). Second, the formula uses the vector space structure of \emph{both} spaces, in two different places: that of $X$ to form the line $p + tv$, and that of $Y$ to form the difference quotient $\frac1t\big(F(p+tv) - F(p)\big)$. Neither can be dropped, which is why the same formula will \emph{not} serve as the definition of the differential on a general manifold: there is no ``$p + tv$'' and no ``$F(p+tv) - F(p)$.'' That is the problem \ref{sec:tangent} begins to address.
\end{rembox}

\begin{exbox}[Directional Derivatives That Are Not Linear in the Direction]\exlabel{ex:directional-derivative-not-linear}
\textit{(Example supplied; not from lecture.)} Let $f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$,
\[
f(x, y) = \frac{x^2 y}{x^2 + y^2} \quad \text{for } (x, y) \neq (0, 0), \qquad f(0, 0) = 0.
\]
To be shown: every directional derivative $D(v) = \frac{d}{dt}\big|_0 f(tv)$ exists, but $v \mapsto D(v)$ is not linear, so $f$ is not differentiable at $0$.
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
\item \emph{The directional derivatives.} $D(0) = 0$. For $v = (v_1, v_2) \neq 0$ and $t \neq 0$,
\[
\frac{f(tv) - f(0)}{t} = \frac1t \cdot \frac{t^3 v_1^2 v_2}{t^2 (v_1^2 + v_2^2)} = \frac{v_1^2 v_2}{v_1^2 + v_2^2},
\]
independent of $t$; so $D(v) = \dfrac{v_1^2 v_2}{v_1^2 + v_2^2}$.
\item \emph{Not linear.} $D(1,0) = 0$ and $D(0,1) = 0$, but $D(1,1) = \tfrac12 \neq D(1,0) + D(0,1)$.
\item \emph{Not differentiable.} If $f$ were differentiable at $0$, the chain rule along the line $t \mapsto tv$ would give $D(v) = Df_0\, v$, which is linear in $v$.
\end{itemize}
\end{exbox}

\begin{exbox}[All Directional Derivatives but Not Differentiable]\exlabel{ex:directional-not-differentiable}
\textit{(Not from lecture; added on request.)} Let $f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$,
\[
f(x, y) = \frac{x^3 y}{x^6 + y^2} \quad \text{for } (x, y) \neq (0, 0), \qquad f(0, 0) = 0.
\]
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \emph{Every directional derivative at $0$ exists and is $0$.} Let $v = (v_1, v_2) \neq 0$ and $t \neq 0$. If $v_2 \neq 0$,
    \[
    \frac{f(tv) - f(0)}{t} = \frac{1}{t} \cdot \frac{t^4 v_1^3 v_2}{t^6 v_1^6 + t^2 v_2^2} = \frac{t\, v_1^3 v_2}{t^4 v_1^6 + v_2^2} \longrightarrow \frac{0}{v_2^2} = 0 \quad (t \to 0);
    \]
    if $v_2 = 0$, then $f(tv) = 0$ for all $t$. So $\frac{d}{dt}\big|_0 f(tv) = 0$ for every $v$, which is even linear in $v$: the candidate derivative would be the zero map.
    \item \emph{$f$ is not differentiable at $0$; it is not even continuous there.} Along the curve $y = x^3$, $x \neq 0$: $f(x, x^3) = \dfrac{x^6}{x^6 + x^6} = \dfrac12$, while $f(0, 0) = 0$. A map differentiable at a point is continuous there, since $f(p + v) - f(p) = Df_p\, v + o(|v|) \to 0$.
\end{enumerate}
So the formula $Df_p(v) = \frac{d}{dt}\big|_0 f(p + tv)$ cannot be used to \emph{prove} differentiability. The lines miss the problem: a line $y = mx$ meets the curve $y = x^3$ only at $0$ and at $x = \pm\sqrt{m}$ (when $m > 0$), a fixed distance away, and the axes meet it only at $0$; so near $0$ no line sees the value $\tfrac12$.
\end{exbox}

\begin{defbox}[Regular Value of a Map Between Vector Spaces]\deflabel{def:vs-regular-value}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} Suppose $\dim X \ge \dim Y$ and $F : X \to Y$ is smooth (Definition~\ref{def:vs-smooth}). A point $c \in Y$ is a \textbf{regular value} of $F$ if, for a choice of linear coordinates $L$ on $X$ and $K$ on $Y$ (Definition~\ref{def:linear-coords}), the point $K(c)$ is a regular value (Definition~\ref{def:regular-value}) of the coordinate representation $\widetilde F = K \circ F \circ L^{-1} : \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^n$ (Definition~\ref{def:vs-coordinate-representation}). By Corollary~\ref{cor:vs-regular}, this holds for one choice of linear coordinates if and only if it holds for every choice.
\end{defbox}

\begin{corbox}[Regular Values Without Coordinates]\thmlabel{cor:vs-regular}
Suppose $\dim X \ge \dim Y$ and $F : X \to Y$ is smooth, and let $\widetilde F = K \circ F \circ L^{-1}$ and $\tilde p = L(p)$ be taken in linear coordinates $L$, $K$, as in Definition~\ref{def:vs-differential}. Then for $p \in X$,
\[
\widetilde F'(\tilde p) \text{ has maximal rank } (= \dim Y) \iff dF_p : X \to Y \text{ is surjective},
\]
and this holds for one choice of coordinates iff for all. Hence $c \in Y$ is a regular value of $F$ (Definition~\ref{def:vs-regular-value}), in one choice of linear coordinates or in any, iff $dF_p$ is surjective for every $p \in F^{-1}(c)$, a statement that involves no bases.
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
Write $m = \dim X$ and $n = \dim Y$, so $m \ge n$ and $\widetilde F'(\tilde p)$ is an $n \times m$ matrix.

\emph{Maximal rank means surjective.} Since $m \ge n$, the maximal possible rank of an $n \times m$ matrix is $n$ (it has $n$ rows). The rank of $\widetilde F'(\tilde p)$ is the dimension of the image of the linear map $\mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^n$ it defines (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(3)), so it has rank $n$ iff that image is all of $\mathbb{R}^n$, i.e.\ iff the map is surjective.

\emph{Bottom arrow surjective iff top arrow surjective.} In the square of Definition~\ref{def:vs-differential} the vertical arrows are bijections, and $dF_p = K^{-1} \circ \widetilde F'(\tilde p) \circ L$, equivalently $\widetilde F'(\tilde p) = K \circ dF_p \circ L^{-1}$. If $\widetilde F'(\tilde p)$ is surjective and $y \in Y$, choose $a \in \mathbb{R}^m$ with $\widetilde F'(\tilde p)\,a = K(y)$; then $dF_p(L^{-1}a) = K^{-1}\big(\widetilde F'(\tilde p)\,a\big) = y$. If $dF_p$ is surjective and $b \in \mathbb{R}^n$, choose $x \in X$ with $dF_p(x) = K^{-1}(b)$; then $\widetilde F'(\tilde p)(Lx) = K\big(dF_p(x)\big) = b$. So the bottom arrow is surjective iff the top arrow $dF_p$ is.

\emph{Independence of coordinates.} The top arrow is independent of coordinates by Theorem~\ref{thm:vs-differential-curves}, so surjectivity of $\widetilde F'(\tilde p)$ is too: if it holds for one choice $L, K$, then $dF_p$ is surjective, and by the previous paragraph applied to any other choice $L', K'$, the Jacobian of $K' F L'^{-1}$ at $L'(p)$ is surjective as well.

\emph{Regular values.} Fix linear coordinates $L$, $K$. By Definition~\ref{def:vs-regular-value}, read in these linear coordinates, $c$ is a regular value of $F$ when $K(c)$ is a regular value of $\widetilde F$ (Definition~\ref{def:regular-value}): $\widetilde F'(\tilde q)$ is surjective at every $\tilde q \in \widetilde F^{-1}(K(c))$ (Definition~\ref{def:regular-point}). These points are exactly the $\tilde q = L(q)$ with $q \in F^{-1}(c)$, since $\widetilde F(L(q)) = K(F(q))$ equals $K(c)$ iff $F(q) = c$ ($K$ is injective) and $L$ is a bijection. By the equivalence above at each such $q$, $c$ is a regular value in the coordinates $L$, $K$ iff $dF_q$ is surjective for every $q \in F^{-1}(c)$, a statement that involves no bases. In particular the condition of Definition~\ref{def:vs-regular-value} holds for one choice of linear coordinates iff it holds for every choice.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[What the Curve Method Computes]\label{rem:what-curve-method-computes}
Read together, Theorem~\ref{thm:vs-differential-curves} and Corollary~\ref{cor:vs-regular} are the license for the computation in Example~\ref{ex:On-smooth}. The board computation $\frac{d}{dt}\big|_0 F(g + tA)$ is not a shortcut around the Jacobian --- it \emph{is} the Jacobian, packaged as the linear map $A \mapsto dF_g(A)$ and read off without coordinates; and the surjectivity of that linear map \emph{is} the maximal-rank condition, likewise without coordinates. Written as a matrix, $dF_g$ for $\Ogp(n)$ would have $n(n+1)/2$ rows and $n^2$ columns of partial derivatives. None of it is needed. Using curves to compute differentials is a basic technique in this subject.
\end{rembox}

% ============================================================================
% SECTION: THE ORTHOGONAL AND UNITARY GROUPS AS SMOOTH MANIFOLDS
% ============================================================================

\section{The Orthogonal and Unitary Groups as Smooth Manifolds}\label{sec:on-un-smooth}\label{sub:on-smooth}

\roadmark{Stage: linear}{The matrix groups become smooth level sets: $\Ogp(n)$ and $\Ugp(n)$ by the regular value theorem, with the differential computed along straight lines.}

The classical groups through the course: defined in Section~\ref{sec:topgroups}, with the examples of Section~\ref{sec:ex-classical}; topological manifolds as level sets in Theorem~\ref{thm:classical-manifolds}; $\SO(2)$ and $\SO(3)$ acting on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\mathbb{R}^3$ in Examples~\ref{ex:so2-orbits} and~\ref{ex:so3-orbits}, and $\SO(3)$ on $S^2$ in Examples~\ref{ex:so3-isotropy} and~\ref{ex:s2-homogeneous}; $\Ogp(n)$ acting on the Grassmannians in Corollary~\ref{cor:grassmannian}; smooth manifolds in Examples~\ref{ex:On-smooth} and~\ref{ex:Un-smooth}; their tangent spaces at the identity in Theorem~\ref{thm:classical-summary}, with the infinitesimal rotations of Example~\ref{ex:so3-infinitesimal}; the double cover $\mathrm{SU}(2) \to \SO(3)$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:double-cover}; the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ and the cross product in Example~\ref{ex:cross-product-lie}; and Lie groups in Proposition~\ref{prop:classical-lie-groups}.


The promise of \ref{sub:classical-manifolds} can now be kept, with \ref{sub:vs-differential} supplying the meaning of every step.

\begin{defbox}[Symmetric Matrices as a Euclidean Space]\deflabel{def:sym}
Let $\Sym(n,\mathbb{R}) = \{\, S \in \Mat(n,\mathbb{R}) \mid S^{\mathsf T} = S \,\}$. It is a linear subspace of $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$, and the entries on and above the diagonal are free while those below are determined, so
\[
\dim \Sym(n,\mathbb{R}) = n + (n-1) + \cdots + 1 = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}.
\]
Reading off those entries in a fixed order gives a linear isomorphism $\Sym(n,\mathbb{R}) \cong \mathbb{R}^{n(n+1)/2}$, which we use to regard maps into $\Sym(n,\mathbb{R})$ as maps into a Euclidean space. Being linear, it changes neither smoothness nor rank. Explicitly, the free entries are the $s_{ij}$ with $i \le j$:
\[
S = \begin{pmatrix}
s_{11} & s_{12} & \cdots & s_{1n} \\
s_{12} & s_{22} & \cdots & s_{2n} \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
s_{1n} & s_{2n} & \cdots & s_{nn}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
\end{defbox}

\begin{exbox}[$\Ogp(n)$ Is a Smooth Manifold of Dimension $\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$]\exlabel{ex:On-smooth}
Define
\[
F : \Mat(n,\mathbb{R}) \longrightarrow \Sym(n,\mathbb{R}), \qquad F(g) = g\, g^{\mathsf T}.
\]
Then $\Ogp(n) = F^{-1}(I)$, the identity $I$ is a regular value of $F$, and consequently $\Ogp(n)$ is a smooth manifold of dimension $n^2 - \tfrac{n(n+1)}{2} = \tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$.
\leeref{Example 7.27}
\end{exbox}

\begin{proof}
Four things have to be shown: $F$ is a smooth map into $\Sym(n,\mathbb{R})$; its level set $F^{-1}(I)$ is $\Ogp(n)$; $dF_g$ is surjective at every $g \in F^{-1}(I)$; and this makes $\Ogp(n)$ a smooth manifold of the stated dimension.

\emph{$F$ is well defined and smooth.} For $F$ to land in $\Sym(n,\mathbb{R})$ we need $F(g)^{\mathsf T} = F(g)$. Using $(PQ)^{\mathsf T} = Q^{\mathsf T} P^{\mathsf T}$ and $g^{\mathsf T\mathsf T} = (g^{\mathsf T})^{\mathsf T} = g$,
\[
(gg^{\mathsf T})^{\mathsf T} = g^{\mathsf T\mathsf T} g^{\mathsf T} = g g^{\mathsf T},
\]
so $F$ does land in $\Sym(n,\mathbb{R})$. For smoothness, take the linear coordinates $L$ on $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$ of Definition~\ref{def:mat-euclid} and $K$ on $\Sym(n,\mathbb{R})$ of Definition~\ref{def:sym}. The components of the coordinate representation $K \circ F \circ L^{-1}$ (Definition~\ref{def:vs-coordinate-representation}) are the entries $(gg^{\mathsf T})_{ij}$ with $i \le j$, and by the definition of the matrix product each of them is
\[
(gg^{\mathsf T})_{ij} = \sum_{m=1}^n g_{im}\,(g^{\mathsf T})_{mj} = \sum_{m=1}^n g_{im}\,g_{jm},
\]
a quadratic polynomial in the coordinates $g_{11}, \ldots, g_{nn}$ of Definition~\ref{def:mat-euclid}. Polynomials are smooth, so $K \circ F \circ L^{-1}$ is smooth, and $F$ is smooth by Definition~\ref{def:vs-smooth}.

\emph{$\Ogp(n) = F^{-1}(I)$.} By Proposition~\ref{prop:orth-equiv}, $g \in \Ogp(n) \iff g^{-1} = g^{\mathsf T} \iff gg^{\mathsf T} = I$. In detail, both inclusions: if $g \in \Ogp(n)$, then $g^{-1} = g^{\mathsf T}$ by (i)$\Rightarrow$(iii) of Proposition~\ref{prop:orth-equiv}, so $F(g) = gg^{\mathsf T} = gg^{-1} = I$. Conversely, let $F(g) = gg^{\mathsf T} = I$. Taking determinants, $\det(g)\det(g^{\mathsf T}) = \det I = 1$, so $\det g \neq 0$ and $g \in \GL(n,\mathbb{R})$; multiplying $gg^{\mathsf T} = I$ on the left by $g^{-1}$ gives $g^{\mathsf T} = g^{-1}$, which is (iii) of Proposition~\ref{prop:orth-equiv}, so $g \in \Ogp(n)$ by (iii)$\Rightarrow$(i).

\emph{The differential as a linear map.} \textit{(Lecture~6: no Jacobian is computed; the differential is computed along curves.)} $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$ and $\Sym(n,\mathbb{R})$ are finite-dimensional vector spaces and $F$ is smooth between them (first step), so by Theorem~\ref{thm:vs-differential-curves}, applied to these two vector spaces with $p = g$ and $v = A$, the differential is computed along lines: for $g \in F^{-1}(I)$ and any $A \in \Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$,
\[
dF_g(A) = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} F(g+tA).
\]
Expanding, with $(g + tA)^{\mathsf T} = g^{\mathsf T} + tA^{\mathsf T}$ because transposition is linear, and multiplying out by distributivity,
\[
F(g+tA) = (g+tA)(g^{\mathsf T} + tA^{\mathsf T}) = g g^{\mathsf T} + t\big(A g^{\mathsf T} + g A^{\mathsf T}\big) + t^2 A A^{\mathsf T}.
\]
This is a polynomial in $t$ with matrix coefficients. Its derivative at $t = 0$ is the coefficient of $t$: the constant term $gg^{\mathsf T}$ contributes $0$, and the term $t^2 AA^{\mathsf T}$ has derivative $2t\,AA^{\mathsf T}$, which is $0$ at $t = 0$. So
\[
dF_g(A) = A g^{\mathsf T} + g A^{\mathsf T}.
\]
This is visibly symmetric, as it must be, $dF_g$ taking values in $\Sym(n,\mathbb{R})$: the transpose of a sum is the sum of the transposes, and $(Ag^{\mathsf T})^{\mathsf T} = gA^{\mathsf T}$, $(gA^{\mathsf T})^{\mathsf T} = Ag^{\mathsf T}$, so $(Ag^{\mathsf T} + gA^{\mathsf T})^{\mathsf T} = gA^{\mathsf T} + Ag^{\mathsf T}$.

\emph{$dF_g$ is surjective.} \textit{(Lecture~6 observed that the left side is twice the symmetric part of a matrix, which is the substitution below; Lecture~7 finished with the explicit choice $A = \tfrac12 Sg$, which uses that $S$ is symmetric and that $g$ is orthogonal.)} Fix $g \in F^{-1}(I) = \Ogp(n)$. We must show that every $S \in \Sym(n,\mathbb{R})$ is $dF_g(A)$ for some $A$. Put $X = Ag^{\mathsf T}$. Then $gA^{\mathsf T} = (g^{\mathsf T})^{\mathsf T} A^{\mathsf T} = (Ag^{\mathsf T})^{\mathsf T} = X^{\mathsf T}$, so that
\[
dF_g(A) = Ag^{\mathsf T} + gA^{\mathsf T} = X + X^{\mathsf T}.
\]
The map $A \mapsto Ag^{\mathsf T}$ is linear, and since $g$ is invertible so is $g^{\mathsf T}$; hence $A \mapsto Ag^{\mathsf T}$ is a linear \emph{bijection} of $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$, with inverse $X \mapsto X (g^{\mathsf T})^{-1}$. So as $A$ runs over $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$, $X$ runs over all of $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$, and therefore
\[
\operatorname{im} dF_g = \{\, X + X^{\mathsf T} \mid X \in \Mat(n,\mathbb{R}) \,\} = \Sym(n,\mathbb{R}),
\]
the last equality because $X + X^{\mathsf T}$ is always symmetric ($(X + X^{\mathsf T})^{\mathsf T} = X^{\mathsf T} + X$), and conversely any symmetric $S$ arises from $X = \tfrac12 S$: $\tfrac12 S + (\tfrac12 S)^{\mathsf T} = \tfrac12 S + \tfrac12 S^{\mathsf T} = \tfrac12 S + \tfrac12 S = S$. Unwinding the substitution gives the matrix explicitly: $A = X (g^{\mathsf T})^{-1} = \tfrac12 S g$, using $(g^{\mathsf T})^{-1} = g$ for orthogonal $g$ (from $g^{\mathsf T} = g^{-1}$, the previous step). Directly, with $A = \tfrac12 Sg$:
\[
A g^{\mathsf T} = \tfrac12 S g g^{\mathsf T} = \tfrac12 S, \qquad
g A^{\mathsf T} = g \big(\tfrac12 S g\big)^{\mathsf T} = \tfrac12 g\, g^{\mathsf T} S^{\mathsf T} = \tfrac12 S,
\]
using $(Sg)^{\mathsf T} = g^{\mathsf T} S^{\mathsf T}$, $gg^{\mathsf T} = I$ and $S^{\mathsf T} = S$; adding gives $dF_g(A) = S$.

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.8em, column sep=2.2em]
\Mat(n,\mathbb{R}) \arrow[rr, "dF_g"] \arrow[dr, "A \,\mapsto\, Ag^{\mathsf T}"', "\cong"] & & \Sym(n,\mathbb{R}) \\
& \Mat(n,\mathbb{R}) \arrow[ur, "X \,\mapsto\, X + X^{\mathsf T}"'] &
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

The same argument as a diagram: a bijection followed by symmetrization, which is onto. The unitary case, Example~\ref{ex:Un-smooth}, has exactly this shape, with $^{\mathsf T}$ replaced by $^*$.

\emph{Conclusion.} $dF_g$ is surjective onto $\Sym(n,\mathbb{R})$ for every $g \in F^{-1}(I)$. By Corollary~\ref{cor:vs-regular} (here $\dim \Mat = n^2 \ge \tfrac{n(n+1)}{2} = \dim \Sym$, since the difference is $\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2} \ge 0$), this says that in any linear coordinates the Jacobian has maximal rank $k = \tfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$ at every point of $F^{-1}(I)$, i.e.\ $I$ is a regular value (Definition~\ref{def:regular-value}). Concretely, with the linear coordinates $L$ and $K$ of the first step, the coordinate representation $\widetilde F = K \circ F \circ L^{-1} : \mathbb{R}^{n^2} \to \mathbb{R}^{n(n+1)/2}$ is smooth, its Jacobian $\widetilde F'(L(g))$ has rank $k$ for every $g \in F^{-1}(I)$, and since $K$ is injective,
\[
\widetilde F(L(g)) = K(F(g)) = K(I) \iff F(g) = I, \qquad\text{so}\qquad \widetilde F^{-1}(K(I)) = L\big(F^{-1}(I)\big) = L(\Ogp(n)).
\]
So $K(I)$ is a regular value of $\widetilde F$. Proposition~\ref{prop:level-set-smooth} applies with $W = \mathbb{R}^{n^2}$, $n + k = n^2$ and $k = \tfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$: $L(\Ogp(n))$ is a smooth manifold of dimension $n^2 - \tfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$. The topology of $\Ogp(n)$ is the subspace topology of $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$, defined by declaring $L$ a homeomorphism (Definition~\ref{def:mat-euclid}), so $L$ restricts to a homeomorphism $\Ogp(n) \to L(\Ogp(n))$; transporting the smooth structure along it (Proposition~\ref{prop:transport-structure}) makes $\Ogp(n)$ a smooth manifold of the same dimension, its charts being the graph charts composed with $L$. Finally
\[
n^2 - \frac{n(n+1)}{2} = \frac{2n^2 - n^2 - n}{2} = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}.
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:vector-spaces-5}
\textbf{The codomain is not a cosmetic choice.} It is essential that $F$ be regarded as a map into $\Sym(n,\mathbb{R})$ and not into $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$: with the larger codomain the regular value theorem yields nothing (Example~\ref{ex:gg-transpose-into-mat-not-regular}). Choosing the codomain to be exactly the space the map lands in is what makes the rank condition attainable --- and it is also what produces the right dimension count, since $\dim \Ogp(n) = n^2 - \dim(\text{codomain})$.
\end{rembox}

\begin{exbox}[{The Map $g \mapsto gg^{\mathsf T}$ into All Matrices}]\exlabel{ex:gg-transpose-into-mat-not-regular}
Let $n \ge 2$ and regard the map of Example~\ref{ex:On-smooth} as a map into all matrices,
\[
G : \Mat(n,\mathbb{R}) \longrightarrow \Mat(n,\mathbb{R}), \qquad G(g) = g\, g^{\mathsf T}.
\]
Then $G^{-1}(I) = \Ogp(n)$, exactly as for $F$, but $dG_g$ is surjective at no point $g$; so $I$ fails to be a regular value of $G$ at every point of $G^{-1}(I)$, and the regular value theorem says nothing about $\Ogp(n)$ through $G$.

What has to be shown is that $dG_g : \Mat(n,\mathbb{R}) \to \Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$ is not surjective, for every $g$.
\begin{itemize}
    \item \emph{The image lies in $\Sym(n,\mathbb{R})$.} $G(g + tA)$ is the same polynomial in $t$ as $F(g + tA)$ in the proof of Example~\ref{ex:On-smooth}, so by Theorem~\ref{thm:vs-differential-curves} $dG_g(A) = Ag^{\mathsf T} + gA^{\mathsf T}$, which is symmetric (shown in that proof). Behind this: $G(g)$ is always symmetric, $\operatorname{im} G \subseteq \Sym(n,\mathbb{R})$, and so the velocities $dG_g(A)$ of the curves $t \mapsto G(g + tA)$ lie in $\Sym(n,\mathbb{R})$ too.
    \item \emph{$\Sym(n,\mathbb{R})$ is a proper subspace.} $\dim \Sym(n,\mathbb{R}) = \tfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$ (Definition~\ref{def:sym}), and $n^2 - \tfrac{n(n+1)}{2} = \tfrac{n(n-1)}{2} > 0$ for $n \ge 2$; so $\Sym(n,\mathbb{R}) \subsetneq \Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$.
\end{itemize}
Hence $\operatorname{im} dG_g \subseteq \Sym(n,\mathbb{R}) \subsetneq \Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$ and $dG_g$ is never surjective; in particular not at the points of $G^{-1}(I) = \Ogp(n)$, which is nonempty since $I \in \Ogp(n)$. By Corollary~\ref{cor:vs-regular} (with $\dim X = \dim Y = n^2$), $I$ is not a regular value of $G$. (For $n = 1$, $\Sym(1,\mathbb{R}) = \Mat(1,\mathbb{R})$ and nothing changes.)
\end{exbox}

\begin{lembox}[{The Smooth Structure on $\Ogp(n)$ Does Not Depend on the Linear Coordinates}]\thmlabel{lem:On-structure-independent-of-linear-coordinates}
The smooth structure on $\Ogp(n)$ obtained in Example~\ref{ex:On-smooth} is independent of the linear coordinates used to identify $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$ with $\mathbb{R}^{n^2}$ and $\Sym(n,\mathbb{R})$ with $\mathbb{R}^{n(n+1)/2}$.
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
The idea: two such identifications differ by linear isomorphisms, which are diffeomorphisms (Proposition~\ref{prop:vs-manifold}), so the level set $F^{-1}(I)$ and its graph charts transport across them without change. In detail, let $(L, K)$ and $(L', K')$ be two choices of linear coordinates on $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$ and $\Sym(n,\mathbb{R})$, with $\widetilde F = K \circ F \circ L^{-1}$ and $\widetilde F' = K' \circ F \circ L'^{-1}$. Put $Z = L(\Ogp(n)) = \widetilde F^{-1}(K(I))$ and $Z' = L'(\Ogp(n)) = \widetilde F'^{-1}(K'(I))$ (proof of Example~\ref{ex:On-smooth}), with the smooth structures of Proposition~\ref{prop:level-set-smooth} given by the graph charts of $\widetilde F$ and of $\widetilde F'$. The structure $\mathcal S_L$ on $\Ogp(n)$ is the one transported along the homeomorphism $L|_{\Ogp(n)} : \Ogp(n) \to Z$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:transport-structure}), and $\mathcal S_{L'}$ the one transported along $L'|_{\Ogp(n)}$. In both cases the topology of $\Ogp(n)$ is the subspace topology of $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$, which does not depend on the linear coordinates (Proposition~\ref{prop:vs-manifold}).

\emph{Step 1: $A = L' \circ L^{-1}$ restricts to a diffeomorphism $Z \to Z'$.} $A$ is a linear isomorphism of $\mathbb{R}^{n^2}$ with $A(Z) = Z'$. Let $(U_J, \varphi_J)$ be a graph chart of $Z$ and $(U'_{J'}, \varphi'_{J'})$ a graph chart of $Z'$, the latter the restriction of a coordinate projection $\pi_{I'}$. The set $\varphi_J\big(U_J \cap A^{-1}(U'_{J'})\big)$ is open, because $A|_Z$ is continuous and $\varphi_J$ is a homeomorphism, and on it
\[
\varphi'_{J'} \circ A \circ \varphi_J^{-1} = \pi_{I'} \circ A \circ \varphi_J^{-1} .
\]
Here $\varphi_J^{-1}$ is smooth in the Euclidean sense (observation~1 in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:level-set-smooth}) and $A$, $\pi_{I'}$ are linear, so the composite is smooth. Every coordinate representation of $A|_Z$ in graph charts is therefore smooth, and $A|_Z : Z \to Z'$ is smooth (Proposition~\ref{prop:smooth-map-charts}). The same argument with $A^{-1} = L \circ L'^{-1}$ and the roles of $Z$ and $Z'$ exchanged shows that $A^{-1}|_{Z'}$, the inverse of $A|_Z$, is smooth. So $A|_Z$ is a diffeomorphism (Definition~\ref{def:diffeomorphism}).

\emph{Step 2: the two structures agree.} With the structure $\mathcal S_L$, $L|_{\Ogp(n)}$ is a diffeomorphism onto $Z$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:transport-structure}(2)), so $L'|_{\Ogp(n)} = A|_Z \circ L|_{\Ogp(n)}$ is a composite of diffeomorphisms, hence a diffeomorphism onto $Z'$. By the uniqueness in Proposition~\ref{prop:transport-structure}(3), applied to $h = L'|_{\Ogp(n)}$, the only structure on $\Ogp(n)$ for which $L'|_{\Ogp(n)}$ is a diffeomorphism is $\mathcal S_{L'}$; so $\mathcal S_L = \mathcal S_{L'}$. The coordinates $K$ and $K'$ entered only through the defining maps $\widetilde F$ and $\widetilde F'$, whose graph charts Step~1 used only through observations valid for every graph chart.
\end{proof}

\begin{defbox}[Skew-Symmetric Matrices]\deflabel{def:skew-symmetric-matrices}
Let $\Skew(n,\mathbb{R}) = \{\, B \in \Mat(n,\mathbb{R}) \mid B^{\mathsf T} = -B \,\}$, the \textbf{skew-symmetric matrices}. \textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} It is a linear subspace of $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$: if $B^{\mathsf T} = -B$ and $B'^{\mathsf T} = -B'$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$, then $(B + B')^{\mathsf T} = B^{\mathsf T} + B'^{\mathsf T} = -(B + B')$ and $(cB)^{\mathsf T} = cB^{\mathsf T} = -cB$. Its dimension, $\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$, is computed in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:On-kernel}.
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[The Kernel of the Differential]\thmlabel{prop:On-kernel}
With $F(g) = gg^{\mathsf T}$ as above, for every $g \in \Ogp(n)$,
\[
\ker dF_g = \{\, A \in \Mat(n,\mathbb{R}) \mid gA^{\mathsf T} + Ag^{\mathsf T} = 0 \,\} = g \cdot \Skew(n,\mathbb{R}),
\]
where $\Skew(n,\mathbb{R})$ is the space of skew-symmetric matrices (Definition~\ref{def:skew-symmetric-matrices}). In particular $\ker dF_I = \Skew(n,\mathbb{R})$, and $\dim \ker dF_g = \tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$ for every $g$.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\emph{First equality.} By definition $\ker dF_g = \{A \in \Mat(n,\mathbb{R}) \mid dF_g(A) = 0\}$, and $dF_g(A) = Ag^{\mathsf T} + gA^{\mathsf T}$ was computed in the proof of Example~\ref{ex:On-smooth}; matrix addition is commutative, so the condition reads $gA^{\mathsf T} + Ag^{\mathsf T} = 0$.

\emph{Second equality.} Since $g$ is invertible, every $A$ can be written uniquely as $A = gB$ with $B = g^{-1}A$ (the map $B \mapsto gB$ is a bijection of $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$ with inverse $A \mapsto g^{-1}A$). Substituting, and using $A^{\mathsf T} = (gB)^{\mathsf T} = B^{\mathsf T} g^{\mathsf T}$, then distributivity,
\[
gA^{\mathsf T} + Ag^{\mathsf T} = g B^{\mathsf T} g^{\mathsf T} + g B g^{\mathsf T} = g\,(B^{\mathsf T} + B)\,g^{\mathsf T}.
\]
As $g$ and $g^{\mathsf T}$ are invertible, this vanishes iff $B + B^{\mathsf T} = 0$: if $g(B^{\mathsf T} + B)g^{\mathsf T} = 0$, multiplying on the left by $g^{-1}$ and on the right by $(g^{\mathsf T})^{-1}$ gives $B^{\mathsf T} + B = 0$, and conversely $B^{\mathsf T} + B = 0$ makes the product $0$. And $B + B^{\mathsf T} = 0$ says $B^{\mathsf T} = -B$, i.e.\ $B$ is skew-symmetric. Hence $\ker dF_g = \{gB \mid B \in \Skew(n,\mathbb{R})\}$. At $g = I$ the description reads $\ker dF_I = \Skew(n,\mathbb{R})$ directly: $dF_I(A) = A^{\mathsf T} + A$.

\emph{Dimension.} Left multiplication by $g$, $B \mapsto gB$, is a linear isomorphism of $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$: it is linear since $g(B + B') = gB + gB'$ and $g(cB) = c\,gB$, and bijective with inverse $A \mapsto g^{-1}A$. By the second equality it maps the subspace $\Skew(n,\mathbb{R})$ onto $\ker dF_g$, and it is injective, so it restricts to a linear isomorphism $\Skew(n,\mathbb{R}) \to \ker dF_g$. So $\dim \ker dF_g = \dim \Skew(n,\mathbb{R})$ for every $g$.

\emph{Counting.} The condition $B^{\mathsf T} = -B$ says $B_{ji} = -B_{ij}$ for all $i, j$. For $i = j$ it gives $B_{ii} = -B_{ii}$, so a skew-symmetric matrix has zero diagonal; for $i < j$ it says that the entry $B_{ji}$ below the diagonal is the negative of the entry $B_{ij}$ above. Conversely, any choice of the entries $B_{ij}$ with $i < j$, completed by $B_{ii} = 0$ and $B_{ji} = -B_{ij}$, is skew-symmetric. So $B$ is determined by the $\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$ entries strictly above the diagonal, which may be chosen freely --- reading them off is a linear isomorphism $\Skew(n,\mathbb{R}) \cong \mathbb{R}^{n(n-1)/2}$, the number of positions $(i,j)$ with $i < j$ being $(n-1) + (n-2) + \cdots + 1 + 0 = \binom{n}{2}$:
\[
B = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \ast \\ -(\ast)^{\mathsf T} & \ddots \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \dim \Skew(n,\mathbb{R}) = \binom{n}{2} = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}. \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[Two Readings of the Dimension]\label{rem:two-readings-dimension}
There are now two reasons that $\dim \Ogp(n) = \tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$, the second a combinatorial one (choosing two out of $n$): the level-set count $n^2 - \tfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$ from the regular value theorem, and the kernel count $\binom{n}{2}$ from Proposition~\ref{prop:On-kernel}. They agree by rank--nullity: $dF_g$ is surjective onto a space of dimension $\tfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$, so its kernel has dimension $n^2 - \tfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$. The kernel is not yet officially anything, but it is the \emph{geometric tangent space} $T^{\geo}_g\Ogp(n)$ to $\Ogp(n)$ at $g$ (see \ref{sec:tangent}), and at $g = I$ the skew-symmetric matrices will be the \emph{Lie algebra} $\mathfrak{so}(n)$. The same move produced $\nabla\det$ in Proposition~\ref{prop:jacobi}, and it will recur whenever a classical group is presented as a level set.
\end{rembox}

\begin{corbox}[{$\SO(n)$ Is a Smooth Manifold; $\Ogp(n)$ Is Compact}]\thmlabel{cor:On-consequences}
$\SO(n)$ is a smooth manifold of dimension $\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$, and $\Ogp(n)$ is compact.
\leeref{Example 7.27}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\emph{$\SO(n)$ is open (and closed) in $\Ogp(n)$.} By Definition~\ref{def:special-orthogonal-group}, $\SO(n) = \{g \in \Ogp(n) \mid \det g = 1\}$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:orth-equiv}, $\det g = \pm 1$ for every $g \in \Ogp(n)$, so for $g \in \Ogp(n)$ the conditions $\det g = 1$ and $\det g > 0$ are the same, and $\SO(n) = \Ogp(n) \cap \det^{-1}(0,\infty)$ is an open subset of $\Ogp(n)$: $\det$ is a polynomial in the entries, hence continuous on $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$, so $\det^{-1}(0,\infty)$ is open in $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$, and its intersection with $\Ogp(n)$ is open in the subspace topology. ($\det$ is continuous and takes only the values $\pm1$ on $\Ogp(n)$, so $\SO(n)$ is also closed: its complement in $\Ogp(n)$ is $\Ogp(n) \cap \det^{-1}(-\infty, 0)$, open by the same argument.)

\emph{$\SO(n)$ is a smooth manifold of dimension $\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$.} An open subset of a smooth $m$-manifold is a smooth $m$-manifold, its charts being restrictions of the given ones (Proposition~\ref{prop:open-smooth}). Here $M = \Ogp(n)$, a smooth manifold of dimension $m = \tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$ (Example~\ref{ex:On-smooth}), and $S = \SO(n)$ is open in it, as just shown; so $\SO(n)$ is a smooth manifold, and $\dim \SO(n) = m = \tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$.

\emph{$\Ogp(n)$ is compact.} Compactness of $\Ogp(n)$ was shown in Corollary~\ref{cor:grassmannian}: it is closed as $F^{-1}(I)$ with $F$ continuous, and bounded because every column of an orthogonal matrix is a unit vector. In detail: $F$ is smooth (Example~\ref{ex:On-smooth}), hence continuous, and the point $\{I\}$ is closed in $\Sym(n,\mathbb{R})$, so $\Ogp(n) = F^{-1}(I)$ is closed in $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R}) \cong \mathbb{R}^{n^2}$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:orth-equiv}(ii), $g^{\mathsf T} g = I$; its $(j,j)$ entry is
\[
1 = (g^{\mathsf T} g)_{jj} = \sum_{i=1}^n (g^{\mathsf T})_{ji}\, g_{ij} = \sum_{i=1}^n g_{ij}^2 ,
\]
which says that the $j$-th column is a unit vector. Hence $|g_{ij}| \le 1$ for all $i, j$, and $\|g\|^2 = \sum_{i,j} g_{ij}^2 = n$ in the norm of Definition~\ref{def:mat-euclid}, so $\Ogp(n)$ lies in the closed ball of radius $\sqrt n$. Closed and bounded in $\mathbb{R}^{n^2}$, it is compact by Heine--Borel (Proposition~\ref{fact:compact}(1)).
\end{proof}

\textbf{Transcription note.} Page 20 of the handwritten notes writes ``$\ker dF_g(A) = \{A \mid gA^{\mathsf T} + Ag^{\mathsf T} = 0\}$''; the kernel is of the linear map $dF_g$, and the ``$(A)$'' does not belong. The transposes sit to the right of $g$ throughout because that is how $F$ was written ($gg^{\mathsf T}$, not $g^{\mathsf T}g$); either convention defines $\Ogp(n)$.

The unitary group $\Ugp(n)$ is treated the same way, with $F(g) = gg^*$ mapping into the Hermitian matrices, in \S\ref{sub:un-smooth}. The analogue for $\SL(n,\mathbb{R})$ was Corollary~\ref{prop:SL-loc-euc}, which Proposition~\ref{prop:level-set-smooth} now upgrades from a topological to a smooth manifold.

\begin{rembox}[Where This Leaves Us]\label{rem:where-this-leaves-us}
Every level set met so far is now a smooth manifold: $\SL(n,\mathbb{R})$, $\Ogp(n)$, $\SO(n)$, the spheres, and any surface cut out by a regular value. What remains owed is the global half of the internal picture: a manifold defined abstractly, not sitting inside any $\mathbb{R}^N$, has no external description until one knows it can be embedded in a Euclidean space at all. That is Whitney's embedding theorem, later in the course.
\end{rembox}
