% SECTION: TRANSVERSALITY
% ============================================================================

\section{Transversality}\label{sec:transversality}\label{sub:transversality}

\roadmark{Stage: geometric}{When is the preimage of a regular level set again a regular level set? A condition that does not mention the defining map.}

\textit{Assignment 2, Problem 5. The problem ends with a parenthetical that is the point of the whole exercise: the transversality condition ``does not mention $G$ explicitly --- keep this in mind, for the future.''}

Throughout this section $F : \mathbb{R}^N \to \mathbb{R}^k$ and $G : \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^\ell$ are smooth, $0$ is a regular value of $G$, and
\[
S = G^{-1}(0) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^k ,
\]
a smooth manifold of dimension $k - \ell$ with $T^{\geo}_qS = \ker G'(q)$ for $q \in S$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel}). Its codimension, in the sense of the next definition, is $\operatorname{codim} S = k - \dim S = \ell$, the number of equations cutting it out.

\begin{defbox}[Codimension]\deflabel{def:codimension}
If $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^k$ is a manifold of dimension $s$ --- for instance a regular level set --- its \textbf{codimension} in $\mathbb{R}^k$ is $\operatorname{codim} S = k - s$.
\leeref{Ch.~5, \emph{Embedded Submanifolds}}
\end{defbox} (Everything below works verbatim with $F$ and $G$ defined only on open subsets.)

\begin{defbox}[Transversality]\deflabel{def:transverse}
$F$ is \textbf{transverse} to $S$, written $F \pitchfork S$, if
\[
\operatorname{im} F'(p) \;+\; T^{\geo}_{F(p)}S \;=\; \mathbb{R}^k \qquad \text{for every } p \in F^{-1}(S).
\]
The condition is imposed only at points of the preimage, and holds vacuously if $F^{-1}(S) = \emptyset$.
\end{defbox}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:tangent-7}
In words: at each point where $F$ meets $S$, the directions $F$ can move in, together with the directions along $S$, fill up the whole ambient space. The condition involves $F$ and $S$ only --- not the function $G$ used to cut $S$ out.
\end{rembox}

\begin{thmbox}[Preimages of Transverse Level Sets]\thmlabel{thm:transverse-preimage}
If $F \pitchfork S$, then $M = F^{-1}(S)$ is a smooth manifold of dimension $N - \ell$ (or empty), and for $p \in M$
\[
T^{\geo}_pM = F'(p)^{-1}\big(T^{\geo}_{F(p)}S\big) = \{\, v \in \mathbb{R}^N \mid F'(p)v \in T^{\geo}_{F(p)}S \,\}.
\]
In particular $\operatorname{codim} M = \operatorname{codim} S = \ell$.
\leeref{Theorem 6.30(a)}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=3em, column sep=3.6em]
M \arrow[r, hook] \arrow[d, "F|_M"'] & \mathbb{R}^N \arrow[d, "F"'] \arrow[dr, "G \circ F"] & \\
S \arrow[r, hook] & \mathbb{R}^k \arrow[r, "G"'] & \mathbb{R}^\ell
\end{tikzcd}
\\[1.2em]
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=3em, column sep=3.6em]
T^{\geo}_pM \arrow[r, hook] \arrow[d, "F'(p)|"'] & \mathbb{R}^N \arrow[d, "F'(p)"'] \arrow[dr, "(G \circ F)'(p)"] & \\
T^{\geo}_qS \arrow[r, hook] & \mathbb{R}^k \arrow[r, "G'(q)"'] & \mathbb{R}^\ell
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

Top, the spaces; bottom, their linearizations at $p$ and $q = F(p)$. In each, the square says the top-left corner is everything upstairs that lands in the bottom-left corner --- $M = F^{-1}(S)$ and $T^{\geo}_pM = F'(p)^{-1}(T^{\geo}_qS)$ --- and the triangle says the same set is cut out by the composite, $M = (G\circ F)^{-1}(0)$ and $T^{\geo}_pM = \ker (G\circ F)'(p)$. The theorem asserts that the preimage in the lower diagram is the geometric tangent space of the preimage in the upper one; Example~\ref{ex:transverse-failures}(b) shows this can fail without transversality.


\begin{proof}
If $M = \emptyset$ there is nothing to prove, so assume otherwise; then $S \neq \emptyset$ (a point $p \in M$ has $F(p) \in S$), and surjectivity of $G'(q) : \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^\ell$ at some $q \in S$ gives $k \ge \ell$ (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)). The plan: write $M$ as a level set of $G \circ F$, show $0$ is a regular value, and read off the dimension and the geometric tangent space from the regular value theorem and Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel}.

\emph{$M$ is a level set.} For $p \in \mathbb{R}^N$, by the definitions of preimage and of $S$,
\[
p \in F^{-1}(S) \iff F(p) \in G^{-1}(0) \iff G(F(p)) = 0 ,
\]
so $M = (G \circ F)^{-1}(0)$, with $G \circ F : \mathbb{R}^N \to \mathbb{R}^\ell$ smooth as a composite of smooth maps.

\emph{$0$ is a regular value of $G \circ F$.} Let $p \in M$ and $q = F(p) \in S$. By the chain rule $(G \circ F)'(p) = G'(q)\,F'(p)$. We show this is surjective. Given $w \in \mathbb{R}^\ell$, choose $u \in \mathbb{R}^k$ with $G'(q)u = w$, possible as $G'(q)$ is surjective ($0$ is a regular value of $G$ and $q \in G^{-1}(0)$). Transversality at $p$ (Definition~\ref{def:transverse}) says $\operatorname{im} F'(p) + T^{\geo}_qS = \mathbb{R}^k$, so we can write $u = F'(p)v + t$ with $v \in \mathbb{R}^N$ and $t \in T^{\geo}_qS = \ker G'(q)$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel} for $S$). Then, by linearity of $G'(q)$ and $G'(q)t = 0$,
\[
w = G'(q)u = G'(q)F'(p)v + G'(q)t = G'(q)F'(p)v ,
\]
so $w$ is in the image and $(G\circ F)'(p)$ is surjective. As $p \in M$ was arbitrary, $0$ is a regular value (Definition~\ref{def:regular-value}), and surjectivity at a point of $M$ forces $N \ge \ell$ (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)).

\emph{Conclusion.} By Theorem~\ref{thm:regular-value} and Proposition~\ref{prop:level-set-smooth}, applied to $G \circ F$ on $\mathbb{R}^N = \mathbb{R}^{(N-\ell)+\ell}$, $M$ is a smooth manifold of dimension $N - \ell$, so (Definition~\ref{def:codimension}) $\operatorname{codim} M = N - (N - \ell) = \ell = \operatorname{codim} S$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel} applied to $M = (G\circ F)^{-1}(0)$, then the chain rule, then the definition of the kernel, then Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel} for $S$,
\[
T^{\geo}_pM = \ker (G\circ F)'(p) = \ker\big(G'(q)F'(p)\big) = \{v \mid G'(q)\big(F'(p)v\big) = 0\} = \{v \mid F'(p)v \in \ker G'(q)\} = F'(p)^{-1}(T^{\geo}_qS). \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{lembox}[The Image of a Subspace Plus the Kernel]\thmlabel{lem:linear-image-subspace-plus-kernel}
Let $B : V \to Y$ be a linear map of vector spaces and $W \subseteq V$ a linear subspace of its domain. Then
\[
B(W + \ker B) = B(W).
\]
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture.)} Both inclusions are shown.
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\subseteq$: an element of the left side is $B(w + t)$ with $w \in W$ and $t \in \ker B$, and $B(w + t) = Bw + Bt = Bw$ by linearity and $Bt = 0$; so it lies in $B(W)$.
    \item $\supseteq$: $W \subseteq W + \ker B$ (take $t = 0$), so $B(W) \subseteq B(W + \ker B)$.
\end{itemize}
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[The Surjectivity Step as an Image Computation]\label{rem:transverse-image-computation}
\textit{(Not from lecture; the route of the official solution of Assignment~2, Problem~5.)} Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:linear-image-subspace-plus-kernel} with $B = G'(q)$ and $W = \operatorname{im} F'(p)$. Then $\ker G'(q) = T^{\geo}_qS$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel}), transversality says $\operatorname{im} F'(p) + T^{\geo}_qS = \mathbb{R}^k$, and
\[
\operatorname{im}\,(G \circ F)'(p) = G'(q)\big(\operatorname{im} F'(p)\big) = G'(q)\big(\operatorname{im} F'(p) + \ker G'(q)\big) = G'(q)\big(\mathbb{R}^k\big) = \mathbb{R}^\ell ,
\]
by the chain rule, the lemma, transversality, and surjectivity of $G'(q)$ ($0$ is a regular value of $G$ and $q \in G^{-1}(0)$). This is the lifting step of the proof in one line; it is used again in the second proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-submanifold-preimage}.
\end{rembox}

\textbf{Comparison with Lee.} Lee's Theorem~6.30 states this for a smooth map transverse to an \emph{embedded submanifold} $S \subseteq M$, after the theory of submanifolds (Chapter~5). The course's version, for level sets in Euclidean space, needs only the regular value theorem. It is the case where $S$ is cut out by a single global defining map $G$, and the proof --- pull $G$ back along $F$ --- is the one Lee uses locally.

\begin{propbox}[Transversality Is the Regular Value Condition]\thmlabel{prop:transverse-iff}
For $p \in F^{-1}(S)$ with $q = F(p)$,
\[
\operatorname{im} F'(p) + T^{\geo}_qS = \mathbb{R}^k \iff (G \circ F)'(p) \text{ is surjective.}
\]
Consequently $F \pitchfork S$ if and only if $0$ is a regular value of $G \circ F$.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
Throughout, $T^{\geo}_qS = \ker G'(q)$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel}) and $(G \circ F)'(p) = G'(q)F'(p)$ (chain rule).

($\Rightarrow$) is the middle step of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-preimage}, written out here at the single point $p$. Suppose $\operatorname{im} F'(p) + T^{\geo}_qS = \mathbb{R}^k$ and let $w \in \mathbb{R}^\ell$. Since $q \in S$ and $0$ is a regular value of $G$, $G'(q)$ is surjective, so $w = G'(q)u$ for some $u \in \mathbb{R}^k$. By the hypothesis, $u = F'(p)v + t$ with $v \in \mathbb{R}^N$ and $t \in \ker G'(q)$, and then
\[
w = G'(q)u = G'(q)F'(p)v + G'(q)t = G'(q)F'(p)v = (G\circ F)'(p)\,v ,
\]
so $(G \circ F)'(p)$ is surjective.

($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $G'(q)F'(p)$ is surjective and let $u \in \mathbb{R}^k$. Then $G'(q)u = G'(q)F'(p)v$ for some $v \in \mathbb{R}^N$, so by linearity $G'(q)\big(u - F'(p)v\big) = 0$, i.e.\ $u - F'(p)v \in \ker G'(q) = T^{\geo}_qS$, and
\[
u = F'(p)v + \big(u - F'(p)v\big) \in \operatorname{im} F'(p) + T^{\geo}_qS.
\]

\emph{Consequently.} $F \pitchfork S$ means the left condition holds at every $p \in F^{-1}(S)$ (Definition~\ref{def:transverse}); by the equivalence just proved, this says $(G\circ F)'(p)$ is surjective at every $p \in F^{-1}(S)$. Since $F^{-1}(S) = (G \circ F)^{-1}(0)$ (first step of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-preimage}), that is exactly the statement that $0$ is a regular value of $G \circ F$ (Definitions~\ref{def:regular-value} and~\ref{def:regular-point}).
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[An Intrinsic Statement with a Chosen Proof]\label{rem:intrinsic-statement-chosen-proof}
Proposition~\ref{prop:transverse-iff} is the precise content of the parenthetical. Transversality is not merely a sufficient condition: it \emph{is} the regular value condition for $G \circ F$, rewritten so that $G$ disappears. The hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-preimage} and both of its conclusions --- that $M$ is a manifold, and the formula for $T^{\geo}_pM$ --- involve only $F$ and $S$; only the proof picks a defining function $G$. This is the same pattern as for charts: a statement that does not depend on a choice, proved by making one. Two things remain for later. The smooth structure on $M$ is built through $G$, and its independence of $G$ is a statement about submanifolds. And $S$ need only be cut out by some $G$ \emph{near each point}, which will turn out to hold for every embedded submanifold, so the theorem localizes.
\end{rembox}

\begin{corbox}[The Regular Value Theorem as a Special Case]\thmlabel{cor:rvt-transverse}
Let $c \in \mathbb{R}^k$ and $S = \{c\}$. Then $F \pitchfork \{c\}$ if and only if $c$ is a regular value of $F$, and in that case Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-preimage} returns Theorem~\ref{thm:regular-value} together with $T^{\geo}_pM = \ker F'(p)$.
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
To apply the theorem we present $\{c\}$ as a regular level set. $\{c\} = G^{-1}(0)$ for $G(y) = y - c$, $G : \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^k$, since $y - c = 0 \iff y = c$. Its Jacobian is the identity, $G'(y) = I$ for every $y$, which is surjective, so $0$ is a regular value of $G$ with $\ell = k$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel}, $T^{\geo}_c\{c\} = \ker G'(c) = \ker I = 0$.

\emph{Transversality is the regular value condition.} With $T^{\geo}_{F(p)}S = 0$, the condition of Definition~\ref{def:transverse} at $p \in F^{-1}(c)$ reads
\[
\operatorname{im} F'(p) + 0 = \operatorname{im} F'(p) = \mathbb{R}^k ,
\]
i.e.\ $F'(p)$ is surjective. Transversality then reads $\operatorname{im} F'(p) = \mathbb{R}^k$ at every $p \in F^{-1}(c)$ --- the definition of a regular value (Definitions~\ref{def:regular-value} and~\ref{def:regular-point}).

\emph{The conclusions.} With $\ell = k$, Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-preimage} gives that $M = F^{-1}(c)$ is a smooth manifold of dimension $\dim M = N - k$ --- the conclusion of Theorem~\ref{thm:regular-value} with $N = n + k$ --- and
\[
T^{\geo}_pM = F'(p)^{-1}\big(T^{\geo}_c\{c\}\big) = F'(p)^{-1}(0) = \ker F'(p) .
\]
This is the description of Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel} for the regular level set $F^{-1}(c)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{defbox}[Transverse Intersection]\deflabel{def:transverse-intersection}
Regular level sets $S_1, S_2 \subseteq \mathbb{R}^k$ \textbf{intersect transversally} if
\[
T^{\geo}_qS_1 + T^{\geo}_qS_2 = \mathbb{R}^k \qquad\text{for every } q \in S_1 \cap S_2 ,
\]
a condition that holds vacuously when $S_1 \cap S_2 = \emptyset$.
\leeref{Theorem 6.30(b)}
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[Transverse Intersections]\thmlabel{prop:transverse-intersection}
Let $G_i : \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^{\ell_i}$, $i = 1,2$, be smooth with $0$ a regular value, and $S_i = G_i^{-1}(0)$. For $q \in S_1 \cap S_2$,
\[
T^{\geo}_qS_1 + T^{\geo}_qS_2 = \mathbb{R}^k \iff (G_1, G_2)'(q) : \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^{\ell_1 + \ell_2} \text{ is surjective.}
\]
If $S_1$ and $S_2$ intersect transversally (Definition~\ref{def:transverse-intersection}), then $S_1 \cap S_2$ is a smooth manifold with
\[
\operatorname{codim}(S_1 \cap S_2) = \operatorname{codim} S_1 + \operatorname{codim} S_2, \qquad T^{\geo}_q(S_1 \cap S_2) = T^{\geo}_qS_1 \cap T^{\geo}_qS_2 .
\]
\leeref{Theorem 6.30(b)}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
Write $T_i = T^{\geo}_qS_i = \ker G_i'(q)$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel}). Since $q \in S_i$ and $0$ is a regular value of $G_i$, $G_i'(q)$ is surjective, so by rank--nullity (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)) $T_i$ has dimension $k - \ell_i$. We show that both sides of the equivalence are the same condition on $\dim(T_1 \cap T_2)$.

\emph{The right side.} The rows of the Jacobian of $(G_1, G_2)$ are the gradients of the components (Definition~\ref{def:jacobian}): first those of $G_1$, then those of $G_2$. So the Jacobian is the stacked matrix $(G_1,G_2)'(q) = \begin{pmatrix} G_1'(q) \\ G_2'(q)\end{pmatrix}$, and $(G_1,G_2)'(q)v = \big(G_1'(q)v,\ G_2'(q)v\big)$. This is $0$ iff $G_1'(q)v = 0$ and $G_2'(q)v = 0$, so the kernel is $T_1 \cap T_2$. By rank--nullity,
\[
\dim \operatorname{im}\,(G_1,G_2)'(q) = k - \dim(T_1 \cap T_2) ,
\]
and the image is all of $\mathbb{R}^{\ell_1+\ell_2}$ iff its dimension is $\ell_1 + \ell_2$. So $(G_1,G_2)'(q)$ is surjective iff $\dim(T_1 \cap T_2) = k - \ell_1 - \ell_2$.

\emph{The left side.} On the other hand, by the dimension formula for a sum of two subspaces,
\[
\dim(T_1 + T_2) = \dim T_1 + \dim T_2 - \dim(T_1 \cap T_2) = (k - \ell_1) + (k - \ell_2) - \dim(T_1 \cap T_2),
\]
and the subspace $T_1 + T_2$ of $\mathbb{R}^k$ is all of $\mathbb{R}^k$ iff its dimension is $k$, which happens iff $\dim(T_1 \cap T_2) = k - \ell_1 - \ell_2$. The two conditions coincide.

\emph{The transverse intersection.} A point $q$ lies in $S_1 \cap S_2$ iff $G_1(q) = 0$ and $G_2(q) = 0$, iff $(G_1,G_2)(q) = 0$; so $S_1 \cap S_2 = (G_1,G_2)^{-1}(0)$. When the conditions hold throughout $S_1 \cap S_2$ (Definition~\ref{def:transverse-intersection}), the equivalence shows that $(G_1,G_2)'(q)$ is surjective at every point of this level set, i.e.\ the point $0$ is a regular value of $(G_1, G_2)$ (Definition~\ref{def:regular-value}). Theorem~\ref{thm:regular-value} with Proposition~\ref{prop:level-set-smooth} then makes $S_1 \cap S_2$ a smooth manifold of dimension $k - (\ell_1 + \ell_2)$, so by Definition~\ref{def:codimension}
\[
\operatorname{codim}(S_1 \cap S_2) = k - \big(k - \ell_1 - \ell_2\big) = \ell_1 + \ell_2 = \operatorname{codim} S_1 + \operatorname{codim} S_2 ,
\]
using $\operatorname{codim} S_i = k - (k - \ell_i) = \ell_i$. And Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel} gives the geometric tangent space $T^{\geo}_q(S_1 \cap S_2) = \ker(G_1,G_2)'(q) = T_1 \cap T_2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{exbox}[The Sphere and the Plane Re-read]\exlabel{ex:sphere-plane-transverse}
The figure in \S\ref{sub:regular-values} was a transversality picture. Let $S_1 = S^2$ and $S_2 = \{z = c\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$, so $T^{\geo}_qS_1 = q^\perp$ and $T^{\geo}_qS_2 = e_3^\perp$, the horizontal plane. Two planes through the origin in $\mathbb{R}^3$ sum to $\mathbb{R}^3$ iff they are distinct, so the intersection is transverse at $q$ iff $q^\perp \neq e_3^\perp$, i.e.\ iff $q \neq \pm e_3$ --- iff the two normals $q$ and $e_3$ are independent, which is what the figure's caption said in the language of gradients. \textit{(Computed; not from lecture.)} In the form of Proposition~\ref{prop:transverse-intersection}, cut out $S_1$ by $G_1(x,y,z) = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 1$ and $S_2$ by $G_2(x,y,z) = z - c$; at $q = (x,y,z)$ the stacked $2 \times 3$ Jacobian is
\[
(G_1, G_2)'(q) = \begin{pmatrix} G_1'(q) \\ G_2'(q) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2x & 2y & 2z \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix},
\]
whose $2 \times 2$ minors are $2x$, $2y$ (columns $1,3$ and $2,3$) and $0$ (columns $1,2$); so it has rank $2$ iff $(x,y) \neq (0,0)$, which on $S^2$ means $q \neq \pm e_3$.
\begin{itemize}
    \item $|c| < 1$: every point of $S_1 \cap S_2$ has $x^2 + y^2 = 1 - c^2 > 0$, so $q \neq \pm e_3$ and the intersection is transverse. Codimensions add, $1 + 1 = 2$, and $S_1 \cap S_2$ is a curve: the circle of radius $\sqrt{1-c^2}$.
    \item $c = \pm 1$: $S_1 \cap S_2 = \{\pm e_3\}$, where $T^{\geo}_qS_1 = T^{\geo}_qS_2$. Not transverse, and the intersection is a point rather than the predicted curve.
    \item $|c| > 1$: the intersection is empty, and transversality holds vacuously.
\end{itemize}
\end{exbox}

The sphere through the course: a topological manifold with hemisphere charts in Section~\ref{sec:ex-spheres}; the homogeneous space $\SO(3)/\SO(2)$ in Example~\ref{ex:s2-homogeneous}; the Riemann sphere $\mathbb{CP}^1$ in Proposition~\ref{prop:cp1-sphere}; its geometric tangent spaces in Example~\ref{ex:tangent-sphere} and its transverse intersection with a plane in Example~\ref{ex:sphere-plane-transverse}; the double cover $S^n \to \mathbb{RP}^n$ and the Hopf fibration $S^{2n+1} \to \mathbb{CP}^n$ in Section~\ref{sec:ex-hopf}; and $S^3 = \mathrm{SU}(2)$ in Proposition~\ref{prop:s3-su2}.


\begin{exbox}[Two Ways Transversality Can Fail]\exlabel{ex:transverse-failures}
Let $S$ be the $x$-axis in $\mathbb{R}^2$, cut out by $G(x,y) = y$, so $T^{\geo}_qS$ is the $x$-axis at every $q \in S$, and $\ell = 1$. For $F : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^2$ the theorem predicts $\dim F^{-1}(S) = 1 - 1 = 0$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(a)] $F(t) = (t, 0)$. Then $F^{-1}(S) = \mathbb{R}$, of dimension $1$: the \emph{dimension} is wrong. Here $\operatorname{im} F'(t)$ is the $x$-axis, so $\operatorname{im} F'(t) + T^{\geo}_{F(t)}S$ is the $x$-axis, not $\mathbb{R}^2$.
    \item[(b)] $F(t) = (t, t^2)$. Then $F^{-1}(S) = \{0\}$, which has the predicted dimension $0$; but $F'(0) = (1,0)$ lies in $T^{\geo}_0S$, so $F'(0)^{-1}(T^{\geo}_0S) = \mathbb{R}$, while the geometric tangent space of a point is $0$: the \emph{tangent formula} is wrong. Correspondingly $(G \circ F)(t) = t^2$ has $(G\circ F)'(0) = 0$, as Proposition~\ref{prop:transverse-iff} predicts. \textit{(Computed; not from lecture.)} As a product of Jacobians, with the $1 \times 2$ Jacobian $G'(x,y) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ of $G(x,y) = y$ and the $2 \times 1$ Jacobian $F'(t) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2t \end{pmatrix}$,
\[
(G \circ F)'(0) = G'(F(0))\,F'(0) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = 0 .
\]
    \item[(c)] $F(t) = (t, t^2 - \varepsilon)$ with $\varepsilon > 0$. Now $F^{-1}(S) = \{\pm\sqrt\varepsilon\}$, and at these points $F'(t) = (1, 2t)$ has nonzero second component, so $\operatorname{im} F'(t) + T^{\geo}_{F(t)}S = \mathbb{R}^2$: transverse, two points, and every conclusion of the theorem holds.
\end{enumerate}
\end{exbox}
