The same construction as a diagram: the curve is built downstairs as $c$ and lifted by $\varphi^{-1}$, and the triangle commutes, $\varphi \circ \gamma = c$.

Assignment~3's solution first treats the basis vectors $\partial/\partial x^i|_p$, using curves with $c'(0) = e_i$, and then the general case. The general argument contains the basis case, with $a = e_i$ and $c(t) = \varphi(p) + t\,e_i$, so it is presented here alone.

\begin{corbox}[Velocity of a Composite --- Computing Differentials by Curves]\thmlabel{cor:velocity-composite}
Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth and $\gamma$ a smooth curve in $M$ with $\gamma(0) = p$. Then $D_{F \circ \gamma} = F_{*p}(D_\gamma)$. Consequently, for every $D \in T_pM$,
\[
F_{*p}(D) = D_{F \circ \gamma} \qquad \text{for any smooth curve } \gamma \text{ with } \gamma(0) = p \text{ and } D_\gamma = D,
\]
and such a curve exists by Theorem~\ref{thm:every-vector-velocity}.
\leeref{Proposition 3.24 and Corollary 3.25}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\emph{The identity $D_{F \circ \gamma} = F_{*p}(D_\gamma)$.} The composite $F \circ \gamma : J \to N$ is a smooth curve (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}) with $(F \circ \gamma)(0) = F(p)$, so its velocity $D_{F \circ \gamma} \in T_{F(p)}N$ is defined. The Chain Rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}), applied to the maps $\gamma : J \to M$ and $F : M \to N$ at the point $0 \in J$, reads $(F \circ \gamma)_{*0} = F_{*\gamma(0)} \circ \gamma_{*0} = F_{*p} \circ \gamma_{*0}$. Hence, using Definition~\ref{def:velocity} at the first and last steps,
\[
D_{F \circ \gamma} = (F \circ \gamma)_{*0}\Big(\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_0\Big) = F_{*p}\Big(\gamma_{*0}\Big(\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_0\Big)\Big) = F_{*p}(D_\gamma) .
\]

\emph{Consequence.} Let $D \in T_pM$ and let $\gamma$ be any smooth curve with $\gamma(0) = p$ and $D_\gamma = D$; such a curve exists by Theorem~\ref{thm:every-vector-velocity}. Then, by the identity just proved, $F_{*p}(D) = F_{*p}(D_\gamma) = D_{F \circ \gamma}$.
\end{proof}

This is Lee's main computational tool: to find $F_{*p}(D)$, choose any curve with velocity $D$ and differentiate $F$ along it. It is the manifold version of Theorem~\ref{thm:vs-differential-curves}, and it is how Lee computes the differential of the determinant (Problem~7-4). \textit{(Computed; not from lecture.)} With $m = \dim M$, $n = \dim N$, charts $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$ at $p$ and $(V, \psi = (y^1, \ldots, y^n))$ at $F(p)$ with $F(U) \subseteq V$, and $F^j = y^j \circ F$, the coefficients of $D_\gamma$ and $D_{F \circ \gamma}$ are $(x^i \circ \gamma)'(0)$ and $(y^j \circ F \circ \gamma)'(0)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:velocity-coords}), and by Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix} the identity $D_{F \circ \gamma} = F_{*p}(D_\gamma)$ reads
\[
\begin{pmatrix} (y^1 \circ F \circ \gamma)'(0) \\ \vdots \\ (y^n \circ F \circ \gamma)'(0) \end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^m}(p) \\[2mm]
\vdots & & \vdots \\[1mm]
\dfrac{\partial F^n}{\partial x^1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^n}{\partial x^m}(p)
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} (x^1 \circ \gamma)'(0) \\ \vdots \\ (x^m \circ \gamma)'(0) \end{pmatrix} :
\]
the Jacobian carries the velocity of the coordinate curve $\varphi \circ \gamma$ to that of $\psi \circ F \circ \gamma$.

\begin{corbox}[Tangent Vectors as Classes of Curves]\thmlabel{cor:tangent-vectors-as-curve-classes}
Let $p \in M$, let $\gamma_1, \gamma_2$ be smooth curves in $M$ with $\gamma_1(0) = \gamma_2(0) = p$ (Definition~\ref{def:smooth-curve}), and let $(U, \varphi)$ be a chart at $p$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $D_{\gamma_1} = D_{\gamma_2}$ if and only if $(\varphi \circ \gamma_1)'(0) = (\varphi \circ \gamma_2)'(0)$. In particular the coordinate velocities agree in one chart at $p$ if and only if they agree in every chart at $p$.
    \item Write $\gamma_1 \sim \gamma_2$ when this holds. Then $\gamma \mapsto D_\gamma$ induces a bijection from the set of smooth curves through $p$, modulo $\sim$, onto $T_pM$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\emph{(1)} Let $x^1, \ldots, x^n$ be the coordinate functions of $\varphi$; the coordinate curves $\varphi \circ \gamma_k$ are defined near $0$, since $\gamma_k^{-1}(U)$ is open and contains $0$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:velocity-coords},
\[
D_{\gamma_k} = \sum_{j=1}^n \big(x^j \circ \gamma_k\big)'(0)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_p \qquad (k = 1, 2),
\]
and the $\partial/\partial x^j|_p$ form a basis of $T_pM$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}), so the coefficients in it are unique. Hence $D_{\gamma_1} = D_{\gamma_2}$ if and only if $(x^j \circ \gamma_1)'(0) = (x^j \circ \gamma_2)'(0)$ for every $j$, that is, $(\varphi \circ \gamma_1)'(0) = (\varphi \circ \gamma_2)'(0)$. The condition $D_{\gamma_1} = D_{\gamma_2}$ mentions no chart: if the coordinate velocities agree in one chart at $p$, then $D_{\gamma_1} = D_{\gamma_2}$, and so they agree in every chart at $p$.

\emph{(2)} By (1), $\gamma_1 \sim \gamma_2$ means $D_{\gamma_1} = D_{\gamma_2}$; so $\sim$ is an equivalence relation, and $[\gamma] \mapsto D_\gamma$ is well defined and injective on equivalence classes. It is surjective by Theorem~\ref{thm:every-vector-velocity}.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[The Two Faces Reconciled]\label{rem:two-faces-reconciled}
Theorem~\ref{thm:every-vector-velocity} says the map $\gamma \mapsto D_\gamma$, from smooth curves through $p$ to $T_pM$, is onto. By Proposition~\ref{prop:velocity-coords}, two curves have the same velocity exactly when their coordinate curves have the same velocity in one chart, and then in every chart. So (Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vectors-as-curve-classes}) $T_pM$ may equally be described as \emph{curves through $p$, modulo having the same velocity in coordinates} --- the intrinsic ``velocities of curves'' definition of the tangent space, now a theorem, on every manifold, with no ambient space. For a regular level set, the abstract velocity $D_\gamma$ is the derivation $D_{\gamma'(0)}$ attached to the geometric velocity $\gamma'(0) \in T^{\geo}_pM$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:Dv-properties}(2)). So the identification of Theorem~\ref{thm:ambient-abstract} is the statement that the two notions of velocity agree.
\end{rembox}

% ============================================================================
% Lecture 17 (Fri Oct 9, 2026): remark on tangent spaces
% ============================================================================

\begin{rembox}[From Lecture~17 On: One Tangent Space]\label{rem:identify-tangent-spaces}
\textit{Lecture~17.} For $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ the course built two tangent spaces at $p$: the geometric one, $T^{\geo}_pM \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$, a vector subspace consisting of the velocities $\gamma'(0)$ of curves $\gamma : (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \to M$ with $\gamma(0) = p$; and the abstract one, $T_pM$, the derivations of germs at $p$. The homework (Theorem~\ref{thm:every-vector-velocity}, Assignment~3, Problem~2) showed that every derivation is realized by a curve, $D = D_\gamma$, and $D_\gamma = D_{\gamma'(0)}$ (the remark \emph{The Two Faces Reconciled} above). So the two are identified,
\[
T^{\geo}_pM \;\cong\; T_pM, \qquad \gamma'(0) \longleftrightarrow D_\gamma ,
\]
and \emph{from now on the course always makes this identification without further notice}: for submanifolds of $\mathbb{R}^N$ the geometric tangent space may be used in computations, since it agrees with the abstract one. For a regular level set the precise statement is Theorem~\ref{thm:ambient-abstract}. Earlier chapters keep the notations $T^{\geo}_pM$ and $T_pM$ apart, and are left as they are.
\end{rembox}

\begin{rembox}[Review Session: The Two Definitions of $T_pM$]\label{rem:review-tangent-definitions}
\textit{Review session, Oct 16, on the characterizations of the tangent space.} There are only two, derivations and curves; the ambient one is essentially the same as curves. For a regular submanifold $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$, the ambient tangent space is $\{\, \tilde\gamma'(0) : \gamma : (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \to M,\ \gamma(0) = p \,\}$, where $\tilde\gamma = \iota \circ \gamma$ is $\gamma$ regarded as a curve in $\mathbb{R}^N$: the derivative $\tilde\gamma'(0)$ uses the vector space structure of the ambient space, through the difference quotient. ``Ambient'' is the course's own terminology, not used elsewhere, kept because it is pedagogically useful. On an abstract manifold, $T_pM$ is the space of derivations of germs. The bridge is the homework proposition: a curve $\gamma$ through $p$ defines a derivation, $D_\gamma[f] = \frac{d}{dt}\big|_{0} f(\gamma(t))$, the $\dot\gamma(0)$ of the lecture (Definition~\ref{def:velocity}), and every derivation arises this way (Theorem~\ref{thm:every-vector-velocity}); this is what identifies the two for $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ (the remark \emph{From Lecture~17 On: One Tangent Space}). Lee's order of definitions differs.
\end{rembox}

\subsection{Tangent Spaces of Products}\label{sub:tangent-products}

\textit{Lecture 11. There is a natural isomorphism --- natural meaning coordinate-free --- between the tangent space of a product and the direct sum of the tangent spaces of the factors. There are three ways to see it: by the inclusions of the factors, by curves, and in coordinates.}

Throughout, $m_i = \dim M_i$, $p = (p_1, p_2) \in M_1 \times M_2$, and $\iota_1 = \iota^{p_2} : M_1 \to M_1 \times M_2$, $\iota_2 = \iota^{p_1} : M_2 \to M_1 \times M_2$ are the slice inclusions through $p$ (Definition~\ref{def:slice-inclusions}).

\begin{thmbox}[The Tangent Space of a Product]\thmlabel{thm:tangent-product}
The linear map
\[
\Theta : T_{p_1}M_1 \oplus T_{p_2}M_2 \longrightarrow T_p(M_1 \times M_2), \qquad \Theta(v, w) = \iota_{1*}v + \iota_{2*}w,
\]
is an isomorphism, defined without charts, with inverse $\Psi(D) = (\pi_{1*}D, \pi_{2*}D)$. In particular $\iota_{1*}$ and $\iota_{2*}$ are injective, and $T_p(M_1 \times M_2)$ is the internal direct sum of their images, $\Theta\big(T_{p_1}M_1 \oplus \{0\}\big)$ and $\Theta\big(\{0\} \oplus T_{p_2}M_2\big)$.
\leeref{Proposition 3.14}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Stated in lecture, with the injectivity left as a check.)} To show: $\Theta$ is a linear bijection with inverse $\Psi$; then the two consequences in the last sentence.

\emph{The maps.} Since $\iota_1(p_1) = (p_1, p_2) = p$ and $\iota_2(p_2) = p$, the pushforwards are $\iota_{1*} = (\iota_1)_{*p_1} : T_{p_1}M_1 \to T_pM$ and $\iota_{2*} = (\iota_2)_{*p_2} : T_{p_2}M_2 \to T_pM$, where $M = M_1 \times M_2$; since $\pi_i(p) = p_i$, also $\pi_{i*} = (\pi_i)_{*p} : T_pM \to T_{p_i}M_i$. All four maps $\iota_i$, $\pi_i$ are smooth (Proposition~\ref{prop:product-maps}), so the four pushforwards are linear (Proposition~\ref{prop:pushforward-derivation}). Hence $\Theta(v, w) = \iota_{1*}v + \iota_{2*}w$ and $\Psi(D) = (\pi_{1*}D, \pi_{2*}D)$ are linear, with the componentwise operations of the direct sum (Definition~\ref{def:direct-sum}). They are built from pushforwards alone, so no chart is involved.

\emph{The pushforward along a constant map is zero.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:constant-pushforward}(1), if $\kappa : X \to Y$ is constant, then $\kappa_{*x} = 0$ for every $x \in X$: for every $D \in T_xX$ and every germ $[g]$ at the value of $\kappa$, $(\kappa_{*x}D)[g] = D[g \circ \kappa] = 0$, since $g \circ \kappa$ is constant and derivations kill constants.

\emph{Four identities.} For $q \in M_1$, $\pi_1(\iota_1(q)) = \pi_1(q, p_2) = q$ and $\pi_2(\iota_1(q)) = \pi_2(q, p_2) = p_2$; for $q \in M_2$, $\pi_2(\iota_2(q)) = \pi_2(p_1, q) = q$ and $\pi_1(\iota_2(q)) = p_1$. So $\pi_1 \circ \iota_1 = \mathrm{id}_{M_1}$ and $\pi_2 \circ \iota_2 = \mathrm{id}_{M_2}$, while $\pi_2 \circ \iota_1$ and $\pi_1 \circ \iota_2$ are constant. By the Chain Rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}), which also gives $(\mathrm{id})_* = \mathrm{id}$, and the previous step for the constant maps $\pi_2 \circ \iota_1$ and $\pi_1 \circ \iota_2$ --- that is, Lemma~\ref{lem:constant-pushforward}(2) with $F = \pi_2$, $\iota = \iota_1$ and with $F = \pi_1$, $\iota = \iota_2$ ---
\[
\pi_{1*}\iota_{1*} = \mathrm{id}, \qquad \pi_{2*}\iota_{2*} = \mathrm{id}, \qquad \pi_{2*}\iota_{1*} = 0, \qquad \pi_{1*}\iota_{2*} = 0 .
\]

\emph{$\Psi \circ \Theta = \mathrm{id}$.} For $(v, w) \in T_{p_1}M_1 \oplus T_{p_2}M_2$, by the linearity of $\pi_{1*}$ and $\pi_{2*}$ and the four identities,
\[
\Psi\big(\Theta(v, w)\big) = \big(\pi_{1*}\iota_{1*}v + \pi_{1*}\iota_{2*}w,\ \pi_{2*}\iota_{1*}v + \pi_{2*}\iota_{2*}w\big) = (v + 0,\ 0 + w) = (v, w) .
\]
So $\Theta$ is injective: if $\Theta(v, w) = 0$, then $(v, w) = \Psi(\Theta(v,w)) = \Psi(0) = 0$.

\emph{$\Theta$ is an isomorphism with inverse $\Psi$.} Both spaces have dimension $m_1 + m_2$: $\dim T_{p_i}M_i = m_i$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}), so $\dim(T_{p_1}M_1 \oplus T_{p_2}M_2) = m_1 + m_2$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:direct-sum}(2)); and $M_1 \times M_2$ has dimension $m_1 + m_2$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:product-manifold}), so $\dim T_p(M_1 \times M_2) = m_1 + m_2$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}). An injective linear map between spaces of the same finite dimension is bijective (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)). So $\Theta$ is an isomorphism, and composing $\Psi \circ \Theta = \mathrm{id}$ on the right with $\Theta^{-1}$ gives $\Psi = \Theta^{-1}$.

\emph{The last sentence.} $\iota_{1*}v = \iota_{1*}v + \iota_{2*}0 = \Theta(v, 0)$, and $\pi_{1*}\iota_{1*} = \mathrm{id}$, so $\iota_{1*}$ is injective (if $\iota_{1*}v = 0$ then $v = \pi_{1*}\iota_{1*}v = 0$); likewise $\iota_{2*}w = \Theta(0, w)$ and $\pi_{2*}\iota_{2*} = \mathrm{id}$ make $\iota_{2*}$ injective. So the images of $\iota_{1*}$ and $\iota_{2*}$ are $\Theta(T_{p_1}M_1 \oplus \{0\})$ and $\Theta(\{0\} \oplus T_{p_2}M_2)$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:direct-sum}(1), $T_{p_1}M_1 \oplus T_{p_2}M_2$ is the internal direct sum of $T_{p_1}M_1 \oplus \{0\}$ and $\{0\} \oplus T_{p_2}M_2$; carried across the isomorphism $\Theta$: every $D \in T_p(M_1 \times M_2)$ is $D = \Theta(\Psi D) = \Theta(v, 0) + \Theta(0, w)$ with $(v, w) = \Psi(D)$, and if also $D = \Theta(v', 0) + \Theta(0, w')$, then $\Theta(v, w) = \Theta(v', w')$ and injectivity gives $(v, w) = (v', w')$. So $T_p(M_1 \times M_2)$ is the internal direct sum of the two images (Definition~\ref{def:internal-direct-sum}).
\end{proof}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=4.6em, row sep=2.4em]
M_1 \arrow[r, shift left=0.8ex, "\iota_1"] & M_1 \times M_2 \arrow[l, shift left=0.8ex, "\pi_1"] \arrow[r, shift right=0.8ex, "\pi_2"'] & M_2 \arrow[l, shift right=0.8ex, "\iota_2"']
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad\qquad
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=4.6em]
T_{p_1}M_1 \oplus T_{p_2}M_2 \arrow[r, shift left=0.8ex, "\Theta"] & T_p(M_1 \times M_2) \arrow[l, shift left=0.8ex, "\Psi"]
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

The slice inclusions and the projections through $p$. The four identities $\pi_1 \iota_1 = \mathrm{id}$, $\pi_2 \iota_2 = \mathrm{id}$, and $\pi_2 \iota_1$, $\pi_1 \iota_2$ constant, pushed forward to tangent spaces, are the whole proof that $\Psi \circ \Theta = \mathrm{id}$.

\textbf{Partial derivatives in the $M_1$ variables.} For $v \in T_{p_1}M_1$ and a germ $[f]$ at $p$,
\[
(\iota_{1*}v)[f] = v\big[f \circ \iota_1\big], \qquad (f \circ \iota_1)(q) = f(q, p_2) :
\]
to push $v$ forward, restrict $f$ to the slice $M_1 \times \{p_2\}$ and differentiate there. So the first summand consists of derivations only with respect to the $M_1$ variables, with $p_2$ held fixed --- partial derivatives in the direction of $M_1$ --- and the second of partial derivatives in the direction of $M_2$.

\draw[gray!55, dashed] (2.30,1.65) -- (2.30,-0.65); \draw[gray!55, dashed] (2.25,1.70) -- (-0.65,1.70);
\fill[violet!75!black] (2.30,-0.65) circle (1.5pt) node[below, font=\scriptsize] {$p_1$}; \draw[->, very thick, violet!75!black] (2.30,-0.65) -- (3.30,-0.65) node[below, font=\scriptsize] {$v$};
\fill[teal!60!black] (-0.65,1.70) circle (1.5pt) node[left, font=\scriptsize] {$p_2$}; \draw[->, very thick, teal!60!black] (-0.65,1.70) -- (-0.65,2.45) node[left, font=\scriptsize] {$w$};
\node[font=\scriptsize, gray!70!black] at (2.50,-0.28) {$\pi_1$}; \node[font=\scriptsize, gray!70!black] at (-0.3,1.50) {$\pi_2$};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

The isomorphism in one picture. Through $p$ run the two slices, $M_1 \times \{p_2\}$ and $\{p_1\} \times M_2$. Pushing $v$ and $w$ forward along the slice inclusions gives tangent vectors along the slices, and every $D \in T_p(M_1 \times M_2)$ is uniquely their sum. The projections take $D$ back to $v$ and $w$: $\Psi(D) = (\pi_{1*}D, \pi_{2*}D) = (v, w)$.

\begin{corbox}[Product Coordinates]\thmlabel{cor:tangent-product-coords}
In product coordinates $(x^1, \ldots, x^{m_1}, y^1, \ldots, y^{m_2})$ at $p$,
\[
\iota_{1*}\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_{p_1}\Big) = \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p, \qquad \iota_{2*}\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial y^j}\Big|_{p_2}\Big) = \frac{\partial}{\partial y^j}\Big|_p .
\]
So the $\partial/\partial x^i|_p$ form a basis of the first summand and the $\partial/\partial y^j|_p$ a basis of the second.
\leeref{Proposition 3.14}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
Let $(U_1, \varphi_1 = (x^1, \ldots, x^{m_1}))$ be a chart of $M_1$ at $p_1$ and $(U_2, \varphi_2 = (y^1, \ldots, y^{m_2}))$ a chart of $M_2$ at $p_2$; the product chart $(U_1 \times U_2, \varphi_1 \times \varphi_2)$ has the coordinate functions $x^i \circ \pi_1$ and $y^j \circ \pi_2$, written again $x^i$ and $y^j$ (Definition~\ref{def:product-manifold}).

\emph{The first summand.} The slice inclusion $\iota_1$ maps $U_1$ into $U_1 \times U_2$, since $p_2 \in U_2$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:product-maps} its coordinate representation in the charts $\varphi_1$ and $\varphi_1 \times \varphi_2$ is $r \mapsto (r, \varphi_2(p_2))$ on $\varphi_1(U_1)$: its first $m_1$ components are $r \mapsto r^k$, and its last $m_2$ components are the constants $y^l(p_2)$. At $\varphi_1(p_1)$ the partial derivatives are $\partial r^k/\partial r^i = \delta^k_i$ and $0$ for the constants, so the Jacobian is
\[
\begin{pmatrix} I_{m_1} \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}
\qquad (\text{$m_1$ rows from the $x$'s, then $m_2$ rows from the $y$'s}).
\]
By Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix}, whose matrix entries are these Jacobian entries (Proposition~\ref{prop:upstairs-downstairs}), the $i$-th column says
\[
\iota_{1*}\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_{p_1}\Big) = \sum_{k=1}^{m_1} \delta^k_i\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^k}\Big|_p + \sum_{l=1}^{m_2} 0 \cdot \frac{\partial}{\partial y^l}\Big|_p = \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p .
\]

\emph{The second summand.} The slice inclusion $\iota_2$ maps $U_2$ into $U_1 \times U_2$, and by Proposition~\ref{prop:product-maps} its coordinate representation is $s \mapsto (\varphi_1(p_1), s)$ on $\varphi_2(U_2)$: the first $m_1$ components are the constants $x^k(p_1)$, the last $m_2$ are $s \mapsto s^l$. Its Jacobian at $\varphi_2(p_2)$ is $\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ I_{m_2} \end{pmatrix}$, and the $j$-th column says, by Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix},
\[
\iota_{2*}\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial y^j}\Big|_{p_2}\Big) = \sum_{k=1}^{m_1} 0 \cdot \frac{\partial}{\partial x^k}\Big|_p + \sum_{l=1}^{m_2} \delta^l_j\, \frac{\partial}{\partial y^l}\Big|_p = \frac{\partial}{\partial y^j}\Big|_p .
\]

\emph{The bases.} The $\partial/\partial x^i|_{p_1}$ form a basis of $T_{p_1}M_1$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}), and $\iota_{1*}$ is linear and injective (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-product}). An injective linear map carries a basis of its domain to a basis of its image (the images span the image, and a linear relation among them pulls back to one among the originals). So the $\partial/\partial x^i|_p = \iota_{1*}(\partial/\partial x^i|_{p_1})$ form a basis of the first summand $\iota_{1*}(T_{p_1}M_1)$; in the same way, with $\iota_{2*}$ and the basis $\partial/\partial y^j|_{p_2}$ of $T_{p_2}M_2$, the $\partial/\partial y^j|_p$ form a basis of the second summand. \textit{(Computed; not from lecture.)} Placing the two Jacobians side by side: in the basis $(\partial/\partial x^i|_{p_1}, 0), (0, \partial/\partial y^j|_{p_2})$ of $T_{p_1}M_1 \oplus T_{p_2}M_2$ and the product-coordinate basis of $T_p(M_1 \times M_2)$, the matrix of $\Theta(v, w) = \iota_{1*}v + \iota_{2*}w$ is
\[
\left(\begin{array}{c|c} I_{m_1} & 0 \\ \hline 0 & I_{m_2} \end{array}\right) = I_{m_1 + m_2},
\]
its first $m_1$ columns being the Jacobian of $\iota_1$ and its last $m_2$ columns that of $\iota_2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[Velocities of Curves in a Product]\thmlabel{cor:tangent-product-curves}
Let $\gamma = (\gamma_1, \gamma_2)$ be a smooth curve in $M_1 \times M_2$ with $\gamma(0) = p$. Then $\Psi(D_\gamma) = (D_{\gamma_1}, D_{\gamma_2})$, that is, $D_\gamma = \iota_{1*}D_{\gamma_1} + \iota_{2*}D_{\gamma_2}$. In particular, if $\gamma_2$ is constant --- a ``horizontal'' curve $\gamma(t) = (\gamma_1(t), p_2)$ --- then $D_\gamma = \iota_{1*}D_{\gamma_1}$ lies in the first summand.
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\emph{The components.} The components of $\gamma$ are $\gamma_i = \pi_i \circ \gamma$, smooth curves (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}) with $\gamma_i(0) = \pi_i(p) = p_i$. By Corollary~\ref{cor:velocity-composite}, applied to the smooth map $\pi_i : M_1 \times M_2 \to M_i$ and the curve $\gamma$,
\[
\pi_{i*}D_\gamma = D_{\pi_i \circ \gamma} = D_{\gamma_i} \qquad (i = 1, 2).
\]
So $\Psi(D_\gamma) = (\pi_{1*}D_\gamma, \pi_{2*}D_\gamma) = (D_{\gamma_1}, D_{\gamma_2})$. Applying $\Theta = \Psi^{-1}$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-product}),
\[
D_\gamma = \Theta\big(D_{\gamma_1}, D_{\gamma_2}\big) = \iota_{1*}D_{\gamma_1} + \iota_{2*}D_{\gamma_2} .
\]

\emph{Horizontal curves.} If $\gamma_2$ is constant, $\gamma_2(t) = p_2$, then $D_{\gamma_2} = (\gamma_2)_{*0}(d/dt|_0) = 0$ by Definition~\ref{def:velocity} and Lemma~\ref{lem:constant-pushforward}(1), the pushforward along the constant map $\gamma_2$ being $0$. Explicitly, for every germ $[g]$ at $p_2$, $D_{\gamma_2}[g] = \frac{d}{dt}\big|_{t=0}\, g(p_2) = 0$, the derivative of a constant. So $D_{\gamma_2} = 0$, and $D_\gamma = \iota_{1*}D_{\gamma_1} + \iota_{2*}0 = \iota_{1*}D_{\gamma_1}$ lies in the first summand.
\end{proof}

This is the second of the three views of the isomorphism, and it uses the velocities of Assignment~3, Problem~2 (Definition~\ref{def:velocity}).

% ============================================================================
% Lecture 18 (Mon Oct 12, 2026): partial differentiation
% ============================================================================

\textit{Lecture 18. Without this construction the proof that left-invariant fields are smooth (Proposition~\ref{prop:left-invariant-extension-smooth}) cannot be completed; the lecture opened with it to finish that proof. It is the partial derivative in the $M_1$ variables above, now with the base point in the other factor allowed to vary. From here to the end of the section the lettering is that of Lecture~18: the factors are $M$ and $N$, $p$ is a point of $M$ and no longer the point $(p_1, p_2)$ of the product, and $\varphi$ is a smooth function on $M \times N$, not a chart.}

\begin{defbox}[Partial Derivative in One Factor]\deflabel{def:partial-derivative-factor}
Let $\varphi : M \times N \to \mathbb{R}$ be smooth, $p \in M$ and $v \in T_pM$. The \textbf{partial derivative of $\varphi$ in the direction $v$} is the function $\partial_v\varphi : N \to \mathbb{R}$,
\[
\partial_v\varphi(q) = \Theta(v, 0)[\varphi] = (\iota^q_{*}v)[\varphi] = v\big[\varphi(\cdot, q)\big], \qquad q \in N,
\]
where $\Theta(v, 0) \in T_{(p,q)}(M \times N)$ is the vector $(v, 0)$ under $T_{(p,q)}(M \times N) = T_pM \oplus T_qN$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-product}), $0 \in T_qN$, and $\iota^q : M \to M \times N$, $x \mapsto (x, q)$, is the slice inclusion (Definition~\ref{def:slice-inclusions}). In the same way, for $w \in T_qN$, the partial derivative \textbf{in the second variable} is $\partial_w\varphi : M \to \mathbb{R}$, $\partial_w\varphi(p) = \Theta(0, w)[\varphi] = w\big[\varphi(p, \cdot)\big]$.
\end{defbox}

This notation is the course's own, not Lee's. The dependence on $q$ is hidden in the fact that the pair $(v, 0)$ is a tangent vector at $(p, q)$: the $0$ is the zero of $T_qN$, so the point at which $(v,0)$ sits moves with $q$. The three equal expressions in the definition are equal by the definition of $\Theta$ and of the pushforward (Definition~\ref{def:pushforward}): $\Theta(v, 0) = \iota^q_*v + \iota^p_*0 = \iota^q_*v$, and $(\iota^q_*v)[\varphi] = v[\varphi \circ \iota^q]$ with $(\varphi \circ \iota^q)(x) = \varphi(x, q)$.

\begin{propbox}[Partial Derivatives by Curves and in Coordinates]\thmlabel{prop:partial-derivative-factor}
Let $\varphi \in C^\infty(M \times N)$, $p \in M$ and $v \in T_pM$.
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item If $\gamma : (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \to M$ is a smooth curve \emph{adapted to $v$}, i.e.\ $\gamma(0) = p$ and $D_\gamma = v$, then for every $q \in N$
\[
\partial_v\varphi(q) = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} \varphi\big(\gamma(t), q\big).
\]
\item In charts $(x^1, \ldots, x^m)$ near $p$ and $(y^1, \ldots, y^n)$ near $q$, if $v = \sum_{j=1}^m v^j\, \partial/\partial x^j|_p$, then
\[
\partial_v\varphi(q) = \sum_{j=1}^m v^j\, \frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial x^j}(p, q) .
\]
\item $\partial_v\varphi \in C^\infty(N)$.
\end{enumerate}
The same holds in the second variable: for $w \in T_qN$, $\partial_w\varphi \in C^\infty(M)$.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~18, in the lecture's order: curves, then coordinates, from which smoothness is read off. Details filled in.)}

\emph{1. Curves.} The curve $t \mapsto (\gamma(t), q) = \iota^q(\gamma(t))$ is a horizontal curve, changing the first entry and not the second. By Definition~\ref{def:partial-derivative-factor} and Definition~\ref{def:velocity},
\[
\partial_v\varphi(q) = v[\varphi \circ \iota^q] = D_\gamma[\varphi \circ \iota^q] = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} (\varphi \circ \iota^q)(\gamma(t)) = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} \varphi\big(\gamma(t), q\big).
\]
Equivalently, $\Theta(v, 0)$ is the velocity of the horizontal curve (Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-product-curves}).

\emph{2. Coordinates.} The $x$ and the $y$ together form a coordinate chart of $M \times N$ (Definition~\ref{def:product-manifold}). By linearity of $\Theta$ and Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-product-coords}, $\Theta(v, 0) = \sum_j v^j\, \iota^q_*\big(\partial/\partial x^j|_p\big) = \sum_j v^j\, \partial/\partial x^j|_{(p,q)}$, and applying this to $\varphi$ gives the formula: $\partial_v\varphi$ just differentiates in the $x$ variables.

\emph{3. Smoothness.} The coordinate description makes it clear that this construction always gives a smooth function on $N$. \textit{(Filled in.)} Fix charts $(U, \phi_U = (x^j))$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V, \psi = (y^k))$ of $N$, and let $\hat\varphi(r, s) = \varphi\big(\phi_U^{-1}(r), \psi^{-1}(s)\big)$, a smooth function on $\phi_U(U) \times \psi(V)$, the coordinate representation of $\varphi$ in the product chart. By 2, for $q \in V$,
\[
\partial_v\varphi\big(\psi^{-1}(s)\big) = \sum_{j=1}^m v^j\, \frac{\partial\hat\varphi}{\partial r^j}\big(\phi_U(p), s\big), \qquad s \in \psi(V).
\]
Each $\partial\hat\varphi/\partial r^j$ is smooth, as a partial derivative of the smooth function $\hat\varphi$ --- by Lemma~\ref{lem:partials-smooth}, applied to $\varphi$ in the product chart on $U \times V$, it is the coordinate representation of the smooth function $\partial\varphi/\partial x^j$ --- and $s \mapsto (\phi_U(p), s)$ is smooth, so the right side is a smooth function of $s$: the coordinate representation of $\partial_v\varphi$ on $V$ is smooth. Charts $(V, \psi)$ cover $N$, so $\partial_v\varphi \in C^\infty(N)$. The second variable is the same with the factors exchanged.
\end{proof}

The picture of the definition: one horizontal curve through $(p, q)$ for each $q$, all with the same velocity $v$ in the $M$ direction. Differentiating $\varphi$ along each gives one number per $q$, and Proposition~\ref{prop:partial-derivative-factor}(3) says these numbers vary smoothly with $q$.

\textbf{Transcription note (Lecture 18).} Page~47 of the handwritten notes writes the splitting as ``$T_{(p,q)}(M \times N) = T_pM \oplus T_qM$'' (corrected in lecture); it is $T_pM \oplus T_qN$. The curves line has ``$\forall\, q \in M$'' for $q \in N$, and the coordinate formula sums to $n$ and evaluates at $q$; the sum runs to $m = \dim M$, and the partials are evaluated at $(p, q)$.

\section{The Cotangent Space}\label{sec:cotangent}

\roadmark{Stage: abstract, dual}{The cotangent space as the dual of the tangent space, and the differential of a function as a covector; in coordinates (\ref{sec:covector-coords}) and from germs alone (\ref{sec:cotangent-germs}) after this.}

% ============================================================================
% Lecture 10 (Wed Sep 23, 2026)
% ============================================================================
\subsection{Differentials of Functions and the Cotangent Space}\label{sub:cotangent}

\textit{Lecture 10: a very special and very important case. The target is $N = \mathbb{R}$, and the differential of a scalar function becomes a covector.}

The target $\mathbb{R}$ is itself a smooth manifold, so $f_{*p}$ lands in a tangent space of $\mathbb{R}$. The lecture disposed of these tangent spaces in one line --- each is identified with $\mathbb{R}$ once and for all --- and the next three boxes spell that line out: the chart and coordinate of $\mathbb{R}$, its coordinate derivation, and the identification.

\begin{defbox}[The Standard Coordinate on $\mathbb{R}$]\deflabel{def:standard-coordinate-R}
$\mathbb{R}$ is a smooth $1$-manifold, with the smooth structure of the single global chart $(\mathbb{R}, \mathrm{id}_\mathbb{R})$ (Definition~\ref{def:vs-structure}, with $X = \mathbb{R}$ and $L = \mathrm{id}_\mathbb{R}$). Its coordinate function (Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-functions}) is written $r$:
\[
r : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad r(t) = t .
\]
Because the chart is the identity, a smooth function $h$ on an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is its own coordinate representation: $h_{\mathrm{id}} = h \circ \mathrm{id}^{-1} = h$.
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[The Coordinate Derivation on $\mathbb{R}$]\deflabel{def:coordinate-derivation-R}
For $c \in \mathbb{R}$, $\partial/\partial r|_c \in T_c\mathbb{R}$ is the coordinate derivation (Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation}) of the chart $(\mathbb{R}, \mathrm{id}_\mathbb{R})$ at $c$. Since $h_{\mathrm{id}} = h$ (Definition~\ref{def:standard-coordinate-R}), it is the ordinary derivative at $c$:
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\Big|_c [h] = h'(c) \qquad \text{for every germ } [h] \text{ at } c .
\]
In particular $\partial/\partial r|_c\,[r] = r'(c) = 1$.
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[The Tangent Spaces of $\mathbb{R}$]\thmlabel{prop:tangent-space-R}
Let $c \in \mathbb{R}$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $T_c\mathbb{R}$ is one-dimensional, with basis $\{\partial/\partial r|_c\}$.
    \item Every $v \in T_c\mathbb{R}$ is $v = v[r]\,\partial/\partial r|_c$: its coefficient on the basis vector is its value on the coordinate function $r$.
    \item The map $\iota_c : T_c\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $\iota_c(v) = v[r]$, is a linear isomorphism, with $\iota_c\big(a\,\partial/\partial r|_c\big) = a$ for $a \in \mathbb{R}$ and inverse $a \mapsto a\,\partial/\partial r|_c$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} (1) and (2) are the Basis Theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}) for the chart $(\mathbb{R}, \mathrm{id}_\mathbb{R})$, with $n = 1$ and $x^1 = r$; (2) is its universal formula. (3) $\iota_c$ is linear because the vector-space operations of $T_c\mathbb{R}$ are pointwise on germs (Definition~\ref{def:abstract-tangent}): $(v + w)[r] = v[r] + w[r]$ and $(av)[r] = a\,v[r]$. By Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation-R}, $\iota_c(a\,\partial/\partial r|_c) = a \cdot 1 = a$, so $\iota_c$ is surjective, and $a \mapsto a\,\partial/\partial r|_c$ is a right inverse; it is also a left inverse by (2), $v = \iota_c(v)\,\partial/\partial r|_c$.
\end{proof}

\begin{defbox}[The Standard Identification of $T_c\mathbb{R}$ with $\mathbb{R}$]\deflabel{def:identification-TR}
For every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, $T_c\mathbb{R}$ is identified with $\mathbb{R}$ by the isomorphism $\iota_c$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:tangent-space-R}:
\[
T_c\mathbb{R} \xrightarrow{\ \iota_c\ } \mathbb{R}, \qquad a\,\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\Big|_c \longmapsto a, \qquad \text{equivalently} \quad v \longmapsto v[r] .
\]
\end{defbox}

Concretely, $a\,\partial/\partial r|_c$ is the derivation $h \mapsto a\,h'(c)$: differentiation at $c$ at speed $a$, the velocity of the curve $t \mapsto c + at$. The identification records the speed $a$ and forgets the base point $c$; this is why it can be made for all $c$ at once.


\begin{defbox}[Cotangent Space]\deflabel{def:cotangent}
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $p \in M$. The \textbf{cotangent space} of $M$ at $p$ is the dual of the abstract tangent space,
\[
T_p^*M = (T_pM)^* .
\]
\leeref{Ch.~11, \emph{Covectors}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[The Differential of a Function]\deflabel{def:differential-function}
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $p \in M$, and let $f : M \to \mathbb{R}$ be smooth (or defined and smooth only near $p$). Its pushforward at $p$ (Definition~\ref{def:pushforward}) is a linear map into the tangent space of $\mathbb{R}$ at the point $f(p)$:
\[
f_{*p} : T_pM \longrightarrow T_{f(p)}\mathbb{R}, \qquad \big(f_{*p}D\big)[h] = D[\,h \circ f\,] .
\]
The \textbf{differential} of $f$ at $p$ is this map followed by the standard identification $\iota_{f(p)} : T_{f(p)}\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ (Definition~\ref{def:identification-TR}):
\[
df_p = \iota_{f(p)} \circ f_{*p} : T_pM \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}, \qquad df_p(D) = \big(f_{*p}D\big)[r] .
\]
So $df_p(D)$ is the coefficient of $f_{*p}D$ on the basis vector $\partial/\partial r|_{f(p)}$ of $T_{f(p)}\mathbb{R}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:tangent-space-R}): $f_{*p}D = df_p(D)\,\partial/\partial r|_{f(p)}$. As a composite of linear maps, $df_p$ is linear, so $df_p \in T_p^*M$, the cotangent space of Definition~\ref{def:cotangent}. Proposition~\ref{prop:df-derivation} computes it: $df_p(D) = D[f]$.
\leeref{Ch.~11, \emph{Covectors}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=4.4em, row sep=2.6em]
T_pM \arrow[r, "f_{*p}"] \arrow[rr, bend right=22, "df_p"'] & T_{f(p)}\mathbb{R} \arrow[r, "\iota_{f(p)}", "\cong"'] & \mathbb{R}
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

The differential of a function is its pushforward followed by the permanent identification of every tangent space of $\mathbb{R}$ with $\mathbb{R}$; so $df_p$ is the pushforward $f_{*p}$ under another name. The notation $T_p^*M$ puts the star on the $T$, as a shorthand for $(T_pM)^*$.

\begin{propbox}[The Differential Evaluates Derivations]\thmlabel{prop:df-derivation}
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, $p \in M$, and $f$ a smooth function defined near $p$. For every $D \in T_pM$, $\ df_p(D) = D[f]$. In particular $df_p\big(\partial/\partial x^j|_p\big) = \partial f/\partial x^j(p)$ in any chart.
\leeref{Ch.~11, \emph{Covectors}}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
By Definition~\ref{def:differential-function} and the definition of the pushforward (Definition~\ref{def:pushforward}), $df_p(D) = (f_{*p}D)[r] = D[r \circ f] = D[f]$, since $r \circ f = f$ ($r$ is the identity of $\mathbb{R}$, Definition~\ref{def:standard-coordinate-R}). For $D = \partial/\partial x^j|_p$ this is $\partial/\partial x^j|_p\,[f] = \partial f/\partial x^j(p)$ (Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation}).
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[Properties of the Differential of a Function]\thmlabel{cor:df-properties}
Let $f, g$ be smooth near $p$ and $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \emph{Linearity:} $d(af + bg)_p = a\,df_p + b\,dg_p$.
    \item \emph{Product rule:} $d(fg)_p = f(p)\,dg_p + g(p)\,df_p$.
    \item \emph{Chain rule:} if $h$ is smooth on an open interval containing the values of $f$ near $p$, then $d(h \circ f)_p = h'(f(p))\,df_p$.
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Proposition 11.20}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} All three are equalities in $T_p^*M = (T_pM)^*$ (Definition~\ref{def:cotangent}), whose elements are functions on $T_pM$; two of them are equal when they take the same value at every $D \in T_pM$, and sums and scalar multiples in a dual space are taken pointwise, $(a\alpha + b\beta)(D) = a\,\alpha(D) + b\,\beta(D)$ (Definition~\ref{def:dual}). So fix $D \in T_pM$. Each step below uses one of: Proposition~\ref{prop:df-derivation}, $dk_p(D) = D[k]$ for any $k$ smooth near $p$; the algebra operations on germs (Proposition~\ref{prop:germ-algebra}), $[af + bg] = a[f] + b[g]$ and $[fg] = [f][g]$; and the two defining properties of the derivation $D$ (Definition~\ref{def:derivation}).

\emph{(1)} By $\mathbb{R}$-linearity of $D$:
\[
d(af + bg)_p(D) = D\big[af + bg\big] = D\big(a[f] + b[g]\big) = a\,D[f] + b\,D[g] = a\,df_p(D) + b\,dg_p(D) = \big(a\,df_p + b\,dg_p\big)(D).
\]

\emph{(2)} By the Leibniz rule $D([f][g]) = f(p)\,D[g] + g(p)\,D[f]$, applied to the germs $[f]$ and $[g]$:
\[
d(fg)_p(D) = D\big[fg\big] = D\big([f][g]\big) = f(p)\,D[g] + g(p)\,D[f] = f(p)\,dg_p(D) + g(p)\,df_p(D) = \big(f(p)\,dg_p + g(p)\,df_p\big)(D).
\]
Here $f(p)$ and $g(p)$ are numbers, the values of the germs at $p$, so the right side is a linear combination of the covectors $dg_p$ and $df_p$.

\emph{(3)} The composite $h \circ f$ is smooth near $p$, and $h$ is smooth near $f(p)$, so $[h]$ is a germ at $f(p)$ on $\mathbb{R}$. By the definition of the pushforward (Definition~\ref{def:pushforward}), $D[h \circ f] = (f_{*p}D)[h]$. By Definition~\ref{def:differential-function}, $f_{*p}D = df_p(D)\,\partial/\partial r|_{f(p)}$; this is an equality of derivations at $f(p)$, so both sides take the same value on $[h]$. With Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation-R}:
\[
d(h \circ f)_p(D) = D[h \circ f] = (f_{*p}D)[h] = df_p(D)\,\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\Big|_{f(p)}[h] = df_p(D)\,h'(f(p)) = \big(h'(f(p))\,df_p\big)(D).
\]
Since $D$ was arbitrary, the three identities hold in $T_p^*M$.
\end{proof}

% ============================================================================
% SECTION: COVECTORS IN COORDINATES
% ============================================================================

\section{Covectors in Coordinates}\label{sec:covector-coords}

\roadmark{Stage: abstract, dual}{In a chart, the differentials $dx^i|_p$ of the coordinate functions form the basis of $T_p^*M$ dual to the coordinate derivations, and a covector is determined by its components.}

\textit{Lecture 10, continued. The cotangent space and the differential of a function were defined in \ref{sec:cotangent} without coordinates; a chart now gives $T_p^*M$ a basis, and every covector components.}

\begin{lembox}[The Differential of a Function in Coordinates]\thmlabel{lem:df-coords}
Let $(x^1, \ldots, x^m)$ be coordinates near $p$, and write $dx^i|_p$ for the differential at $p$ of the coordinate function $x^i$. Then $\{dx^1|_p, \ldots, dx^m|_p\}$ is the dual basis of $\{\partial/\partial x^1|_p, \ldots, \partial/\partial x^m|_p\}$, so $\dim T_p^*M = m$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:dual-basis}), and for every smooth $f$ defined near $p$,
\[
df_p = \sum_{i=1}^m \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^i}(p)\, dx^i\big|_p .
\]
\leeref{Ch.~11, \emph{Covectors}}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~10: it suffices to check the identity on basis vectors. In lecture the left side came from the matrix of $f_{*p}$ (Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix}), a $1 \times m$ row --- gradients go across --- whose $j$-th entry is $\partial f/\partial x^j(p)$. Proposition~\ref{prop:df-derivation} gives the same value directly.)}

\emph{Step 1: the $dx^i|_p$ are the dual basis.} Let $\varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^m)$ be the chart, so that $x^i \circ \varphi^{-1} = r^i$, the $i$-th standard coordinate of $\mathbb{R}^m$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:coordinate-functions-own-chart}). For each $i$ and $j$, Proposition~\ref{prop:df-derivation} with $f = x^i$ and $D = \partial/\partial x^j|_p$, followed by Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation}, gives
\[
dx^i|_p\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_p\Big) = \frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_p\big[x^i\big] = \frac{\partial (x^i \circ \varphi^{-1})}{\partial r^j}\big(\varphi(p)\big) = \frac{\partial r^i}{\partial r^j}\big(\varphi(p)\big) = \delta^i_j .
\]
This is the defining property of the dual basis (Definition~\ref{def:dual-basis}) of the basis $\{\partial/\partial x^j|_p\}$ of $T_pM$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}). By Proposition~\ref{prop:dual-basis} the $dx^i|_p$ form a basis of $T_p^*M$, and $\dim T_p^*M = m$.

\emph{Step 2: the formula.} Both sides are linear functionals on $T_pM$, so by Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(2) it suffices that they agree on each basis vector $\partial/\partial x^j|_p$. The left side gives, by Proposition~\ref{prop:df-derivation},
\[
df_p\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_p\Big) = \frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_p[f] = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^j}(p) .
\]
The right side is a linear combination of covectors, evaluated pointwise (Definition~\ref{def:dual}); by Step 1 only the term $i = j$ survives:
\[
\Big(\sum_{i=1}^m \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^i}(p)\, dx^i\big|_p\Big)\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_p\Big) = \sum_{i=1}^m \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^i}(p)\, dx^i\big|_p\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_p\Big) = \sum_{i=1}^m \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^i}(p)\, \delta^i_j = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^j}(p) .
\]
The two values agree for every $j$, so the two covectors are equal.
\end{proof}

\begin{defbox}[Components of a Covector]\deflabel{def:covector-components}
Let $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$ be a chart at $p$ and $\xi \in T_p^*M$. The \textbf{components} of $\xi$ in the chart are the numbers
\[
\xi_i = \xi\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p\Big), \qquad i = 1, \ldots, m,
\]
the values of $\xi$ on the coordinate basis of $T_pM$. They are the covector counterpart of the components $v^i = v[x^i]$ of a tangent vector $v \in T_pM$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}). The letters $\xi$ and $\xi_i$ are used for a covector and its components from here on, as in the coordinates $(x^1, \ldots, x^m, \xi_1, \ldots, \xi_m)$ of $T^*M$ (\ref{sub:cotangent-bundle}).
\end{defbox}

\begin{corbox}[Covectors in the Dual Basis]\thmlabel{cor:covector-components}
In a chart $(x^1, \ldots, x^m)$ near $p$, every covector $\xi \in T_p^*M$ is the combination of the dual basis $dx^1|_p, \ldots, dx^m|_p$ whose coefficients are its components (Definition~\ref{def:covector-components}):
\[
\xi = \sum_{j=1}^m \xi_j\, dx^j\big|_p, \qquad \xi_j = \xi\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_p\Big),
\]
and these are the only coefficients for which the expansion holds.
\leeref{Ch.~11, \emph{Covectors}}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~15 recalled the basis $dx^j|_p$ and read off the components by evaluation.)} Two things are claimed: the expansion, and the uniqueness of its coefficients.

\emph{The expansion.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:df-coords}, $(dx^1|_p, \ldots, dx^m|_p)$ is the dual basis (Definition~\ref{def:dual-basis}) of the basis $(\partial/\partial x^1|_p, \ldots, \partial/\partial x^m|_p)$ of $T_pM$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}). So the second formula of Proposition~\ref{prop:dual-basis} applies, with $V = T_pM$, $e_j = \partial/\partial x^j|_p$, $\varepsilon^j = dx^j|_p$ and $\lambda = \xi$; with Definition~\ref{def:covector-components} it reads
\[
\xi = \sum_{j=1}^m \xi\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_p\Big)\, dx^j\big|_p = \sum_{j=1}^m \xi_j\, dx^j\big|_p .
\]

\emph{Uniqueness.} By the same proposition the $dx^j|_p$ form a basis of $T_p^*M$, so the coefficients are unique. Explicitly: if $\xi = \sum_j c_j\, dx^j|_p$, evaluate both sides at $\partial/\partial x^k|_p$, using that covectors are added and scaled pointwise (Definition~\ref{def:dual}) and that $dx^j|_p(\partial/\partial x^k|_p) = \delta^j_k$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:df-coords}):
\[
\xi_k = \xi\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^k}\Big|_p\Big) = \sum_{j=1}^m c_j\, dx^j\big|_p\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^k}\Big|_p\Big) = \sum_{j=1}^m c_j\, \delta^j_k = c_k .
\]
So the coefficients are the components, $c_k = \xi_k$.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:cotangent}
The formula of Lemma~\ref{lem:df-coords} can also be read off from Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix}: with the coordinate $r$ on the target, the matrix of $f_{*p}$ is the $1 \times m$ row
\[
\Big( \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^1}(p) \ \ \cdots \ \ \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^m}(p) \Big).
\]
The matrix is $1 \times m$, not $m \times 1$ --- gradients go across --- since the target is one-dimensional. The lecture's proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:df-coords} took this route; the proof given for the lemma goes through Proposition~\ref{prop:df-derivation} instead, where the shape of the matrix does not arise.
\end{rembox}

The differential as a covector, for $f(x,y) = y + 0.3x^2$ near $p = (0.8, 0)$. Left: level curves of $f$ at equal spacing $\Delta$, and a tangent vector $v$ at $p$. Right: in $T_pM$, the level lines of the linear functional $df_p$ at the same spacing --- the linearization of the curves on the left, straight and parallel. The value $df_p(v)$ counts, in units of $\Delta$, how many lines $v$ crosses: here exactly $2\Delta$, since $v$ ends on the line $df_p = 2\Delta$. On the left, $v$ crosses \emph{approximately} two level curves; the curvature is what the linearization discards.

\begin{rembox}[Differential --- Not Gradient]\label{rem:differential-not-gradient}
The formula $df = \sum \partial f/\partial x^i\,dx^i$ of multivariable calculus is now a statement about covectors: the $dx^i|_p$ are not infinitesimals but the dual basis of the coordinate derivations, the coefficients are numbers, and the dual basis extracts the components of a vector in the original basis. What does \emph{not} survive on a manifold is the gradient. A function on $M$ has no gradient \emph{vector} --- converting $df_p$ into a vector requires an inner product on $T_pM$, i.e.\ a Riemannian metric --- but it always has its differential $df_p \in T_p^*M$, and that is where differentials of scalar functions live. Differential forms, later in the term, will be built from covectors, and will pull back as naturally as germs do. Tangent vectors, written $D$ while thought of as derivations, will soon be written $v$. On $\mathbb{R}^n$ there is such an inner product, the dot product: Definition~\ref{def:gradient} and Proposition~\ref{prop:dot-product-identification} below make the conversion between the gradient and the differential precise. They are used later, for Lagrange multipliers (Theorem~\ref{thm:lagrange-multipliers}) and for the normal bundle (\ref{sec:normal-bundle}).
\end{rembox}

\textit{Not from lecture: the gradient of calculus, used informally since \ref{sec:rvt}, and the dot-product identification of vectors with covectors on open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$, which turns the gradient into the differential.}

\begin{defbox}[Gradient]\deflabel{def:gradient}
Let $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be open, $p \in U$, and $h$ a smooth function defined near $p$. The \textbf{gradient} of $h$ at $p$ is the vector of its ordinary partial derivatives,
\[
\nabla h(p) = \Big( \frac{\partial h}{\partial r^1}(p), \ldots, \frac{\partial h}{\partial r^n}(p) \Big) \in \mathbb{R}^n ,
\]
the single row of the Jacobian of $h$ at $p$ (Definition~\ref{def:jacobian}), read as a vector of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Each $\partial h/\partial r^i(p)$ is also the coordinate derivation $\partial/\partial r^i|_p[h]$ of the identity chart (Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation}), in which $h$ is its own coordinate representation.
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[Vectors as Covectors through the Dot Product]\thmlabel{prop:dot-product-identification}
Let $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be open and $p \in U$, with $T_pU = T_p\mathbb{R}^n$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:germs-local}), and for $w \in \mathbb{R}^n$ let $D_w|_p \in T_p\mathbb{R}^n$ be the directional derivative of Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs}. For $v \in \mathbb{R}^n$ define $\xi_v : T_pU \to \mathbb{R}$ by
\[
\xi_v\big(D_w|_p\big) = v \cdot w \qquad (w \in \mathbb{R}^n).
\]
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\xi_v \in T_p^*U$, and $\mathbb{R}^n \to T_p^*U$, $v \mapsto \xi_v$, is a linear isomorphism.
    \item In the identity chart, with coordinates $r^1, \ldots, r^n$, $\xi_v = \sum_{i=1}^n v^i\, dr^i|_p$: the components of $\xi_v$ are the entries of $v$.
    \item For $h$ smooth near $p$, $\xi_{\nabla h(p)} = dh_p$ (Definition~\ref{def:gradient}). That is, $dh_p(D_w|_p) = \nabla h(p) \cdot w$ for every $w \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and the components of $dh_p$ in the identity chart are the entries of $\nabla h(p)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} Two facts about the vectors $D_w|_p$ are used throughout. By Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs}, with $V = \mathbb{R}^n$ and $a = p$, the map $w \mapsto D_w|_p$ is a linear isomorphism $\mathbb{R}^n \to T_p\mathbb{R}^n$, so every tangent vector at $p$ is $D_w|_p$ for exactly one $w \in \mathbb{R}^n$. And by Proposition~\ref{prop:differential-agree} (its second statement, with $W = U$ and $a = p$), $D_w|_p[g] = \frac{d}{dt}\big|_{t=0}\, g(p + tw) = \sum_i w^i\, \partial g/\partial r^i(p)$ for every germ $[g]$ at $p$, the partial derivatives being the coordinate derivations of the identity chart; two derivations that agree on every germ are equal, so
\[
D_w|_p = \sum_{i=1}^n w^i\, \frac{\partial}{\partial r^i}\Big|_p, \qquad\text{in particular}\qquad D_{e_i}|_p = \frac{\partial}{\partial r^i}\Big|_p .
\]

\emph{(1) $\xi_v$ is a covector.} $\xi_v$ is the composite of the inverse isomorphism $T_p\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$, $D_w|_p \mapsto w$, with the linear map $w \mapsto v \cdot w$; so it is well defined and linear, $\xi_v \in T_p^*U$ (Definition~\ref{def:cotangent}).

\emph{(1) Linearity in $v$.} For $v, v' \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$, at every $D_w|_p$, by the bilinearity of the dot product and the pointwise operations of $T_p^*U$ (Definition~\ref{def:dual}),
\[
\xi_{av + bv'}\big(D_w|_p\big) = (av + bv') \cdot w = a\, v \cdot w + b\, v' \cdot w = \big(a\,\xi_v + b\,\xi_{v'}\big)\big(D_w|_p\big) .
\]
Every tangent vector at $p$ is some $D_w|_p$, so $\xi_{av + bv'} = a\,\xi_v + b\,\xi_{v'}$.

\emph{(1) Isomorphism.} If $\xi_v = 0$, then $0 = \xi_v(D_v|_p) = v \cdot v = |v|^2$, so $v = 0$: the map is injective. Both spaces have dimension $n$: $\mathbb{R}^n$, and $T_p^*U$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:df-coords} in the identity chart. An injective linear map between spaces of the same finite dimension is bijective (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)), so $v \mapsto \xi_v$ is a linear isomorphism: the dot product identifies vectors with covectors.

\emph{(2)} By $D_{e_i}|_p = \partial/\partial r^i|_p$, the components of $\xi_v$ (Definition~\ref{def:covector-components}) are
\[
\xi_v\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial r^i}\Big|_p\Big) = \xi_v\big(D_{e_i}|_p\big) = v \cdot e_i = v^i ,
\]
and Corollary~\ref{cor:covector-components}, in the identity chart, gives $\xi_v = \sum_i v^i\, dr^i|_p$.

\emph{(3)} Let $w \in \mathbb{R}^n$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:df-derivation}, the formula for $D_w|_p$ above (derivations are added and scaled pointwise, Definition~\ref{def:abstract-tangent}), and Definition~\ref{def:gradient},
\[
dh_p\big(D_w|_p\big) = D_w|_p[h] = \sum_{i=1}^n w^i\, \frac{\partial}{\partial r^i}\Big|_p[h] = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial h}{\partial r^i}(p)\, w^i = \nabla h(p) \cdot w = \xi_{\nabla h(p)}\big(D_w|_p\big) .
\]
The covectors $dh_p$ and $\xi_{\nabla h(p)}$ agree at every $D_w|_p$, that is, at every tangent vector at $p$, so they are equal. By (2), the components of $dh_p = \xi_{\nabla h(p)}$ are the entries $\partial h/\partial r^i(p)$ of $\nabla h(p)$ --- which is also Lemma~\ref{lem:df-coords} in the identity chart, $dh_p = \sum_i \partial h/\partial r^i(p)\, dr^i|_p$.
\end{proof}

% SECTION: THE COTANGENT SPACE FROM GERMS
% ============================================================================

\section{The Cotangent Space from Germs}\label{sec:cotangent-germs}\label{sub:cotangent-germs}

\roadmark{Stage: abstract, dual}{The cotangent space recovered from germs alone, $T_p^*M \cong I_p/I_p^2$, with no dualizing; covectors then pull back along smooth maps, as germs do.}

\textit{Assignment 3, Problem 3. The cotangent space was defined in Lecture 10 as the dual $(T_pM)^*$. This section shows that it also has a description with no dualizing at all, in terms of germs alone: the natural definition $I_p/I_p^2$. The proof splits into four results: a characterization of $I_p^2$, a basis of the quotient, a non-degenerate pairing, and the isomorphism, which then comes from the Linear Algebra Toolkit for free.}

\begin{defbox}[The Space $I_p/I_p^2$]\deflabel{def:Ip-quotient}
$I_p/I_p^2$ is the quotient vector space (Definition~\ref{def:quotient-vs}) of $I_p$ by its subspace $I_p^2$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:Ip-subspaces}). The class of $[f] \in I_p$ is written $[[f]] = [f] + I_p^2$, and $[[f]] = [[f']]$ iff $[f'] - [f] \in I_p^2$.
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[Germs Vanishing to Second Order]\thmlabel{prop:second-order}
For $[f] \in C_p^\infty(M)$ the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $[f] \in I_p^2$;
    \item $f(p) = 0$ and $df_p = 0$;
    \item $f(p) = 0$ and $\partial f/\partial x^i(p) = 0$ for all $i$, in one --- hence every --- chart at $p$.
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Problem 11-4(a)}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\emph{(2)$\iff$(3).} Both conditions contain $f(p) = 0$; compare the rest. By Lemma~\ref{lem:df-coords}, in any chart at $p$,
\[
df_p = \sum_{i=1}^m \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^i}(p)\, dx^i\big|_p ,
\]
and the $dx^i|_p$ are linearly independent, so this combination is $0$ exactly when every coefficient is $0$: $df_p = 0 \iff \partial f/\partial x^i(p) = 0$ for all $i$. Condition (2) mentions no chart, so (3) in one chart gives (2), which gives (3) in every chart --- which is why ``one'' chart implies ``every''.

\emph{(1)$\Rightarrow$(2).} Let $[f] \in I_p^2$, so $[f] = \sum_k [u_k][w_k]$ with all $[u_k], [w_k] \in I_p$ (Definition~\ref{def:Ip-square}), i.e.\ $u_k(p) = w_k(p) = 0$. Evaluation at $p$ is an algebra homomorphism (Proposition~\ref{prop:germ-algebra}), so $f(p) = \sum_k u_k(p)\, w_k(p) = 0$. For $D \in T_pM$, by Proposition~\ref{prop:df-derivation}, the linearity of $D$, and its Leibniz rule (Definition~\ref{def:derivation}),
\[
df_p(D) = D[f] = \sum_k D\big([u_k][w_k]\big) = \sum_k \big(u_k(p)\, D[w_k] + w_k(p)\, D[u_k]\big) = \sum_k \big(0 \cdot D[w_k] + 0 \cdot D[u_k]\big) = 0 .
\]
This holds for every $D$, so $df_p = 0$. (The middle steps are Lemma~\ref{lem:derivation-properties}(2).)

\emph{(3)$\Rightarrow$(1).} \textit{(Assignment 3, Problem 3.)} Fix a chart $(U,\varphi)$ at $p$, a representative $f : V \to \mathbb{R}$, and put $a = \varphi(p)$ and $f_\varphi = f \circ \varphi^{-1}$. The hypotheses say $f_\varphi(a) = f(p) = 0$ and $\partial f_\varphi/\partial r^i(a) = \partial f/\partial x^i(p) = 0$ (Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation}). On an open ball $B \subseteq \varphi(U \cap V)$ centred at $a$, Hadamard's lemma (Lemma~\ref{lem:hadamard}) gives smooth $f_i$ on $B$ with $f_\varphi(r) = f_\varphi(a) + \sum_i (r^i - a^i) f_i(r)$; here the constant term $f_\varphi(a)$ is $0$, so
\[
f_\varphi(r) = \sum_{i=1}^m (r^i - a^i)\, f_i(r) \quad (r \in B), \qquad f_i(a) = \frac{\partial f_\varphi}{\partial r^i}(a) = 0 .
\]
On the open neighbourhood $W = \varphi^{-1}(B)$ of $p$, substitute $r = \varphi(q)$; then $r^i = x^i(q)$, $a^i = x^i(p)$ and $f_\varphi(\varphi(q)) = f(q)$, so
\[
f(q) = \sum_{i=1}^m \big(x^i(q) - x^i(p)\big)\,(f_i \circ \varphi)(q) \qquad (q \in W).
\]
Two functions that agree on a neighbourhood of $p$ have the same germ, so $[f] = \sum_i [x^i - x^i(p)]\,[f_i \circ \varphi]$. In each term both factors lie in $I_p$: $x^i(p) - x^i(p) = 0$, and $(f_i \circ \varphi)(p) = f_i(a) = 0$. So $[f]$ is a finite sum of products of two elements of $I_p$, that is, $[f] \in I_p^2$ (Definition~\ref{def:Ip-square}).
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[First and Second Order Vanishing]\label{rem:cotangent-2}
The proposition is the conceptual centre of Problem~3. $I_p$ consists of the germs vanishing to \emph{first} order at $p$, and $I_p^2$ of those vanishing to \emph{second} order --- value and first derivatives zero. So the quotient $I_p/I_p^2$ remembers exactly the first derivatives of a germ that vanishes at $p$, and nothing else. It only needs first-order Hadamard: the vanishing of $f_i(a)$ is what puts the second factor in $I_p$.
\end{rembox}

\begin{propbox}[A Basis of $I_p/I_p^2$]\thmlabel{prop:ideal-basis}
Let $(U, \varphi)$ be a chart at $p$ with coordinate functions $x^1, \ldots, x^m$. For every $[f] \in I_p$,
\[
[[f]] = \sum_{i=1}^m \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^i}(p)\, [[x^i - x^i(p)]],
\]
and the classes $[[x^1 - x^1(p)]], \ldots, [[x^m - x^m(p)]]$ form a basis of $I_p/I_p^2$. In particular $\dim I_p/I_p^2 = m$.
\leeref{cf.\ Problem 11-4(a)}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
Each $x^i - x^i(p)$ is smooth on $U$ and vanishes at $p$, so its germ lies in $I_p$. Two facts about partial derivatives at $p$ are used. They are linear, since $\partial/\partial x^j|_p$ is a derivation (Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation}, Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}); and
\[
\frac{\partial\big(x^i - x^i(p)\big)}{\partial x^j}(p) = \frac{\partial x^i}{\partial x^j}(p) - 0 = \delta^i_j ,
\]
because a derivation kills constants (Lemma~\ref{lem:derivation-properties}(1)) and $\partial x^i/\partial x^j(p) = dx^i|_p(\partial/\partial x^j|_p) = \delta^i_j$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:df-derivation}, then Lemma~\ref{lem:df-coords}: the $dx^i|_p$ are the basis dual to the $\partial/\partial x^j|_p$, Definition~\ref{def:dual-basis}).

\emph{The expansion.} Let $[f] \in I_p$, write $c_i = \partial f/\partial x^i(p)$, and put $g = f - \sum_i c_i\,(x^i - x^i(p))$ near $p$. Then $g(p) = f(p) - \sum_i c_i \cdot 0 = 0$, and for each $j$
\[
\frac{\partial g}{\partial x^j}(p) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^j}(p) - \sum_{i=1}^m c_i\, \delta^i_j = c_j - c_j = 0 .
\]
By Proposition~\ref{prop:second-order} ((3)$\Rightarrow$(1)), $[g] \in I_p^2$, that is, $[[g]] = 0$. The projection $[f] \mapsto [[f]]$ is linear (Proposition~\ref{prop:quotient-vs}(1)), so from $[f] = [g] + \sum_i c_i\,[x^i - x^i(p)]$,
\[
[[f]] = [[g]] + \sum_{i=1}^m c_i\, [[x^i - x^i(p)]] = \sum_{i=1}^m \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^i}(p)\, [[x^i - x^i(p)]] .
\]

\emph{Spanning.} Every element of $I_p/I_p^2$ is a class $[[f]]$ with $[f] \in I_p$, so by the expansion the classes $[[x^i - x^i(p)]]$ span.

\emph{Independence.} Suppose $\sum_i c_i\,[[x^i - x^i(p)]] = 0$. By linearity of the projection, the germ $[h] = \sum_i c_i\,[x^i - x^i(p)]$ has $[[h]] = 0$, i.e.\ $[h] \in I_p^2$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:second-order} ((1)$\Rightarrow$(3)), $\partial h/\partial x^j(p) = 0$ for every $j$; and by the two facts above, $\partial h/\partial x^j(p) = \sum_i c_i\, \delta^i_j = c_j$. So every $c_j = 0$.

So the $m$ classes form a basis, and $\dim I_p/I_p^2 = m$.
\end{proof}

This is the cotangent counterpart of the basis theorem for $T_pM$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}): the coefficients of $[[f]]$ are the first partials of $f$, just as the coefficients of a derivation $D$ were its values $D[x^i]$.

\begin{defbox}[The Pairing Between Tangent Vectors and $I_p/I_p^2$]\deflabel{def:cotangent-pairing}
The \textbf{pairing} of $T_pM$ with $I_p/I_p^2$ is
\[
\langle\ ,\ \rangle : T_pM \times I_p/I_p^2 \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad \langle D, [[f]] \rangle = D[f] .
\]
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[The Pairing Is Well Defined and Non-Degenerate]\thmlabel{prop:cotangent-pairing}
The pairing of Definition~\ref{def:cotangent-pairing} is well defined, bilinear, and non-degenerate in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:non-degenerate-pairing}.
\leeref{no counterpart; Lee proves Problem 11-4(b) without a pairing}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Well defined} \textit{(Problem~3(a))}. The value $\langle D, [[f]] \rangle = D[f]$ must not depend on the representative $[f]$ of the class. If $[[f]] = [[f']]$, then $[f'] - [f] \in I_p^2$ (Definition~\ref{def:Ip-quotient}), say $[f'] - [f] = \sum_k [u_k][w_k]$ with $[u_k], [w_k] \in I_p$. By the linearity and the Leibniz rule of $D$ (Definition~\ref{def:derivation}),
\[
D[f'] - D[f] = D\big([f'] - [f]\big) = \sum_k \big(u_k(p)\, D[w_k] + w_k(p)\, D[u_k]\big) = 0,
\]
since $u_k(p) = w_k(p) = 0$. (Equivalently: $D$ restricted to $I_p$ is linear and vanishes on $I_p^2$, Lemma~\ref{lem:derivation-properties}(2), so it descends to $I_p/I_p^2$ by the universal property of quotient spaces, Proposition~\ref{prop:quotient-vs}(2).)

\emph{Bilinear.} In the second argument, by the quotient operations (Definition~\ref{def:quotient-vs}) and the linearity of $D$:
\[
\big\langle D,\ a[[f]] + b[[g]] \big\rangle = \big\langle D, [[af + bg]] \big\rangle = D[af + bg] = a\,D[f] + b\,D[g] = a\,\langle D, [[f]] \rangle + b\,\langle D, [[g]] \rangle .
\]
In the first argument, because derivations are added and scaled pointwise (Definition~\ref{def:abstract-tangent}):
\[
\big\langle aD + bE,\ [[f]] \big\rangle = (aD + bE)[f] = a\,D[f] + b\,E[f] = a\,\langle D, [[f]] \rangle + b\,\langle E, [[f]] \rangle .
\]

\emph{Left non-degenerate.} Suppose $\langle D, [[f]] \rangle = D[f] = 0$ for every $[f] \in I_p$. Let $[f] \in C_p^\infty(M)$ be any germ. Then $[f] - \underline{f(p)} \in I_p$, since it vanishes at $p$, and $D$ kills the constant germ $\underline{f(p)}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:derivation-properties}(1)); so
\[
D[f] = D\big[f - \underline{f(p)}\big] + D\big[\underline{f(p)}\big] = 0 + 0 = 0 .
\]
So $D$ vanishes on all germs: $D = 0$.

\emph{Right non-degenerate.} Suppose $[f] \in I_p$ and $\langle D, [[f]] \rangle = D[f] = 0$ for every $D \in T_pM$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:df-derivation}, $df_p(D) = D[f] = 0$ for every $D$, so $df_p = 0$; and $f(p) = 0$ since $[f] \in I_p$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:second-order} ((2)$\Rightarrow$(1)), $[f] \in I_p^2$, that is, $[[f]] = 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{thmbox}[The Cotangent Space from Germs]\thmlabel{thm:cotangent-ideal}
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The pairing induces isomorphisms
    \[
    T_pM \xrightarrow{\ \cong\ } \big(I_p/I_p^2\big)^*, \qquad\qquad \Phi : I_p/I_p^2 \xrightarrow{\ \cong\ } (T_pM)^* = T_p^*M .
    \]
    \item $\Phi([[f]]) = df_p$: the isomorphism sends the class of a germ to its differential.
    \item In any chart, $\Phi$ carries the basis $[[x^i - x^i(p)]]$ of $I_p/I_p^2$ to the basis $dx^i|_p$ of $T_p^*M$, which is dual to the basis $\partial/\partial x^i|_p$ of $T_pM$.
\end{enumerate}
The isomorphisms are defined without any chart.
\leeref{Problem 11-4(b), with global functions in place of germs (see the comparison below)}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\emph{(1)} Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:pairing} with $V = T_pM$, $W = I_p/I_p^2$ and $B = \langle\ ,\ \rangle$. Its hypotheses hold: the pairing is bilinear and non-degenerate (Proposition~\ref{prop:cotangent-pairing}), and $T_pM$ is finite-dimensional, of dimension $m$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}). So the two induced maps of Definition~\ref{def:pairing},
\[
B^\flat : T_pM \to \big(I_p/I_p^2\big)^*, \ \ D \mapsto \langle D, \cdot\,\rangle, \qquad\qquad \Phi = B^\sharp : I_p/I_p^2 \to (T_pM)^*, \ \ [[f]] \mapsto \langle \cdot\,, [[f]] \rangle,
\]
are isomorphisms.

\emph{(2)} For every $D \in T_pM$, by the definition of $\Phi$, the definition of the pairing, and Proposition~\ref{prop:df-derivation},
\[
\Phi([[f]])(D) = \langle D, [[f]] \rangle = D[f] = df_p(D) .
\]
The covectors $\Phi([[f]])$ and $df_p$ agree at every $D$, so they are equal.

\emph{(3)} By (2) and the linearity of $d$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:df-properties}(1)), applied to $x^i$ and the constant function $x^i(p)$,
\[
\Phi\big([[x^i - x^i(p)]]\big) = d\big(x^i - x^i(p)\big)_p = dx^i|_p - d\big(x^i(p)\big)_p = dx^i|_p ,
\]
because the differential of a constant function $c$ is $0$: by Definition~\ref{def:differential-function}, $dc_p = \iota_c \circ c_{*p}$, and $c_{*p} = 0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:constant-pushforward}(1), $c$ being a constant map $M \to \mathbb{R}$. Directly, $dc_p(D) = D[\underline{c}] = 0$ for every $D$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:df-derivation}, Lemma~\ref{lem:derivation-properties}(1)). The $dx^i|_p$ are the basis dual to the $\partial/\partial x^i|_p$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:df-coords}.

\emph{No chart.} The pairing $\langle D, [[f]] \rangle = D[f]$ is defined without coordinates, and so are $B^\flat$ and $\Phi$, which are built from it alone; a chart enters only in (3), to name the bases.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[The Most Natural Description]\label{rem:cotangent-natural}
\textit{Lecture~15, coming back to this theorem; and the review session of Oct 16, recalling this homework problem.} From the point of view of functions, the cotangent space is the more natural of the two. The tangent space needed derivations; the cotangent space needs only functions --- germs vanishing at $p$, modulo those vanishing to second order. $I_p$, the germs vanishing at $p$, is an ideal, and $T_p^*M \cong I_p/I_p^2$ naturally, with nothing about curves and nothing about ambient spaces --- a general and short description, with a one-page definition. This is one reason why the cotangent bundle will turn out to carry structure that the tangent bundle does not: the cotangent bundle carries a symplectic structure with no choices made.
\end{rembox}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.4em, column sep=3.6em]
I_p/I_p^2 \arrow[r, "\Phi", "\cong"'] & T_p^*M \arrow[r, dash, "\text{dual to}"] & T_pM \\
{[[f]]} \arrow[r, mapsto] & df_p & \\
{[[x^i - x^i(p)]]} \arrow[r, mapsto] & dx^i|_p \arrow[r, leftrightarrow, "\text{dual}"] & \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

The three spaces and their three bases. $\Phi$ sends the class of a germ to its differential, so the coordinate classes go to the coordinate covectors, and those are the dual basis of the coordinate derivations. The $dx^i|_p$ of Lecture 10 and the classes $[[x^i - x^i(p)]]$ of Problem~3 are the same objects, seen through $\Phi$.

\begin{thmbox}[Dimension of the Cotangent Space]\thmlabel{thm:cotangent-dimension}
Let $M$ be a smooth $m$-manifold and $p \in M$. Then
\[
\dim T_p^*M \;=\; \dim \big(I_p/I_p^2\big) \;=\; \dim T_pM \;=\; m .
\]
The cotangent space has the same dimension as the tangent space, at every point.
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Collected from the results above; not stated as a single theorem in lecture.)} $T_p^*M = (T_pM)^*$ is the dual of a space of dimension $m$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-dimension}), and the dual of a finite-dimensional space has the same dimension (Proposition~\ref{prop:dual-basis}); explicitly, the $m$ covectors $dx^i|_p$ form a basis (Lemma~\ref{lem:df-coords}). And $I_p/I_p^2$ has the basis of $m$ classes $[[x^i - x^i(p)]]$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:ideal-basis}), or equivalently is isomorphic to $T_p^*M$ by $\Phi$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:cotangent-ideal}).
\end{proof}

Equal dimension is what makes the isomorphisms of Theorem~\ref{thm:cotangent-ideal} possible, but the dimension count alone does not produce them: any two spaces of dimension $m$ are isomorphic, by choosing bases. What Theorem~\ref{thm:cotangent-ideal} adds is that $\Phi$ needs no choice. Between $T_pM$ and $T_p^*M$ themselves there is no such choice-free isomorphism, which is why the tangent and cotangent bundles are isomorphic, but not naturally (\ref{sub:cotangent-bundle}).

\textbf{Assignment 3, Problem 3.} Part (a) is the well-definedness in Proposition~\ref{prop:cotangent-pairing}. Part (b) is its non-degeneracy, and the ``therefore'' of (b) is Theorem~\ref{thm:pairing}, which uses \emph{both} halves: right non-degeneracy bounds $\dim I_p/I_p^2 \le m$, left non-degeneracy gives $m \le \dim I_p/I_p^2$. The submitted solution reaches the isomorphism by another route: it shows $\Phi$ injective by right non-degeneracy and surjective by checking that $\Phi([[x^i - x^i(p)]])$ is the dual basis --- which is part (3) of the theorem.

\textbf{Comparison with Lee.} In the text of Chapter~11, Lee defines the cotangent space as the dual $(T_pM)^*$, motivated as the coordinate-independent replacement for the gradient. The description of this section is his Problem~11-4. Part~(a) is Proposition~\ref{prop:second-order}, down to the phrase ``vanishes to second order'', and part~(b) is Theorem~\ref{thm:cotangent-ideal}(1)--(2). There are two differences. First, Lee's $I_p$ consists of smooth functions on all of $M$ vanishing at $p$, not germs, so his version needs bump functions to pass between local and global, as everywhere in his treatment (Proposition~\ref{prop:germ-global}). Second, Lee proves the isomorphism directly, showing that $f \mapsto df_p$ vanishes on $I_p^2$ and descends to the quotient, where Assignment~3 goes through a non-degenerate pairing and the pairing theorem. His remark to the problem adds two points: some treatments define $T_p^*M$ first, as $I_p/I_p^2$, and then $T_pM$ as its dual --- in some ways the more natural order --- and covectors, as classes of functions $M \to \mathbb{R}$, are dual to tangent vectors as classes of curves $\mathbb{R} \to M$ (his Problem~3-8; here Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vectors-as-curve-classes}). The quotient $I_p/I_p^2$ is also the manifold analogue of the Zariski cotangent space of algebraic geometry.
