% SECTION: TRANSVERSALITY AND LAGRANGE MULTIPLIERS
% ============================================================================

\section{Transversality and Lagrange Multipliers}\label{sec:transversality-submanifolds}

\roadmark{Stage: submanifolds}{Preimages of transverse submanifolds are submanifolds; normal and conormal spaces, critical points of restrictions, Lagrange multipliers, and transverse intersections.}

\textit{Assignment~5, Problem~2.} \ref{sec:transversality} treated transversality in Euclidean space: a smooth map $F : \mathbb{R}^N \to \mathbb{R}^k$ transverse to a regular level set $S = G^{-1}(0)$ (Definition~\ref{def:transverse}) pulls $S$ back to a manifold of the same codimension, with $T^{\geo}_pF^{-1}(S) = F'(p)^{-1}(T^{\geo}_{F(p)}S)$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-preimage}). That proof needed a global defining map $G$. With regular submanifolds and their adapted charts, the same statement holds for any smooth map between manifolds and any regular submanifold of the target --- an adapted chart supplies a defining map $x_b$ near each point, which is the localization announced in the remark \emph{An Intrinsic Statement with a Chosen Proof} in \ref{sec:transversality}.

\begin{defbox}[Transversality to a Submanifold]\deflabel{def:transverse-submanifold}
Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth, $S \subseteq N$ a regular submanifold, and $\iota : S \to N$ the inclusion. For $p \in F^{-1}(S)$, $F$ is \textbf{transverse to $S$ at $p$} if
\[
F_{*p}\big(T_pM\big) + \iota_{*F(p)}\big(T_{F(p)}S\big) = T_{F(p)}N ,
\]
the sum of two subspaces of $T_{F(p)}N$; and $F$ is \textbf{transverse to $S$}, written $F \pitchfork S$, if it is transverse to $S$ at every $p \in F^{-1}(S)$. Here $T_qS$ is regarded as a subspace of $T_qN$ through the injective map $\iota_{*q}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-tangent}). The condition is imposed only at points of the preimage, and holds vacuously if $F^{-1}(S) = \emptyset$.
\leeref{Ch.~6, \emph{Transversality}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{thmbox}[Preimages of Transverse Submanifolds]\thmlabel{thm:transverse-submanifold-preimage}
Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth, with $\dim M = m$ and $\dim N = n$, let $S \subseteq N$ be a regular submanifold of codimension $k$, and suppose $F \pitchfork S$ (Definition~\ref{def:transverse-submanifold}). Let $\iota : S \to N$ and $j : F^{-1}(S) \to M$ be the inclusions.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $F^{-1}(S)$ is a regular submanifold of $M$ of codimension $k$, the codimension of $S$ in $N$ (possibly empty). If it is nonempty, then $k \le m$ and $\dim F^{-1}(S) = m - k$.
    \item For every $p \in F^{-1}(S)$,
    \[
    j_{*p}\big(T_pF^{-1}(S)\big) = (F_{*p})^{-1}\big(\iota_{*F(p)}(T_{F(p)}S)\big) = \big\{\, v \in T_pM : F_{*p}v \in \iota_{*F(p)}(T_{F(p)}S) \,\big\} .
    \]
\end{enumerate}
Identifying the tangent spaces of the two submanifolds with their images (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-tangent}), (2) reads $T_pF^{-1}(S) = F_{*p}^{-1}\big(T_{F(p)}S\big)$, the formula of Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-preimage}.
\leeref{Theorem 6.30(a)}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~5, Problem~2; the student's route, with two steps completed --- the normal form is applied at a single point, and the kernel of $(x_b)_{*q}$ is computed directly, without the regular value theorem.)} \textit{(The two completions are now separate statements, Proposition~\ref{prop:adapted-defining-map} and Lemma~\ref{lem:rvt-local}, which Steps~2, 6 and~7 and part~(2) below cite; the details are written out in their proofs.)} For (1) we must produce, at every $p \in F^{-1}(S)$, a smooth chart of $M$ adapted to $F^{-1}(S)$ with $k$ equations (Definition~\ref{def:adapted-chart}). If $F^{-1}(S) = \emptyset$ there is nothing to check, since the condition of Definition~\ref{def:submanifold} is one condition at each point of the subset (the convention of Theorem~\ref{thm:rvt-manifolds}, whose fibres may be empty); and (2) is then vacuous. So fix $p \in F^{-1}(S)$ and put $q = F(p)$, a point of $S$. The plan: an adapted chart of $S$ at $q$ supplies a local defining map $x_b$ for $S$; transversality makes $G = x_b \circ F$ a submersion at $p$; the normal form of $G$ then straightens $F^{-1}(S)$ near $p$. Throughout, the tangent space of an open subset at a point is identified with that of the ambient manifold (Lemma~\ref{lem:germs-local}), as everywhere in the notes; by the Chain Rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}), applied to a restriction $F|_V = F \circ \iota_V$ with $\iota_V$ the inclusion of the open set $V$, this identification turns the differential of a restriction of $F$ into $F_{*p}$.

\emph{Step 1: an adapted chart at $q$.} Since $q \in S$ and $S$ is a regular submanifold of codimension $k$, there is a smooth chart $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^n))$ of $N$ with $q \in U$ and
\[
U \cap S = \{\, q' \in U : x_b(q') = \vec 0 \,\}, \qquad x_a = (x^1, \ldots, x^{n-k}), \quad x_b = (x^{n-k+1}, \ldots, x^n)
\]
(Definitions~\ref{def:submanifold} and~\ref{def:adapted-chart}). By Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-tangent}, applied to $S \subseteq N$,
\[
\iota_{*q}\big(T_qS\big) = \Span\Big\{\frac{\partial}{\partial x^1}\Big|_q, \ldots, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^{n-k}}\Big|_q\Big\} .
\]

\emph{Step 2: the map $x_b$ and its differential.} Regard $x_b : U \to \mathbb{R}^k$ as a map from the open submanifold $U$ to $\mathbb{R}^k$, the latter with the identity chart, whose coordinate functions are $r^1, \ldots, r^k$. Proposition~\ref{prop:adapted-defining-map}, applied to the regular submanifold $S \subseteq N$ of codimension $k$ and the adapted chart $(U, \varphi)$ of Step~1 (so with $n$ in place of $m$), gives: $x_b$ is smooth, and at $q$ (where $x_b(q) = \vec 0$, as $q \in U \cap S$) $(x_b)_{*q}(\partial/\partial x^i|_q)$ is $0$ for $i \le n - k$ and $\partial/\partial r^{\,i-(n-k)}|_{\vec 0}$ for $i > n - k$. Two consequences.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(a)] \emph{$(x_b)_{*q}$ is onto $T_{\vec 0}\mathbb{R}^k$}: by part~(2) of the proposition, $x_b$ is a submersion at every point of $U$, in particular at $q$.
    \item[(b)] \emph{$\ker (x_b)_{*q} = \iota_{*q}(T_qS)$}: part~(4) of the proposition, at the point $q \in U \cap S$.
\end{enumerate}

\emph{Step 3: a chart at $p$ mapped into $U$, and the map $G$.} $F$ is continuous, so $F^{-1}(U)$ is an open set containing $p$. Take any smooth chart $(\tilde V, \tilde\psi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and put $V = \tilde V \cap F^{-1}(U)$, an open set containing $p$ with $F(V) \subseteq U$; the restriction of $\tilde\psi$ to $V$ is again a smooth chart (Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(1), with $U' = V$). Define
\[
G = x_b \circ F|_V : V \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^k .
\]
It is smooth: $F|_V$ is smooth (Proposition~\ref{prop:open-inclusion-smooth}(2)), and smooth as a map into the open submanifold $U$, since it takes values in $U$ and its composite with the inclusion $U \hookrightarrow N$ is the smooth map $F|_V$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:open-inclusion-smooth}(3)); then $G$ is a composite of smooth maps (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}). By the Chain Rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}) and the identifications $T_pV = T_pM$, $T_qU = T_qN$,
\[
G_{*p} = (x_b)_{*q} \circ F_{*p} : T_pM \longrightarrow T_{\vec 0}\mathbb{R}^k .
\]

\emph{Step 4: $G$ cuts out $F^{-1}(S)$ in $V$.} For $p' \in V$ we have $F(p') \in U$, so
\[
G(p') = \vec 0 \iff x_b\big(F(p')\big) = \vec 0 \iff F(p') \in U \cap S \iff F(p') \in S \iff p' \in F^{-1}(S) :
\]
the first equivalence is the definition of $G$; the second is Step~1, $F(p')$ being a point of $U$; the third holds because $F(p') \in U$ anyway. Hence $G^{-1}(\vec 0) = V \cap F^{-1}(S)$.

\emph{Step 5: $G$ is a submersion at $p$.} We show $G_{*p}$ is onto. Let $w \in T_{\vec 0}\mathbb{R}^k$. By Step~2(a) there is $u \in T_qN$ with $(x_b)_{*q}u = w$. By transversality at $p$ (Definition~\ref{def:transverse-submanifold}), $u = F_{*p}v + t$ with $v \in T_pM$ and $t \in \iota_{*q}(T_qS)$, and $(x_b)_{*q}t = 0$ by Step~2(b). By linearity of $(x_b)_{*q}$ and Step~3,
\[
w = (x_b)_{*q}u = (x_b)_{*q}F_{*p}v + (x_b)_{*q}t = (x_b)_{*q}F_{*p}v + 0 = G_{*p}v .
\]
So $G_{*p}$ is onto, i.e.\ $G$ is a submersion at $p$ (Definition~\ref{def:submersion}). In particular $k \le m$: a surjective linear map $T_pM \to T_{\vec 0}\mathbb{R}^k$ has $\dim T_pM \ge \dim T_{\vec 0}\mathbb{R}^k$ (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)), and these dimensions are $m$ and $k$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-dimension}).

\emph{Step 6: the normal form of $G$ at $p$.} Lemma~\ref{lem:rvt-local} requires $G$ to be a submersion only at the one point $p$, which is Step~5; no shrinking of $V$ is needed. Its part~(1), applied to $G : V \to \mathbb{R}^k$ at $p$ with $c = G(p) = \vec 0$ (and $k$ in place of $n$), gives --- by the normal form of $G$ --- a smooth chart $(W, \theta = (z^1, \ldots, z^m))$ of $M$ at $p$ with $W \subseteq V$ and a smooth chart $(Y, \chi)$ of $\mathbb{R}^k$ at $\vec 0$ with $G(W) \subseteq Y$ and $\chi\big(G(p')\big) = \big(z^1(p'), \ldots, z^k(p')\big)$ for $p' \in W$; and, with $\vec c = \chi(\vec 0) = (c_1, \ldots, c_k)$,
\[
W \cap G^{-1}(\vec 0) = \{\, p' \in W : z^1(p') = c_1, \ \ldots, \ z^k(p') = c_k \,\} .
\]

\emph{Step 7: an adapted chart at $p$.} Since $W \subseteq V$, Step~4 gives $W \cap F^{-1}(S) = W \cap V \cap F^{-1}(S) = W \cap G^{-1}(\vec 0)$, so
\[
W \cap F^{-1}(S) = \{\, p' \in W : z^1(p') = c_1, \ \ldots, \ z^k(p') = c_k \,\} ,
\]
the intersection cut out in the smooth chart $(W, \theta)$ of $M$ by setting $k$ of its coordinates equal to constants. By Lemma~\ref{lem:rvt-local}(2), with the subset $F^{-1}(S)$ --- that is, Proposition~\ref{prop:adapted-flex} with the coordinates $z^1, \ldots, z^k$ and the constant vector $\vec c$ --- there is a chart of $M$ with domain $W$ adapted to $F^{-1}(S)$, of codimension $k$: explicitly, $\big(z^{k+1}, \ldots, z^m, \ z^1 - c_1, \ldots, z^k - c_k\big)$, the translation and permutation of the student's solution. Here $k \le m$ by Step~5.

\emph{Conclusion of (1).} As $p \in F^{-1}(S)$ was arbitrary, every point of $F^{-1}(S)$ lies in a chart of $M$ adapted to $F^{-1}(S)$ with $k$ equations, so $F^{-1}(S)$ is a regular submanifold of $M$ of codimension $k$ (Definition~\ref{def:submanifold}), and $\dim F^{-1}(S) = m - k$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-structure}. The codimension of $S$ in $N$ is also $k$, by hypothesis.

\emph{(2): $j_{*p}(T_pF^{-1}(S)) \subseteq \ker G_{*p}$.} Lemma~\ref{lem:rvt-local}(3) applies to $G : V \to \mathbb{R}^k$, a submersion at $p$ (Step~5) with $c = G(p) = \vec 0$, to the regular submanifold $F^{-1}(S)$ of $M$ of codimension $k$ (part~(1)) with inclusion $j$, and to $W' = V$: by Step~4, $F^{-1}(S) \cap V = G^{-1}(\vec 0) = G^{-1}(\vec 0) \cap V$. The inclusion is the first half of its proof: on the open neighbourhood $V \cap F^{-1}(S)$ of $p$ in $F^{-1}(S)$ the composite $G \circ j$ is constant with value $\vec 0$, by Step~4, so $G_{*p} \circ j_{*p} = (G \circ j)_{*p} = 0$ by the Chain Rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}) and Lemma~\ref{lem:constant-pushforward}; that is, $G_{*p}(j_{*p}v) = 0$ for every $v \in T_pF^{-1}(S)$.

\emph{(2): dimensions.} The second half of the lemma's proof: $\dim j_{*p}(T_pF^{-1}(S)) = \dim F^{-1}(S) = m - k$, since $j_{*p}$ is injective (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-tangent}) and by (1); and $\dim \ker G_{*p} = m - k$ by rank--nullity (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)), $G_{*p}$ being onto the $k$-dimensional $T_{\vec 0}\mathbb{R}^k$ (Step~5). A subspace of the same finite dimension is the whole space, so $j_{*p}(T_pF^{-1}(S)) = \ker G_{*p}$.

\emph{(2): the kernel of $G_{*p}$.} By Step~3, the definition of the kernel, and Step~2(b),
\begin{align*}
\ker G_{*p} &= \big\{\, v \in T_pM : (x_b)_{*q}\big(F_{*p}v\big) = 0 \,\big\} \\
&= \big\{\, v \in T_pM : F_{*p}v \in \ker (x_b)_{*q} \,\big\} = \big\{\, v \in T_pM : F_{*p}v \in \iota_{*q}(T_qS) \,\big\} ,
\end{align*}
which is $(F_{*p})^{-1}\big(\iota_{*q}(T_qS)\big)$. With the previous paragraph, $j_{*p}(T_pF^{-1}(S)) = (F_{*p})^{-1}\big(\iota_{*q}(T_qS)\big)$. This is Lemma~\ref{lem:rvt-local}(3) --- the argument of the tangent-space half of Theorem~\ref{thm:rvt-manifolds} --- run for $G$, followed by the computation of $\ker G_{*p}$ that ends the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-preimage}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Second proof (reduction to Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-preimage} in charts)]
\textit{(Not from lecture; the route of the official solution of Assignment~5, Problem~2, and the one its hint intends. The three facts that transport the Euclidean theorem are checked explicitly.)} Fix $p \in F^{-1}(S)$ and $q = F(p)$. As in Steps~1 and~3 of the first proof, take a chart $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^n))$ of $N$ adapted to $S$ at $q$, so $U \cap S = x_b^{-1}(\vec 0)$, and a chart $(V, \psi)$ of $M$ at $p$ with $F(V) \subseteq U$. Downstairs, set
\[
\tilde F = \varphi \circ F \circ \psi^{-1} : \psi(V) \to \mathbb{R}^n, \qquad \tilde G : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^k, \quad \tilde G(y) = (y^{n-k+1}, \ldots, y^n) .
\]
$\tilde G$ is linear with $\tilde G' = (0 \mid I_k)$ surjective everywhere, so $\tilde S = \tilde G^{-1}(\vec 0) = \mathbb{R}^{n-k} \times \{\vec 0\}$ is a regular level set with $T^{\geo}_y\tilde S = \ker\tilde G' = \mathbb{R}^{n-k} \times \{\vec 0\}$, and $\varphi(U \cap S) = \tilde S \cap \varphi(U)$. As $\tilde F$ takes values in $\varphi(U)$,
\[
\tilde F^{-1}(\tilde S) = \psi\big(V \cap F^{-1}(S)\big) .
\]

\emph{Fact 1: transversality survives the charts.} Let $p' \in V \cap F^{-1}(S)$, $q' = F(p')$, $x' = \psi(p')$. By the Chain Rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}), $\tilde F_{*x'} = \varphi_{*q'} \circ F_{*p'} \circ (\psi^{-1})_{*x'}$, and $(\psi^{-1})_{*x'}$ is onto (Proposition~\ref{prop:chart-diffeo}), so $\operatorname{im}\tilde F_{*x'} = \varphi_{*q'}(\operatorname{im}F_{*p'})$. The chart is adapted at $q'$ too, so $\iota_{*q'}(T_{q'}S)$ is spanned by the $\partial/\partial x^i|_{q'}$ with $i \le n - k$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-tangent}), which $\varphi_{*q'}$ sends to the $\partial/\partial r^i|_{\varphi(q')}$, that is, to $e_1, \ldots, e_{n-k}$ under the identification of Proposition~\ref{prop:differential-agree}. Applying the isomorphism $\varphi_{*q'}$ to $\operatorname{im}F_{*p'} + \iota_{*q'}(T_{q'}S) = T_{q'}N$ gives
\[
\operatorname{im}\tilde F'(x') + T^{\geo}_{\tilde F(x')}\tilde S = \mathbb{R}^n .
\]

\emph{Fact 2: Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-preimage} on an open set.} Its proof is pointwise until the regular value theorem is invoked: the surjectivity step (or the remark \emph{The Surjectivity Step as an Image Computation} in \ref{sec:transversality}) uses only Fact~1 at each point. So $0$ is a regular value of $\tilde H = \tilde G \circ \tilde F : \psi(V) \to \mathbb{R}^k$, and $\tilde H^{-1}(\vec 0) = \tilde F^{-1}(\tilde S) = \psi(V \cap F^{-1}(S))$. Note $\tilde H = x_b \circ F \circ \psi^{-1}$.

\emph{Fact 3: slice charts pull back.} By the Regular Value Theorem for manifolds (Theorem~\ref{thm:rvt-manifolds}), applied to $\tilde H$ on the open submanifold $\psi(V)$ of $\mathbb{R}^m$, there is a chart $(W', \theta)$ of $\psi(V)$ at $\psi(p)$ adapted to $\tilde H^{-1}(\vec 0)$, with $k$ equations. Then $\theta \circ \psi : \psi^{-1}(W') \to \theta(W')$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open set, so a smooth chart of $M$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:diffeo-chart}), and for $p'' \in \psi^{-1}(W') \subseteq V$, the last $k$ coordinates of $\theta(\psi(p''))$ vanish if and only if $\psi(p'') \in \tilde H^{-1}(\vec 0)$, if and only if $p'' \in F^{-1}(S)$. So $(\psi^{-1}(W'), \theta \circ \psi)$ is a chart of $M$ adapted to $F^{-1}(S)$ at $p$, with $k$ equations.

As $p$ was arbitrary, $F^{-1}(S)$ is a regular submanifold of codimension $k$, which is (1). For (2), $G = x_b \circ F|_V = \tilde H \circ \psi$ is the map of the first proof; it is a submersion at $p$, since $\tilde H$ is one at $\psi(p)$ and $\psi_{*p}$ is an isomorphism; and (2) follows as there.
\end{proof}

\begin{defbox}[Normal Space]\deflabel{def:normal-space}
Let $S \subseteq M$ be a regular submanifold with inclusion $\iota$, and $p \in S$. The \textbf{normal space} of $S$ at $p$ is the quotient vector space (Definition~\ref{def:quotient-vs})
\[
T_pM / \iota_{*p}(T_pS) ,
\]
written $T_pM / T_pS$ when $T_pS$ is identified with its image (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-tangent}).
\end{defbox}

\begin{lembox}[Dimension of the Normal Space]\thmlabel{lem:normal-space-dimension}
\textit{(Not from lecture.)} Let $M$ be a smooth manifold of dimension $m$, $S \subseteq M$ a regular submanifold of codimension $k$ with inclusion $\iota$, and $p \in S$. Then the normal space $T_pM/\iota_{*p}(T_pS)$ of $S$ at $p$ (Definition~\ref{def:normal-space}) has dimension $k$.
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
We compute the dimension of the quotient from those of $T_pM$ and of the subspace $\iota_{*p}(T_pS)$: $\dim T_pM = m$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-dimension}), $\dim \iota_{*p}(T_pS) = \dim T_pS = m - k$ because $\iota_{*p}$ is injective (Propositions~\ref{prop:submanifold-tangent} and~\ref{prop:submanifold-structure}), and $\dim T_pM/\iota_{*p}(T_pS) = m - (m - k) = k$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:quotient-vs}(3).
\end{proof}

The normal space needs no metric, unlike the normal vectors of the remark \emph{No Normal Vectors Without a Metric} in \ref{sec:submanifolds}; its dimension is that of the conormal space $N_pS$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:conormal-basis}).

\begin{propbox}[Normal Spaces Under a Transverse Map]\thmlabel{prop:transverse-normal-spaces}
Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth, $S \subseteq N$ a regular submanifold of codimension $k$ with inclusion $\iota$, $p \in F^{-1}(S)$ and $q = F(p)$. Put
\[
K_p = (F_{*p})^{-1}\big(\iota_{*q}(T_qS)\big) \subseteq T_pM .
\]
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $F_{*p}$ induces a well-defined linear map of quotient spaces (Definition~\ref{def:quotient-vs})
    \[
    \bar F_{*p} : T_pM / K_p \longrightarrow T_qN / \iota_{*q}(T_qS), \qquad v + K_p \longmapsto F_{*p}v + \iota_{*q}(T_qS) .
    \]
    \item $\bar F_{*p}$ is injective.
    \item $\bar F_{*p}$ is surjective if and only if $F$ is transverse to $S$ at $p$ (Definition~\ref{def:transverse-submanifold}).
\end{enumerate}
So if $F \pitchfork S$, then $K_p = j_{*p}(T_pF^{-1}(S))$, with $j$ the inclusion of $F^{-1}(S)$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-submanifold-preimage}) and $\bar F_{*p}$ is an isomorphism $T_pM/T_pF^{-1}(S) \cong T_qN/T_qS$ of the normal spaces (Definition~\ref{def:normal-space}): both have dimension $k$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:normal-space-dimension}), which is the reason the codimension is preserved.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture.)} Write $E = \iota_{*q}(T_qS)$, a subspace of $T_qN$ (the image of a linear map), and $\pi_N : T_qN \to T_qN/E$, $\pi_M : T_pM \to T_pM/K_p$ for the projections. $K_p$ is a subspace of $T_pM$, as the preimage of the subspace $E$ under the linear map $F_{*p}$: if $F_{*p}v, F_{*p}v' \in E$, then $F_{*p}(v + cv') = F_{*p}v + c\,F_{*p}v' \in E$. Throughout, two vectors have the same coset iff their difference lies in the subspace (Definition~\ref{def:quotient-vs}).

\emph{(1)} Let $A = \pi_N \circ F_{*p} : T_pM \to T_qN/E$, $A(v) = F_{*p}v + E$, linear as a composite of linear maps (Proposition~\ref{prop:quotient-vs}(1)). Its kernel is $K_p$: by $\ker \pi_N = E$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:quotient-vs}(1)),
\[
A(v) = 0 \iff \pi_N\big(F_{*p}v\big) = 0 \iff F_{*p}v \in E \iff v \in K_p .
\]
In particular $K_p \subseteq \ker A$, so by the universal property (Proposition~\ref{prop:quotient-vs}(2)) there is a unique linear $\bar F_{*p} : T_pM/K_p \to T_qN/E$ with $\bar F_{*p} \circ \pi_M = A$, namely $\bar F_{*p}(v + K_p) = A(v) = F_{*p}v + E$ --- the map of (1), well defined and linear.

\emph{(2)} Suppose $\bar F_{*p}(v + K_p) = 0$. Then $A(v) = 0$, so $v \in \ker A = K_p$ by (1), i.e.\ $v + K_p = 0 + K_p$, the zero of $T_pM/K_p$. A linear map with zero kernel is injective.

\emph{(3)} Since $\pi_M$ is surjective (Proposition~\ref{prop:quotient-vs}(1)), every element of $T_pM/K_p$ is some $v + K_p$, and the image of $\bar F_{*p}$ is $\{F_{*p}v + E : v \in T_pM\}$. So, by the criterion for equal cosets,
\begin{align*}
\bar F_{*p} \text{ is surjective} &\iff \text{for every } u \in T_qN \text{ there is } v \in T_pM \text{ with } u + E = F_{*p}v + E \\
&\iff \text{for every } u \in T_qN \text{ there is } v \in T_pM \text{ with } u - F_{*p}v \in E \\
&\iff \text{every } u \in T_qN \text{ lies in } F_{*p}(T_pM) + E .
\end{align*}
For the last equivalence: if $u - F_{*p}v = t \in E$, then $u = F_{*p}v + t$ lies in the sum; conversely if $u = F_{*p}v + t$ with $t \in E$, then $u - F_{*p}v = t \in E$. The last condition says $F_{*p}(T_pM) + \iota_{*q}(T_qS) = T_qN$, since the sum is a subspace of $T_qN$ in any case; this is transversality at $p$ (Definition~\ref{def:transverse-submanifold}).

\emph{The transverse case.} If $F \pitchfork S$, then $\bar F_{*p}$ is injective by (2) and surjective by (3), hence an isomorphism, and $K_p = j_{*p}(T_pF^{-1}(S))$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-submanifold-preimage}(2). The dimensions are $\dim T_pM = m$ and $\dim T_qN = n$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-dimension}); $\dim E = \dim T_qS = n - k$, as $\iota_{*q}$ is injective (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-tangent}); and $\dim K_p = m - k$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-submanifold-preimage}(1)). So by Proposition~\ref{prop:quotient-vs}(3)
\[
\dim T_pM/K_p = m - (m - k) = k = n - (n - k) = \dim T_qN/E ,
\]
as an isomorphism requires. Read backwards, the isomorphism alone gives $\dim K_p = m - \dim T_qN/E = m - k$: the codimension of $F^{-1}(S)$ in $M$ is the dimension of its normal space $T_pM/K_p$, and transversality makes $F_{*p}$ carry that normal space isomorphically onto the normal space of $S$, of dimension $k$.
\end{proof}

\textit{Review session, Oct 16 (and Uribe's email before it). The homework defined a map transverse to a submanifold (Definition~\ref{def:transverse-submanifold}). Two submanifolds can also be transverse to each other; historically this was the original definition, later generalized to maps. The Euclidean version is Definition~\ref{def:transverse-intersection}.} \textit{(Placed here because Corollary~\ref{cor:transverse-special-cases}(2) uses them; the theorem of the review session on the intersection is Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-intersection-manifold} in \ref{sub:transverse-submanifolds}.)}

\begin{defbox}[Transverse Submanifolds]\deflabel{def:transverse-submanifolds}
Let $S_1, S_2 \subseteq N$ be regular submanifolds. $S_1$ \textbf{intersects $S_2$ transversally}, written $S_1 \pitchfork S_2$, if
\[
T_qS_1 + T_qS_2 = T_qN \qquad \text{for every } q \in S_1 \cap S_2 ,
\]
with $T_qS_i \subseteq T_qN$ through the inclusions (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-tangent}). The condition holds vacuously if $S_1 \cap S_2 = \varnothing$. The notation $S_1 \pitchfork S_2$ is a statement about the pair, not a set: unlike $S_1 \cap S_2$, it is not the result of an operation.
\leeref{Ch.~6, \emph{Transversality}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[Transverse Submanifolds and Transverse Maps]\thmlabel{prop:transverse-submanifolds-maps}
$S_1 \pitchfork S_2$ if and only if the inclusion $\iota_1 : S_1 \hookrightarrow N$ is transverse to $S_2$ (Definition~\ref{def:transverse-submanifold}).
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Stated in the review session as immediate from the definitions; written out.)} $\iota_1^{-1}(S_2) = S_1 \cap S_2$, and for $q$ in it, $(\iota_1)_{*q}(T_qS_1)$ is $T_qS_1$ regarded as a subspace of $T_qN$. So the condition of Definition~\ref{def:transverse-submanifold} for $F = \iota_1$ at $q$ is $T_qS_1 + T_qS_2 = T_qN$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[Special Cases of Transversality]\thmlabel{cor:transverse-special-cases}
Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth, $\dim M = m$, $\dim N = n$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \emph{A point.} For $c \in N$, $\{c\}$ is a regular submanifold of $N$ of codimension $n$, and $F \pitchfork \{c\}$ if and only if $c$ is a regular value of $F$. In that case Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-submanifold-preimage} returns the regular value theorem, Theorem~\ref{thm:rvt-manifolds}: $F^{-1}(c)$ is a regular submanifold of $M$ of codimension $n$, and $j_{*p}(T_pF^{-1}(c)) = \ker F_{*p}$ for $p \in F^{-1}(c)$.
    \item \emph{Two submanifolds.} Let $S, S' \subseteq N$ be regular submanifolds of codimensions $k$ and $k'$, with inclusions $\iota$ and $\iota'$, that intersect transversally, $S' \pitchfork S$ (Definition~\ref{def:transverse-submanifolds}) --- that is, $\iota' \pitchfork S$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:transverse-submanifolds-maps}; a condition symmetric in $S$ and $S'$). Then $S' \cap S$ is a regular submanifold of $S'$ of codimension $k$. (It is also a regular submanifold of $N$ of codimension $k + k'$, and, with all tangent spaces regarded as subspaces of $T_pN$, $T_p(S' \cap S) = T_pS' \cap T_pS$: this is Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-intersection-manifold}.)
    \item \emph{Submersions.} If $F$ is a submersion, then $F \pitchfork S$ for every regular submanifold $S \subseteq N$, and $F^{-1}(S)$ is a regular submanifold of $M$ of the same codimension as $S$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)}

\emph{(1)} $\{c\}$ is a regular submanifold of $N$ of codimension $n$: it is the fibre $\mathrm{id}_N^{-1}(c)$ of the identity, a submersion since $(\mathrm{id}_N)_{*} = \mathrm{id}$ (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}), so Corollary~\ref{cor:submersion-fibres} applies. Its tangent space is $0$ (dimension $n - n = 0$, Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-dimension} and Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-structure}), so transversality at $p \in F^{-1}(c)$ (Definition~\ref{def:transverse-submanifold}) reads $F_{*p}(T_pM) + 0 = T_cN$: $F_{*p}$ is onto. Thus $F \pitchfork \{c\}$ iff $F$ is a submersion at every point of $F^{-1}(c)$, iff $c$ is a regular value (Definitions~\ref{def:manifold-regular-point} and~\ref{def:manifold-regular}; the empty case is Definition~\ref{def:regular-critical-value}(2)). Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-submanifold-preimage}, with $S = \{c\}$ and $k = n$, then gives that $F^{-1}(c)$ is a regular submanifold of codimension $n$, and $j_{*p}(T_pF^{-1}(c)) = (F_{*p})^{-1}(0) = \ker F_{*p}$.

\emph{(2)} The inclusion $\iota' : S' \to N$ is smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}(1)), $(\iota')^{-1}(S) = S' \cap S$, and $\iota'_{*p}(T_pS')$ is the image of the differential of $\iota'$ at $p$; so $\iota' \pitchfork S$ (Definition~\ref{def:transverse-submanifold}) is the condition
\[
\iota'_{*p}\big(T_pS'\big) + \iota_{*p}\big(T_pS\big) = T_pN \qquad \text{for every } p \in S' \cap S ,
\]
which is $S' \pitchfork S$ (Definition~\ref{def:transverse-submanifolds}; Proposition~\ref{prop:transverse-submanifolds-maps} with $S_1 = S'$ and $S_2 = S$), and which is symmetric in $S$ and $S'$ because a sum of subspaces is. Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-submanifold-preimage}, applied to $\iota'$ in place of $F$, makes $S' \cap S$ a regular submanifold of $S'$ of codimension $k = \operatorname{codim} S$, so of dimension $(n - k') - k = n - (k' + k)$, $S'$ having dimension $n - k'$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-structure}). Its tangent space, and $S' \cap S$ as a submanifold of $N$, are treated in the second proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-intersection-manifold}.

\emph{(3)} If $F$ is a submersion, then $F_{*p}(T_pM) = T_{F(p)}N$ already, so the sum in Definition~\ref{def:transverse-submanifold} is all of $T_{F(p)}N$ at every $p \in F^{-1}(S)$: $F \pitchfork S$. Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-submanifold-preimage} then makes $F^{-1}(S)$ a regular submanifold of $M$ of the same codimension as $S$.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[Special Cases and the Euclidean Versions]\label{rem:transversality-special-cases}
\textit{(Not from lecture.)} Corollary~\ref{cor:transverse-special-cases}(1) is the manifold version of Corollary~\ref{cor:rvt-transverse}, and (2), together with Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-intersection-manifold}, that of Proposition~\ref{prop:transverse-intersection}: the codimensions add, as for level sets. For $S = \{c\}$ a point, (3) is Corollary~\ref{cor:submersion-fibres}: a submersion is transverse to every point, and its fibres are regular submanifolds of codimension $n$.
\end{rembox}

\textit{Assignment~5, Problem~4 (``Revisiting Lagrange multipliers''), in the notation of these notes: the assignment's submanifold $M \subset N$ is here $S \subseteq M$, with $M$ the ambient manifold of dimension $m$; its conormal space $\mathcal{N}_pM$ is $N_pS$ (Definition~\ref{def:conormal}); and $d(G^j)_p$ is written $dG^j|_p$. The problem: (a) a point is a critical point of the restriction $f = \Phi|_S$ of a smooth function $\Phi$ on $M$ exactly when $d\Phi_p$ is conormal to $S$; (b) for a regular level set $S = G^{-1}(0)$ the differentials $dG^1|_p, \ldots, dG^k|_p$ form a basis of $N_pS$, and the method of Lagrange multipliers follows. The proofs are the submitted solution's, written out.}

\begin{propbox}[Critical Points of a Restriction]\thmlabel{prop:restriction-critical}
Let $S \subseteq M$ be a regular submanifold, $\iota : S \to M$ the inclusion, $p \in S$, and $\iota_p^* : T_p^*M \to T_p^*S$ the pullback of covectors (Definition~\ref{def:pullback-covector}). Let $\Phi : M \to \mathbb{R}$ be smooth and $f = \Phi \circ \iota = \Phi|_S : S \to \mathbb{R}$ its restriction.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $N_pS = \ker \iota_p^*$.
    \item $df_p = \iota_p^*\big(d\Phi_p\big)$.
    \item $p$ is a critical point of $f$ if and only if $d\Phi_p \in N_pS$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~5, Problem~4(a).)} The restriction $f = \Phi \circ \iota$ is smooth, as a composite of smooth maps (Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}(1) and Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}), so $df_p \in T_p^*S$ is defined. By Definition~\ref{def:pullback-covector} with $F = \iota$ and $F(p) = \iota(p) = p$, the pullback of a covector $\xi \in T_p^*M$ is the covector on $T_pS$
\[
\big(\iota_p^*\xi\big)(v) = \xi\big(\iota_{*p}v\big), \qquad v \in T_pS .
\]

\emph{(1)} Let $\xi \in T_p^*M$. A covector is zero when it vanishes at every vector, and every element of $\iota_{*p}(T_pS)$ is $\iota_{*p}v$ for some $v \in T_pS$; so
\[
\iota_p^*\xi = 0 \iff \xi\big(\iota_{*p}v\big) = 0 \ \text{ for all } v \in T_pS \iff \xi(w) = 0 \ \text{ for all } w \in \iota_{*p}(T_pS) \iff \xi \in N_pS ,
\]
the last step by Definition~\ref{def:conormal}. So the annihilator of the tangent space, which is how Definition~\ref{def:conormal} describes $N_pS$, is the kernel of the pullback, which is how the assignment describes it.

\emph{(2)} This is Proposition~\ref{prop:pullback-d} with $F = \iota$ and the function $\Phi$, smooth near $\iota(p) = p$: it gives $\iota_p^*(d\Phi_p) = d(\Phi \circ \iota)_p = df_p$. Written out for $v \in T_pS$, by Proposition~\ref{prop:df-derivation}, the definition of the pushforward (Definition~\ref{def:pushforward}), Proposition~\ref{prop:df-derivation} again, and the formula for $\iota_p^*$ above,
\[
df_p(v) = v\big[\Phi \circ \iota\big] = \big(\iota_{*p}v\big)[\Phi] = d\Phi_p\big(\iota_{*p}v\big) = \big(\iota_p^*(d\Phi_p)\big)(v) .
\]
Two covectors on $T_pS$ that agree at every $v$ are equal.

\emph{(3)} By Proposition~\ref{prop:critical-functions}, applied to the smooth function $f$ on the manifold $S$, then (2), then (1),
\[
p \text{ is a critical point of } f \iff df_p = 0 \iff \iota_p^*\big(d\Phi_p\big) = 0 \iff d\Phi_p \in \ker \iota_p^* = N_pS .
\]
In words: $p$ is critical for the restriction exactly when $d\Phi_p$ vanishes on every vector tangent to $S$ at $p$.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[The Conormal Space of a Regular Level Set]\thmlabel{prop:conormal-defining-functions}
Let $G = (G^1, \ldots, G^k) : M \to \mathbb{R}^k$ be smooth, with $0$ a regular value of $G$ (Definition~\ref{def:manifold-regular}), and let $S = G^{-1}(0)$. Then for every $p \in S$ the covectors $dG^1|_p, \ldots, dG^k|_p$ form a basis of the conormal space $N_pS$.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~5, Problem~4(b), first part. The dimension count cites Proposition~\ref{prop:conormal-basis}, which the submitted solution re-derives in an adapted chart; the submitted solution's independence argument, and its second, Jacobian form, are now the two proofs of Proposition~\ref{prop:submersion-independent-differentials}.)} Let $r^1, \ldots, r^k$ be the standard coordinates of $\mathbb{R}^k$, so that $G^j = r^j \circ G$; each $G^j$ is smooth, as a composite of smooth maps (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}). Fix $p \in S$. We show three things: $\dim N_pS = k$; each $dG^j|_p$ lies in $N_pS$; and the $k$ covectors $dG^j|_p$ are linearly independent. Then they span a $k$-dimensional subspace of the $k$-dimensional space $N_pS$, and a subspace of the same finite dimension is the whole space; so they are a basis.

\emph{$S$ is a regular submanifold, and $\dim N_pS = k$.} By Theorem~\ref{thm:rvt-manifolds}, applied to $G : M \to \mathbb{R}^k$ and the regular value $0$ (so $n = k$ there), $S$ is a regular submanifold of $M$ of codimension $k$; so $N_pS$ is defined, and $\dim N_pS = k$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:conormal-basis}(2). In an adapted chart $(x^1, \ldots, x^m)$ at $p$, a covector $\xi = \sum_i \xi_i\, dx^i|_p$ lies in $N_pS$ exactly when $\xi_i = 0$ for $i \le m - k$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:conormal-basis}(1)), so $N_pS$ has basis $dx^{m-k+1}|_p, \ldots, dx^m|_p$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:conormal-basis}(2)).

\emph{Each $dG^j|_p$ lies in $N_pS$.} Let $1 \le j \le k$. Every $q \in S = G^{-1}(0)$ has $G(q) = 0$, so $(G^j \circ \iota)(q) = G^j(q) = 0$: the function $G^j \circ \iota$ is the constant $0$ on $S$, and its germ at $p$ is the constant germ $[\underline 0]$. So $(G^j \circ \iota)_{*p} = 0$, the pushforward along a constant map being zero (Lemma~\ref{lem:constant-pushforward}), and hence $d(G^j \circ \iota)_p = 0$, the differential being this pushforward followed by the identification $T_0\mathbb{R} \cong \mathbb{R}$ (Definition~\ref{def:differential-function}). By Proposition~\ref{prop:restriction-critical}(2) with $\Phi = G^j$,
\[
\iota_p^*\big(dG^j|_p\big) = d\big(G^j \circ \iota\big)_p = 0 ,
\]
so $dG^j|_p \in \ker \iota_p^* = N_pS$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:restriction-critical}(1).

\emph{Linear independence.} Since $0$ is a regular value and $p \in G^{-1}(0)$, $G$ is a submersion at $p$ (Definitions~\ref{def:manifold-regular} and~\ref{def:manifold-regular-point}: $p$ is a regular point, so $G_{*p}$ is onto). By Proposition~\ref{prop:submersion-independent-differentials}(2), direction ($\Rightarrow$), the covectors $dG^1|_p, \ldots, dG^k|_p$ are therefore linearly independent. Its proof is the submitted solution's argument: by its formula (1), $G_{*p}v = \sum_j dG^j|_p(v)\, \partial/\partial r^j|_0$, a relation $\sum_j c_j\, dG^j|_p = 0$ says $c \cdot G_{*p}(v) = 0$ for every $v$, and since $G_{*p}$ is onto we may take $G_{*p}(v) = c$, which gives $|c|^2 = 0$. Its second proof is the Jacobian form: the relation says $J^{\mathsf T} c = 0$ for the $k \times m$ matrix $J = [\partial G^j/\partial x^i(p)]$ of $G_{*p}$ in any chart, and $J^{\mathsf T}$ has rank $k$.

\emph{Conclusion.} $dG^1|_p, \ldots, dG^k|_p$ are $k$ linearly independent elements of $N_pS$, which has dimension $k$, so they form a basis of $N_pS$. As $p \in S$ was arbitrary, this holds at every point of $S$.
\end{proof}

The assignment adds that a regular submanifold is \emph{locally} always a regular level set: this is Proposition~\ref{prop:adapted-defining-map}. Given an adapted chart $(U, \varphi = (x_a, x_b))$, put $G = x_b : U \to \mathbb{R}^k$. By that proposition, $U \cap S = G^{-1}(0)$ and $0$ is a regular value of $G$ (part~(3)), $G$ being a submersion at every point of $U$ (part~(2)). So Proposition~\ref{prop:conormal-defining-functions} and the theorem below apply to $U \cap S \subseteq U$. For this $G$ the basis $dG^j|_p = dx^{m-k+j}|_p$ is the basis of Proposition~\ref{prop:conormal-basis}(2).

\begin{thmbox}[Lagrange Multipliers]\thmlabel{thm:lagrange-multipliers}
Let $G = (G^1, \ldots, G^k) : M \to \mathbb{R}^k$ be smooth with $0$ a regular value, $S = G^{-1}(0)$, $\Phi : M \to \mathbb{R}$ smooth, and $f = \Phi|_S$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item If $f$ has a local extremum at $p \in S$ --- $f(q) \le f(p)$ for all $q$ in some neighbourhood of $p$ in $S$, or $f(q) \ge f(p)$ for all such $q$ --- then $p$ is a critical point of $f$.
    \item A point $p \in S$ is a critical point of $f$ if and only if there are $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_k \in \mathbb{R}$ with
    \[
    d\Phi_p = \sum_{j=1}^k \lambda_j\, dG^j|_p ,
    \]
    and the \textbf{Lagrange multipliers} $\lambda_j$ are then unique. Equivalently, the critical points of $f$ are the points $p \in M$ for which there is $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}^k$ with
    \[
    d\Big(\Phi - \sum_{j=1}^k \lambda_j G^j\Big)_p = 0, \qquad G(p) = 0 .
    \]
    \item If $M = \mathbb{R}^m$, with the gradient $\nabla h(p) = \big(\partial h/\partial r^1(p), \ldots, \partial h/\partial r^m(p)\big)$ (Definition~\ref{def:gradient}), the vector with $\nabla h(p) \cdot v = dh_p(v)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:dot-product-identification}), the conditions of (2) read
    \[
    \nabla\Phi(p) = \sum_{j=1}^k \lambda_j\, \nabla G^j(p), \qquad G^1(p) = \cdots = G^k(p) = 0 ,
    \]
    $m + k$ equations in the $m + k$ unknowns $(p, \lambda) \in \mathbb{R}^m \times \mathbb{R}^k$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~5, Problem~4(b), second part: ``explain how the method of Lagrange multipliers follows.'')} By Theorem~\ref{thm:rvt-manifolds}, $S$ is a regular submanifold of $M$, and $f = \Phi \circ \iota$ is smooth on it (Proposition~\ref{prop:restriction-critical}).

\emph{(1)} This is Proposition~\ref{prop:extremum-critical}, applied to the smooth function $f$ on the manifold $S$ (with its induced structure) and the neighbourhood of $p$ in $S$ on which $f \le f(p)$ (or $f \ge f(p)$): it gives $df_p = 0$, which by Proposition~\ref{prop:critical-functions} says that $p$ is a critical point of $f$. Its proof is the argument along curves: every $v \in T_pS$ is the velocity $D_\gamma$ of a smooth curve $\gamma$ in $S$ with $\gamma(0) = p$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:every-vector-velocity}), $f \circ \gamma$ has a local extremum at the interior point $0$, and $df_p(v) = (f \circ \gamma)'(0) = 0$. So the method, which looks for the critical points of $f$, finds in particular all local extrema of $\Phi$ subject to the constraint $G = 0$.

\emph{(2)} By Proposition~\ref{prop:restriction-critical}(3), $p$ is a critical point of $f$ iff $d\Phi_p \in N_pS$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:conormal-defining-functions}, $N_pS$ is the span of $dG^1|_p, \ldots, dG^k|_p$. So if $p$ is critical, $d\Phi_p$ is a linear combination $\sum_j \lambda_j\, dG^j|_p$; conversely, such a combination lies in $N_pS$, which is a subspace (the kernel of the linear map $\iota_p^*$, Proposition~\ref{prop:restriction-critical}(1)) containing every $dG^j|_p$, so $p$ is critical. \emph{Uniqueness:} if $\sum_j \lambda_j\, dG^j|_p = \sum_j \mu_j\, dG^j|_p$, then $\sum_j (\lambda_j - \mu_j)\, dG^j|_p = 0$, and linear independence of the $dG^j|_p$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:conormal-defining-functions}, or directly Proposition~\ref{prop:submersion-independent-differentials}(2), $G$ being a submersion at $p \in G^{-1}(0)$) gives $\lambda_j = \mu_j$ for every $j$. \emph{The equivalent form:} the function $\Phi - \sum_j \lambda_j G^j$ is smooth on $M$, and linearity of $d$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:df-properties}(1), applied once for each of the $k$ terms) gives
\[
d\Big(\Phi - \sum_{j=1}^k \lambda_j G^j\Big)_p = d\Phi_p - \sum_{j=1}^k \lambda_j\, dG^j|_p ,
\]
which is $0$ iff $d\Phi_p = \sum_j \lambda_j\, dG^j|_p$; and a point $p \in M$ lies in $S = G^{-1}(0)$ iff $G(p) = 0$.

\emph{(3)} Use the identity chart of $\mathbb{R}^m$, with coordinate functions $r^1, \ldots, r^m$; its coordinate derivations are the ordinary partial derivatives, $\partial/\partial r^i|_p[h] = \partial h/\partial r^i(p)$ (Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation}, the chart being the identity). For a smooth $h$ on $\mathbb{R}^m$, Lemma~\ref{lem:df-coords} gives $dh_p = \sum_i \partial h/\partial r^i(p)\, dr^i|_p$: the components of $dh_p$ are the entries of the gradient $\nabla h(p)$ (Definition~\ref{def:gradient}). This is the identification of Proposition~\ref{prop:dot-product-identification}: under the linear isomorphism $v \mapsto \xi_v$ of $\mathbb{R}^m$ onto $T_p^*\mathbb{R}^m$, $\xi_v(D_w|_p) = v \cdot w$, the vector $\nabla h(p)$ goes to $dh_p$. (So for $w = \sum_i w^i\, \partial/\partial r^i|_p$, identified with $(w^1, \ldots, w^m) \in \mathbb{R}^m$ as in Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs}, $dh_p(w) = \sum_i \partial h/\partial r^i(p)\, w^i = \nabla h(p) \cdot w$.) Two covectors are equal iff their components in the basis $dr^i|_p$ are equal, so, applying this to $h = \Phi$ and $h = G^j$,
\[
d\Phi_p = \sum_{j=1}^k \lambda_j\, dG^j|_p \iff \frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial r^i}(p) = \sum_{j=1}^k \lambda_j\, \frac{\partial G^j}{\partial r^i}(p) \ \ (i = 1, \ldots, m) \iff \nabla\Phi(p) = \sum_{j=1}^k \lambda_j\, \nabla G^j(p) .
\]
Equivalently, by Proposition~\ref{prop:dot-product-identification}: $v \mapsto \xi_v$ is linear and injective, with $\xi_{\nabla\Phi(p)} = d\Phi_p$ and $\xi_{\nabla G^j(p)} = dG^j|_p$, so $d\Phi_p = \sum_j \lambda_j\, dG^j|_p$ says $\xi_{\nabla\Phi(p)} = \xi_{\sum_j \lambda_j \nabla G^j(p)}$, that is, $\nabla\Phi(p) = \sum_j \lambda_j\, \nabla G^j(p)$.
With $G(p) = 0$ from (2) this is the system stated: $m$ scalar equations from the gradients and $k$ from the constraints, in the $m$ coordinates of $p$ and the $k$ multipliers. (The count makes a finite set of solutions plausible; it is not a theorem that there are any, or finitely many.)
\end{proof}

\textit{(Not from the assignment.)} In (3) the system is the vanishing of the gradient of the single function $L(x, \lambda) = \Phi(x) - \sum_j \lambda_j G^j(x)$ on $\mathbb{R}^{m+k}$: its partial derivatives at $(p, \lambda)$ are $\partial\Phi/\partial r^i(p) - \sum_j \lambda_j\, \partial G^j/\partial r^i(p)$ in the direction of $x^i$ and $-G^j(p)$ in the direction of $\lambda_j$, so $\nabla L(p, \lambda) = 0$ is exactly the $m + k$ equations above.

\begin{rembox}[The Conormal Bundle]\label{rem:conormal-bundle}
\textit{(Not from the assignment.)} The conormal spaces $N_pS$, $p \in S$, can be put together, as the cotangent spaces are put together in the cotangent bundle $T^*M$, into the \emph{conormal bundle} $N^*S \subseteq T^*M$. This is done later, in \ref{sub:ctb-zero-section}, once $T^*M$ and its standard coordinates are available (Definition~\ref{def:conormal-bundle}). There $N^*S$ is shown to be a regular submanifold of $T^*M$ of dimension $m$, whatever the codimension of $S$, cut out in the standard coordinates over an adapted chart by the description of $N_pS$ in Proposition~\ref{prop:conormal-basis}(1) (Proposition~\ref{prop:conormal-bundle-submanifold}); the critical points of a restriction $\Phi|_S$ are where the graph of $d\Phi$ meets it, by Proposition~\ref{prop:restriction-critical}(3) (Corollary~\ref{cor:crit-restriction-conormal}); and for $S = G^{-1}(0)$ the Lagrange multipliers of Theorem~\ref{thm:lagrange-multipliers} are the coordinates of $(p, d\Phi_p) \in N^*S$ in its fibre, in the basis $dG^1|_p, \ldots, dG^k|_p$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:conormal-defining-functions}.
\end{rembox}

\subsection{Transverse Submanifolds}\label{sub:transverse-submanifolds}

\textit{Review session, Oct 16. The definition of transverse submanifolds and its reformulation through the inclusion map, from the same session, stand before Corollary~\ref{cor:transverse-special-cases}, whose second case uses them (Definition~\ref{def:transverse-submanifolds}, Proposition~\ref{prop:transverse-submanifolds-maps}); what remains here is the theorem on the intersection.}

\begin{thmbox}[Transverse Intersections in a Manifold]\thmlabel{thm:transverse-intersection-manifold}
If $S_1 \pitchfork S_2$ in $N$, then $S_1 \cap S_2$ is a regular submanifold of $N$, with
\[
\operatorname{codim}(S_1 \cap S_2) = \operatorname{codim} S_1 + \operatorname{codim} S_2, \qquad T_q(S_1 \cap S_2) = T_qS_1 \cap T_qS_2 .
\]
\leeref{Theorem 6.30(b)}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Proved in the homework in the Euclidean case, Proposition~\ref{prop:transverse-intersection}, where it is a linear-algebra fact. The manifold version is filled in, along the Euclidean proof.)} Let $n = \dim N$, $k_i = \operatorname{codim} S_i$, and $q \in S_1 \cap S_2$.

\emph{Local defining functions.} Take a slice chart $(U_i, \varphi_i)$ for $S_i$ at $q$ (Definition~\ref{def:submanifold}), so that $U_i \cap S_i = G_i^{-1}(0)$, where $G_i : U_i \to \mathbb{R}^{k_i}$ is the last $k_i$ coordinates of $\varphi_i$. $G_i$ is a submersion (a coordinate projection composed with a chart), so by the regular value theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:rvt-manifolds}) $T_qS_i = \ker (dG_i)_q$, a subspace of $T_qN$ of dimension $n - k_i$.

\emph{Transversality is a regular value condition.} On $W = U_1 \cap U_2$ put $G = (G_1, G_2) : W \to \mathbb{R}^{k_1 + k_2}$, so that $W \cap S_1 \cap S_2 = G^{-1}(0)$ and $\ker dG_q = K_1 \cap K_2$, with $K_i = \ker (dG_i)_q = T_qS_i$. By the dimension formula for subspaces,
\[
\dim(K_1 \cap K_2) = \dim K_1 + \dim K_2 - \dim(K_1 + K_2) = 2n - k_1 - k_2 - \dim(K_1 + K_2).
\]
So $K_1 + K_2 = T_qN$ if and only if $\dim \ker dG_q = n - k_1 - k_2$, if and only if $dG_q$ has rank $k_1 + k_2$, that is, is onto. In a chart $(x^1, \ldots, x^n)$ at $q$, with $G_i = (G_i^1, \ldots, G_i^{k_i})$, the matrix of $dG_q$ is the $(k_1 + k_2) \times n$ matrix that stacks those of $(dG_1)_q$ and $(dG_2)_q$:
\[
\left(\begin{array}{ccc} \dfrac{\partial G_1^1}{\partial x^1}(q) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial G_1^1}{\partial x^n}(q) \\ \vdots & & \vdots \\ \dfrac{\partial G_1^{k_1}}{\partial x^1}(q) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial G_1^{k_1}}{\partial x^n}(q) \\ \hline \dfrac{\partial G_2^1}{\partial x^1}(q) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial G_2^1}{\partial x^n}(q) \\ \vdots & & \vdots \\ \dfrac{\partial G_2^{k_2}}{\partial x^1}(q) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial G_2^{k_2}}{\partial x^n}(q) \end{array}\right) ,
\]
so a vector is in its kernel exactly when it is killed by both blocks. Since $S_1 \pitchfork S_2$, this holds at every point of $G^{-1}(0)$: $0$ is a regular value of $G$.

\emph{Conclusion.} By Theorem~\ref{thm:rvt-manifolds}, $G^{-1}(0) = W \cap S_1 \cap S_2$ is a regular submanifold of $W$ of codimension $k_1 + k_2$, with $T_q(S_1 \cap S_2) = \ker dG_q = T_qS_1 \cap T_qS_2$. Being a regular submanifold is a local condition (slice charts at each point), and $W$ is open in $N$; $q$ was arbitrary, so $S_1 \cap S_2$ is a regular submanifold of $N$ of codimension $k_1 + k_2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Second proof (through the inclusion of one submanifold and adapted charts)]
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in. The letters are those of Corollary~\ref{cor:transverse-special-cases}(2): $S' = S_1$ and $S = S_2$, with inclusions $\iota'$ and $\iota$ and codimensions $k' = k_1$ and $k = k_2$; $n = \dim N$; and the point of $S' \cap S$ is called $p$.)}

\emph{The tangent space, through $S'$.} By Corollary~\ref{cor:transverse-special-cases}(2), $S' \cap S = (\iota')^{-1}(S)$ is a regular submanifold of $S'$ of codimension $k$, by Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-submanifold-preimage} applied to $\iota'$ in place of $F$. Part (2) of that theorem gives, with $j : S' \cap S \to S'$ the inclusion, $j_{*p}(T_p(S' \cap S)) = (\iota'_{*p})^{-1}\big(\iota_{*p}(T_pS)\big)$: the vectors of $T_pS'$ whose image in $T_pN$ lies in $\iota_{*p}(T_pS)$. Applying $\iota'_{*p}$, and using that $\iota' \circ j$ is the inclusion of $S' \cap S$ into $N$ (Chain Rule), the tangent space of $S' \cap S$ inside $T_pN$ is
\[
\iota'_{*p}\Big((\iota'_{*p})^{-1}\big(\iota_{*p}(T_pS)\big)\Big) = \iota'_{*p}\big(T_pS'\big) \cap \iota_{*p}\big(T_pS\big) ,
\]
since for a linear map $A$ and a subspace $E$ of its target, $A\big(A^{-1}(E)\big) = \operatorname{im} A \cap E$: an element $Av$ with $Av \in E$ lies in both; conversely $w = Av \in E$ gives $v \in A^{-1}(E)$. With all tangent spaces regarded as subspaces of $T_pN$: $T_p(S' \cap S) = T_pS' \cap T_pS$.

\emph{In $N$.} Fix $p \in S' \cap S$ (if $S' \cap S = \emptyset$ there is nothing to check). Take charts $(U, \varphi)$ adapted to $S$ and $(U', \varphi')$ adapted to $S'$ at $p$, with local defining maps $x_b : U \to \mathbb{R}^k$ and $x'_b : U' \to \mathbb{R}^{k'}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:adapted-defining-map}), and on the open set $V = U \cap U' \ni p$ put
\[
H = (x_b, x'_b) : V \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^{k + k'} ,
\]
smooth because its components are. Its first $k$ components are those of $x_b$ and its last $k'$ those of $x'_b$.
\begin{itemize}
    \item \emph{$H^{-1}(\vec 0) = V \cap S \cap S'$}: $H(q) = \vec 0$ iff $x_b(q) = \vec 0$ and $x'_b(q) = \vec 0$, iff $q \in U \cap S$ and $q \in U' \cap S'$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:adapted-defining-map}(3)).
    \item \emph{$\ker H_{*p} = \iota_{*p}(T_pS) \cap \iota'_{*p}(T_pS')$}: by Proposition~\ref{prop:submersion-independent-differentials}(1), $H_{*p}v = \sum_j dH^j|_p(v)\, \partial/\partial r^j|_{\vec 0}$, which is $0$ iff every coefficient $dH^j|_p(v)$ is $0$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}); by the same formula for $x_b$ and $x'_b$, $(x_b)_{*p}v = 0$ iff $dH^j|_p(v) = 0$ for $j \le k$, and $(x'_b)_{*p}v = 0$ iff $dH^j|_p(v) = 0$ for $j > k$. So $\ker H_{*p} = \ker (x_b)_{*p} \cap \ker (x'_b)_{*p}$, which is $\iota_{*p}(T_pS) \cap \iota'_{*p}(T_pS')$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:adapted-defining-map}(4).
    \item \emph{$H$ is a submersion at $p$}: by the dimension formula for a sum of two subspaces, with $\dim \iota_{*p}(T_pS) = n - k$ and $\dim \iota'_{*p}(T_pS') = n - k'$ ($\iota_{*p}$, $\iota'_{*p}$ injective, Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-tangent}) and their sum $T_pN$ by transversality,
    \[
    \dim \ker H_{*p} = (n - k) + (n - k') - n = n - k - k' ,
    \]
    so by rank--nullity (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)) $\operatorname{rank} H_{*p} = n - (n - k - k') = k + k'$, and $H_{*p}$ is onto the $(k + k')$-dimensional $T_{\vec 0}\mathbb{R}^{k+k'}$.
\end{itemize}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:rvt-local}(2), applied to $H : V \to \mathbb{R}^{k+k'}$ at $p$ with $c = \vec 0$, there is a chart $(W, \hat\theta)$ of $N$ at $p$, $W \subseteq V$, whose last $k + k'$ components vanish exactly on $W \cap H^{-1}(\vec 0) = W \cap S \cap S'$; it is adapted to $S' \cap S$, of codimension $k + k'$. As $p$ was arbitrary, $S' \cap S$ is a regular submanifold of $N$ of codimension $k + k'$ (Definition~\ref{def:submanifold}), of dimension $n - k - k'$, in agreement with Corollary~\ref{cor:transverse-special-cases}(2), where it is a submanifold of codimension $k$ of the $(n - k')$-dimensional $S'$. And Lemma~\ref{lem:rvt-local}(3), with $W' = V$, gives again that its tangent space at $p$ is $\ker H_{*p} = \iota_{*p}(T_pS) \cap \iota'_{*p}(T_pS')$.
\end{proof}

\textit{The picture.} In $\mathbb{R}^3$, if $S_1$ is a surface and $S_2$ a curve, at a point of intersection the tangent plane and the tangent line must add up to all of $\mathbb{R}^3$, so the curve has to pierce the surface. If both are surfaces, two planes add up to $\mathbb{R}^3$ exactly when they are different, and then they meet in a line: the surfaces cut through each other along a curve. The picture is local: it is the vector-space picture of the tangent spaces at a point of intersection.

Codimensions add: $1 + 2 = 3$ for a surface and a curve, a point; $1 + 1 = 2$ for two surfaces, a curve. In the Morse problem of the homework the same thing happened in $T^*M$: the section $s_f = df$ is an embedding, because it is a section, so the question is the same as intersecting the image of this embedding with the zero section (Theorem~\ref{thm:morse-transverse}), and there $m + m = 2m$, the full dimension: the intersection is a set of isolated points.

\section{Fibrations}\label{sec:fibrations}

\roadmark{Stage: bundles}{Submersions that are locally products.}

\textit{References: Lee Ch.~10. Lectures 11--13.} The submersions that look locally like the projection $U \times F \to U$. Their fibres are submanifolds (\ref{sec:rvt-manifolds}), all copies of one fibre; the tangent bundle, later (\ref{sec:tangent-bundle}), is the first major example.

\subsection{Fibrations}\label{sub:fibrations}

\textit{Lecture 11. Fibrations are an important class within the submersions. They are introduced now because the tangent bundle, the cotangent bundle and vector bundles, coming soon, are all fibrations. The idea: surjective maps $\pi : M \to B$ that are locally like the projection $U \times F \to U$, with $U$ open in the \textbf{base} $B$ and $F$ a third, fixed manifold. There is a notation clash: $F$ now names the fibre, not the map, which is called $\pi$.}

\begin{defbox}[Fibration]\deflabel{def:fibration}
Let $M$, $B$ and $F$ be smooth manifolds and $\pi : M \to B$ smooth. Then $\pi$ is a \textbf{fibration with fibre $F$} if there are an open cover $\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ of $B$ and, for each $\alpha$, a diffeomorphism
\[
\phi_\alpha : \pi^{-1}(U_\alpha) \longrightarrow U_\alpha \times F \qquad \text{with} \qquad \mathrm{pr}_1 \circ \phi_\alpha = \pi|_{\pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)},
\]
where $\pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)$ is an open submanifold of $M$ (Definition~\ref{def:open-submanifold-smooth}), $U_\alpha \times F$ a product manifold (Definition~\ref{def:product-manifold}) --- equivalently, an open submanifold of $B \times F$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:open-product}) --- and
\[
\mathrm{pr}_1 : U_\alpha \times F \to U_\alpha, \qquad \mathrm{pr}_1(b, y) = b ,
\]
the projection onto the first factor (Definition~\ref{def:projections}; written $\mathrm{pr}_1$ rather than $\pi_1$ because $\pi$ already names the fibration), which is smooth (Proposition~\ref{prop:product-maps}). The condition $\mathrm{pr}_1 \circ \phi_\alpha = \pi|_{\pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)}$ says that $\phi_\alpha$ keeps the base point: for $x \in \pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)$ the first component of $\phi_\alpha(x)$ is $\pi(x)$, that is, $\phi_\alpha(x) = \big(\pi(x), y\big)$ for some $y \in F$. The $\phi_\alpha$ are called \textbf{local trivializations}. $M$ is the \textbf{total space} and $B$ the \textbf{base}.
\leeref{Ch.~10, smooth fiber bundles}
\end{defbox}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=3em, column sep=4.5em]
\pi^{-1}(U_\alpha) \arrow[rr, "\phi_\alpha", "\cong"'] \arrow[dr, "\pi|"'] & & U_\alpha \times F \arrow[dl, "\mathrm{pr}_1"] \\
& U_\alpha \subseteq B &
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

The diagram \emph{commutes}: all the compositions that can be formed along its arrows from one place to another give the same answer. Here there are two routes from $\pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)$ to $U_\alpha$, and they agree: $\mathrm{pr}_1 \circ \phi_\alpha = \pi|$. Concretely, $\phi_\alpha(p) = (\pi(p), \ast)$ --- its first component \emph{is} $\pi(p)$, and only the second, a point of $F$, is new information.

The cartoon of a fibration. On the left, the global product $B \times F$, with each fibre $\{b\} \times F$ standing over its point. On the right, a total space that need not be a product: its fibres may twist as they travel over $B$. But over each $U_\alpha$ the part $\pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)$ is identified by $\phi_\alpha$ with the straight product $U_\alpha \times F$, and the identification respects the base points, which is the commuting diagram.

\begin{defbox}[Trivial Fibration]\deflabel{def:trivial-fibration}
A fibration $\pi : M \to B$ with fibre $F$ (Definition~\ref{def:fibration}) is \textbf{trivial} if it has a local trivialization over all of $B$: a diffeomorphism $\phi : M \to B \times F$ with $\mathrm{pr}_1 \circ \phi = \pi$.
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[Fibres and Fibrations]\thmlabel{prop:fibration-properties}
Let $\pi : M \to B$ be a fibration with fibre $F$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item For every $b \in B$ and every $\alpha$ with $b \in U_\alpha$, the local trivialization $\phi_\alpha$ restricts to a bijection $\pi^{-1}(b) \to \{b\} \times F$, which is a homeomorphism for the subspace topologies; so the fibre $\pi^{-1}(b)$ is homeomorphic to $F$: every fibre is a copy of the model fibre.
    \item $\pi$ is a submersion, and it is surjective if $F \ne \emptyset$.
    \item $\pi$ is an open map.
\end{enumerate}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Stated in lecture; (2) by the chain rule.)} Throughout, recall from Definition~\ref{def:fibration} that the sets $U_\alpha$ cover $B$, that each $\pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)$ is open in $M$ (the preimage of an open set under the continuous map $\pi$), and that on it $\pi = \mathrm{pr}_1 \circ \phi_\alpha$ --- the commuting diagram.

\emph{(1)} Fix $b \in B$ and $\alpha$ with $b \in U_\alpha$ (there is one, the $U_\alpha$ covering $B$); then $\pi^{-1}(b) \subseteq \pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)$, the domain of $\phi_\alpha$.

\emph{$\phi_\alpha$ maps $\pi^{-1}(b)$ onto $\mathrm{pr}_1^{-1}(b) = \{b\} \times F$.} This is where the commuting diagram and the bijectivity of $\phi_\alpha$ are used. If $x \in \pi^{-1}(b)$, then $\mathrm{pr}_1(\phi_\alpha(x)) = \pi(x) = b$, so $\phi_\alpha(x) \in \{b\} \times F$. Conversely, if $(b, f) \in \{b\} \times F \subseteq U_\alpha \times F$, then $x = \phi_\alpha^{-1}(b, f)$ is defined, $\phi_\alpha$ being a bijection onto $U_\alpha \times F$, and
\[
\pi(x) = \mathrm{pr}_1\big(\phi_\alpha(x)\big) = \mathrm{pr}_1(b, f) = b ,
\]
so $x \in \pi^{-1}(b)$ with $\phi_\alpha(x) = (b, f)$. Thus $\phi_\alpha$ restricts to a bijection $\pi^{-1}(b) \to \{b\} \times F$.

\emph{The restriction is a homeomorphism with the subspace topologies.} $\phi_\alpha$ is a diffeomorphism, in particular a homeomorphism, so its restriction to the subset $\pi^{-1}(b)$ is a homeomorphism onto its image $\{b\} \times F$ (Proposition~\ref{fact:cont}(3)). The subspace topology of $\pi^{-1}(b)$ is the same whether it is taken from $\pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)$ or from $M$, since $\big(O \cap \pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)\big) \cap \pi^{-1}(b) = O \cap \pi^{-1}(b)$ for every $O$ open in $M$.

\emph{$\{b\} \times F$ is a copy of $F$.} The map $\{b\} \times F \to F$, $(b, f) \mapsto f$, is a homeomorphism, with inverse $f \mapsto (b, f)$. The first is the restriction of the projection $\mathrm{pr}_2$, which is continuous; the second is continuous into $U_\alpha \times F$ because its two components, the constant map $b$ and $\mathrm{id}_F$, are continuous (Proposition~\ref{fact:cont}(4)), hence continuous into the subspace $\{b\} \times F$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:univ-subspace}(2)); and the two maps are inverse to each other. Composing, $\pi^{-1}(b) \to \{b\} \times F \to F$ is a homeomorphism.

\emph{(2)} \emph{$\pi$ is a submersion.} Fix $p \in M$; we show that $\pi_{*p}$ is onto $T_{\pi(p)}B$. Choose $\alpha$ with $\pi(p) \in U_\alpha$, let $W = \pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)$, an open submanifold of $M$ containing $p$, and write $\pi|_W : W \to U_\alpha$ for the restriction. On the open set $W$, $\pi|_W = \mathrm{pr}_1 \circ \phi_\alpha$; by the Chain Rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}),
\[
(\pi|_W)_{*p} = (\mathrm{pr}_1)_{*\phi_\alpha(p)} \circ (\phi_\alpha)_{*p} ,
\]
a composite of an isomorphism and a surjection. Indeed $(\phi_\alpha)_{*p}$ is an isomorphism because $\phi_\alpha$ is a diffeomorphism (Corollary~\ref{lem:germs-diffeo}), and $(\mathrm{pr}_1)_{*\phi_\alpha(p)}$ is onto because the projection of the product manifold $U_\alpha \times F$ onto its first factor is a submersion (Example~\ref{ex:product-projection-submersion}, with $M_1 = U_\alpha$ and $M_2 = F$). So, given $w \in T_{\pi(p)}U_\alpha$, choose $u$ with $(\mathrm{pr}_1)_{*\phi_\alpha(p)}u = w$ and put $v = (\phi_\alpha)_{*p}^{-1}u$; then $(\pi|_W)_{*p}v = w$, and $(\pi|_W)_{*p}$ is onto.

It remains to pass from $\pi|_W$ to $\pi$. With the inclusions $\iota_W : W \hookrightarrow M$ and $\iota_{U_\alpha} : U_\alpha \hookrightarrow B$ we have $\pi \circ \iota_W = \iota_{U_\alpha} \circ \pi|_W$, so by the Chain Rule
\[
\pi_{*p} \circ (\iota_W)_{*p} = (\iota_{U_\alpha})_{*\pi(p)} \circ (\pi|_W)_{*p} .
\]
The right side is onto $T_{\pi(p)}B$, because $(\iota_{U_\alpha})_{*\pi(p)}$ is an isomorphism (Lemma~\ref{lem:germs-local}) and $(\pi|_W)_{*p}$ is onto. Hence the left side is onto, and therefore so is $\pi_{*p}$. As $p$ was arbitrary, $\pi$ is a submersion (Definition~\ref{def:submersion}).

\emph{$\pi$ is surjective if $F \neq \emptyset$.} Every $b$ lies in some $U_\alpha$, and its fibre is a copy of $F$ by (1), nonempty if $F$ is; any $x \in \pi^{-1}(b)$ has $\pi(x) = b$.

\emph{(3)} By (2), $\pi$ is a submersion, so by Corollary~\ref{cor:submersion-open-map} $\pi(O)$ is open in $B$ for every open $O \subseteq M$: $\pi$ is an open map.
\end{proof}

The Hopf fibration $S^{2n+1} \to \mathbb{CP}^n$, the first example of a fibration, and its local but not global sections are collected in Section~\ref{sec:ex-hopf}.

\begin{rembox}[What Comes Next]\label{rem:what-comes-next}
Tangent bundles, cotangent bundles and vector bundles are fibrations with additional structure, where the fibres are vector spaces. The basic notion of fibration is more general: its fibre $F$ is any manifold.
\end{rembox}

\textbf{Transcription note.} Stating the idea of a fibration, Uribe first said ``$U$ open in $M$''; a student corrected it to open in $B$, as in the definition.

\subsection{Fibres}\label{sub:fibrations-revisited}

\textit{Lecture 12. The notation changes once more, to conform to more general usage: the fibration is $\pi : E \to B$, with total space $E$, base $B$, and fibre $F$ --- the definition as before (Definition~\ref{def:fibration}), with $E$ in place of $M$.}

\begin{propbox}[Fibres Are Copies of the Model Fibre]\thmlabel{prop:fibres-diffeo}
Let $\pi : E \to B$ be a fibration with fibre $F$ and $b \in B$. Then $\pi^{-1}(b)$ is a regular submanifold of $E$, and for every $\alpha$ with $b \in U_\alpha$ the local trivialization $\phi_\alpha$ restricts to a diffeomorphism
\[
\pi^{-1}(b) \longrightarrow \{b\} \times F \cong F .
\]
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Claimed in Lecture~12; filled in.)} Three things are claimed: $\pi^{-1}(b)$ is a regular submanifold of $E$; $\phi_\alpha$ restricts to a diffeomorphism $\pi^{-1}(b) \to \{b\} \times F$; and $\{b\} \times F$ is diffeomorphic to $F$.

\emph{The two submanifolds.} $\pi$ is a submersion (Proposition~\ref{prop:fibration-properties}(2)), so its fibre $\pi^{-1}(b)$ is a regular submanifold of $E$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:submersion-fibres}). Likewise the projection $\mathrm{pr}_1 : U_\alpha \times F \to U_\alpha$ is a submersion (Example~\ref{ex:product-projection-submersion}), so its fibre $\{b\} \times F = \mathrm{pr}_1^{-1}(b)$ is a regular submanifold of $U_\alpha \times F$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:submersion-fibres} again). Both carry their induced smooth structures (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-structure}).

\emph{A bijection.} Because the diagram commutes, $\phi_\alpha$ maps $\pi^{-1}(b)$ bijectively onto $\{b\} \times F$: this is Proposition~\ref{prop:fibration-properties}(1), for this $\alpha$; explicitly, $\mathrm{pr}_1(\phi_\alpha(x)) = \pi(x) = b$ for $x \in \pi^{-1}(b)$, and $\pi\big(\phi_\alpha^{-1}(b, f)\big) = \mathrm{pr}_1(b, f) = b$ for $(b, f) \in \{b\} \times F$. Write $\Phi : \pi^{-1}(b) \to \{b\} \times F$ for the restriction of $\phi_\alpha$; its inverse is the restriction of $\phi_\alpha^{-1}$ to $\{b\} \times F$.

\emph{$\Phi$ is smooth.} The inclusion $\iota : \pi^{-1}(b) \hookrightarrow E$ is smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}(1)). It takes values in the open subset $\pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)$, so it is also smooth as a map into the open submanifold $\pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)$, whose smooth charts are the charts of $E$ with domain inside $\pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)$. Hence $\phi_\alpha \circ \iota : \pi^{-1}(b) \to U_\alpha \times F$ is smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}). It takes values in the submanifold $\{b\} \times F$, so it is smooth as a map into $\{b\} \times F$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}(2)); that map is $\Phi$.

\emph{$\Phi^{-1}$ is smooth.} The inclusion $\iota' : \{b\} \times F \hookrightarrow U_\alpha \times F$ is smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}(1)), and $\phi_\alpha^{-1} \circ \iota'$ is smooth into $\pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)$, hence into $E$, the inclusion of an open submanifold being smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}). It takes values in the submanifold $\pi^{-1}(b)$, so it is smooth as a map into $\pi^{-1}(b)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}(2)); that map is $\Phi^{-1}$. So $\Phi$ is a diffeomorphism (Definition~\ref{def:diffeomorphism}): the restriction and its inverse are smooth as maps into $U_\alpha \times F$ and into $E$, hence smooth into the submanifolds $\{b\} \times F$ and $\pi^{-1}(b)$.

\emph{$\{b\} \times F \cong F$.} Finally $\{b\} \times F \to F$, $(b, f) \mapsto f$, is a diffeomorphism by the same lemma, with inverse $f \mapsto (b, f)$. Explicitly: the first map is $\mathrm{pr}_2 \circ \iota'$, smooth because $\mathrm{pr}_2$ and $\iota'$ are (Proposition~\ref{prop:product-maps}, Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}(1)). The second is the slice inclusion $\iota^{b} : F \to U_\alpha \times F$, $f \mapsto (b, f)$ (Definition~\ref{def:slice-inclusions}), smooth by Proposition~\ref{prop:product-maps}; it takes values in $\{b\} \times F$, so it is smooth into $\{b\} \times F$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}(2). The two maps are inverse to each other. Composing with $\Phi$ gives the diffeomorphism $\pi^{-1}(b) \to \{b\} \times F \cong F$.
\end{proof}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=4.4em, row sep=2.8em]
\pi^{-1}(b) \arrow[r, hook] \arrow[d, "\phi_\alpha|"', "\cong"] & \pi^{-1}(U_\alpha) \arrow[d, "\phi_\alpha", "\cong"'] \\
\{b\} \times F \arrow[r, hook] \arrow[d, "\mathrm{pr}_2"', "\cong"] & U_\alpha \times F \\
F &
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

The fibre over $b$ and the model fibre. The trivialization $\phi_\alpha$ carries the submanifold $\pi^{-1}(b)$ onto the submanifold $\{b\} \times F$ --- this is where the commuting triangle of Definition~\ref{def:fibration} is used --- and $\mathrm{pr}_2$ identifies that with $F$.

This upgrades Proposition~\ref{prop:fibration-properties}(1) from homeomorphic to diffeomorphic. Not every submersion has this property: its fibres are submanifolds, but they can change type from one point to another.

\begin{exbox}[A Submersion That Is Not a Fibration]\exlabel{ex:punctured-plane}
Let $E = \mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{(0, 1)\}$ and $\pi : E \to \mathbb{R}$, $\pi(x, y) = x$. Then $\pi$ is a surjective submersion, but not a fibration.
\end{exbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~12.)} Three things are claimed: $\pi$ is a submersion, it is onto, and it is not a fibration.

\emph{Submersion.} $E$ is open in $\mathbb{R}^2$, the complement of the closed set $\{(0, 1)\}$. $\pi$ is the restriction of the projection $\mathrm{pr} : \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ to an open subset, so it is a submersion (Example~\ref{ex:projection-submersion}, with $k = l = 1$). In detail: with $\iota_E : E \hookrightarrow \mathbb{R}^2$ the inclusion, $\pi = \mathrm{pr} \circ \iota_E$, so by the Chain Rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}) $\pi_{*q} = \mathrm{pr}_{*q} \circ (\iota_E)_{*q}$ for $q \in E$; here $(\iota_E)_{*q}$ is an isomorphism (Lemma~\ref{lem:germs-local}) and $\mathrm{pr}_{*q}$ is onto, so $\pi_{*q}$ is onto.

\emph{Onto.} For $x \in \mathbb{R}$, the point $(x, 0)$ is not $(0, 1)$, so it lies in $E$, and $\pi(x, 0) = x$.

\emph{The fibres.} Its fibres are the vertical lines $\{x\} \times \mathbb{R}$ for $x \ne 0$, except for one: over $0$ the fibre is $\{0\} \times (\mathbb{R} \setminus \{1\})$, a vertical line with a point missing, that is, two half-lines. Indeed $\pi^{-1}(x) = \{(x, y) : (x, y) \neq (0, 1)\}$, and the excluded point has $x = 0$.

\emph{Not a fibration.} If $\pi$ were a fibration with fibre $F$, all fibres would be diffeomorphic to $F$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:fibres-diffeo}), hence to each other (compose one diffeomorphism with the inverse of the other), and in particular homeomorphic. But $\{1\} \times \mathbb{R}$ is connected and $\{0\} \times (\mathbb{R} \setminus \{1\})$ is not, and connectedness is preserved by homeomorphisms. In detail: $\{1\} \times \mathbb{R}$ is homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}$ by $(1, y) \mapsto y$, hence connected (Proposition~\ref{fact:conn}(4)). $\{0\} \times (\mathbb{R} \setminus \{1\})$ is the union of the two disjoint nonempty sets $\{0\} \times (-\infty, 1)$ and $\{0\} \times (1, \infty)$, each open in it, being its intersection with the open half-plane $\{y < 1\}$, resp.\ $\{y > 1\}$; so it is not connected. And the image of a connected space under a homeomorphism, a continuous map, is connected (Proposition~\ref{fact:conn}(1)).
\end{proof}

The converse question: if all the fibres of a surjective submersion are diffeomorphic to one manifold, must it be a fibration? It was raised in Lecture~12 and answered at the start of Lecture~13: yes when $\pi$ is proper, no in general (Theorem~\ref{thm:ehresmann} and Example~\ref{ex:ehresmann-counter} below).

\subsection{When Is a Submersion a Fibration?}\label{sub:ehresmann}

\textit{Lecture 13 (Wed Sep 30). The answer to the question left open in Lecture~12: no in general, but there is a partial yes.}

\begin{thmbox}[Ehresmann's Theorem]\thmlabel{thm:ehresmann}
Let $\pi : E \to B$ be a surjective submersion which is \emph{proper}: the preimage of every compact set is compact. If $B$ is connected, then $\pi$ is a fibration.
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}[Proof (to be filled)]
Stated in Lecture~13, not proved: the proof uses connections, which the course does not cover. To be filled.
\end{proof}

\textit{Status.} Stated in Lecture~13, not proved: the proof uses connections, which the course does not cover. The lecture first recalled the case of a compact fibre, then the general statement for proper maps, which is the form given here. The intuition: a connection lets one lift a path from $b$ to $b'$ in the base to paths in $E$, and flow the fibre over $b$ onto the fibre over $b'$; properness is what lets the flow run for as long as needed, so that it identifies the fibres not just one at a time but over a whole neighbourhood --- a local trivialization. The transcript renders the name as ``Aristotle''; it is Ehresmann.

\begin{exbox}[All Fibres Diffeomorphic but Not a Fibration]\exlabel{ex:ehresmann-counter}
Let
\[
E = \big\{ (x, y, t) \in \mathbb{R}^3 : (x, y) \ne (0, 0), \ \text{and } (x, y) \ne (t, 0) \text{ if } t \ne 0, \ (x, y) \ne (1, 0) \text{ if } t = 0 \big\},
\]
and $\pi(x, y, t) = t$. Then $\pi : E \to \mathbb{R}$ is a surjective submersion, and every fibre is the plane minus two points:
\[
\pi^{-1}(t) \cong \begin{cases} \mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{(0,0), (t,0)\}, & t \ne 0, \\ \mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{(0,0), (1,0)\}, & t = 0, \end{cases}
\]
all diffeomorphic to one another. But $\pi$ is not a fibration.
\end{exbox}

\begin{proof}[Proof (partial)]
\textit{(Completion.)} $E$ is open in $\mathbb{R}^3$: its complement is the $t$-axis $\{(0,0,t)\}$, together with the line $\{(t, 0, t)\}$ and the single point $(1, 0, 0)$, a closed set. So $\pi$ is the restriction of a projection to an open set, hence a submersion (Example~\ref{ex:projection-submersion}), and it is onto. Any two copies of the plane with two points removed are diffeomorphic by an affine map.

\emph{Not a fibration (sketch).} \textit{(Not from lecture; filled in. The argument uses the fundamental group, which these notes do not develop; it is a sketch for that reason.)} Suppose $\pi$ were a fibration with fibre $F$. By Definition~\ref{def:fibration} some open $U \ni 0$ of $\mathbb{R}$ would carry a local trivialization $\phi : \pi^{-1}(U) \to U \times F$ with $\mathrm{pr}_1 \circ \phi = \pi$. Choose $\varepsilon > 0$ with $I = (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \subseteq U$. Since $\mathrm{pr}_1 \circ \phi = \pi$, $\phi$ maps $\pi^{-1}(I)$ onto $I \times F$, and $F$ is diffeomorphic to the fibre $\pi^{-1}(0)$, the plane minus two points (Proposition~\ref{prop:fibres-diffeo}). So $\pi^{-1}(I)$ would be homeomorphic to $I \times \big(\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{\text{two points}\}\big)$. We compare fundamental groups.
\begin{itemize}
    \item $I \times \big(\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{\text{two points}\}\big)$ deformation retracts onto a copy of $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{\text{two points}\}$, the interval $I$ being contractible; its fundamental group is free of rank $2$.
    \item By the definition of $E$, a point $(x, y, t)$ with $t \in I$ fails to lie in $E$ exactly when $(x, y) = (0, 0)$, or $t \ne 0$ and $(x, y) = (t, 0)$, or $t = 0$ and $(x, y) = (1, 0)$. So
    \[
    \pi^{-1}(I) = \big(\mathbb{R}^2 \times I\big) \setminus \big(L_0 \cup L_1 \cup \{P\}\big), \qquad L_0 = \{(0, 0, t) : t \in I\}, \quad L_1 = \{(t, 0, t) : t \in I\}, \quad P = (1, 0, 0) ,
    \]
    where $L_0$ and $L_1$ are two segments of lines through the origin, which is their only common point, and $P$ lies on neither. The slab $\mathbb{R}^2 \times I$ is star-shaped about the origin, and $L_0 \cup L_1$ is its intersection with two lines through the origin; so moving each point along its ray from the origin deformation retracts $(\mathbb{R}^2 \times I) \setminus (L_0 \cup L_1)$ onto the sphere of radius $\varepsilon/2$ about the origin minus the four points where the two lines pierce it. A sphere minus four points is homeomorphic to a plane minus three points, whose fundamental group is free of rank $3$. Removing the further point $P$ from this $3$-dimensional manifold does not change the fundamental group: in dimension $3$, loops and homotopies between loops can be moved off a point.
\end{itemize}
Free groups of ranks $2$ and $3$ are not isomorphic (their abelianizations are $\mathbb{Z}^2$ and $\mathbb{Z}^3$), while homeomorphic spaces have isomorphic fundamental groups. This contradiction shows that there is no local trivialization over any neighbourhood of $0$, so $\pi$ is not a fibration.
\end{proof}

\textit{Status.} From a mathematics forum (located with ChatGPT); given in lecture as a picture, without proof. That $\pi$ is not a fibration was stated, not proved, there; the proof above is complete except for the facts about fundamental groups that the sketch quotes. The intuition: as $t \to 0$ the missing point $(t, 0)$ collides with $(0,0)$, while over $t = 0$ the second missing point sits away at $(1, 0)$. \textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} The example is subtler than it looks: the failure is not visible in any single fibre, each of which is a plane minus two points; it lies in the way the fibres over a neighbourhood of $0$ fit together, and it takes the fundamental group of $\pi^{-1}(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$ to detect it, because that set is connected, like the product it is compared with. With lines in place of planes the corresponding map is not locally trivial either, and there counting connected components is enough: for $E' = \{(x, t) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : x \ne 0, \ \text{and } x \ne t \text{ if } t \ne 0, \ x \ne 1 \text{ if } t = 0\}$ and $\pi'(x, t) = t$, every fibre is a line minus two points, but $\pi'^{-1}(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$ is the strip $\mathbb{R} \times (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$ minus the two crossing lines $x = 0$ and $x = t$ and the point $(1, 0)$, which has four connected components ($x < \min(0, t)$; $x > \max(0, t)$ without the point $(1, 0)$; $0 < x < t$; $t < x < 0$), while the product of $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$ with a line minus two points has three.

\subsection{Sections and Local Sections}\label{sub:local-sections}

\textit{From Assignment~4, Problem~4, whose hint --- ``declare that $\Phi_i \circ s_i$ includes $U_i \to U_i \times \{1\}$, and extend the definition of $\Phi_i$ by equivariance'' --- contains a general principle: local trivializations and local sections are two descriptions of the same thing.}

\begin{defbox}[Section]\deflabel{def:section}
Let $\pi : E \to B$ be a fibration. A \textbf{section} of $\pi$ is a smooth map $s : B \to E$ with $\pi \circ s = \mathrm{id}_B$: going up by $s$ and then down by $\pi$ gives the identity on the base. It picks, smoothly in $b$, one point $s(b)$ of each fibre $\pi^{-1}(b)$.
\leeref{Ch.~10, \emph{Sections of Vector Bundles}}
\end{defbox}

E \arrow[d, shift right=0.9ex, "\pi"'] \\
B \arrow[u, shift right=0.9ex, "s"']
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad
\raisebox{1.6em}{$\pi \circ s = \mathrm{id}_B$}
\end{center}

A section goes up, the projection comes down, and the round trip is the identity on the base.
