The key step. $V$ may contain other parts of $F(M)$ (black) besides $F(U)$ (orange). Because $F(U)$ is open in $F(M)$, it is $W \cap F(M)$ for an open $W$ (shaded), and $W$ cuts the other parts away; $F(M)$ continues beyond $F(U)$ only by leaving $W$. For the irrational line no such $W$ exists, which is exactly the failure of openness.

\textbf{Transcription note.} Page~39 of the handwritten notes writes the target as $F(M) \cap V = \{0 = y^{n-m+1} = \cdots = y^m\}$; the vanishing coordinates are the last $n - m$ of them, $y^{m+1}, \ldots, y^n$, as the lecture said.

\begin{rembox}[Where Is Injectivity Used?]\label{rem:where-injectivity-used}
In lecture the use of injectivity was first located at the last equality. But $(*)$ concerns only $F(U)$, and the proof needs only that $F$ be an immersion which is open onto its image. Covering-type maps show that a map need not be injective for its image to be a manifold (Examples~\ref{ex:line-circle-noninjective-image} and~\ref{ex:sphere-rp2-noninjective-image} below).

\emph{The conclusion, confirmed in Uribe's follow-up email.} The proof given shows that for an immersion that is open as a map onto its image (so for all $U$ open in $M$, $F(U)$ is open in $F(M)$), $F(M)$ is a submanifold; the map $F$ does not have to be injective. The proof uses exactly two things: the normal form (the immersion hypothesis), and that $F(U)$ is open in $F(M)$ for the $U$ of the normal form; with the completion via Corollary~\ref{cor:immersion-local-image} nothing else enters. Injectivity belongs to the \emph{idea} of an embedding --- an isomorphism between $M$ and its image (Corollary~\ref{cor:embedding-diffeo}) --- not to this proof. Immersions that are open maps onto their images form an unusual class of maps.
\end{rembox}

\begin{exbox}[A Non-Injective Map onto the Circle]\exlabel{ex:line-circle-noninjective-image}
The map $F : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^2$, $F(t) = (\cos t, \sin t)$, is not injective, but its image $S^1$ is a regular submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^2$.

\emph{Not injective.} $F(0) = (1, 0) = F(2\pi)$.

\emph{The image is $S^1$.} $\cos^2 t + \sin^2 t = 1$, so $F(\mathbb{R}) \subseteq S^1$; and every point of $S^1$ is $(\cos t, \sin t)$ for some $t$, its polar angle, so $F(\mathbb{R}) = S^1$.

\emph{$S^1$ is a regular submanifold.} $S^1 = g^{-1}(1)$ for $g(x, y) = x^2 + y^2$, and $dg = 2x\, dx + 2y\, dy$ vanishes only at the origin, which is not on $S^1$; so $1$ is a regular value of $g$, and $S^1$ is a regular submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^2$ of codimension $1$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:rvt-manifolds}.

$F$ is moreover an immersion ($F'(t) = (-\sin t, \cos t) \neq 0$) that is open onto its image: as a map into $S^1$ it is a local diffeomorphism (Example~\ref{ex:line-circle}), and a local diffeomorphism is an open map. So it is an instance of Proposition~\ref{prop:immersion-open-image} below.
\end{exbox}

\begin{exbox}[{The Two-to-One Map $S^2 \to \mathbb{RP}^2$}]\exlabel{ex:sphere-rp2-noninjective-image}
The projection $\pi : S^2 \to \mathbb{RP}^2$, $x \mapsto [x]$, is two-to-one, so not injective, but its image is the manifold $\mathbb{RP}^2$.

\emph{Two-to-one.} For $x, y \in S^2$, $[x] = [y]$ means $y = \lambda x$ for a real $\lambda \neq 0$; then $1 = |y| = |\lambda|\,|x| = |\lambda|$, so $\lambda = \pm 1$. Hence $\pi^{-1}([x]) = \{x, -x\}$, two distinct points since $x \neq 0$.

\emph{The image.} Every point of $\mathbb{RP}^2$ is a line $[y]$, $y \neq 0$, and $y/|y| \in S^2$ lies on it; so $\pi$ is onto. Its image $\mathbb{RP}^2$ is a smooth manifold (Corollary~\ref{cor:rpn-atlas}), a regular submanifold of codimension $0$ of itself (Proposition~\ref{prop:open-codim0}(1)). That $\pi$ is a local diffeomorphism is Example~\ref{ex:sn-rpn}, later.
\end{exbox}

\begin{propbox}[Immersions That Are Open onto Their Images]\thmlabel{prop:immersion-open-image}
Let $F : M \to N$ be an immersion, with $\dim M = m$ and $\dim N = n$, such that $F : M \to F(M)$ is an open map, $F(M)$ carrying the subspace topology. Then $F(M)$ is a regular submanifold of $N$ of codimension $n - m$.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(The conclusion of the class discussion, confirmed in Uribe's follow-up email.)} The proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image}, word for word: openness of $F$ onto its image is all it used to produce $W$. Written out, with the one changed justification marked:

Let $q = F(p) \in F(M)$; we need an adapted chart at $q$. \emph{Normal form.} $F$ is an immersion, so Theorem~\ref{thm:immersion-normal-form} gives charts $(U, \varphi)$ at $p$ and $(V, \psi = (y^1, \ldots, y^n))$ at $q$, and Corollary~\ref{cor:immersion-local-image} gives an open $V' \subseteq V$ containing $F(U)$ with
\[
F(U) = \{\, x \in V' : y^{m+1}(x) = \cdots = y^n(x) = 0 \,\}. \tag{$*$}
\]
Neither result uses injectivity of $F$: the injectivity used in the corollary is that of the chart $\psi$. \emph{Openness} (the changed step). $U$ is open in $M$ and, by hypothesis, $F : M \to F(M)$ is an open map, so $F(U)$ is open in $F(M)$; since $F(M)$ carries the subspace topology, $F(U) = W \cap F(M)$ for some open $W \subseteq N$ (Definition~\ref{def:subspace}). In Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image} this step used that $F$ is a homeomorphism onto its image, but only through its consequence that $F$ is open onto its image. \emph{Shrinking.} Since $F(U) \subseteq V'$ and $F(U) = W \cap F(M) \subseteq W$,
\[
F(M) \cap (V' \cap W) = \big(F(M) \cap W\big) \cap V' = F(U) \cap V' = F(U) = F(U) \cap W = \{\, x \in V' \cap W : y^{m+1}(x) = \cdots = y^n(x) = 0 \,\},
\]
the last equality by $(*)$ intersected with $W$. So the smooth chart $(V' \cap W, \psi|_{V' \cap W})$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(1), $V' \cap W$ being an open subset of $V$), whose domain contains $q$, is adapted at $q$ (Definition~\ref{def:adapted-chart}, with $k = n - m$), and $F(M)$ is a regular submanifold of codimension $n - m$.

For example, $t \mapsto (\cos t, \sin t)$ is an immersion of $\mathbb{R}$, open onto $S^1$ and far from injective --- every point of $S^1$ has infinitely many preimages --- and its image $S^1$ is a submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^2$. (It is an immersion into $\mathbb{R}^2$ because its velocity $(-\sin t, \cos t)$ never vanishes, as in Example~\ref{ex:nodal-cubic}. It is open onto $S^1$ because it is a local diffeomorphism onto $S^1$ (Example~\ref{ex:line-circle}): each $t$ has an open neighbourhood $U_t$ mapped homeomorphically onto an open subset of $S^1$, so for $O \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ open the image of $O \cap U_t$ is open in that subset, hence in $S^1$, and the image of $O$ is the union of these open sets.) The figure-eight is not open onto its image, consistent with its image not being a submanifold. (For $\beta(t) = (\sin 2t, \sin t)$ on $(-\pi, \pi)$, the set $\beta\big((-\pi/2, \pi/2)\big)$ is not open in the image: every open set of $\mathbb{R}^2$ around $\beta(0) = (0, 0)$ contains $\beta(t)$ for $t$ near $\pm\pi$, because $\beta(t) \to (\sin(\pm 2\pi), \sin(\pm\pi)) = (0, 0)$ as $t \to \pm\pi$, and these points are not in $\beta\big((-\pi/2, \pi/2)\big)$ since $\beta$ is injective.)
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[An Embedding Is a Diffeomorphism onto Its Image]\thmlabel{cor:embedding-diffeo}
If $F : M \to N$ is an embedding, then $F : M \to F(M)$ is a diffeomorphism, $F(M)$ carrying its induced smooth structure as a regular submanifold.
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Stated in Lecture~14; filled in.)} Write $\bar F : M \to F(M)$ for $F$ regarded as a map onto its image and $\iota : F(M) \hookrightarrow N$ for the inclusion, so that $F = \iota \circ \bar F$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image}, $F(M)$ is a regular submanifold of $N$ of codimension $n - m$, so with its induced structure it is a smooth manifold of dimension $n - (n - m) = m$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-structure}).

\emph{Smooth.} $F$ is smooth into $N$ with values in $F(M)$, so $\bar F : M \to F(M)$ is smooth by Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}(2).

\emph{Immersion.} Its differential followed by the injective $\iota_*$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-tangent}) is the injective $F_*$: by the Chain Rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}), $F_{*p} = \iota_{*F(p)} \circ \bar F_{*p}$ for $p \in M$. If $\bar F_{*p} v = 0$, then $F_{*p} v = \iota_{*F(p)}(0) = 0$, so $v = 0$ because $F$ is an immersion. So $\bar F_{*p}$ is injective for every $p$.

\emph{Local diffeomorphism.} Both manifolds have dimension $m$ and $\bar F$ is an immersion at every point, so it is a local diffeomorphism (Proposition~\ref{prop:dimension-constraints}(3)).

\emph{Diffeomorphism.} $\bar F$ is bijective: injective because $F : M \to F(M)$ is a homeomorphism (Definition~\ref{def:embedding}), and onto $F(M)$ by the definition of $F(M)$. Being a bijective local diffeomorphism, it is a diffeomorphism, its inverse being smooth near every point (Corollary~\ref{cor:bijective-local-diffeo}).
\end{proof}

\subsection{Proper Maps}\label{sub:proper-maps}

\textit{Lecture 14. When is an injective immersion an embedding? The homeomorphism condition is point-set topology, and a convenient sufficient condition is properness --- the same hypothesis as in Ehresmann's theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:ehresmann}).}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Definition~\ref{def:proper} (Proper Map).} A continuous map is \textbf{proper} if the preimage of every compact set is compact.
\end{quote}

In symbols: a continuous map $F : X \to Y$ is proper if $F^{-1}(K)$ is compact for every compact $K \subseteq Y$. (Lee, App.~A, \emph{Proper Maps}.)

\begin{propbox}[Proper Maps into Manifolds Are Closed]\thmlabel{prop:proper-closed}
Let $F : M \to N$ be a continuous proper map, $N$ a topological manifold. Then $F$ is closed: $F(C)$ is closed in $N$ for every closed $C \subseteq M$.
\leeref{Theorem A.57}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~14. Claim~2 was not finished in lecture; the complete proof came in Uribe's follow-up email, and the completion of Claim~2 below is the notes' own.)} Let $C \subseteq M$ be closed. We show $\overline{F(C)} \subseteq F(C)$, so that $F(C)$ is closed. Recall that $N$, a topological manifold, is Hausdorff, and that a point lies in the closure of a set $A$ exactly when every open set containing the point meets $A$.

\emph{Claim 1: $F(C) \cap K$ is closed for every compact $K \subseteq N$.} $F^{-1}(K)$ is compact, because $F$ is proper (Definition~\ref{def:proper}). So $C \cap F^{-1}(K)$, a closed subset of it, is compact: it is closed in the subspace $F^{-1}(K)$, its complement there being $(M \setminus C) \cap F^{-1}(K)$, and a closed subset of a compact space is compact (Proposition~\ref{fact:compact}(5)). Its image $F\big(C \cap F^{-1}(K)\big)$ is compact, as the continuous image of a compact space (Proposition~\ref{fact:compact}(2)), hence closed in the Hausdorff space $N$ (Proposition~\ref{fact:compact}(4)). And $F\big(C \cap F^{-1}(K)\big) = F(C) \cap K$: a point of the left side is $F(c)$ with $c \in C$ and $F(c) \in K$, hence lies in $F(C) \cap K$; and conversely, a point $y \in F(C) \cap K$ is $y = F(c)$ with $c \in C$, and $F(c) = y \in K$ gives $c \in F^{-1}(K)$.

\emph{Claim 2.} Let $q \in \overline{F(C)}$, and let $V$ be a neighbourhood of $q$ with compact closure (Proposition~\ref{prop:locally-compact}). Then $q \in \overline{F(C) \cap \overline V}$. \textit{(Completion.)} If $O$ is any open set containing $q$, then $O \cap V$ is an open set containing $q$, so it meets $F(C)$; hence $O$ meets $F(C) \cap V \subseteq F(C) \cap \overline V$.

\emph{Conclusion.} By Claim~1 with $K = \overline V$, the set $F(C) \cap \overline V$ is closed, so it equals its closure, and $q \in F(C) \cap \overline V \subseteq F(C)$. As $q \in \overline{F(C)}$ was arbitrary, $\overline{F(C)} \subseteq F(C)$; the reverse inclusion always holds. Thus $\overline{F(C)} = F(C)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{thmbox}[Injective Proper Immersions Are Embeddings]\thmlabel{thm:proper-embedding}
An injective proper immersion $F : M \to N$ is an embedding.
\leeref{Proposition 4.22}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~14 reduced this to Proposition~\ref{prop:proper-closed}; the last step is filled in.)} $F$ is an immersion by hypothesis, so by Definition~\ref{def:embedding} it remains to see that $F : M \to F(M)$ is a homeomorphism, $F(M)$ carrying the subspace topology.

It is a continuous bijection: continuous into $F(M)$ because it is continuous into $N$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:univ-subspace}(2)), injective by hypothesis, and onto $F(M)$ by the definition of $F(M)$. Let $G : F(M) \to M$ be its inverse. A map is continuous when the preimage of every closed set is closed (take complements in the definition of continuity), and for $C \subseteq M$ the preimage $G^{-1}(C)$ is $F(C)$. If $C \subseteq M$ is closed, then $F(C)$ is closed in $N$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:proper-closed} ($F$ is continuous and proper, and $N$ is a manifold), hence $F(C) = F(C) \cap F(M)$ is closed in $F(M)$: its complement in $F(M)$ is $(N \setminus F(C)) \cap F(M)$, open in the subspace topology (Definition~\ref{def:subspace}). So the inverse $F(M) \to M$ is continuous, and $F : M \to F(M)$ is a homeomorphism.
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[Injective Immersions of Compact Manifolds]\thmlabel{cor:compact-embedding}
If $M$ is compact, every injective immersion $F : M \to N$ is an embedding.
\leeref{Proposition 4.22}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(From Uribe's follow-up email; the proof is filled in.)} $F$ is proper (Definition~\ref{def:proper}): if $K \subseteq N$ is compact, it is closed, as a compact subset of the Hausdorff space $N$ (Proposition~\ref{fact:compact}(4)); so $F^{-1}(K)$ is closed in $M$, $F$ being continuous; and a closed subset of the compact $M$ is compact (Proposition~\ref{fact:compact}(5)). So $F$ is an injective proper immersion. Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:proper-embedding}: $F$ is an embedding.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Closedness and Density}\label{sub:closedness-density}

\textit{Why does density of the irrational line rule out an embedding? Because the image of an embedding is always closed \emph{locally}, and a dense set that is locally closed is open. Prompted by Assignment~4, Problem~5.}

\begin{defbox}[Locally Closed Subset]\deflabel{def:locally-closed}
A subset $S$ of a topological space $N$ is \textbf{locally closed} if every point of $S$ has an open neighbourhood $V$ in $N$ such that $S \cap V$ is closed in $V$. Equivalently, $S$ is closed in some open subset of $N$ containing it, namely the union $U$ of these $V$'s (Lemma~\ref{lem:locally-closed-equivalence}).
\end{defbox}

\begin{lembox}[The Two Forms of Local Closedness]\thmlabel{lem:locally-closed-equivalence}
Let $S$ be a subset of a topological space $N$. The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item every point of $S$ has an open neighbourhood $V$ in $N$ such that $S \cap V$ is closed in $V$, that is, $S$ is locally closed (Definition~\ref{def:locally-closed});
    \item $S$ is closed in some open subset $U$ of $N$ containing $S$.
\end{enumerate}
In (1) $\Rightarrow$ (2), $U$ can be taken to be the union of the neighbourhoods $V$ of (1), one for each point of $S$.
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} \emph{(1) $\Rightarrow$ (2).} For each point of $S$ choose a neighbourhood $V$ as in (1). If $U$ is the union of these $V$ --- one for each point of $S$ --- then $U$ is open and contains $S$. A point of $U \setminus S$ lies in some $V \setminus S$, which is open: it is open in $V$, as the complement of the closed set $S \cap V$, hence open in $N$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:open-in-open}); and $V \setminus S \subseteq U \setminus S$. So $U \setminus S$ is open, and $S = U \setminus (U \setminus S)$ is closed in $U$.

\emph{(2) $\Rightarrow$ (1).} Conversely, if $S$ is closed in an open $U \supseteq S$, then every point of $S$ has the open neighbourhood $V = U$, with $S \cap V = S$ closed in $V$.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[Images of Embeddings Are Locally Closed]\thmlabel{prop:embedding-locally-closed}
Every regular submanifold of $N$ --- in particular the image of an embedding (Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image}) --- is locally closed in $N$.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} Let $S$ be a regular submanifold of $N$, of codimension $k$, and put $n = \dim N$ and $m = n - k$. (By Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image}, the image of an embedding is such an $S$, so the ``in particular'' follows.)

\emph{Locally closed.} At each point of the submanifold $S$ there is an adapted chart $(V, \psi = (y^1, \ldots, y^n))$ (Definitions~\ref{def:submanifold} and~\ref{def:adapted-chart}), in which $S \cap V = \{x \in V : y^{m+1}(x) = \cdots = y^n(x) = 0\}$, a closed subset of $V$ as the zero set of continuous functions: it is the preimage of the closed set $\{\vec 0\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{k}$ under the continuous map $(y^{m+1}, \ldots, y^n) : V \to \mathbb{R}^k$. This is the condition of Definition~\ref{def:locally-closed}, with this $V$.

\emph{The equivalent form.} The second form in Definition~\ref{def:locally-closed} --- $S$ is closed in an open $U \supseteq S$, the union of these $V$, one for each point of $S$ --- then holds by Lemma~\ref{lem:locally-closed-equivalence}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[Dense Regular Submanifolds Are Open]\thmlabel{cor:dense-submanifold}
A dense regular submanifold $S$ of $N$ is an open subset of $N$, and has codimension $0$. In particular, the image of an embedding $F : M \to N$ with $\dim M < \dim N$ is never dense.
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} \emph{$S$ is open.} By Proposition~\ref{prop:embedding-locally-closed}, $S$ is locally closed, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:locally-closed-equivalence} $S$ is closed in an open $U \supseteq S$. $S$ is dense in $N$, hence in $U$: a point $u \in U$ lies in the closure of $S$ in $U$ when every open set of $U$ containing $u$ meets $S$, and such a set is open in $N$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:open-in-open}), so it meets $S$ by density. A closed dense subset of $U$ is all of $U$, since it equals its closure in $U$, which is $U$; so $S = U$ is open.

\emph{Codimension $0$.} If $S = \emptyset$, density forces $N = \overline{S} = \emptyset$, and there is nothing to prove; so let $x \in S$. If $S$ had codimension $k \ge 1$, take an adapted chart $(V, \psi)$ at $x$ (Definition~\ref{def:adapted-chart}): then $\psi(S \cap V)$ would be a nonempty subset of $\mathbb{R}^{n-k} \times \{0\}$, open in $\mathbb{R}^n$ because $S \cap V$ is open in $V$ --- impossible, since no nonempty open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ lies in a hyperplane. In detail: $S \cap V$ is open in $V$ because $S$ is open in $N$; $\psi$ is a homeomorphism of $V$ onto the open set $\psi(V)$, so $\psi(S \cap V)$ is open in $\psi(V)$ (Proposition~\ref{fact:cont}(3)), hence in $\mathbb{R}^n$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:open-in-open}). It contains $\psi(x) = (a, \vec 0)$, hence an open ball of some radius $\varepsilon > 0$ around it, which contains the point obtained from $(a, \vec 0)$ by changing its last coordinate from $0$ to $\varepsilon/2$; since $k \ge 1$, that coordinate is one of the last $k$, so this point is not in $\mathbb{R}^{n-k} \times \{0\}$, a contradiction. So $k = 0$.

\emph{In particular.} Let $F : M \to N$ be an embedding with $m = \dim M < \dim N = n$, and $M \neq \emptyset$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image}, $F(M)$ is a nonempty regular submanifold with adapted charts of codimension $n - m \ge 1$ at each of its points. If $F(M)$ were dense, it would be open by the first part, and the argument just given, applied to one of these adapted charts, would give a contradiction. So $F(M)$ is not dense.
\end{proof}

This is the precise form of the statement that no shrinking of $V$ isolates the piece $F(U)$ of the irrational line: at every point of the irrational line, local closedness fails (Corollary~\ref{cor:irrational-line-not-locally-closed}, after Proposition~\ref{prop:irrational-line}).

\begin{propbox}[Closed Embeddings Are the Proper Ones]\thmlabel{prop:proper-iff-closed}
An embedding $F : M \to N$ is proper if and only if its image $F(M)$ is closed in $N$. In particular, an injective proper immersion is exactly an embedding with closed image.
\leeref{Proposition 5.5}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} \emph{Proper $\Rightarrow$ closed image.} If $F$ is proper, it is closed (Proposition~\ref{prop:proper-closed}, $N$ being a manifold), so $F(M)$, the image of the closed set $M$, is closed.

\emph{Closed image $\Rightarrow$ proper.} Conversely, let $F(M)$ be closed and $K \subseteq N$ compact. Then $K \cap F(M)$ is a closed subset of $K$ (in the subspace topology of $K$, as the intersection of $K$ with a closed subset of $N$), hence compact (Proposition~\ref{fact:compact}(5)). Since $F$ takes all its values in $F(M)$, $F^{-1}(K) = F^{-1}\big(K \cap F(M)\big)$. And $F^{-1}\big(K \cap F(M)\big)$ is its image under the inverse of the homeomorphism $F : M \to F(M)$ (Definition~\ref{def:embedding}), a continuous map, hence compact (Proposition~\ref{fact:compact}(2)). So $F$ is proper (Definition~\ref{def:proper}).

\emph{The last sentence.} The last sentence combines this with Theorem~\ref{thm:proper-embedding}. An injective proper immersion is an embedding by that theorem, and its image is closed by the first part. Conversely, an embedding with closed image is proper by the second part, and it is an injective immersion by Definition~\ref{def:embedding}.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[Sections Are Closed Embeddings]\thmlabel{prop:sections-embeddings}
Let $\pi : E \to M$ and $s : M \to E$ be smooth with $\pi \circ s = \mathrm{id}_M$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $s$ is an embedding (Definition~\ref{def:embedding});
    \item its image $s(M) = \{ y \in E : s(\pi(y)) = y \}$ is closed in $E$.
\end{enumerate}
So $s(M)$ is a closed regular submanifold of $E$ of dimension $\dim M$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image}), and $s$ is proper (Proposition~\ref{prop:proper-iff-closed}). In particular the image of every section of a fibration (Definition~\ref{def:section}) is one.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~5, Problem~1, which assumed $\pi$ to be a surjective submersion; the proof uses only $\pi \circ s = \mathrm{id}_M$. Part (2) is not from the assignment.)} Throughout, $p, p'$ denote points of $M$ and $y$ points of $E$.

\emph{(1) $s$ is an immersion.} By Proposition~\ref{prop:section-splitting}(1), $s_{*p}$ is injective for every $p$ (Definition~\ref{def:immersion}).

\emph{(1) $s : M \to s(M)$ is a homeomorphism.} It is injective: if $s(p) = s(p')$, then $p = \pi(s(p)) = \pi(s(p')) = p'$. It is onto $s(M)$ by definition, so it is a bijection. Its inverse is the restriction $\pi|_{s(M)}$: on one hand $\pi|_{s(M)} \circ s = \pi \circ s = \mathrm{id}_M$; on the other, for $y = s(p) \in s(M)$,
\[
s\big(\pi|_{s(M)}(y)\big) = s\big(\pi(s(p))\big) = s(p) = y .
\]
Both maps are continuous: $s : M \to E$ is continuous with values in $s(M)$, which carries the subspace topology, so $s : M \to s(M)$ is continuous; and $\pi|_{s(M)}$ is the restriction of the continuous map $\pi$ to a subspace. So $s$ is an immersion and a homeomorphism onto its image, an embedding.

\emph{(2) The image.} If $y = s(p)$, then $s(\pi(y)) = s(p) = y$; conversely, if $s(\pi(y)) = y$, then $y \in s(M)$. So $s(M) = \{ y : s(\pi(y)) = y \}$. Its complement is open: let $s(\pi(y)) \ne y$. $E$ is Hausdorff (Definition~\ref{def:manifold}), so there are disjoint open sets $O \ni s(\pi(y))$ and $O' \ni y$. The set $(s \circ \pi)^{-1}(O) \cap O'$ is open, as $s \circ \pi$ is continuous, and contains $y$; for $y'$ in it, $s(\pi(y')) \in O$ and $y' \in O'$, so $s(\pi(y')) \ne y'$. So every point outside $s(M)$ has a neighbourhood outside $s(M)$, and $s(M)$ is closed.

The last two sentences: $s(M)$ is a regular submanifold of codimension $\dim E - \dim M$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image}, closed by (2), so $s$ is proper by Proposition~\ref{prop:proper-iff-closed}. For a fibration, a section is such an $s$ (Definition~\ref{def:section}).
\end{proof}

\begin{exbox}[Sections of the Tangent and Cotangent Bundles]\exlabel{ex:sections-embeddings-bundles}
The main examples come later: the zero sections of $TM$ and $T^*M$ (Definitions~\ref{def:tb-zero-section} and~\ref{def:ctb-zero-section}, later, in \ref{sec:tangent-bundle} and \ref{sec:cotangent-bundle}), and the section $p \mapsto (p, df_p)$ of $T^*M$ given by a smooth function $f$, smooth by Proposition~\ref{prop:d-operator} (later, in \ref{sec:d-operator}). Each is such an $s$, so by Proposition~\ref{prop:sections-embeddings} its image --- the zero section, resp.\ the image $\{(p, df_p)\}$ of the one-form $df$ --- is a closed regular submanifold of dimension $\dim M$.
\end{exbox}


\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}
\begin{tabular}{p{0.27\textwidth} p{0.33\textwidth} p{0.3\textwidth}}
\hline
Map & Image & Example separating it from the row above \\
\hline
injective proper immersion & closed regular submanifold & --- \\
embedding & locally closed regular submanifold & an open interval embedded in $\mathbb{R}^2$ \\
injective immersion & possibly not locally closed, even dense & the irrational line \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Closedness of the image alone is not enough: the image of the figure-eight (Lee's Example~4.19) is compact, hence closed, but the figure-eight is not an embedding. Local closedness is necessary for an embedding, not sufficient.

\begin{lembox}[Dirichlet's Approximation Theorem]\thmlabel{lem:dirichlet}
For every $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and every integer $N \ge 1$ there are integers $n, m$ with $1 \le n \le N$ and $|n\alpha - m| < 1/N$.
\leeref{Lemma 4.21}
\end{lembox}

\textit{Status.} Used in Assignment~4, Problem~5, citing Lee; not proved here. (Lee's proof is a pigeonhole argument on the fractional parts of $0, \alpha, \ldots, N\alpha$.)

\begin{propbox}[The Irrational Line on the Torus]\thmlabel{prop:irrational-line}
Let $\alpha$ be irrational and $\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to T^2 = S^1 \times S^1$, $\gamma(t) = (e^{2\pi i t}, e^{2\pi i \alpha t})$ --- the curve $F(t) = [t, \alpha t]$ introduced before Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image}, under the identification $[x, y] \mapsto (e^{2\pi i x}, e^{2\pi i y})$. Then $\gamma$ is an injective immersion, its image is dense in $T^2$, and $\gamma$ is not an embedding.
\leeref{Example 4.20}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~4, Problem~5: the submitted solution, condensed; the second proof of the last claim is new.)} Distances below are taken in $\mathbb{C}^2$, whose subspace topology $T^2$ carries; write $\gamma_{\mathbb{C}} = \iota \circ \gamma : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}^2$ for $\gamma$ followed by the inclusion $\iota : T^2 \hookrightarrow \mathbb{C}^2$. Two elementary facts are used: $e^{2\pi i s} = 1$ if and only if $s \in \mathbb{Z}$; and $|e^{is} - e^{it}| \le |s - t|$ for real $s, t$ (a chord of the unit circle is no longer than the arc it subtends).

\emph{Immersion.} $\gamma$ is smooth into $\mathbb{C}^2$ with values in the submanifold $T^2$, hence smooth into $T^2$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}(2)). Its velocity in $\mathbb{C}^2$, $\big(2\pi i e^{2\pi i t}, 2\pi i\alpha e^{2\pi i \alpha t}\big)$, has first entry of modulus $2\pi \ne 0$, so by the chain rule $\gamma_{*t}$ is nonzero, hence injective. In detail: by Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix} in the identity charts, $(\gamma_{\mathbb{C}})_{*t}(\partial/\partial r|_t)$ is the velocity above, which is nonzero; by the Chain Rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}) $(\gamma_{\mathbb{C}})_{*t} = \iota_{*\gamma(t)} \circ \gamma_{*t}$, so $\gamma_{*t}(\partial/\partial r|_t) \neq 0$, for otherwise its image under $\iota_{*\gamma(t)}$ would be $0$. As $T_t\mathbb{R}$ is spanned by $\partial/\partial r|_t$, the linear map $\gamma_{*t}$ has kernel $0$.

\emph{Injective.} If $\gamma(t_1) = \gamma(t_2)$, then $e^{2\pi i (t_1 - t_2)} = 1$ and $e^{2\pi i \alpha(t_1 - t_2)} = 1$, so $t_1 - t_2 \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $\alpha(t_1 - t_2) \in \mathbb{Z}$; if $t_1 \ne t_2$ this makes $\alpha = \alpha(t_1 - t_2)/(t_1 - t_2)$ a quotient of integers with nonzero denominator, that is, rational. So $t_1 = t_2$.

\emph{Dense.} Using $|e^{is} - e^{it}| \le |s - t|$: by Lemma~\ref{lem:dirichlet} there are $n_N \ge 1$ and $m_N$ with $|n_N\alpha - m_N| < 1/N$, so $w_N = e^{2\pi i \alpha n_N} = e^{i\theta_N}$ with $\theta_N = 2\pi(n_N\alpha - m_N)$, $0 < |\theta_N| < 2\pi/N$ (nonzero by injectivity). Here $e^{2\pi i \alpha n_N} = e^{2\pi i (\alpha n_N - m_N)}$ because $e^{-2\pi i m_N} = 1$; and $\theta_N = 0$ would give $\gamma(n_N) = (1, 1) = \gamma(0)$ with $n_N \neq 0$, contradicting injectivity. The powers $w_N^k = e^{2\pi i \alpha (k n_N)}$ are $2\pi/N$-dense in $S^1$, since consecutive ones differ in angle by $|\theta_N|$. In detail: let $\delta = |\theta_N|$, and note $e^{ik\delta} = w_N^{\pm k} = e^{2\pi i \alpha (\pm k n_N)}$, with the sign of $\theta_N$. Given $e^{i\phi} \in S^1$ with $\phi \in [0, 2\pi)$, let $k \ge 0$ be the integer with $k\delta \le \phi < (k+1)\delta$; then $0 \le \phi - k\delta < \delta$, so $|e^{i\phi} - e^{ik\delta}| \le |\phi - k\delta| < \delta < 2\pi/N$, and $e^{ik\delta}$ is a power of $w_N$. So $D = \{e^{2\pi i\alpha k} : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}$ is dense in $S^1$: every point of $S^1$ lies within $2\pi/N$ of $D$, for every $N$. Given $(e^{2\pi i a}, e^{2\pi i b}) \in T^2$, the points $\gamma(a + k) = (e^{2\pi i a}, e^{2\pi i \alpha a} e^{2\pi i \alpha k})$ have the right first coordinate, and their second coordinates come arbitrarily close to $e^{2\pi i b}$ because $D$ is dense. In detail: given $\varepsilon > 0$, choose $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $|e^{2\pi i \alpha k} - e^{2\pi i (b - \alpha a)}| < \varepsilon$; multiplying by $e^{2\pi i \alpha a}$, of modulus $1$,
\[
\big|\gamma(a + k) - (e^{2\pi i a}, e^{2\pi i b})\big| = \big|e^{2\pi i \alpha a} e^{2\pi i \alpha k} - e^{2\pi i \alpha a} e^{2\pi i (b - \alpha a)}\big| = \big|e^{2\pi i \alpha k} - e^{2\pi i (b - \alpha a)}\big| < \varepsilon .
\]
So every open set of $T^2$ meets $\gamma(\mathbb{R})$: the image is dense.

\emph{Not an embedding: the submitted proof.} $\gamma(n_N) \to \gamma(0)$, since
\[
|\gamma(n_N) - \gamma(0)| = \big|(e^{2\pi i n_N}, e^{2\pi i \alpha n_N}) - (1, 1)\big| = \big|e^{2\pi i \alpha n_N} - e^{2\pi i m_N}\big| \le 2\pi|n_N\alpha - m_N| < 2\pi/N ,
\]
using $e^{2\pi i n_N} = 1 = e^{2\pi i m_N}$. So $\gamma(n_N) \to \gamma(0)$ in the image $\gamma(\mathbb{R})$ with its subspace topology. If $\gamma^{-1} : \gamma(\mathbb{R}) \to \mathbb{R}$ were continuous, as it is for an embedding (Definition~\ref{def:embedding}), then $n_N = \gamma^{-1}(\gamma(n_N)) \to \gamma^{-1}(\gamma(0)) = 0$, which is false because $n_N \ge 1$ for every $N$.

\emph{Not an embedding: via density.} The image is dense and $\dim \mathbb{R} = 1 < 2 = \dim T^2$, so by Corollary~\ref{cor:dense-submanifold} it is not the image of an embedding.
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[The Irrational Line Is Not Locally Closed]\thmlabel{cor:irrational-line-not-locally-closed}
Let $\gamma$ be the curve of Proposition~\ref{prop:irrational-line} and $S = \gamma(\mathbb{R}) \subseteq T^2$ its image. For every $x \in S$ and every open set $V \subseteq T^2$ containing $x$, the set $S \cap V$ is not closed in $V$. So the condition of Definition~\ref{def:locally-closed} fails at every point of $S$; in particular, $S$ is not locally closed in $T^2$.
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} Let $x \in S$ and let $V \subseteq T^2$ be open with $x \in V$. We show: $S \cap V$ is dense in $V$; $V$ is not contained in $S$; and hence $S \cap V$ is not closed in $V$.

\emph{$S \cap V$ is dense in $V$.} Let $O$ be a nonempty open subset of $V$. Then $O$ is open in $T^2$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:open-in-open}), so it meets $S$, because $S$ is dense in $T^2$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:irrational-line}); and a point of $O \cap S$ lies in $S \cap V$, as $O \subseteq V$. So every nonempty open subset of $V$ meets $S \cap V$. A point $v \in V$ lies in the closure of $S \cap V$ in $V$ when every open set of $V$ containing $v$ meets $S \cap V$; so that closure is all of $V$.

\emph{$V$ is not contained in $S$.} Write $x = (e^{2\pi i a}, e^{2\pi i b})$ with $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$, and let
\[
c : \mathbb{R} \to T^2, \qquad c(s) = \big(e^{2\pi i a}, e^{2\pi i s}\big) ,
\]
a parametrization of the circle $\{e^{2\pi i a}\} \times S^1$. It is continuous into $\mathbb{C}^2$ with values in $T^2$, hence continuous into $T^2$, which carries the subspace topology (Proposition~\ref{prop:univ-subspace}(2)). Since $c(b) = x \in V$, the set $c^{-1}(V)$ is open in $\mathbb{R}$ and contains $b$, so it contains an interval $J = (b - \varepsilon, b + \varepsilon)$ with $0 < \varepsilon < \tfrac12$. On $J$ the map $c$ is injective: if $c(s) = c(s')$, then $e^{2\pi i (s - s')} = 1$, so $s - s' \in \mathbb{Z}$, and $|s - s'| < 2\varepsilon < 1$ gives $s = s'$. So $c(J)$ is a subset of $V$ in bijection with the interval $J$, hence uncountable. On the other hand, $c(J)$ lies in the circle $\{e^{2\pi i a}\} \times S^1$, and $S$ meets that circle in a countable set: $\gamma(t) = (e^{2\pi i t}, e^{2\pi i \alpha t})$ has first coordinate $e^{2\pi i a}$ exactly when $e^{2\pi i (t - a)} = 1$, that is, when $t - a \in \mathbb{Z}$; so
\[
S \cap \big(\{e^{2\pi i a}\} \times S^1\big) = \{\gamma(a + k) : k \in \mathbb{Z}\} .
\]
An uncountable set is not contained in a countable one, so some point of $c(J) \subseteq V$ is not in $S$.

\emph{Conclusion.} If $S \cap V$ were closed in $V$, it would equal its closure in $V$, which is $V$ by the first step; then $V \subseteq S$, contradicting the second step. So $S \cap V$ is not closed in $V$. As $x \in S$ and $V$ were arbitrary, no point of $S$ has an open neighbourhood $V$ in $T^2$ with $S \cap V$ closed in $V$; since $S \neq \emptyset$, $S$ is not locally closed (Definition~\ref{def:locally-closed}).
\end{proof}

\subsection{Regular and Immersed Submanifolds}\label{sub:immersed-submanifolds}

\textit{Not from lecture: the notion announced with Definition~\ref{def:submanifold}.} A regular submanifold carries the subspace topology, and its smooth structure is forced on it by the ambient manifold. The images of the injective immersions seen so far --- the figure-eight (\ref{sub:immersion-images}), the irrational line on the torus (Proposition~\ref{prop:irrational-line}) --- do not fit that definition, but each is a perfectly good manifold in the topology it inherits from its \emph{domain}. Allowing that topology gives the second kind of submanifold.

\begin{defbox}[Immersed Submanifold]\deflabel{def:immersed-submanifold}
Let $N$ be a smooth manifold. An \textbf{immersed submanifold} of $N$ is a subset $S \subseteq N$ together with a topology on $S$, in which it is a topological manifold, and a smooth structure on $S$, such that the inclusion $\iota : S \hookrightarrow N$ is a smooth immersion (Definition~\ref{def:immersion}). The topology need not be the subspace topology.
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[Images of Injective Immersions]\thmlabel{prop:immersion-image}
Let $F : M \to N$ be an injective immersion and $S = F(M)$. There is exactly one topology and smooth structure on $S$ for which $F : M \to S$ is a diffeomorphism, and with them $S$ is an immersed submanifold of $N$.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture.)} \emph{The topology.} Declare $U \subseteq S$ open if $F^{-1}(U)$ is open in $M$. This is a topology on $S$, because $F^{-1}(\emptyset) = \emptyset$, $F^{-1}(S) = M$, and preimages commute with unions and intersections. Let $h = F^{-1} : S \to M$ be the inverse of the bijection $F : M \to S$ ($F$ is injective). For $U \subseteq S$, $h(U) = F^{-1}(U)$, so $U$ is open in $S$ exactly when $h(U)$ is open in $M$: $h$ is a bijection that matches open sets with open sets, a homeomorphism (Proposition~\ref{fact:cont}(2)).

\emph{The smooth structure.} By Proposition~\ref{prop:transport-structure}, applied to the homeomorphism $h : S \to M$, $S$ is a topological manifold and carries exactly one smooth structure for which $h$, and hence $F = h^{-1}$, is a diffeomorphism (Definition~\ref{def:transported}); a map is a diffeomorphism exactly when its inverse is (Definition~\ref{def:diffeomorphism}).

\emph{Uniqueness.} The topology is forced as well, since a diffeomorphism is a homeomorphism: if some topology on $S$ makes $F : M \to S$ a homeomorphism, then a set $U \subseteq S$ is open in it exactly when $F^{-1}(U)$ is open in $M$ (Proposition~\ref{fact:cont}(2)), which is the topology declared above. And for that topology the smooth structure is unique by Proposition~\ref{prop:transport-structure}(3).

\emph{Immersed submanifold.} The inclusion is $\iota = F \circ h$, with $F : M \to N$: indeed $F(h(q)) = q$ for $q \in S$. It is a composite of smooth maps (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}); by the chain rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}) $\iota_{*q} = F_{*h(q)} \circ h_{*q}$, which is injective because $h_{*q}$ is an isomorphism (Corollary~\ref{lem:germs-diffeo}) and $F_{*h(q)}$ is injective: if $\iota_{*q}v = 0$, then $h_{*q}v \in \ker F_{*h(q)} = 0$, so $v = 0$. So $\iota$ is an immersion, and $S$, with this topology and smooth structure, is an immersed submanifold of $N$ (Definition~\ref{def:immersed-submanifold}).
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[Every Regular Submanifold Is an Immersed Submanifold]\thmlabel{prop:regular-is-immersed}
A regular submanifold $S \subseteq N$, with the subspace topology and its induced smooth structure (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-structure}), is an immersed submanifold of $N$.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture.)} Check Definition~\ref{def:immersed-submanifold}. With the subspace topology and the induced smooth structure, $S$ is a topological manifold and a smooth manifold (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-structure}). The inclusion $\iota : S \hookrightarrow N$ is smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}) and $\iota_{*p}$ is injective at every $p \in S$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-tangent}), so $\iota$ is a smooth immersion (Definition~\ref{def:immersion}).
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[When an Immersed Submanifold Is Regular]\thmlabel{prop:immersed-regular}
Let $F : M \to N$ be an injective immersion, and give $S = F(M)$ the structure of Proposition~\ref{prop:immersion-image}. The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $F$ is an embedding (Definition~\ref{def:embedding});
    \item the topology of $S$ is the subspace topology;
    \item $S$ is a regular submanifold of $N$ whose induced smooth structure is the structure of Proposition~\ref{prop:immersion-image}.
\end{enumerate}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture.)} Write $\mathcal{T}_S$ for the topology of Proposition~\ref{prop:immersion-image} and $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{sub}}$ for the subspace topology on $S$. We show (1)~$\Leftrightarrow$~(2), (1)~$\Rightarrow$~(3) and (3)~$\Rightarrow$~(2), which together give all the equivalences.

\emph{(1)~$\Leftrightarrow$~(2).} The topology of $S$ is the one for which $F : M \to S$ is a homeomorphism; it equals the subspace topology exactly when $F$ is a homeomorphism onto its image with the subspace topology, which, for an immersion, is the definition of an embedding. In detail: $F$ is an immersion by hypothesis, so by Definition~\ref{def:embedding}, (1) says that $F : M \to (S, \mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{sub}})$ is a homeomorphism. If $\mathcal{T}_S = \mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{sub}}$, this holds, because $F : M \to (S, \mathcal{T}_S)$ is a homeomorphism (Proposition~\ref{prop:immersion-image}). Conversely, if $F : M \to (S, \mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{sub}})$ is a homeomorphism, then for $U \subseteq S$, by Proposition~\ref{fact:cont}(2) applied to both homeomorphisms,
\[
U \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{sub}} \iff F^{-1}(U) \text{ is open in } M \iff U \in \mathcal{T}_S ,
\]
so $\mathcal{T}_S = \mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{sub}}$.

\emph{(1)~$\Rightarrow$~(3).} $S$ is a regular submanifold by Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image}, and $F : M \to S$ is a diffeomorphism for its induced structure by Corollary~\ref{cor:embedding-diffeo}. By the uniqueness in Proposition~\ref{prop:immersion-image} --- exactly one topology and smooth structure on $S$ make $F : M \to S$ a diffeomorphism --- the two structures coincide.

\emph{(3)~$\Rightarrow$~(2).} The induced structure of a regular submanifold has the subspace topology (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-structure}, and Definition~\ref{def:submanifold}, where $S$ carries the subspace topology). By (3) the induced structure is the structure of Proposition~\ref{prop:immersion-image}, so its topology $\mathcal{T}_S$ is $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{sub}}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{exbox}[Immersed but Not Regular]\exlabel{ex:immersed-not-regular}
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \emph{The figure-eight.} $\beta(t) = (\sin 2t, \sin t)$, $t \in (-\pi, \pi)$ (Lee, Example~4.19), is an injective immersion, so its image is an immersed submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^2$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:immersion-image}). It is not a regular submanifold: in the subspace topology every small neighbourhood of the origin in the image is an X --- the strand through $\beta(0)$ and the two ends returning as $t \to \pm\pi$ --- and removing the origin leaves four components, which cannot happen in a $1$-manifold (as in Example~\ref{ex:nodal-cubic}).
    \item \emph{The irrational line.} The curve $\gamma$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:irrational-line} is an injective immersion, so its image is an immersed submanifold of $T^2$, a copy of $\mathbb{R}$ in its own topology. It is not a regular submanifold. The image is dense, so if it were regular it would be open in $T^2$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:dense-submanifold}). But a nonempty open subset of $T^2$ containing $(e^{2\pi i a}, w)$ meets the circle $\{e^{2\pi i a}\} \times S^1$ in an open arc, which is uncountable, while the image meets that circle only in the countable set $\{\gamma(a + k) : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{exbox}

In the immersed topology, a short interval of the irrational line is an open subset of the image; in the subspace topology, every neighbourhood of a point of the image also contains points from arbitrarily far along the line, because the line comes back densely. That is the whole difference between the two kinds of submanifold.


% ============================================================================
% SECTION: GEOMETRIC AND ABSTRACT MANIFOLDS (comparison; not from lecture)
% ============================================================================

\section{Geometric and Abstract Manifolds}\label{sec:geometric-abstract}

\roadmark{Stage: recap}{The two pictures of a manifold --- a subset of Euclidean space, and a space with an atlas --- set side by side, definition by definition and theorem by theorem, with the result that bridges each pair.}

\textit{Not from lecture: a comparison written for these notes in Chapter~6, after immersions and embeddings, when every bridge between the two pictures is in place. Nothing here is new; every object is defined, and every fact proved, where the cross-reference points.}

The course has built manifolds in two ways. The \emph{geometric} picture is the equations thread of the roadmap: a manifold is a subset of some $\mathbb{R}^N$, cut out by equations or swept out by a parametrization, and everything --- smoothness, tangent vectors, differentials, regular values --- is inherited from the ambient space. The \emph{abstract} picture needs no ambient space: a manifold is a topological space with a maximal smooth atlas, and every notion is defined through charts. Almost every definition and theorem of the geometric picture has a counterpart in the abstract one, usually proved by reducing to the geometric version in charts. Each part below lists the pairs one to one, recalls the central ones verbatim, and names the result that shows the two agree wherever both make sense.

\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}
\small
\begin{tabular}{p{0.17\textwidth} p{0.25\textwidth} p{0.25\textwidth} p{0.22\textwidth}}
\hline
Aspect & Geometric (inside $\mathbb{R}^N$) & Abstract (charts only) & Bridge \\
\hline
the object & external, internal or graph description & maximal atlas; submanifold & Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-euclidean} \\
smooth structure & graph charts & chosen or induced atlas & Proposition~\ref{prop:rvt-agree}(1) \\
smooth maps & smooth between vector spaces & smooth in charts & Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold} \\
tangent space & velocities, $\ker F'(p)$ & derivations of germs & Theorem~\ref{thm:ambient-abstract} \\
differential & Jacobian $F'(p)$ & pushforward $F_{*p}$ & Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix} \\
covectors & gradient $\nabla f$, transpose $J^{\mathsf T}$ & $df_p$, pullback $F_p^*$ & the remark \emph{The Two Differentials Meet} \\
regular points & $F'(p)$ surjective & $F_{*p}$ surjective & Proposition~\ref{prop:regular-one-chart} \\
key theorems & implicit and inverse function theorems & normal form; local diffeomorphism criterion & proved through charts \\
regular values & level sets are manifolds & level sets are submanifolds & Proposition~\ref{prop:rvt-agree} \\
global picture & inside $\mathbb{R}^N$ by construction & no ambient space & Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image} \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\subsection{The Object and Its Smooth Structure}

\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.25}
\small
\begin{tabular}{p{0.3\textwidth} p{0.3\textwidth} p{0.3\textwidth}}
\hline
Geometric & Abstract & How they correspond \\
\hline
Definition~\ref{def:ext-int} (external: a regular level set) & Definition~\ref{def:submanifold} (a coordinate slice of an adapted chart, Definition~\ref{def:adapted-chart}) & Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-euclidean}: the slice is a fourth equivalent description \\
Definition~\ref{def:internal-description}, Definition~\ref{def:parametrization} (a parametrization) & the inverse of a chart (the remark \emph{A Parametrization Is an Inverse Chart}); Definition~\ref{def:immersion} & rank $n$ Jacobian = immersion; homeomorphism onto the image = embedding (Definition~\ref{def:embedding}) \\
Theorem~\ref{thm:ext-int} (the descriptions agree) & Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-euclidean}, Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image} & straightening a graph gives an adapted chart \\
Proposition~\ref{prop:level-set-smooth} (graph charts) & Definition~\ref{def:smooth-structure}; Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-structure} (induced structure) & Proposition~\ref{prop:rvt-agree}(1): the same structure \\
Definition~\ref{def:vs-structure} (a vector space) & Proposition~\ref{prop:vs-manifold} & a vector space is a manifold with one global chart \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Geometrically, a manifold is a subset of a Euclidean space with one of three equivalent local descriptions (Theorem~\ref{thm:ext-int}):

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Definition~\ref{def:ext-int} (External Description).} Let $X \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ and $p \in X$. Near $p$, $X$ is described \textbf{externally} if there are an open $W \ni p$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ and a smooth $F : W \to \mathbb{R}^k$ having $\vec 0$ as a regular value, with $X \cap W = F^{-1}(\vec 0)$ --- the level-set or implicit description.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Definition~\ref{def:internal-description} (Internal Description).} Let $X \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ and $p \in X$. Near $p$, $X$ is described \textbf{internally} if there are an open $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, an open $W \ni p$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$, and a smooth $\alpha : V \to \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ which is a homeomorphism onto $X \cap W$ and whose Jacobian $D\alpha_q$ has rank $n$ at every $q \in V$ --- the parametric description.
\end{quote}

--- or a graph over $n$ of the coordinates. Abstractly, a manifold is a topological manifold with a choice of charts, and the subsets that look like the geometric ones are the submanifolds:

\begin{quote}
\sloppy \textbf{Recall: Definition~\ref{def:smooth-structure} (Smooth Manifold Structure).} A \textbf{differentiable (smooth) structure} on a topological manifold $M$ is a maximal atlas $\mathcal{A}$ on $M$. A \textbf{smooth manifold} is a pair $\mathcal{M} = (M, \mathcal{A})$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-atlas}, specifying any atlas specifies a smooth structure, and two atlases specify the same structure exactly when they are compatible.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Definition~\ref{def:submanifold} (Regular Submanifold).} Let $M$ be a smooth manifold of dimension $m$, $S \subseteq M$ a subset with the subspace topology, and $0 \le k \le m$. For a chart $\varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^m)$ write $x_a = (x^1, \ldots, x^{m-k})$ for its first $m - k$ components and $x_b = (x^{m-k+1}, \ldots, x^m)$ for its last $k$. Then $S$ is a \textbf{regular submanifold of $M$ of codimension $k$} if every $p \in S$ lies in the domain of a smooth chart $(U, \varphi)$ of $M$ with
\[
U \cap S = \{\, q \in U : x_b(q) = \vec 0 \,\}.
\]
Regular submanifolds are also called \textbf{embedded} submanifolds, as opposed to the immersed submanifolds of Definition~\ref{def:immersed-submanifold}. In these notes, ``submanifold'' without qualification means a regular submanifold.
\end{quote}

A subset of $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ has the three Euclidean descriptions near each point exactly when it is a submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-euclidean}), and the graph-chart structure of Proposition~\ref{prop:level-set-smooth} is then the induced one (Proposition~\ref{prop:rvt-agree}(1)). The circle shows all of this at once: its external, graph and internal descriptions (Example~\ref{ex:circle-three-ways}), and three atlases --- four charts, stereographic and angle --- that define one smooth structure (\ref{sec:ex-circle}).

\subsection{Where the Examples Come From}

The geometric examples are level sets: the spheres (\ref{sec:ex-spheres}), and the classical groups $\SL(n,\mathbb{R})$, $\Ogp(n)$, $\SO(n)$, $\Ugp(n)$ as level sets in spaces of matrices (Theorem~\ref{thm:classical-manifolds}, smooth by \ref{sec:on-un-smooth}). The abstract picture adds the spaces built by gluing: $\mathbb{CP}^n$ (\ref{sec:ex-cpn}, with its standard charts in \ref{sub:projective-atlas}), coset spaces $G/H$ (\ref{sec:homogeneous}) and the Grassmannians (Corollary~\ref{cor:grassmannian}). These arrive with no ambient space: a point of $\mathbb{CP}^n$ is a line, not a point of some $\mathbb{R}^N$. Some of them can be placed in a Euclidean space afterwards --- that is what an embedding does (below) --- but not as constructed.

\subsection{Smooth Maps}

\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.25}
\small
\begin{tabular}{p{0.3\textwidth} p{0.3\textwidth} p{0.3\textwidth}}
\hline
Geometric & Abstract & How they correspond \\
\hline
Definition~\ref{def:vs-smooth} (smooth between vector spaces) & Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map} (smooth in charts) & Proposition~\ref{prop:diffeo-agree}: the two notions of diffeomorphism agree \\
Lemma~\ref{lem:level-set-maps} (maps into and out of level sets) & Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold} (maps into and out of submanifolds) & the same statement, for submanifolds of any manifold \\
Theorem~\ref{thm:inverse-function} (inverse function theorem) & Theorem~\ref{thm:local-diffeo-criterion} (local diffeomorphism criterion) & the criterion is the inverse function theorem in charts \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Theorem~\ref{thm:inverse-function} (Inverse Function Theorem).} Let $W \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be open, $\Phi : W \to \mathbb{R}^n$ smooth, and $a \in W$ with $\Phi'(a)$ invertible. Then there are open sets $U_0 \ni a$ in $W$ and $V_0 \ni \Phi(a)$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ such that $\Phi(U_0) = V_0$ and $\Phi|_{U_0} : U_0 \to V_0$ is bijective with smooth inverse.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Theorem~\ref{thm:local-diffeo-criterion} (Local Diffeomorphisms Are Detected by the Differential).} A smooth map $F : M \to N$ is a local diffeomorphism if and only if $F_{*p} : T_pM \to T_{F(p)}N$ is bijective for every $p \in M$.
\end{quote}

A map into or out of a level set is smooth when it is a restriction of, or lands in, a smooth map between Euclidean spaces; abstractly, when its coordinate representations are. Every abstract statement about smoothness is proved by reading it in charts, where it becomes the Euclidean one: the local diffeomorphism criterion is the inverse function theorem applied to a coordinate representation.

\subsection{Tangent Vectors}

\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.25}
\small
\begin{tabular}{p{0.3\textwidth} p{0.3\textwidth} p{0.3\textwidth}}
\hline
Geometric & Abstract & How they correspond \\
\hline
Definition~\ref{def:geometric-tangent} (velocities $\gamma'(0)$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$) & Definition~\ref{def:abstract-tangent} (derivations of germs, Definition~\ref{def:derivation}) & Theorem~\ref{thm:ambient-abstract}: $v \mapsto D_v$ is an isomorphism \\
Definition~\ref{def:Dv} (the directional derivative $D_v$) & Definition~\ref{def:derivation} (a derivation at $p$) & Proposition~\ref{prop:Dv-properties}, Proposition~\ref{prop:Dv-determines-v}: $D_v$ is a derivation and determines $v$ \\
$\gamma'(0)$, the velocity in the ambient space & Definition~\ref{def:velocity}; Theorem~\ref{thm:every-vector-velocity} & every abstract tangent vector is a velocity \\
Lemma~\ref{lem:tangent-local} (locality) & Lemma~\ref{lem:germs-local} (open subsets have the same tangent spaces) & both depend only on a neighbourhood of $p$ \\
Lemma~\ref{lem:tangent-graph} (tangent space of a graph) & Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-tangent} (tangent space of a submanifold) & the span of the first coordinate directions of a slice \\
Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel} ($T^{\geo}_pM = \ker F'(p)$) & Theorem~\ref{thm:rvt-manifolds} ($\iota_{*p}(T_pS) = \ker F_{*p}$) & Proposition~\ref{prop:rvt-agree}(2) \\
Corollary~\ref{thm:geo-tangent-dimension} (dimension) & Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis} (basis theorem) & both give dimension $n$ \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Definition~\ref{def:geometric-tangent} (Geometric Tangent Space).} The \textbf{geometric} (or \textbf{ambient}) \textbf{tangent space} to $M$ at $p$ is
\[
\begin{aligned}
T^{\geo}_pM \;=\; \Big\{\, \gamma'(0) \;\Big|\;& \gamma : (-\varepsilon,\varepsilon) \to \mathbb{R}^{n+k} \text{ smooth},\ \varepsilon > 0, \\
& \gamma\big((-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\big) \subseteq M,\ \gamma(0) = p \,\Big\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+k},
\end{aligned}
\]
where $\gamma'(0) = \frac{d\gamma}{dt}\big|_{t=0}$ is the ordinary derivative of a curve in $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$. In words: $T^{\geo}_pM$ is the set of velocities at $p$ of smooth curves that pass through $p$ while staying on $M$. The same definition applies verbatim with $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ replaced by any finite-dimensional real vector space containing $M$, such as $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$, with $\gamma'(0)$ computed in that space.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Definition~\ref{def:abstract-tangent} (The Abstract Tangent Space).} The \textbf{(abstract) tangent space} to $M$ at $p$ is
\[
T_pM \;=\; \{\, \text{all derivations at } p \,\},
\]
a real vector space under the pointwise operations $(D + D')[f] = D[f] + D'[f]$ and $(\lambda D)[f] = \lambda\, D[f]$. An element $D \in T_pM$ is a \textbf{tangent vector} at $p$. It is not an arrow in any ambient space but a function on germs, $D : C^\infty_p(M) \to \mathbb{R}$, so $D[f]$ is a real number for each germ $[f]$ at $p$.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel} (The Geometric Tangent Space Is the Kernel of the Jacobian).} $T^{\geo}_pM = \ker F'(p)$, where $F'(p) : \mathbb{R}^{n+k} \to \mathbb{R}^k$ is the Jacobian at $p$. In particular $T^{\geo}_pM$ is a linear subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ of dimension $n = \dim M$.
\end{quote}

A geometric tangent vector is an arrow in the ambient space; an abstract one is a machine that differentiates germs. The arrow $v$ becomes the machine $D_v$, and for a level set $v \mapsto D_v$ is an isomorphism $T^{\geo}_pM \to T_pM$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:ambient-abstract}); conversely every abstract tangent vector is the velocity of a curve (Theorem~\ref{thm:every-vector-velocity}), which restores the arrow picture without an ambient space. For a submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ the inclusion carries $T_pS$ onto $T^{\geo}_pS$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:rvt-agree}(2) and the remark \emph{The Tangent Spaces Match} in \ref{sec:submanifolds}).

\subsection{Differentials: the Jacobian and the Pushforward}

\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.25}
\small
\begin{tabular}{p{0.3\textwidth} p{0.3\textwidth} p{0.3\textwidth}}
\hline
Geometric & Abstract & How they correspond \\
\hline
Definition~\ref{def:jacobian} (Jacobian matrix $DF_p$); Definition~\ref{def:vs-differential} ($dF_p$ between vector spaces) & Definition~\ref{def:pushforward} (pushforward $F_{*p}$) & Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix}: the matrix of $F_{*p}$ is the Jacobian of the coordinate representation \\
composition $g \circ F$ inside the chain rule & Definition~\ref{def:germ-pullback} (pullback of germs $F_p^*$) & $F_{*p}D = D \circ F_p^*$: the pushforward is defined through the pullback \\
Theorem~\ref{thm:vs-differential-curves} ($dF_p(v) = \frac{d}{dt}F(p + tv)$) & Corollary~\ref{cor:velocity-composite} (differentials by curves) & both compute the differential along curves \\
Definition~\ref{def:rank} (rank of a matrix) & Definition~\ref{def:manifold-rank} (rank of $F_{*p}$) & the rank of the Jacobian of any coordinate representation \\
the chain rule for Jacobians & Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}; Corollary~\ref{cor:chain-rule-coords} & $(G \circ F)_{*p} = G_{*F(p)} \circ F_{*p}$ is matrix multiplication in coordinates \\
$\mathbb{R}^n$ is its own tangent space & Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs}; Proposition~\ref{prop:differential-agree} & on open subsets of vector spaces $F_{*p}$ is the ordinary derivative \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Definition~\ref{def:jacobian} (Jacobian Matrix).} Let $F = (F_1, \ldots, F_m) : \mathbb{R}^N \to \mathbb{R}^m$ be $C^1$ and $p \in \mathbb{R}^N$. The \textbf{Jacobian matrix} of $F$ at $p$ is the $m \times N$ matrix of partial derivatives
\[
DF_p = \begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_N}(p) \\[2mm]
\vdots & & \vdots \\[1mm]
\dfrac{\partial F_m}{\partial x_1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F_m}{\partial x_N}(p)
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \text{row } a = \nabla F_a(p),
\]
regarded as the linear map $DF_p : \mathbb{R}^N \to \mathbb{R}^m$, $v \mapsto DF_p\, v$. It is the derivative of $F$ at $p$: $F(p + v) = F(p) + DF_p\, v + o(|v|)$, and the chain rule for a curve reads $\frac{d}{dt} F(\gamma(t)) = DF_{\gamma(t)}\, \gamma'(t)$. For $m = 1$ the Jacobian is the single row $\nabla F(p)$, and $DF_p\, v = \nabla F(p) \cdot v$.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Definition~\ref{def:germ-pullback} (Pullback of Germs).} Let $F : M \to N$ be a smooth map between smooth manifolds, and $p \in M$, so that $F(p)$ is a point of $N$. Let $[g] \in C^\infty_{F(p)}(N)$ be a germ \emph{at the point $F(p)$ of $N$}, with a representative $(g, V)$: $V \subseteq N$ is open with $F(p) \in V$, and $g : V \to \mathbb{R}$ is smooth. Then $F^{-1}(V)$ is an open neighbourhood of $p$ in $M$, and $g \circ F : F^{-1}(V) \to \mathbb{R}$ is smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}), so $(g \circ F, F^{-1}(V))$ represents a germ at $p$ on $M$. The \textbf{pullback} of germs along $F$ at $p$ is the map
\[
F_p^* : C^\infty_{F(p)}(N) \longrightarrow C^\infty_p(M), \qquad F_p^*[g] = [\,g \circ F\,],
\]
which takes a germ on $N$ at $F(p)$ to a germ on $M$ at $p$. It does not depend on the representative $(g, V)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:pullback-properties}).
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Definition~\ref{def:pushforward} (Pushforward --- the Differential).} Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth and $p \in M$, and let $D \in T_pM$ be a tangent vector at $p$ --- that is, a derivation at $p$, a linear map $D : C^\infty_p(M) \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying the Leibniz rule. The \textbf{pushforward} of $D$ along $F$ is the map
\[
F_{*p}D : C^\infty_{F(p)}(N) \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}, \qquad \big(F_{*p}D\big)[g] \;:=\; D\big(F_p^*[g]\big) = D[\,g \circ F\,],
\]
defined on germs $[g]$ at $F(p)$ on $N$: pull the germ back to $p$, then apply $D$. In one line, $F_{*p}D = D \circ F_p^*$. It is a derivation at $F(p)$, i.e.\ an element of $T_{F(p)}N$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:pushforward-derivation}). Letting $D$ vary gives the \textbf{pushforward}, or \textbf{differential}, of $F$ at $p$,
\[
F_{*p} : T_pM \longrightarrow T_{F(p)}N, \qquad D \longmapsto F_{*p}D,
\]
a map from tangent vectors at $p$ in $M$ to tangent vectors at $F(p)$ in $N$, also written $dF_p$. So $F_{*p}$ acts on derivations; its value $F_{*p}D$ is again a derivation, which acts on germs at $F(p)$.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix} (The Matrix of the Differential).} Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth and $p \in M$, with smooth charts $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V, \psi = (y^1, \ldots, y^n))$ of $N$ such that $F(U) \subseteq V$, components $F^j = y^j \circ F$, coordinate representation $\tilde F = \psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}$, and the coordinate bases $\mathcal{B}_M = \{\partial/\partial x^i|_p\}$ of $T_pM$ and $\mathcal{B}_N = \{\partial/\partial y^j|_{F(p)}\}$ of $T_{F(p)}N$. Then $F_{*p}$ is linear, and
\[
F_{*p}\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p\Big) = \sum_{j=1}^n \frac{\partial F^j}{\partial x^i}(p)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial y^j}\Big|_{F(p)} .
\]
So the matrix of $F_{*p}$ in the bases $\mathcal{B}_M$, $\mathcal{B}_N$ has the upstairs partials $\partial F^j/\partial x^i(p)$ as entries, and by Proposition~\ref{prop:upstairs-downstairs} it is the $n \times m$ Jacobian of the coordinate representation,
\[
\Big[\, \frac{\partial F^j}{\partial x^i}(p) \,\Big]_{j, i} = \tilde F'\big(\varphi(p)\big),
\]
with $j$ the row index and $i$ the column index.
\end{quote}

The two differentials are built in opposite directions. The Jacobian is computed from $F$ directly: differentiate the components. The pushforward is defined by duality: to see how $F_{*p}D$ differentiates a function $g$ near $F(p)$, pull $g$ back to $g \circ F$ and let $D$ differentiate that. In coordinates the result is the same matrix (Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix}), and on open subsets of Euclidean space the pushforward is the ordinary derivative (Proposition~\ref{prop:differential-agree}).

\subsection{Covectors: Gradients, Transposes and Pullbacks}

\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.25}
\small
\begin{tabular}{p{0.3\textwidth} p{0.3\textwidth} p{0.3\textwidth}}
\hline
Geometric & Abstract & How they correspond \\
\hline
the gradient $\nabla f(p)$, a row of the Jacobian & Definition~\ref{def:differential-function} ($df_p \in T_p^*M$); Lemma~\ref{lem:df-coords} & the remark \emph{Differential --- Not Gradient}: a gradient needs an inner product \\
the transpose $J_F^{\mathsf T}$ of the Jacobian & Definition~\ref{def:pullback-covector} (pullback of covectors, the dual map of $F_{*p}$) & in dual bases the matrix of $F_p^*$ is the transpose of the matrix of $F_{*p}$ \\
$\nabla(f \circ F) = J_F^{\mathsf T} \nabla f$ (chain rule) & Proposition~\ref{prop:pullback-d} ($F_p^*\, df = d(f \circ F)$) & the remark \emph{The Two Differentials Meet} \\
normal vectors, spanned by $\nabla F^1, \ldots, \nabla F^k$ & Definition~\ref{def:conormal} (conormal space); Proposition~\ref{prop:conormal-basis} (basis $dF^i|_p$) & the remark \emph{No Normal Vectors Without a Metric} \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Definition~\ref{def:differential-function} (The Differential of a Function).} Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $p \in M$, and let $f : M \to \mathbb{R}$ be smooth (or defined and smooth only near $p$). Its pushforward at $p$ (Definition~\ref{def:pushforward}) is a linear map into the tangent space of $\mathbb{R}$ at the point $f(p)$:
\[
f_{*p} : T_pM \longrightarrow T_{f(p)}\mathbb{R}, \qquad \big(f_{*p}D\big)[h] = D[\,h \circ f\,] .
\]
The \textbf{differential} of $f$ at $p$ is this map followed by the standard identification $\iota_{f(p)} : T_{f(p)}\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ (Definition~\ref{def:identification-TR}):
\[
df_p = \iota_{f(p)} \circ f_{*p} : T_pM \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}, \qquad df_p(D) = \big(f_{*p}D\big)[r] .
\]
So $df_p(D)$ is the coefficient of $f_{*p}D$ on the basis vector $\partial/\partial r|_{f(p)}$ of $T_{f(p)}\mathbb{R}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:tangent-space-R}): $f_{*p}D = df_p(D)\,\partial/\partial r|_{f(p)}$. As a composite of linear maps, $df_p$ is linear, so $df_p \in T_p^*M$, the cotangent space of Definition~\ref{def:cotangent}. Proposition~\ref{prop:df-derivation} computes it: $df_p(D) = D[f]$.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Definition~\ref{def:pullback-covector} (Pullback of Covectors).} Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth and $p \in M$. The \textbf{pullback of covectors} at $p$ is the dual map (Definition~\ref{def:dual-map}) of the pushforward $F_{*p} : T_pM \to T_{F(p)}N$:
\[
F_p^* : T^*_{F(p)}N \longrightarrow T_p^*M, \qquad (F_p^*\xi)(v) = \xi\big(F_{*p}v\big) \qquad (\xi \in T^*_{F(p)}N,\ v \in T_pM) .
\]
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Proposition~\ref{prop:pullback-d} (Pullback Commutes with $d$).} Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth, $p \in M$, and $f$ smooth near $F(p)$. Then
\[
F_p^*\big(df_{F(p)}\big) = d(f \circ F)_p \quad \text{in } T_p^*M .
\]
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: the remark \emph{The Two Differentials Meet}.} In $\mathbb{R}^n$, with the dot-product identification $v \mapsto \xi_v$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:dot-product-identification}, under which $dh_p = \xi_{\nabla h(p)}$ (its part (3), with the gradient of Definition~\ref{def:gradient}), the proposition is the chain rule in the form $\nabla(f \circ F) = J_F^{\mathsf T}\, \nabla f$, with the gradients written as columns. (Definition~\ref{def:jacobian} writes the gradients $\nabla F_a(p)$ as the rows of the Jacobian; in that row convention the same identity reads $\nabla(f \circ F) = \nabla f \; J_F$, the transpose of this one.) The pushforward $F_*$ is really the differential of $F$: for a function $f : M \to \mathbb{R}$, $df_p$ is $f_{*p}$ followed by the identification $T_{f(p)}\mathbb{R} \cong \mathbb{R}$.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Definition~\ref{def:conormal} (Conormal Space).} Let $S \subseteq M$ be a regular submanifold and $p \in S$. The \textbf{conormal space} of $S$ at $p$ is
\[
N_pS = \{\, \xi \in T_p^*M : \xi(v) = 0 \text{ for all } v \in \iota_{*p}(T_pS) \,\},
\]
the covectors at $p$ that vanish on the tangent space of $S$ --- the annihilator of $T_pS$ in $T_p^*M$.
\end{quote}

In $\mathbb{R}^n$ the dot product identifies covectors with vectors, so the differential $df_p$ appears as the gradient, a pulled-back covector as the transpose of the Jacobian applied to a gradient, and a conormal covector $dF^i|_p$ as the normal vector $\nabla F^i(p)$. For $F = (F_1, \ldots, F_m) : \mathbb{R}^N \to \mathbb{R}^m$ as in the recalled Definition~\ref{def:jacobian}, $f$ smooth near $F(p)$, and $y_1, \ldots, y_m$ the coordinates of $\mathbb{R}^m$, the chain rule $\nabla(f \circ F) = J_F^{\mathsf T}\, \nabla f$, with the gradients written as columns, reads
\[
\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\partial (f \circ F)}{\partial x_1}(p) \\ \vdots \\ \dfrac{\partial (f \circ F)}{\partial x_N}(p) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F_m}{\partial x_1}(p) \\ \vdots & & \vdots \\ \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_N}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F_m}{\partial x_N}(p) \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y_1}\big(F(p)\big) \\ \vdots \\ \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y_m}\big(F(p)\big) \end{pmatrix} ,
\]
the $N \times m$ matrix in the middle being $(DF_p)^{\mathsf T}$. An abstract manifold has no dot product, so the covector versions are the intrinsic ones; an inner product on each tangent space --- a metric --- would turn them back into vectors.

\subsection{Regular Points, Regular Values and the Theorems Behind Them}

\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.25}
\small
\begin{tabular}{p{0.3\textwidth} p{0.3\textwidth} p{0.3\textwidth}}
\hline
Geometric & Abstract & How they correspond \\
\hline
Definition~\ref{def:regular-point} ($DF_p$ surjective) & Definition~\ref{def:manifold-regular-point}, Definition~\ref{def:regular-critical} ($F_{*p}$ surjective) & Proposition~\ref{prop:regular-one-chart}: regular for $F$ iff for its coordinate representation \\
Definition~\ref{def:regular-value} (every point of $F^{-1}(c)$ regular) & Definition~\ref{def:manifold-regular}, Definition~\ref{def:regular-critical-value} & the same condition, read through charts; Corollary~\ref{cor:vs-regular} without coordinates \\
Theorem~\ref{thm:ift-general} (implicit function theorem) & Theorem~\ref{thm:submersion-normal-form} (local normal form for submersions) & the normal form is the implicit function theorem in charts \\
Theorem~\ref{thm:regular-value} (a regular level set is a topological manifold) & Corollary~\ref{cor:manifold-level-sets} (the same for $F : M \to N$) & proved through Proposition~\ref{prop:regular-one-chart} \\
Proposition~\ref{prop:level-set-smooth} (a regular level set is a smooth manifold) & Theorem~\ref{thm:rvt-manifolds} (a regular level set is a submanifold) & Proposition~\ref{prop:rvt-agree}: the same structure and tangent spaces \\
Corollary~\ref{cor:rvt-open} (open domains, arbitrary values) & Corollary~\ref{cor:submersion-fibres} (fibres of submersions) & every value of a submersion is regular \\
Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-preimage}, Corollary~\ref{cor:rvt-transverse} (transversality) & (no manifold version yet) & the regular value theorem is the case of a point \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Definition~\ref{def:regular-point} (Regular Point).} Let $F : \mathbb{R}^N \to \mathbb{R}^m$ be $C^1$. A point $p \in \mathbb{R}^N$ is a \textbf{regular point} of $F$ if the Jacobian $DF_p : \mathbb{R}^N \to \mathbb{R}^m$ (Definition~\ref{def:jacobian}) is surjective, i.e.\ has rank $m$ (Definition~\ref{def:rank}). Otherwise $p$ is a \textbf{critical point}.
For scalar-valued $F$ ($m = 1$) the Jacobian is the row vector $\nabla F(p)$, and $p$ is a regular point iff $\nabla F(p) \neq 0$.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Definition~\ref{def:manifold-regular-point} (Regular Point of a Smooth Map).} Let $F : M \to N$ be a smooth map. A point $p$ is a \textbf{regular point} of $F$ if $F_{*p}$ is surjective.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Definition~\ref{def:regular-value} (Regular Value).} Let $F : \mathbb{R}^N \to \mathbb{R}^m$ be $C^1$. A value $c \in \mathbb{R}^m$ is a \textbf{regular value} of $F$ if every point of the level set $F^{-1}(c)$ is a regular point (Definition~\ref{def:regular-point}). Otherwise $c$ is a \textbf{critical value}. (If $F^{-1}(c) = \emptyset$, then $c$ is vacuously a regular value.)
So for scalar-valued $F$, $c \in \mathbb{R}$ is a regular value iff $\nabla F$ vanishes nowhere on $F^{-1}(c)$.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Definition~\ref{def:manifold-regular} (Regular Value of a Smooth Map).} Let $F : M \to N$ be a smooth map. A value $c \in N$ is a \textbf{regular value} if every $p \in F^{-1}(c)$ is a regular point (Definition~\ref{def:manifold-regular-point}).
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Theorem~\ref{thm:ift-general} (Implicit Function Theorem --- Lee Theorem C.40).} Let $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}^k$ be an open subset, with standard coordinates written $(x, y) = (x^1, \ldots, x^n, y^1, \ldots, y^k)$. Suppose $\Phi : U \to \mathbb{R}^k$ is smooth, $(a, b) \in U$, and $c = \Phi(a,b)$. If the $k \times k$ matrix
\[
\left( \frac{\partial \Phi^i}{\partial y^j}(a, b) \right)_{1 \le i, j \le k}
\]
is nonsingular, then there exist neighborhoods $V_0 \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ of $a$ and $W_0 \subseteq \mathbb{R}^k$ of $b$ and a smooth function $F : V_0 \to W_0$ such that $\Phi^{-1}(c) \cap (V_0 \times W_0)$ is the graph of $F$; that is, for $(x,y) \in V_0 \times W_0$,
\[
\Phi(x, y) = c \iff y = F(x).
\]
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Theorem~\ref{thm:submersion-normal-form} (Local Normal Form for Submersions).} Let $F : M \to N$ be a submersion at $p$, with $\dim M = m$ and $\dim N = n$. Then there are charts $(U, \varphi)$ at $p$ and $(V, \psi)$ at $F(p)$ with $F(U) \subseteq V$ in which the coordinate representation $\tilde F = \psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1} : \varphi(U) \to \psi(V)$ is the projection onto the first $n$ coordinates:
\[
\tilde F\big(r^1, \ldots, r^m\big) = \big(r^1, \ldots, r^n\big).
\]
Equivalently, with coordinate functions $x^i = r^i \circ \varphi$ on $U$ and $y^j = r^j \circ \psi$ on $V$: $\;y^j \circ F = x^j$ on $U$ for $j = 1, \ldots, n$. In particular $n \le m$.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Theorem~\ref{thm:regular-value} (Regular Value Theorem).} Let $F : \mathbb{R}^{n+k} \to \mathbb{R}^k$ be smooth and suppose $\vec 0 \in \mathbb{R}^k$ is a regular value of $F$, i.e.\ the Jacobian $F'(p) = DF_p$ (Definition~\ref{def:jacobian}) has rank $k$ at every $p \in X := F^{-1}(\vec 0)$. Then $X$, with the subspace topology, is a topological manifold of dimension $n$.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Theorem~\ref{thm:rvt-manifolds} (The Regular Value Theorem for Manifolds).} Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth, with $\dim M = m$ and $\dim N = n$, and let $q \in N$ be a regular value of $F$ (Definition~\ref{def:manifold-regular}). Then $S = F^{-1}(q)$ is a regular submanifold of $M$ of codimension $n$ (possibly empty), so $\dim S = m - n$, and for every $p \in S$
\[
\iota_{*p}(T_pS) = \ker F_{*p} .
\]
\end{quote}

The pattern is the one of the whole course: a definition is transplanted by replacing the Jacobian $DF_p$ with the pushforward $F_{*p}$, and a theorem is proved by reading it in charts, where it becomes the Euclidean one. Proposition~\ref{prop:regular-one-chart} is the bridge for regular points --- a point is regular for $F$ exactly when it is regular for the coordinate representation, because the matrix of $F_{*p}$ is that Jacobian. The local normal form for submersions plays the role of the implicit function theorem, and it upgrades the conclusion from ``topological manifold'' to ``submanifold'' with its tangent space. The remark \emph{The Regular Value Theorems --- Old and New} (\ref{sec:rvt-manifolds}) lists all five versions with their roles.

\subsection{The Global Picture: Embeddings}

A geometric manifold sits in $\mathbb{R}^N$ by construction; an abstract one need not sit anywhere. The bridge is an embedding:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Definition~\ref{def:embedding} (Embedding).} A smooth map $F : M \to N$ is an \textbf{embedding} if it is an immersion and, as a map onto its image, $F : M \to F(M)$ is a homeomorphism, $F(M)$ carrying the subspace topology of $N$. Injectivity is part of being a homeomorphism, so it need not be required separately.
\end{quote}

The image of an embedding is a submanifold (Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image}), so an abstract manifold with an embedding into $\mathbb{R}^N$ is diffeomorphic to a geometric one, and all the comparisons above apply to it. The internal description of Definition~\ref{def:internal-description} is exactly a local embedding: an injective immersion that is a homeomorphism onto its image. Injective immersions alone are not enough: their images are immersed submanifolds (Definition~\ref{def:immersed-submanifold}, Proposition~\ref{prop:immersion-image}), regular exactly when the immersion is an embedding (Proposition~\ref{prop:immersed-regular}); the figure-eight and the irrational line on the torus are immersed but not regular (Example~\ref{ex:immersed-not-regular}).

Whether every abstract manifold has an embedding into some $\mathbb{R}^N$ is answered by the Whitney embedding theorem, proved later in the course (\ref{sec:whitney}):

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Theorem~\ref{thm:whitney} (The Whitney Embedding and Immersion Theorems).} Let $M$ be a smooth manifold of dimension $m$. Then there is an embedding $M \to \mathbb{R}^{2m+1}$ and an immersion $M \to \mathbb{R}^{2m}$.
\end{quote}

\begin{rembox}[Abstract Manifolds Embed in Euclidean Space]\label{rem:whitney}
\textit{(Not from lecture at this point; the theorem is stated here ahead of its proof, which is given with Theorem~\ref{thm:whitney}.)} By Theorem~\ref{thm:whitney}, every smooth $m$-manifold --- Hausdorff and second countable, as in Definition~\ref{def:smooth-structure} --- admits a smooth embedding into $\mathbb{R}^{2m+1}$ (Lee, Theorem~6.15), and Whitney improved the dimension to $2m$. So no manifold is out of reach of the geometric picture: every abstract manifold is diffeomorphic to a submanifold of some Euclidean space. The abstract definition is still the right one, because the embedding is not part of the manifold: the same manifold has many embeddings, none of them preferred, and quotients such as $\mathbb{CP}^n$ come with none.
\end{rembox}

\subsection{What Each Picture Gives}

The geometric picture gives computations: a tangent space is a kernel, a differential is a Jacobian, a normal vector is a gradient, and all of it can be drawn. The abstract picture gives intrinsic definitions: the tangent space of $\mathbb{CP}^n$ or of $G/H$ makes sense without choosing where to put them, and every notion is independent of an embedding --- which is why the bundles, fields and forms of the next chapters are built on the abstract side. The bridges in the table are what let the course compute in the geometric picture and conclude in the abstract one.

\section{Projective Spaces and the Hopf Fibration}\label{sec:ex-hopf}

\roadmark{Stage: bundles}{The maps of this chapter on projective spaces: $S^n \to \mathbb{RP}^n$ is a two-to-one local diffeomorphism, and $S^{2n+1} \to \mathbb{CP}^n$ is a submersion and a fibration, the Hopf fibration, with local sections but no global one.}

The projections $S^n \to \mathbb{RP}^n$ and $S^{2n+1} \to \mathbb{CP}^n$ through the course: the second is the quotient map that defines $\mathbb{CP}^n$ in Section~\ref{sec:ex-cpn}, an orbit map in Example~\ref{ex:cpn-orbit}; the first is the quotient map of Proposition~\ref{prop:rpn-topologies}, and both are read in the standard atlases of Section~\ref{sec:projective-smooth}; Section~\ref{sec:ex-hopf} shows the first is a two-to-one local diffeomorphism and the second a submersion and a fibration, the Hopf fibration, with local but no global sections; and for $n = 3$ the first returns as $S^3 = \mathrm{SU}(2) \to \SO(3) \cong \mathbb{RP}^3$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:double-cover}.

\begin{exbox}[Spheres Cover Projective Spaces]\exlabel{ex:sn-rpn}
The projection $\pi : S^n \to \mathbb{RP}^n$, $x \mapsto [x]$, is a local diffeomorphism, exactly two-to-one.
\end{exbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Stated in Lecture~10 as an example, without proof --- the covering-map distinction was postponed; filled in.)} Three things are claimed: $\pi$ is smooth; it is a local diffeomorphism, that is (Definition~\ref{def:local-diffeo}), every $x \in S^n$ has a neighbourhood $U$ that $\pi$ maps onto a neighbourhood $V$ of $\pi(x)$ with $\pi|_U^V$ having a smooth inverse; and every fibre of $\pi$ has exactly two points.

\emph{Setup.} Use coordinates $x_0, \ldots, x_n$ on $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$, matching the charts $(U_i, \varphi_i)$ of Corollary~\ref{cor:rpn-atlas}: $U_i = \{[x] \mid x_i \neq 0\}$ and $\varphi_i([x]) = (x_k/x_i)_{k \neq i}$.
