\section{Differential Operators}\label{sec:diff-ops}\label{sub:diff-ops}

\roadmark{Stage: fields}{Vector fields and multiplications by functions generate a ring of operators on $C^\infty(M)$; its elements have an order, and in a chart they are the linear partial differential operators with smooth coefficients.}

\textit{Lecture~15 introduced the ring of differential operators in passing, as an aside to the locality of derivations (Lemma~\ref{lem:derivation-local}): its definition, the fact that its elements are local, and, without proof, Peetre's theorem. Those are collected here. Everything else in this section --- the algebra of multiplications and vector fields, the order of an operator, the coordinate form and the commutator estimate in \ref{sec:lie-bracket} --- is not from lecture; it makes precise the remark that differential operators are given by differential expressions in local coordinates.}

\begin{defbox}[Multiplication Operator]\deflabel{def:multiplication-operator}
For $g \in C^\infty(M)$, the \textbf{multiplication operator} $m_g : C^\infty(M) \to C^\infty(M)$ is $m_g f = g f$.
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[Multiplication Operators]\thmlabel{prop:mult-operators}
Let $g, h \in C^\infty(M)$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $m_g$ is an $\mathbb{R}$-linear operator (Definition~\ref{def:linear-operator}), and
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $m_{g + h} = m_g + m_h$, $m_{gh} = m_g \circ m_h$, $m_1 = \mathrm{id}$ and $m_c = c\, \mathrm{id}$ (writing $c$ also for the constant function);
    \item $m_g$ determines $g$: $g = m_g(1)$, so $m_g = m_h$ only if $g = h$.
\end{enumerate}
So $g \mapsto m_g$ is an injective ring homomorphism from $C^\infty(M)$ into the linear operators, whose image $\{ m_g \}$ is a \emph{commutative} subring: $m_g \circ m_h = m_{gh} = m_{hg} = m_h \circ m_g$.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} Two operators are equal when they give the same function on every $f \in C^\infty(M)$, and two functions are equal when they agree at every point; operators are added pointwise, $(P + Q)f = Pf + Qf$, and composed by $(P \circ Q)f = P(Qf)$ (Definition~\ref{def:operator-sum-composite}). So each claim is checked at a function $f$ and a point $p$.

\emph{$m_g$ is a linear operator.} $m_g f = gf$ is a product of smooth functions, so $m_g$ maps $C^\infty(M)$ to $C^\infty(M)$. For $f_1, f_2 \in C^\infty(M)$ and $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$, by distributivity in $\mathbb{R}$,
\[
\big(m_g(af_1 + bf_2)\big)(p) = g(p)\big(a f_1(p) + b f_2(p)\big) = a\, g(p) f_1(p) + b\, g(p) f_2(p) = \big(a\, m_g f_1 + b\, m_g f_2\big)(p) .
\]

\emph{(1)} The four identities, by the arithmetic of $\mathbb{R}$ at the point $p$:
\[
(m_{g+h} f)(p) = \big(g(p) + h(p)\big) f(p) = g(p) f(p) + h(p) f(p) = (m_g f)(p) + (m_h f)(p) = \big((m_g + m_h) f\big)(p),
\]
\[
(m_{gh} f)(p) = \big(g(p) h(p)\big) f(p) = g(p)\big(h(p) f(p)\big) = g(p)\,(m_h f)(p) = \big(m_g(m_h f)\big)(p) = \big((m_g \circ m_h) f\big)(p),
\]
\[
(m_1 f)(p) = 1 \cdot f(p) = f(p) = (\mathrm{id}\, f)(p), \qquad (m_c f)(p) = c\, f(p) = \big((c\,\mathrm{id}) f\big)(p) .
\]

\emph{(2)} Applying $m_g$ to the constant function $1$: $m_g(1) = g \cdot 1 = g$. So if $m_g = m_h$, then $g = m_g(1) = m_h(1) = h$.

\emph{The final sentence.} By (1), $g \mapsto m_g$ sends sums to sums, products to composites, and the unit $1$ to the unit $\mathrm{id}$, so it is a ring homomorphism; by (2) it is injective. Its image is commutative because $C^\infty(M)$ is, $gh = hg$ pointwise: by (1), $m_g \circ m_h = m_{gh} = m_{hg} = m_h \circ m_g$.
\end{proof}

\begin{defbox}[Differential Operators]\deflabel{def:differential-operator}
The \textbf{ring of differential operators} on $M$, written $\mathrm{Diff}(M)$ here, is the subring of the $\mathbb{R}$-linear maps $C^\infty(M) \to C^\infty(M)$ (with sum and composition) generated by
\[
D_\mathbf{X} \quad (\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)) \qquad \text{and} \qquad m_g \quad (g \in C^\infty(M)) ,
\]
the operators of Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-derivation} and Definition~\ref{def:multiplication-operator}. Its elements, the \textbf{differential operators}, are the finite sums of finite composites of such operators.
\end{defbox}

In words: apply a vector field, compose with multiplication by a function or with another vector field, do finitely many of these things, and take linear combinations of the results. (The name $\mathrm{Diff}(M)$ is not from lecture.)

\begin{propbox}[Vector Fields and Multiplication Operators]\thmlabel{prop:vf-mult-commutation}
Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ and $g \in C^\infty(M)$. Then
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $m_g \circ D_\mathbf{X} = D_{g\mathbf{X}}$, for the vector field $g\mathbf{X}$ of Definition~\ref{def:function-times-field};
    \item $D_\mathbf{X} \circ m_g = m_g \circ D_\mathbf{X} + m_{\mathbf{X}g}$, where $\mathbf{X}g = D_\mathbf{X} g$.
\end{enumerate}
In words: a multiplication can always be moved to the \emph{left} of a vector field, at the cost of the extra term $m_{\mathbf{X}g}$, which contains no vector field.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} Both parts are equalities of operators on $C^\infty(M)$: two operators are equal when they give the same function on every $f$, and two functions are equal when they agree at every point. So let $f \in C^\infty(M)$ and $p \in M$.

\emph{(1)} $g\mathbf{X}$ is a vector field by Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-vector-space}(4), so $D_{g\mathbf{X}}$ is defined (Definition~\ref{def:vf-operator}). Using in turn Definition~\ref{def:multiplication-operator}, the definition of $D_\mathbf{X}$ (Definition~\ref{def:vf-operator}), the pointwise scalar multiplication of derivations (Definition~\ref{def:abstract-tangent}), and Definition~\ref{def:function-times-field}:
\[
\big((m_g \circ D_\mathbf{X}) f\big)(p) = g(p)\,(D_\mathbf{X} f)(p) = g(p)\, \mathbf{X}_p[f] = \big(g(p)\, \mathbf{X}_p\big)[f] = (g\mathbf{X})_p[f] = (D_{g\mathbf{X}} f)(p) .
\]

\emph{(2)} By the product rule for the derivation $D_\mathbf{X}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-derivation}), applied to the product $gf$:
\[
D_\mathbf{X}(m_g f) = D_\mathbf{X}(gf) = g\, D_\mathbf{X} f + f\, D_\mathbf{X} g = (m_g \circ D_\mathbf{X}) f + m_{\mathbf{X}g} f = \big(m_g \circ D_\mathbf{X} + m_{\mathbf{X}g}\big) f .
\]
The third equality uses $g\, D_\mathbf{X} f = m_g(D_\mathbf{X} f)$ and $f\, D_\mathbf{X} g = (\mathbf{X}g)\, f = m_{\mathbf{X}g} f$, with $\mathbf{X}g = D_\mathbf{X} g \in C^\infty(M)$; the last is the pointwise sum of operators. As $f$ was arbitrary, $D_\mathbf{X} \circ m_g = m_g \circ D_\mathbf{X} + m_{\mathbf{X}g}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{exbox}[Differential Operators in Coordinates]\exlabel{ex:differential-operators}
\textit{(Not from lecture.)} On $M = \mathbb{R}$ with coordinate $x$, write $\partial = D_{\partial/\partial x}$. Then $P = \partial \circ \partial + m_x \circ \partial$ is a differential operator, $Pf = f'' + x f'$, of order $2$ (Definition~\ref{def:diff-op-order} below). On $M = \mathbb{R}^2$ the Laplacian $\Delta = \partial_x \circ \partial_x + \partial_y \circ \partial_y$ is one, also of order $2$. Composites can always be rewritten with the multiplications in front, because of the product rule $\partial \circ m_g = m_{\partial g} + m_g \circ \partial$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-mult-commutation}(2)): for instance $\partial \circ m_x \circ \partial = \partial + m_x \circ \partial \circ \partial$, that is, $(x f')' = f' + x f''$. Rewriting every composite in this way is how Proposition~\ref{prop:diff-op-coords} below puts any differential operator, in a chart, in the form $\sum_\alpha a_\alpha\, \partial^\alpha$ with smooth coefficients $a_\alpha$: differential operators are given by differential expressions in local coordinates.
\end{exbox}

\begin{defbox}[Order of a Differential Operator]\deflabel{def:diff-op-order}
For an integer $k \ge 0$, $\mathrm{Diff}_k(M)$ is the set of finite sums of composites $A_1 \circ \cdots \circ A_r$ of generators (each $A_i$ a $D_\mathbf{X}$ or an $m_g$, Definition~\ref{def:differential-operator}) in which \emph{at most $k$} of the factors are of the form $D_\mathbf{X}$; the empty composite ($r = 0$) is $\mathrm{id}$. Set $\mathrm{Diff}_{-1}(M) = \{0\}$. A differential operator $P$ has \textbf{order at most $k$} if $P \in \mathrm{Diff}_k(M)$, and \textbf{order $k$} if moreover $P \notin \mathrm{Diff}_{k-1}(M)$.
\end{defbox}

The order counts the fewest vector-field factors with which $P$ can be written, not the number in a given expression: the next example is written with one vector field but has order $0$.

\begin{exbox}[A Commutator in One Variable]\exlabel{ex:weyl-commutator}
\textit{(Not from lecture.)} On $M = \mathbb{R}$, with $\partial = D_{\partial/\partial x}$ and $m_x$ multiplication by the coordinate $x$,
\[
\partial \circ m_x - m_x \circ \partial = \mathrm{id}, \qquad \text{that is,} \quad (xf)' - x f' = f .
\]
So $\mathrm{Diff}(\mathbb{R})$ is not commutative, unlike its subring of multiplications (Proposition~\ref{prop:mult-operators}); and the operator on the left, written with one vector-field factor in each term, has order $0$. The operators with polynomial coefficients, generated by $\partial$ and $m_x$, form the \emph{Weyl algebra}; in quantum mechanics the same relation, for $i\hbar\,\partial$ and $m_x$, is the canonical commutation relation.
\end{exbox}

\begin{proof}
\emph{The identity.} By Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-mult-commutation}(2) with $\mathbf{X} = \partial/\partial x$ and $g = x$: $\partial \circ m_x = m_x \circ \partial + m_{\mathbf{X}x}$. Here $\mathbf{X}x = D_{\partial/\partial x}\, x = x' = 1$, the derivative of the coordinate function (Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-derivation} with the single coefficient $1$). So
\[
\partial \circ m_x = m_x \circ \partial + m_{x'} = m_x \circ \partial + m_1 ,
\]
and $m_1 = \mathrm{id}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:mult-operators}(1)). Subtracting $m_x \circ \partial$ gives $\partial \circ m_x - m_x \circ \partial = \mathrm{id}$. Applied to $f$ this reads $(xf)' - xf' = f$, the product rule $(xf)' = f + xf'$.

\emph{The two consequences.} $\mathrm{Diff}(\mathbb{R})$ is not commutative, because $\partial \circ m_x \ne m_x \circ \partial$: their difference $\mathrm{id}$ sends the constant function $1$ to $1 \ne 0$. And the operator $\partial \circ m_x - m_x \circ \partial$ has order $0$ (Definition~\ref{def:diff-op-order}): it equals $\mathrm{id}$, the empty composite ($r = 0$), so it lies in $\mathrm{Diff}_0(\mathbb{R})$; and it is not in $\mathrm{Diff}_{-1}(\mathbb{R}) = \{0\}$, being nonzero.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[The Order Filtration]\thmlabel{prop:diff-filtration}
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\mathrm{Diff}_0(M) \subseteq \mathrm{Diff}_1(M) \subseteq \mathrm{Diff}_2(M) \subseteq \cdots$, each $\mathrm{Diff}_k(M)$ is closed under sums, and $\bigcup_k \mathrm{Diff}_k(M) = \mathrm{Diff}(M)$.
    \item $\mathrm{Diff}_k(M) \circ \mathrm{Diff}_l(M) \subseteq \mathrm{Diff}_{k+l}(M)$: orders add, at most, under composition.
\end{enumerate}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} Throughout, ``composite'' means a composite $A_1 \circ \cdots \circ A_r$ of generators, each $A_i$ a $D_\mathbf{X}$ or an $m_g$, and $\mathrm{Diff}_k(M)$ consists of the finite sums of composites with at most $k$ factors of the form $D_\mathbf{X}$ (Definition~\ref{def:diff-op-order}). The empty sum is the operator $0 = m_0$.

\emph{(1)} \emph{Inclusions.} A composite with at most $k$ vector-field factors has at most $k + 1$; so a finite sum of such composites is also a finite sum of composites with at most $k + 1$, and $\mathrm{Diff}_k(M) \subseteq \mathrm{Diff}_{k+1}(M)$. \emph{Sums.} The sum of two finite sums of composites with at most $k$ vector-field factors is again a finite sum of such composites. \emph{Union.} Each $\mathrm{Diff}_k(M)$ consists of finite sums of finite composites of generators, so lies in $\mathrm{Diff}(M)$ (Definition~\ref{def:differential-operator}). Conversely, let $P = C_1 + \cdots + C_s \in \mathrm{Diff}(M)$ with composites $C_i$, and let $k_i$ be the number of vector-field factors of $C_i$. With $k = \max_i k_i$ (and $k = 0$ if $s = 0$), every $C_i$ has at most $k$ vector-field factors, so $P \in \mathrm{Diff}_k(M)$.

\emph{(2)} Let $P = \sum_i C_i \in \mathrm{Diff}_k(M)$ and $Q = \sum_j E_j \in \mathrm{Diff}_l(M)$, with composites $C_i$ having at most $k$ and $E_j$ at most $l$ vector-field factors. Composition distributes over sums on both sides: for every $f$,
\[
\big((P_1 + P_2) \circ Q\big) f = P_1(Qf) + P_2(Qf), \qquad \big(Q \circ (P_1 + P_2)\big) f = Q(P_1 f + P_2 f) = Q(P_1 f) + Q(P_2 f),
\]
the first by the pointwise sum of operators, the second because $Q$ is linear. Hence $P \circ Q = \sum_i \sum_j C_i \circ E_j$. Each $C_i \circ E_j$ is a composite of generators --- the factors of $C_i$ followed by those of $E_j$ --- whose vector-field factors number at most $k + l$. So $P \circ Q$ is a finite sum of composites with at most $k + l$ vector-field factors: $P \circ Q \in \mathrm{Diff}_{k+l}(M)$. (If $k = -1$ or $l = -1$, then $P = 0$ or $Q = 0$, so $P \circ Q = 0$, which lies in $\mathrm{Diff}_{k+l}(M)$ whenever $k + l \ge -1$.)
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[Differential Operators of Order 0 and 1]\thmlabel{prop:diff-low-order}
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\mathrm{Diff}_0(M) = \{ m_g : g \in C^\infty(M) \}$.
    \item $\mathrm{Diff}_1(M) = \{ m_g + D_\mathbf{X} : g \in C^\infty(M),\ \mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M) \}$, and $g$ and $\mathbf{X}$ are determined by the operator $P = m_g + D_\mathbf{X}$: $g = P(1)$ and $D_\mathbf{X} = P - m_{P(1)}$.
\end{enumerate}
In particular the derivations of $C^\infty(M)$ are exactly the $P \in \mathrm{Diff}_1(M)$ with $P(1) = 0$.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} As in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:diff-filtration}, ``composite'' means a composite of generators, each a $D_\mathbf{X}$ or an $m_g$, and $\mathrm{Diff}_k(M)$ consists of the finite sums of composites with at most $k$ factors of the form $D_\mathbf{X}$ (Definition~\ref{def:diff-op-order}).

\emph{(1)} A composite with no vector-field factor is $m_{g_1} \circ \cdots \circ m_{g_r}$. By $m_{gh} = m_g \circ m_h$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:mult-operators}(1)), applied $r - 1$ times, it equals $m_{g_1 \cdots g_r}$; for $r = 0$ it is $\mathrm{id} = m_1$. A finite sum of multiplication operators is again one, $\sum_i m_{h_i} = m_{\sum_i h_i}$, by $m_{g+h} = m_g + m_h$ (same proposition). So every element of $\mathrm{Diff}_0(M)$ is some $m_g$. Conversely $m_g$ is a composite of one generator with no vector-field factor, so $m_g \in \mathrm{Diff}_0(M)$.

\emph{(2)} \emph{Every element has the form $m_g + D_\mathbf{Y}$.} A composite with no vector-field factor is $m_g$ by (1), and $m_g = m_g + D_\mathbf{0}$, since $(D_\mathbf{0} f)(p) = 0_p[f] = 0$. A composite with exactly one vector-field factor $D_\mathbf{X}$ is $m_a \circ D_\mathbf{X} \circ m_b$, where $m_a$ is the composite of the multiplications to the left of it and $m_b$ that of those to the right (by (1); $a = 1$ or $b = 1$ if there are none). Then, by Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-mult-commutation}(2) with $g = b$, the linearity of $m_a$, Proposition~\ref{prop:mult-operators}(1), and Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-mult-commutation}(1) with $g = ab$,
\[
m_a \circ D_\mathbf{X} \circ m_b = m_a \circ \big( m_b \circ D_\mathbf{X} + m_{\mathbf{X}b} \big) = m_a \circ m_b \circ D_\mathbf{X} + m_a \circ m_{\mathbf{X}b} = m_{ab} \circ D_\mathbf{X} + m_{a\,\mathbf{X}b} = D_{ab\mathbf{X}} + m_{a\,\mathbf{X}b} ,
\]
where $ab\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-vector-space}(4). Finally, a sum of two operators of this form is again of this form:
\[
(m_g + D_\mathbf{X}) + (m_h + D_\mathbf{Y}) = m_{g+h} + D_{\mathbf{X}+\mathbf{Y}} ,
\]
because $m_g + m_h = m_{g+h}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:mult-operators}(1)), and $D_\mathbf{X} + D_\mathbf{Y} = D_{\mathbf{X}+\mathbf{Y}}$: for every $f$ and $p$, $\mathbf{X}_p[f] + \mathbf{Y}_p[f] = (\mathbf{X}_p + \mathbf{Y}_p)[f] = (\mathbf{X} + \mathbf{Y})_p[f]$ (Definitions~\ref{def:abstract-tangent} and~\ref{def:vector-fields-space}), with $\mathbf{X} + \mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-vector-space}(1)). The empty sum is $0 = m_0 + D_\mathbf{0}$. So every element of $\mathrm{Diff}_1(M)$ is of the form $m_g + D_\mathbf{Y}$. Conversely $m_g + D_\mathbf{X}$ is a sum of two composites of one generator each, with at most one vector-field factor, so it lies in $\mathrm{Diff}_1(M)$.

\emph{$g$ and $\mathbf{X}$ are determined by $P$.} First, $D_\mathbf{X}$ kills the constant function $1$: for every $p \in M$, $(D_\mathbf{X} 1)(p) = \mathbf{X}_p[1] = 0$ (Definition~\ref{def:vf-operator}), because the derivation $\mathbf{X}_p$ at $p$ annihilates constants (Lemma~\ref{lem:derivation-properties}(1)).
Hence for $P = m_g + D_\mathbf{X}$,
\[
P(1) = m_g(1) + D_\mathbf{X}(1) = g \cdot 1 + 0 = g ,
\]
and then $D_\mathbf{X} = P - m_g = P - m_{P(1)}$. If also $P = m_h + D_\mathbf{Y}$, the same computation gives $h = P(1) = g$ and $D_\mathbf{Y} = P - m_{P(1)} = D_\mathbf{X}$, and $D_\mathbf{Y} = D_\mathbf{X}$ forces $\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X}$ by the uniqueness in Proposition~\ref{prop:derivations-are-fields}.

For the last sentence. \emph{Derivations lie in $\mathrm{Diff}_1(M)$ and kill $1$:} a derivation of $C^\infty(M)$ is $D_\mathbf{X}$ for some $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:derivations-are-fields}); $D_\mathbf{X} = m_0 + D_\mathbf{X} \in \mathrm{Diff}_1(M)$ by (2), and $D_\mathbf{X}(1) = 0$ as just shown. \emph{Conversely}, if $P \in \mathrm{Diff}_1(M)$ has $P(1) = 0$, write $P = m_g + D_\mathbf{X}$ by (2); then $g = P(1) = 0$, so $P = m_0 + D_\mathbf{X} = D_\mathbf{X}$ (as $m_0 f = 0$), a derivation (Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-derivation}).
\end{proof}

\begin{lembox}[Coordinate Derivations on a Chart]\thmlabel{lem:coord-derivations}
Let $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$ be a chart and $\partial_i = \partial/\partial x^i : C^\infty(U) \to C^\infty(U)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:partials-smooth}).
\begin{enumerate}
    \item Each $\partial_i$ is a derivation of $C^\infty(U)$: $\partial_i(bu) = (\partial_i b)\, u + b\, \partial_i u$.
    \item The $\partial_i$ commute: $\partial_i \circ \partial_j = \partial_j \circ \partial_i$. Hence $\partial_i \circ \partial^\alpha = \partial^{\alpha + e_i}$ for every multi-index $\alpha$ (Definition~\ref{def:multi-index}).
\end{enumerate}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} \emph{(1)} $\partial_i$ is the operator $D_{\partial/\partial x^i}$ of the vector field $\partial/\partial x^i$ on the manifold $U$ (a vector field by Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}, its coefficients being the constants $0$ and $1$), so it is a derivation of $C^\infty(U)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-derivation}): $\partial_i(bu) = (\partial_i b)\, u + b\, \partial_i u$. \emph{(2)} The $\partial_i$ commute: by Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation}, $(\partial_i u) \circ \varphi^{-1} = \partial u_\varphi/\partial r^i$, so $(\partial_i \partial_j u) \circ \varphi^{-1} = \partial^2 u_\varphi/\partial r^i \partial r^j$, and mixed partials of the smooth function $u_\varphi = u \circ \varphi^{-1}$ are equal (Clairaut's theorem); hence $\partial_i \circ \partial_j = \partial_j \circ \partial_i$. Finally, $\partial^\alpha = \partial_1^{\alpha_1} \circ \cdots \circ \partial_m^{\alpha_m}$, and moving the extra factor $\partial_i$ past $\partial_1^{\alpha_1}, \ldots, \partial_{i-1}^{\alpha_{i-1}}$ one factor at a time gives $\partial_i \circ \partial^\alpha = \partial_1^{\alpha_1} \circ \cdots \circ \partial_i^{\alpha_i + 1} \circ \cdots \circ \partial_m^{\alpha_m} = \partial^{\alpha + e_i}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[Differential Operators in a Chart]\thmlabel{prop:diff-op-coords}
Let $P \in \mathrm{Diff}_k(M)$ and let $(U, (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$ be a chart. Then there are \emph{unique} functions $a_\alpha \in C^\infty(U)$, one for each multi-index $\alpha$ with $|\alpha| \le k$ (Definition~\ref{def:multi-index}), such that
\[
(Pf)\big|_U = \sum_{|\alpha| \le k} a_\alpha\, \partial^\alpha \big(f|_U\big) \qquad \text{for all } f \in C^\infty(M).
\]
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} Write $\varphi$ for the chart map. By Lemma~\ref{lem:coord-derivations}, the $\partial_i$ are commuting derivations of $C^\infty(U)$, and $\partial_i \circ \partial^\alpha = \partial^{\alpha + e_i}$.

\emph{Existence.} Call an operator $Q$ on $C^\infty(U)$ \emph{of form $j$} if $Q = \sum_{|\alpha| \le j} b_\alpha\, \partial^\alpha$ with $b_\alpha \in C^\infty(U)$. An operator of form $j$ is of form $k$ for $j \le k$ (take $b_\alpha = 0$ for $j < |\alpha| \le k$), and a sum of operators of form $k$ is of form $k$ (add the coefficients of equal $\partial^\alpha$). Now $P$ is a finite sum $\sum_s C_s$ of composites $C_s$ of generators with at most $k$ vector-field factors (Definition~\ref{def:diff-op-order}), and $(Pf)|_U = \sum_s (C_s f)|_U$. So it suffices to show: if $A_1 \circ \cdots \circ A_r$ is a composite of generators with $j$ vector-field factors, then $(A_1 \cdots A_r f)|_U = Q(f|_U)$ for all $f \in C^\infty(M)$, for some $Q$ of form $j$. Induct on $r$. For $r = 0$ take $Q = \mathrm{id} = \partial^{(0, \ldots, 0)}$, of form $0$. For $r \ge 1$ let $B = A_2 \circ \cdots \circ A_r$, with $j'$ vector-field factors; by the induction hypothesis $(Bf)|_U = Q'(f|_U)$ with $Q' = \sum_{|\alpha| \le j'} b_\alpha\, \partial^\alpha$ of form $j'$. Write $u = f|_U$.
\begin{itemize}
    \item If $A_1 = m_g$ then $j = j'$, and restricting the product $g\,(Bf)$ to $U$,
    \[
    (m_g B f)|_U = g|_U\, (Bf)|_U = g|_U \sum_{|\alpha| \le j'} b_\alpha\, \partial^\alpha u = \sum_{|\alpha| \le j'} \big(g|_U\, b_\alpha\big)\, \partial^\alpha u ,
    \]
    of form $j$ with the smooth coefficients $g|_U\, b_\alpha$.
    \item If $A_1 = D_\mathbf{X}$ then $j = j' + 1$. For $h \in C^\infty(M)$, Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-derivation} gives $(D_\mathbf{X} h)|_U = \sum_i \mathbf{X}^i\, \partial_i (h|_U)$; here $\partial h/\partial x^i(q) = \partial_i(h|_U)(q)$, both being computed from $h \circ \varphi^{-1}$ on $\varphi(U)$ (Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation}). With $h = Bf$, the product rule for $\partial_i$, and $\partial_i \circ \partial^\alpha = \partial^{\alpha + e_i}$,
    \[
    (D_\mathbf{X} B f)|_U = \sum_i \mathbf{X}^i\, \partial_i \Big( \sum_\alpha b_\alpha\, \partial^\alpha u \Big) = \sum_i \sum_\alpha \mathbf{X}^i \Big( (\partial_i b_\alpha)\, \partial^\alpha u + b_\alpha\, \partial_i \partial^\alpha u \Big) = \sum_i \sum_\alpha \Big( \mathbf{X}^i\, (\partial_i b_\alpha)\, \partial^\alpha + \mathbf{X}^i\, b_\alpha\, \partial^{\alpha + e_i} \Big) u ,
    \]
    the sums over $|\alpha| \le j'$. The last step uses $\partial_i \circ \partial^\alpha = \partial^{\alpha + e_i}$, which reorders partial derivatives (Lemma~\ref{lem:coord-derivations}). The coefficients $\mathbf{X}^i\, \partial_i b_\alpha$ and $\mathbf{X}^i\, b_\alpha$ are smooth on $U$ ($\mathbf{X}^i$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}), and the multi-indices occurring have $|\alpha| \le j'$ and $|\alpha + e_i| = |\alpha| + 1 \le j' + 1$. Collecting the terms with the same multi-index, the right side has form $j' + 1 = j$.
\end{itemize}

\emph{Uniqueness.} Suppose $\sum_{|\alpha| \le k} c_\alpha\, \partial^\alpha (f|_U) = 0$ for all $f \in C^\infty(M)$, with $c_\alpha \in C^\infty(U)$; we show every $c_\beta = 0$. Fix $p \in U$, let $c = (x^1(p), \ldots, x^m(p)) = \varphi(p)$, and fix $\beta$ with $|\beta| \le k$. The function $(x - c)^\beta/\beta!$ is smooth on $U$, so by Corollary~\ref{cor:germ-extension} there is $f_\beta \in C^\infty(M)$ that agrees with it on an open $W$ with $p \in W \subseteq U$. Partial derivatives on $U$ are computed from the coordinate representation on open subsets (Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation}), so two functions that agree on $W$ have all their iterated partial derivatives equal on $W$; hence $\partial^\alpha (f_\beta|_U)(p) = \partial^\alpha\big((x - c)^\beta/\beta!\big)(p)$ for every $\alpha$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:monomial-derivatives}, $\partial^\alpha (x - c)^\beta(p)$ vanishes unless $\alpha = \beta$, where it is $\beta!$. Applying the hypothesis to $f = f_\beta$ and evaluating at $p$,
\[
0 = \sum_{|\alpha| \le k} c_\alpha(p)\, \partial^\alpha (f_\beta|_U)(p) = \sum_{|\alpha| \le k} c_\alpha(p)\, \partial^\alpha\Big(\frac{(x - c)^\beta}{\beta!}\Big)(p) = c_\beta(p)\, \frac{\beta!}{\beta!} = c_\beta(p) .
\]
As $p$ and $\beta$ were arbitrary, all $c_\beta = 0$. Applied to the difference of two expressions for $P$, $(Pf)|_U = \sum a_\alpha\, \partial^\alpha (f|_U) = \sum a'_\alpha\, \partial^\alpha (f|_U)$, with $c_\alpha = a_\alpha - a'_\alpha$, this gives $a_\alpha = a'_\alpha$ for every $\alpha$: uniqueness.
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[Differential Operators on Euclidean Space]\thmlabel{cor:diff-op-euclidean}
On $\mathbb{R}^m$, with its standard coordinates and $\partial_i = D_{\partial/\partial x^i}$,
\[
\mathrm{Diff}_k(\mathbb{R}^m) = \Big\{ \sum_{|\alpha| \le k} a_\alpha\, \partial^\alpha \;:\; a_\alpha \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^m) \Big\},
\]
with the coefficients $a_\alpha$ uniquely determined by the operator. In particular $\mathrm{Diff}(\mathbb{R}^m)$ is exactly the set of linear partial differential operators with smooth coefficients, and the order of Definition~\ref{def:diff-op-order} is the usual order: the largest $|\alpha|$ with $a_\alpha \ne 0$.
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} Here $\partial_i$ in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:multi-index} for the identity chart, $f \mapsto \partial f/\partial x^i$, is the operator $D_{\partial/\partial x^i}$ of the vector field $\partial/\partial x^i$ on $\mathbb{R}^m$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-derivation}, with coefficients $\delta^j_i$); $\partial/\partial x^i$ is a vector field by Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}, its coefficients being constant.

\emph{$\subseteq$ and uniqueness.} The identity chart $(\mathbb{R}^m, \mathrm{id})$ covers $\mathbb{R}^m$, so Proposition~\ref{prop:diff-op-coords} with $U = \mathbb{R}^m$ (where $f|_U = f$) gives, for $P \in \mathrm{Diff}_k(\mathbb{R}^m)$, unique $a_\alpha \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^m)$ with $Pf = \sum_{|\alpha| \le k} a_\alpha\, \partial^\alpha f$ for all $f$.

\emph{$\supseteq$.} Conversely, each term is
\[
a_\alpha\, \partial^\alpha = m_{a_\alpha} \circ \underbrace{\partial_1 \circ \cdots \circ \partial_1}_{\alpha_1} \circ \cdots \circ \underbrace{\partial_m \circ \cdots \circ \partial_m}_{\alpha_m} ,
\]
a composite of generators with $\alpha_1 + \cdots + \alpha_m = |\alpha|$ vector-field factors, so it lies in $\mathrm{Diff}_{|\alpha|}(\mathbb{R}^m) \subseteq \mathrm{Diff}_k(\mathbb{R}^m)$ for $|\alpha| \le k$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:diff-filtration}(1)). A finite sum of such terms lies in $\mathrm{Diff}_k(\mathbb{R}^m)$, which is closed under sums (same proposition).

\emph{$\mathrm{Diff}(\mathbb{R}^m)$.} Since $\mathrm{Diff}(\mathbb{R}^m) = \bigcup_k \mathrm{Diff}_k(\mathbb{R}^m)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:diff-filtration}(1)), the differential operators are exactly the finite expressions $\sum_\alpha a_\alpha\, \partial^\alpha$ with smooth coefficients.

\emph{The order.} Let $P \in \mathrm{Diff}_k(\mathbb{R}^m)$ with its unique coefficients $a_\alpha$, $|\alpha| \le k$. For $-1 \le j \le k$: $P \in \mathrm{Diff}_j(\mathbb{R}^m)$ if and only if $a_\alpha = 0$ for all $|\alpha| > j$. Indeed, if $P \in \mathrm{Diff}_j(\mathbb{R}^m)$, its expansion with $|\alpha| \le j$ (by $\subseteq$; for $j = -1$, $P = 0$ with the empty expansion), padded with zero coefficients for $j < |\alpha| \le k$, is an expansion with $|\alpha| \le k$, so by uniqueness it equals $(a_\alpha)$, and $a_\alpha = 0$ for $|\alpha| > j$. Conversely, if $a_\alpha = 0$ for $|\alpha| > j$, then $P = \sum_{|\alpha| \le j} a_\alpha\, \partial^\alpha \in \mathrm{Diff}_j(\mathbb{R}^m)$ by $\supseteq$ (for $j = -1$, $P = 0$). So for $P \ne 0$, with $\ell$ the largest $|\alpha|$ such that $a_\alpha \ne 0$, $P \in \mathrm{Diff}_\ell(\mathbb{R}^m)$ and $P \notin \mathrm{Diff}_{\ell - 1}(\mathbb{R}^m)$: $P$ has order $\ell$ (Definition~\ref{def:diff-op-order}).
\end{proof}

\begin{lembox}[Differential Operators Are Local]\thmlabel{lem:differential-operators-are-local}
Every differential operator (Definition~\ref{def:differential-operator}) is a local operator (Definition~\ref{def:local-operator}).
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Stated in Lecture~15; the reason is filled in.)} Let $U \subseteq M$ be open and $f, g \in C^\infty(M)$ with $f|_U = g|_U$.

\emph{The generators are local.} $(m_h f)(p) = h(p) f(p)$ depends only on $f(p)$, so $(m_h f)|_U = (m_h g)|_U$. And $(D_\mathbf{X} f)(p) = \mathbf{X}_p[f]$ depends only on the germ of $f$ at $p$, because $\mathbf{X}_p$ is a derivation at $p$, acting on germs (Definition~\ref{def:derivation}); for $p \in U$, $f$ and $g$ agree on the neighbourhood $U$ of $p$, so they have the same germ at $p$, and $(D_\mathbf{X} f)(p) = (D_\mathbf{X} g)(p)$.

\emph{Sums and composites of local operators are local.} Let $P$, $Q$ be local. Then $(Pf)|_U = (Pg)|_U$ and $(Qf)|_U = (Qg)|_U$, so $((P + Q)f)|_U = ((P + Q)g)|_U$. Applying the locality of $Q$ to the functions $Pf$ and $Pg$, which agree on $U$, gives $(QPf)|_U = (QPg)|_U$.

A differential operator is a finite sum of finite composites of generators (Definition~\ref{def:differential-operator}), so by induction on the number of operations it is local.
\end{proof}

\begin{thmbox}[Local Operators Are Differential Operators]\thmlabel{thm:peetre}
Let $P : C^\infty(M) \to C^\infty(M)$ be an $\mathbb{R}$-linear local operator. Then $P$ is a differential operator near each point: every $p \in M$ has a chart neighbourhood $U$ on which $(Pf)|_U = \sum_{|\alpha| \le k} a_\alpha\, \partial^\alpha (f|_U)$ for all $f \in C^\infty(M)$, for some $k$ and some $a_\alpha \in C^\infty(U)$ --- the form of Proposition~\ref{prop:diff-op-coords}. Conversely, every differential operator is local (Lemma~\ref{lem:differential-operators-are-local}).
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}[Proof (not given in this course)]
Stated without proof in Lecture~15, for information, with the remark that the converse is the easy direction. It is Peetre's theorem. The statement is local because on a non-compact $M$ the order $k$ need not be bounded as $p$ varies, and then $P$ is not a finite sum of composites on all of $M$.
\end{proof}

% SECTION: THE LIE BRACKET
% ============================================================================

\section{Lie Bracket and Lie Algebra}\label{sec:lie-bracket}\label{sub:lie-bracket}

\roadmark{Stage: fields}{Two vector fields, composed as operators, give a second-order operator; their commutator cancels the second derivatives and is again a vector field, so $\mathfrak{X}(M)$ is a Lie algebra.}

\textit{Lecture 16. Differential operators matter here because of commutators.}

\begin{defbox}[The Lie Bracket of Vector Fields]\deflabel{def:lie-bracket}
For $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$, regarded as operators on $C^\infty(M)$ (Definition~\ref{def:operator}), the \textbf{commutator} or \textbf{Lie bracket} is the operator
\[
[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}](f) = \mathbf{X}\big(\mathbf{Y}(f)\big) - \mathbf{Y}\big(\mathbf{X}(f)\big), \qquad f \in C^\infty(M).
\]
\leeref{Ch.~8, \emph{Lie Brackets}}
\end{defbox}

Each composite $\mathbf{X} \circ \mathbf{Y}$ is a second-order operator, in $\mathrm{Diff}_2(M)$ (Definition~\ref{def:diff-op-order}), with second derivatives in local coordinates; but the commutator is much better behaved.

\begin{lembox}[The Bracket of Vector Fields Is a Vector Field]\thmlabel{lem:bracket-field}
$[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]$ is a derivation of $C^\infty(M)$; hence, by Proposition~\ref{prop:derivations-are-fields}, it is a vector field.
\leeref{Lemma 8.25}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~16: routine algebra, the key ingredient being the product rule.)} By Definition~\ref{def:global-derivation}, three things have to be shown: that $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]$ takes $C^\infty(M)$ to $C^\infty(M)$, that it is $\mathbb{R}$-linear, and that it satisfies the product rule. Throughout, $\mathbf{X}f$ is the function $p \mapsto \mathbf{X}_p[f]$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-derivation}, $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ are derivations of $C^\infty(M)$: each is linear, and $\mathbf{X}(fg) = f\,\mathbf{X}g + g\,\mathbf{X}f$, $\mathbf{Y}(fg) = f\,\mathbf{Y}g + g\,\mathbf{Y}f$.

\emph{An operator.} For $f \in C^\infty(M)$, $\mathbf{Y}f \in C^\infty(M)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-derivation}, and then $\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{Y}f) \in C^\infty(M)$ by the same lemma applied to the smooth function $\mathbf{Y}f$. Likewise $\mathbf{X}f$ and then $\mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{X}f)$ are smooth. So their difference $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}](f)$ is smooth.

\emph{Linearity.} Linearity is clear, as a difference of composites of linear maps. Explicitly, for $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ and $f, g \in C^\infty(M)$, by linearity of $\mathbf{Y}$ and then of $\mathbf{X}$,
\[
\mathbf{X}\big(\mathbf{Y}(af + bg)\big) = \mathbf{X}\big(a\,\mathbf{Y}f + b\,\mathbf{Y}g\big) = a\,\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Y}f + b\,\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Y}g ,
\]
and by linearity of $\mathbf{X}$ and then of $\mathbf{Y}$,
\[
\mathbf{Y}\big(\mathbf{X}(af + bg)\big) = \mathbf{Y}\big(a\,\mathbf{X}f + b\,\mathbf{X}g\big) = a\,\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{X}f + b\,\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{X}g .
\]
Subtracting the second line from the first and grouping the terms with $a$ and with $b$,
\[
[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}](af + bg) = a\,\big(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Y}f - \mathbf{Y}\mathbf{X}f\big) + b\,\big(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Y}g - \mathbf{Y}\mathbf{X}g\big) = a\,[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}](f) + b\,[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}](g) .
\]

\emph{Product rule.} For the product rule, apply the product rule for $\mathbf{Y}$, then the linearity of $\mathbf{X}$, and then the product rule for $\mathbf{X}$ to each of the two products $f \cdot \mathbf{Y}g$ and $g \cdot \mathbf{Y}f$:
\[
\mathbf{X}\big(\mathbf{Y}(fg)\big) = \mathbf{X}\big(f\, \mathbf{Y}g + g\, \mathbf{Y}f\big) = \mathbf{X}\big(f\, \mathbf{Y}g\big) + \mathbf{X}\big(g\, \mathbf{Y}f\big) = \mathbf{X}f\; \mathbf{Y}g + f\, \mathbf{X}\mathbf{Y}g + \mathbf{X}g\; \mathbf{Y}f + g\, \mathbf{X}\mathbf{Y}f .
\]
The same expression with $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ exchanged --- the product rule for $\mathbf{X}$, the linearity of $\mathbf{Y}$, the product rule for $\mathbf{Y}$ --- is
\[
\mathbf{Y}\big(\mathbf{X}(fg)\big) = \mathbf{Y}\big(f\, \mathbf{X}g + g\, \mathbf{X}f\big) = \mathbf{Y}\big(f\, \mathbf{X}g\big) + \mathbf{Y}\big(g\, \mathbf{X}f\big) = \mathbf{Y}f\; \mathbf{X}g + f\, \mathbf{Y}\mathbf{X}g + \mathbf{Y}g\; \mathbf{X}f + g\, \mathbf{Y}\mathbf{X}f .
\]
Subtracting, the first-order cross terms $\mathbf{X}f\,\mathbf{Y}g$ and $\mathbf{X}g\,\mathbf{Y}f$ cancel, because functions multiply commutatively: $\mathbf{X}f\;\mathbf{Y}g - \mathbf{Y}g\;\mathbf{X}f = 0$ and $\mathbf{X}g\;\mathbf{Y}f - \mathbf{Y}f\;\mathbf{X}g = 0$. That leaves
\[
[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}](fg) = f\,\big(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Y}g - \mathbf{Y}\mathbf{X}g\big) + g\,\big(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Y}f - \mathbf{Y}\mathbf{X}f\big) = f\, [\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}](g) + g\, [\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}](f).
\]
So $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]$ is a derivation of $C^\infty(M)$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:derivations-are-fields} it is the operator $D_\mathbf{Z}$ of a unique vector field $\mathbf{Z}$, and this field is again written $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]$.
\end{proof}

\begin{exbox}[A Bracket in the Plane]\exlabel{ex:bracket-plane}
On $\mathbb{R}^2$ with coordinates $(x, y)$, let $\mathbf{X} = a\, \partial_x$ and $\mathbf{Y} = b\, \partial_y$ with $a, b \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^2)$. Then
\[
[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}] = a\, \frac{\partial b}{\partial x}\, \frac{\partial}{\partial y} \;-\; b\, \frac{\partial a}{\partial y}\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x} .
\]
\end{exbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~16: an exercise in multivariable calculus.)} Both sides are vector fields: the left side by Lemma~\ref{lem:bracket-field}, the right side by Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}, since its coefficients are products of smooth functions. A vector field is determined by its operator (the uniqueness in Proposition~\ref{prop:derivations-are-fields}), so it suffices that both sides give the same function when applied to any $f \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^2)$. In the standard chart, Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-derivation} gives $\mathbf{X}h = a\, \partial h/\partial x$ and $\mathbf{Y}h = b\, \partial h/\partial y$ for every smooth $h$.

Apply both composites to $f$ and use the product rule for the partial derivatives $\partial/\partial x$ and $\partial/\partial y$:
\[
\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Y}f = a\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\Big(b\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\Big) = a\, \frac{\partial b}{\partial x}\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} + ab\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\, \partial y}, \qquad
\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{X}f = b\, \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\Big(a\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\Big) = b\, \frac{\partial a}{\partial y}\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} + ba\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\, \partial x} .
\]
The second derivatives are equal, $ab\, \partial^2 f/\partial x\, \partial y = ba\, \partial^2 f/\partial y\, \partial x$, because $ab = ba$ and the mixed partials of the smooth function $f$ agree (Clairaut's theorem). So they cancel in the difference, leaving
\[
[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]f = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{Y}f - \mathbf{Y}\mathbf{X}f = a\, \frac{\partial b}{\partial x}\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} - b\, \frac{\partial a}{\partial y}\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} .
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-derivation} again, the right side is the field $a\, (\partial b/\partial x)\, \partial/\partial y - b\, (\partial a/\partial y)\, \partial/\partial x$ applied to $f$. So the two fields have the same operator, and the bracket is the stated first-order operator.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[The Bracket in Coordinates]\thmlabel{prop:bracket-coords}
In a chart with $\mathbf{X} = \sum_i \mathbf{X}^i\, \partial_i$ and $\mathbf{Y} = \sum_i \mathbf{Y}^i\, \partial_i$, where $\partial_i = \partial/\partial x^i$,
\[
[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}] = \sum_j \big( \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{Y}^j) - \mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{X}^j) \big)\, \partial_j = \sum_j \sum_i \Big( \mathbf{X}^i\, \frac{\partial \mathbf{Y}^j}{\partial x^i} - \mathbf{Y}^i\, \frac{\partial \mathbf{X}^j}{\partial x^i} \Big)\, \partial_j .
\]
\textit{(Computed; not from lecture.)} In matrix form, with the columns of components and the Jacobian matrices $\big[\partial \mathbf{Y}^j/\partial x^i\big]$ and $\big[\partial \mathbf{X}^j/\partial x^i\big]$ of the coefficient functions (row $j$, column $i$), the components $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]^j$ of the bracket are
\[
\begin{pmatrix} [\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]^1 \\ \vdots \\ [\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]^m \end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial \mathbf{Y}^1}{\partial x^1} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial \mathbf{Y}^1}{\partial x^m} \\
\vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
\dfrac{\partial \mathbf{Y}^m}{\partial x^1} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial \mathbf{Y}^m}{\partial x^m}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{X}^1 \\ \vdots \\ \mathbf{X}^m \end{pmatrix}
-
\begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial \mathbf{X}^1}{\partial x^1} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial \mathbf{X}^1}{\partial x^m} \\
\vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
\dfrac{\partial \mathbf{X}^m}{\partial x^1} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial \mathbf{X}^m}{\partial x^m}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{Y}^1 \\ \vdots \\ \mathbf{Y}^m \end{pmatrix} .
\]
\leeref{Proposition 8.26}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in --- Example~\ref{ex:bracket-plane} is the case $\mathbf{X} = a\,\partial_x$, $\mathbf{Y} = b\,\partial_y$.)} Let $U$ be the chart domain. The $\mathbf{X}^i, \mathbf{Y}^i \in C^\infty(U)$ are the coefficient functions of Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}, $\mathbf{X}^i(q) = \mathbf{X}_q[x^i]$ and $\mathbf{Y}^i(q) = \mathbf{Y}_q[x^i]$; and for $h \in C^\infty(U)$, $\mathbf{X}(h)$ denotes the function $q \mapsto \mathbf{X}_q[h]$ on $U$. The $j$-th coefficient of a vector field is its value on the coordinate function $x^j$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}); applied to the vector field $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:bracket-field}), this gives $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]_q = \sum_j [\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]^j(q)\, \partial_j|_q$ at each $q \in U$, with $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]^j(q) = [\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]_q[x^j]$. So what has to be shown is
\[
[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]_p[x^j] = \mathbf{X}_p[\mathbf{Y}^j] - \mathbf{Y}_p[\mathbf{X}^j] \qquad \text{for every } p \in U \text{ and every } j,
\]
followed by the expansion of the right side. Informally this is $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}](x^j) = \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{Y}x^j) - \mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{X}x^j) = \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{Y}^j) - \mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{X}^j)$; the one point to take care of is that the bracket acts on $C^\infty(M)$, while $x^j$ is defined only on $U$.

\emph{A global stand-in for $x^j$.} Fix $p \in U$. Let $\chi$ be a bump function at $p$ with $\operatorname{supp}\chi \subseteq U$ (Corollary~\ref{prop:bump-existence}), equal to $1$ on an open $V \ni p$; then $V \subseteq \operatorname{supp}\chi \subseteq U$. By Corollary~\ref{cor:germ-extension}, $\tilde x^j = \chi x^j$, extended by $0$ outside $U$, lies in $C^\infty(M)$, and it equals $x^j$ on $V$. So at every $q \in V$ the germs of $\tilde x^j$ and $x^j$ coincide, and
\[
(\mathbf{Y}\tilde x^j)(q) = \mathbf{Y}_q[\tilde x^j] = \mathbf{Y}_q[x^j] = \mathbf{Y}^j(q), \qquad (\mathbf{X}\tilde x^j)(q) = \mathbf{X}_q[\tilde x^j] = \mathbf{X}_q[x^j] = \mathbf{X}^j(q) \qquad (q \in V).
\]

\emph{The coefficient at $p$.} By the last display, $\mathbf{Y}\tilde x^j$ and $\mathbf{Y}^j$ agree on the open neighbourhood $V$ of $p$, so they have the same germ at $p$, and $\mathbf{X}_p$, which acts on germs, gives them the same value; likewise for $\mathbf{X}\tilde x^j$, $\mathbf{X}^j$ and $\mathbf{Y}_p$. Hence, using first $[\tilde x^j] = [x^j]$ at $p$ and then Definition~\ref{def:lie-bracket} evaluated at $p$,
\[
[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]_p[x^j] = [\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]_p[\tilde x^j] = \mathbf{X}_p[\mathbf{Y}\tilde x^j] - \mathbf{Y}_p[\mathbf{X}\tilde x^j] = \mathbf{X}_p[\mathbf{Y}^j] - \mathbf{Y}_p[\mathbf{X}^j] .
\]
As $p \in U$ was arbitrary, this is the first formula: $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]^j = \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{Y}^j) - \mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{X}^j)$ on $U$.

\emph{The second form.} By the universal formula of Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}, $\mathbf{X}_p = \sum_i \mathbf{X}_p[x^i]\, \partial_i|_p = \sum_i \mathbf{X}^i(p)\, \partial_i|_p$. Applied to the germ of $\mathbf{Y}^j$, with Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation}, this expands $\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{Y}^j) = \sum_i \mathbf{X}^i\, \partial \mathbf{Y}^j/\partial x^i$; with the letters $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ exchanged, $\mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{X}^j) = \sum_i \mathbf{Y}^i\, \partial \mathbf{X}^j/\partial x^i$. Substituting,
\[
[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}] = \sum_j \big( \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{Y}^j) - \mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{X}^j) \big)\, \partial_j = \sum_j \sum_i \Big( \mathbf{X}^i\, \frac{\partial \mathbf{Y}^j}{\partial x^i} - \mathbf{Y}^i\, \frac{\partial \mathbf{X}^j}{\partial x^i} \Big)\, \partial_j \qquad \text{on } U.
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[The Hessian at a Critical Point via Vector Fields]\thmlabel{prop:hessian-vector-fields}
Let $p$ be a critical point of $f \in C^\infty(M)$, and $v, w \in T_pM$. For every vector field $\mathbf{W}$ with $\mathbf{W}_p = w$,
\[
\mathrm{Hess}_p f(v, w) = v\big[\mathbf{W} f\big]
\]
(Definition~\ref{def:hessian-critical}). In particular the right side does not depend on the choice of $\mathbf{W}$; and, with $\mathbf{V}$ a vector field with $\mathbf{V}_p = v$, the symmetry of the Hessian is the vanishing of $df_p$ on a bracket:
\[
\mathrm{Hess}_p f(v, w) - \mathrm{Hess}_p f(w, v) = \big([\mathbf{V}, \mathbf{W}]f\big)(p) = df_p\big([\mathbf{V}, \mathbf{W}]_p\big) = 0 .
\]
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; suggested by Assignment~5, Problem~3.)} Choose a chart $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$ at $p$. On $U$, $\mathbf{W} = \sum_j \mathbf{W}^j\, \partial/\partial x^j$ with smooth $\mathbf{W}^j$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}), and $\mathbf{W}f = \sum_j \mathbf{W}^j\, \partial f/\partial x^j$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-derivation}). The tangent vector $v$ is a derivation at $p$, acting on germs (Definition~\ref{def:derivation}), so by its linearity and Leibniz rule
\[
v\big[\mathbf{W} f\big] = \sum_{j=1}^m \Big( v\big[\mathbf{W}^j\big]\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^j}(p) + \mathbf{W}^j(p)\, v\Big[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x^j}\Big] \Big) .
\]
At a critical point $\partial f/\partial x^j(p) = df_p(\partial/\partial x^j|_p) = 0$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:critical-functions}), so the first terms vanish. In the second, $\mathbf{W}^j(p) = w^j$, the components of $w = \mathbf{W}_p$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:df-derivation} and Proposition~\ref{prop:hessian-flat}(1), in its form $(\mathrm{Hess}_p f)^\sharp(\partial/\partial x^j|_p) = d(\partial f/\partial x^j)_p$, which does not use the symmetry of the Hessian,
\[
v\Big[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x^j}\Big] = d\Big(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x^j}\Big)_p(v) = (\mathrm{Hess}_p f)^\sharp\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_p\Big)(v) = \mathrm{Hess}_p f\Big(v, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_p\Big) ;
\]
in components, with $v = \sum_i v^i\, \partial/\partial x^i|_p$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}) and Proposition~\ref{prop:hessian-forms}(1), this is $\sum_i v^i\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\big|_p\big(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x^j}\big) = \sum_i v^i\, H_{ij}(p)$. So, by the bilinearity of $\mathrm{Hess}_p f$ (Definition~\ref{def:hessian-critical}),
\[
v\big[\mathbf{W}f\big] = \sum_{j=1}^m w^j\, \mathrm{Hess}_p f\Big(v, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_p\Big) = \mathrm{Hess}_p f\Big(v, \sum_{j=1}^m w^j\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_p\Big) = \mathrm{Hess}_p f(v, w) = \sum_{i,j} H_{ij}(p)\, v^i w^j ,
\]
which involves $\mathbf{W}$ only through $w$.

For the last display: by what was just shown, $\mathrm{Hess}_p f(v, w) = v[\mathbf{W}f] = \mathbf{V}_p[\mathbf{W}f] = (\mathbf{V}(\mathbf{W}f))(p)$, and likewise $\mathrm{Hess}_p f(w, v) = (\mathbf{W}(\mathbf{V}f))(p)$. Their difference is $([\mathbf{V}, \mathbf{W}]f)(p)$ (Definition~\ref{def:lie-bracket}); $[\mathbf{V}, \mathbf{W}]$ is a vector field (Lemma~\ref{lem:bracket-field}), so this is $[\mathbf{V}, \mathbf{W}]_p[f] = df_p([\mathbf{V}, \mathbf{W}]_p)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:df-derivation}), which is $0$ because $df_p = 0$. This is a second proof of the symmetry of $\mathrm{Hess}_p f$, without Clairaut's theorem.
\end{proof}


\begin{defbox}[Lie Algebra]\deflabel{def:lie-algebra}
A (real) \textbf{Lie algebra} $\mathfrak{g}$ is a real vector space together with a bilinear, skew-symmetric operation $[\cdot,\cdot] : \mathfrak{g} \times \mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{g}$, the \textbf{Lie bracket}, satisfying the \textbf{Jacobi identity}
\[
[X, [Y, Z]] + [Y, [Z, X]] + [Z, [X, Y]] = 0 \qquad \text{for all } X, Y, Z \in \mathfrak{g}.
\]
\leeref{Ch.~8, \emph{Lie Algebras}}
\end{defbox}

The three terms come from one by permuting $X, Y, Z$ cyclically: $Y$ moves to the left position, $Z$ one place to the left, and $X$ to the last position.

\begin{defbox}[Lie Algebra Morphism]\deflabel{def:lie-algebra-morphism}
Let $\mathfrak{h}$ and $\mathfrak{g}$ be Lie algebras (Definition~\ref{def:lie-algebra}). A \textbf{Lie algebra morphism} is a linear map $\phi : \mathfrak{h} \to \mathfrak{g}$ that preserves brackets: $\phi([A, B]) = [\phi(A), \phi(B)]$ for all $A, B \in \mathfrak{h}$.
\leeref{Ch.~8, \emph{Induced Lie Algebra Homomorphisms}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[Lie Algebra Isomorphism]\deflabel{def:lie-algebra-isomorphism}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} A \textbf{Lie algebra isomorphism}, or \textbf{isomorphism of Lie algebras}, is a Lie algebra morphism $\phi : \mathfrak{h} \to \mathfrak{g}$ (Definition~\ref{def:lie-algebra-morphism}) that is bijective.
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[Commutators of an Associative Product]\thmlabel{prop:commutator-jacobi}
Let $A$ be a real vector space with a bilinear \emph{associative} product $(X, Y) \mapsto X * Y$. Then the commutator $[X, Y] = X * Y - Y * X$ is bilinear, skew-symmetric, and satisfies the Jacobi identity; so $(A, [\cdot,\cdot])$ is a Lie algebra.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Stated in Lecture~16 as a general fact, the key hypothesis being that the product is associative; filled in.)} By Definition~\ref{def:lie-algebra}, three properties of the commutator have to be checked; it takes values in $A$, since $A$ is closed under $*$ and subtraction. Bilinearity of $*$ means $(aX + bX') * Y = a\,X * Y + b\,X' * Y$ and $X * (aY + bY') = a\,X * Y + b\,X * Y'$ for $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$.

\emph{Skew-symmetry.} Directly from the definition, $[Y, X] = Y * X - X * Y = -(X * Y - Y * X) = -[X, Y]$.

\emph{Bilinearity.} In the first argument, by the bilinearity of $*$ in each of its two slots,
\[
[aX + bX', Y] = (aX + bX') * Y - Y * (aX + bX') = a\,X * Y + b\,X' * Y - a\,Y * X - b\,Y * X' = a\,[X, Y] + b\,[X', Y] .
\]
In the second argument it follows from the first and skew-symmetry:
\[
[X, aY + bY'] = -[aY + bY', X] = -a\,[Y, X] - b\,[Y', X] = a\,[X, Y] + b\,[X, Y'] .
\]

\emph{Jacobi identity.} By associativity, triple products can be written without parentheses, $XYZ = (X * Y) * Z = X * (Y * Z)$. Expanding the inner bracket and then the outer one with the bilinearity of $*$,
\[
[X, [Y, Z]] = X * (Y * Z - Z * Y) - (Y * Z - Z * Y) * X = XYZ - XZY - YZX + ZYX .
\]
The other two terms of the Jacobi identity come from this one by the cyclic renaming $X \to Y \to Z \to X$, applied once and twice. Permuting cyclically gives
\[
[Y,[Z,X]] = YZX - YXZ - ZXY + XZY, \qquad [Z,[X,Y]] = ZXY - ZYX - XYZ + YXZ .
\]
In the sum of the three lines, each of the six words appears once with each sign: $XYZ$ with $+$ in the first and $-$ in the third; $XZY$ with $-$ in the first and $+$ in the second; $YZX$ with $-$ in the first and $+$ in the second; $ZYX$ with $+$ in the first and $-$ in the third; $YXZ$ with $-$ in the second and $+$ in the third; $ZXY$ with $-$ in the second and $+$ in the third. So the sum is $0$, and $(A, [\cdot,\cdot])$ is a Lie algebra.
\end{proof}

\begin{exbox}[Matrices]\exlabel{ex:mat-lie-algebra}
$\Mat(n, \mathbb{R})$, with the commutator $[A, B] = AB - BA$ of matrix multiplication, is a Lie algebra, by Proposition~\ref{prop:commutator-jacobi}.
\end{exbox}

\begin{corbox}[Vector Fields Form a Lie Algebra]\thmlabel{cor:vf-lie-algebra}
$\big(\mathfrak{X}(M), [\cdot,\cdot]\big)$ is a Lie algebra.
\leeref{Proposition 8.28}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~16: the bracket of fields comes from a product, composition, which is associative. Filled in.)} By Definition~\ref{def:lie-algebra}, what has to be shown is that $\mathfrak{X}(M)$ is a real vector space, that the bracket maps $\mathfrak{X}(M) \times \mathfrak{X}(M)$ into $\mathfrak{X}(M)$, and that it is bilinear, skew-symmetric and satisfies the Jacobi identity. In this proof write $D_\mathbf{X}$ for $\mathbf{X}$ regarded as an operator (Definition~\ref{def:vf-operator}), to keep the field and its operator apart.

\emph{The space and the bracket.} $\mathfrak{X}(M)$ is a real vector space by Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-vector-space}. By Lemma~\ref{lem:bracket-field}, $\mathfrak{X}(M)$, identified with the derivations, is closed under the commutator: for $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ the commutator of $D_\mathbf{X}$ and $D_\mathbf{Y}$ is the operator of the vector field $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]$,
\[
D_{[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]} = D_\mathbf{X} \circ D_\mathbf{Y} - D_\mathbf{Y} \circ D_\mathbf{X} .
\]

\emph{The operators form an associative algebra.} Let $A$ be the set of $\mathbb{R}$-linear operators on $C^\infty(M)$ (Definition~\ref{def:linear-operator}), a real vector space under $(aP + bQ)f = a\,Pf + b\,Qf$, with the product $P * Q = P \circ Q$, again a linear operator (Lemma~\ref{lem:linear-operators-closed}). Composition of maps is associative. It is bilinear: $\big((aP + bP') \circ Q\big)f = a\,P(Qf) + b\,P'(Qf)$ by the definition of the operations, and $\big(P \circ (aQ + bQ')\big)f = P(a\,Qf + b\,Q'f) = a\,P(Qf) + b\,P(Q'f)$ because $P$ is linear. So the linear operators on $C^\infty(M)$ form an associative algebra under composition, and by Proposition~\ref{prop:commutator-jacobi} their commutator $[P, Q] = P \circ Q - Q \circ P$ is bilinear, skew-symmetric and satisfies the Jacobi identity. The display above reads $D_{[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]} = [D_\mathbf{X}, D_\mathbf{Y}]$.

\emph{From operators to fields.} The map $\mathbf{X} \mapsto D_\mathbf{X}$ is linear: for $f \in C^\infty(M)$ and $p \in M$, by Definition~\ref{def:vector-fields-space} and the pointwise operations of $T_pM$ (Definition~\ref{def:abstract-tangent}),
\[
\big(D_{a\mathbf{X} + b\mathbf{Y}} f\big)(p) = \big(a\,\mathbf{X}_p + b\,\mathbf{Y}_p\big)[f] = a\,\mathbf{X}_p[f] + b\,\mathbf{Y}_p[f] = \big((a\,D_\mathbf{X} + b\,D_\mathbf{Y}) f\big)(p) .
\]
It is injective, by the uniqueness in Proposition~\ref{prop:derivations-are-fields}. So an identity between fields holds as soon as the corresponding identity between their operators holds. Using $D_{[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]} = [D_\mathbf{X}, D_\mathbf{Y}]$ and the linearity of $\mathbf{X} \mapsto D_\mathbf{X}$:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \emph{bilinearity:} $D_{[a\mathbf{X} + b\mathbf{X}', \mathbf{Y}]} = [a\,D_\mathbf{X} + b\,D_{\mathbf{X}'}, D_\mathbf{Y}] = a\,[D_\mathbf{X}, D_\mathbf{Y}] + b\,[D_{\mathbf{X}'}, D_\mathbf{Y}] = D_{a[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}] + b[\mathbf{X}', \mathbf{Y}]}$, and in the second argument $D_{[\mathbf{X}, a\mathbf{Y} + b\mathbf{Y}']} = [D_\mathbf{X}, a\,D_\mathbf{Y} + b\,D_{\mathbf{Y}'}] = a\,[D_\mathbf{X}, D_\mathbf{Y}] + b\,[D_\mathbf{X}, D_{\mathbf{Y}'}] = D_{a[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}] + b[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}']}$;
    \item \emph{skew-symmetry:} $D_{[\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}]} = [D_\mathbf{Y}, D_\mathbf{X}] = -[D_\mathbf{X}, D_\mathbf{Y}] = D_{-[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]}$;
    \item \emph{Jacobi:} applying the identity twice, $D_{[\mathbf{X}, [\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{Z}]]} = [D_\mathbf{X}, D_{[\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{Z}]}] = [D_\mathbf{X}, [D_\mathbf{Y}, D_\mathbf{Z}]]$, and the same with $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{Z}$ renamed cyclically; adding the three,
    \[
    D_{[\mathbf{X}, [\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{Z}]] + [\mathbf{Y}, [\mathbf{Z}, \mathbf{X}]] + [\mathbf{Z}, [\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]]} = [D_\mathbf{X}, [D_\mathbf{Y}, D_\mathbf{Z}]] + [D_\mathbf{Y}, [D_\mathbf{Z}, D_\mathbf{X}]] + [D_\mathbf{Z}, [D_\mathbf{X}, D_\mathbf{Y}]] = 0 = D_\mathbf{0} .
    \]
\end{itemize}
By injectivity each identity holds between the fields themselves; in particular the Jacobi identity holds on $\mathfrak{X}(M)$.
\end{proof}

Checking the Jacobi identity for vector fields directly by hand is a big computation. The Lie algebra $\mathfrak{X}(M)$ is infinite-dimensional (for $\dim M \ge 1$). The finite-dimensional Lie algebras of \ref{sec:lie-groups} sit inside it.

The bracket of two vector fields is one instance of a general fact about the ring of differential operators (\ref{sec:diff-ops}): a commutator is always of lower order than the composites it is made from.

\begin{propbox}[Commutators Lower the Order]\thmlabel{prop:diff-commutator-order}
For operators $P, Q$ write $[P, Q] = P \circ Q - Q \circ P$, as in Definition~\ref{def:lie-bracket}. For the generators of $\mathrm{Diff}(M)$, with $g, h \in C^\infty(M)$ and $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $[m_g, m_h] = 0$;
    \item $[D_\mathbf{X}, m_g] = m_{\mathbf{X}g}$;
    \item $[D_\mathbf{X}, D_\mathbf{Y}] = D_{[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]}$.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently, if $P \in \mathrm{Diff}_k(M)$ and $Q \in \mathrm{Diff}_l(M)$, then $[P, Q] \in \mathrm{Diff}_{k+l-1}(M)$ (Definition~\ref{def:diff-op-order}).
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} (1) is Proposition~\ref{prop:mult-operators}, (2) is Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-mult-commutation}(2), and (3) is Lemma~\ref{lem:bracket-field}, read with $D_\mathbf{X}$ written out. So for generators $A, B$ of orders $a, b \in \{0, 1\}$ ($0$ for a multiplication, $1$ for a vector field), $[A, B] \in \mathrm{Diff}_{a+b-1}(M)$. Two identities, checked by expanding (each side of the first is $PQR - QRP$),
\[
[P, Q \circ R] = [P, Q] \circ R + Q \circ [P, R], \qquad [P \circ Q, R] = P \circ [Q, R] + [P, R] \circ Q ,
\]
carry this to composites, using Proposition~\ref{prop:diff-filtration}(2).
\begin{itemize}
    \item \emph{A generator against a composite.} Let $A$ have order $a$ and $B = B_1 \circ \cdots \circ B_s$ be a composite of generators of orders $b_i$, $l = \sum_i b_i$. By induction on $s$ ($s = 0$: $[A, \mathrm{id}] = 0$), with $B' = B_2 \circ \cdots \circ B_s$,
    \[
    [A, B_1 \circ B'] = [A, B_1] \circ B' + B_1 \circ [A, B'] \in \mathrm{Diff}_{a + b_1 - 1} \circ \mathrm{Diff}_{l - b_1} + \mathrm{Diff}_{b_1} \circ \mathrm{Diff}_{a + l - b_1 - 1} \subseteq \mathrm{Diff}_{a + l - 1} .
    \]
    \item \emph{A composite against a composite.} Let $A = A_1 \circ \cdots \circ A_r$ have orders $a_i$, $k = \sum_i a_i$; by induction on $r$ ($r = 0$: $[\mathrm{id}, B] = 0$), with $A' = A_2 \circ \cdots \circ A_r$,
    \[
    [A_1 \circ A', B] = A_1 \circ [A', B] + [A_1, B] \circ A' \in \mathrm{Diff}_{a_1} \circ \mathrm{Diff}_{k - a_1 + l - 1} + \mathrm{Diff}_{a_1 + l - 1} \circ \mathrm{Diff}_{k - a_1} \subseteq \mathrm{Diff}_{k + l - 1} .
    \]
    \item \emph{Sums.} The commutator is bilinear. A $P \in \mathrm{Diff}_k(M)$ is a sum of composites with $k' \le k$ vector-field factors, a $Q \in \mathrm{Diff}_l(M)$ one of composites with $l' \le l$, and each $[\text{composite}, \text{composite}]$ lies in $\mathrm{Diff}_{k' + l' - 1} \subseteq \mathrm{Diff}_{k + l - 1}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:diff-filtration}(1)). \qedhere
\end{itemize}
\end{proof}

So two differential operators commute ``up to lower order''. For $k = l = 1$, applied to $D_\mathbf{X}$ and $D_\mathbf{Y}$, the second-order parts of $\mathbf{X} \circ \mathbf{Y}$ and $\mathbf{Y} \circ \mathbf{X}$ cancel, as in Example~\ref{ex:bracket-plane}; what is left lies in $\mathrm{Diff}_1(M)$ and kills constants, and is the vector field $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:diff-low-order}(2)).


\begin{exbox}[The Cross Product]\exlabel{ex:cross-product-lie}
$\mathbb{R}^3$ with the cross product is a Lie algebra, and the hat map of Definition~\ref{def:hat-map} is an isomorphism of Lie algebras (Definition~\ref{def:lie-algebra-isomorphism}) onto $\Skew(3, \mathbb{R}) = \mathfrak{so}(3)$ with the matrix commutator:
\[
[\hat a, \hat b] = \hat a \hat b - \hat b \hat a = \widehat{a \times b} .
\]
Here, written out (Definition~\ref{def:hat-map}), for $a = (a_1, a_2, a_3)$,
\[
\hat a = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -a_3 & a_2 \\ a_3 & 0 & -a_1 \\ -a_2 & a_1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} .
\]
\end{exbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~16 mentioned only that the cross product satisfies the Jacobi identity. The proof via the hat map is filled in.)} There are three steps: the bracket identity $[\hat a, \hat b] = \widehat{a \times b}$; that $\Skew(3,\mathbb{R})$ is a Lie algebra under the commutator; and the transfer of the Lie algebra axioms to $(\mathbb{R}^3, \times)$ along the hat map.

\emph{The identity.} Two $3 \times 3$ matrices are equal if they agree on every $x \in \mathbb{R}^3$, so fix $x$. By Definition~\ref{def:hat-map}, $\hat v\, y = v \times y$ for all $v, y$, so $\hat a \hat b\, x = a \times (b \times x)$ and $\hat b \hat a\, x = b \times (a \times x)$. The vector identity $u \times (v \times w) = v\,(u \cdot w) - w\,(u \cdot v)$, with $(u, v, w) = (a, b, x)$ and with $(u, v, w) = (b, a, x)$, gives
\[
a \times (b \times x) = b\,(a \cdot x) - x\,(a \cdot b), \qquad b \times (a \times x) = a\,(b \cdot x) - x\,(b \cdot a) ,
\]
and the terms in $x$ cancel in the difference because $a \cdot b = b \cdot a$. The same identity with $(u, v, w) = (x, a, b)$, together with the antisymmetry of the cross product, gives $(a \times b) \times x = -\,x \times (a \times b) = -\big(a\,(x \cdot b) - b\,(x \cdot a)\big) = b\,(a \cdot x) - a\,(b \cdot x)$. Together, for every $x \in \mathbb{R}^3$,
\[
[\hat a, \hat b]\, x = a \times (b \times x) - b \times (a \times x) = b\,(a \cdot x) - a\,(b \cdot x) = (a \times b) \times x = \widehat{a \times b}\, x .
\]

\emph{$\Skew(3,\mathbb{R})$ is a Lie algebra.} It is a linear subspace of $\Mat(3,\mathbb{R})$, since $A^{\mathsf T} = -A$ is a linear condition. It is closed under the commutator: for skew $A, B$, using $(XY)^{\mathsf T} = Y^{\mathsf T} X^{\mathsf T}$,
\[
[A,B]^{\mathsf T} = B^{\mathsf T} A^{\mathsf T} - A^{\mathsf T} B^{\mathsf T} = [B^{\mathsf T}, A^{\mathsf T}] = (-B)(-A) - (-A)(-B) = [B, A] = -[A,B] .
\]
So the commutator restricts to a bracket $\Skew(3,\mathbb{R}) \times \Skew(3,\mathbb{R}) \to \Skew(3,\mathbb{R})$, and bilinearity, skew-symmetry and the Jacobi identity hold there because they hold for all matrices; so it is a Lie algebra by Example~\ref{ex:mat-lie-algebra}.

\emph{Transfer.} The hat map is a linear isomorphism (Definition~\ref{def:hat-map}) carrying $\times$ to the commutator, $\widehat{a \times b} = [\hat a, \hat b]$; so the cross product inherits bilinearity, skew-symmetry and the Jacobi identity --- without the big computation. In detail, for $a, a', b, b', c \in \mathbb{R}^3$ and $s, t \in \mathbb{R}$, using the linearity of the hat map, the identity, and the properties of the commutator on $\Skew(3,\mathbb{R})$:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \emph{bilinearity:} $\widehat{(sa + ta') \times b} = [s\hat a + t\hat a', \hat b] = s\,[\hat a, \hat b] + t\,[\hat a', \hat b] = s\,\widehat{a \times b} + t\,\widehat{a' \times b}$, and $\widehat{a \times (sb + tb')} = [\hat a, s\hat b + t\hat b'] = s\,\widehat{a \times b} + t\,\widehat{a \times b'}$;
    \item \emph{skew-symmetry:} $\widehat{b \times a} = [\hat b, \hat a] = -[\hat a, \hat b] = -\widehat{a \times b}$;
    \item \emph{Jacobi:} applying the identity twice, $\widehat{a \times (b \times c)} = [\hat a, \widehat{b \times c}] = [\hat a, [\hat b, \hat c]]$, and likewise with $a, b, c$ renamed cyclically, so
    \[
    \widehat{a \times (b \times c)} + \widehat{b \times (c \times a)} + \widehat{c \times (a \times b)} = [\hat a, [\hat b, \hat c]] + [\hat b, [\hat c, \hat a]] + [\hat c, [\hat a, \hat b]] = 0 .
    \]
\end{itemize}
Since the hat map is linear and injective, each equality between hats is the corresponding equality in $\mathbb{R}^3$. So $(\mathbb{R}^3, \times)$ is a Lie algebra, and the hat map, a linear bijection with $\widehat{a \times b} = [\hat a, \hat b]$, is an isomorphism of Lie algebras onto $\Skew(3,\mathbb{R})$ (Definition~\ref{def:lie-algebra-isomorphism}).
\end{proof}

The classical groups through the course: defined in Section~\ref{sec:topgroups}, with the examples of Section~\ref{sec:ex-classical}; topological manifolds as level sets in Theorem~\ref{thm:classical-manifolds}; $\SO(2)$ and $\SO(3)$ acting on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\mathbb{R}^3$ in Examples~\ref{ex:so2-orbits} and~\ref{ex:so3-orbits}, and $\SO(3)$ on $S^2$ in Examples~\ref{ex:so3-isotropy} and~\ref{ex:s2-homogeneous}; $\Ogp(n)$ acting on the Grassmannians in Corollary~\ref{cor:grassmannian}; smooth manifolds in Examples~\ref{ex:On-smooth} and~\ref{ex:Un-smooth}; their tangent spaces at the identity in Theorem~\ref{thm:classical-summary}, with the infinitesimal rotations of Example~\ref{ex:so3-infinitesimal}; the double cover $\mathrm{SU}(2) \to \SO(3)$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:double-cover}; the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ and the cross product in Example~\ref{ex:cross-product-lie}; and Lie groups in Proposition~\ref{prop:classical-lie-groups}.

\section{Related Vector Fields}\label{sec:related-fields}\label{sub:related-fields}

\roadmark{Stage: fields}{Vector fields cannot be pushed forward along an arbitrary smooth map, but two fields can be related by one; related fields have related brackets, and a diffeomorphism carries fields and brackets across.}

\textit{Lecture 17. Back to vector fields, still from the operator point of view; vector fields as generators of dynamics come later. Recap: every vector field defines a derivation of $C^\infty(M)$, and conversely (Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-derivation}, Proposition~\ref{prop:derivations-are-fields}); so the commutator of two fields is again a field (Lemma~\ref{lem:bracket-field}). Officially, a vector field is a smooth section of the tangent bundle (Definition~\ref{def:vector-field}).}

\begin{rembox}[Vector Fields Do Not Push Forward]\label{rem:fields-not-functorial}
Given a smooth map $F : M \to N$, in general vector fields can be neither pushed forward nor pulled back: vector fields have no functorial properties, as opposed to differential forms, which can always be pulled back. Single tangent vectors \emph{can} be pushed forward, by $dF_p$; the trouble is assembling the results into a field on $N$.
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
\item If $F$ is not injective, two points $p_1 \ne p_2$ with $F(p_1) = F(p_2) = q$ give two candidates $dF_{p_1}(\mathbf{X}_{p_1})$ and $dF_{p_2}(\mathbf{X}_{p_2})$ at $q$, in general different, so the would-be pushforward is multi-valued.
\item If $F$ is not surjective, a point $q' \notin F(M)$ gets no candidate at all, so nothing defines the field outside the image.
\end{itemize}
\end{rembox}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.95]
\draw[thick, violet!70!black, fill=violet!4] (0,0) ellipse (1.6 and 1.05);
\node[violet!70!black, font=\footnotesize] at (-1.25,0.95) {$M$};
\fill (-0.60,0.25) circle (1.6pt) node[below left, font=\scriptsize] {$p_1$};
\fill (0.20,-0.25) circle (1.6pt) node[below left, font=\scriptsize] {$p_2$};
\draw[->, very thick, orange!85!black] (-0.60,0.25) -- ++(0.6,0.35) node[right, font=\scriptsize] {$\mathbf{X}_{p_1}$};
\draw[->, very thick, teal!65!black] (0.20,-0.25) -- ++(0.4,-0.4) node[right, font=\scriptsize] {$\mathbf{X}_{p_2}$};

\node[teal!60!black, font=\scriptsize] at (4.75,-1.0) {$F(M)$};
\fill (4.75,0.00) circle (1.6pt) node[below, xshift=-1.5pt, font=\scriptsize] {$q$};

\node[font=\scriptsize, anchor=west] at (5.35,-0.52) {$dF_{p_2}(\mathbf{X}_{p_2})$};

\node[font=\scriptsize, align=center] at (3.0,-1.85) {$F(p_1) = F(p_2) = q$: two candidates at $q$; \quad $q' \notin F(M)$: no candidate};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

The exception is a diffeomorphism, where each $q \in N$ is $F(p)$ for exactly one $p$.

\begin{rembox}[Notation: $dF_p$]\label{rem:dF-notation}
\textit{Lecture~17} switches to the more common notation $dF$, which replaces $F_*$. From here on the pushforward of Definition~\ref{def:pushforward} is written
\[
dF_p = F_{*p} : T_pM \to T_{F(p)}N ,
\]
as in Lee. It agrees with the differential of a map between vector spaces (Definition~\ref{def:vs-differential}) under the identification $v \leftrightarrow D_v|_a$ of Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs} (the remark in \ref{sec:differential-coords}), so the two uses of $dF_p$ do not clash. Earlier sections keep $F_{*p}$. Both notations are used below, with the same meaning: $\iota_{*p} = d\iota_p$, $(L_g)_{*h} = d(L_g)_h$ and $F_{*p} = dF_p$.
\end{rembox}

\begin{defbox}[Pushforward of a Vector Field by a Diffeomorphism]\deflabel{def:vf-pushforward}
Let $F : M \to N$ be a diffeomorphism and $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$. The \textbf{pushforward} of $\mathbf{X}$ is the section $F_*\mathbf{X}$ of $TN$ given by
\[
(F_*\mathbf{X})_q = dF_{F^{-1}(q)}\big(\mathbf{X}_{F^{-1}(q)}\big), \qquad q \in N .
\]
\leeref{Ch.~8, \emph{Pushforwards of Vector Fields}}
\end{defbox}

It is smooth, so $F_*\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(N)$: this is Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-pushforward} below. For a general $F$, however, a field on $M$ and a field on $N$ can still be related by $F$, corresponding to one another: relatedness is not a construction but something that may happen.

\begin{defbox}[$F$-Related Vector Fields]\deflabel{def:F-related}
Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth, $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ and $\mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{X}(N)$. Then $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ are \textbf{$F$-related} if
\[
dF_p(\mathbf{X}_p) = \mathbf{Y}_{F(p)} \in T_{F(p)}N \qquad \text{for every } p \in M .
\]
\leeref{Ch.~8, \emph{Vector Fields and Smooth Maps}}
\end{defbox}

In words: push the value of $\mathbf{X}$ at $p$ forward; if every time this gives the value of $\mathbf{Y}$ at the image point $F(p)$, the two vector fields are related by $F$. No injectivity or surjectivity is assumed. Points outside $F(M)$ impose nothing on $\mathbf{Y}$, and two points with the same image must push forward to the same vector. \textit{(Computed; not from lecture.)} In charts $(U, (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$ of $M$ and $(V, (y^1, \ldots, y^n))$ of $N$ with $F(U) \subseteq V$, $m = \dim M$, $n = \dim N$, write $F^j = y^j \circ F$, $\mathbf{X} = \sum_i \mathbf{X}^i\, \partial/\partial x^i$ and $\mathbf{Y} = \sum_j \mathbf{Y}^j\, \partial/\partial y^j$. The matrix of $dF_p$ is the Jacobian of Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix}, so the condition reads, at every $p \in U$,
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^m}(p) \\
\vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
\dfrac{\partial F^n}{\partial x^1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^n}{\partial x^m}(p)
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{X}^1(p) \\ \vdots \\ \mathbf{X}^m(p) \end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{Y}^1(F(p)) \\ \vdots \\ \mathbf{Y}^n(F(p)) \end{pmatrix} .
\]

\begin{exbox}[Fields Related by a Projection]\exlabel{ex:projection-related}
Let $\pi : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$, $\pi(x, y) = x$, and $\mathbf{Y} = b(x)\, \dfrac{d}{dx}$ with $b \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ --- every vector field on $\mathbb{R}$ can be written like this. The fields on $\mathbb{R}^2$ that are $\pi$-related to $\mathbf{Y}$ are exactly
\[
\mathbf{X} = b(x)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x} + c(x, y)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial y}, \qquad c \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^2) \text{ arbitrary.}
\]
\end{exbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~17, as a question to the class: which components can a $\pi$-related field have? The first component is forced to be $b(x)$; the second is arbitrary. The computation is filled in.)} By Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords} in the standard chart of $\mathbb{R}^2$, every vector field on $\mathbb{R}^2$ can be written $\mathbf{X} = a\, \partial_x + c\, \partial_y$ with $a, c \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^2)$. Since $\pi(x, y) = x$, Definition~\ref{def:F-related} says that $\mathbf{X}$ is $\pi$-related to $\mathbf{Y}$ if and only if $d\pi_{(x,y)}(\mathbf{X}_{(x,y)}) = \mathbf{Y}_x$ for every $(x, y)$. So compute the left side.

\emph{The pushforwards of the coordinate vectors.} Let $[g]$ be a germ at $x$ on $\mathbb{R}$. The function $g \circ \pi$ is $(x', y') \mapsto g(x')$. By Definition~\ref{def:pushforward} and then Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation} in the standard chart,
\[
d\pi\big(\partial_x|_{(x,y)}\big)[g] = \partial_x|_{(x,y)}[g \circ \pi] = \partial_x (g \circ \pi)(x,y) = g'(x) = \frac{d}{dx}\Big|_x [g], \qquad
d\pi\big(\partial_y|_{(x,y)}\big)[g] = \partial_y|_{(x,y)}[g \circ \pi] = \partial_y\, g(x) = 0 ,
\]
where $d/dx|_x$ is the coordinate derivation of $\mathbb{R}$ at $x$ (Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation-R}, with the coordinate written $x$), and $\partial_y\, g(x) = 0$ because $g(x)$ does not depend on $y$. Derivations that agree on every germ are equal, so $d\pi(\partial_x|_{(x,y)}) = d/dx|_x$ and $d\pi(\partial_y|_{(x,y)}) = 0$. In matrix form (Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix}), the matrix of $d\pi_{(x,y)}$ is the $1 \times 2$ Jacobian of $\pi$, and it sends the column of components of $\mathbf{X}_{(x,y)} = a\,\partial_x + c\,\partial_y$ to
\[
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} a(x, y) \\ c(x, y) \end{pmatrix} = a(x, y) .
\]

\emph{The condition.} $d\pi_{(x,y)}$ is linear (Proposition~\ref{prop:pushforward-derivation}), so
\[
d\pi_{(x,y)}(\mathbf{X}_{(x,y)}) = a(x, y)\, d\pi\big(\partial_x|_{(x,y)}\big) + c(x, y)\, d\pi\big(\partial_y|_{(x,y)}\big) = a(x, y)\, \frac{d}{dx}\Big|_x .
\]
This equals $\mathbf{Y}_x = b(x)\, \frac{d}{dx}\big|_x$ if and only if $\big(a(x,y) - b(x)\big)\, \frac{d}{dx}\big|_x = 0$, that is, if and only if $a(x, y) = b(x)$, because $d/dx|_x \ne 0$ (it is a basis of $T_x\mathbb{R}$, Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}). So the fields $\pi$-related to $\mathbf{Y}$ are those with $a(x, y) = b(x)$ for all $(x, y)$, and $c$ is not constrained. Conversely, for every $c \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^2)$ the section $b(x)\,\partial_x + c\,\partial_y$ has smooth coefficients ($(x, y) \mapsto b(x)$ is $b \circ \pi$), so it is a vector field (Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}), and by the computation it is $\pi$-related to $\mathbf{Y}$.
\end{proof}

Only the horizontal component matters, and it must be the same along each vertical line, the fibre $\pi^{-1}(x)$, equal to the value of $\mathbf{Y}$ at $x$ below.
