\textit{The operator viewpoint.} The definition is geometric --- ``arrows''. There is an equivalent characterization in terms of operators, using the pullback of functions, $F^*g = g \circ F$.

\begin{propbox}[Related Fields as Operators]\thmlabel{prop:F-related-operator}
Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth, $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ and $\mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{X}(N)$. Then $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ are $F$-related if and only if
\[
\mathbf{X}(g \circ F) = (\mathbf{Y}g) \circ F \qquad \text{for every } g \in C^\infty(N),
\]
that is, $\mathbf{X} \circ F^* = F^* \circ \mathbf{Y}$: the pullback $F^*$ intertwines $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ as derivations.
\leeref{Proposition 8.16}
\end{propbox}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=4em, row sep=2.6em]
C^\infty(N) \arrow[r, "\mathbf{Y}"] \arrow[d, "F^*"'] & C^\infty(N) \arrow[d, "F^*"] \\
C^\infty(M) \arrow[r, "\mathbf{X}"'] & C^\infty(M)
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~17, a sketch of the proof; the step for the converse is filled in.)} The two forms of the condition are the same, since $(\mathbf{X} \circ F^*)(g) = \mathbf{X}(g \circ F)$ and $(F^* \circ \mathbf{Y})(g) = (\mathbf{Y}g) \circ F$; and both sides are functions on $M$, so the condition says that they agree at every $p \in M$, for every $g$. Let $g \in C^\infty(N)$ and $p \in M$. The value at $p$ of a field applied to a function is the tangent vector at $p$ applied to its germ (Definition~\ref{def:vf-operator}). With this, and the definition of the pushforward (Definition~\ref{def:pushforward}) for $D = \mathbf{X}_p$ --- germs pull back, so derivations push forward ---
\[
\mathbf{X}(g \circ F)(p) = \mathbf{X}_p[g \circ F] = dF_p(\mathbf{X}_p)[g],
\qquad
\big((\mathbf{Y}g) \circ F\big)(p) = (\mathbf{Y}g)\big(F(p)\big) = \mathbf{Y}_{F(p)}[g] .
\]

\emph{Related implies intertwining.} If the fields are $F$-related, then $dF_p(\mathbf{X}_p) = \mathbf{Y}_{F(p)}$ (Definition~\ref{def:F-related}), so the right-hand sides agree, for every $g$ and $p$; that is, $\mathbf{X}(g \circ F) = (\mathbf{Y}g) \circ F$.

\emph{Intertwining implies related.} Conversely, suppose $\mathbf{X}(g \circ F) = (\mathbf{Y}g) \circ F$ for every $g \in C^\infty(N)$, and fix $p \in M$. By the display, the two derivations $dF_p(\mathbf{X}_p)$ and $\mathbf{Y}_{F(p)}$ at $F(p)$ agree on every global function $g$. Every germ $[h]$ at $F(p)$ has a global representative $g \in C^\infty(N)$, $[g] = [h]$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:germ-extension}), so
\[
dF_p(\mathbf{X}_p)[h] = dF_p(\mathbf{X}_p)[g] = \mathbf{Y}_{F(p)}[g] = \mathbf{Y}_{F(p)}[h] .
\]
So the two derivations agree on every germ, and are equal as maps on $C^\infty_{F(p)}(N)$: $dF_p(\mathbf{X}_p) = \mathbf{Y}_{F(p)}$. As $p$ was arbitrary, the fields are $F$-related.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[Pushforward by a Diffeomorphism]\thmlabel{prop:vf-pushforward}
Let $F : M \to N$ be a diffeomorphism and $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$. Then $F_*\mathbf{X}$ is smooth, it is the unique vector field on $N$ that is $F$-related to $\mathbf{X}$, and for every $g \in C^\infty(N)$
\[
(F_*\mathbf{X})\, g = \big(\mathbf{X}(g \circ F)\big) \circ F^{-1} .
\]
\leeref{Proposition 8.19, Corollary 8.21}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} Four things are claimed: the formula, smoothness, $F$-relatedness, and uniqueness. Here $(F_*\mathbf{X})\,g$ denotes the function $q \mapsto (F_*\mathbf{X})_q[g]$ on $N$, as in Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-smooth-criterion}.

\emph{The formula.} For $q \in N$ put $p = F^{-1}(q)$. By Definition~\ref{def:vf-pushforward}, then Definition~\ref{def:pushforward} with $D = \mathbf{X}_p$, then Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-derivation},
\[
(F_*\mathbf{X})_q[g] = dF_p(\mathbf{X}_p)[g] = \mathbf{X}_p[g \circ F] = \mathbf{X}(g \circ F)(p) = \big(\mathbf{X}(g \circ F) \circ F^{-1}\big)(q) ,
\]
which is the formula.

\emph{Smoothness.} At each $q$, $(F_*\mathbf{X})_q = dF_p(\mathbf{X}_p)$ lies in $T_{F(p)}N = T_qN$, so $F_*\mathbf{X}$ is a section of $TN$. In the formula, $g \circ F \in C^\infty(M)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}), so $\mathbf{X}(g \circ F)$ is smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-derivation}); and $F^{-1}$ is smooth because $F$ is a diffeomorphism (Definition~\ref{def:diffeomorphism}), so the composite $\mathbf{X}(g \circ F) \circ F^{-1}$ is smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}). This holds for every $g \in C^\infty(N)$, so $F_*\mathbf{X}$ is smooth by Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-smooth-criterion}.

\emph{$F$-related.} For $p \in M$, $F^{-1}(F(p)) = p$, so Definition~\ref{def:vf-pushforward} at $q = F(p)$ reads $(F_*\mathbf{X})_{F(p)} = dF_p(\mathbf{X}_p)$. This is Definition~\ref{def:F-related} with $\mathbf{Y} = F_*\mathbf{X}$.

\emph{Uniqueness.} If $\mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{X}(N)$ is also $F$-related to $\mathbf{X}$, let $q \in N$. Since $F$ is onto, $q = F(p)$ with $p = F^{-1}(q)$, and by Definition~\ref{def:F-related} and then Definition~\ref{def:vf-pushforward},
\[
\mathbf{Y}_q = \mathbf{Y}_{F(p)} = dF_p(\mathbf{X}_p) = (F_*\mathbf{X})_q .
\]
This holds for every $q$, so $\mathbf{Y} = F_*\mathbf{X}$.
\end{proof}

The reason for the characterization through operators is the following proposition.

\begin{propbox}[Naturality of the Bracket]\thmlabel{prop:bracket-naturality}
Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth, $\mathbf{X}_1, \mathbf{X}_2 \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ and $\mathbf{Y}_1, \mathbf{Y}_2 \in \mathfrak{X}(N)$. If $\mathbf{X}_i$ is $F$-related to $\mathbf{Y}_i$ for $i = 1, 2$, then $[\mathbf{X}_1, \mathbf{X}_2]$ is $F$-related to $[\mathbf{Y}_1, \mathbf{Y}_2]$.
\leeref{Proposition 8.30}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Omitted in Lecture~17 as an exercise in chasing the definitions: being $F$-related means that $F^*$ commutes with the derivations. Filled in.)} The brackets $[\mathbf{X}_1, \mathbf{X}_2] \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ and $[\mathbf{Y}_1, \mathbf{Y}_2] \in \mathfrak{X}(N)$ are vector fields (Lemma~\ref{lem:bracket-field}). By Proposition~\ref{prop:F-related-operator}, it suffices to show
\[
[\mathbf{X}_1, \mathbf{X}_2](g \circ F) = \big([\mathbf{Y}_1, \mathbf{Y}_2]\, g\big) \circ F \qquad \text{for every } g \in C^\infty(N).
\]
Let $g \in C^\infty(N)$. The same proposition, applied to the pairs $(\mathbf{X}_i, \mathbf{Y}_i)$, gives $\mathbf{X}_i(h \circ F) = (\mathbf{Y}_i h) \circ F$ for every $h \in C^\infty(N)$ and $i = 1, 2$.

\emph{The composite $\mathbf{X}_1\mathbf{X}_2$.} Apply this first for $i = 2$ with $h = g$, and then for $i = 1$ with $h = \mathbf{Y}_2 g$, which lies in $C^\infty(N)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-derivation}:
\[
\mathbf{X}_1\mathbf{X}_2(g \circ F) = \mathbf{X}_1\big((\mathbf{Y}_2 g) \circ F\big) = (\mathbf{Y}_1\mathbf{Y}_2 g) \circ F .
\]

\emph{The composite $\mathbf{X}_2\mathbf{X}_1$.} Apply it first for $i = 1$ with $h = g$, and then for $i = 2$ with $h = \mathbf{Y}_1 g$:
\[
\mathbf{X}_2\mathbf{X}_1(g \circ F) = \mathbf{X}_2\big((\mathbf{Y}_1 g) \circ F\big) = (\mathbf{Y}_2\mathbf{Y}_1 g) \circ F .
\]

\emph{Subtracting.} By Definition~\ref{def:lie-bracket}, and since $u \circ F - v \circ F = (u - v) \circ F$ for functions $u, v$ on $N$,
\[
[\mathbf{X}_1, \mathbf{X}_2](g \circ F) = (\mathbf{Y}_1\mathbf{Y}_2 g) \circ F - (\mathbf{Y}_2\mathbf{Y}_1 g) \circ F = \big(\mathbf{Y}_1\mathbf{Y}_2 g - \mathbf{Y}_2\mathbf{Y}_1 g\big) \circ F = \big([\mathbf{Y}_1, \mathbf{Y}_2]\, g\big) \circ F ,
\]
and Proposition~\ref{prop:F-related-operator} again, with $\mathbf{X} = [\mathbf{X}_1, \mathbf{X}_2]$ and $\mathbf{Y} = [\mathbf{Y}_1, \mathbf{Y}_2]$, gives the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[Diffeomorphisms Preserve Brackets]\thmlabel{cor:diffeo-bracket}
If $F : M \to N$ is a diffeomorphism and $\mathbf{X}_1, \mathbf{X}_2 \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$, then $F_*[\mathbf{X}_1, \mathbf{X}_2] = [F_*\mathbf{X}_1, F_*\mathbf{X}_2]$.
\leeref{Corollary 8.31}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} By Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-pushforward}, each $F_*\mathbf{X}_i$ is a vector field on $N$ and $\mathbf{X}_i$ is $F$-related to $F_*\mathbf{X}_i$, for $i = 1, 2$. So Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket-naturality}, with $\mathbf{Y}_i = F_*\mathbf{X}_i$, shows that $[\mathbf{X}_1, \mathbf{X}_2]$ is $F$-related to $[F_*\mathbf{X}_1, F_*\mathbf{X}_2]$. On the other hand $[\mathbf{X}_1, \mathbf{X}_2] \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:bracket-field}), so Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-pushforward}, applied to this field, says that the only field on $N$ that is $F$-related to $[\mathbf{X}_1, \mathbf{X}_2]$ is $F_*[\mathbf{X}_1, \mathbf{X}_2]$. Both $[F_*\mathbf{X}_1, F_*\mathbf{X}_2]$ and $F_*[\mathbf{X}_1, \mathbf{X}_2]$ are such fields, so they are equal.
\end{proof}

\textit{(Not from lecture; the conversion diagram of the midterm check sheet, added on request.)} A vector field $\mathbf{X}$ on $M$, pointwise, globally and in components. Chart $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$; the numbers on the arrows refer to the remark below.

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=3.6em, row sep=3.2em, font=\footnotesize]
\text{section } p \mapsto \mathbf{X}_p \in T_pM \arrow[r, shift left, "(1)"] \arrow[d, shift left, "(3)"] & \text{operator } \mathbf{X} : C^\infty(M) \to C^\infty(M) \arrow[l, shift left, "(2)"] \\
\mathbf{X} = \sum_j \mathbf{X}^j \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x^j} \ \text{on } U \arrow[u, shift left, "(4)"] &
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

\begin{rembox}[Conversion Diagram for Vector Fields]\label{rem:conversion-vector-fields}
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \emph{Section to operator.} $(\mathbf{X}f)(p) = \mathbf{X}_p[f]$, a derivation of $C^\infty(M)$: $\mathbf{X}(fg) = f\,\mathbf{X}g + g\,\mathbf{X}f$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-derivation}); $\mathbf{X}f$ is smooth for every smooth $f$ exactly when $\mathbf{X}$ is smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-smooth-criterion}).
    \item \emph{Operator to section.} Every derivation of $C^\infty(M)$ is a vector field: $\mathbf{X}_p[f] = (\mathbf{X}\tilde f)(p)$ for a global $\tilde f$ with the same germ at $p$, which exists by bump functions and does not depend on the choice (Corollary~\ref{cor:germ-extension}, Lemma~\ref{lem:derivation-local}, Proposition~\ref{prop:derivations-are-fields}).
    \item \emph{Section to components.} On $U$, $\mathbf{X}^j = \mathbf{X}(x^j)$, that is, $\mathbf{X}^j(p) = \mathbf{X}_p[x^j] = dx^j|_p(\mathbf{X}_p)$.
    \item \emph{Components to section.} $\mathbf{X}_p = \sum_j \mathbf{X}^j(p)\, \partial/\partial x^j|_p$, smooth if and only if all $\mathbf{X}^j$ are (Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}); then $\mathbf{X}f = \sum_j \mathbf{X}^j\, \partial f/\partial x^j$.
\end{enumerate}
\emph{The same three faces for:}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \emph{the bracket.} Globally $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]f = \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{Y}f) - \mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{X}f)$ (Definition~\ref{def:lie-bracket}). Pointwise $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]_p[f] = \mathbf{X}_p[\mathbf{Y}f] - \mathbf{Y}_p[\mathbf{X}f]$, which needs the global function $\mathbf{Y}f$, not only the vector $\mathbf{Y}_p$. In components $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]^j = \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{Y}^j) - \mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{X}^j) = \sum_i \big(\mathbf{X}^i\, \partial \mathbf{Y}^j/\partial x^i - \mathbf{Y}^i\, \partial \mathbf{X}^j/\partial x^i\big)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket-coords}).
    \item \emph{$F$-related fields.} Pointwise $F_{*p}\mathbf{X}_p = \mathbf{Y}_{F(p)}$ (Definition~\ref{def:F-related}). Globally $\mathbf{X}(g \circ F) = (\mathbf{Y}g) \circ F$ for all $g$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:F-related-operator}). In components $\mathbf{Y}^i(F(p)) = \sum_j \frac{\partial F^i}{\partial x^j}(p)\, \mathbf{X}^j(p)$. For a diffeomorphism, $\mathbf{Y} = F_*\mathbf{X}$ with $(F_*\mathbf{X})_q = dF_{F^{-1}(q)}\big(\mathbf{X}_{F^{-1}(q)}\big)$ (Definition~\ref{def:vf-pushforward}).
    \item \emph{one-forms.} Pointwise $\theta_p \in T_p^*M$; globally the function $p \mapsto \theta_p(\mathbf{X}_p)$ for each vector field $\mathbf{X}$; in components $\theta_j = \theta(\partial/\partial x^j)$ and $\theta = \sum_j \theta_j\, dx^j$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:one-form-coords}). For $\theta = df$, $df(\mathbf{X}) = \mathbf{X}f$.
    \item \emph{the tangent bundle.} The section $\mathbf{X}$ in the standard chart of $TM$ (\ref{sec:tangent-bundle}) is $p \mapsto (x^1, \ldots, x^m, \mathbf{X}^1, \ldots, \mathbf{X}^m)$, with transition $(r, v) \mapsto (\tau(r), \tau'(r)v)$, $\tau$ the transition function of the base.
\end{itemize}
\end{rembox}


\textit{Lecture 21 opened with the last problem of the midterm.}

\begin{defbox}[Vector Field Tangent to a Submanifold]\deflabel{def:field-tangent}
Let $S \subseteq M$ be a regular submanifold, $\iota : S \hookrightarrow M$ the inclusion, and $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$. Then $\mathbf{X}$ is \textbf{tangent to $S$} if
\[
\mathbf{X}_p \in \iota_{*p}(T_pS) \qquad \text{for every } p \in S .
\]
Identifying $T_pS$ with the subspace $\iota_{*p}(T_pS) \subseteq T_pM$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-tangent}), this reads $\mathbf{X}_p \in T_pS$ for every $p \in S$. Nothing is required at points of $M \setminus S$.
\leeref{Ch.~8, \emph{Vector Fields on Submanifolds}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{lembox}[Tangency in an Adapted Chart]\thmlabel{lem:tangent-adapted}
Let $S \subseteq M$ be a regular submanifold of dimension $k$, and $(U, (x, y)) = (U, (x^1, \ldots, x^k, y^1, \ldots, y^{m-k}))$ an adapted chart with $S \cap U = \{ y = 0 \}$ (Definition~\ref{def:adapted-chart}). Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ be written on $U$ as
\[
\mathbf{X} = \sum_{i=1}^k f^i\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i} + \sum_{a=1}^{m-k} g^a\, \frac{\partial}{\partial y^a}
\]
(Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}). Then $\mathbf{X}_p \in T_pS$ for every $p \in S \cap U$ if and only if $g^a(x, 0) = 0$ for every $a$ and every point $(x, 0)$ of $S \cap U$: along $S$, there is no $y$ component.
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; the step the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket-tangent} uses, written out.)} Let $p \in S \cap U$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-tangent}, applied to the adapted chart with the coordinates along $S$ listed first, $\iota_{*p}(T_pS) = \Span\{ \partial/\partial x^1|_p, \ldots, \partial/\partial x^k|_p \}$. The $m$ vectors $\partial/\partial x^i|_p$, $\partial/\partial y^a|_p$ form a basis of $T_pM$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}), and
\[
\mathbf{X}_p = \sum_i f^i(p)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p + \sum_a g^a(p)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial y^a}\Big|_p .
\]
Since coefficients in a basis are unique, $\mathbf{X}_p$ lies in the span of the $\partial/\partial x^i|_p$ exactly when every $g^a(p) = 0$. The points of $S \cap U$ are those with $y = 0$, so the condition for all $p \in S \cap U$ is $g^a(x, 0) = 0$ for all $a$.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[Brackets of Fields Tangent to a Submanifold]\thmlabel{prop:bracket-tangent}
Let $S \subseteq M$ be a regular submanifold and $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ tangent to $S$ (Definition~\ref{def:field-tangent}). Then $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]$ is also tangent to $S$.
\leeref{Corollary 8.32}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~21, in outline; the bookkeeping is filled in.)} Use adapted coordinates: near $p \in S$ take a slice chart $(x, y) = (x^1, \ldots, x^k, y^1, \ldots, y^{m-k})$ with $S = \{ y = 0 \}$ (Definitions~\ref{def:submanifold} and~\ref{def:adapted-chart}); on the exam, $M$ was two-dimensional, but $x$ and $y$ may be vector-valued: neither the dimension nor the codimension matters. Write
\[
\mathbf{X} = \sum_i f^i\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i} + \sum_a g^a\, \frac{\partial}{\partial y^a}, \qquad
\mathbf{Y} = \sum_i u^i\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i} + \sum_a v^a\, \frac{\partial}{\partial y^a} .
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:tangent-adapted}, tangency says $g^a(x, 0) = 0$ and $v^a(x, 0) = 0$: there is no $y$ component along $S$. We show the $\partial/\partial y^b$ components of $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]$ have the same property. By Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket-coords}, that component is
\[
\mathbf{X}(v^b) - \mathbf{Y}(g^b) = \sum_i f^i\, \frac{\partial v^b}{\partial x^i} + \sum_a g^a\, \frac{\partial v^b}{\partial y^a} - \sum_i u^i\, \frac{\partial g^b}{\partial x^i} - \sum_a v^a\, \frac{\partial g^b}{\partial y^a} .
\]
Evaluate at $y = 0$. The terms with $\partial/\partial x^i$ vanish for one reason: a partial with respect to $x$ at $y = 0$ is computed by first setting $y = 0$ and then differentiating in $x$, and with $y = 0$ the function is already zero --- $\frac{\partial v^b}{\partial x^i}(x, 0) = \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\big(v^b(x, 0)\big) = 0$, and likewise for $g^b$. The terms with $\partial/\partial y^a$ vanish for a different reason: the partials $\partial v^b/\partial y^a$ and $\partial g^b/\partial y^a$ need not be zero, but their coefficients $g^a(x, 0)$ and $v^a(x, 0)$ are. So the $y$-components of $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]$ vanish on $S$, and $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]_p \in T_pS$ for $p \in S$.
\end{proof}

A field tangent to $S$, near $S$. Left: $S$ in $M$ and the domain $U$ of a slice chart $\varphi = (x, y)$. Right: in the chart, $\varphi(S \cap U) = \{y = 0\}$, and $\mathbf{X} = f\,\partial_x + g\,\partial_y$ is tangent to $S$ exactly when $g(x, 0) = 0$: on the slice its arrows point along it.

\textbf{Comparison with Lee.} Lee proves this (Corollary~8.32) with related fields: on $S$, $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ restrict to fields $\iota$-related to them, and the naturality of the bracket (Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket-naturality}) applied to the inclusion $\iota : S \to M$ does the rest. The coordinate proof above is the one given in class.

\textbf{Transcription note (Lecture 21).} Page~55 of the handwritten notes records the $\partial_y$ component of $[f\partial_x, v\partial_y]$ as $\partial v/\partial x|_{y = 0}$; it is $f\, \partial v/\partial x|_{y = 0}$, which vanishes for the same reason.

\begin{lembox}[Vector Fields on a Submanifold Extend Locally]\thmlabel{lem:vf-local-extension}
Let $S \subseteq M$ be a regular submanifold of dimension $k$, $\iota : S \hookrightarrow M$ the inclusion, and $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(S)$. Let $(U, (x, y))$ be an adapted chart with $S \cap U = \{y = 0\}$ and image a product $V \times W$, $\vec 0 \in W$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:adapted-product}, where the codimension is $m - k$), and $\pi : U \to U \cap S$ the retraction of Lemma~\ref{lem:local-retraction}. Write $\mathbf{X} = \sum_{i=1}^k \mathbf{X}^i\, \partial/\partial x^i|^S$ on $U \cap S$, in the induced chart $x|_{U \cap S}$ of $S$. Then
\[
\mathbf{Y} = \sum_{i=1}^k (\mathbf{X}^i \circ \pi)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i} \in \mathfrak{X}(U)
\]
satisfies $\mathbf{Y}_p = \iota_{*p}(\mathbf{X}_p)$ for every $p \in U \cap S$. In particular $\mathbf{Y}$ is tangent to $S$ (Definition~\ref{def:field-tangent}).
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~7, Problem~1: the submitted solution, the step ``the local extension''.)} \emph{$\mathbf{Y}$ is smooth.} Since $\mathbf{X}$ is a smooth vector field on $S$, its coefficients $\mathbf{X}^i$ in the chart $x|_{U \cap S}$ of $S$ are smooth functions on $U \cap S$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}, on the manifold $S$). By Lemma~\ref{lem:local-function-extension}, each $\mathbf{X}^i \circ \pi$ is smooth on $U$; the coefficients of $\partial/\partial y^a$ are $0$, also smooth. By Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}, $\mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{X}(U)$.

\emph{$\mathbf{Y}$ extends $\mathbf{X}$.} Let $p \in U \cap S$. Since $\pi(p) = p$, the coefficients of $\mathbf{Y}_p$ are $\mathbf{X}^i(p)$ for $i \le k$ and $0$ for the $\partial/\partial y^a$. By linearity of $\iota_{*p}$ and Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-tangent} (with $x^1, \ldots, x^k$ the coordinates of $S$), $\iota_{*p}(\partial/\partial x^i|^S_p) = \partial/\partial x^i|_p$, so
\[
\iota_{*p}(\mathbf{X}_p) = \sum_{i=1}^k \mathbf{X}^i(p)\, \iota_{*p}\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|^S_p\Big) = \sum_{i=1}^k \mathbf{X}^i(p)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p = \mathbf{Y}_p .
\]
\emph{Tangency} \textit{(filled in)}: $\mathbf{Y}_p = \iota_{*p}(\mathbf{X}_p) \in \iota_{*p}(T_pS)$ for $p \in U \cap S$; equivalently, $\mathbf{Y}$ has no $\partial/\partial y$ component at all (Lemma~\ref{lem:tangent-adapted}).
\end{proof}

The local extension depends on the chart; a global one is glued from local ones with a partition of unity, in Theorem~\ref{thm:vf-extension}.

\section{Lie Groups and Left-Invariant Vector Fields}\label{sec:lie-groups}

\roadmark{Stage: symmetry}{Groups that are manifolds, and the vector fields that respect the group: the start of Lie theory.}

\textit{Lecture 16. References: Lee Ch.~7 and Ch.~8. Lie algebras and Lie groups are related, and in one direction the relationship is very nice: every Lie group has a Lie algebra associated to it.}

\begin{defbox}[Lie Group]\deflabel{def:lie-group}
A \textbf{Lie group} is a topological group $G$ (Definition~\ref{def:top-group}) together with a smooth structure, such that multiplication $G \times G \to G$, $(g, h) \mapsto gh$, and inversion $G \to G$, $g \mapsto g^{-1}$, are smooth maps.
\leeref{Ch.~7, \emph{Basic Definitions}}
\end{defbox}

For a topological group the two maps had to be continuous; now they are required to be smooth, which makes sense because $G$ has a manifold structure.

\begin{propbox}[The Classical Groups Are Lie Groups]\thmlabel{prop:classical-lie-groups}
$\GL(n,\mathbb{R})$, $\GL(n,\mathbb{C})$, $\SL(n,\mathbb{R})$, $\Ogp(n)$, $\SO(n)$, $\Ugp(n)$ and $\mathrm{SU}(2)$, with the smooth structures of Theorem~\ref{thm:classical-summary} and \ref{sec:double-cover}, are Lie groups.
\leeref{Examples 7.3, 7.27--7.30}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Stated in Lecture~16 for all the matrix groups seen so far; filled in.)} By Definition~\ref{def:lie-group}, for each group $G$ of the list it has to be shown that multiplication $G \times G \to G$ and inversion $G \to G$ are smooth; they are then continuous, so $G$ is also a topological group (Definition~\ref{def:top-group}).

\emph{The setting.} Each group $G$ is an open subset or a submanifold of a space of matrices $\Mat$, which is $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R}) = \mathbb{R}^{n^2}$ or $\Mat(n,\mathbb{C}) \cong \mathbb{R}^{2n^2}$ (real and imaginary parts of the entries) (Theorem~\ref{thm:classical-summary}; for $\mathrm{SU}(2)$, Proposition~\ref{prop:s3-su2}). The inclusion $\iota : G \hookrightarrow \Mat$ is smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}). And a smooth map into $\Mat$ that lands in $G$ is smooth into $G$: by Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}(2) for a submanifold; for an open subset because its chart is the restriction of the linear chart of $\Mat$ (proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:classical-summary}), so the map has the same coordinate representations as a map into $G$ and as a map into $\Mat$.

\emph{Multiplication} is the composite of $\iota \times \iota : G \times G \to \Mat \times \Mat$, $(g, h) \mapsto (g, h)$, with matrix multiplication $\Mat \times \Mat \to \Mat$.
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\iota \times \iota$ is smooth since its components are: they are $\iota \circ \pi_1$ and $\iota \circ \pi_2$, smooth by Proposition~\ref{prop:product-maps} and Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}, and a map into the Euclidean space $\Mat \times \Mat$ is smooth when its components are.
    \item Matrix multiplication is smooth: the entries $(AB)_{ij} = \sum_k A_{ik} B_{kj}$ are polynomials in the real coordinates (in the complex case, the real and imaginary parts of $\sum_k A_{ik} B_{kj}$ are polynomials in the real and imaginary parts of the entries).
\end{itemize}
So the composite $(g, h) \mapsto gh$ is smooth into $\Mat$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}). It lands in $G$, because $G$ is a group under matrix multiplication; so it is smooth into $G$, by the last sentence of the setting.

\emph{Inversion} is the restriction of a smooth map on the open set of invertible matrices --- $g \mapsto \adj(g)/\det g$ by the cofactor formula, a rational map with nonvanishing denominator --- landing in $G$, hence smooth into $G$ in the same way. In detail: the set of invertible matrices in $\Mat$ is $\det^{-1}$ of the nonzero numbers, open since $\det$ is continuous. On it, the entries of $\adj(g)$ and $\det g$ are polynomials in the entries of $g$, and $\det g \ne 0$, so $g \mapsto \adj(g)/\det g = g^{-1}$ is smooth; in the complex case, dividing by $\det g$ is multiplying by $\overline{\det g}/|\det g|^2$, again rational in the real coordinates with nonvanishing denominator $|\det g|^2$. Every $G$ of the list consists of invertible matrices, so $g \mapsto g^{-1}$ on $G$ is this map composed with $\iota$, smooth into $\Mat$; it lands in $G$, because $G$ is closed under inverses; so it is smooth into $G$. (For $\Ogp(n)$ and $\Ugp(n)$ it is even linear: $g \mapsto g^{\mathsf T}$, $g \mapsto g^*$.)
\end{proof}

The classical groups through the course: defined in Section~\ref{sec:topgroups}, with the examples of Section~\ref{sec:ex-classical}; topological manifolds as level sets in Theorem~\ref{thm:classical-manifolds}; $\SO(2)$ and $\SO(3)$ acting on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\mathbb{R}^3$ in Examples~\ref{ex:so2-orbits} and~\ref{ex:so3-orbits}, and $\SO(3)$ on $S^2$ in Examples~\ref{ex:so3-isotropy} and~\ref{ex:s2-homogeneous}; $\Ogp(n)$ acting on the Grassmannians in Corollary~\ref{cor:grassmannian}; smooth manifolds in Examples~\ref{ex:On-smooth} and~\ref{ex:Un-smooth}; their tangent spaces at the identity in Theorem~\ref{thm:classical-summary}, with the infinitesimal rotations of Example~\ref{ex:so3-infinitesimal}; the double cover $\mathrm{SU}(2) \to \SO(3)$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:double-cover}; the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ and the cross product in Example~\ref{ex:cross-product-lie}; and Lie groups in Proposition~\ref{prop:classical-lie-groups}.

The unit quaternions $S^3$ are a Lie group as well (Proposition~\ref{prop:s3-lie-group}), isomorphic to $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:s3-su2}).

\textit{Assignment~6, Problem~1: the differentials of multiplication and inversion at the identity. Not from lecture; the submitted solution, with the notation of these notes ($\mu$ for the multiplication, written $m$ in the assignment).}

\begin{propbox}[The Differential of Multiplication at the Identity]\thmlabel{prop:dmu-identity}
Let $G$ be a Lie group with identity $e$ and multiplication $\mu : G \times G \to G$, $\mu(g, h) = gh$. Under the identification $T_{(e,e)}(G \times G) = T_eG \oplus T_eG$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-product},
\[
d\mu_{(e,e)}(A, B) = A + B, \qquad A, B \in T_eG .
\]
\leeref{Problem 7-2(a)}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~6, Problem~1(a); the submitted solution.)} Let $\pi_1, \pi_2 : G \times G \to G$ be the projections and $\iota_1, \iota_2 : G \to G \times G$ the slice inclusions through $(e, e)$ (Definition~\ref{def:slice-inclusions}),
\[
\iota_1(g) = (g, e), \qquad \iota_2(g) = (e, g) .
\]
\emph{The vectors $(A, 0)$ and $(0, B)$.} The identification of Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-product} sends $v \in T_{(e,e)}(G \times G)$ to $\big(d(\pi_1)_{(e,e)}(v),\, d(\pi_2)_{(e,e)}(v)\big)$. Since $\pi_1 \circ \iota_1 = \mathrm{id}_G$ and $\pi_2 \circ \iota_1$ is the constant map to $e$, the chain rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}) and Lemma~\ref{lem:constant-pushforward} give, for $A \in T_eG$,
\[
d(\pi_1)_{(e,e)}\big(d(\iota_1)_e(A)\big) = A, \qquad d(\pi_2)_{(e,e)}\big(d(\iota_1)_e(A)\big) = 0,
\]
so $d(\iota_1)_e(A) = (A, 0)$. In the same way, $d(\iota_2)_e(B) = (0, B)$ for $B \in T_eG$. With $n = \dim G$ and $I_n = \mathrm{id}_{T_eG}$, in block form with respect to $T_eG \oplus T_eG$,
\[
d(\iota_1)_e = \begin{pmatrix} I_n \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad d(\iota_2)_e = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ I_n \end{pmatrix}.
\]

\emph{Computing $d\mu_{(e,e)}(A, 0)$.} For $g \in G$, $\mu(\iota_1(g)) = \mu(g, e) = ge = g$, so $\mu \circ \iota_1 = \mathrm{id}_G$. By the chain rule,
\[
d\mu_{(e,e)} \circ d(\iota_1)_e = d(\mu \circ \iota_1)_e = d(\mathrm{id}_G)_e = \mathrm{id}_{T_eG},
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
d\mu_{(e,e)}(A, 0) = d\mu_{(e,e)}\big(d(\iota_1)_e(A)\big) = A .
\]

\emph{Computing $d\mu_{(e,e)}(0, B)$.} Likewise $\mu(\iota_2(g)) = \mu(e, g) = eg = g$, so $\mu \circ \iota_2 = \mathrm{id}_G$, and the chain rule gives
\[
d\mu_{(e,e)}(0, B) = d\mu_{(e,e)}\big(d(\iota_2)_e(B)\big) = d(\mu \circ \iota_2)_e(B) = B .
\]

\emph{Conclusion.} Since $(A, B) = (A, 0) + (0, B)$ in $T_eG \oplus T_eG$ and $d\mu_{(e,e)}$ is linear (Proposition~\ref{prop:pushforward-derivation}),
\[
d\mu_{(e,e)}(A, B) = d\mu_{(e,e)}(A, 0) + d\mu_{(e,e)}(0, B) = A + B .
\]
In block form,
\[
d\mu_{(e,e)} = \begin{pmatrix} I_n & I_n \end{pmatrix}, \qquad d\mu_{(e,e)}\begin{pmatrix} A \\ B \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} I_n & I_n \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} A \\ B \end{pmatrix} = A + B . \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[The Differential of Inversion at the Identity]\thmlabel{prop:dinv-identity}
Let $G$ be a Lie group with identity $e$ and inversion $j : G \to G$, $j(g) = g^{-1}$. Then
\[
dj_e(A) = -A, \qquad A \in T_eG .
\]
\leeref{Problem 7-2(b)}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~6, Problem~1(b), ``a version of implicit differentiation''; the submitted solution.)} Define
\[
F = (\mathrm{id}_G, j) : G \to G \times G, \qquad F(g) = (g, j(g)),
\]
which is smooth since its components $\mathrm{id}_G$ and $j$ are (Definition~\ref{def:lie-group}), with $\pi_1 \circ F = \mathrm{id}_G$ and $\pi_2 \circ F = j$. Since $j(e) = e^{-1} = e$, $F(e) = (e, e)$. For every $g \in G$,
\[
\mu(F(g)) = \mu(g, j(g)) = gg^{-1} = e,
\]
so $\mu \circ F = c_e$, the constant map $G \to G$ with value $e$.

\emph{The differential of $F$.} By the chain rule, for $A \in T_eG$,
\[
d(\pi_1)_{(e,e)}\big(dF_e(A)\big) = d(\mathrm{id}_G)_e(A) = A, \qquad d(\pi_2)_{(e,e)}\big(dF_e(A)\big) = dj_e(A),
\]
so under the identification of Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-product}, $dF_e(A) = (A, dj_e(A))$. In block form,
\[
dF_e = \begin{pmatrix} I_n \\ dj_e \end{pmatrix}.
\]

\emph{The differential of $c_e$.} For $v \in T_eG$ and a smooth function $f$ defined near $e$, $f \circ c_e$ is constant, so $d(c_e)_e(v)f = v(f \circ c_e) = 0$. Hence $d(c_e)_e = 0$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:constant-pushforward}).

\emph{Conclusion.} Applying the chain rule to $\mu \circ F = c_e$ at $e$, and using Proposition~\ref{prop:dmu-identity},
\[
0 = d(c_e)_e = d\mu_{(e,e)} \circ dF_e = \begin{pmatrix} I_n & I_n \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} I_n \\ dj_e \end{pmatrix} = I_n + dj_e .
\]
Therefore $dj_e = -I_n$, that is, $dj_e(A) = -A$ for all $A \in T_eG$.
\end{proof}

For a matrix group both are first-order expansions: $(I + tA)(I + tB) = I + t(A + B) + O(t^2)$ and $(I + tA)^{-1} = I - tA + O(t^2)$. At a general point the same proofs give the formulas of Propositions~\ref{prop:dmu-general} and~\ref{prop:dinv-general}, in \ref{sub:right-invariant}, once right translations are available.


\begin{defbox}[Left Translation]\deflabel{def:left-translation-lie}
For $g$ in a Lie group $G$, \textbf{left translation} by $g$ is $L_g : G \to G$, $L_g(h) = gh$.
\leeref{Ch.~7, \emph{Basic Definitions}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{lembox}[Left Translations Are Diffeomorphisms]\thmlabel{lem:Lg-diffeo}
$L_g$ is a diffeomorphism, with inverse $L_{g^{-1}}$.
\leeref{Ch.~7, \emph{Basic Definitions}}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Filled in, as for topological groups in Lemma~\ref{lem:Lg}.)} By Definition~\ref{def:diffeomorphism}, it has to be shown that $L_g$ is a smooth bijection with smooth inverse, and that the inverse is $L_{g^{-1}}$.

\emph{Smooth.} $L_g$ is smooth as the composite of $h \mapsto (g, h)$ with multiplication: $L_g(h) = gh = \mu\big(\iota^{g}(h)\big)$, where $\iota^{g} : G \to G \times G$, $h \mapsto (g, h)$, is the slice inclusion of Definition~\ref{def:slice-inclusions} (with $M_1 = M_2 = G$ and $p_1 = g$), smooth by Proposition~\ref{prop:product-maps}, and $\mu : G \times G \to G$ is multiplication, smooth by Definition~\ref{def:lie-group}. So $L_g = \mu \circ \iota^{g}$ is smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}). The same holds for every element of $G$, in particular for $g^{-1}$: $L_{g^{-1}}$ is smooth.

\emph{Inverse.} For $h \in G$, by associativity of the group product,
\[
L_g\big(L_{g^{-1}}(h)\big) = g\,(g^{-1}h) = (gg^{-1})\,h = h, \qquad L_{g^{-1}}\big(L_g(h)\big) = g^{-1}(gh) = (g^{-1}g)\,h = h .
\]
So $L_g \circ L_{g^{-1}} = L_{g^{-1}} \circ L_g = \mathrm{id}$: $L_g$ is a bijection with inverse $L_{g^{-1}}$, and both are smooth, so $L_g$ is a diffeomorphism.
\end{proof}

\begin{defbox}[Left-Invariant Vector Field]\deflabel{def:left-invariant}
A vector field $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(G)$ is \textbf{left-invariant} if for all $g, h \in G$
\[
(L_g)_{*h}\, \mathbf{X}_h = \mathbf{X}_{gh} .
\]
\leeref{Ch.~8, \emph{Lie Algebras}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=6em, row sep=3em]
T_hG \arrow[r, "(L_g)_{*h}"] & T_{gh}G \\[-2.2em]
\mathbf{X}_h \arrow[r, mapsto] & \mathbf{X}_{gh}
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

Left invariance in one line: pushing vectors of the field forward by left translations always gives the corresponding vectors of the field. The value at one point determines the field everywhere: taking $h = e$, $\mathbf{X}_g = (L_g)_{*e}\, \mathbf{X}_e$. This is the left translation of tangent spaces from the discussion of moving the base point (Lemma~\ref{lem:group-morphism-translation}), applied to a whole field.

\begin{exbox}[Left-Invariant Fields on $\GL({n,\mathbb{R}})$]\exlabel{ex:left-invariant-GL}
On $G = \GL(n,\mathbb{R})$, open in $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$, so that $T_gG = \Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$, the left-invariant vector fields are exactly
\[
\mathbf{X}^A_g = gA, \qquad A \in \Mat(n,\mathbb{R}) = T_IG .
\]
\end{exbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} \emph{The identification.} $G$ is open in the vector space $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$, so $T_gG = T_g\Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:germs-local}), and $T_g\Mat(n,\mathbb{R}) \cong \Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$ by $v \leftrightarrow D_v|_g$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs}); this is the identification $T_gG = \Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$ of the statement.

\emph{The differential of $L_g$.} $L_g$ is the restriction to $G$ of the linear map $\ell_g : \Mat(n,\mathbb{R}) \to \Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$, $h \mapsto gh$, so its differential at every point is that same linear map: $(L_g)_{*h}(v) = gv$. Indeed, $\iota \circ L_g = \ell_g \circ \iota$ for the inclusion $\iota : G \hookrightarrow \Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$, so by the chain rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}) $\iota_{*gh} \circ (L_g)_{*h} = (\ell_g)_{*h} \circ \iota_{*h}$, and $\iota_{*}$ is the identification of Lemma~\ref{lem:germs-local}; and by Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs} for the linear map $\ell_g$, $(\ell_g)_{*h}(D_v|_h) = D_{gv}|_{gh}$.

\emph{Left-invariant fields are of the form $\mathbf{X}^A$.} By the last step, left invariance (Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant}) reads
\[
g\,\mathbf{X}_h = \mathbf{X}_{gh} \qquad \text{for all } g, h \in G,
\]
with $\mathbf{X}_h \in \Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$. Taking $h = I$ gives $\mathbf{X}_g = \mathbf{X}_{gI} = g\,\mathbf{X}_I$, so $\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{X}^A$ with $A = \mathbf{X}_I$.

\emph{Every $\mathbf{X}^A$ is a left-invariant field.} Conversely, let $A \in \Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$. By associativity of matrix multiplication,
\[
(L_g)_{*h}\big(\mathbf{X}^A_h\big) = g\,(hA) = (gh)A = \mathbf{X}^A_{gh},
\]
so every $\mathbf{X}^A$ is left-invariant. It is smooth because its entries are linear in those of $g$: in the global chart of $G$ given by the matrix entries $x^{ij}$, the coefficients of $\mathbf{X}^A$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}) are $\mathbf{X}^A_g[x^{ij}] = D_{gA}|_g[x^{ij}] = \frac{d}{dt}\big|_{t=0}\, x^{ij}(g + t\,gA) = (gA)_{ij} = \sum_k g_{ik} A_{kj}$, linear in the entries of $g$, hence smooth.
\end{proof}

Compare Theorem~\ref{thm:classical-summary}, where $T^{\geo}_g G = g \cdot T^{\geo}_I G$ for the classical groups: a left-invariant field moves the tangent space at the identity around the group by left multiplication. In the language of \ref{sub:lie-algebra-TeG}, later in this section, $\mathbf{X}^A$ is the left-invariant extension of $A \in T_IG$ (Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant-extension}): by the differential of $L_g$ computed in the proof above, $(L_g)_{*I}(A) = gA = \mathbf{X}^A_g$.

\begin{defbox}[The Lie Algebra of a Lie Group]\deflabel{def:lie-algebra-of-group}
The \textbf{Lie algebra} of a Lie group $G$ is
\[
\mathfrak{g} = \{\, \mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(G) \mid \mathbf{X} \text{ is left-invariant} \,\},
\]
with the Lie bracket of vector fields.
\leeref{Ch.~8, \emph{Lie Algebras}}
\end{defbox}

\textit{Status.} Defined in Lecture~16, where $\mathfrak{g}$ was announced to be soon identified with the tangent space at the identity; originally, though, its elements are a very special type of vector field, because that is where the Lie bracket comes from. For $\GL(n,\mathbb{R})$ the identification is $\mathbf{X}^A \mapsto A$ (Example~\ref{ex:left-invariant-GL}). The two facts announced then were proved in Lecture~17, in \S\ref{sub:lie-algebra-TeG} below: $\mathfrak{g}$ is closed under the bracket, and $\mathbf{X} \mapsto \mathbf{X}_e$ is an isomorphism onto $T_eG$ (its last step, smoothness, completed in Lecture~18).

\subsection{The Lie Algebra and the Tangent Space at the Identity}\label{sub:lie-algebra-TeG}

\textit{Lecture 17. Back to Lie groups: with the language of related fields, some of the definitions can be rephrased.}

\begin{lembox}[Left-Invariance as Relatedness]\thmlabel{lem:left-invariant-related}
A vector field $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(G)$ is left-invariant (Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant}) if and only if, for every $g \in G$, $\mathbf{X}$ is \emph{$L_g$-related to itself} (Definition~\ref{def:F-related} with $F = L_g$ and $\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X}$).
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~17, a rephrasing of the definition.)} Being $L_g$-related to itself means $d(L_g)_h(\mathbf{X}_h) = \mathbf{X}_{L_g(h)} = \mathbf{X}_{gh}$ for every $h \in G$, which is the condition of Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant} for this $g$.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[Why Left?]\label{rem:left-invariant-related}
Lecture~17 abbreviates ``left-invariant'' to l.i. Nothing is wrong with right: a choice has to be made, and left is the universal choice. Right-invariant fields, $R_g$-related to themselves for $R_g(h) = hg$, give an equivalent theory; the one place the choice shows is the sign of the bracket, at the end of this subsection. Right-invariant fields are worked out in \ref{sub:right-invariant}.
\end{rembox}

\begin{corbox}[$\mathfrak{g}$ Is a Lie Subalgebra of $\mathfrak{X}(G)$]\thmlabel{cor:lie-subalgebra}
If $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{g}$ then $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}] \in \mathfrak{g}$. So $\mathfrak{g}$, a linear subspace of $\mathfrak{X}(G)$, is a Lie algebra under the bracket of vector fields.
\leeref{Proposition 8.33}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~17: a consequence of Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket-naturality}.)} \emph{Closed under the bracket.} Let $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{g}$ and fix $g \in G$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:left-invariant-related}, $\mathbf{X}$ is $L_g$-related to $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ to $\mathbf{Y}$. So by Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket-naturality} with $F = L_g$, $\mathbf{X}_1 = \mathbf{Y}_1 = \mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{X}_2 = \mathbf{Y}_2 = \mathbf{Y}$, $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]$ is $L_g$-related to $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]$. This holds for every $g$, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:left-invariant-related} again (in the converse direction) this for every $g$ is left-invariance: $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}] \in \mathfrak{g}$.

\textit{(Filled in.)} \emph{A linear subspace.} $\mathfrak{g}$ is a linear subspace because each $d(L_g)_h$ is linear (Proposition~\ref{prop:pushforward-derivation}). Explicitly, let $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{g}$ and $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$. For all $g, h \in G$, by the pointwise operations of Definition~\ref{def:vector-fields-space}, the linearity of $d(L_g)_h$, and left-invariance of $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$,
\[
d(L_g)_h\big((a\mathbf{X} + b\mathbf{Y})_h\big) = d(L_g)_h\big(a\,\mathbf{X}_h + b\,\mathbf{Y}_h\big) = a\, d(L_g)_h(\mathbf{X}_h) + b\, d(L_g)_h(\mathbf{Y}_h) = a\,\mathbf{X}_{gh} + b\,\mathbf{Y}_{gh} = (a\mathbf{X} + b\mathbf{Y})_{gh} .
\]
So $a\mathbf{X} + b\mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{g}$; and the zero field is in $\mathfrak{g}$, since a linear map sends $0$ to $0$.

\emph{A Lie algebra.} By the first step the bracket of vector fields restricts to a map $\mathfrak{g} \times \mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{g}$. The bracket on $\mathfrak{g}$ is bilinear, skew and satisfies Jacobi because it does on $\mathfrak{X}(G)$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:vf-lie-algebra}): these are identities for all elements of $\mathfrak{X}(G)$, so in particular for all elements of $\mathfrak{g}$. So $\mathfrak{g}$ is a Lie algebra (Definition~\ref{def:lie-algebra}).
\end{proof}

So $\mathfrak{g}$ is a Lie subalgebra of the infinite-dimensional Lie algebra of all vector fields on $G$. Vector fields can be added and scaled, so $\mathfrak{X}(G)$ is a vector space (in fact a module over the smooth functions, but here it is regarded as a vector space). At this point it is not yet clear what $\mathfrak{g}$ is: a priori it could still be infinite-dimensional, or zero. The theorem below settles it. Its proof rests on a construction, made in Lecture~17 and finished in Lecture~18, which comes first.

\begin{defbox}[Left-Invariant Extension]\deflabel{def:left-invariant-extension}
Let $G$ be a Lie group with identity $e$, and $v \in T_eG$. The \textbf{left-invariant extension} of $v$ is the map $\mathbf{X}^v : G \to TG$, $g \mapsto \mathbf{X}^v_g$, with
\[
\mathbf{X}^v_g = d(L_g)_e(v) \in T_gG, \qquad g \in G :
\]
the vector $v$ carried from $e$ to $g$ by the differential of the left translation $L_g$ (Definition~\ref{def:left-translation-lie}). It is a \emph{rough} vector field (Lee's term), a tangent vector at every point, not yet known to be smooth.
\leeref{proof of Theorem 8.37}
\end{defbox}

As with vector fields on a vector space (Proposition~\ref{prop:translations-identify}), there is a unique left translation carrying $e$ to $g$, and $\mathbf{X}^v_g$ is $v$ carried along it.

\begin{lembox}[The Left-Invariant Extension Is Left-Invariant]\thmlabel{lem:left-invariant-extension}
Let $G$ be a Lie group with identity $e$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item For $v \in T_eG$, $\mathbf{X}^v_g \in T_gG$ for every $g \in G$, and $\mathbf{X}^v_e = v$.
    \item For $v \in T_eG$, $\mathbf{X}^v$ satisfies the identity of Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant}: $d(L_g)_h\big(\mathbf{X}^v_h\big) = \mathbf{X}^v_{gh}$ for all $g, h \in G$.
    \item Every $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{g}$ is the left-invariant extension of its value at $e$: $\mathbf{X}_g = d(L_g)_e(\mathbf{X}_e)$ for every $g \in G$, that is, $\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{X}^{\mathbf{X}_e}$.
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{proof of Theorem 8.37}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~17, steps of the proof that $\mathfrak{g}$ is $T_eG$; (2) was left to check, and done in the review at the start of Lecture~19.)}

\emph{(1)} $L_g$ maps $e$ to $g$, so $d(L_g)_e : T_eG \to T_{L_g(e)}G = T_{ge}G = T_gG$, and $\mathbf{X}^v_g = d(L_g)_e(v)$ lies in $T_gG$. And $L_e = \mathrm{id}_G$ (as $eh = h$), so $\mathbf{X}^v_e = (\mathrm{id}_G)_{*e}(v) = v$ by Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}.

\emph{(2)} \textit{(Lecture~19.)} Fix $h, g \in G$. To end up at $g$ one has to start at $h^{-1}g$: $L_h$ maps $h^{-1}g$ to $g$. By Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant-extension} and the chain rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}),
\[
d(L_h)_{h^{-1}g}\big(\mathbf{X}^v_{h^{-1}g}\big) = d(L_h)_{h^{-1}g}\, d(L_{h^{-1}g})_e(v) = d\big(L_h \circ L_{h^{-1}g}\big)_e(v) = d(L_g)_e(v) = \mathbf{X}^v_g ,
\]
because $L_h \circ L_{h^{-1}g} = L_g$: multiplying on the left by $h^{-1}g$ and then on the left by $h$, the $h$ and the $h^{-1}$ cancel. Writing $k = h^{-1}g$, this says $d(L_h)_k(\mathbf{X}^v_k) = \mathbf{X}^v_{hk}$ for all $h, k \in G$, the identity of Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant}.

\emph{(3)} Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{g}$ and $g \in G$. Left-invariance (Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant}) with $h = e$ reads $d(L_g)_e(\mathbf{X}_e) = \mathbf{X}_{ge} = \mathbf{X}_g$, and by Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant-extension} with $v = \mathbf{X}_e$ the left side is $\mathbf{X}^{\mathbf{X}_e}_g$.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[The Left-Invariant Extension Is Smooth]\thmlabel{prop:left-invariant-extension-smooth}
Let $G$ be a Lie group with identity $e$ and $v \in T_eG$. For $f \in C^\infty(G)$ let $\varphi : G \times G \to \mathbb{R}$, $\varphi(g, x) = f(gx)$. Then $\varphi$ is smooth, and
\[
\mathbf{X}^v f = \partial_v\varphi \in C^\infty(G),
\]
the partial derivative of $\varphi$ in the second variable in the direction $v$ (Definition~\ref{def:partial-derivative-factor}). Hence $\mathbf{X}^v$ is smooth: $\mathbf{X}^v \in \mathfrak{g}$, a left-invariant vector field with $\mathbf{X}^v_e = v$.
\leeref{proof of Theorem 8.37}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~18, completing the proof of Lecture~17.)} Lecture~17 stopped here: what was missing is that $\mathbf{X}^v$ is $C^\infty$, an important technical point for which the tools were not yet available. Lecture~18 finished it with the partial derivative construction (Definition~\ref{def:partial-derivative-factor}). So far $\mathbf{X}^v$ is a left-invariant \emph{rough} field (Lemma~\ref{lem:left-invariant-extension}(1) and (2)), Lee's term for a section not yet known to be smooth; the piece of the construction not yet justified is its smoothness.

\emph{The claim.} It suffices to show that for every $f \in C^\infty(G)$ the function $\mathbf{X}^v f : g \mapsto \mathbf{X}^v_g[f]$ is smooth. This function is well defined whether or not $\mathbf{X}^v$ is smooth, because there is a vector at every point, and it can act on any function. The lecture's proof of the claim: in local coordinates $(x^1, \ldots, x^m)$, $m = \dim G$, there is still a pointwise expansion $\mathbf{X}^v = \sum_j a^j\, \partial/\partial x^j$, and $\mathbf{X}^v$ is smooth exactly when the $a^j$ are (Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}); and $a^j$ is precisely the action of $\mathbf{X}^v$ on the coordinate $x^j$. This is Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-smooth-criterion}, whose proof also handles the point that $x^j$ is defined only on the chart, by extending it with a bump function.

\emph{The construction.} Let $f \in C^\infty(G)$ and $g \in G$. By the definition of $\mathbf{X}^v$ and of the pushforward (Definition~\ref{def:pushforward}),
\[
(\mathbf{X}^v f)(g) = d(L_g)_e(v)[f] = v[f \circ L_g] \in \mathbb{R},
\]
and the point is that, as a function of $g$, this is smooth. The trick is to construct
\[
\varphi : G \times G \xrightarrow{\ \text{multiplication}\ } G \xrightarrow{\ f\ } \mathbb{R}, \qquad \varphi(g, x) = f(gx) = (f \circ L_g)(x).
\]
It is smooth, as the composite of the multiplication, smooth by Definition~\ref{def:lie-group}, with $f$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}). Fixing $g$ in the first variable, $f \circ L_g = \varphi(g, \cdot)$, so by Definition~\ref{def:partial-derivative-factor}, in the second variable with $w = v \in T_eG$,
\[
(\mathbf{X}^v f)(g) = v\big[\varphi(g, \cdot)\big] = \partial_v\varphi(g) .
\]
Here $v$ acts on the second variable, and so the result is smooth: $\partial_v\varphi \in C^\infty(G)$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:partial-derivative-factor}(3). By the claim, $\mathbf{X}^v$ is smooth. It is left-invariant (Lemma~\ref{lem:left-invariant-extension}(2)), so $\mathbf{X}^v \in \mathfrak{g}$ (Definition~\ref{def:lie-algebra-of-group}), and $\mathbf{X}^v_e = v$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:left-invariant-extension}(1)).
\end{proof}

\begin{thmbox}[The Lie Algebra Is the Tangent Space at the Identity]\thmlabel{thm:lie-algebra-TeG}
Let $G$ be a Lie group with identity $e$. The evaluation map
\[
\mathrm{ev} : \mathfrak{g} \to T_eG, \qquad \mathbf{X} \mapsto \mathbf{X}_e ,
\]
is a linear isomorphism. In particular $\dim \mathfrak{g} = \dim G$.
\leeref{Theorem 8.37}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~17, incomplete by one detail that could not yet be proved there; completed in Lecture~18. The lecture's steps.)} $\mathrm{ev}$ is linear: for $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{g}$ and $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$, $\mathrm{ev}(a\mathbf{X} + b\mathbf{Y}) = (a\mathbf{X} + b\mathbf{Y})_e = a\,\mathbf{X}_e + b\,\mathbf{Y}_e$ by Definition~\ref{def:vector-fields-space}. It remains to show that $\mathrm{ev}$ is injective and surjective.

\textit{The basic idea.} For $g \in G$, $L_g$ maps $e$ to $g$, so $d(L_g)_e : T_eG \to T_gG$, and for $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{g}$, left-invariance (Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant}) with $h = e$ reads
\[
d(L_g)_e(\mathbf{X}_e) = \mathbf{X}_g ;
\]
more generally $d(L_g)_h(\mathbf{X}_h) = \mathbf{X}_{gh}$ for all $h$. So there is only one choice: $\mathbf{X}$ is the left-invariant extension of $\mathbf{X}_e$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:left-invariant-extension}(3)).

\emph{Injective.} By the basic idea, $\mathbf{X}$ is determined by its value at $e$. So $\mathbf{X}_e = 0$ forces $\mathbf{X}_g = d(L_g)_e(0) = 0$ for all $g$, since $d(L_g)_e$ is linear (Proposition~\ref{prop:pushforward-derivation}). So the kernel of the linear map $\mathrm{ev}$ is $\{\mathbf{0}\}$, and $\mathrm{ev}$ is injective.

\emph{Surjective.} Start with $v \in T_eG$; we want a left-invariant $\mathbf{X}$ with $\mathbf{X}_e = v$. The basic idea says there is no choice: we must take the left-invariant extension of $v$ (Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant-extension}),
\[
\mathbf{X}^v_g = d(L_g)_e(v), \qquad g \in G .
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:left-invariant-extension}(1) and (2), which are Lecture~17's steps, $\mathbf{X}^v$ is a rough vector field, a tangent vector at every point, with $\mathbf{X}^v_e = v$ and satisfying the left-invariance identity. \emph{Smooth.} This is where Lecture~17 stopped; Lecture~18 finished it, and by Proposition~\ref{prop:left-invariant-extension-smooth} $\mathbf{X}^v$ is smooth, through $\mathbf{X}^v f = \partial_v\varphi$ for $\varphi(g, x) = f(gx)$. So $\mathbf{X}^v \in \mathfrak{g}$ and $\mathrm{ev}(\mathbf{X}^v) = v$.

Finally, a linear isomorphism preserves dimension, so $\dim \mathfrak{g} = \dim T_eG = \dim G$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-dimension}).
\end{proof}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.95]

\node[gray!70!black, font=\footnotesize] at (-2.25,0.95) {$G$};

\end{center}

\textbf{Comparison with Lee.} Lee's proof (Theorem~8.37) differentiates $f(g\,\gamma(t))$ along a curve $\gamma$ adapted to $v$, which is Proposition~\ref{prop:partial-derivative-factor}(1) applied to the function $\varphi(g, x) = f(gx)$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:left-invariant-extension-smooth}: $(\mathbf{X}^v f)(g) = \frac{d}{dt}\big|_{t=0} \varphi(g, \gamma(t))$. The course packages that step once and for all as the partial derivative $\partial_v\varphi$.

\begin{exbox}[The Additive Group of a Vector Space]\exlabel{ex:vs-lie-algebra}
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space, a Lie group under addition with identity $0$, so that $L_p = \tau_p$ is translation by $p$. Its left-invariant vector fields are the constant fields $\mathbf{X}^v : p \mapsto D_v|_p$, $v \in V$, and all their brackets vanish: $\mathfrak{g} \cong V$ with the zero bracket.
\end{exbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in, after the remark in Lecture~17 that the translations of a vector space give a left-invariant vector field.)} \emph{$V$ is a Lie group.} In linear coordinates (Definition~\ref{def:vs-structure}), addition $(p, q) \mapsto p + q$ and inversion $p \mapsto -p$ are linear, hence smooth; so $V$ is a Lie group (Definition~\ref{def:lie-group}), with $L_p(q) = p + q = \tau_p(q)$.

\emph{The left-invariant fields.} By Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs}, every element of $T_0V$ is $D_v|_0$ for a unique $v \in V$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:lie-algebra-TeG} and Lemma~\ref{lem:left-invariant-extension}(3), the left-invariant fields are exactly the left-invariant extensions $\mathbf{X}^w$, $w \in T_0V$ (Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant-extension}), with $\mathbf{X}^w_p = d(L_p)_0(w)$. For $w = D_v|_0$, Proposition~\ref{prop:translations-identify}(2) gives
\[
\mathbf{X}^{w}_p = d(\tau_p)_0\big(D_v|_0\big) = D_v|_p ,
\]
so the field $\mathbf{X}^v$ of the example, the left-invariant extension of $D_v|_0$, is $p \mapsto D_v|_p$; by the theorem these are all the left-invariant fields. The map $v \mapsto \mathbf{X}^v$ is the composite of the isomorphism $v \mapsto D_v|_0$ of Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs} with $\mathrm{ev}^{-1}$, so it is a linear isomorphism $V \cong \mathfrak{g}$.

\emph{The brackets vanish.} Choose a basis of $V$ and the corresponding linear coordinates $x^1, \ldots, x^n$, a global chart, and write $v = \sum_i v^i e_i$. The coefficients of $\mathbf{X}^v$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}) are, using Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs} and the linearity of $x^i$,
\[
\mathbf{X}^v_p[x^i] = D_v|_p[x^i] = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} x^i(p + tv) = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} \big(x^i(p) + t\,v^i\big) = v^i .
\]
So in linear coordinates $\mathbf{X}^v = \sum_i v^i\, \partial_i$ has constant coefficients, and likewise $\mathbf{X}^w = \sum_i w^i\, \partial_i$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket-coords}, the $j$-th coefficient of $[\mathbf{X}^v, \mathbf{X}^w]$ is $\sum_i \big(v^i\, \partial w^j/\partial x^i - w^i\, \partial v^j/\partial x^i\big) = 0$, since the partial derivatives of constants vanish. So $[\mathbf{X}^v, \mathbf{X}^w] = 0$ for all $v, w$: $\mathfrak{g} \cong V$ with the zero bracket.
\end{proof}

\begin{defbox}[The Lie Bracket on $T_eG$]\deflabel{def:bracket-TeG}
Let $G$ be a Lie group and, for $v \in T_eG$, let $\mathbf{X}^v \in \mathfrak{g}$ be its left-invariant extension (Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant-extension} and Proposition~\ref{prop:left-invariant-extension-smooth}), the left-invariant field with $\mathbf{X}^v_e = v$, unique by Theorem~\ref{thm:lie-algebra-TeG}. The \textbf{Lie bracket} on $T_eG$ is
\[
[v, w] = \big[\mathbf{X}^v, \mathbf{X}^w\big]_e , \qquad v, w \in T_eG .
\]
\end{defbox}

By construction $\mathrm{ev}$ is then an isomorphism of Lie algebras (Definition~\ref{def:lie-algebra-isomorphism}): $T_eG$ inherits the bracket that makes it one. The question is what this bracket is.

\begin{thmbox}[{The Lie Algebra of $\GL({d,\mathbb{R}})$}]\thmlabel{thm:gl-bracket}
Let $G = \GL(d, \mathbb{R})$, the $d \times d$ invertible matrices, an open subset of $\Mat(d, \mathbb{R}) \cong \mathbb{R}^{d^2}$, so that $T_IG = \Mat(d,\mathbb{R})$. The Lie bracket on $T_IG$ (Definition~\ref{def:bracket-TeG}) is the matrix commutator
\[
[A, B] = AB - BA .
\]
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~19: here diagram chasing no longer suffices, and something has to be computed. The lecture's computation, with the index bookkeeping written out. Lecture~19 proved this together with Theorem~\ref{thm:linear-group-bracket}, which reduces every linear group in $\GL(d, \mathbb{R})$ to this case; the linear groups in $\GL(d, \mathbb{C})$ are reduced to it through Proposition~\ref{prop:glc-bracket}.)}

\emph{Coordinates.} Write $A = (a^i_j)$, with $i$ the row index and $j$ the column index, and call a general group element $X = (x^i_j) \in \GL(d, \mathbb{R})$ rather than $g$, to think of it as a variable. Written out,
\[
A = \begin{pmatrix} a^1_1 & \cdots & a^1_d \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ a^d_1 & \cdots & a^d_d \end{pmatrix},
\qquad
X = \begin{pmatrix} x^1_1 & \cdots & x^1_d \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ x^d_1 & \cdots & x^d_d \end{pmatrix},
\]
the upper index numbering the rows and the lower index the columns. The entries $x^i_j$ are the standard coordinates of $\Mat(d,\mathbb{R}) \cong \mathbb{R}^{d^2}$, indexed by pairs, and a tangent vector $V = (V^i_j) \in \Mat(d, \mathbb{R}) = T_X\GL(d,\mathbb{R})$ is $\sum_{i,j} V^i_j\, \partial/\partial x^i_j|_X$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs}). The basic computation is
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i_j}\big(x^l_n\big) = \delta_{il}\, \delta_{jn} ,
\]
one or zero according to whether the coordinate being differentiated is the one the partial is taken with respect to.

\emph{The left-invariant field.} $\mathbf{X}^A_X = d(L_X)_I(A)$, and $L_X : \mathbb{R}^{d^2} \to \mathbb{R}^{d^2}$, $Y \mapsto XY$, is linear, so it is its own differential (Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs}): $\mathbf{X}^A_X = XA$ (Example~\ref{ex:left-invariant-GL}). The $(i,j)$ entry of $XA$ is $\sum_k x^i_k a^k_j$, so
\[
\mathbf{X}^A = \sum_{i,j} \Big( \sum_k x^i_k\, a^k_j \Big) \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i_j}, \qquad
\mathbf{X}^B = \sum_{l,n} \Big( \sum_m x^l_m\, b^m_n \Big) \frac{\partial}{\partial x^l_n},
\]
with independent indices for the second field, since the two sums are independent. The $a^k_j$ and $b^m_n$ are constants; the $x$'s are functions. (So the sums can be taken out of the commutator, which is bilinear over constants, but the $x$'s cannot be pulled out, because they are functions.)

\emph{The bracket.} The second derivatives can be ignored, because they cancel in the bracket (Lemma~\ref{lem:bracket-field}): by Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket-coords}, the coefficient of $\partial/\partial x^l_n$ in $[\mathbf{X}^A, \mathbf{X}^B]$ is $\mathbf{X}^A$ applied to the coefficient of $\mathbf{X}^B$, minus the same with $A$ and $B$ exchanged. Applying the basic computation,
\[
\mathbf{X}^A\Big( \sum_m x^l_m\, b^m_n \Big) = \sum_{i,j,k,m} x^i_k\, a^k_j\, b^m_n\, \delta_{il}\, \delta_{jm} = \sum_{k} x^l_k \Big( \sum_j a^k_j\, b^j_n \Big) = \sum_k x^l_k\, (AB)^k_n :
\]
setting $i = l$ and $m = j$ is all that happens, and then $\sum_j a^k_j\, b^j_n$ is an entry of a matrix, the $(k, n)$ entry of $AB$. So
\[
[\mathbf{X}^A, \mathbf{X}^B] = \sum_{l,n} \Big( \sum_k x^l_k\, (AB)^k_n \Big) \frac{\partial}{\partial x^l_n} - \big(\text{the same with } A \text{ and } B \text{ exchanged}\big) = \mathbf{X}^{AB} - \mathbf{X}^{BA},
\]
comparing with the formula for $\mathbf{X}^A$ with $AB$, resp.\ $BA$, in place of $A$.

\emph{Evaluate at the identity.} By Definition~\ref{def:bracket-TeG} and $\mathbf{X}^C_I = C$,
\[
[A, B] = [\mathbf{X}^A, \mathbf{X}^B]_I = \mathbf{X}^{AB}_I - \mathbf{X}^{BA}_I = AB - BA . \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

Coordinate-free, the computation says: a field $X \mapsto XC$ on an open subset of $\Mat(d,\mathbb{R})$ is linear in $X$, and the bracket of the linear fields $X \mapsto XA$ and $X \mapsto XB$ is the linear field $X \mapsto X(AB - BA)$.

\begin{rembox}[Left or Right: The Sign of the Bracket]\label{rem:bracket-on-TeG}
The formula $[A, B] = AB - BA$ holds because left-invariant fields are used; with right-invariant fields the bracket would be minus that. Why left, then? Many things would work better if functions were written to the right of their arguments, $(x)f$ instead of $f(x)$: in that notation, composites read in the order the maps are applied. \textit{(Proved in \ref{sub:right-invariant}: Theorem~\ref{thm:right-bracket}, Assignment~6, Problem~2(b).)}
\end{rembox}

\textbf{Transcription note (Lecture 17).} Page~46 of the handwritten notes says the construction gives ``$\mathbf{X} : M \to TM$''; the manifold is the group, $\mathbf{X} : G \to TG$.

\subsection{Right-Invariant Vector Fields}\label{sub:right-invariant}

\textit{Assignment~6, Problem~2, with what its solution contains. Not from lecture. Lecture~17 said there is nothing wrong with right (the remark \emph{Why Left?}) and Lecture~19 that right-invariant fields give the bracket with the opposite sign (the remark \emph{Left or Right: The Sign of the Bracket}); this subsection proves both. Elements of $T_eG$ are written $A, B$, as in the assignment. The general formulas for the differentials of multiplication and inversion, which need right translations, are filled in here as well.}

\begin{defbox}[Right Translation]\deflabel{def:right-translation-lie}
For $g$ in a Lie group $G$, \textbf{right translation} by $g$ is $R_g : G \to G$, $R_g(k) = kg$.
\leeref{Ch.~7, \emph{Basic Definitions}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{lembox}[Right Translations]\thmlabel{lem:Rg}
Let $G$ be a Lie group with identity $e$ and $g, h \in G$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $R_g \circ R_h = R_{hg}$ and $R_e = \mathrm{id}_G$. Note the order: first $h$, then $g$.
    \item $R_g$ is a diffeomorphism, with inverse $R_{g^{-1}}$.
    \item Left and right translations commute: $L_g \circ R_h = R_h \circ L_g$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\emph{(1)} \textit{(The submitted solution.)} For $k \in G$, $(R_g \circ R_h)(k) = R_g(kh) = khg = R_{hg}(k)$, so $R_g \circ R_h = R_{hg}$. Also $R_e(k) = ke = k$, so $R_e = \mathrm{id}_G$.

\textit{(Filled in.)} \emph{(2)} As in Lemma~\ref{lem:Lg-diffeo}: $R_g = \mu \circ \iota^{g}$, where $\iota^{g} : G \to G \times G$, $k \mapsto (k, g)$, is the slice inclusion (Definition~\ref{def:slice-inclusions}, with $p_2 = g$), smooth by Proposition~\ref{prop:product-maps}, and $\mu$ is the multiplication, smooth by Definition~\ref{def:lie-group}; so $R_g$ is smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}), and so is $R_{g^{-1}}$. By (1), $R_g \circ R_{g^{-1}} = R_{g^{-1}g} = R_e = \mathrm{id}_G$ and $R_{g^{-1}} \circ R_g = R_{gg^{-1}} = \mathrm{id}_G$. So $R_g$ is a smooth bijection with smooth inverse $R_{g^{-1}}$, a diffeomorphism (Definition~\ref{def:diffeomorphism}).

\emph{(3)} For $k \in G$, by associativity, $L_g(R_h(k)) = g(kh) = (gk)h = R_h(L_g(k))$.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[The Differential of Multiplication]\thmlabel{prop:dmu-general}
Let $G$ be a Lie group with multiplication $\mu$, and $g, h \in G$. Under the identification $T_{(g,h)}(G \times G) = T_gG \oplus T_hG$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-product},
\[
d\mu_{(g,h)}(v, w) = d(R_h)_g(v) + d(L_g)_h(w), \qquad v \in T_gG,\ w \in T_hG .
\]
At $(g, h) = (e, e)$, where $R_e = L_e = \mathrm{id}_G$, this is Proposition~\ref{prop:dmu-identity}.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from the assignment; the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:dmu-identity} at the point $(g, h)$.)} Let $\iota_1(x) = (x, h)$ and $\iota_2(y) = (g, y)$ be the slice inclusions through $(g, h)$ (Definition~\ref{def:slice-inclusions}), so that $(v, w)$ stands for $\Theta(v, w) = d(\iota_1)_g(v) + d(\iota_2)_h(w)$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-product}). For $x, y \in G$,
\[
(\mu \circ \iota_1)(x) = xh = R_h(x), \qquad (\mu \circ \iota_2)(y) = gy = L_g(y),
\]
so $\mu \circ \iota_1 = R_h$ and $\mu \circ \iota_2 = L_g$. By the linearity of $d\mu_{(g,h)}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:pushforward-derivation}) and the chain rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}),
\[
d\mu_{(g,h)}(v, w) = d\mu_{(g,h)}\big(d(\iota_1)_g(v)\big) + d\mu_{(g,h)}\big(d(\iota_2)_h(w)\big) = d(\mu \circ \iota_1)_g(v) + d(\mu \circ \iota_2)_h(w) = d(R_h)_g(v) + d(L_g)_h(w) . \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{lembox}[Inversion Exchanges Left and Right Translations]\thmlabel{lem:inversion-translations}
Let $G$ be a Lie group with inversion $j$, and $g \in G$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $j \circ L_g = R_{g^{-1}} \circ j$.
    \item $j$ is a diffeomorphism, and $j^{-1} = j$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\emph{(1)} \textit{(Assignment~6, Problem~2(a): the submitted solution's ``key identity''.)} For $k \in G$,
\[
(j \circ L_g)(k) = j(gk) = (gk)^{-1} = k^{-1}g^{-1} = R_{g^{-1}}(k^{-1}) = (R_{g^{-1}} \circ j)(k) .
\]

\emph{(2)} \textit{(Filled in.)} $j$ is smooth (Definition~\ref{def:lie-group}), and $j(j(k)) = (k^{-1})^{-1} = k$, so $j \circ j = \mathrm{id}_G$: $j$ is a smooth bijection whose inverse $j$ is smooth.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[The Differential of Inversion]\thmlabel{prop:dinv-general}
Let $G$ be a Lie group with identity $e$ and inversion $j$, and $g \in G$. Then
\[
dj_g = -\,d(R_{g^{-1}})_e \circ d(L_{g^{-1}})_g : T_gG \longrightarrow T_{g^{-1}}G .
\]
At $g = e$ this is Proposition~\ref{prop:dinv-identity}.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from the assignment.)} By Lemma~\ref{lem:inversion-translations}(1), $j \circ L_g = R_{g^{-1}} \circ j$. Both sides map $e$ to $g^{-1}$; by the chain rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}) at $e$, with $L_g(e) = g$, $j(e) = e$ and $dj_e = -\mathrm{id}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:dinv-identity}),
\[
dj_g \circ d(L_g)_e = d(R_{g^{-1}})_e \circ dj_e = -\,d(R_{g^{-1}})_e .
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:Lg-diffeo}, $L_{g^{-1}} \circ L_g = \mathrm{id}_G$ and $L_g \circ L_{g^{-1}} = \mathrm{id}_G$, so by the chain rule $d(L_g)_e$ is invertible with inverse $d(L_{g^{-1}})_g$. Composing the display on the right with $d(L_{g^{-1}})_g$ gives the formula.
\end{proof}

For a matrix group, where $d(L_g)$ and $d(R_g)$ are multiplication by $g$ on the left and on the right (Example~\ref{ex:left-invariant-GL} and Example~\ref{ex:right-invariant-GL} below), this reads $d\mu_{(g,h)}(v, w) = vh + gw$ and $dj_g(v) = -g^{-1}vg^{-1}$: the product rule and the derivative of the inverse matrix.

\begin{defbox}[Right-Invariant Vector Field]\deflabel{def:right-invariant}
A vector field $\mathbf{Y}$ on a Lie group $G$ is \textbf{right-invariant} if it is $R_g$-related to itself for every $g \in G$ (Definition~\ref{def:F-related}): for all $g, h \in G$,
\[
d(R_g)_h\, \mathbf{Y}_h = \mathbf{Y}_{R_g(h)} = \mathbf{Y}_{hg} .
\]
The same identity defines a right-invariant \emph{rough} field, a tangent vector at every point not yet known to be smooth (Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant-extension}).
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[Right-Invariant Extension]\deflabel{def:right-invariant-extension}
Let $G$ be a Lie group with identity $e$ and $A \in T_eG$. The \textbf{right-invariant extension} of $A$ is the rough field $\mathbf{Y}^A : G \to TG$,
\[
\mathbf{Y}^A_g = d(R_g)_e(A) \in T_gG, \qquad g \in G,
\]
which makes sense since $R_g(e) = g$. Beside it, $\mathbf{X}^A_g = d(L_g)_e(A)$ is the left-invariant extension (Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant-extension}).
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[Right-Invariant Fields and the Tangent Space at the Identity]\thmlabel{prop:right-invariant-TeG}
Let $G$ be a Lie group with identity $e$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item For $A \in T_eG$, $\mathbf{Y}^A$ is right-invariant and $\mathbf{Y}^A_e = A$.
    \item Every right-invariant (rough) field $\mathbf{Y}$ is $\mathbf{Y}^A$ for $A = \mathbf{Y}_e$.
    \item The map $A \mapsto \mathbf{Y}^A$ is linear, and it is a bijection from $T_eG$ onto the right-invariant rough fields, with inverse $\mathbf{Y} \mapsto \mathbf{Y}_e$. In particular $\mathbf{Y}^{-A} = -\mathbf{Y}^A$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~6, Problem~2(a), ``following what we did in class'' (Lemma~\ref{lem:left-invariant-extension}); the submitted solution. The linearity in (3) is from its part (b).)}

\emph{(1) $\mathbf{Y}^A$ is right-invariant.} For $g, h \in G$, by the chain rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}, as $R_h(e) = h$) and Lemma~\ref{lem:Rg}(1),
\[
d(R_g)_h\,\mathbf{Y}^A_h = d(R_g)_h\, d(R_h)_e(A) = d(R_g \circ R_h)_e(A) = d(R_{hg})_e(A) = \mathbf{Y}^A_{hg} .
\]
\emph{$\mathbf{Y}^A_e = A$.} Since $R_e = \mathrm{id}_G$, $\mathbf{Y}^A_e = d(R_e)_e(A) = d(\mathrm{id}_G)_e(A) = A$.

\emph{(2) Every right-invariant field is of this form.} Let $\mathbf{Y}$ be right-invariant and $A = \mathbf{Y}_e$. Taking $h = e$ in the right-invariance identity, for every $g \in G$,
\[
\mathbf{Y}_g = \mathbf{Y}_{eg} = d(R_g)_e\,\mathbf{Y}_e = d(R_g)_e(A) = \mathbf{Y}^A_g,
\]
so $\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{Y}^A$.

\emph{(3)} By (1) and (2), $A \mapsto \mathbf{Y}^A$ and $\mathbf{Y} \mapsto \mathbf{Y}_e$ are mutually inverse. The map $A \mapsto \mathbf{Y}^A$ is linear since each $d(R_g)_e$ is (Proposition~\ref{prop:pushforward-derivation}); in particular $\mathbf{Y}^{-A}_g = d(R_g)_e(-A) = -\mathbf{Y}^A_g$ for all $g$.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[Inversion Carries Left-Invariant to Right-Invariant Fields]\thmlabel{prop:inversion-left-right}
Let $G$ be a Lie group with inversion $j$, and $A \in T_eG$. For every $g \in G$,
\[
dj_g\big(\mathbf{X}^A_g\big) = \mathbf{Y}^{-A}_{j(g)} = \mathbf{Y}^{-A}_{g^{-1}} .
\]
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~6, Problem~2(a); the submitted solution.)} \emph{The right-hand side.} Since $j(g) = g^{-1}$ and $d(R_{g^{-1}})_e$ is linear,
\[
\mathbf{Y}^{-A}_{j(g)} = \mathbf{Y}^{-A}_{g^{-1}} = d(R_{g^{-1}})_e(-A).
\]
\emph{The left-hand side.} By the chain rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}), using $L_g(e) = g$, $j(e) = e$, Lemma~\ref{lem:inversion-translations}(1), and $dj_e(A) = -A$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:dinv-identity}),
\[
dj_g\,\mathbf{X}^A_g = dj_g\, d(L_g)_e(A) = d(j \circ L_g)_e(A) = d(R_{g^{-1}} \circ j)_e(A) = d(R_{g^{-1}})_e\, dj_e(A) = d(R_{g^{-1}})_e(-A).
\]
Comparing the two sides, $dj_g\,\mathbf{X}^A_g = \mathbf{Y}^{-A}_{j(g)}$ for every $g \in G$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[Right-Invariant Extensions Are Smooth]\thmlabel{cor:right-invariant-smooth}
Let $G$ be a Lie group with inversion $j$, and $A \in T_eG$. Then $\mathbf{Y}^{-A} = j_*\mathbf{X}^A$, the pushforward of the left-invariant field $\mathbf{X}^A$ by the diffeomorphism $j$ (Definition~\ref{def:vf-pushforward}). Hence every $\mathbf{Y}^A$ is smooth, and $\mathbf{X}^A$ and $\mathbf{Y}^{-A}$ are $j$-related (Definition~\ref{def:F-related}).
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from the assignment, which did not ask for smoothness: ``You do not have to prove that $Y^A$ is smooth.'' It follows from its part (a).)} By Lemma~\ref{lem:inversion-translations}(2), $j$ is a diffeomorphism with $j^{-1} = j$. For $q \in G$, by Definition~\ref{def:vf-pushforward} and Proposition~\ref{prop:inversion-left-right} at $g = j^{-1}(q) = q^{-1}$,
\[
(j_*\mathbf{X}^A)_q = dj_{q^{-1}}\big(\mathbf{X}^A_{q^{-1}}\big) = \mathbf{Y}^{-A}_{j(q^{-1})} = \mathbf{Y}^{-A}_q .
\]
$\mathbf{X}^A$ is smooth (Proposition~\ref{prop:left-invariant-extension-smooth}), so $\mathbf{Y}^{-A} = j_*\mathbf{X}^A$ is smooth by Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-pushforward}. As $A$ ranges over $T_eG$, so does $-A$: every $\mathbf{Y}^A$ is smooth. Now both are vector fields, and Proposition~\ref{prop:inversion-left-right} is the $j$-relatedness condition of Definition~\ref{def:F-related}.
\end{proof}

So the right-invariant vector fields are exactly the $\mathbf{Y}^A$, $A \in T_eG$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:right-invariant-TeG}), and they are smooth: the right-handed version of Theorem~\ref{thm:lie-algebra-TeG}, here obtained from the left-handed one through $j$ rather than by repeating Proposition~\ref{prop:left-invariant-extension-smooth}.

\begin{defbox}[The Right Bracket]\deflabel{def:right-bracket}
Let $G$ be a Lie group with identity $e$. For $A, B \in T_eG$, the \textbf{right bracket} is
\[
[A, B]^R = \big[\mathbf{Y}^A, \mathbf{Y}^B\big]_e \in T_eG,
\]
with $\mathbf{Y}^A, \mathbf{Y}^B$ the right-invariant extensions (Definition~\ref{def:right-invariant-extension}).
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[The Right Bracket Is a Lie Bracket]\thmlabel{prop:right-bracket-lie}
Let $G$ be a Lie group and $A, B \in T_eG$. The bracket $[\mathbf{Y}^A, \mathbf{Y}^B]$ is right-invariant, and
\[
\big[\mathbf{Y}^A, \mathbf{Y}^B\big] = \mathbf{Y}^{[A,B]^R} .
\]
$[\ ,\ ]^R$ is a Lie bracket on $T_eG$ (Definition~\ref{def:lie-algebra}).
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~6, Problem~2(b); the submitted solution.)} \emph{The bracket is right-invariant.} Let $g \in G$. Since $\mathbf{Y}^A$ and $\mathbf{Y}^B$ are right-invariant, each is $R_g$-related to itself (Definition~\ref{def:right-invariant}); they are smooth (Corollary~\ref{cor:right-invariant-smooth}), so by the naturality of the bracket (Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket-naturality}) $[\mathbf{Y}^A, \mathbf{Y}^B]$ is $R_g$-related to itself. As $g$ is arbitrary, $[\mathbf{Y}^A, \mathbf{Y}^B]$ is right-invariant, and by Proposition~\ref{prop:right-invariant-TeG}(2) it is $\mathbf{Y}^C$ with $C = [\mathbf{Y}^A, \mathbf{Y}^B]_e = [A, B]^R$.

\emph{A Lie bracket.} The map $A \mapsto \mathbf{Y}^A$ is linear and injective (Proposition~\ref{prop:right-invariant-TeG}(3)), and it carries $[\ ,\ ]^R$ to the bracket of vector fields. Hence bilinearity, antisymmetry and the Jacobi identity for $[\ ,\ ]^R$ follow from those of the bracket on $\mathfrak{X}(G)$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:vf-lie-algebra}). \textit{(Filled in.)} For instance, for bilinearity in the first slot, with $a, a' \in \mathbb{R}$,
\[
\mathbf{Y}^{[aA + a'A', B]^R} = \big[a\mathbf{Y}^A + a'\mathbf{Y}^{A'}, \mathbf{Y}^B\big] = a\,\mathbf{Y}^{[A,B]^R} + a'\,\mathbf{Y}^{[A',B]^R} = \mathbf{Y}^{a[A,B]^R + a'[A',B]^R},
\]
and injectivity gives $[aA + a'A', B]^R = a[A,B]^R + a'[A',B]^R$; antisymmetry and Jacobi are the same three steps.
\end{proof}

\begin{thmbox}[The Right Bracket Is the Negative of the Left Bracket]\thmlabel{thm:right-bracket}
Let $G$ be a Lie group, and $[\ ,\ ]$ the Lie bracket on $T_eG$ (Definition~\ref{def:bracket-TeG}). For all $A, B \in T_eG$,
\[
[A, B]^R = -[A, B] .
\]
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~6, Problem~2(b); the submitted solution.)} By Definition~\ref{def:bracket-TeG}, $[\mathbf{X}^A, \mathbf{X}^B] = \mathbf{X}^{[A,B]}$ (both are left-invariant, Corollary~\ref{cor:lie-subalgebra}, with the same value at $e$, Theorem~\ref{thm:lie-algebra-TeG}). By Corollary~\ref{cor:right-invariant-smooth}, $\mathbf{X}^A$ is $j$-related to $\mathbf{Y}^{-A}$ and $\mathbf{X}^B$ is $j$-related to $\mathbf{Y}^{-B}$, so by the naturality of the bracket (Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket-naturality})
\[
[\mathbf{X}^A, \mathbf{X}^B] = \mathbf{X}^{[A,B]} \text{ is $j$-related to } [\mathbf{Y}^{-A}, \mathbf{Y}^{-B}] .
\]
Since $\mathbf{Y}^{-A} = -\mathbf{Y}^A$ and $\mathbf{Y}^{-B} = -\mathbf{Y}^B$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:right-invariant-TeG}(3)), by bilinearity of the bracket and Proposition~\ref{prop:right-bracket-lie},
\[
[\mathbf{Y}^{-A}, \mathbf{Y}^{-B}] = [-\mathbf{Y}^A, -\mathbf{Y}^B] = (-1)(-1)[\mathbf{Y}^A, \mathbf{Y}^B] = \mathbf{Y}^{[A,B]^R} .
\]
On the other hand, Corollary~\ref{cor:right-invariant-smooth} applied to $[A, B] \in T_eG$ shows that $\mathbf{X}^{[A,B]}$ is $j$-related to $\mathbf{Y}^{-[A,B]}$. So $\mathbf{X}^{[A,B]}$ is $j$-related to both $\mathbf{Y}^{[A,B]^R}$ and $\mathbf{Y}^{-[A,B]}$; that is, for every $p \in G$,
\[
\mathbf{Y}^{[A,B]^R}_{j(p)} = dj_p\,\mathbf{X}^{[A,B]}_p = \mathbf{Y}^{-[A,B]}_{j(p)} .
\]
Since $j$ is a bijection, every point of $G$ is of the form $j(p)$, so $\mathbf{Y}^{[A,B]^R} = \mathbf{Y}^{-[A,B]}$. Evaluating at $e$ and using $\mathbf{Y}^C_e = C$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:right-invariant-TeG}(1)),
\[
[A, B]^R = -[A, B] . \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Second proof]
\textit{(Not from the assignment.)} $j$ is a diffeomorphism, so pushing forward by it preserves brackets (Corollary~\ref{cor:diffeo-bracket}). With $j_*\mathbf{X}^C = \mathbf{Y}^{-C}$ for every $C \in T_eG$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:right-invariant-smooth}) and $\mathbf{Y}^{-C} = -\mathbf{Y}^C$,
\[
\mathbf{Y}^{-[A,B]} = j_*\mathbf{X}^{[A,B]} = j_*[\mathbf{X}^A, \mathbf{X}^B] = [j_*\mathbf{X}^A, j_*\mathbf{X}^B] = [-\mathbf{Y}^A, -\mathbf{Y}^B] = [\mathbf{Y}^A, \mathbf{Y}^B] .
\]
Evaluating at $e$: $-[A, B] = [A, B]^R$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[Abelian Lie Groups Have Zero Bracket]\thmlabel{cor:abelian-bracket}
If the Lie group $G$ is abelian, its Lie bracket on $T_eG$ is identically zero.
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~6, Problem~2(c), ``use the result of part (b)''; the submitted solution.)} Suppose $G$ is abelian. For $g, k \in G$, $L_g(k) = gk = kg = R_g(k)$, so $L_g = R_g$. Hence for $A \in T_eG$ and $g \in G$,
\[
\mathbf{X}^A_g = d(L_g)_e(A) = d(R_g)_e(A) = \mathbf{Y}^A_g,
\]
so $\mathbf{X}^A = \mathbf{Y}^A$. Therefore, for $A, B \in T_eG$,
\[
[A, B]^R = [\mathbf{Y}^A, \mathbf{Y}^B]_e = [\mathbf{X}^A, \mathbf{X}^B]_e = [A, B].
\]
Combining with Theorem~\ref{thm:right-bracket}, $[A, B] = [A, B]^R = -[A, B]$, so $2[A, B] = 0$. Since $T_eG$ is a real vector space, $[A, B] = 0$ for all $A, B \in T_eG$.
\end{proof}

This agrees with Example~\ref{ex:vs-lie-algebra}, where the bracket of the additive group of a vector space was computed to vanish.

\begin{exbox}[The Torus]\exlabel{ex:torus-bracket}
Corollary~\ref{cor:abelian-bracket} applies as well to the torus $S^1 \times \cdots \times S^1$, a product of the abelian Lie group $S^1 = \Ugp(1)$: its Lie bracket is identically zero.
\end{exbox}

\begin{exbox}[{$\Ogp(2)$: Zero Bracket but Not Abelian}]\exlabel{ex:o2-bracket}
\textit{(Not from the assignment.)} The converse of Corollary~\ref{cor:abelian-bracket} needs connectedness: $\Ogp(2)$ is not abelian, but its tangent space at $I$ is that of $\SO(2) \cong S^1$, one-dimensional, so its bracket vanishes by antisymmetry.
\end{exbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} \emph{Not abelian.} The rotation by a quarter turn and a reflection lie in $\Ogp(2)$ and do not commute:
\[
\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} .
\]
\emph{Zero bracket.} $T_I\Ogp(2) = \Skew(2, \mathbb{R})$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:classical-summary}), the multiples of one matrix, so it is one-dimensional. Let $A, B \in T_I\Ogp(2)$. If $A = 0$, then $[A, B] = 0$ because the bracket is bilinear. Otherwise $B = cA$ for some $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and $[A, B] = c\,[A, A] = 0$: by antisymmetry $[A, A] = -[A, A]$, so $[A, A] = 0$. The bracket on $T_I\Ogp(2)$ (Definition~\ref{def:bracket-TeG}) is bilinear and antisymmetric because the bracket of vector fields is (Corollary~\ref{cor:vf-lie-algebra}) and $A \mapsto \mathbf{X}^A$ is linear (Theorem~\ref{thm:lie-algebra-TeG}).
\end{proof}

For connected groups the converse holds, a fact that needs the exponential map (Lee, Ch.~20).

\begin{exbox}[Right-Invariant Fields on $\GL({n,\mathbb{R}})$]\exlabel{ex:right-invariant-GL}
On $G = \GL(n,\mathbb{R})$, with $T_gG = \Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$ as in Example~\ref{ex:left-invariant-GL}, the right-invariant extension of $A \in \Mat(n,\mathbb{R}) = T_IG$ is
\[
\mathbf{Y}^A_g = Ag ,
\]
and the left- and right-invariant extensions are related by the adjoint action (Proposition~\ref{prop:adjoint}): $\mathbf{X}^A_g = gA = (gAg^{-1})\,g = \mathbf{Y}^{gAg^{-1}}_g$. The right bracket is $[A, B]^R = BA - AB$.
\end{exbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from the assignment.)} $R_g$ is the restriction to $G$ of the linear map $h \mapsto hg$ of $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$, so, exactly as for $L_g$ in the proof of Example~\ref{ex:left-invariant-GL}, $d(R_g)_h(v) = vg$; at $h = I$, $\mathbf{Y}^A_g = d(R_g)_I(A) = Ag$. Then $\mathbf{X}^A_g = gA = gAg^{-1}g = \mathbf{Y}^{gAg^{-1}}_g$. Finally $[A, B]^R = -[A, B] = -(AB - BA) = BA - AB$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:right-bracket} and Theorem~\ref{thm:gl-bracket}. As a check without the theorem: the fields $X \mapsto AX$ are the column-vector linear fields of Proposition~\ref{prop:column-action-fields-antihomomorphism}, applied to each column of $X$, and their brackets carry the same sign $BA - AB$.
\end{proof}
