% SECTION: LIE GROUP MORPHISMS AND LINEAR GROUPS
% ============================================================================

\section{Lie Group Morphisms and Linear Groups}\label{sec:lie-morphisms}\label{sub:lie-group-morphisms}

\roadmark{Stage: symmetry}{Maps of Lie groups induce maps of Lie algebras that preserve brackets; for a linear group the bracket is the matrix commutator.}

\textit{Lecture 18. Lie group morphisms and the Lie algebra, which the identification $\mathfrak{g} \cong T_eG$ now puts within reach.}

\begin{rembox}[Recap: $\mathfrak{g}$ Is $T_eG$]\label{rem:g-is-TeG}
\textit{(The opening of Lecture~18. A recap: Definition~\ref{def:bracket-TeG}, Theorem~\ref{thm:gl-bracket} and \ref{sub:right-invariant} already work on $T_eG$ and write its elements with capital letters.)} The Lie algebra is identified with the tangent space at the identity, $\mathfrak{g} \cong T_eG$ by $\mathrm{ev}$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:lie-algebra-TeG}), as vector spaces, keeping in mind that the Lie bracket comes from commuting left-invariant fields. That is Definition~\ref{def:lie-algebra-of-group} read through Definition~\ref{def:bracket-TeG}: to compute the bracket of $A, B \in T_eG$,
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item extend $A$ and $B$ to the left-invariant fields $\mathbf{X}^A$, $\mathbf{X}^B$, their left-invariant extensions (Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant-extension}; they lie in $\mathfrak{g}$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:left-invariant-extension-smooth});
\item take the commutator $[\mathbf{X}^A, \mathbf{X}^B]$ of vector fields;
\item evaluate it at the identity: $[A, B] = [\mathbf{X}^A, \mathbf{X}^B]_e$.
\end{enumerate}
This is the definition. Elements of $T_eG$ are written with capital letters, since they are thought of as matrices.
\end{rembox}

\begin{defbox}[Linear Group]\deflabel{def:linear-group}
A \textbf{linear group}, or \textbf{matrix group}, is a Lie group $G$ (Definition~\ref{def:lie-group}) that is a subgroup of $\GL(n,\mathbb{R})$ or $\GL(n,\mathbb{C})$ for some $n$, with matrix multiplication as its group product --- for instance each classical group of Proposition~\ref{prop:classical-lie-groups}.
\end{defbox}

\begin{exbox}[{The Universal Cover of $\SL({2,\mathbb{R}})$}]\exlabel{ex:universal-cover-sl2r-nonlinear}
\textit{(Filled in; not from lecture.)} The universal cover $\widetilde G$ of $\SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ is a Lie group isomorphic to no group of matrices: it admits no injective Lie group morphism (Definition~\ref{def:lie-group-morphism} below) into any $\GL(n,\mathbb{C})$, hence none into $\GL(n,\mathbb{R}) \subseteq \GL(n,\mathbb{C})$. So not every Lie group is a linear group (Definition~\ref{def:linear-group}).

\emph{Justification (a sketch: covering spaces and the passage from Lie algebra morphisms to Lie group morphisms are beyond these notes).} An isomorphism of $\widetilde G$ onto a linear group, followed by the inclusion, would be an injective Lie group morphism into some $\GL(n,\mathbb{C})$; so it suffices to show that every Lie group morphism $\rho : \widetilde G \to \GL(n,\mathbb{C})$ fails to be injective.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \emph{The group.} By the polar decomposition, $\SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ is homeomorphic to $\SO(2) \times P$, where $P$, the positive definite symmetric $2 \times 2$ matrices of determinant $1$, is homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^2$; so $\pi_1(\SL(2,\mathbb{R})) \cong \pi_1(S^1) \cong \mathbb{Z}$. The universal covering map $p : \widetilde G \to \SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ of the connected Lie group $\SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ makes $\widetilde G$ a connected Lie group and $p$ a Lie group morphism, with $\ker p \cong \pi_1(\SL(2,\mathbb{R})) \cong \mathbb{Z}$, a nontrivial subgroup.
    \item \emph{Every $\rho$ factors through $p$.} The differential of $\rho$ at the identity is a Lie algebra morphism (Definition~\ref{def:lie-algebra-morphism}) $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{R}) \to \mathfrak{gl}(n,\mathbb{C})$; it extends complex-linearly to a Lie algebra morphism on $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{C}) = \mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{R}) \oplus i\,\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{R})$. Since $\SL(2,\mathbb{C})$ is simply connected, this extension is the differential of a Lie group morphism $\sigma : \SL(2,\mathbb{C}) \to \GL(n,\mathbb{C})$. With $\iota : \SL(2,\mathbb{R}) \hookrightarrow \SL(2,\mathbb{C})$ the inclusion, $\rho$ and $\sigma \circ \iota \circ p$ are Lie group morphisms with the same differential at the identity, on the connected group $\widetilde G$; so they are equal.
    \item \emph{Conclusion.} Hence $\rho = \sigma \circ \iota \circ p$ is trivial on $\ker p \neq \{e\}$, and $\rho$ is not injective.
\end{enumerate}
\end{exbox}

\begin{rembox}[Nonlinear Groups]\label{rem:linear-groups}
Matrix groups are also called linear groups (Definition~\ref{def:linear-group}). Not every Lie group is isomorphic to a matrix group: nonlinear groups arise naturally as covers of matrix groups, as Example~\ref{ex:universal-cover-sl2r-nonlinear} shows. The question of Lecture~17, restated: for a matrix group, can the bracket be identified directly on the tangent space at the identity? The answer is the matrix commutator (Theorem~\ref{thm:linear-group-bracket} below; its base cases are $\GL(d, \mathbb{R})$, Theorem~\ref{thm:gl-bracket}, and $\GL(d, \mathbb{C})$, Proposition~\ref{prop:glc-bracket}); to get there, the course uses the general idea below.
\end{rembox}

\begin{defbox}[Lie Group Morphism]\deflabel{def:lie-group-morphism}
Let $H$ and $G$ be Lie groups. A \textbf{Lie group morphism} (homomorphism) $F : H \to G$ is a map that is both smooth and a group morphism: $F(gh) = F(g)F(h)$ for all $g, h \in H$.
\leeref{Ch.~7, \emph{Lie Group Homomorphisms}}
\end{defbox}

A Lie group is a manifold and a group whose group operations are smooth, so a morphism preserves both structures. In particular $F(e_H) = e_G$. \textit{(Filled in: $F(e_H) = F(e_He_H) = F(e_H)F(e_H)$; multiply on the left by $F(e_H)^{-1}$.)} So $F$ has a differential at the identity,
\[
dF_e : T_{e}H \longrightarrow T_{e}G, \qquad \text{that is,} \qquad dF_e : \mathfrak{h} \longrightarrow \mathfrak{g},
\]
a linear map between the Lie algebras, and the natural question is whether this map preserves commutators.

A linear map between Lie algebras that preserves brackets is a Lie algebra morphism (Definition~\ref{def:lie-algebra-morphism}); so the question is whether $dF_e$ is one.

\begin{lembox}[Left-Invariant Fields Related by a Morphism]\thmlabel{lem:morphism-related}
Let $F : H \to G$ be a Lie group morphism (Definition~\ref{def:lie-group-morphism}) and $A \in T_eH$, and put $\tilde A = dF_e(A) \in T_eG$. Let $\mathbf{X}^A \in \mathfrak{X}(H)$ and $\mathbf{Y}^{\tilde A} \in \mathfrak{X}(G)$ be the left-invariant extensions of $A$ and of $\tilde A$ (Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant-extension}; smooth by Proposition~\ref{prop:left-invariant-extension-smooth}). Here the letter $\mathbf{Y}$ only marks a field on $G$: $\mathbf{Y}^{\tilde A}$ is the left-invariant extension of $\tilde A$, not its right-invariant extension of Definition~\ref{def:right-invariant-extension}. Then $\mathbf{X}^A$ and $\mathbf{Y}^{\tilde A}$ are $F$-related (Definition~\ref{def:F-related}):
\[
dF_h\big(\mathbf{X}^A_h\big) = \mathbf{Y}^{\tilde A}_{F(h)} \in T_{F(h)}G \qquad \text{for every } h \in H .
\]
\leeref{proof of Theorem 8.44}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~18: the claim in the proof that Lie group morphisms preserve brackets. The final diagram chase, left to the class, is completed.)} Fix $h \in H$; the displayed equality is to be shown. \emph{$F(e) = e$.} As noted after Definition~\ref{def:lie-group-morphism}, $F(e_H) = F(e_He_H) = F(e_H)F(e_H)$, and multiplying on the left by $F(e_H)^{-1}$ gives $F(e_H) = e_G$; so $dF_e$ maps $T_eH$ to $T_eG$, and $\tilde A \in T_eG$.

\emph{The square.} Here it is essential that $F$ is a group morphism. Consider the square
\[
F \circ L_h = L_{F(h)} \circ F : H \to G .
\]
It commutes: for $x \in H$, $F(L_h(x)) = F(hx) = F(h)F(x) = L_{F(h)}(F(x))$, where $L$ always denotes left multiplication in the corresponding group. Differentiate it at $e \in H$. Since $L_h(e) = h$ and $F(e) = e$, the chain rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}) gives the commutative square of differentials
\[
dF_h \circ d(L_h)_e = d\big(L_{F(h)}\big)_e \circ dF_e : T_eH \to T_{F(h)}G .
\]

\emph{The chase.} \textit{(Completed.)} Chase where $A$ goes under this diagram:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{along the bottom, then up:} && A \mapsto d(L_h)_e(A) = \mathbf{X}^A_h \mapsto dF_h(\mathbf{X}^A_h), \\
&\text{up, then along the top:} && A \mapsto dF_e(A) = \tilde A \mapsto d(L_{F(h)})_e(\tilde A) = \mathbf{Y}^{\tilde A}_{F(h)},
\end{aligned}
\]
both by Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant-extension}, for $H$ at the point $h$ and for $G$ at the point $F(h)$. The square commutes, so $dF_h(\mathbf{X}^A_h) = \mathbf{Y}^{\tilde A}_{F(h)}$; as $h$ was arbitrary, this is the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=5em, row sep=3em]
G \arrow[r, "L_{F(h)}"] & G \\
H \arrow[u, "F"] \arrow[r, "L_h"'] & H \arrow[u, "F"']
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad\qquad
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=5em, row sep=3em]
T_eG \arrow[r, "d(L_{F(h)})_e"] & T_{F(h)}G \\
T_eH \arrow[u, "dF_e"] \arrow[r, "d(L_h)_e"'] & T_hH \arrow[u, "dF_h"']
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=5em, row sep=3em]
\tilde A \arrow[r, mapsto] & \mathbf{Y}^{\tilde A}_{F(h)} \\
A \arrow[u, mapsto] \arrow[r, mapsto] & \mathbf{X}^A_h \arrow[u, mapsto]
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

Top left: the group square, which commutes because $F$ is a morphism. Top right: its differential at $e$, which commutes by the chain rule. Below: where $A$ goes. Both routes end at the same vector, which is the statement that $\mathbf{X}^A$ and $\mathbf{Y}^{\tilde A}$ are $F$-related.

\begin{propbox}[Lie Group Morphisms Preserve Brackets]\thmlabel{prop:morphism-preserves-bracket}
Let $F : H \to G$ be a Lie group morphism. For all $A, B \in T_eH$,
\[
dF_e\big([A, B]\big) = \big[dF_e(A), dF_e(B)\big] \in T_eG ,
\]
that is, $dF_e : \mathfrak{h} \to \mathfrak{g}$ is a Lie algebra morphism (Definition~\ref{def:lie-algebra-morphism}).
\leeref{Theorem 8.44}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~18, a soft proof.)} Since the bracket is defined in terms of vector fields, the proof has to pass to vector fields. For $A \in T_eH$ let $\mathbf{X}^A \in \mathfrak{X}(H)$ be the left-invariant extension of $A$, the left-invariant field with $\mathbf{X}^A_e = A$; put $\tilde A = dF_e(A) \in T_eG$, and let $\mathbf{Y}^{\tilde A} \in \mathfrak{X}(G)$ be the left-invariant extension of $\tilde A$, with $\mathbf{Y}^{\tilde A}_e = \tilde A$ (Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant-extension} and Proposition~\ref{prop:left-invariant-extension-smooth}, applied to $H$ and to $G$).

\emph{Claim.} $\mathbf{X}^A$ and $\mathbf{Y}^{\tilde A}$ are $F$-related (Definition~\ref{def:F-related}).

\emph{The proposition follows from the claim.} Let also $B \in T_eH$ and $\tilde B = dF_e(B)$. By the claim, $\mathbf{X}^A$ is $F$-related to $\mathbf{Y}^{\tilde A}$ and $\mathbf{X}^B$ to $\mathbf{Y}^{\tilde B}$, so by Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket-naturality}, $[\mathbf{X}^A, \mathbf{X}^B]$ is $F$-related to $[\mathbf{Y}^{\tilde A}, \mathbf{Y}^{\tilde B}]$. Evaluate at $e \in H$, using $F(e) = e$:
\[
dF_e\big([\mathbf{X}^A, \mathbf{X}^B]_e\big) = [\mathbf{Y}^{\tilde A}, \mathbf{Y}^{\tilde B}]_{F(e)} = [\mathbf{Y}^{\tilde A}, \mathbf{Y}^{\tilde B}]_e .
\]
By Definition~\ref{def:bracket-TeG} the left side is $dF_e([A, B])$ and the right side is $[\tilde A, \tilde B] = [dF_e(A), dF_e(B)]$: that is exactly the proposition. So the work lies in the claim: it is Lemma~\ref{lem:morphism-related}, applied to $F$ and $A$, whose proof is the diagram chase above.
\end{proof}

The commutator for the general linear group $\GL(d, \mathbb{R})$ is Theorem~\ref{thm:gl-bracket}; next, the commutator for $\GL(d, \mathbb{C})$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:glc-bracket}) and for any linear group (Theorem~\ref{thm:linear-group-bracket}).

\textbf{Transcription note (Lecture 18).} Page~47 of the handwritten notes begins the proof with ``take $A \in T_hH$''; $A \in T_eH$. Page~48 writes the second field as $\mathbf{Y}^{\hat B}$ in one place; it is $\mathbf{Y}^{\tilde B}$, with $\tilde B = dF_e(B)$.

% Lecture 19 (Wed Oct 14, 2026): the bracket of a matrix group
% ============================================================================

\subsection{The Bracket of a Matrix Group}\label{sub:matrix-group-bracket}

\textit{Lecture 19 began with a review: the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ of left-invariant fields, closed under commutators (Corollary~\ref{cor:lie-subalgebra}); the isomorphism $\mathrm{ev} : \mathfrak{g} \to T_eG$ with inverse $A \mapsto \mathbf{X}^A$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:lie-algebra-TeG}), including the check that $\mathbf{X}^A$ is left-invariant (Lemma~\ref{lem:left-invariant-extension}(2)); and the bracket on $T_eG$ (Definition~\ref{def:bracket-TeG}), defined so that $\mathrm{ev}$ is an isomorphism of Lie algebras (Definition~\ref{def:lie-algebra-isomorphism}).}

\begin{rembox}[The Lie Algebra in Practice]\label{rem:lie-algebra-practice}
In practice, the Lie algebra of a group such as the orthogonal group is never described as a space of left-invariant fields; it is always the tangent space at the identity --- with the bracket of Definition~\ref{def:bracket-TeG}, which for matrix groups is the matrix commutator (Theorem~\ref{thm:linear-group-bracket} below). The notation $\mathfrak{gl}(d, \mathbb{R}) = T_I\GL(d,\mathbb{R}) = \Mat(d,\mathbb{R})$ is standard, and likewise $\mathfrak{gl}(d, \mathbb{C}) = T_I\GL(d,\mathbb{C}) = \Mat(d,\mathbb{C})$.
\end{rembox}

\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in: Definition~\ref{def:realification}, Lemma~\ref{lem:realification} and Proposition~\ref{prop:glc-bracket}. Definition~\ref{def:linear-group} allows subgroups of $\GL(n,\mathbb{C})$, while Theorem~\ref{thm:gl-bracket} computes the bracket of $\GL(d,\mathbb{R})$ only. The complex general linear group is brought back to the real one by writing a complex matrix as a real matrix of twice the size; no second index computation is needed.)}

\begin{defbox}[Realification of a Complex Matrix]\deflabel{def:realification}
Write $Z \in \Mat(n,\mathbb{C})$ as $Z = A + iB$, with $A, B \in \Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$ the matrices of the real parts and of the imaginary parts of the entries of $Z$. The \textbf{realification} of $Z$ is the real $2n \times 2n$ block matrix
\[
\rho(Z) = \begin{pmatrix} A & -B \\ B & A \end{pmatrix} \in \Mat(2n,\mathbb{R}) .
\]
\end{defbox}

The realification is the matrix of $z \mapsto Zz$ on $\mathbb{C}^n$ in real coordinates: for $z = x + iy$ with $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $(A + iB)(x + iy) = (Ax - By) + i\,(Bx + Ay)$, and $\rho(Z)$ takes the column $(x, y)$ to the column $(Ax - By,\ Bx + Ay)$.

\begin{lembox}[Realification Is an Injective Lie Group Morphism]\thmlabel{lem:realification}
Let $\rho : \Mat(n,\mathbb{C}) \to \Mat(2n,\mathbb{R})$ be the realification (Definition~\ref{def:realification}), with $\Mat(n,\mathbb{C})$ regarded as a real vector space (Definition~\ref{def:complex-groups}).
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\rho$ is $\mathbb{R}$-linear and injective.
    \item $\rho(ZW) = \rho(Z)\,\rho(W)$ for all $Z, W \in \Mat(n,\mathbb{C})$, and $\rho(I_n) = I_{2n}$.
    \item $\rho$ maps $\GL(n,\mathbb{C})$ into $\GL(2n,\mathbb{R})$, and its restriction $F : \GL(n,\mathbb{C}) \to \GL(2n,\mathbb{R})$, $F(Z) = \rho(Z)$, is an injective Lie group morphism (Definition~\ref{def:lie-group-morphism}).
    \item Under the identifications $T_I\GL(n,\mathbb{C}) = \Mat(n,\mathbb{C})$ and $T_I\GL(2n,\mathbb{R}) = \Mat(2n,\mathbb{R})$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:germs-local} and Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs}), the differential of $F$ at the identity is $\rho$ itself: $dF_I(V) = \rho(V)$ for every $V \in \Mat(n,\mathbb{C})$. In particular $dF_I$ is injective.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} Throughout, $Z = A + iB$ and $W = C + iD$ with $A, B, C, D \in \Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$.

\emph{(1)} Let $s, t \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $sZ + tW = (sA + tC) + i\,(sB + tD)$, and $sA + tC$ and $sB + tD$ are real matrices, so they are the real and the imaginary part of $sZ + tW$. By Definition~\ref{def:realification},
\[
\rho(sZ + tW) = \begin{pmatrix} sA + tC & -(sB + tD) \\ sB + tD & sA + tC \end{pmatrix} = s \begin{pmatrix} A & -B \\ B & A \end{pmatrix} + t \begin{pmatrix} C & -D \\ D & C \end{pmatrix} = s\,\rho(Z) + t\,\rho(W) .
\]
So $\rho$ is $\mathbb{R}$-linear. If $\rho(Z) = 0$, then its blocks $A$ and $B$ are zero, so $Z = A + iB = 0$; a linear map with zero kernel is injective.

\emph{(2)} Multiplying out, with $i^2 = -1$ and the scalar $i$ commuting with every matrix,
\[
ZW = (A + iB)(C + iD) = AC + i\,AD + i\,BC + i^2\,BD = (AC - BD) + i\,(AD + BC) ,
\]
and $AC - BD$ and $AD + BC$ are real matrices, so they are the real and the imaginary part of $ZW$. On the other side, by block multiplication,
\[
\rho(Z)\,\rho(W) = \begin{pmatrix} A & -B \\ B & A \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} C & -D \\ D & C \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} AC - BD & -AD - BC \\ BC + AD & -BD + AC \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} AC - BD & -(AD + BC) \\ AD + BC & AC - BD \end{pmatrix} = \rho(ZW) .
\]
For $Z = I_n$ the real part is $A = I_n$ and the imaginary part is $B = 0$, so $\rho(I_n)$ is the block matrix with diagonal blocks $I_n$ and zero off-diagonal blocks, which is $I_{2n}$.

\emph{(3)} Let $Z \in \GL(n,\mathbb{C})$. By (2), $\rho(Z)\,\rho(Z^{-1}) = \rho(ZZ^{-1}) = \rho(I_n) = I_{2n}$ and $\rho(Z^{-1})\,\rho(Z) = \rho(Z^{-1}Z) = I_{2n}$, so $\rho(Z)$ is invertible, with inverse $\rho(Z^{-1})$: $\rho(Z) \in \GL(2n,\mathbb{R})$. So $F$ is defined; it is a group morphism by (2) and injective by (1). It remains to see that $F$ is smooth. In the linear coordinates of $\Mat(n,\mathbb{C})$, the real and imaginary parts of the entries (Definition~\ref{def:complex-groups}), and of $\Mat(2n,\mathbb{R})$, the entries, each entry of $\rho(Z)$ is an entry of $A$ or of $B$ or the negative of one, that is, plus or minus one of the coordinates of $Z$; so the coordinate representation of $\rho$ is a linear map $\mathbb{R}^{2n^2} \to \mathbb{R}^{4n^2}$, and $\rho$ is smooth. The inclusion $\iota : \GL(n,\mathbb{C}) \hookrightarrow \Mat(n,\mathbb{C})$ is smooth, so $\rho \circ \iota$ is smooth into $\Mat(2n,\mathbb{R})$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}); it lands in the open subset $\GL(2n,\mathbb{R})$, so it is smooth as a map into $\GL(2n,\mathbb{R})$, whose chart is the restriction of the linear chart of $\Mat(2n,\mathbb{R})$ (both facts as in the setting of the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:classical-lie-groups}). This map is $F$.

\emph{(4)} This is the argument for $L_g$ in the proof of Example~\ref{ex:left-invariant-GL}. Let $\iota : \GL(n,\mathbb{C}) \hookrightarrow \Mat(n,\mathbb{C})$ and $j : \GL(2n,\mathbb{R}) \hookrightarrow \Mat(2n,\mathbb{R})$ be the inclusions of the open subsets. Then $j \circ F = \rho \circ \iota$, so by the chain rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}), at the point $I = I_n$ with $F(I_n) = I_{2n}$,
\[
j_{*I_{2n}} \circ dF_{I_n} = \rho_{*I_n} \circ \iota_{*I_n} .
\]
Here $\iota_{*I_n}$ and $j_{*I_{2n}}$ are the identifications of Lemma~\ref{lem:germs-local}, and by Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs} for the linear map $\rho$, $\rho_{*I_n}(D_V|_{I_n}) = D_{\rho(V)}|_{\rho(I_n)} = D_{\rho(V)}|_{I_{2n}}$. So under the identifications $V \leftrightarrow D_V|_{I_n}$ and $\rho(V) \leftrightarrow D_{\rho(V)}|_{I_{2n}}$ of Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs}, $dF_I(V) = \rho(V)$. It is injective by (1).
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[{The Lie Algebra of $\GL({n,\mathbb{C}})$}]\thmlabel{prop:glc-bracket}
Let $G = \GL(n, \mathbb{C})$, an open subset of the real vector space $\Mat(n, \mathbb{C}) \cong \mathbb{R}^{2n^2}$ (Definition~\ref{def:complex-groups}), so that $T_IG = \Mat(n,\mathbb{C})$. The Lie bracket on $T_IG$ (Definition~\ref{def:bracket-TeG}) is the commutator of complex matrices
\[
[A, B] = AB - BA .
\]
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} $G$ is a Lie group (Proposition~\ref{prop:classical-lie-groups}), so $T_IG$ has the bracket of Definition~\ref{def:bracket-TeG}; write it $[A, B]_G$ until it is computed. Let $F : \GL(n,\mathbb{C}) \to \GL(2n,\mathbb{R})$ be the Lie group morphism of Lemma~\ref{lem:realification}(3), with $dF_I = \rho$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:realification}(4)), and let $A, B \in \Mat(n,\mathbb{C}) = T_IG$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:morphism-preserves-bracket} applied to $F$,
\[
\rho\big([A, B]_G\big) = dF_I\big([A, B]_G\big) = \big[dF_I(A), dF_I(B)\big]_{\GL(2n,\mathbb{R})} = \big[\rho(A), \rho(B)\big]_{\GL(2n,\mathbb{R})} .
\]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:gl-bracket} with $d = 2n$, the bracket of $\GL(2n,\mathbb{R})$ is the commutator of real matrices; then by Lemma~\ref{lem:realification}(2), which holds for all complex matrices, and the linearity of $\rho$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:realification}(1)),
\[
\big[\rho(A), \rho(B)\big]_{\GL(2n,\mathbb{R})} = \rho(A)\,\rho(B) - \rho(B)\,\rho(A) = \rho(AB) - \rho(BA) = \rho(AB - BA) .
\]
So $\rho\big([A, B]_G\big) = \rho(AB - BA)$, and $\rho$ is injective (Lemma~\ref{lem:realification}(1)); hence $[A, B]_G = AB - BA$.
\end{proof}

\begin{thmbox}[The Bracket of a Linear Group]\thmlabel{thm:linear-group-bracket}
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let $G \subseteq \GL(d, \mathbb{K})$ be a linear group (Definition~\ref{def:linear-group}) that is a \emph{Lie subgroup}: the inclusion $i : G \hookrightarrow \GL(d, \mathbb{K})$ is smooth and $di_I$ is injective --- for instance, $G$ a regular submanifold of $\Mat(d, \mathbb{K})$, as are the classical groups (Proposition~\ref{prop:classical-lie-groups}). Identify $T_IG$ with its image $di_I(T_IG) \subseteq \mathfrak{gl}(d,\mathbb{K}) = \Mat(d,\mathbb{K})$. Then the Lie bracket on $T_IG$ is
\[
[A, B] = AB - BA ,
\]
with matrix multiplication.
\leeref{Proposition 8.41, Theorem 8.46}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~19, for $\GL(d, \mathbb{R})$; the case of $\GL(d, \mathbb{C})$ is the same argument with Proposition~\ref{prop:glc-bracket} as the base case, filled in.)} By assumption, $G$ is included in some general linear group as a Lie subgroup, and the differential of the inclusion map at the identity is the inclusion $di_I : T_IG \hookrightarrow \mathfrak{gl}(d, \mathbb{K})$. The inclusion is a Lie group morphism (Definition~\ref{def:lie-group-morphism}): smooth by hypothesis, and a group morphism because the product on $G$ is matrix multiplication. So by Proposition~\ref{prop:morphism-preserves-bracket}, for $A, B \in T_IG$,
\[
di_I\big([A, B]_G\big) = \big[di_I(A), di_I(B)\big]_{\GL(d,\mathbb{K})} = di_I(A)\, di_I(B) - di_I(B)\, di_I(A),
\]
the last step by Theorem~\ref{thm:gl-bracket} for $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ and by Proposition~\ref{prop:glc-bracket} for $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{C}$. Under the identification of $T_IG$ with its image, which $di_I$ injective makes legitimate, this is $[A, B] = AB - BA$. So once the bracket of the general linear group is known to be the commutator, the bracket of every linear group that is a Lie subgroup of $\GL(d, \mathbb{K})$ is the commutator too, by algebra alone. \textit{(Filled in: a regular submanifold qualifies, since $i$ is smooth by Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}(1), with coordinate representation $r \mapsto (r, \vec 0)$ in an adapted chart, whose differential is injective.)}
\end{proof}

In particular $di_I(T_IG)$ is closed under the matrix commutator, as the image of a bracket. Lecture~19 checked this directly in one case.

\begin{exbox}[The Commutator of Skew-Symmetric Matrices]\exlabel{ex:skew-bracket}
$T_I\Ogp(n) = \Skew(n, \mathbb{R}) = \{A : A^{\mathsf T} = -A\}$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:classical-summary}). Written out, an element of $\Skew(n, \mathbb{R})$ has zero diagonal, and its entries below the diagonal are the negatives of those above:
\[
A = \begin{pmatrix}
0 & a_{12} & \cdots & a_{1n} \\
-a_{12} & 0 & \cdots & a_{2n} \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
-a_{1n} & -a_{2n} & \cdots & 0
\end{pmatrix} .
\]
 If $A, B \in \Skew(n,\mathbb{R})$, then $[A, B] = AB - BA \in \Skew(n,\mathbb{R})$.
\end{exbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~19.)} $[A, B]^{\mathsf T} = (AB - BA)^{\mathsf T} = B^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T} - A^{\mathsf T}B^{\mathsf T} = (-B)(-A) - (-A)(-B) = BA - AB = -[A, B]$. The same computation works for the unitary group, with the conjugate transpose $^*$ in place of the transpose.
\end{proof}

\textbf{Transcription note (Lecture 19).} Page~49 of the handwritten notes writes the evaluation map as $\mathfrak{g} \to T_eM$ and its inverse from $T_eM$; the group is $G$, so $T_eG$. The definition of the bracket there reads ``$[A, B] = [\mathbf{X}^A, \mathbf{X}^B]$''; the field bracket is evaluated at the identity, $[A, B] = [\mathbf{X}^A, \mathbf{X}^B]_e$ (Definition~\ref{def:bracket-TeG}), as stated in lecture.

\textit{Assignment~6, Problem~3: linear vector fields on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Not from lecture. ``This is a special case of a Lie group (in this case $\GL(n,\mathbb{R})$) acting on the right on a manifold, in this case $\mathbb{R}^n$. Such an action induces a Lie algebra homomorphism from the Lie algebra of the group to the Lie algebra of vector fields on the manifold.''}

\begin{defbox}[Linear Vector Field]\deflabel{def:linear-field}
For an $n \times n$ real matrix $A = (a_{ij})$, the \textbf{linear vector field} $\mathbf{X}^A$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is
\[
\mathbf{X}^A_p = pA \in T_p\mathbb{R}^n \cong \mathbb{R}^n ,
\]
where $p \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is a \emph{row} vector and $T_p\mathbb{R}^n \cong \mathbb{R}^n$ by $v \leftrightarrow D_v|_p$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs}).
\end{defbox}

The letter is that of Example~\ref{ex:left-invariant-GL} on purpose: the left-invariant field $g \mapsto gA$ on $\GL(n,\mathbb{R})$ is $\mathbf{X}^A$ acting on each row of $g$ (the remark \emph{Linear Fields and the Bracket of} $\GL(n,\mathbb{R})$ below).

\begin{propbox}[The Derivation of a Linear Field]\thmlabel{prop:linear-field-derivation}
In the standard coordinates $p = (x^1, \ldots, x^n)$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$, with $\partial_j = \partial/\partial x^j$,
\[
\mathbf{X}^A = \sum_{j=1}^n \Big(\sum_{i=1}^n a_{ij}\,x^i\Big) \partial_j .
\]
The map $A \mapsto \mathbf{X}^A$ is linear: $\mathbf{X}^{A + B} = \mathbf{X}^A + \mathbf{X}^B$ and $\mathbf{X}^{cA} = c\,\mathbf{X}^A$ for $c \in \mathbb{R}$.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~6, Problem~3; the submitted solution.)} The $j$-th entry of the row vector $pA$ is
\[
(pA)_j = \sum_{i=1}^n x^i a_{ij}.
\]
For $f \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$, $\mathbf{X}^A f$ is the derivative of $f$ at $p$ in the direction $\mathbf{X}^A_p = pA$; by the chain rule,
\[
(\mathbf{X}^A f)(p) = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} f(p + t\,pA) = \sum_{j=1}^n (pA)_j\, \partial_j f(p).
\]
Hence $\mathbf{X}^A = \sum_j \big(\sum_i a_{ij}\,x^i\big) \partial_j$. The coefficients are linear in the entries of $A$, so $A \mapsto \mathbf{X}^A$ is linear.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[Brackets of Linear Fields]\thmlabel{prop:linear-field-bracket}
For any two $n \times n$ real matrices $A$, $B$,
\[
\big[\mathbf{X}^A, \mathbf{X}^B\big] = \mathbf{X}^{[A,B]}, \qquad [A, B] = AB - BA .
\]
So $A \mapsto \mathbf{X}^A$ is a Lie algebra morphism $\mathfrak{gl}(n,\mathbb{R}) \to \mathfrak{X}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ (Definition~\ref{def:lie-algebra-morphism}).
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~6, Problem~3, ``show directly''; the submitted solution.)} \emph{Computing $\mathbf{X}^A(\mathbf{X}^B f)$.} Let $f \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$. We have $\mathbf{X}^B f = \sum_k (pB)_k\, \partial_k f$ with $(pB)_k = \sum_l b_{lk}x^l$. By the product rule,
\[
\mathbf{X}^A(\mathbf{X}^B f) = \sum_{j,k} (pA)_j\, \partial_j\big[(pB)_k\big]\, \partial_k f + \sum_{j,k} (pA)_j\,(pB)_k\, \partial_j\partial_k f.
\]
For the first sum, $\partial_j\big(\sum_l b_{lk}x^l\big) = \sum_l b_{lk}\,\delta_{jl} = b_{jk}$, so
\[
\sum_{j,k} \Big(\sum_i a_{ij}x^i\Big) b_{jk}\, \partial_k f = \sum_k \Big(\sum_i x^i \sum_j a_{ij}b_{jk}\Big) \partial_k f = \sum_k \Big(\sum_i (AB)_{ik}\,x^i\Big) \partial_k f = \mathbf{X}^{AB} f.
\]
Writing $S(A,B) = \sum_{j,k} (pA)_j\,(pB)_k\, \partial_j\partial_k f$, we get $\mathbf{X}^A(\mathbf{X}^B f) = \mathbf{X}^{AB}f + S(A,B)$, and in the same way, with $A$ and $B$ interchanged, $\mathbf{X}^B(\mathbf{X}^A f) = \mathbf{X}^{BA}f + S(B,A)$.

\emph{The second-order terms cancel.} Relabelling the summation indices $j \leftrightarrow k$, and using $\partial_k\partial_j f = \partial_j\partial_k f$ (symmetry of second derivatives, as $f$ is smooth),
\[
S(B,A) = \sum_{j,k} (pB)_j\,(pA)_k\, \partial_j\partial_k f = \sum_{j,k} (pB)_k\,(pA)_j\, \partial_k\partial_j f = \sum_{j,k} (pA)_j\,(pB)_k\, \partial_j\partial_k f = S(A,B).
\]

\emph{Conclusion.} Therefore, using the linearity of $A \mapsto \mathbf{X}^A$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:linear-field-derivation}),
\[
[\mathbf{X}^A, \mathbf{X}^B]f = \mathbf{X}^A(\mathbf{X}^B f) - \mathbf{X}^B(\mathbf{X}^A f) = \mathbf{X}^{AB}f - \mathbf{X}^{BA}f = \mathbf{X}^{AB - BA}f = \mathbf{X}^{[A,B]}f.
\]
Since this holds for every $f \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$, $[\mathbf{X}^A, \mathbf{X}^B] = \mathbf{X}^{[A,B]}$.

\textit{(Filled in.)} The last sentence of the statement: $A \mapsto \mathbf{X}^A$ is linear and carries the commutator to the bracket of vector fields, which is what Definition~\ref{def:lie-algebra-morphism} asks of a map between Lie algebras.
\end{proof}

The second-order terms cancel as they must (Lemma~\ref{lem:bracket-field}); the shortcut of Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket-coords}, which computes only the first-order part, gives the same coefficients $\sum_i (AB - BA)_{ik} x^i$ at once.

\begin{rembox}[Linear Fields and the Bracket of $\GL({n,\mathbb{R}})$]\label{rem:linear-fields-gl}
\textit{(Not from the assignment.)} Write $g \in \Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$ by its rows $g_1, \ldots, g_n \in \mathbb{R}^n$. The $l$-th row of $gA$ is $g_lA$, so the left-invariant field $\mathbf{X}^A_g = gA$ of Example~\ref{ex:left-invariant-GL} is the linear field $\mathbf{X}^A$ of Definition~\ref{def:linear-field} acting on each row separately, the $n$ rows being independent variables. Proposition~\ref{prop:linear-field-bracket}, applied row by row, is therefore the computation of Theorem~\ref{thm:gl-bracket}: $[\mathbf{X}^A, \mathbf{X}^B] = \mathbf{X}^{AB - BA}$, the ``coordinate-free'' sentence after its proof.
\end{rembox}

\begin{propbox}[Fields of the Left Action on Column Vectors]\thmlabel{prop:column-action-fields-antihomomorphism}
$\GL(n,\mathbb{R})$ acts on \emph{column} vectors on the left, $g \cdot p = gp$. For $A = (a_{kj}) \in \Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$ let $\mathbf{Z}_A$ be the corresponding field on $\mathbb{R}^n$, $(\mathbf{Z}_A)_p = \frac{d}{dt}\big|_{t=0} (I + tA)\,p = Ap$, that is, $\mathbf{Z}_A = \sum_k \big(\sum_j a_{kj}x^j\big)\partial_k$. Then
\[
[\mathbf{Z}_A, \mathbf{Z}_B] = \mathbf{Z}_{BA - AB} = -\,\mathbf{Z}_{[A,B]} :
\]
$A \mapsto \mathbf{Z}_A$ is an anti-homomorphism.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from the assignment; computed.)} Let $f \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$. Write $(Bp)_k = \sum_l b_{kl}x^l$, so that $\mathbf{Z}_B f = \sum_k (Bp)_k\, \partial_k f$. By the product rule,
\[
\mathbf{Z}_A(\mathbf{Z}_B f) = \sum_{j,k} (Ap)_j\, \partial_j\big[(Bp)_k\big]\, \partial_k f + \sum_{j,k} (Ap)_j\,(Bp)_k\, \partial_j\partial_k f .
\]
\emph{The first-order part.} $\partial_j\big(\sum_l b_{kl}x^l\big) = b_{kj}$, so the first sum is
\[
\sum_{k} \Big(\sum_j b_{kj}\, (Ap)_j\Big)\partial_k f = \sum_k (BAp)_k\, \partial_k f = \mathbf{Z}_{BA}f .
\]
\emph{The second-order parts cancel.} The second sum, $T(A, B) = \sum_{j,k} (Ap)_j\,(Bp)_k\, \partial_j\partial_k f$, is symmetric in $A$ and $B$: relabel $j \leftrightarrow k$ and use $\partial_k\partial_j f = \partial_j\partial_k f$, as in Proposition~\ref{prop:linear-field-bracket}.

\emph{Conclusion.} So $\mathbf{Z}_A(\mathbf{Z}_B f) = \mathbf{Z}_{BA}f + T(A, B)$ and $\mathbf{Z}_B(\mathbf{Z}_A f) = \mathbf{Z}_{AB}f + T(A, B)$, and since $A \mapsto \mathbf{Z}_A$ is linear ($Ap$ is linear in $A$),
\[
[\mathbf{Z}_A, \mathbf{Z}_B]f = \mathbf{Z}_{BA}f - \mathbf{Z}_{AB}f = \mathbf{Z}_{BA - AB}f = -\,\mathbf{Z}_{[A,B]}f .
\]
As $f$ was arbitrary, $[\mathbf{Z}_A, \mathbf{Z}_B] = -\,\mathbf{Z}_{[A,B]}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[Left and Right Actions]\label{rem:left-right-actions}
\textit{(Not from the assignment.)} $\GL(n,\mathbb{R})$ acts on row vectors on the right, $p \cdot g = pg$, and $A \mapsto \mathbf{X}^A$, $\mathbf{X}^A_p = \frac{d}{dt}\big|_{t=0}\, p\,(I + tA)$, preserves brackets (Proposition~\ref{prop:linear-field-bracket}); the left action on column vectors gives an anti-homomorphism instead (Proposition~\ref{prop:column-action-fields-antihomomorphism}). This is the same sign as for right-invariant fields (Theorem~\ref{thm:right-bracket}, Example~\ref{ex:right-invariant-GL}): left multiplication $X \mapsto AX$ generates right-invariant fields, and right multiplication $X \mapsto XA$ left-invariant ones. It is the lecture's aside on writing $(x)f$ (the remark \emph{Left or Right: The Sign of the Bracket}): with maps written on the right, the right action is the one whose composites read in order, and it is the one that preserves brackets.
\end{rembox}

\chapter{Sard's Theorem}

\textit{Lecture 19. A change of subject, to a very useful theorem that is not about vector fields. Sard's theorem is a very important theorem whose proof, a complicated one, uses techniques that are never used again in the course; so it is not proved in class, and the proof is in Lee. The proofs below are filled in, following Lee, Chapter~6, and marked as such. The dynamical side of vector fields resumes after the midterm; meanwhile, self-contained topics.}

% ============================================================================
% SECTION: SETS OF MEASURE ZERO

\section{Sets of Measure Zero}\label{sec:measure-zero}

\roadmark{Stage: analysis}{Sets that are negligible, in Euclidean space and then on manifolds. Only the notion of a set of measure zero is needed, not measure theory.}

\begin{defbox}[Measure Zero in $\mathbb{R}^n$]\deflabel{def:measure-zero-Rn}
A set $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ has \textbf{measure zero} if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a countable cover $\{C_a\}$ of $S$ such that each $C_a$ is an open \textbf{rectangle}, a product of open intervals $C_a = (\alpha_1, \beta_1) \times \cdots \times (\alpha_n, \beta_n)$, and
\[
\sum_a \operatorname{Vol}(C_a) < \varepsilon, \qquad \operatorname{Vol}(C_a) = \prod_{i=1}^n (\beta_i - \alpha_i) \ \ \text{(Euclidean volume)}.
\]
\leeref{Ch.~6, \emph{Sets of Measure Zero}; Appendix C}
\end{defbox}

The rectangles could equally be taken closed (Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(3)). In three dimensions the rectangles are solid boxes. They should be thought of as very small and very thin; for example, a set of measure zero cannot contain an open set (Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(4)), but the condition is much stronger than that.

A curve $S$ in the plane, covered by rectangles. Refining the cover shrinks the total area: about $0.79$ with $8$ rectangles, about $0.34$ with $32$, and as small as desired with more --- so $S$ has measure zero.

\begin{lembox}[Basic Properties of Measure Zero]\thmlabel{lem:measure-zero-basic}
In $\mathbb{R}^n$:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item a subset of a set of measure zero has measure zero;
\item a countable union of sets of measure zero has measure zero;
\item in Definition~\ref{def:measure-zero-Rn}, the open rectangles may be replaced by closed rectangles, or by open or closed cubes;
\item a nonempty open set does not have measure zero (for $n \ge 1$).
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Proposition C.18, Exercise 6.1, Corollary C.25}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in. Item (4) is the observation after Definition~\ref{def:measure-zero-Rn} that a set of measure zero cannot contain an open set.)}

\emph{(1)} A cover of the larger set covers the smaller one.

\emph{(2)} Let $S = \bigcup_{k \ge 1} S_k$ with each $S_k$ of measure zero, and $\varepsilon > 0$. Cover $S_k$ by countably many open rectangles of total volume $< \varepsilon/2^k$. All of these together, a countable family, cover $S$ with total volume $< \sum_k \varepsilon/2^k = \varepsilon$.

\emph{(3)} \emph{Closed rectangles.} A closed rectangle $\prod[\alpha_i, \beta_i]$ lies in the open rectangle $\prod(\alpha_i - \eta, \beta_i + \eta)$, whose volume tends to $\prod(\beta_i - \alpha_i)$ as $\eta \to 0$; so given a cover by closed rectangles of total volume $< \varepsilon/2$, enlarging the $a$-th rectangle ($a = 1, 2, \ldots$) so that its volume grows by less than $\varepsilon/2^{a+1}$ gives an open cover of total volume $< \varepsilon$. Conversely an open rectangle lies in its closure, of the same volume.

\emph{Cubes.} Cubes are rectangles, so a cover by cubes is a cover by rectangles. Conversely, let $R = \prod(\alpha_i, \beta_i)$ with sides $\ell_i = \beta_i - \alpha_i > 0$, and $0 < \delta \le \min_i \ell_i$. The closed cubes of side $\delta$ with corners in $\prod_i (\alpha_i + \delta\mathbb{Z})$ that meet $\overline R$ cover $R$; in the $i$-th direction at most $\lfloor \ell_i / \delta \rfloor + 2 \le \ell_i/\delta + 2 \le 3\ell_i/\delta$ of the intervals $[\alpha_i + t\delta, \alpha_i + (t+1)\delta]$ meet $[\alpha_i, \beta_i]$, so there are at most $\prod_i 3\ell_i/\delta$ such cubes, of total volume at most $3^n \operatorname{Vol}(R)$. Doing this for each rectangle of a cover of total volume $< \varepsilon/3^n$ gives a countable cover by closed cubes of total volume $< \varepsilon$; enlarging them as before gives open cubes.

\emph{(4)} A nonempty open set contains a closed cube $Q$ of some side $s > 0$, so by (1) it suffices to show that $Q$ is not covered by open rectangles of total volume $< s^n = \operatorname{Vol}(Q)$. Suppose $Q \subseteq \bigcup_a C_a$. $Q$ is compact, so finitely many $C_1, \ldots, C_r$ cover it. Cut $\mathbb{R}^n$ by the hyperplanes $x^i = $ (an endpoint of a side of $Q$ or of some $C_b$): this divides $Q$ into finitely many closed grid cells $P$, and each $\overline{C_b} \cap Q$ into cells too, with $\operatorname{Vol}(Q) = \sum_{P \subseteq Q} \operatorname{Vol}(P)$ and $\operatorname{Vol}(C_b) \ge \sum_{P \subseteq \overline{C_b}} \operatorname{Vol}(P)$, since the volume of a rectangle is the sum of the volumes of the cells it is divided into (expand the product of the side lengths). An interior point of a cell $P \subseteq Q$ lies in some $C_b$; no cutting hyperplane passes through the interior of $P$, so $P$ lies on one side of each face of $C_b$, hence $P \subseteq \overline{C_b}$. So every cell of $Q$ is counted in some $\operatorname{Vol}(C_b)$, and $\operatorname{Vol}(Q) \le \sum_{b=1}^r \operatorname{Vol}(C_b) \le \sum_a \operatorname{Vol}(C_a)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lembox}[Smooth Maps Preserve Measure Zero]\thmlabel{lem:smooth-measure-zero}
Let $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be open, $F : U \to \mathbb{R}^n$ smooth, and $S \subseteq U$ a set of measure zero. Then $F(S)$ has measure zero.
\leeref{Proposition 6.5}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~19 gave only the idea of the proof; the details are filled in.)}

\emph{The idea.} Smooth maps are locally Lipschitz: for every compact $K \subseteq U$ there is a constant $C$ with
\[
|F(x) - F(y)| \le C\, |x - y| \qquad \text{for all } x, y \in K,
\]
and $C$ is essentially, though not exactly, the supremum of the partial derivatives over $K$. This implies continuity but is much stronger: $F$ maps cubes into cubes of comparable volume.

\emph{Reduction to a closed cube.} $U$ is the union of the countably many closed cubes with rational corners and rational side lengths that lie in $U$ (each $x \in U$ has an open ball in $U$ about it, and a small rational cube containing $x$ inside that ball). So $F(S) = \bigcup_Q F(S \cap Q)$ over countably many closed cubes $Q \subseteq U$, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(2) it suffices to show that $F(S \cap Q)$ has measure zero.

\emph{The Lipschitz estimate on $Q$, in the sup norm $\|x\|_\infty = \max_i |x^i|$.} The partial derivatives $\partial F^i/\partial x^j$ are continuous on the compact set $Q$, so $M = \max_{i,j} \sup_Q |\partial F^i/\partial x^j|$ is finite. $Q$ is convex, so for $x, y \in Q$ the segment between them lies in $Q$, and the mean value theorem applied to $t \mapsto F^i(x + t(y - x))$ gives a point $\xi$ on the segment with
\[
|F^i(y) - F^i(x)| = \Big| \sum_j \frac{\partial F^i}{\partial x^j}(\xi)\, (y^j - x^j) \Big| \le n M\, \|y - x\|_\infty ,
\]
so $\|F(y) - F(x)\|_\infty \le C \|y - x\|_\infty$ with $C = nM + 1 > 0$.

\emph{Cubes go to cubes.} A cube of side $t$ is a sup-norm ball. Let $\varepsilon > 0$, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(3) cover $S \cap Q$ by countably many open cubes $Q_a$, of sides $t_a$, with $\sum_a t_a^n < \varepsilon$. For each $a$ with $Q_a \cap Q \ne \varnothing$ pick $c_a \in Q_a \cap Q$. For $x \in Q_a \cap Q$, $\|x - c_a\|_\infty < t_a$, so $\|F(x) - F(c_a)\|_\infty < C t_a$: $F(Q_a \cap Q)$ lies in the open cube of side $2Ct_a$ centred at $F(c_a)$. These cubes cover $F(S \cap Q)$, with total volume $\sum_a (2C t_a)^n < (2C)^n \varepsilon$, as small as desired.
\end{proof}

\textbf{Transcription note (Lecture 19).} Page~50 of the handwritten notes states the image lemma for ``$F : U \to \mathbb{R}^n$, $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ open''. As written, with $m$ unrestricted, it is false for $m > n$: the projection $\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$, $(x, y) \mapsto x$, maps the $x$-axis, of measure zero in $\mathbb{R}^2$, onto $\mathbb{R}$. Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-measure-zero} takes $m = n$, as Lee does and as the application to transition maps needs. (For $m < n$ the conclusion holds for every $S$, by Corollary~\ref{cor:sard-low-dim} in \ref{sec:sard}.)

\begin{exbox}[The Cantor Function]\exlabel{ex:cantor-function-measure-zero}
In Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-measure-zero}, $F(S)$ may not have measure zero if $F$ is only continuous; the Cantor function is the standard counterexample. \textit{(Filled in.)} The Cantor function $c : [0,1] \to [0,1]$ is continuous, nondecreasing, and maps the Cantor set $C$, which has measure zero, onto all of $[0,1]$, which does not.

\emph{Setup.} $C = \bigcap_k C_k$, where $C_0 = [0,1]$ and $C_{k+1}$ is obtained from $C_k$ by removing the open middle third of each of its intervals; so $C_k$ is a union of $2^k$ closed intervals of length $3^{-k}$. The Cantor function $c$ is continuous and nondecreasing, with $c(0) = 0$ and $c(1) = 1$, and constant on each removed open interval (its standard construction is taken as known).

\emph{$C$ has measure zero.} For each $k$, $C \subseteq C_k$ is covered by $2^k$ closed intervals of total length $(2/3)^k$, which tends to $0$; closed intervals are allowed by Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(3).

\emph{$c(C) = [0,1]$.} Let $y \in [0,1]$. By the intermediate value theorem there is $x \in [0,1]$ with $c(x) = y$. If $x \in C$ we are done. Otherwise $x$ lies in one of the removed open intervals $(a, b)$; its endpoints $a, b$ are never removed, so $a \in C$, and $c$ is constant on $(a, b)$, hence by continuity on $[a, b]$. So $c(a) = c(x) = y$ with $a \in C$.

\emph{$[0,1]$ does not have measure zero.} It contains the nonempty open set $(0,1)$, which does not have measure zero (Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(4)), and a subset of a set of measure zero has measure zero (Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(1)).

The smoothness used in Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-measure-zero} is exactly the Lipschitz estimate, which $c$ lacks: if $|c(x) - c(y)| \le L\,|x - y|$ on $[0,1]$, the step \emph{Cubes go to cubes} of that proof, with $n = 1$, would show that $c(C)$ has measure zero, contradicting what was just shown.
\end{exbox}

\textit{(Not from lecture.)} The Cantor function $c$: constant on each removed middle third, it climbs only on the Cantor set. So $c$ maps a set of measure zero (orange; shown at the second stage of the construction) onto the whole interval $[0,1]$ (teal). Its slopes are unbounded near the Cantor set, which is the Lipschitz estimate of Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-measure-zero} failing.

Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-measure-zero} is what makes it possible to define sets of measure zero on a manifold.

\begin{defbox}[Measure Zero in a Manifold]\deflabel{def:measure-zero-manifold}
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold of dimension $m$ and $S \subseteq M$ any subset, not necessarily a submanifold. $S$ has \textbf{measure zero} if $S$ can be covered by coordinate charts $\{(U_\alpha, \varphi_\alpha)\}$, $S \subseteq \bigcup_\alpha U_\alpha$, such that for every $\alpha$ the set $\varphi_\alpha(S \cap U_\alpha) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ has measure zero (Definition~\ref{def:measure-zero-Rn}).
\leeref{Ch.~6, \emph{Sets of Measure Zero}; Lemma 6.6}
\end{defbox}

Any number of charts is allowed in Definition~\ref{def:measure-zero-manifold}, but countably many always suffice, because $M$ is second countable --- the next lemma.

\begin{lembox}[Countable Subcovers]\thmlabel{lem:countable-subcover}
Let $X$ be a second-countable space (Definition~\ref{def:second-countable}), $A \subseteq X$, and $\{U_\alpha\}$ a family of open sets covering $A$. Then countably many of the $U_\alpha$ cover $A$.
\leeref{Proposition A.16}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Filled in.)} Let $\mathcal{B}$ be a countable basis. For each $B \in \mathcal{B}$ that is contained in some $U_\alpha$, choose one such $U_{\alpha(B)}$; there are countably many choices. If $x \in A$, then $x \in U_\alpha$ for some $\alpha$, and since $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis there is $B \in \mathcal{B}$ with $x \in B \subseteq U_\alpha$; so $B$ was given a set $U_{\alpha(B)} \supseteq B \ni x$. So the chosen sets cover $A$.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[Measure Zero Is Seen in Every Chart]\thmlabel{prop:measure-zero-every-chart}
If $S \subseteq M$ has measure zero, then $\varphi(S \cap U)$ has measure zero in $\mathbb{R}^m$ for \emph{every} chart $(U, \varphi)$ of $M$. Consequently subsets and countable unions of sets of measure zero in $M$ have measure zero in $M$.
\leeref{Lemma 6.6, Exercise 6.7}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Stated in Lecture~19 as an observation; filled in.)} Let $\{(U_\alpha, \varphi_\alpha)\}$ be as in Definition~\ref{def:measure-zero-manifold}, and $(U, \varphi)$ any chart. By Lemma~\ref{lem:countable-subcover} (manifolds are second countable), countably many $U_\alpha$ cover $S \cap U$, and
\[
\varphi(S \cap U \cap U_\alpha) = \big(\varphi \circ \varphi_\alpha^{-1}\big)\big(\varphi_\alpha(S \cap U \cap U_\alpha)\big),
\]
where the transition map $\varphi \circ \varphi_\alpha^{-1} : \varphi_\alpha(U \cap U_\alpha) \to \varphi(U \cap U_\alpha)$ is a smooth map between open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^m$ (Definition~\ref{def:compatible}), and $\varphi_\alpha(S \cap U \cap U_\alpha) \subseteq \varphi_\alpha(S \cap U_\alpha)$ has measure zero (Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(1)). By Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-measure-zero}, each $\varphi(S \cap U \cap U_\alpha)$ has measure zero, and $\varphi(S \cap U)$ is their countable union (Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(2)).

For the consequences: if $T \subseteq S$, the charts covering $S$ cover $T$, and $\varphi_\alpha(T \cap U_\alpha) \subseteq \varphi_\alpha(S \cap U_\alpha)$. If $S = \bigcup_k S_k$ with each $S_k$ of measure zero, cover $S$ by all charts of $M$: for each chart, $\varphi(S \cap U) = \bigcup_k \varphi(S_k \cap U)$ is a countable union of sets of measure zero, by the first part.
\end{proof}

\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=1.2em, row sep=3.2em]
 & S \cap U \cap U_\alpha \arrow[dl, "\varphi_\alpha"'] \arrow[dr, "\varphi"] & \\
\varphi_\alpha(S \cap U \cap U_\alpha) \arrow[rr, "\varphi \circ \varphi_\alpha^{-1}"'] & & \varphi(S \cap U \cap U_\alpha)
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

The same piece of $S$ seen in two charts. The transition map carries one picture to the other, and it is smooth, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-measure-zero} measure zero in one picture means measure zero in the other.

\begin{lembox}[A Fubini Lemma for Compact Sets]\thmlabel{lem:fubini-measure-zero}
Let $n \ge 2$ and $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n = \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ compact, such that for every $c \in \mathbb{R}$ the slice $A_c = \{ x \in \mathbb{R}^{n-1} : (c, x) \in A \}$ has measure zero in $\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$. Then $A$ has measure zero in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
\leeref{Lemma 6.2}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in, as a tool for Sard's theorem.)} Choose $a < b$ with $A \subseteq [a, b] \times \mathbb{R}^{n-1}$, and let $\delta > 0$.

\emph{Each slice, thickened.} Fix $c \in [a, b]$. $A_c$ is compact (its image $\{c\} \times A_c = A \cap (\{c\} \times \mathbb{R}^{n-1})$ is compact) and has measure zero, so it is covered by countably many open rectangles of total volume $< \delta$, hence by finitely many of them; let $U_c \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ be their union. There is an open interval $J_c \ni c$, which we may take inside $(a - 1, b + 1)$, with $A \cap (J_c \times \mathbb{R}^{n-1}) \subseteq J_c \times U_c$. Otherwise there are points $(c_k, x_k) \in A$ with $c_k \to c$ and $x_k \notin U_c$; by compactness a subsequence converges to some $(c, x) \in A$, with $x \notin U_c$ because the complement of $U_c$ is closed; but $x \in A_c \subseteq U_c$.

\emph{Finitely many strips.} The $J_c$ cover $[a, b]$; take a finite subcover, and from it a minimal one, $J_1, \ldots, J_r$ (for $c_1, \ldots, c_r$). No point lies in three of them: if $x$ lay in three, the one with the smallest left endpoint and the one with the largest right endpoint would both contain $x$, so their union, an interval, would contain the third, contradicting minimality. So $\sum_k \operatorname{length}(J_k) \le 2\,\operatorname{length}\big(\bigcup_k J_k\big) \le 2(b - a + 2)$.

\emph{The cover.} $A \subseteq \bigcup_k J_k \times U_{c_k}$, and $J_k \times U_{c_k}$ is a union of finitely many open rectangles, (interval) $\times$ (rectangle of $U_{c_k}$), of total volume $< \operatorname{length}(J_k)\,\delta$. In total, finitely many open rectangles of total volume $< 2(b - a + 2)\,\delta$, which is as small as desired.
\end{proof}

\textit{(Not from lecture.)} The proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:fubini-measure-zero} for a compact $A$ in the plane ($n = 2$). The slice of $A$ at $c$ (teal) has measure zero, so it is covered by finitely many small intervals, $U_c$. By compactness the same intervals still cover the slices at all $c'$ near $c$, in an interval $J_c$, so $A \cap (J_c \times \mathbb{R})$ lies in the thin boxes $J_c \times U_c$ (orange). Finitely many $J_c$ cover the first coordinate's range, overlapping at most twice, and the total area is at most $2 \times$ (length) $\times$ (the slices' cover size).

\begin{rembox}[Measure Zero and Lebesgue Measure]\label{rem:measure-zero-lebesgue}
\textit{(Not from lecture.)} The course uses only the notion of a set of measure zero, not measure theory. For readers who know Lebesgue measure the dictionary is short.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ has measure zero in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:measure-zero-Rn} exactly when its Lebesgue outer measure is $m^*(S) = 0$ (outer measure is defined with countable covers by rectangles, open or closed, as in Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(3)); such sets are Lebesgue measurable.
\item Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(1)--(2) are monotonicity and countable subadditivity of $m^*$; item (4) is $m^*(\text{closed rectangle}) = $ its volume.
\item Lemma~\ref{lem:fubini-measure-zero} is the cross-section theorem (a consequence of Tonelli's theorem) for a compact, hence measurable, set: $m(A) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} m(A_c)\, dc = 0$. The proof above avoids measurability and integration and uses only compactness.
\end{enumerate}
\end{rembox}

% SECTION: SARD'S THEOREM

\section{Sard's Theorem}\label{sec:sard}

\roadmark{Stage: analysis}{Almost every value of a smooth map is regular.}

\begin{rembox}[Regular and Singular Values (Recall)]\label{rem:singular-values}
For $F : M \to N$ smooth, $q \in N$ is a regular value if $dF_p$ is onto for every $p \in F^{-1}(q)$ (Definition~\ref{def:manifold-regular}); in particular every $q \notin F(M)$ is a regular value (Definition~\ref{def:regular-critical-value}(2)). A value that is not regular is a \emph{singular value} --- the term used in Lecture~19; ``critical value'' in Definition~\ref{def:regular-critical-value} and in Lee. Likewise $p \in M$ is a critical (singular) point if $dF_p$ is not onto (Definition~\ref{def:regular-critical}).
\end{rembox}

\begin{lembox}[Sard's Theorem Reduces to Euclidean Space]\thmlabel{lem:sard-reduction}
Let $m, n \ge 0$. Suppose that for every open $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ and every smooth $G : U \to \mathbb{R}^n$, the set of singular values of $G$ has measure zero in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then for every smooth map $F : M \to N$ with $\dim M = m$ and $\dim N = n$, the set of singular values of $F$ has measure zero in $N$.
\leeref{proof of Theorem 6.10}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; the first step of Lee's proof of Theorem~6.10.)} Let $C \subseteq M$ be the set of critical points of $F$, so that its set of singular values is $S = F(C)$. If $n = 0$, every $dF_p$ is onto the zero space $T_{F(p)}N$, so $S = \varnothing$. Let $n \ge 1$. Each $p \in M$ has a chart $(U_p, \varphi_p)$ with $F(U_p)$ inside the domain of a chart $(V_p, \psi_p)$ of $N$ (shrink a chart at $p$ into $F^{-1}(V_p)$, by continuity). By Lemma~\ref{lem:countable-subcover} countably many $U_i = U_{p_i}$ cover $M$, so $S = \bigcup_i F(C \cap U_i)$. In the charts, $\hat F_i = \psi_i \circ F \circ \varphi_i^{-1} : \varphi_i(U_i) \to \mathbb{R}^n$, and since charts are diffeomorphisms (Proposition~\ref{prop:chart-diffeo}), $p$ is a critical point of $F$ exactly when $\varphi_i(p)$ is one of $\hat F_i$; so $\psi_i\big(F(C \cap U_i)\big)$ is the set of singular values of $\hat F_i$. By hypothesis, applied to $\hat F_i$ on the open set $\varphi_i(U_i) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$, that set has measure zero in $\mathbb{R}^n$. So $F(C \cap U_i)$, covered by the single chart $(V_i, \psi_i)$, has measure zero in $N$, and so does the countable union $S$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:measure-zero-every-chart}).
\end{proof}

\begin{lembox}[Where All Derivatives up to Order $k$ Vanish]\thmlabel{lem:sard-flat-points}
Let $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ be open, $F : U \to \mathbb{R}^n$ smooth with $n \ge 1$, and $k \ge 1$ an integer with $n(k + 1) > m$. Let $Z \subseteq U$ be a set at each point of which all partial derivatives of $F$ of orders $1, \ldots, k$ vanish. Then $F(Z)$ has measure zero in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
\leeref{proof of Theorem 6.10}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; the last step of Lee's proof of Theorem~6.10.)} $U$ is the union of countably many closed cubes $E \subseteq U$ (the reduction to a closed cube in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-measure-zero}), so by Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(2) it suffices to show that $F(Z \cap E)$ has measure zero for a closed cube $E \subseteq U$, of side $R$. Let $A > 0$ bound the absolute values of all partial derivatives of order $k + 1$ of $F$ on $E$ (continuous functions on a compact set; taking $A > 0$ keeps the cubes below nondegenerate). If $x' \in Z \cap E$ and $x \in E$, Taylor's theorem along the segment from $x'$ to $x$, which lies in the convex set $E$, applied to each component $F^i$, has no terms of orders $1, \ldots, k$, so
\[
|F^i(x) - F^i(x')| \le \sum_{|\beta| = k + 1} \frac{A}{\beta!}\, |(x - x')^\beta| \le A'\, \|x - x'\|_\infty^{k + 1},
\]
with $A'$ depending only on $A$, $k$ and $m$. Divide $E$ into $K^m$ closed cubes $E_1, \ldots, E_{K^m}$ of side $R/K$. If $E_j$ contains a point $x'_j \in Z$, then $F(E_j)$ lies in the closed cube of side $2A'(R/K)^{k + 1}$ centred at $F(x'_j)$. So $F(Z \cap E)$ lies in at most $K^m$ cubes of total volume
\[
K^m \big(2A'\big)^n \Big(\frac{R}{K}\Big)^{n(k + 1)} = \big(2A'\big)^n R^{\,n(k + 1)}\, K^{\,m - n(k + 1)} ,
\]
which tends to $0$ as $K \to \infty$ because $n(k + 1) > m$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(3), $F(Z \cap E)$ has measure zero.
\end{proof}

\begin{thmbox}[Sard's Theorem]\thmlabel{thm:sard}
Let $F : M \to N$ be a smooth map, and
\[
S = \{\, q \in N : q \text{ is not a regular value of } F \,\},
\]
the set of singular values. Then $S$ has measure zero in $N$ (Definition~\ref{def:measure-zero-manifold}).
\leeref{Theorem 6.10}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not given in lecture, the proof being long; filled in, following Lee's proof of Theorem~6.10.)} By Lemma~\ref{lem:sard-reduction}, it suffices to prove, for every $m \ge 0$, the Euclidean statement

\textbf{$(\mathrm{S}_m)$:} for every open $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$, every $n \ge 0$ and every smooth $F : U \to \mathbb{R}^n$, the set $F(C)$ has measure zero in $\mathbb{R}^n$, where $C = \{ x \in U : \operatorname{rank} DF(x) < n \}$.

Here $C$ is the set of critical points of $F$, so $F(C)$ is its set of singular values. We prove $(\mathrm{S}_m)$ by induction on $m$.

\emph{$m = 0$.} $\mathbb{R}^0$ is a single point, so $F(C)$ has at most one point. If $n = 0$, then $C = \varnothing$, as no rank is $< 0$. If $n \ge 1$, a point lies in cubes of arbitrarily small volume, so it has measure zero. (Through Lemma~\ref{lem:sard-reduction} this covers manifolds of dimension $0$; directly, such an $M$ is countable, being second countable and discrete, so $F(M)$ is countable and has measure zero by Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(2).)

\emph{$m \ge 1$.} Assume $(\mathrm{S}_{m-1})$, let $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ be open and $F : U \to \mathbb{R}^n$ smooth. If $n = 0$, then $C = \varnothing$; so let $n \ge 1$. Here $DF(x)$ is the $n \times m$ Jacobian
\[
DF(x) = \begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^1}(x) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^m}(x) \\
\vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
\dfrac{\partial F^n}{\partial x^1}(x) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^n}{\partial x^m}(x)
\end{pmatrix} .
\]

\emph{A filtration of $C$.} For $k \ge 1$ let $C_k \subseteq C$ be the set of $x \in C$ at which all partial derivatives of $F$ of orders $1, \ldots, k$ vanish, so $C \supseteq C_1 \supseteq C_2 \supseteq \cdots$. These sets are closed in $U$: $C$ is where all $n \times n$ minors of $DF$ vanish, and $C_k$ is cut out of $C$ by finitely many more continuous functions. Fix an integer $k_0 \ge 1$ with $k_0 > m/n - 1$, that is, $n(k_0 + 1) > m$ (for instance $k_0 = \max(1, \lfloor m/n \rfloor)$; the condition $k_0 \ge 1$ matters when $m < n$). Then
\[
C = (C \setminus C_1) \cup \bigcup_{k=1}^{k_0 - 1} (C_k \setminus C_{k+1}) \cup C_{k_0},
\]
and it suffices to show that the image of each piece has measure zero.

\emph{Step 1: $F(C \setminus C_1)$ has measure zero.} If $n = 1$ then $C \setminus C_1 = \varnothing$: a nonzero first partial at $x$ makes the $1 \times m$ matrix $DF(x)$ have rank $1$. Let $n \ge 2$. Replacing $U$ by the open set $U \setminus C_1$, we may assume $C_1 = \varnothing$. Let $a \in C$. Some first partial of $F$ is nonzero at $a$; renumbering coordinates, $\partial F^1/\partial x^1(a) \neq 0$. Then $h(x) = (F^1(x), x^2, \ldots, x^m)$ has invertible derivative at $a$, so by the inverse function theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:inverse-function}) it is a diffeomorphism from an open $W_a \ni a$ onto an open set; choose a closed ball $K_a \ni a$ in $W_a$ with $a$ in its interior. \textit{(Computed; not from lecture.)} The derivative of $h$ is upper triangular,
\[
Dh(a) = \begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^1}(a) & \dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^2}(a) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^m}(a) \\
0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
0 & 0 & \cdots & 1
\end{pmatrix},
\]
so $\det Dh(a) = \partial F^1/\partial x^1(a) \neq 0$. In the coordinates $(u, v) = h(x)$, $u \in \mathbb{R}$, $v \in \mathbb{R}^{m-1}$, the map $G = F \circ h^{-1}$ has the form $G(u, v) = (u, G^2(u,v), \ldots, G^n(u, v))$, so
\[
DG(u, v) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ * & \big(\partial G^i/\partial v^j\big) \end{pmatrix},
\]
and $(u, v)$ is a critical point of $G$ exactly when the $(n-1) \times (m-1)$ block has rank $< n - 1$. For $c \in \mathbb{R}$ let $G_c(v) = (G^2(c, v), \ldots, G^n(c, v))$, defined on the open set $\{ v : (c, v) \in h(W_a) \} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{m-1}$; then $(c, v)$ is a critical point of $G$ exactly when $v$ is a critical point of $G_c$. The set $F(C \cap K_a) = G(h(C \cap K_a))$ is compact ($C \cap K_a$ is closed in the compact $K_a$), and its slice at $u = c$ consists of points $(c, G_c(v))$ with $v$ a critical point of $G_c$: it lies in $\{c\} \times$ (the singular values of $G_c$), which has measure zero in $\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ by $(\mathrm{S}_{m-1})$, $G_c$ having an $(m-1)$-dimensional domain. By Lemma~\ref{lem:fubini-measure-zero}, $F(C \cap K_a)$ has measure zero. The interiors of the $K_a$ cover $C$, so countably many do (Lemma~\ref{lem:countable-subcover}), and $F(C \setminus C_1)$ is a countable union of sets of measure zero.

\emph{Step 2: $F(C_k \setminus C_{k+1})$ has measure zero, $k \ge 1$.} Replacing $U$ by $U \setminus C_{k+1}$, we may assume that at each $a \in C_k$ some partial derivative of order $k + 1$ of $F$ is nonzero. So there is a $k$-th order partial derivative $y = \partial^\alpha F^i$, $|\alpha| = k$, with $dy_a \neq 0$. Choose an open $V_a \ni a$ on which $dy \neq 0$. Then $0$ is a regular value of $y|_{V_a}$, and $Y = \{ x \in V_a : y(x) = 0 \}$ is a regular submanifold of $V_a$ of dimension $m - 1$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:rvt-manifolds}). All $k$-th order partials of $F$ vanish on $C_k$, so $C_k \cap V_a \subseteq Y$. At $p \in C_k \cap V_a$, all first partials vanish ($k \ge 1$), so $dF_p = 0$, and $d(F|_Y)_p = dF_p \circ d\iota_p = 0$ is not onto $\mathbb{R}^n$, $n \ge 1$ (chain rule, $\iota : Y \to U$ the inclusion, smooth by Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}). So $F(C_k \cap V_a)$ lies in the set of singular values of $F|_Y : Y \to \mathbb{R}^n$, which has measure zero by $(\mathrm{S}_{m-1})$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:sard-reduction}, applied to the $(m-1)$-dimensional manifold $Y$ and $N = \mathbb{R}^n$. Countably many $V_a$ cover $C_k$, so $F(C_k \setminus C_{k+1})$ has measure zero.

\emph{Step 3: $F(C_{k_0})$ has measure zero.} At each point of $C_{k_0}$ all partial derivatives of $F$ of orders $1, \ldots, k_0$ vanish, and $n(k_0 + 1) > m$. So Lemma~\ref{lem:sard-flat-points}, with $k = k_0$ and $Z = C_{k_0}$, shows that $F(C_{k_0})$ has measure zero.

Steps 1--3 cover all of $C$, which completes the induction.
\end{proof}

So almost every value of a smooth map is regular. The theorem has many applications, starting with Corollary~\ref{cor:sard-low-dim} and parametric transversality (\ref{sec:parametric-transversality}).

The simplest picture: $f(x) = x^3 - 3x$ on $M = N = \mathbb{R}$. The critical points are $x = \pm 1$, where $f' = 0$, so the singular values are just $f(\pm 1) = \mp 2$, two points, a set of measure zero. Every other $c$ is a regular value: at each of its preimages the slope is nonzero.

\begin{corbox}[Maps from Lower Dimension]\thmlabel{cor:sard-low-dim}
If $F : M \to N$ is smooth and $\dim M < \dim N$, then the regular values of $F$ are exactly the points of $N \setminus F(M)$, and $F(M)$ has measure zero in $N$.
\leeref{Corollary 6.11}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~19.)} By linear algebra, no point in the image can be a regular value, for dimension reasons: for $p \in M$, the image of $dF_p : T_pM \to T_{F(p)}N$ has dimension at most $\dim M < \dim N$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-dimension}), so $dF_p$ is never onto. So the regular values are exactly the points with empty preimage, where the condition is vacuous, and $F(M)$ is the set of singular values, of measure zero by Sard's theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:sard}).
\end{proof}

For instance, a smooth curve $\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^2$ never fills an open set of the plane: its image has measure zero, and so does every subset of it (Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(1)), while an open set does not (Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(4)) --- in contrast with continuous space-filling curves.

\section{Parametric Transversality}\label{sec:parametric-transversality}

\roadmark{Stage: analysis}{Transversality of a whole family passes, by Sard's theorem, to almost every member.}

\textit{Lecture 20. The transversality theorem of René Thom, or parametric transversality; together with Sard's theorem it has important consequences.}

\begin{defbox}[Smooth Family of Maps]\deflabel{def:smooth-family}
Let $S$, $M$, $N$ be smooth manifolds. A \textbf{smooth family} of maps $M \to N$, parametrized by $S$, is a collection $\{F_s\}_{s \in S}$ of maps $F_s : M \to N$ such that $F : S \times M \to N$, $F(s, p) = F_s(p)$, is smooth. $S$ is the \textbf{parameter space}.
\leeref{Ch.~6, \emph{The Transversality Homotopy Theorem}}
\end{defbox}

Smoothness of the family means smoothness of the single map $F$, jointly in $s$ and $p$. Each $F_s = F \circ \iota_s$, with $\iota_s : M \to S \times M$, $p \mapsto (s, p)$, the slice inclusion (Definition~\ref{def:slice-inclusions}), so each $F_s$ is smooth.

\begin{thmbox}[Parametric Transversality]\thmlabel{thm:parametric-transversality}
Let $F : S \times M \to N$ be smooth, $Z \subseteq N$ a regular submanifold, and suppose $F \pitchfork Z$ (Definition~\ref{def:transverse-submanifold}). Then $W = F^{-1}(Z)$ is a regular submanifold of $S \times M$, and with $\pi : W \to S$ the restriction of the projection $(s, p) \mapsto s$: for $s \in S$,
\[
s \text{ is a regular value of } \pi \iff F_s : M \to N \text{ is transverse to } Z .
\]
\leeref{Theorem 6.35 (proof)}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~20 proved the direction that matters for applications, $(\Rightarrow)$, and left the converse as an exercise; the converse is filled in.)}

\emph{Preliminaries.} $W$ is a regular submanifold of $S \times M$ and, for $(s, p) \in W$ with $q = F(s, p)$,
\[
T_{(s,p)}W = \big(dF_{(s,p)}\big)^{-1}\big(T_qZ\big) \tag{1}
\]
(Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-submanifold-preimage}): the preimage of the tangent space of $Z$ under the differential. $\pi$ is smooth, as the restriction of the smooth projection to a regular submanifold. Write tangent vectors to $S \times M$ as pairs $(\sigma, u) \in T_sS \oplus T_pM$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-product}); then $d\pi(\sigma, u) = \sigma$, and
\[
dF_{(s,p)}(0, u) = d(F_s)_p(u), \tag{2}
\]
because $F_s = F \circ \iota_s$ and $d(\iota_s)_p(u) = (0, u)$: it is a partial derivative, computed with the first entry frozen at $s$ (Definition~\ref{def:partial-derivative-factor}).

\emph{$(\Rightarrow)$} Let $s$ be a regular value of $\pi$, and $p \in M$ with $q = F_s(p) = F(s,p) \in Z$. We must show $\operatorname{Im} d(F_s)_p + T_qZ = T_qN$; the inclusion $\subseteq$ is clear. Let $w \in T_qN$. Since $F \pitchfork Z$, there are $(\sigma, u) \in T_{(s,p)}(S \times M)$ and $v \in T_qZ$ with
\[
w = dF_{(s,p)}(\sigma, u) + v . \tag{$*$}
\]
Since $s$ is a regular value of $\pi$, $\sigma$ is in the image of $d\pi_{(s,p)}$: there is a tangent vector to $W$ at $(s, p)$ projecting to $\sigma$, and since $d\pi$ only reads the first component, it has the form $(\sigma, \tau)$ for some $\tau \in T_pM$. Write $(\sigma, u) = (\sigma, \tau) + (0, u - \tau)$ and substitute into $(*)$:
\[
w = dF_{(s,p)}(\sigma, \tau) + dF_{(s,p)}(0, u - \tau) + v = d(F_s)_p(u - \tau) + \big(dF_{(s,p)}(\sigma, \tau) + v\big),
\]
by (2). By (1), $dF_{(s,p)}(\sigma, \tau) \in T_qZ$, so the bracket is tangent to $Z$, and $w \in \operatorname{Im} d(F_s)_p + T_qZ$. So $F_s$ intersects $Z$ transversely.

\emph{$(\Leftarrow)$} \textit{(Filled in.)} Suppose $F_s \pitchfork Z$, and let $(s, p) \in \pi^{-1}(s)$, so $q = F_s(p) \in Z$; we show $d\pi_{(s,p)}$ is onto $T_sS$. Let $\sigma \in T_sS$. By transversality of $F_s$, $dF_{(s,p)}(\sigma, 0) = d(F_s)_p(u) + v$ for some $u \in T_pM$, $v \in T_qZ$. By (2), $dF_{(s,p)}(\sigma, -u) = dF_{(s,p)}(\sigma, 0) - d(F_s)_p(u) = v \in T_qZ$, so $(\sigma, -u) \in T_{(s,p)}W$ by (1), and $d\pi(\sigma, -u) = \sigma$.
\end{proof}

\textit{(Not from lecture; figure added.)} An explicit instance of the cartoon. Take $S = M = \mathbb{R}$, $N = \mathbb{R}^2$, $Z = \{ y = x^2 \}$ and $F(s, x) = (x, s)$, so $F_s$ parametrizes the horizontal line at height $s$. Then $F$ is a diffeomorphism, so $F \pitchfork Z$, and $W = F^{-1}(Z) = \{ (s, x) : s = x^2 \}$. Parametrizing $W$ by $x \mapsto (x^2, x)$, the projection is $\pi(x^2, x) = x^2$, with derivative $2x$: the only critical point is $x = 0$, and the only critical value is $s = 0$. For $s > 0$, $F_s$ crosses $Z$ transversally at $x = \pm\sqrt{s}$; for $s < 0$, $F_s^{-1}(Z) = \varnothing$; at $s = 0$, $\operatorname{Im} d(F_0)_0 = \operatorname{span}\{(1, 0)\} = T_{(0,0)}Z$, so $F_0$ is tangent to $Z$, not transverse --- exactly as Theorem~\ref{thm:parametric-transversality} predicts.

\begin{corbox}[Almost Every Member Is Transverse]\thmlabel{cor:parametric-sard}
If $F : S \times M \to N$ is smooth and $F \pitchfork Z$, then $F_s \pitchfork Z$ for almost every $s \in S$: the set of $s$ with $F_s$ not transverse to $Z$ has measure zero in $S$.
\leeref{Theorem 6.35}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~20.)} By Sard's theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:sard}) applied to $\pi : W \to S$, the singular values of $\pi$ form a set of measure zero; for every other $s$, $F_s \pitchfork Z$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:parametric-transversality}.
\end{proof}

The corollary passes from transversality of the family to transversality of the individual members of the family.

\begin{exbox}[Translates Are Generically Transverse]\exlabel{ex:translates-transverse}
Let $Y, Z \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ be regular submanifolds. For almost every $a \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the translate $a + Y$ intersects $Z$ transversally.
\end{exbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~20, the first classical geometric application; details filled in.)} The parameter space is $\mathbb{R}^d$ itself: $F : \mathbb{R}^d \times Y \to \mathbb{R}^d$, $F(a, p) = a + p$, using the vector space structure to translate. Then $F_a(Y) = a + Y$. \emph{$F$ is a submersion}: fixing $p$ and varying $a$, $dF_{(a,p)}(\sigma, 0) = \sigma$ for every $\sigma \in T_a\mathbb{R}^d = \mathbb{R}^d$. So $F \pitchfork Z$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:transverse-special-cases}(3)), and $F^{-1}(Z) = \{ (a, p) : a + p \in Z \}$. By Corollary~\ref{cor:parametric-sard}, $F_a \pitchfork Z$ for almost every $a$. Finally $F_a : Y \to \mathbb{R}^d$ is the inclusion of $a + Y$ composed with the diffeomorphism $Y \to a + Y$, $p \mapsto a + p$, and $a + Y$ is a regular submanifold, a translate of one, so $F_a \pitchfork Z$ says $(a + Y) \pitchfork Z$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:transverse-submanifolds-maps}).
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[Transverse Submanifolds of Small Total Dimension Are Disjoint]\thmlabel{cor:transverse-small-dimension-disjoint}
Let $Y, Z \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ be regular submanifolds with $\dim Y + \dim Z < d$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $Y \pitchfork Z$, then $Y \cap Z = \varnothing$: a transverse intersection must be empty.
\item For almost every $a \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the translate $a + Y$ is disjoint from $Z$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(The reason is the one given with the statement in the notes, ``since $T_qY + T_qZ$ has dimension at most $\dim Y + \dim Z$''; details filled in.)}

\emph{(1)} We show that $Y \cap Z$ has no point. Suppose $q \in Y \cap Z$. Since $Y \pitchfork Z$, $T_qY + T_qZ = T_q\mathbb{R}^d$ (Definition~\ref{def:transverse-submanifolds}), a vector space of dimension $d$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-dimension}). On the other hand $T_qY$ has a basis of $\dim Y$ vectors and $T_qZ$ a basis of $\dim Z$ vectors (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-dimension}), and the two bases together span $T_qY + T_qZ$; so $T_qY + T_qZ$ has dimension at most $\dim Y + \dim Z < d$. This is a contradiction, so $Y \cap Z = \varnothing$.

\emph{(2)} By Example~\ref{ex:translates-transverse}, $(a + Y) \pitchfork Z$ for almost every $a \in \mathbb{R}^d$. For each $a$, $a + Y$ is a regular submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^d$ diffeomorphic to $Y$ by $p \mapsto a + p$ (as in the proof of Example~\ref{ex:translates-transverse}), so $\dim(a + Y) + \dim Z = \dim Y + \dim Z < d$. By (1), applied to $a + Y$ and $Z$, $(a + Y) \cap Z = \varnothing$ for every $a$ with $(a + Y) \pitchfork Z$, that is, for almost every $a$.
\end{proof}

\begin{exbox}[Two Curves in Space]\exlabel{ex:two-curves-in-space}
Two curves in $\mathbb{R}^3$ ($1 + 1 < 3$): translating one by a generic vector makes it disjoint from the other (Corollary~\ref{cor:transverse-small-dimension-disjoint}(2)).
\end{exbox}

For two curves in the plane that are tangent, a generic translate either separates them or makes them cross transversally. This is the idea of \emph{general position}: a configuration is not in general position if moving one of the objects a little changes the geometry radically. Objects in general position are transverse, which may mean that they do not intersect; an empty intersection is still a meaningful, and often powerful, statement.
