\fill ({4.3-sqrt(0.75/0.9)},{0.45*0.75/0.9}) circle (1.5pt); \fill ({4.3+sqrt(0.75/0.9)},{0.45*0.75/0.9}) circle (1.5pt);
\draw[->, gray!70!black] (4.3,-1.3) -- node[right] {$a$} (4.3,-0.55);
\draw[->, gray!70!black] (8.6,-0.05) -- node[right] {$a'$} (8.6,-0.7);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

The lecture's picture: $Z$ (blue) and $Y$ (red) tangent at a point, not transverse; a translate $a + Y$ meeting $Z$ in two transverse crossings; another translate $a' + Y$ disjoint from $Z$. Only translates making them tangent again are excluded, and those form a set of measure zero.

A further application, Assignment~6, Problem~5 (\ref{sub:height-functions}): for a submanifold of Euclidean space, almost all linear functions restricted to the submanifold are Morse (Definition~\ref{def:morse-function}), so Morse functions are plentiful.

\textbf{Transcription note (Lecture 20).} Page~54 of the handwritten notes writes ``$\pi$ onto'' under $F^{-1}(Z) \to \mathbb{R}^d$. This does not hold in general: $(a, p) \in F^{-1}(Z)$ exactly when $a + p \in Z$, so the image of $\pi$ is $\{ z - p : z \in Z,\ p \in Y \}$, the set of $a$ for which $a + Y$ meets $Z$ (a single point when $Y$ and $Z$ are points). Surjectivity plays no role in the argument.

\subsection{Height Functions Are Almost Always Morse}\label{sub:height-functions}

\textit{Assignment~6, Problem~5: the homework announced in Lecture~20. Not from lecture; the submitted solution, with the bundle facts it uses filled in (\ref{sub:geo-tangent-bundle}) and its main implication completed to an equivalence.}

\emph{Setting.} Throughout this subsection $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ is a regular submanifold of dimension $m < N$, with the geometric tangent spaces $T^{\geo}_pM$, written $T_pM$ (the Setting of \ref{sec:normal-bundle} with $n = N$); $T^{\geo}M$ is its tangent bundle with zero section $\mathcal{Z}$ and $\pi_p : \mathbb{R}^N \to T_pM$ the orthogonal projection (Definitions~\ref{def:geo-tangent-bundle}, \ref{def:geo-zero-section-set} and~\ref{def:tangent-orthogonal-projection}, Lemma~\ref{lem:tangent-projection}). Points of the parameter space $\mathbb{R}^N$ are written $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}$. From Proposition~\ref{prop:height-transverse} on, $S$ denotes $F^{-1}(\mathcal{Z})$, as in the assignment: it plays the role of the $W$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:parametric-transversality}, not of the parameter space $S$ there, which here is $\mathbb{R}^N$. (If $m = N$, $M$ is open in $\mathbb{R}^N$ and the functions below have no critical points unless $\mathbf{a} = 0$.)

\begin{lembox}[The Zero Section and the Splitting Along It]\thmlabel{lem:geo-zero-section}
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The zero section $\zeta : M \to T^{\geo}M$, $\zeta(p) = (p, 0)$, is smooth, and $\mathcal{Z} = \zeta(M)$ is a closed regular submanifold of $T^{\geo}M$ of dimension $m$.
    \item For $p \in M$, with tangent spaces of the submanifolds $\mathcal{Z} \subseteq T^{\geo}M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{2N}$ taken geometrically,
    \[
    T_{(p,0)}\mathcal{Z} = \{(u, 0) : u \in T_pM\}, \qquad V = \{(0, w) : w \in T_pM\}, \qquad T_{(p,0)}T^{\geo}M = T_{(p,0)}\mathcal{Z} \oplus V = T_pM \times T_pM .
    \]
\end{enumerate}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\emph{(1)} \textit{(Filled in.)} The projection $\pi(q, v) = q$ is the restriction to $T^{\geo}M$ of a linear map, smooth by Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}(1); $\zeta$ is smooth into $\mathbb{R}^{2N}$ and lands in the regular submanifold $T^{\geo}M$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:geo-tangent-bundle-submanifold}), so it is smooth into it (Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}(2)). As $\pi \circ \zeta = \mathrm{id}_M$, Proposition~\ref{prop:sections-embeddings} makes $\zeta$ an embedding with closed image, a closed regular submanifold of dimension $m$.

\emph{(2)} \textit{(Assignment~6, Problem~5(a); the submitted solution.)} If $\gamma$ is a curve in $M$ with $\gamma(0) = p$ and $\gamma'(0) = u$, then $t \mapsto (\gamma(t), 0)$ is a curve in $\mathcal{Z}$ with velocity $(u, 0)$ at $t = 0$; so $\{(u, 0) : u \in T_pM\} \subseteq T_{(p,0)}\mathcal{Z}$, with equality since both have dimension $m$ (by (1) and Corollary~\ref{thm:geo-tangent-dimension}). For $w \in T_pM$, $t \mapsto (p, tw)$ is a curve in $T^{\geo}M$ with velocity $(0, w)$ at $t = 0$, so $V \subseteq T_{(p,0)}T^{\geo}M$. Both $T_{(p,0)}\mathcal{Z}$ and $V$ are $m$-dimensional, and $T_{(p,0)}\mathcal{Z} \cap V = \{0\}$, since $(u, 0) = (0, w)$ forces $u = w = 0$. Hence $T_{(p,0)}\mathcal{Z} + V$ is a $2m$-dimensional subspace of the $2m$-dimensional space $T_{(p,0)}T^{\geo}M$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:geo-tangent-bundle-submanifold}), so they are equal.
\end{proof}

This is the splitting of Proposition~\ref{prop:zero-section-vertical} for $T^*M$, seen inside $\mathbb{R}^{2N}$: horizontal (along the zero section) plus vertical (along the fibre).

\begin{defbox}[Height Function]\deflabel{def:height-function}
For $\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^N$, the \textbf{height function} in the direction $\mathbf{a}$ is $f_{\mathbf{a}} : M \to \mathbb{R}$, $f_{\mathbf{a}}(p) = p \cdot \mathbf{a}$, the restriction to $M$ of a linear function.
\end{defbox}

\begin{lembox}[Critical Points of a Height Function]\thmlabel{lem:height-critical}
For $p \in M$ and $w \in T_pM$, $d(f_{\mathbf{a}})_p(w) = w \cdot \mathbf{a} = w \cdot \pi_p(\mathbf{a})$. Hence
\[
p \in \operatorname{Crit}(f_{\mathbf{a}}) \iff \mathbf{a} \perp T_pM \iff \pi_p(\mathbf{a}) = 0 .
\]
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~6, Problem~5(b); the submitted solution.)} $f_{\mathbf{a}}$ is the restriction to $M$ of the linear function $y \mapsto y \cdot \mathbf{a}$, so along a curve $\gamma$ in $M$ with $\gamma(0) = p$, $\gamma'(0) = w$, $d(f_{\mathbf{a}})_p(w) = \frac{d}{dt}\big|_{t=0}\, \gamma(t) \cdot \mathbf{a} = w \cdot \mathbf{a}$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:velocity-composite}). Since $w \cdot \mathbf{a} = w \cdot \pi_p(\mathbf{a})$ for $w \in T_pM$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:tangent-projection}(1)), this is the identification $T_pM \cong T_p^*M$ by the inner product: $d(f_{\mathbf{a}})_p$ corresponds to $\pi_p(\mathbf{a})$. So $d(f_{\mathbf{a}})_p = 0$ if and only if $\mathbf{a} \perp T_pM$, if and only if $\pi_p(\mathbf{a}) = 0$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:tangent-projection}(1)).
\end{proof}

So $\pi_p(\mathbf{a})$ is the gradient of $f_{\mathbf{a}}$ at $p$, and the family of gradients is the map of the next proposition.

\begin{propbox}[The Gradient Family Is Transverse to the Zero Section]\thmlabel{prop:height-transverse}
Let $F : \mathbb{R}^N \times M \to T^{\geo}M$, $F(\mathbf{a}, p) = (p, \pi_p(\mathbf{a}))$. Then $F$ is smooth, $F \pitchfork \mathcal{Z}$ (Definition~\ref{def:transverse-submanifold}), and
\[
S = F^{-1}(\mathcal{Z}) = \{(\mathbf{a}, p) \in \mathbb{R}^N \times M : \mathbf{a} \perp T_pM\}
\]
is a regular submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^N \times M$ of dimension $N$: the normal bundle $\mathcal{N}$ of $M$ (Definition~\ref{def:normal-bundle}) with the two factors written in the opposite order. For $(\mathbf{a}, p) \in S$ and $\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^N$,
\[
dF_{(\mathbf{a},p)}(\mathbf{b}, 0) = \big(0,\ \pi_p(\mathbf{b})\big) .
\]
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~6, Problem~5(a); the submitted solution. Smoothness, not asked for, is Lemma~\ref{lem:tangent-projection}(3).)} \emph{$F^{-1}(\mathcal{Z})$.} The zero section is $\mathcal{Z} = \{(p, 0) : p \in M\}$, so
\[
F^{-1}(\mathcal{Z}) = \{(\mathbf{a}, p) \in \mathbb{R}^N \times M : \pi_p(\mathbf{a}) = 0\} = \{(\mathbf{a}, p) : p \in M,\ \mathbf{a} \in (T_pM)^\perp\}
\]
by Lemma~\ref{lem:tangent-projection}(1). This is the normal bundle $\mathcal{N} = \{(p, v) : p \in M,\ v \perp T_pM\}$ of $M$, with the two factors written in the opposite order.

\emph{$F \pitchfork \mathcal{Z}$.} Let $(\mathbf{a}, p) \in F^{-1}(\mathcal{Z})$, so $F(\mathbf{a}, p) = (p, 0)$. We must show $\operatorname{Im} dF_{(\mathbf{a}, p)} + T_{(p,0)}\mathcal{Z} = T_{(p,0)}T^{\geo}M$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:geo-zero-section}(2), it suffices to show $V \subseteq \operatorname{Im} dF_{(\mathbf{a}, p)}$. For $\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^N$, the curve $t \mapsto (\mathbf{a} + t\mathbf{b}, p)$ in $\mathbb{R}^N \times M$ has velocity $(\mathbf{b}, 0)$ at $t = 0$, and by linearity of $\pi_p$, $F(\mathbf{a} + t\mathbf{b}, p) = \big(p,\ \pi_p(\mathbf{a}) + t\,\pi_p(\mathbf{b})\big)$, so
\[
dF_{(\mathbf{a}, p)}(\mathbf{b}, 0) = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} F(\mathbf{a} + t\mathbf{b}, p) = \big(0,\ \pi_p(\mathbf{b})\big).
\]
Given $w \in T_pM$, take $\mathbf{b} = w$; since $\pi_p(w) = w$, this gives $(0, w) = dF_{(\mathbf{a},p)}(w, 0) \in \operatorname{Im} dF_{(\mathbf{a}, p)}$. Hence $V \subseteq \operatorname{Im} dF_{(\mathbf{a}, p)}$, and
\[
\operatorname{Im} dF_{(\mathbf{a}, p)} + T_{(p,0)}\mathcal{Z} \supseteq V + T_{(p,0)}\mathcal{Z} = T_{(p,0)}T^{\geo}M.
\]
In block form with respect to $\mathbb{R}^N \oplus T_pM$ and $T_{(p,0)}T^{\geo}M = T_pM \oplus T_pM$ (horizontal $\oplus$ vertical),
\[
dF_{(\mathbf{a}, p)} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & I_m \\ \pi_p & \ast \end{pmatrix},
\]
and the first column alone, together with $T_{(p,0)}\mathcal{Z}$, spans $T_{(p,0)}T^{\geo}M$. Therefore $F \pitchfork \mathcal{Z}$.

\emph{The manifold $S$.} By Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-submanifold-preimage}, applied to $F$ and the submanifold $\mathcal{Z}$ of codimension $2m - m = m$ in $T^{\geo}M$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:geo-zero-section}(1)), $S$ is a regular submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^N \times M$ of codimension $m$, so $\dim S = N + m - m = N$, and $T_{(\mathbf{a},p)}S = \{(\mathbf{b}, u) \in \mathbb{R}^N \oplus T_pM : dF_{(\mathbf{a},p)}(\mathbf{b}, u) \in T_{(p,0)}\mathcal{Z}\}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[The Hessian of a Height Function]\thmlabel{prop:height-hessian}
Let $(\mathbf{a}, p) \in S$, that is, $p \in \operatorname{Crit}(f_{\mathbf{a}})$, and $F_{\mathbf{a}} = F(\mathbf{a}, \cdot) : M \to T^{\geo}M$, $F_{\mathbf{a}}(q) = (q, \pi_q(\mathbf{a}))$. Then
\[
d(F_{\mathbf{a}})_p(u) = (u, A_pu), \qquad A_pu = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}\pi_{\gamma(t)}(\mathbf{a}) \quad (\gamma(0) = p,\ \gamma'(0) = u),
\]
for a linear map $A_p : T_pM \to T_pM$. In an adapted chart as in the Setting of \ref{sec:normal-bundle}, the matrix of $A_p$ in the basis $X_1(p), \ldots, X_m(p)$ is $g(p)^{-1}H_p$, where $g$ is the Gram matrix (Lemma~\ref{lem:tangent-projection}) and $H_p$ the Hessian matrix of $f_{\mathbf{a}}$ in the chart $(x^1, \ldots, x^m)$ of $M$ (Definition~\ref{def:hessian-matrix}). So $A_p$ is invertible if and only if $p$ is a nondegenerate critical point of $f_{\mathbf{a}}$.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~6, Problem~5(b); the submitted solution.)} \emph{The vertical derivative.} For $u \in T_pM$ and a curve $\gamma$ in $M$ with $\gamma(0) = p$, $\gamma'(0) = u$,
\[
d(F_{\mathbf{a}})_p(u) = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}\big(\gamma(t), \pi_{\gamma(t)}(\mathbf{a})\big) = (u, A_pu), \qquad A_pu = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}\pi_{\gamma(t)}(\mathbf{a}).
\]
Since $T_{(p,0)}T^{\geo}M = \{(u, w) : u, w \in T_pM\}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:geo-zero-section}(2)), $A_pu \in T_pM$, and $A_p$ is linear since $d(F_{\mathbf{a}})_p$ is. In block form, $d(F_{\mathbf{a}})_p = \begin{pmatrix} I_m \\ A_p \end{pmatrix}$.

\emph{$A_p$ in coordinates.} Restricted to $U \cap M$, the first $m$ coordinates $(x^1, \ldots, x^m)$ of the adapted chart form a chart of $M$, whose coordinate vectors at $q \in U \cap M$ are the $X_j(q) = \partial_j(q) \in T_qM \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:tangent-projection}(2), $\pi_q(\mathbf{a}) = \sum_{i,j} g^{ij}(q)\,\big(\mathbf{a} \cdot \partial_j(q)\big)\,\partial_i(q)$, and $\frac{\partial f_{\mathbf{a}}}{\partial x^j}(q) = \partial_j(q) \cdot \mathbf{a}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:height-critical} with $w = \partial_j(q)$). Since $p$ is a critical point, $\mathbf{a} \cdot \partial_j(p) = 0$ for all $j$. Differentiating $\pi_q(\mathbf{a})$ in the direction $\partial_k$ at $q = p$ by the product rule, every term in which the derivative does not fall on $\mathbf{a} \cdot \partial_j(q)$ contains the factor $\mathbf{a} \cdot \partial_j(p) = 0$, so
\[
A_p(\partial_k(p)) = \sum_{i,j} g^{ij}(p)\, \frac{\partial^2 f_{\mathbf{a}}}{\partial x^k \partial x^j}(p)\, \partial_i(p).
\]
Thus the matrix of $A_p$ in the basis $(\partial_i(p))$ is $g(p)^{-1}H_p$. As $g(p)$ is invertible, $A_p$ is invertible if and only if $\det H_p \neq 0$, that is (Proposition~\ref{prop:hessian-flat}(2)), if and only if $p$ is nondegenerate.
\end{proof}

\begin{thmbox}[Height Functions and Regular Values]\thmlabel{thm:height-regular-values}
Let $\pi : S \to \mathbb{R}^N$, $\pi(\mathbf{a}, p) = \mathbf{a}$, be the projection of the manifold $S$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:height-transverse} onto the parameter (not to be confused with the orthogonal projections $\pi_p$). Then $\pi^{-1}(\mathbf{a}) = \{\mathbf{a}\} \times \operatorname{Crit}(f_{\mathbf{a}})$, and
\[
\mathbf{a} \text{ is a regular value of } \pi \iff f_{\mathbf{a}} \text{ is a Morse function.}
\]
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~6, Problem~5(b): the direction $(\Rightarrow)$ is the submitted solution; $(\Leftarrow)$ is filled in.)} By Lemma~\ref{lem:height-critical}, $(\mathbf{a}, p) \in S$ if and only if $p \in \operatorname{Crit}(f_{\mathbf{a}})$, so $\pi^{-1}(\mathbf{a}) = \{\mathbf{a}\} \times \operatorname{Crit}(f_{\mathbf{a}})$. Since $\pi$ is the restriction of the linear projection $(\mathbf{a}, p) \mapsto \mathbf{a}$, $\pi_{*(\mathbf{a},p)}(\mathbf{b}, u) = \mathbf{b}$.

\emph{The tangent space of $S$.} Let $(\mathbf{a}, p) \in S$. Since $F(\mathbf{a}, q) = F_{\mathbf{a}}(q)$, the chain rule gives $dF_{(\mathbf{a},p)}(0, u) = d(F_{\mathbf{a}})_p(u) = (u, A_pu)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:height-hessian}), and with Proposition~\ref{prop:height-transverse}, by linearity,
\[
dF_{(\mathbf{a},p)}(\mathbf{b}, u) = \big(u,\ \pi_p(\mathbf{b}) + A_pu\big) .
\]
As $T_{(p,0)}\mathcal{Z} = \{(u', 0) : u' \in T_pM\}$, Proposition~\ref{prop:height-transverse} gives
\[
T_{(\mathbf{a},p)}S = \{(\mathbf{b}, u) : \pi_p(\mathbf{b}) + A_pu = 0\}, \qquad \ker \pi_{*(\mathbf{a},p)} = \{(0, u) : u \in T_pM,\ A_pu = 0\}.
\]

\emph{$(\Rightarrow)$ Regular values give Morse functions.} Suppose $\mathbf{a}$ is a regular value of $\pi$, and let $p$ be a critical point of $f_{\mathbf{a}}$, so $(\mathbf{a}, p) \in \pi^{-1}(\mathbf{a})$. Then $\pi_{*(\mathbf{a},p)} : T_{(\mathbf{a},p)}S \to \mathbb{R}^N$ is surjective, and since $\dim T_{(\mathbf{a},p)}S = N$, it is also injective. By the kernel computation, $A_pu = 0$ implies $u = 0$, so $A_p$ is injective, hence invertible, and $p$ is nondegenerate (Proposition~\ref{prop:height-hessian}). Since $p$ was an arbitrary critical point, $f_{\mathbf{a}}$ is Morse.

\emph{$(\Leftarrow)$} Suppose $f_{\mathbf{a}}$ is Morse, and let $(\mathbf{a}, p) \in \pi^{-1}(\mathbf{a})$. Then $p$ is a nondegenerate critical point, so $A_p$ is invertible (Proposition~\ref{prop:height-hessian}). Given $\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^N$, put $u = -A_p^{-1}\pi_p(\mathbf{b}) \in T_pM$; then $(\mathbf{b}, u) \in T_{(\mathbf{a},p)}S$ and $\pi_{*(\mathbf{a},p)}(\mathbf{b}, u) = \mathbf{b}$. So $\pi_{*(\mathbf{a},p)}$ is onto at every point of $\pi^{-1}(\mathbf{a})$: $\mathbf{a}$ is a regular value.
\end{proof}

The image of $\pi_{*(\mathbf{a},p)}$ is $\{\mathbf{b} : \pi_p(\mathbf{b}) \in \operatorname{Im} A_p\}$; the theorem says this is all of $\mathbb{R}^N$ exactly when $A_p$ is onto.

\begin{corbox}[Almost Every Height Function Is Morse]\thmlabel{cor:height-morse}
For almost every $\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^N$ (all $\mathbf{a}$ outside a set of measure zero), $f_{\mathbf{a}} : M \to \mathbb{R}$ is a Morse function.
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~6, Problem~5(b); the submitted solution.)} By Sard's theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:sard}) applied to the smooth map $\pi : S \to \mathbb{R}^N$, the set of critical values of $\pi$ has measure zero in $\mathbb{R}^N$. Hence almost every $\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^N$ is a regular value of $\pi$, and for all such $\mathbf{a}$, $f_{\mathbf{a}}$ is a Morse function (Theorem~\ref{thm:height-regular-values}).
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Second proof]
\textit{(Not from the assignment: the problem as an instance of Corollary~\ref{cor:parametric-sard}.)} $F$ is a smooth family of maps $F_{\mathbf{a}} : M \to T^{\geo}M$ parametrized by $\mathbb{R}^N$ (Definition~\ref{def:smooth-family}), and $F \pitchfork \mathcal{Z}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:height-transverse}); so $F_{\mathbf{a}} \pitchfork \mathcal{Z}$ for almost every $\mathbf{a}$. At $p \in F_{\mathbf{a}}^{-1}(\mathcal{Z}) = \operatorname{Crit}(f_{\mathbf{a}})$, by Proposition~\ref{prop:height-hessian} and Lemma~\ref{lem:geo-zero-section}(2),
\[
\operatorname{Im} d(F_{\mathbf{a}})_p + T_{(p,0)}\mathcal{Z} = \{(u, A_pu)\} + \{(u', 0)\} = T_pM \times \operatorname{Im} A_p ,
\]
which is all of $T_{(p,0)}T^{\geo}M = T_pM \times T_pM$ if and only if $A_p$ is onto, that is, $p$ is nondegenerate. So $F_{\mathbf{a}} \pitchfork \mathcal{Z}$ exactly when $f_{\mathbf{a}}$ is Morse, and the claim follows. Under the identification $T^{\geo}M \cong T^*M$ of the hint (``one can identify $TM \cong T^*M$ using the inner product''), $F_{\mathbf{a}}$ is the section $s_{f_{\mathbf{a}}} : p \mapsto (p, d(f_{\mathbf{a}})_p)$, and this equivalence is Theorem~\ref{thm:morse-transverse}.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[Directions Outside the Image]\label{rem:height-outside-image}
``Incidentally, what can you say about $f_{\mathbf{a}}$ if $\mathbf{a}$ is not in the image of $\pi$?'' \textit{(The submitted answer.)} If $\mathbf{a} \notin \pi(S)$, then $\pi^{-1}(\mathbf{a}) = \{\mathbf{a}\} \times \operatorname{Crit}(f_{\mathbf{a}})$ is empty, so $f_{\mathbf{a}}$ has no critical points; in particular it is vacuously Morse (Definition~\ref{def:morse-function}). Corollaries~\ref{cor:height-projection-onto-compact} and~\ref{cor:height-projection-zero-critical-value} below add two facts about the image and the critical values of $\pi$.
\end{rembox}

\begin{corbox}[{For Compact $M$ the Projection $\pi$ Is Onto}]\thmlabel{cor:height-projection-onto-compact}
If $M$ is compact and nonempty, then every $\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^N$ lies in the image of $\pi : S \to \mathbb{R}^N$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:height-regular-values}): $\pi$ is onto, and every $f_{\mathbf{a}}$ has a critical point.
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from the assignment.)} Let $\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^N$. The height function $f_{\mathbf{a}}$ (Definition~\ref{def:height-function}) is continuous on the compact nonempty set $M$, so it attains a maximum at some $p \in M$. A local extremum is a critical point (Proposition~\ref{prop:extremum-critical}), so $p \in \operatorname{Crit}(f_{\mathbf{a}})$, and $(\mathbf{a}, p) \in \{\mathbf{a}\} \times \operatorname{Crit}(f_{\mathbf{a}}) = \pi^{-1}(\mathbf{a})$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:height-regular-values}). So $\mathbf{a} = \pi(\mathbf{a}, p)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[{The Direction $0$ Is Always a Critical Value}]\thmlabel{cor:height-projection-zero-critical-value}
If $M$ is nonempty and $m \ge 1$, then $0$ is a critical value of $\pi : S \to \mathbb{R}^N$.
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from the assignment.)} For $\mathbf{a} = 0$, $f_0(p) = p \cdot 0 = 0$: $f_0 \equiv 0$. So $d(f_0)_p = 0$ for every $p$, and every point of $M$ is a critical point of $f_0$. In any chart the Hessian matrix of the constant function is the zero $m \times m$ matrix, with determinant $0$ since $m \ge 1$; so every critical point is degenerate (Proposition~\ref{prop:hessian-flat}(2), (a) $\Leftrightarrow$ (d)). As $M \neq \varnothing$, $f_0$ has a degenerate critical point and is not a Morse function (Definition~\ref{def:morse-function}). By Theorem~\ref{thm:height-regular-values}, $0$ is not a regular value of $\pi$, that is, it is a critical value (Definition~\ref{def:regular-critical-value}).
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[$\bigstar$ The Shape Operator]\label{rem:height-shape-operator}
\textit{(Beyond the course; stated, not proved here.)} For $(\mathbf{a}, p) \in S$, $\mathbf{a}$ is a normal vector at $p$, and $A_p$ is the \emph{shape operator} (Weingarten map) of $M$ at $p$ in the normal direction $\mathbf{a}$: writing $\mathbf{a} = \pi_{\gamma(t)}(\mathbf{a}) + \nu(t)$ with $\nu(t) \perp T_{\gamma(t)}M$, $A_pu = -\nu'(0)$, the classical $S_{\mathbf{a}}(u) = -(D_u\nu)^{\top}$. The Hessian is the second fundamental form $\mathrm{II}$ paired with $\mathbf{a}$: $\operatorname{Hess}_p f_{\mathbf{a}}(u, w) = \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathrm{II}_p(u, w)$. So $f_{\mathbf{a}}$ fails to be Morse exactly when $M$ is curved degenerately in the direction $\mathbf{a}$ at some point where $\mathbf{a}$ is normal. For a hypersurface ($m = N - 1$), $\pi$ restricted to unit normals is the Gauss map, and the excluded directions are those of normals at points of zero Gauss--Kronecker curvature. The companion statement for distances, $L_{\mathbf{a}}(p) = |p - \mathbf{a}|^2$, is Milnor's (\emph{Morse Theory}, \S6): $L_{\mathbf{a}}$ is Morse if and only if $\mathbf{a}$ is not a focal point of $M$ (Definition~\ref{def:focal-point}), the eigenvalue condition of the remark \emph{Focal Points in General} in \ref{sub:endpoint-focal}.
\end{rembox}

\section{Partitions of Unity}\label{sec:partitions-of-unity}

\roadmark{Stage: analysis}{Writing $1$ as a locally finite sum of smooth functions subordinate to any open cover: the tool for gluing local constructions into global ones.}

\textit{Lecture 22. Partitions of unity: a key tool for constructing exhaustion functions and much else, for example for integrating forms. Lee develops them up front (Lee, Chapter~2); the course introduces them where they are first needed. In the lectures they came after the Whitney embedding theorem for compact manifolds (Lecture~21), together with its noncompact case (Lectures~22--23); these notes put them first, since the noncompact case uses them (\ref{sec:whitney}).}

\begin{defbox}[Locally Finite Family]\deflabel{def:locally-finite}
Let $X$ be a topological space. A family $\{S_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ of subsets of $X$, over any index set $A$, is \textbf{locally finite} if every $p \in X$ has a neighbourhood $U$ that meets only finitely many of the sets: $\{ \alpha \in A : U \cap S_\alpha \neq \varnothing \}$ is finite.
\textit{(Lecture~22 stated the condition inside the definition of a partition of unity, and again in that of a paracompact space; stated once here.)}
\leeref{Ch.~1, \emph{Paracompactness}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{exbox}[Intervals Centred at the Integers]\exlabel{ex:locally-finite-integer-intervals}
\textit{(Not from lecture.)} The intervals $S_n = (n - 1, n + 1)$, $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, form a locally finite family in $\mathbb{R}$, although there are infinitely many of them and they cover $\mathbb{R}$. For $p \in \mathbb{R}$ take the neighbourhood $U = (p - 1, p + 1)$. If $U \cap S_n \neq \varnothing$, some $x$ has $|x - p| < 1$ and $|x - n| < 1$, so $|n - p| < 2$; at most four integers $n$ satisfy this. So $U$ meets at most four of the $S_n$.
\end{exbox}

\begin{exbox}[Nested Intervals]\exlabel{ex:nested-intervals}
\textit{(Not from lecture.)} The intervals $S_n = (-n, n)$, $n \ge 1$, do not form a locally finite family in $\mathbb{R}$, and the condition of Definition~\ref{def:locally-finite} fails at every point. Let $p \in \mathbb{R}$ and $U$ any neighbourhood of $p$. For every integer $n > |p|$ we have $p \in S_n$, so $p \in U \cap S_n$; hence $U$ meets the infinitely many $S_n$ with $n > |p|$.
\end{exbox}

\begin{exbox}[Intervals Accumulating at $0$]\exlabel{ex:intervals-accumulating-at-zero}
\textit{(Not from lecture.)} The intervals $S_n = \big(\tfrac{1}{n+1}, \tfrac{1}{n}\big)$, $n \ge 1$, satisfy the condition of Definition~\ref{def:locally-finite} at every $p \neq 0$ but not at $p = 0$; so the family is not locally finite, since the condition must hold at every point.
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
\item $p < 0$: the neighbourhood $(-\infty, 0)$ meets no $S_n$.
\item $p > 0$: the neighbourhood $U = (p/2, \infty)$ meets $S_n$ only if $\tfrac1n > \tfrac p2$, i.e.\ $n < \tfrac2p$; finitely many $n$.
\item $p = 0$: a neighbourhood $U$ of $0$ contains some $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$, which contains $S_n$ for every $n$ with $\tfrac1n < \varepsilon$; infinitely many $n$.
\end{itemize}
\end{exbox}

\begin{lembox}[Closures and Unions in a Locally Finite Family]\thmlabel{lem:locally-finite-closures}
Let $\{S_i\}_{i \in I}$ be a locally finite family of subsets of a topological space $X$ (Definition~\ref{def:locally-finite}).
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item The closures $\{\overline{S_i}\}_{i \in I}$ also form a locally finite family.
\item $\overline{\bigcup_i S_i} = \bigcup_i \overline{S_i}$. In particular, if every $S_i$ is closed, then $\bigcup_i S_i$ is closed.
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Lemma 1.13}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lee leaves the proof as an exercise, Exercise~1.14; the proof of Theorem~2.23 in the assigned reading uses both parts. Filled in.)} Neighbourhoods can be taken open: a neighbourhood meeting only finitely many $S_i$ contains an open neighbourhood with the same property.

(1) Let $p \in X$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $p$ meeting only finitely many $S_i$. If $W$ meets $\overline{S_i}$, say at $x$, then $W$ is an open set containing the point $x$ of the closure of $S_i$, so $W$ meets $S_i$. Hence $\{ i : W \cap \overline{S_i} \neq \varnothing \} \subseteq \{ i : W \cap S_i \neq \varnothing \}$, a finite set.

(2) \emph{$\supseteq$.} For each $i$, $S_i \subseteq \bigcup_j S_j$, so $\overline{S_i} \subseteq \overline{\bigcup_j S_j}$. \emph{$\subseteq$.} Let $p \notin \bigcup_i \overline{S_i}$; we show $p \notin \overline{\bigcup_i S_i}$. Take an open neighbourhood $W$ of $p$ meeting only $S_{i_1}, \ldots, S_{i_k}$. The set $C = \overline{S_{i_1}} \cup \cdots \cup \overline{S_{i_k}}$ is closed, as a finite union of closed sets, and $p \notin C$. So $W' = W \setminus C$ is an open neighbourhood of $p$. It misses $S_{i_1}, \ldots, S_{i_k}$ (they lie in $C$) and every other $S_i$ (which $W$ already misses), so $W' \cap \bigcup_i S_i = \varnothing$ and $p \notin \overline{\bigcup_i S_i}$. If every $S_i$ is closed, this reads $\overline{\bigcup_i S_i} = \bigcup_i S_i$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lembox}[Locally Finite Sums of Smooth Functions Are Smooth]\thmlabel{lem:locally-finite-sum-smooth}
Let $\{f_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ be smooth functions on a smooth manifold $M$ whose supports $\{\operatorname{supp} f_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ form a locally finite family (Definition~\ref{def:locally-finite}). Then every $p \in M$ has an open neighbourhood on which all but finitely many $f_\alpha$ vanish identically; in particular the sum $f = \sum_{\alpha \in A} f_\alpha$ has only finitely many nonzero terms at each point, and $f$ is smooth on $M$.
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; the argument the proofs of Theorem~\ref{thm:partition-of-unity} and Proposition~\ref{prop:exhaustion-exists} use.)} Let $p \in M$. By local finiteness $p$ has a neighbourhood meeting only finitely many supports; shrinking it, take it open, $U$, and let $F = \{ \alpha \in A : U \cap \operatorname{supp} f_\alpha \neq \varnothing \}$, a finite set. For $\alpha \notin F$, $U$ does not meet $\operatorname{supp} f_\alpha$, which contains $\{ f_\alpha \neq 0 \}$; so $f_\alpha = 0$ on $U$. Hence on $U$
\[
f = \sum_{\alpha \in F} f_\alpha ,
\]
a finite sum of smooth functions, so $f|_U$ is smooth. Every point of $M$ has an open neighbourhood on which $f$ is smooth, and smoothness is a local property; so $f$ is smooth on $M$.
\end{proof}

\begin{exbox}[Pointwise Finiteness Is Not Enough]\exlabel{ex:pointwise-finite-sum}
\textit{(Not from lecture.)} Lemma~\ref{lem:locally-finite-sum-smooth} needs the supports to be locally finite; it is not enough that each point lies in only finitely many supports. On $M = \mathbb{R}$ let $a_n = \tfrac{1}{n+1}$, $b_n = \tfrac1n$ ($n \ge 1$), and let $f_n$ be the smooth function equal to $c_n\, e^{-1/((x - a_n)(b_n - x))}$ on $(a_n, b_n)$ and $0$ elsewhere, with $c_n > 0$ chosen so that $\max f_n = 1$, attained at the midpoint $m_n$ of $[a_n, b_n]$ (the exponent is largest there). Then $\operatorname{supp} f_n = [a_n, b_n]$.
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
\item \emph{Pointwise finite.} A point lies in at most two of the supports (the endpoints $\tfrac1n$, $n \ge 2$, lie in two), and $0$ in none, so $f = \sum_n f_n$ is defined everywhere.
\item \emph{Not continuous.} $f(m_n) = f_n(m_n) = 1$, since $m_n$ lies in no other support, and $m_n \to 0$; but $f(0) = 0$. So $f$ is not even continuous at $0$.
\item \emph{Not locally finite.} The supports accumulate at $0$, as in Example~\ref{ex:intervals-accumulating-at-zero}: every neighbourhood of $0$ meets infinitely many of them.
\end{itemize}
\end{exbox}

\begin{defbox}[Partition of Unity]\deflabel{def:partition-of-unity}
A \textbf{partition of unity} on $M$ is an indexed family $\{\chi_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ of smooth functions on $M$, over an arbitrary index set $A$ (possibly uncountable), such that
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item $0 \le \chi_\alpha \le 1$ for every $\alpha$;
\item the family of supports $\{\operatorname{supp}\chi_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ is locally finite (Definition~\ref{def:locally-finite}): every $p \in M$ has a neighbourhood $U$ for which $\{ \alpha \in A : U \cap \operatorname{supp}\chi_\alpha \neq \varnothing \}$ is finite;
\item $\sum_{\alpha \in A} \chi_\alpha(p) = 1$ for every $p \in M$.
\end{enumerate}
By (2) the sum in (3) has only finitely many nonzero terms at each point.
\leeref{Ch.~2, \emph{Partitions of Unity}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[Partition of Unity Subordinate to a Cover]\deflabel{def:subordinate-partition}
A partition of unity $\{\chi_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ on $M$ (Definition~\ref{def:partition-of-unity}) is \textbf{subordinate} to an open cover $\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ of $M$ if $\operatorname{supp}\chi_\alpha \subseteq U_\alpha$ for every $\alpha$.
\leeref{Ch.~2, \emph{Partitions of Unity}}
\end{defbox}

The name: the number one is written as a sum of smooth functions. Partitions of unity allow one to localize; the bump functions so far, and the cutoff functions in the proof of the Whitney embedding theorem (\ref{sec:whitney}), are made of the same material.

The simplest example, on $M = \mathbb{R}$: a function $\chi_1$ that is $1$ far to the left and $0$ far to the right, and $\chi_2 = 1 - \chi_1$.

The main result of this section is that every open cover has a subordinate partition of unity (Theorem~\ref{thm:partition-of-unity} below). Its proof has two steps of different kinds: an analysis step in $\mathbb{R}^m$ (the function $h$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-cutoff}; the lecture's first version used the plateau functions of Lemma~\ref{lem:plateau}), and genuine point-set topology on $M$ (paracompactness, Theorem~\ref{thm:manifolds-paracompact}). The ingredients come first.

\begin{lembox}[Plateau Functions]\thmlabel{lem:plateau}
For all $\varepsilon > \delta > 0$ there is $\rho \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ with $0 \le \rho \le 1$, $\rho \equiv 1$ on $[-\delta, \delta]$ and $\operatorname{supp}\rho \subseteq (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$. Then $f(x) = \rho(|x|)$ is smooth on $\mathbb{R}^m$, $f \equiv 1$ on the closed ball $\overline{B}_\delta$, and $\operatorname{supp} f \subseteq B_\varepsilon = \{ x \in \mathbb{R}^m : |x| < \varepsilon \}$.
\leeref{Lemmas 2.20--2.22}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not proved in Lecture~22, which described the method: start from the function equal to $e^{-1/x}$ for $x$ positive and zero for $x$ negative, then reflect, divide and add. This is step~1 of the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:bump-closed-ball}.)} With $h$ as in Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-cutoff} and $\delta < r' < \varepsilon$, take $\rho(t) = h(r'^2 - t^2)\big/\big(h(r'^2 - t^2) + h(t^2 - \delta^2)\big)$: smooth, between $0$ and $1$, equal to $1$ for $|t| \le \delta$ and $0$ for $|t| \ge r'$, so $\operatorname{supp}\rho \subseteq [-r', r'] \subseteq (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$. Then $f(x) = \rho(|x|)$ is the function $H$ of that proof (with $r = \delta$), smooth on $\mathbb{R}^m$ --- $|x|$ is not smooth at the origin, but $\rho$ is constant equal to one near $0$, so $f$ is constant near $x = 0$ --- with $f \equiv 1$ on $\overline{B}_\delta$ and $\operatorname{supp} f = \overline{B}_{r'} \subseteq B_\varepsilon$.
\end{proof}

\textit{The topology.} The second step needs some point-set topology, which pays for the use of partitions of unity before their construction.

\begin{defbox}[Refinement of a Cover]\deflabel{def:refinement}
Let $\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ be a cover of a topological space $X$. A cover $\{V_i\}_{i \in I}$ of $X$ is a \textbf{refinement} of $\{U_\alpha\}$ if every $V_i$ lies in some $U_\alpha$: for each $i$ there is $\alpha(i) \in A$ with $V_i \subseteq U_{\alpha(i)}$. It is an \textbf{open refinement} if every $V_i$ is open. A subcover is the special case in which every $V_i$ is one of the $U_\alpha$.
\textit{(Lecture~22 stated the condition inside the definition of a paracompact space; stated once here.)}
\leeref{Ch.~1, \emph{Paracompactness}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{exbox}[A Locally Finite Refinement That Is Not a Subcover]\exlabel{ex:refinement-not-subcover}
\textit{(Not from lecture.)} On $\mathbb{R}$, the open cover $\{(-n, n)\}_{n \ge 1}$ is not locally finite (Example~\ref{ex:nested-intervals}). The intervals $V_k = (k - 1, k + 1)$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$, form a locally finite open refinement of it (Definition~\ref{def:refinement}):
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
\item \emph{A cover.} Every $x \in \mathbb{R}$ lies in $V_k$ for $k = \lfloor x \rfloor$, since $k \le x < k + 1$.
\item \emph{A refinement.} If $|x - k| < 1$ then $|x| < |k| + 1$, so $V_k \subseteq (-n, n)$ with $n = |k| + 1$.
\item \emph{Locally finite.} This is Example~\ref{ex:locally-finite-integer-intervals}.
\end{itemize}
It is not a subcover: $V_1 = (0, 2)$ is not one of the intervals $(-n, n)$. Refining, not only passing to a subcover, is needed here: a subcover of $\{(-n, n)\}$ must contain infinitely many of the intervals (finitely many have bounded union), and all of them contain $0$, so no subcover is locally finite at $0$.
\end{exbox}

\begin{defbox}[Paracompact Space]\deflabel{def:paracompact}
A space $X$ is \textbf{paracompact} if every open cover $\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ has an open refinement $\{V_i\}_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ (Definition~\ref{def:refinement}) that covers and is locally finite (Definition~\ref{def:locally-finite}):
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item $X = \bigcup_i V_i$, and for every $i$ there is $\alpha(i)$ with $V_i \subseteq U_{\alpha(i)}$;
\item every $p \in X$ has a neighbourhood $W$ such that $\{ i : W \cap V_i \neq \varnothing \}$ is finite.
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Ch.~1, \emph{Paracompactness}}
\end{defbox}

Compactness gives a finite subcover; paracompactness gives a locally finite refinement, which need not be a subcover. (The usual definition allows refinements indexed by any set; with the countable index set of the lecture it is what holds for manifolds, Theorem~\ref{thm:manifolds-paracompact} below.)

\begin{lembox}[Exhaustion by Compact Sets]\thmlabel{lem:compact-exhaustion}
A second-countable, locally compact Hausdorff space $X$ is the union of compact sets $K_1 \subseteq K_2 \subseteq \cdots$ with $K_j \subseteq \operatorname{Int}K_{j+1}$ for every $j$.
\leeref{Proposition A.60}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in, following Lee.)} \emph{A countable basis of precompact sets.} Let $\mathcal{B}$ be a countable basis, and $\mathcal{B}'$ the set of $B \in \mathcal{B}$ with compact closure. $\mathcal{B}'$ is still a basis: if $x \in W$ open, local compactness gives an open $V \ni x$ with $\overline V$ compact, and some $B \in \mathcal{B}$ has $x \in B \subseteq V \cap W$; then $\overline B$ is a closed subset of the compact $\overline V$ (closures computed in the Hausdorff space $X$), so compact. Enumerate $\mathcal{B}' = \{B_1, B_2, \ldots\}$ (if it is finite, $X$ is compact and $K_j = X$ works).

\emph{The exhaustion.} Put $K_1 = \overline{B_1}$. Given $K_j$ compact, it is covered by the $B_i$, hence by $B_1, \ldots, B_n$ for some $n$; take the least such $n$ with $n \ge j + 1$, and $K_{j+1} = \overline{B_1} \cup \cdots \cup \overline{B_n}$, compact as a finite union of compact sets. Then $K_j \subseteq B_1 \cup \cdots \cup B_n \subseteq \operatorname{Int}K_{j+1}$, and $B_j \subseteq K_j$ for all $j$, so $\bigcup_j K_j = X$.
\end{proof}

\begin{thmbox}[Manifolds Are Paracompact]\thmlabel{thm:manifolds-paracompact}
Let $M$ be a topological manifold, $\{U_\alpha\}$ an open cover, and $\mathcal{B}$ any basis of the topology of $M$. Then $\{U_\alpha\}$ has a countable, locally finite open refinement that covers $M$ and consists of elements of $\mathcal{B}$. In particular $M$ is paracompact. More generally, every second-countable, locally compact Hausdorff space is paracompact, by the same proof.
\leeref{Theorem 1.15}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Stated in Lecture~22, with the proof left to Lee; filled in, following Lee.)} $M$ is Hausdorff, second countable (Definition~\ref{def:second-countable}) and locally compact (Proposition~\ref{prop:locally-compact}); let $K_1 \subseteq K_2 \subseteq \cdots$ be as in Lemma~\ref{lem:compact-exhaustion}, and $K_0 = K_{-1} = \varnothing$. For $j \ge 0$ put
\[
A_j = K_{j+1} \setminus \operatorname{Int}K_j \ \ \text{(compact)}, \qquad W_j = \operatorname{Int}K_{j+2} \setminus K_{j-1} \ \ \text{(open)}, \qquad A_j \subseteq W_j .
\]
For each $x \in A_j$ choose $\alpha$ with $x \in U_\alpha$, and $B_x \in \mathcal{B}$ with $x \in B_x \subseteq U_\alpha \cap W_j$. Finitely many $B_x$ cover the compact set $A_j$. The union over $j$ of these finite families is a countable family of elements of $\mathcal{B}$; it covers $M$, because the $A_j$ do (each point lies in some $K_{j+1} \setminus \operatorname{Int}K_j$); and it refines $\{U_\alpha\}$. \emph{Locally finite:} the sets chosen for $j$ lie in $W_j$, and $W_j \cap W_k = \varnothing$ when $|j - k| \ge 3$; a point of $A_j$ has the neighbourhood $W_j$, which meets only the sets chosen for $j - 2, \ldots, j + 2$, finitely many.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[Is Local Compactness Needed?]\label{rem:paracompact-hypotheses}
\textit{(Transcription note, Lecture~22.)} Page~58 of the handwritten notes states the theorem as ``if $X$ is $T_2$ and 2nd countable, then it is paracompact (need locally compact?)'', leaving open whether local compactness is needed. Local compactness is needed: as stated the theorem is false in general, and local compactness, which manifolds have, is the missing hypothesis; Hausdorff, second countable and locally compact imply paracompact, and Lee proves directly what is needed for manifolds in Theorem~1.15 (p.~9). So the theorem is stated with local compactness, as above. \textit{(Filled in.)} Some hypothesis beyond Hausdorff and second countable is needed: the $K$-topology on $\mathbb{R}$ is Hausdorff and second countable but not paracompact (Example~\ref{ex:k-topology-not-paracompact} below). Local compactness, as above, suffices; so does regularity. For manifolds nothing changes: they are locally compact. Second countability is essential here; it was used once before, for countable subcovers in measure zero (Lemma~\ref{lem:countable-subcover}).
\end{rembox}

\begin{exbox}[The K-Topology on the Real Line]\exlabel{ex:k-topology-not-paracompact}
\textit{(Filled in; not from lecture.)} Let $K = \{1/n : n \ge 1\}$. The \emph{$K$-topology} on $\mathbb{R}$ is generated by the open intervals $(a, b)$ and the sets $(a, b) \setminus K$. It is Hausdorff and second countable but not regular (Munkres, \S31), so not paracompact.

\emph{Basis.} The open intervals and the sets $(a, b) \setminus K$ cover $\mathbb{R}$, and the intersection of two of them is empty or again of one of the two forms, since $\big((a, b) \setminus K\big) \cap (c, d) = \big((a, b) \cap (c, d)\big) \setminus K$. So they form a basis, and the open sets are their unions.

\emph{Hausdorff.} Every open interval is open, so the $K$-topology is finer than the standard one; two distinct points have disjoint open intervals around them.

\emph{Second countable.} The intervals $(p, q)$ and the sets $(p, q) \setminus K$ with $p < q$ rational form a countable family. It is a basis: if $x$ lies in a basic set $(a, b)$, respectively $(a, b) \setminus K$, choose rationals $p, q$ with $a \le p < x < q \le b$; then $x \in (p, q) \subseteq (a, b)$, respectively $x \in (p, q) \setminus K \subseteq (a, b) \setminus K$.

\emph{Not regular.} $K$ is closed: $K \cup \{0\}$ is closed in the standard topology, so $\mathbb{R} \setminus (K \cup \{0\})$ is open, and $\mathbb{R} \setminus K$ is its union with the basic set $(-1, 1) \setminus K$. Suppose $U \ni 0$ and $V \supseteq K$ are disjoint open sets. $U$ contains a basic set $B \ni 0$. $B$ is not an interval: an interval around $0$ contains some $1/n \in K \subseteq V$, while $B \subseteq U$ and $U \cap V = \varnothing$. So $B = (a, b) \setminus K$ with $a < 0 < b$. Choose $n$ with $1/n < b$. $V$ contains a basic set $C \ni 1/n$, which is an interval $(c, d)$, since the sets $(c, d) \setminus K$ do not contain $1/n$; replacing it by $(\max(c, 0), \min(d, b))$, which still contains $1/n$, we may assume $(c, d) \subseteq (0, b)$. The interval $(c, d)$ is uncountable and $K$ is countable, so there is $z \in (c, d) \setminus K$. Then $z \in (a, b) \setminus K = B \subseteq U$ and $z \in (c, d) \subseteq V$, contradicting $U \cap V = \varnothing$. So the point $0$ and the closed set $K$ cannot be separated by open sets.

\emph{Not paracompact.} A paracompact Hausdorff space is normal, in particular regular (Munkres, Theorem~41.1). Munkres's paracompactness asks only for a locally finite open refinement, not a countable one, so it follows from Definition~\ref{def:paracompact}. As the $K$-topology is Hausdorff but not regular, it is not paracompact.
\end{exbox}

\begin{defbox}[Regular Coordinate Ball]\deflabel{def:regular-coordinate-ball}
An open set $B \subseteq M$ is a \textbf{regular coordinate ball} if there are a chart $(U, \varphi)$ with $B \subseteq U$ and numbers $0 < \delta < \varepsilon$ such that $\varphi(B) = B_\delta(0)$, the $\delta$-ball centred at $0$, and $B_\varepsilon(0) \subseteq \varphi(U)$ --- an $\varepsilon$-ball centred at $0$ containing $\varphi(B)$, with room to spare. The room makes $\varphi^{-1}\big(\overline{B}_\delta(0)\big)$ a compact subset of $U$, which is then the closure of $B$ in $M$ (Step~2 of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:partition-of-unity}); the lecture's first version of that proof also uses it to pull back the plateau function of Lemma~\ref{lem:plateau}, equal to $1$ on $\overline{B}_\delta$ and supported in $B_\varepsilon$.
\leeref{Ch.~1, \emph{Regular Coordinate Balls}}
\end{defbox}

\textit{(Figure redrawn with the manifold side.)} Definition~\ref{def:regular-coordinate-ball} in pictures. Left, in $M$: the chart domain $U$, the regular coordinate ball $B$ around $p = \varphi^{-1}(0)$, and the larger set $\varphi^{-1}(B_\varepsilon(0))$, which still lies in $U$. Right, their images under $\varphi$: the open set $\varphi(U) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$, the $\varepsilon$-ball inside it, and $\varphi(B) = B_\delta(0)$. The room between the two balls is where the plateau function of Lemma~\ref{lem:plateau}, used in the lecture's first version of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:partition-of-unity}, falls from $1$ to $0$.

\begin{lembox}[Regular Coordinate Balls Form a Basis]\thmlabel{lem:regular-balls-basis}
Let $\{U_\alpha\}$ be an open cover of $M$. The regular coordinate balls $B$ whose chart $(U, \varphi)$ can be chosen with $U$ inside some $U_\alpha$ form a basis of the topology of $M$.
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Filled in.)} Let $W$ be open and $x \in W$, say $x \in U_\alpha$. Take a chart $(V, \psi)$ at $x$, restrict it to $U = V \cap W \cap U_\alpha$, and translate so that $\varphi = \psi|_U - \psi(x)$ sends $x$ to $0$. $\varphi(U)$ is open, so it contains some $B_\varepsilon(0)$; for $0 < \delta < \varepsilon$, $B = \varphi^{-1}(B_\delta(0))$ is a regular coordinate ball with $x \in B \subseteq U \subseteq W$, and its chart domain $U$ lies in $U_\alpha$.
\end{proof}

\begin{thmbox}[Existence of Partitions of Unity]\thmlabel{thm:partition-of-unity}
If $\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ is any open cover of $M$, there is a partition of unity $\{\chi_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ subordinate to it.
\leeref{Theorem 2.23}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}[Proof (Lee's proof of Theorem~2.23)]
\textit{(The assigned reading, email of Oct 26: Lee, Chapter~2, from Lemma~2.20 to the beginning of the section on applications of partitions of unity, p.~44; for paracompactness, Theorem~1.15, p.~9. Lecture~22 began the proof; its first version is compared in the remark after this proof.)} Let $\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ be an open cover of $M$.

\emph{Step 1: a locally finite cover by regular coordinate balls.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:regular-balls-basis}, the regular coordinate balls whose chart domain lies in some $U_\alpha$ form a basis $\mathcal{B}$ of the topology of $M$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:manifolds-paracompact}, applied with this basis, $\{U_\alpha\}$ has a countable, locally finite open refinement $\{B_i\}_{i \ge 1}$ covering $M$ with every $B_i \in \mathcal{B}$. So for each $i$ there are a chart $(U_i, \varphi_i)$ and numbers $0 < \delta_i < \varepsilon_i$ with
\[
\varphi_i(B_i) = B_{\delta_i}(0), \qquad B_{\varepsilon_i}(0) \subseteq \varphi_i(U_i), \qquad U_i \subseteq U_{\alpha(i)} \ \text{ for some } \alpha(i) \in A
\]
(Definition~\ref{def:regular-coordinate-ball}). By Lemma~\ref{lem:locally-finite-closures}(1), the closures $\{\overline{B_i}\}$ also form a locally finite family.

\emph{Step 2: a function positive exactly on $B_i$.} With $h(t) = e^{-1/t}$ for $t > 0$ and $h(t) = 0$ for $t \le 0$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-cutoff}), define
\[
f_i = h\big(\delta_i^2 - |\varphi_i|^2\big) \ \text{ on } U_i, \qquad f_i = 0 \ \text{ on } M \setminus \overline{B_i} .
\]
\emph{Well defined.} The set $K_i = \varphi_i^{-1}\big(\overline{B}_{\delta_i}(0)\big)$ is compact, because $\overline{B}_{\delta_i}(0) \subseteq B_{\varepsilon_i}(0) \subseteq \varphi_i(U_i)$ is compact and $\varphi_i^{-1}$ is continuous; so $K_i$ is closed in $M$ (Hausdorff). It contains $B_i$ and lies in the closure of $B_i$ (every point of $\overline{B}_{\delta_i}(0)$ is a limit of points of $B_{\delta_i}(0)$), so $K_i = \overline{B_i}$. On the overlap $U_i \setminus \overline{B_i}$ of the two formulas, $|\varphi_i| > \delta_i$, so $h(\delta_i^2 - |\varphi_i|^2) = 0$: the two formulas agree. \emph{Smooth.} $f_i$ is smooth on the open set $U_i$ (a composition of smooth maps) and zero on the open set $M \setminus \overline{B_i}$, and these two open sets cover $M$. \emph{Support.} $f_i > 0$ exactly on $B_i$, so $\operatorname{supp} f_i = \overline{B_i} \subseteq U_i \subseteq U_{\alpha(i)}$.

\emph{Step 3: normalize.} The supports $\operatorname{supp} f_i = \overline{B_i}$ form a locally finite family (Step~1), so $f = \sum_i f_i$ is smooth by Lemma~\ref{lem:locally-finite-sum-smooth}. Each $f_i \ge 0$, and every $p$ lies in some $B_i$, where $f_i(p) > 0$; so $f > 0$ on $M$. Hence $g_i = f_i / f$ is smooth, $0 \le g_i \le 1$, $\operatorname{supp} g_i = \overline{B_i}$, and $\sum_i g_i = f / f = 1$.

\emph{Step 4: re-index by $A$.} For $\alpha \in A$ put
\[
\chi_\alpha = \sum_{i \,:\, \alpha(i) = \alpha} g_i ,
\]
the zero function if no $i$ has $\alpha(i) = \alpha$. The family $\{\operatorname{supp} g_i\} = \{\overline{B_i}\}$ is locally finite, so each $\chi_\alpha$ is smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:locally-finite-sum-smooth}); $0 \le \chi_\alpha \le \sum_i g_i = 1$; and $\sum_\alpha \chi_\alpha = \sum_i g_i = 1$, since each $i$ has exactly one $\alpha(i)$. \emph{Subordinate.} $\{\chi_\alpha \neq 0\} \subseteq \bigcup_{\alpha(i) = \alpha} B_i$, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:locally-finite-closures}(2) (the subfamily $\{B_i\}_{\alpha(i) = \alpha}$ is still locally finite)
\[
\operatorname{supp}\chi_\alpha \subseteq \overline{\bigcup_{\alpha(i) = \alpha} B_i} = \bigcup_{\alpha(i) = \alpha} \overline{B_i} \subseteq \bigcup_{\alpha(i) = \alpha} U_i \subseteq U_\alpha .
\]
\emph{Locally finite.} If an open set $W$ meets only finitely many $\overline{B_i}$, it meets $\operatorname{supp}\chi_\alpha$ only for the finitely many $\alpha = \alpha(i)$ of those $i$. So $\{\chi_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ is a partition of unity subordinate to $\{U_\alpha\}$ (Definitions~\ref{def:partition-of-unity} and~\ref{def:subordinate-partition}).
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[Lecture 22's First Version of the Construction]\label{rem:pou-lecture-version}
Lecture~22 built the functions differently: pull back the plateau function of Lemma~\ref{lem:plateau} (with $\delta_i < \varepsilon_i$) by $\varphi_i$ and extend by zero, as in step~2 of the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:bump-closed-ball}, which gives smooth $f_i$ with
\[
f_i|_{B_i} \equiv 1, \qquad \operatorname{supp} f_i \subseteq U_i \subseteq U_{\alpha(i)} ,
\]
so that $\sum_j f_j \ge 1$ everywhere; then $g_i = f_i / \sum_j f_j$ and $\chi_\alpha = \sum_{\alpha(i) = \alpha} g_i$, as in Steps~3 and~4. One point needs care in that version: local finiteness of $\{B_i\}$ does not by itself make $\{\operatorname{supp} f_i\}$ locally finite, since $\operatorname{supp} f_i$ then sits in the larger ball $\varphi_i^{-1}(B_{\varepsilon_i}(0))$, not in $\overline{B_i}$. Lee's choice in Step~2, $f_i$ positive exactly on $B_i$ and supported in $\overline{B_i}$, avoids this; $f_i$ is then no longer $\equiv 1$ on $B_i$, only positive there, which is all the division needs.
\end{rembox}

\begin{propbox}[Bump Functions for Closed Sets]\thmlabel{prop:bump-closed-set}
Let $A \subseteq M$ be closed and $U \subseteq M$ open with $A \subseteq U$. Then there is a smooth $\psi : M \to [0, 1]$ with $\psi \equiv 1$ on $A$ and $\operatorname{supp}\psi \subseteq U$.
\leeref{Proposition 2.25}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lee's proof. Not part of the assigned reading, which stops before the applications of partitions of unity; Lee's proof of the Whitney embedding theorem, Theorem~\ref{thm:whitney}, uses it.)} Put $U_0 = U$ and $U_1 = M \setminus A$. Both are open ($A$ is closed), and they cover $M$, since a point not in $U$ is not in $A \subseteq U$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:partition-of-unity} there is a partition of unity $\{\chi_0, \chi_1\}$ subordinate to $\{U_0, U_1\}$. Let $\psi = \chi_0$. It is smooth, $0 \le \psi \le 1$, and $\operatorname{supp}\psi \subseteq U_0 = U$. For $p \in A$: $\operatorname{supp}\chi_1 \subseteq M \setminus A$, so $\chi_1(p) = 0$, and $\psi(p) = \chi_0(p) + \chi_1(p) = 1$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Application: Extending Functions and Vector Fields from a Submanifold}\label{sub:extension-submanifold}

\textit{(Assignment~7, Problem~1, and what its proof gives.)} The standard use of a partition of unity: build an object locally, in charts, and glue the local pieces. Here the local pieces come from adapted charts (Lemmas~\ref{lem:local-function-extension} and~\ref{lem:vf-local-extension}), and the gluing is the next lemma.

\begin{lembox}[Gluing Vector Fields with a Partition of Unity]\thmlabel{lem:vf-gluing}
Let $\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ be an open cover of $M$, $\mathbf{Y}_\alpha \in \mathfrak{X}(U_\alpha)$ for each $\alpha \in A$, and $\{\chi_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ a partition of unity subordinate to the cover (Definitions~\ref{def:partition-of-unity} and~\ref{def:subordinate-partition}). Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item each field $\chi_\alpha \mathbf{Y}_\alpha$, extended by $0$ outside $U_\alpha$, is a smooth vector field on $M$;
\item $\widetilde{\mathbf{X}} = \sum_{\alpha \in A} \chi_\alpha \mathbf{Y}_\alpha$ is a well-defined smooth vector field on $M$;
\item if $p \in M$ and $v \in T_pM$ satisfy $(\mathbf{Y}_\alpha)_p = v$ for every $\alpha$ with $p \in U_\alpha$, then $\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_p = v$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~7, Problem~1: the submitted solution, the steps ``Gluing'' and ``$\widetilde X$ extends $X$''.)} \emph{(1)} The field $\chi_\alpha \mathbf{Y}_\alpha$, $(\chi_\alpha \mathbf{Y}_\alpha)_q = \chi_\alpha(q)(\mathbf{Y}_\alpha)_q$ for $q \in U_\alpha$ and $0$ outside $U_\alpha$, is smooth on the open set $U_\alpha$, as the product of a smooth function and a smooth vector field; it vanishes on the open set $M \setminus \operatorname{supp}\chi_\alpha$; and these two open sets cover $M$, since $\operatorname{supp}\chi_\alpha \subseteq U_\alpha$. Smoothness is local, so $\chi_\alpha \mathbf{Y}_\alpha \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$.

\emph{(2)} Let $q \in M$. Since $\{\operatorname{supp}\chi_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ is locally finite, $q$ has an open neighbourhood $N$ for which $F = \{\alpha \in A : N \cap \operatorname{supp}\chi_\alpha \neq \varnothing\}$ is finite. For $\alpha \notin F$, $\chi_\alpha \mathbf{Y}_\alpha \equiv 0$ on $N$, so on $N$
\[
\widetilde{\mathbf{X}} = \sum_{\alpha \in F} \chi_\alpha \mathbf{Y}_\alpha ,
\]
a finite sum of smooth vector fields. Hence $\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}$ is a well-defined vector field, smooth on $N$; as $q$ was arbitrary, $\widetilde{\mathbf{X}} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$.

\emph{(3)} For $\alpha$ with $p \notin U_\alpha$, $\chi_\alpha(p) = 0$, since $\operatorname{supp}\chi_\alpha \subseteq U_\alpha$. Let $A_p = \{\alpha \in A : p \in U_\alpha\}$. Then $\sum_{\alpha \in A_p} \chi_\alpha(p) = \sum_{\alpha \in A} \chi_\alpha(p) = 1$, and
\[
\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_p = \sum_{\alpha \in A_p} \chi_\alpha(p)\, (\mathbf{Y}_\alpha)_p = \Big(\sum_{\alpha \in A_p} \chi_\alpha(p)\Big)\, v = v . \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[Extension of Smooth Functions from a Closed Submanifold]\thmlabel{prop:function-extension}
Let $S \subseteq M$ be a regular submanifold that is closed in $M$, and $f \in C^\infty(S)$. Then there is $\tilde f \in C^\infty(M)$ with $\tilde f|_S = f$.
\leeref{Lemma 5.34}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from the assignment; filled in: the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:vf-extension} below, with functions in place of vector fields.)} By Lemma~\ref{lem:adapted-product}, $S$ is covered by the domains of adapted charts $(U_\alpha, \varphi_\alpha)$, $\alpha \in A'$, with product images; let $\pi_\alpha : U_\alpha \to U_\alpha \cap S$ be their retractions (Lemma~\ref{lem:local-retraction}). Since $S$ is closed, $U_0 = M \setminus S$ is open, and $\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$, $A = A' \sqcup \{0\}$, is an open cover of $M$. Take a subordinate partition of unity $\{\chi_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:partition-of-unity}). Put $f_\alpha = f|_{U_\alpha \cap S} \circ \pi_\alpha \in C^\infty(U_\alpha)$ for $\alpha \in A'$, equal to $f$ on $U_\alpha \cap S$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:local-function-extension}, and $f_0 = 0$. As in Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-gluing}(1), each $\chi_\alpha f_\alpha$, extended by $0$, is smooth on $M$, with support in $\operatorname{supp}\chi_\alpha$; these supports are locally finite, so $\tilde f = \sum_{\alpha \in A} \chi_\alpha f_\alpha$ is smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:locally-finite-sum-smooth}). For $p \in S$: $\chi_0(p) = 0$, since $\operatorname{supp}\chi_0 \subseteq M \setminus S$; $\chi_\alpha(p) = 0$ if $p \notin U_\alpha$; and $f_\alpha(p) = f(p)$ if $p \in U_\alpha$, $\alpha \in A'$. So $\tilde f(p) = \big(\sum_{\alpha} \chi_\alpha(p)\big) f(p) = f(p)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{thmbox}[Extension of Vector Fields from a Submanifold]\thmlabel{thm:vf-extension}
Let $S \subseteq M$ be a regular submanifold, $\iota : S \hookrightarrow M$ the inclusion, and $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(S)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item There are an open set $W \supseteq S$ of $M$ and $\widetilde{\mathbf{X}} \in \mathfrak{X}(W)$ with $\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_p = \iota_{*p}(\mathbf{X}_p)$ for every $p \in S$.
\item If $S$ is closed in $M$, one can take $W = M$: there is $\widetilde{\mathbf{X}} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ with $\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_p = \iota_{*p}(\mathbf{X}_p)$ for every $p \in S$, that is, $\mathbf{X}$ is $\iota$-related to $\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}$ (Definition~\ref{def:F-related}).
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Problem 8-15}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~7, Problem~1: the submitted solution, which proves (2); its steps are stated above as Lemmas~\ref{lem:adapted-product}, \ref{lem:local-retraction}, \ref{lem:local-function-extension}, \ref{lem:vf-local-extension} and~\ref{lem:vf-gluing}. The problem as posted did not assume $S$ closed; the submitted solution adds this hypothesis, which Example~\ref{ex:vf-no-extension} shows is needed for (2). Part (1) is filled in.)} For $p \in S$, $\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_p \in T_pM$ while $\mathbf{X}_p \in T_pS$, so ``$\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}$ extends $\mathbf{X}$'' means $\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_p = \iota_{*p}(\mathbf{X}_p)$; $\iota_{*p}$ is kept explicit throughout.

\emph{(2) The open cover.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:adapted-product}, every point of $S$ lies in the domain of an adapted chart with product image; let $\{(U_\alpha, \varphi_\alpha)\}_{\alpha \in A'}$ be a family of such charts whose domains cover $S$. Since $S$ is closed in $M$, $U_0 = M \setminus S$ is open in $M$. With $A = A' \sqcup \{0\}$, $\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ is an open cover of $M$: every $p \in S$ lies in some $U_\alpha$ with $\alpha \in A'$, and every $p \notin S$ lies in $U_0$.

\emph{The partition of unity.} By Theorem~\ref{thm:partition-of-unity} there is a partition of unity $\{\chi_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ subordinate to $\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$.

\emph{The local extensions.} For $\alpha \in A'$, Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-local-extension} gives $\mathbf{Y}_\alpha \in \mathfrak{X}(U_\alpha)$ with $(\mathbf{Y}_\alpha)_p = \iota_{*p}(\mathbf{X}_p)$ for $p \in U_\alpha \cap S$; let $\mathbf{Y}_0 = 0 \in \mathfrak{X}(U_0)$.

\emph{Gluing.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-gluing}(1) and~(2), $\widetilde{\mathbf{X}} = \sum_{\alpha \in A} \chi_\alpha \mathbf{Y}_\alpha \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$. Let $p \in S$. Then $p \notin U_0$, and $(\mathbf{Y}_\alpha)_p = \iota_{*p}(\mathbf{X}_p)$ for every $\alpha \in A'$ with $p \in U_\alpha$; by Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-gluing}(3) with $v = \iota_{*p}(\mathbf{X}_p)$, $\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_p = \iota_{*p}(\mathbf{X}_p)$.

\emph{(1)} \textit{(Filled in.)} Without closedness, let $W = \bigcup_{\alpha \in A'} U_\alpha$, an open set containing $S$ and an open submanifold of $M$ (Definition~\ref{def:open-submanifold-smooth}). The $U_\alpha$, $\alpha \in A'$, form an open cover of $W$; Theorem~\ref{thm:partition-of-unity} on the manifold $W$ gives a subordinate partition of unity, and the gluing step, without the index $0$, gives $\widetilde{\mathbf{X}} \in \mathfrak{X}(W)$ with $\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_p = \iota_{*p}(\mathbf{X}_p)$ for $p \in S$.
\end{proof}

\begin{exbox}[A Vector Field on a Non-Closed Submanifold That Does Not Extend]\exlabel{ex:vf-no-extension}
\textit{(Not from the assignment.)} In $M = \mathbb{R}^2$ let $S = \{(x, 0) : x > 0\}$, and on $S$ let $\mathbf{X} = \frac{1}{x}\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\big|^S$. There is no $\widetilde{\mathbf{X}} \in \mathfrak{X}(\mathbb{R}^2)$ with $\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_p = \iota_{*p}(\mathbf{X}_p)$ for every $p \in S$. So the hypothesis ``$S$ closed'' in Theorem~\ref{thm:vf-extension}(2) cannot be dropped; by part~(1), $\mathbf{X}$ does extend to the open set $W = \{(x, y) : x > 0\}$, for instance by $\frac{1}{x}\, \partial/\partial x$.
\end{exbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Filled in.)} \emph{The setting.} On $U = \{(x, y) : x > 0\}$ the identity chart $(x, y)$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ is adapted to $S$, with $S \cap U = S = \{y = 0\}$; so $S$ is a regular submanifold of dimension $1$, with chart $x|_S$, and $\mathbf{X}$ is smooth on $S$, its coefficient $1/x$ being smooth for $x > 0$. $S$ is not closed: $(0, 0) \in \overline{S} \setminus S$.

\emph{No extension.} Suppose $\widetilde{\mathbf{X}} \in \mathfrak{X}(\mathbb{R}^2)$ extends $\mathbf{X}$, and write $\widetilde{\mathbf{X}} = a\, \partial/\partial x + b\, \partial/\partial y$ with $a, b$ smooth, hence continuous, on $\mathbb{R}^2$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}). For $p = (x, 0) \in S$, $\iota_{*p}(\partial/\partial x|^S_p) = \partial/\partial x|_p$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-tangent}), so $\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_p = \frac{1}{x}\, \partial/\partial x|_p$ and $a(x, 0) = 1/x$. As $x \to 0^+$, $a(x, 0) \to +\infty$; but $a$ is continuous at $(0, 0)$, so $a(x, 0) \to a(0, 0)$, a real number. This contradiction shows that no extension exists.
\end{proof}

% Lecture 23 (Wed Oct 28, 2026): exhaustion functions from partitions of unity
% ============================================================================

\subsection{An Application: Exhaustion Functions}\label{sub:exhaustion-proof}

\textit{Lecture 23. The application of partitions of unity needed for the sketch of the noncompact Whitney embedding theorem (\ref{sub:whitney-noncompact}): the existence of exhaustion functions, which partitions of unity make quick. Exhaustion functions were defined, and their existence stated, in Lecture~22 with that sketch; they are collected here so that the proof follows the statement.}

\begin{defbox}[Exhaustion Function]\deflabel{def:exhaustion-function}
An \textbf{exhaustion function} on $M$ is a smooth function $f : M \to \mathbb{R}$, $f \ge 0$, such that for every $c \in \mathbb{R}$ the \textbf{sublevel set} $f^{-1}\big((-\infty, c]\big)$ is compact.
\leeref{Ch.~2, \emph{Exhaustion Functions}}
\end{defbox}

The cartoon, also used in Morse theory: stand $M$ up with $f$ as the height. The level set at $c$ is the slice at height $c$, and the sublevel set is everything below it, compact for every $c$. It is not obvious that exhaustion functions always exist (Proposition~\ref{prop:exhaustion-exists}).

The proof starts from a countable cover by open sets with compact closures, which was set as an exercise.

\begin{lembox}[Countable Precompact Covers]\thmlabel{lem:precompact-cover}
Every manifold $M$ has a countable open cover $\{V_i\}_{i \ge 1}$ such that $\overline{V_i}$ is compact for every $i$.
\leeref{Proposition 2.28 (proof)}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Set in Lecture~23 as an exercise, the intended argument using paracompactness; filled in, by paracompactness.)} Every $p \in M$ has an open neighbourhood $W_p$ with $\overline{W_p}$ compact (Proposition~\ref{prop:locally-compact}). By Theorem~\ref{thm:manifolds-paracompact} the cover $\{W_p\}_{p \in M}$ has a countable open refinement $\{V_i\}$ covering $M$; if it is finite, repeat one of its sets to index it by $i \ge 1$. Each $V_i$ lies in some $W_{p(i)}$, so $\overline{V_i}$ is a closed subset of the compact set $\overline{W_{p(i)}}$, hence compact. (Another way: the countable basis of precompact sets built in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:compact-exhaustion} is already such a cover. Local finiteness of the refinement is not needed here.)
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[Exhaustion Functions Exist]\thmlabel{prop:exhaustion-exists}
Every smooth manifold admits an exhaustion function.
\leeref{Proposition 2.28}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~23. The proposition was announced in Lecture~22, where the sketch of the noncompact Whitney theorem used it before it was proved.)} Let $\{V_i\}_{i \ge 1}$ be as in Lemma~\ref{lem:precompact-cover}, and let $\{\chi_i\}_{i \ge 1}$ be a partition of unity subordinate to it (Theorem~\ref{thm:partition-of-unity}). Reviewing what this means (Definitions~\ref{def:partition-of-unity} and~\ref{def:subordinate-partition}):
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item $0 \le \chi_i \le 1$ for all $i$;
\item $\{\operatorname{supp}\chi_i\}$ is locally finite;
\item $\sum_i \chi_i(p) = 1$ for all $p \in M$ --- a finite sum at each point, by (2);
\item $\operatorname{supp}\chi_i \subseteq V_i$ for all $i$ --- this is what \emph{subordinate} means.
\end{enumerate}
The key construction is to define
\[
f = \sum_{j \ge 1} j\, \chi_j .
\]
Without the weights $j$ the sum would be identically $1$; the weights are what make the sublevel sets compact. Again this is a locally finite sum of smooth functions, so $f$ is smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:locally-finite-sum-smooth}); and $f \ge 0$ because the $\chi_j$ are nonnegative (in fact $f \ge \sum_j \chi_j = 1$). It remains to show that the sublevel sets are compact.

\emph{Claim.} For every $c \in \mathbb{R}$ and every integer $N \ge 0$ with $N \ge c$,
\[
f^{-1}\big((-\infty, c]\big) \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^N V_i \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^N \overline{V_i} .
\]
\emph{The claim implies the proposition.} $\bigcup_{i=1}^N \overline{V_i}$ is a finite union of compact sets, so it is compact. $f^{-1}((-\infty, c])$ is closed, since $f$ is continuous, and a closed subset of a compact set is compact.

\emph{Proof of the claim.} We prove the contrapositive. Let $p \notin \bigcup_{i=1}^N V_i$. For $i = 1, \ldots, N$, $p \notin V_i \supseteq \operatorname{supp}\chi_i$, so $\chi_i(p) = 0$. Hence the sum defining $f(p)$ really starts at $N + 1$, and since every coefficient is at least $N + 1$,
\[
f(p) = \sum_{j = N+1}^\infty j\, \chi_j(p) \ \ge\ (N + 1) \underbrace{\sum_{j = N+1}^\infty \chi_j(p)}_{=\, \sum_j \chi_j(p) \,=\, 1} = N + 1 > c .
\]
So $p \notin f^{-1}((-\infty, c])$.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[Why the Closures]\label{rem:why-closures}
Should the contrapositive use the union of the \emph{closures}? The proof shows the inclusion in $\bigcup_{i \le N} V_i$, which is contained in the union of the closures, so it makes no difference. The open sets give the stronger statement; the closures are where compactness lives, since the $V_i$ were chosen so that the $\overline{V_i}$ are compact, and $\bigcup_{i \le N} V_i$ alone need not be compact. Lee runs the contrapositive from $p \notin \bigcup_{j \le N} \overline{V_j}$ instead (Proposition~2.28); either way the sublevel set lands inside the compact set $\bigcup_{j \le N} \overline{V_j}$.
\end{rembox}

\textit{(Not from lecture; figure added, computed.)} The construction on $M = \mathbb{R}$, with $V_1 = (-1, 1)$ and $V_j = \{ j - 1.6 < |x| < j \}$ for $j \ge 2$, and $\chi_j$ obtained by normalizing bumps positive exactly on $V_j$. Then $f = \sum_j j\chi_j$ climbs one step on each successive $V_j$, so it grows like $|x|$. The sublevel set $f^{-1}((-\infty, 2.5])$ (red) lies inside $\overline{V_1} \cup \overline{V_2} \cup \overline{V_3} = [-3, 3]$, as the claim with $N = 3$ says.

Partitions of unity are a very common technique in the subject; an application from the assignments is the extension of vector fields from a closed submanifold (Theorem~\ref{thm:vf-extension}, Assignment~7, Problem~1).

\textbf{Transcription note (Lecture 23).} The board defined $f = \sum_{j \ge 0} j\chi_j$ but wrote the union in the claim from $i = 1$. These notes index the cover and the partition from $1$, as Lee does. If the index starts at $0$, the union in the claim must start at $i = 0$ too. Otherwise a point of $V_0$ outside $V_1, \ldots, V_N$ can have $f(p) = \sum_{j > N} j\chi_j(p) < N + 1$, since then $\sum_{j > N}\chi_j(p) = 1 - \chi_0(p)$.

% SECTION: THE WHITNEY EMBEDDING THEOREM (Lecture 21)
% ============================================================================
\section{The Whitney Embedding Theorem}\label{sec:whitney}

\roadmark{Stage: analysis}{Every manifold sits inside some Euclidean space; Sard's theorem pushes the dimension down to $2m + 1$.}

\textit{Lecture 21: the Whitney embedding and immersion theorems.}

The proof, for $M$ compact, has two parts with entirely different ideas: bump functions embed $M$ in some $\mathbb{R}^k$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:compact-embeds}), and projections along well-chosen lines lower the dimension (Lemmas~\ref{lem:projection-injective} and~\ref{lem:projection-immersion}). The lemmas come first; Theorem~\ref{thm:whitney-compact} assembles them. The general case, Theorem~\ref{thm:whitney}, is sketched in \ref{sub:whitney-noncompact}.

\begin{lembox}[Compact Manifolds Embed in Some $\mathbb{R}^k$]\thmlabel{lem:compact-embeds}
Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold of dimension $m$. Then there is an embedding $F : M \to \mathbb{R}^k$ for some $k$.
\leeref{proof of Theorem 6.15}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~21, Part~I of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:whitney-compact}, in the lecture's steps with details filled in.)} The tool is bump functions; the idea of a partition of unity (\ref{sec:partitions-of-unity}) is behind the construction.

\emph{The cover.} For every $x \in M$ choose a chart $(U_x, \varphi_x)$ at $x$ and an open coordinate ball $B_x \ni x$ with $\overline{B_x} \subseteq U_x$ and $\varphi_x(\overline{B_x})$ a closed ball in $\mathbb{R}^m$ --- possible because $\varphi_x(U_x)$ is open, so it contains a closed Euclidean ball $\overline{B}(\varphi_x(x), r')$ about $\varphi_x(x)$; fix $0 < r < r'$ and let $\overline{B_x}$ be the preimage under $\varphi_x$ of the smaller closed ball $\overline{B}(\varphi_x(x), r)$. Let $\chi_x \in C^\infty_0(M)$ with $\operatorname{supp}\chi_x \subseteq U_x$ and $\chi_x \equiv 1$ on $\overline{B_x}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:bump-closed-ball}, with these radii $r < r'$). The \emph{open} balls $B_x$ cover $M$; it matters that the cover is by the $B_x$, not the $U_x$, since the steps below use $\chi_i \equiv 1$ on $B_i$. $M$ is compact, so finitely many cover; relabel them $B_1, \ldots, B_n$, with charts $(U_i, \varphi_i)$ and bump functions $\chi_i$.

\emph{The map.} Each $\chi_i\varphi_i : M \to \mathbb{R}^m$, defined as $\chi_i \varphi_i$ on $U_i$ and $0$ outside, is smooth: it is smooth on $U_i$ and zero on the open set $M \setminus \operatorname{supp}\chi_i$, and these cover $M$ ($\operatorname{supp}\chi_i$ is compact, hence closed). Define
\[
F = \big(\chi_1\varphi_1, \ldots, \chi_n\varphi_n, \chi_1, \ldots, \chi_n\big) : M \to \mathbb{R}^{nm + n},
\]
a large Euclidean space: $n$ blocks of $m$ components, then $n$ scalars.

\emph{$F$ is injective.} Suppose $F(p) = F(q)$. There is $i$ with $p \in B_i$, so $\chi_i(p) = 1$. The last $n$ components of $F$ are the $\chi$'s, so $\chi_i(q) = \chi_i(p) = 1$; in particular $\chi_i(q) \neq 0$, so $q \in U_i$, because $\chi_i$ vanishes outside $U_i$ ($q$ need not lie in $B_i$). The $i$-th block gives $\chi_i(p)\varphi_i(p) = \chi_i(q)\varphi_i(q)$, that is, $\varphi_i(p) = \varphi_i(q)$; the charts are bijective, so $p = q$. The last $n$ components, the $\chi$'s, are what place $p$ and $q$ in the same coordinate chart.

\emph{$F$ is an immersion.} Write $F = (F_1, \ldots, F_n, \chi_1, \ldots, \chi_n)$ with $F_j = \chi_j\varphi_j : M \to \mathbb{R}^m$. Let $p \in M$, $v \in T_pM$, and $\gamma$ a curve with $\gamma(0) = p$ and $D_\gamma = v$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:every-vector-velocity}). Using curves, $dF_p(v) = \frac{d}{dt}\big|_{t=0} F(\gamma(t)) = (v_1, \ldots, v_n, \ldots)$, with $v_j = d(F_j)_p(v) \in \mathbb{R}^m$, componentwise. Choose $i$ with $p \in B_i$. Then $\chi_i \equiv 1$ on the open set $B_i \ni p$, so $F_i = \varphi_i$ near $p$ and $v_i = d(\varphi_i)_p(v)$ --- equivalently $d(\chi_i)_p = 0$, since $\chi_i \equiv 1$ in a neighbourhood of $p$. As $\varphi_i$ is a diffeomorphism onto its image (Proposition~\ref{prop:chart-diffeo}), $v \neq 0$ gives $v_i \neq 0$, so $dF_p(v) \neq 0$: $dF_p$ is injective.

\emph{An embedding.} An injective immersion of a compact manifold is an embedding (Corollary~\ref{cor:compact-embedding}).
\end{proof}

The lecture's cartoon for injectivity: $\chi_i \equiv 1$ on $\overline{B}_i$ (possibly also a little outside it), and zero outside $U_i$. So $\chi_i(q) = 1$ forces $q \in U_i$, where the chart $\varphi_i$ separates points.


\textit{Part~II: lower the ambient dimension.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:compact-embeds}, a compact $M$ may be taken to be a regular submanifold $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ (the image of the embedding, Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image}). Regard $\mathbb{R}^{N-1} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ by $x \mapsto (x, 0)$. To every line $\ell \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ through $0$ that is transverse to $\mathbb{R}^{N-1}$, that is, not contained in it, so that $\mathbb{R}^N = \mathbb{R}^{N-1} \oplus \ell$, associate the projection along $\ell$, a linear map $\mathbb{R}^N \to \mathbb{R}^{N-1}$ with kernel $\ell$, and its restriction
\[
\pi_\ell : M \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^{N-1} .
\]
We want: \emph{if $N > 2m + 1$, there is an $\ell$ such that $\pi_\ell$ is an embedding.} Applying this repeatedly lowers $N$ to $2m + 1$, where the hypothesis $N > 2m + 1$ stops holding.

\begin{lembox}[Lines in a Hyperplane Have Measure Zero]\thmlabel{lem:hyperplane-lines}
Identify $\mathbb{R}^{N-1}$ with $\{y \in \mathbb{R}^N : y^N = 0\}$. The set
\[
H = \{\, [y] \in \mathbb{RP}^{N-1} : y^N = 0 \,\}
\]
of lines through $0$ contained in $\mathbb{R}^{N-1}$ is an embedded submanifold of $\mathbb{RP}^{N-1}$ of dimension $N - 2$, and it has measure zero in $\mathbb{RP}^{N-1}$.
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~6, Problem~4, with $N = 2m + 1$; the submitted solution. The fact is used in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:projection-injective} as well.)} $H$ is well defined, since $y^N = 0$ is unchanged by scaling $y$. Index the coordinates of $\mathbb{R}^N$ by $1, \ldots, N$, and for $i = 1, \ldots, N$ let $U_i = \{[y] : y^i \neq 0\}$ with the affine chart $\varphi_i([y]) = (y^k/y^i)_{k \neq i}$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:rpn-atlas}). Then $H \cap U_N = \varnothing$, and for $i \leq N - 1$, $\varphi_i(H \cap U_i)$ is the coordinate hyperplane $\{y^N/y^i = 0\}$ of $\mathbb{R}^{N-1}$. So the charts $\varphi_i$ are slice charts for $H$, and $H$ is an embedded $(N-2)$-dimensional submanifold of $\mathbb{RP}^{N-1}$. Since $N - 2 < N - 1$, $H$ has measure zero in $\mathbb{RP}^{N-1}$ by Corollary~\ref{cor:sard-low-dim}, applied to its inclusion. \textit{(Filled in: directly from Definition~\ref{def:measure-zero-manifold}, the chart images $\varphi_i(H \cap U_i)$ are hyperplanes, of measure zero in $\mathbb{R}^{N-1}$ by the same corollary applied to a linear map $\mathbb{R}^{N-2} \to \mathbb{R}^{N-1}$ onto each.)}
\end{proof}

\begin{lembox}[Projections That Stay Injective]\thmlabel{lem:projection-injective}
Let $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ be a regular submanifold of dimension $m$, with $N > 2m + 1$. Then the lines $\ell \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ through $0$ for which $\ell \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{N-1}$, or $\pi_\ell : M \to \mathbb{R}^{N-1}$ is not injective, form a set of measure zero in $\mathbb{RP}^{N-1}$. In particular there are lines $\ell \not\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{N-1}$ with $\pi_\ell$ injective.
\leeref{Lemma 6.13}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~21, Part~II of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:whitney-compact}.)} The key idea: let $\Delta = \{ (p, p) : p \in M \}$, closed in $M \times M$ since $M$ is Hausdorff, and
\[
\sigma : (M \times M) \setminus \Delta \longrightarrow \mathbb{RP}^{N-1}, \qquad (p, q) \longmapsto \operatorname{span}(q - p),
\]
the line through $0$ parallel to the secant from $p$ to $q$, the vector $\vec{pq}$; $q - p \neq 0$ because $p \neq q$. \textit{(Filled in.)} $\sigma$ is smooth: it is $(p, q) \mapsto q - p \in \mathbb{R}^N \setminus \{0\}$ followed by the quotient map to $\mathbb{RP}^{N-1}$, which in the chart $\varphi_i$ of Corollary~\ref{cor:rpn-atlas} is $w \mapsto (w^k/w^i)_{k \neq i}$, rational with nonvanishing denominator. Its domain is open in $M \times M$, of dimension $2m$, and $\dim \mathbb{RP}^{N-1} = N - 1$. If $2m < N - 1$, the image of $\sigma$ has measure zero (Corollary~\ref{cor:sard-low-dim}). So do the lines contained in $\mathbb{R}^{N-1}$: they form a copy of $\mathbb{RP}^{N-2}$, of lower dimension, whose image under the smooth inclusion has measure zero by the same corollary (Lemma~\ref{lem:hyperplane-lines}). A union of two sets of measure zero has measure zero (Proposition~\ref{prop:measure-zero-every-chart}), so its complement is dense (Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(4), in charts): pick $\ell$ not in the image of $\sigma$ and transverse to $\mathbb{R}^{N-1}$. For such $\ell$, $\pi_\ell$ is injective: $\pi_\ell(p) = \pi_\ell(q)$ means $q - p \in \ker = \ell$, so for $p \neq q$, $\ell = \operatorname{span}(q - p) = \sigma(p, q)$, contrary to the choice. So injectivity is lost exactly when the secant of some pair $p \neq q$ is parallel to the line of projection. The condition $2m < N - 1$ is $N > 2m + 1$, exactly the bound in the statement.
\end{proof}

Projection along a line $\ell$, in the plane ($N = 2$). Points of $M$ slide along lines parallel to $\ell$ onto $\mathbb{R}^{N-1}$. Two points $p \neq q$ collide exactly when the secant $q - p$ is parallel to $\ell$; choosing $\ell$ outside the image of $\sigma$ avoids every such pair. This argument gives the non-optimal Whitney embedding theorem, into $\mathbb{R}^{2m+1}$.

\textit{(Not from lecture; figure added.)} Why the bound is $2m + 1$. For a curve ($m = 1$) in $\mathbb{R}^3$ ($N = 3$), $(M \times M) \setminus \Delta$ has dimension $2m = 2 = N - 1$, so the secant directions $\sigma(p, q)$ can fill an open set of $\mathbb{RP}^2$ and Corollary~\ref{cor:sard-low-dim} does not apply. Indeed, projecting a curve in space onto a plane along $\ell$ typically produces crossings: here $q - p$ is parallel to $\ell$, and $\pi_\ell(p) = \pi_\ell(q)$. The shadow is still an immersed curve, matching the immersion into $\mathbb{R}^{2m}$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:whitney}, but not an embedded one.
