\begin{lembox}[When a Projection Is an Immersion]\thmlabel{lem:projection-immersion-criterion}
Let $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ be a regular submanifold of dimension $m$, $\ell = \mathbb{R}v$ a line with $v^N \neq 0$, and $UM$ the unit tangent bundle (Definition~\ref{def:unit-tangent-bundle}), with
\[
G : UM \to \mathbb{RP}^{N-1}, \qquad G(x, u) = [u] .
\]
Then $G$ is smooth, and the projection $\pi_\ell : M \to \mathbb{R}^{N-1}$ along $\ell$ satisfies $d(\pi_\ell)_x = \pi_\ell|_{T_xM}$, so that
\[
\pi_\ell \text{ is an immersion} \iff T_xM \cap \ell = \{0\} \text{ for every } x \in M \iff \ell \notin G(UM) .
\]
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~6, Problem~4, with $N = 2m + 1$; the submitted solution, which writes $\pi_v$ for $\pi_\ell$. Tangent spaces are geometric, $T_xM \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$.)} \emph{The projection.} With $\mathbb{R}^{N-1} = \{y : y^N = 0\}$, the projection with kernel $\ell = \mathbb{R}v$ is
\[
\pi_\ell(y) = y - \frac{y^N}{v^N}\,v .
\]
It is linear, its values have last coordinate $0$, and $\pi_\ell(y) = 0$ if and only if $y \in \mathbb{R}v$. On $M$ it is $F = \pi_\ell \circ \iota$, with $\iota : M \hookrightarrow \mathbb{R}^N$ the inclusion.

\emph{The differential of $F$.} Since $\pi_\ell$ is linear, $\pi_\ell(y + tw) = \pi_\ell(y) + t\,\pi_\ell(w)$, so $d(\pi_\ell)_y(w) = \frac{d}{dt}\big|_{t=0}\pi_\ell(y + tw) = \pi_\ell(w)$ for all $y, w \in \mathbb{R}^N$; that is, $d(\pi_\ell)_y = \pi_\ell$. By the chain rule, for $x \in M$, $dF_x = d(\pi_\ell)_x \circ d\iota_x = \pi_\ell|_{T_xM}$.

\emph{Its kernel.} A vector $w \in T_xM$ satisfies $\pi_\ell(w) = 0$ if and only if $w \in \ker \pi_\ell = \mathbb{R}v$, so $\ker dF_x = T_xM \cap \mathbb{R}v$. The linear map $dF_x$ is injective if and only if this is $\{0\}$: no nonzero tangent vector to $M$ at $x$ is parallel to $v$. This is the first equivalence.

\emph{Restating the condition with $G$.} For nonzero $y \in \mathbb{R}^N$, $[y] \in \mathbb{RP}^{N-1}$ is the line $\mathbb{R}y$, so $[y] = [y']$ if and only if $y' = cy$ for some $c \neq 0$. Suppose some nonzero $w \in T_xM$ is parallel to $v$, say $w = cv$; then $c \neq 0$ since $w \neq 0$. Let $u = w/|w|$. Since $T_xM$ is a subspace, $u \in T_xM$, and $|u| = 1$, so $(x, u) \in UM$. Moreover $u = \frac{c}{|w|}\,v$, so $G(x, u) = [u] = [v]$ and $[v] \in G(UM)$. Conversely, suppose $[v] = G(x, u) = [u]$ for some $(x, u) \in UM$. Then $u = cv$ for some $c \neq 0$, so $u$ is a tangent vector to $M$ at $x$, nonzero since $|u| = 1$, and parallel to $v$. Combining both directions with the first equivalence gives the second.

\emph{$G$ is smooth.} It is the composite of the smooth map $(x, u) \mapsto u$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}(1)), which takes values in $\mathbb{R}^N \setminus \{0\}$ since $|u| = 1$, with the smooth quotient map $q : \mathbb{R}^N \setminus \{0\} \to \mathbb{RP}^{N-1}$, $q(y) = [y]$, which in the chart $\varphi_i$ of Corollary~\ref{cor:rpn-atlas} is $y \mapsto (y^k/y^i)_{k \neq i}$, rational with nonvanishing denominator.
\end{proof}

\begin{lembox}[Projections That Stay Immersions]\thmlabel{lem:projection-immersion}
Let $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ be a regular submanifold of dimension $m$, with $N > 2m$. Then the lines $\ell \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ through $0$ for which $\ell \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{N-1}$, or $\pi_\ell : M \to \mathbb{R}^{N-1}$ is not an immersion, form a set of measure zero in $\mathbb{RP}^{N-1}$. In particular there are lines $\ell \not\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{N-1}$ with $\pi_\ell$ an immersion.
\leeref{Lemma 6.13; Problem 6-2}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~6, Problem~4: the submitted solution, written there for $N = 2m + 1$; it uses $N$ only through $2m - 1 < N - 1$, so it proves the lemma for every $N > 2m$, one less than Lemma~\ref{lem:projection-injective} needs.)} Lecture~21 sketched the same idea as for Lemma~\ref{lem:projection-injective}, with tangent vectors in place of pairs $(p, q)$, as if $p$ and $q$ were infinitesimally close together: map nonzero tangent vectors to lines, $(p, v) \mapsto \mathbb{R}v$, with $T_pM \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ (the homework restricts to unit vectors $v$), and choose $\ell$ also outside its image. A line outside this image gives an immersion precisely because the differential of the projection is the projection itself (Lemma~\ref{lem:projection-immersion-criterion}).

\emph{$G(UM)$ has measure zero.} By Proposition~\ref{prop:unit-tangent-bundle}, $UM$ is a regular submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^{2N}$ of dimension $2m - 1$, and $G : UM \to \mathbb{RP}^{N-1}$, $G(x, u) = [u]$, is smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:projection-immersion-criterion}). Since $\dim UM = 2m - 1 < N - 1 = \dim \mathbb{RP}^{N-1}$, Corollary~\ref{cor:sard-low-dim} shows that $G(UM)$ has measure zero in $\mathbb{RP}^{N-1}$.

\emph{The bad lines.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:projection-immersion-criterion}, a line $\ell \not\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{N-1}$ for which $\pi_\ell$ is not an immersion lies in $G(UM)$. So the lines of the statement lie in $G(UM) \cup H$, with $H$ the lines in $\mathbb{R}^{N-1}$, of measure zero by Lemma~\ref{lem:hyperplane-lines}. A union of two sets of measure zero has measure zero (Proposition~\ref{prop:measure-zero-every-chart}), and so does any subset of it.

\emph{Choosing $\ell$.} On the other hand, $\mathbb{RP}^{N-1}$ does not have measure zero, since $\varphi_N(U_N) = \mathbb{R}^{N-1}$ does not have Lebesgue measure zero (Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(4) and Proposition~\ref{prop:measure-zero-every-chart}). Hence there exists $[v] \in \mathbb{RP}^{N-1} \setminus \big(G(UM) \cup H\big)$. Let $v$ be any representative. Since $[v] \notin H$, $v^N \neq 0$, so $v \in \mathbb{R}^N \setminus \mathbb{R}^{N-1}$ and $\pi_\ell$, $\ell = \mathbb{R}v$, is defined; since $[v] \notin G(UM)$, Lemma~\ref{lem:projection-immersion-criterion} shows that $\pi_\ell : M \to \mathbb{R}^{N-1}$ is an immersion.
\end{proof}

\begin{thmbox}[The Whitney Theorems for Compact Manifolds]\thmlabel{thm:whitney-compact}
Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold of dimension $m$. Then there is an embedding $M \to \mathbb{R}^{2m+1}$ and an immersion $M \to \mathbb{R}^{2m}$.
\leeref{Theorems 6.15 and 6.18, compact case}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~21, in two steps with entirely different ideas: Lemma~\ref{lem:compact-embeds} and Lemmas~\ref{lem:projection-injective}--\ref{lem:projection-immersion}; the immersion lemma was a homework problem, Assignment~6, Problem~4, filled in above.)}

\emph{Step 1: some Euclidean space.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:compact-embeds} there is an embedding $M \to \mathbb{R}^N$ for some $N$. Its image is a regular submanifold diffeomorphic to $M$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image}); replace $M$ by it.

\emph{Step 2: one dimension less.} Suppose $N > 2m + 1$. By Lemmas~\ref{lem:projection-injective} and~\ref{lem:projection-immersion}, the lines $\ell$ that lie in $\mathbb{R}^{N-1}$, or for which $\pi_\ell$ is not injective, or not an immersion, form the union of two sets of measure zero in $\mathbb{RP}^{N-1}$, which has measure zero (Proposition~\ref{prop:measure-zero-every-chart}). A set of measure zero contains no nonempty open set (Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(4), in a chart), so it is not all of $\mathbb{RP}^{N-1}$: choose $\ell$ outside it. Then $\pi_\ell : M \to \mathbb{R}^{N-1}$ is an injective immersion of a compact manifold, hence an embedding (Corollary~\ref{cor:compact-embedding}), and its image is a regular submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^{N-1}$ diffeomorphic to $M$.

\emph{Step 3: repeat.} Apply Step~2 while $N > 2m + 1$, lowering $N$ by one each time until $N = 2m + 1$: this ends with an embedding $M \to \mathbb{R}^{2m+1}$.

\emph{Step 4: the immersion.} \textit{(Assignment~6, Problem~4; the submitted solution's reduction.)} Now $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{2m+1}$, and $N = 2m + 1 > 2m$, so Lemma~\ref{lem:projection-immersion} gives a line $\ell \not\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{2m}$ with $\pi_\ell : M \to \mathbb{R}^{2m}$ an immersion. For the original manifold, compose with the diffeomorphism $\iota$ from $M$ onto its image in $\mathbb{R}^{2m+1}$: if $F'$ is an immersion of $\iota(M)$, then so is $F' \circ \iota$, since by the chain rule $d(F' \circ \iota)_x = dF'_{\iota(x)} \circ d\iota_x$, where $d\iota_x$ is an isomorphism onto $T_{\iota(x)}\iota(M)$ and $dF'_{\iota(x)}$ is injective on $T_{\iota(x)}\iota(M)$. So one more projection is possible: where the embedding stops at $2m + 1$, the immersion goes one dimension further.
\end{proof}

% Lecture 22 (Mon Oct 26, 2026): the noncompact case, sketched
% ============================================================================

\subsection{The Noncompact Case: A Sketch}\label{sub:whitney-noncompact}

\textit{Lecture 22. Only a sketch of the proof, with precise references to Lee for the rest. The noncompact proof has the same two parts as the compact one --- first put $M$ in some Euclidean space, then project as much as you can --- and the lecture sketched only the first. The main tool is the existence of exhaustion functions.}

The sketch uses an exhaustion function (Definition~\ref{def:exhaustion-function}): a smooth $f \ge 0$ on $M$ whose sublevel sets $f^{-1}\big((-\infty, c]\big)$ are all compact. Every smooth manifold has one (Proposition~\ref{prop:exhaustion-exists}); both are in \ref{sub:exhaustion-proof}, where partitions of unity give the proof.

\textit{Slicing $M$ into compact pieces.} The idea is to use level sets of an exhaustion function to slice $M$ into compact pieces, which have boundary (ignored in the sketch), to embed each piece, and to keep track of the overlaps. Let $f$ be an exhaustion function. Its singular values have measure zero (Theorem~\ref{thm:sard}), so every interval contains regular values; for each $i = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$ pick regular values $a_i, b_i$ with $i < a_i < b_i < i + 1$, and put
\[
E_i = f^{-1}\big([b_{i-1}, a_{i+1}]\big), \qquad D_i = f^{-1}\big([i, i+1]\big) \qquad (i \ge 1),
\]
with $E_0 = f^{-1}\big((-\infty, a_1]\big)$ and $D_0 = f^{-1}\big((-\infty, 1]\big)$. Each $E_i$ is compact (a closed subset of a sublevel set), and a manifold with boundary, because $b_{i-1}$ and $a_{i+1}$ are regular values. Then $M = \bigcup_i D_i$, $D_i \subseteq \operatorname{Int}E_i$, and, for later use,
\[
E_i \cap E_{i+2} = \varnothing ,
\]
since $E_i \subseteq f^{-1}\big((-\infty, a_{i+1}]\big)$ and $E_{i+2} \subseteq f^{-1}\big([b_{i+1}, \infty)\big)$ with $a_{i+1} < b_{i+1}$; more generally $E_i \cap E_j = \varnothing$ when $|i - j| \ge 2$.

Left: a sublevel set of an exhaustion function on a surface with holes, as on the board. \textit{(Not from lecture: the surface is plotted, not drawn.)} Here $M$ is the boundary of a thickened ladder in $\mathbb{R}^3$, the zero set of a smooth function: a noncompact surface (it continues upward) with a hole between consecutive rungs, and $f$ is the height, an exhaustion function on $M$; the sublevel set $f^{-1}\big((-\infty, c]\big)$ (orange) is compact. Right: the slicing (not pictured in Lee). $E_i$ runs from the regular value $b_{i-1}$, just below $i$, to $a_{i+1}$, just above $i + 1$, and contains the band $D_i$ (teal) between the integer levels $i$ and $i + 1$ in its interior. The height has critical points at the top and bottom of each rung, where the topology of the sublevel sets changes (the starting point of Morse theory); the levels $c$, $a_i$, $b_i$ are regular values, so they miss these heights, and each $E_i$ is a compact manifold with boundary --- here $E_i$ contains two of the holes.

\begin{propbox}[A Proper Embedding from the Slices]\thmlabel{prop:noncompact-embedding}
Let $f$ be an exhaustion function on $M$, $\dim M = m$, and $E_i, D_i$ as above. Suppose that each $E_i$ admits an embedding $F_i : E_i \to \mathbb{R}^{2m+1}$, and let $\rho_i : M \to \mathbb{R}$ be smooth with $\operatorname{supp}\rho_i \subseteq \operatorname{Int}E_i$ and $\rho_i \equiv 1$ on a neighbourhood of $D_i$. Then
\[
F = \Big( \sum_{i \text{ even}} \rho_i F_i,\ \sum_{i \text{ odd}} \rho_i F_i,\ f \Big) : M \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^{2(2m+1)+1}
\]
is a proper injective immersion, hence an embedding.
\leeref{Theorem 6.15 (proof)}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~22 gave the construction and the reason for properness; injectivity and the immersion property, completely analogous to the compact case, are filled in from Lee. The two hypotheses are assumed, not proved, in the lecture: that compact manifolds with boundary embed in $\mathbb{R}^{2m+1}$ (manifolds with boundary are not discussed in the course), and that the cutoffs $\rho_i$ exist, which partitions of unity provide.)}

\emph{$F$ is smooth.} $\rho_iF_i$, a priori defined only on $E_i$, extends smoothly by zero outside $E_i$: it is smooth on the open set $\operatorname{Int}E_i$ and zero on the open set $M \setminus \operatorname{supp}\rho_i$, which together cover $M$. The sums are locally finite: the $E_i$ with $i$ of one parity are pairwise disjoint closed sets, and only finitely many of them meet a neighbourhood $f^{-1}\big((c - 1, c + 1)\big)$, since $E_i \subseteq f^{-1}([i - 1, i + 2])$. So near each point at most one term of each sum is nonzero.

\emph{$F$ is proper} --- properness comes from having $f$ as a component. If $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{2(2m+1)+1}$ is compact, the last coordinate is bounded on $K$, say by $c$, so $F^{-1}(K)$ is a closed subset of the compact sublevel set $f^{-1}\big((-\infty, c]\big)$, hence compact (Definition~\ref{def:proper}).

\emph{$F$ is injective.} Suppose $F(p) = F(q)$. Then $f(p) = f(q)$, so if $p \in D_j$ then $q \in D_j$, and $\rho_j(p) = \rho_j(q) = 1$. In the block of the parity of $j$, every other term vanishes at $p$ and $q$: for $i \neq j$ of that parity $|i - j| \ge 2$, so $\operatorname{supp}\rho_i \subseteq E_i$ misses $E_j \supseteq D_j$. So that block reads $F_j(p) = F_j(q)$, and $F_j$ is injective: $p = q$.

\emph{$F$ is an immersion.} Let $p \in D_j$, and $W \subseteq \operatorname{Int}E_j$ an open neighbourhood of $p$ on which $\rho_j \equiv 1$. On $W$ the block of the parity of $j$ is $F_j$, since the other terms of that block are supported in sets $E_i$ disjoint from $E_j$. So that block of $dF_p$ is $d(F_j)_p$, injective because $F_j$ is an embedding; hence $dF_p$ is injective.

\emph{An embedding.} A proper injective immersion is an embedding (Theorem~\ref{thm:proper-embedding}).
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[{Why the Last Coordinate Is $f$}]\label{rem:q-last-coordinate-proper}
The last coordinate $f$ in Proposition~\ref{prop:noncompact-embedding} is not there for injectivity: it makes $F$ proper, since an exhaustion function is proper, and properness is what turns an injective immersion of a noncompact manifold into an embedding (Theorem~\ref{thm:proper-embedding}).
\end{rembox}

\textit{(Not from lecture; figure added.)} Why the noncompact embedding is made proper. The curve $\gamma(t) = \big(\sin 2s, \sin s\big)$, $s = \pi + 2\arctan t$, is an injective immersion $\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^2$, but both ends approach $\gamma(0)$: the preimage of a small closed disc $\overline{B}$ about $\gamma(0)$ contains two half-lines, so $\gamma$ is not proper, and its image is not an embedded submanifold near $\gamma(0)$. Adding an exhaustion function as an extra coordinate makes the map proper: it pulls the ends apart in height, which is what Proposition~\ref{prop:noncompact-embedding} does with $f$.
%% <<< END ADDED



\textit{The projection step.} For a noncompact manifold the image can spread all over the ambient space, and a projection of an injective immersion need not be proper. Lee's remedy, Lemma~\ref{lem:proper-embedding-2m1}: squeeze the image into a tube, ball $\times\ \mathbb{R}$, where projections can be controlled. Lee's proof of the theorem also embeds each slice $E_i$, a compact manifold with boundary; manifolds with boundary are not treated in these notes, and the two facts used about them are cited after the lemma (Proposition~\ref{prop:whitney-slices}).

\begin{lembox}[{Proper Embeddings into $\mathbb{R}^{2m+1}$}]\thmlabel{lem:proper-embedding-2m1}
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold of dimension $m$. If $M$ admits an embedding into some $\mathbb{R}^N$, then it admits a proper embedding into $\mathbb{R}^{2m+1}$.
\leeref{Lemma 6.14}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lee's proof of Lemma~6.14, the assigned reading of Oct 26; Lee's ``simple geometric argument'' about two tubes is written out in Step~2(e).)} For a line $S$ through $0$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $R > 0$, the \emph{tube} with axis $S$ and radius $R$ is the open set
\[
T_R(S) = \{ x \in \mathbb{R}^n : |x - y| < R \text{ for some } y \in S \} .
\]

\emph{Step 1: a proper embedding into a tube.} Let $F : M \to \mathbb{R}^N$ be an embedding. The map $G : \mathbb{R}^N \to B^N = \{ y : |y| < 1 \}$, $G(x) = x / \sqrt{1 + |x|^2}$, is a diffeomorphism: it is smooth, $|G(x)|^2 = |x|^2 / (1 + |x|^2) < 1$, and $y \mapsto y / \sqrt{1 - |y|^2}$ is a smooth inverse (if $y = G(x)$ then $1 - |y|^2 = 1/(1 + |x|^2)$, so $y / \sqrt{1 - |y|^2} = x$; the other composite is checked the same way). Let $f$ be an exhaustion function on $M$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:exhaustion-exists}) and
\[
\Phi_0 = (G \circ F, f) : M \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^{N+1} .
\]
$\Phi_0$ is injective, because $G \circ F$ is. It is an immersion: the first $N$ components of $d(\Phi_0)_p$ form $dG_{F(p)} \circ dF_p$, injective since $dF_p$ is injective and $dG_{F(p)}$ is invertible. It is proper: if $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{N+1}$ is compact, the last coordinate is at most some $c$ on $K$, so $\Phi_0^{-1}(K)$ is a closed subset ($\Phi_0$ is continuous) of the compact set $f^{-1}\big((-\infty, c]\big)$, hence compact. By Theorem~\ref{thm:proper-embedding}, $\Phi_0$ is a proper embedding. Its image lies in $B^N \times \mathbb{R} \subseteq T_1(S_0)$, with $S_0$ the last coordinate axis: $(y, t)$ with $|y| < 1$ is at distance $|y| < 1$ from $(0, t) \in S_0$.

\emph{Step 2: lowering the dimension by one.} Claim: \emph{if $\Phi : M \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is a proper embedding with $\Phi(M) \subseteq T_R(S)$ for a line $S$ through $0$, and $n > 2m + 1$, then there are a line $\ell$ and a proper embedding $\Phi' = \pi_\ell \circ \Phi : M \to \mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ with $\Phi'(M) \subseteq T_{R'}(S')$ for a line $S'$ through $0$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ and some $R'$.}

(a) \emph{Choice of $\ell$.} $M' = \Phi(M)$ is a regular submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^n$ of dimension $m$, and $\Phi$ is a diffeomorphism onto it (Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image}). By Lemma~\ref{lem:projection-injective} ($n > 2m + 1$) and Lemma~\ref{lem:projection-immersion} ($n > 2m$), the lines $\ell$ with $\ell \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n-1}$, or with $\pi_\ell|_{M'}$ not injective, or not an immersion, form a set of measure zero in $\mathbb{RP}^{n-1}$; so does the single point $S$, and so does the union $Z$ of these sets (Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(2), read in charts, Proposition~\ref{prop:measure-zero-every-chart}). $Z$ is not all of $\mathbb{RP}^{n-1}$: in a chart $(U, \varphi)$ that would make the nonempty open set $\varphi(U)$ of measure zero, contradicting Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(4). Choose $\ell = \mathbb{R}v \notin Z$: then $v^n \neq 0$, $\pi_\ell|_{M'}$ is an injective immersion, and $\ell \neq S$.

(b) \emph{$\Phi'$ is an injective immersion.} It is injective as a composite of injective maps. Since $\pi_\ell$ is linear, $d\Phi'_p = \pi_\ell \circ d\Phi_p$; $d\Phi_p$ is injective with image $T_{\Phi(p)}M'$, and $\pi_\ell$ is injective on $T_{\Phi(p)}M'$ because $\pi_\ell|_{M'}$ is an immersion (Lemma~\ref{lem:projection-immersion-criterion}). So $d\Phi'_p$ is injective.

(c) \emph{The new tube.} Let $s$ be a unit vector with $S = \mathbb{R}s$. Since $s \notin \ell = \ker \pi_\ell$, $s' = \pi_\ell(s) \neq 0$; put $S' = \mathbb{R}s'$. A linear map is bounded: $|\pi_\ell(y)| \le C|y|$ for some $C$ and all $y$. For $p \in M$ there is $t$ with $|\Phi(p) - ts| < R$, so $|\Phi'(p) - ts'| = |\pi_\ell(\Phi(p) - ts)| \le CR$, and $\Phi'(M) \subseteq T_{R'}(S')$ with $R' = CR + 1$.

(d) \emph{$\Phi'$ is proper.} Let $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ be compact, say $K \subseteq B_{R_1}(0)$. If $\Phi'(p) \in K$, put $x = \Phi(p)$. By the formula of Lemma~\ref{lem:projection-immersion-criterion}, $\pi_\ell(x) = x - \tfrac{x^n}{v^n}v$, so $x$ lies at distance $|\pi_\ell(x)| < R_1$ from the point $\tfrac{x^n}{v^n}v \in \ell$: $x \in T_{R_1}(\ell)$. Also $x \in T_R(S)$. By (e), $|x| \le D$ for a constant $D$. So $\Phi'^{-1}(K)$ is a closed subset ($\Phi'$ is continuous) of $\Phi^{-1}\big(\overline{B}_D(0)\big)$, which is compact because $\Phi$ is proper; hence $\Phi'^{-1}(K)$ is compact.

(e) \emph{Two tubes with non-parallel axes meet in a bounded set.} Let $u = v/|v|$. The map $(a, b) \mapsto as - bu$ is linear and injective on $\mathbb{R}^2$, since $s$ and $u$ are linearly independent ($\ell \neq S$). The continuous function $(a, b) \mapsto |as - bu|$ is positive on the compact unit circle, so it has a minimum $\mu > 0$ there, and by homogeneity $|as - bu| \ge \mu\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ for all $(a, b)$. If $x \in T_R(S) \cap T_{R_1}(\ell)$, write $x = as + e_1 = bu + e_2$ with $|e_1| < R$, $|e_2| < R_1$. Then $|as - bu| = |e_2 - e_1| < R + R_1$, so $|a| < (R + R_1)/\mu$ and $|x| \le |a| + |e_1| < (R + R_1)/\mu + R =: D$.

(f) \emph{Conclusion of the claim.} $\Phi'$ is a proper injective immersion, hence an embedding (Theorem~\ref{thm:proper-embedding}), with image in the tube $T_{R'}(S')$.

\emph{Step 3: iterate.} Start from $\Phi_0$ ($n = N + 1$). While $n > 2m + 1$, Step~2 lowers $n$ by one, keeping a proper embedding with image in a tube; it stops at a proper embedding into $\mathbb{R}^{2m+1}$. If already $N + 1 \le 2m + 1$, follow $\Phi_0$ by the inclusion $\mathbb{R}^{N+1} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{2m+1}$, a proper embedding (the preimage of a compact set is its intersection with the closed subspace $\mathbb{R}^{N+1}$); a composite of proper embeddings is a proper embedding.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[{The Slices Are Compact and Embed in $\mathbb{R}^{2m+1}$}]\thmlabel{prop:whitney-slices}
Let $f$ be an exhaustion function on $M$, $\dim M = m$, and let $b < a$ be regular values of $f$. Let $E = f^{-1}\big([b, a]\big)$, or $E = f^{-1}\big((-\infty, a]\big)$.
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item $E$ is compact, and it is a smooth manifold with boundary contained in $f^{-1}(b) \cup f^{-1}(a)$ (a regular domain in $M$).
\item $E$ admits a smooth embedding into $\mathbb{R}^{2m+1}$.
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Proposition 5.47; proof of Theorem 6.15}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}[Proof (not given in this course)]
Compactness: $E$ is closed ($f$ is continuous) and contained in the sublevel set $f^{-1}\big((-\infty, a]\big)$, which is compact (Definition~\ref{def:exhaustion-function}). The rest concerns manifolds with boundary, which these notes do not treat: (1) is Lee, Proposition~5.47, as used in Lee's proof of Theorem~6.15; for (2), Lee's proofs of the compact case (Lemma~\ref{lem:compact-embeds}, with regular coordinate half-balls allowed) and of Lemma~\ref{lem:proper-embedding-2m1} hold for manifolds with boundary.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[Immersions into $\mathbb{R}^{2m}$ from Any Embedding]\thmlabel{prop:immersion-from-embedding}
Let $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ be a regular submanifold of dimension $m$, with $N \ge 2m$. Then there is a linear surjection $L : \mathbb{R}^N \to \mathbb{R}^{2m}$ such that $L|_M : M \to \mathbb{R}^{2m}$ is an immersion. In particular, every manifold that embeds in some $\mathbb{R}^N$ immerses in $\mathbb{R}^{2m}$.
\leeref{Theorem 6.18}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from the assignment. Assignment~6, Problem~4, allows ``that $M$ can be embedded in some $\mathbb{R}^N$''; the submitted solution starts instead from an embedding in $\mathbb{R}^{2m+1}$, which the course proves for compact $M$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:whitney-compact}), and in general in Theorem~\ref{thm:whitney} below. This proof needs only some $\mathbb{R}^N$: Lemma~\ref{lem:projection-immersion} is repeated, keeping the unit tangent bundle of the original $M$, because after one projection the image of $M$ is only immersed, not a submanifold.)} Tangent spaces are geometric, $T_xM \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$, and $UM \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{2N}$ is the unit tangent bundle, of dimension $2m - 1$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:unit-tangent-bundle}).

\emph{The claim, by descending induction on $k$.} For $k = N, N - 1, \ldots, 2m$ there is a linear surjection $L_k : \mathbb{R}^N \to \mathbb{R}^k$ with $\ker L_k \cap T_xM = \{0\}$ for every $x \in M$. For $k = N$ take $L_N = \mathrm{id}$.

\emph{The step.} Suppose $L_k$ is found and $k > 2m$. Since $L_k$ is injective on each $T_xM$, $L_ku \neq 0$ for $(x, u) \in UM$, and
\[
G_k : UM \to \mathbb{RP}^{k-1}, \qquad G_k(x, u) = [L_ku],
\]
is smooth: it is $(x, u) \mapsto L_ku \in \mathbb{R}^k \setminus \{0\}$, smooth as the restriction of a linear map (Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}(1)), followed by the quotient map, smooth as in Lemma~\ref{lem:projection-immersion-criterion}. As $\dim UM = 2m - 1 < k - 1$, $G_k(UM)$ has measure zero (Corollary~\ref{cor:sard-low-dim}); with Lemma~\ref{lem:hyperplane-lines} (in $\mathbb{RP}^{k-1}$) there is a line $\ell \subseteq \mathbb{R}^k$, $\ell \not\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{k-1}$, $\ell \notin G_k(UM)$, as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:projection-immersion}. Put $L_{k-1} = \pi_\ell \circ L_k : \mathbb{R}^N \to \mathbb{R}^{k-1}$, a composite of linear surjections. If $u \in T_xM$, $u \neq 0$, had $L_{k-1}u = 0$, then $L_ku \in \ker \pi_\ell = \ell$ with $L_ku \neq 0$, so $\ell = [L_ku] = G_k(x, u/|u|)$, contrary to the choice of $\ell$. So $\ker L_{k-1} \cap T_xM = \{0\}$.

\emph{Conclusion.} With $L = L_{2m}$: $L|_M = L \circ \iota$ has differential $d(L|_M)_x = L|_{T_xM}$ (the differential of a linear map is the map itself, as in Lemma~\ref{lem:projection-immersion-criterion}), injective for every $x$. So $L|_M$ is an immersion. For the last sentence, an embedding $M \to \mathbb{R}^N$ is a diffeomorphism onto a regular submanifold (Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image}, Corollary~\ref{cor:embedding-diffeo}), and an immersion composed with a diffeomorphism is an immersion, by the chain rule.
\end{proof}

This gives the immersion half of Theorem~\ref{thm:whitney} below (Lee, Theorem~6.18) from an embedding into any Euclidean space, without the dimension $2m + 1$ of the embedding half; for compact $M$, Lemma~\ref{lem:compact-embeds} supplies the embedding.



\begin{thmbox}[The Whitney Embedding and Immersion Theorems]\thmlabel{thm:whitney}
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold of dimension $m$. Then there is an embedding $M \to \mathbb{R}^{2m+1}$ and an immersion $M \to \mathbb{R}^{2m}$.
\leeref{Theorems 6.15 and 6.18}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}[Proof (Lee's proof of Theorem~6.15; the immersion by Proposition~\ref{prop:immersion-from-embedding})]
\textit{(The assigned reading, email of Oct 26: Lee, Lemmas~6.13 and~6.14 and Theorem~6.15; Lecture~22 sketched the noncompact case.)} \emph{Reduction.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:proper-embedding-2m1}, it suffices to embed $M$ in some Euclidean space; the lemma then gives a proper embedding into $\mathbb{R}^{2m+1}$.

\emph{$M$ compact.} Lemma~\ref{lem:compact-embeds} gives an embedding into some $\mathbb{R}^k$.

\emph{$M$ noncompact.} Let $f$ be an exhaustion function (Proposition~\ref{prop:exhaustion-exists}), and let $a_i, b_i$, $D_i$, $E_i$ be as in the slicing above: regular values $i < a_i < b_i < i + 1$ (they exist by Theorem~\ref{thm:sard}), $D_0 = f^{-1}\big((-\infty, 1]\big)$, $E_0 = f^{-1}\big((-\infty, a_1]\big)$, and for $i \ge 1$, $D_i = f^{-1}\big([i, i + 1]\big)$, $E_i = f^{-1}\big([b_{i-1}, a_{i+1}]\big)$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:whitney-slices}, each $E_i$ admits an embedding $F_i : E_i \to \mathbb{R}^{2m+1}$.

\emph{The cutoffs.} For $i \ge 1$ choose $c_i, d_i$ with $b_{i-1} < c_i < i$ and $i + 1 < d_i < a_{i+1}$, and put $A_i = f^{-1}\big([c_i, d_i]\big)$, $U_i = f^{-1}\big((b_{i-1}, a_{i+1})\big)$; for $i = 0$ choose $1 < d_0 < a_1$ and put $A_0 = f^{-1}\big((-\infty, d_0]\big)$, $U_0 = f^{-1}\big((-\infty, a_1)\big)$. $A_i$ is closed, $U_i$ is open, $A_i \subseteq U_i$, and $U_i \subseteq E_i$, so $U_i \subseteq \operatorname{Int}E_i$. Proposition~\ref{prop:bump-closed-set} gives a smooth $\rho_i : M \to [0, 1]$ with $\rho_i \equiv 1$ on $A_i$, hence on the open neighbourhood $f^{-1}\big((c_i, d_i)\big)$ of $D_i$ (for $i = 0$, $f^{-1}\big((-\infty, d_0)\big)$), and $\operatorname{supp}\rho_i \subseteq U_i \subseteq \operatorname{Int}E_i$.

\emph{Gluing.} Proposition~\ref{prop:noncompact-embedding}, with these $F_i$ and $\rho_i$, gives a proper embedding
\[
F = \Big( \sum_{i \text{ even}} \rho_i F_i,\ \sum_{i \text{ odd}} \rho_i F_i,\ f \Big) : M \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^{2(2m+1)+1} ,
\]
and the reduction applies.

\emph{The immersion.} $M$ now embeds in $\mathbb{R}^{2m+1}$, so Proposition~\ref{prop:immersion-from-embedding}, with $N = 2m + 1 \ge 2m$, gives an immersion $M \to \mathbb{R}^{2m}$.
\end{proof}

In other words, every manifold is diffeomorphic to a submanifold of some Euclidean space (Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image}). The course proves the compact case in full (Theorem~\ref{thm:whitney-compact}). The noncompact case, which first makes the embedding proper, was sketched in Lecture~22 and assigned as reading in Lee (Lemma~6.14 and Theorem~6.15, with a figure of the tube construction); the proof above is Lee's, with two facts about manifolds with boundary cited (Proposition~\ref{prop:whitney-slices}).

\begin{rembox}[The Hard Version]\label{rem:strong-whitney}
In the ``hard'' version the dimensions are one less: an embedding into $\mathbb{R}^{2m}$ and an immersion into $\mathbb{R}^{2m-1}$ (for $m > 0$ in the first and $m > 1$ in the second; Lee, Theorems 6.19 and 6.20). The course does not discuss it: the proof is very specialized and long. The smaller the codimension, the tighter the fit, and the harder the manifold must be manipulated to fit in.
\end{rembox}

\begin{corbox}[Every Manifold Has a Morse Function]\thmlabel{cor:morse-exists}
Every smooth manifold $M$ admits a Morse function (Definition~\ref{def:morse-function}). If $M$ is compact, nonempty and of dimension $m \ge 1$, such a function has finitely many critical points, and at least two.
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from the assignment; Assignment~6, Problem~5, with the Whitney embedding theorem.)} By Theorem~\ref{thm:whitney} there is an embedding $\Phi : M \to \mathbb{R}^N$ ($N = 2m + 1$); its image $M' = \Phi(M)$ is a regular submanifold and $\Phi : M \to M'$ is a diffeomorphism (Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image}, Corollary~\ref{cor:embedding-diffeo}). By Corollary~\ref{cor:height-morse} there is $\mathbf{a}$ with $f_{\mathbf{a}} : M' \to \mathbb{R}$ Morse. Then $f = f_{\mathbf{a}} \circ \Phi$ is Morse: for a chart $(U, \psi)$ of $M'$, $(\Phi^{-1}(U), \psi \circ \Phi)$ is a chart of $M$ ($\psi \circ \Phi$ is a diffeomorphism onto the open set $\psi(U)$, Lemma~\ref{lem:diffeo-chart}), in which $f$ has the same coordinate representation $f \circ (\psi \circ \Phi)^{-1} = f_{\mathbf{a}} \circ \psi^{-1}$ as $f_{\mathbf{a}}$ in $\psi$; so $p$ is a critical point of $f$ exactly when $\Phi(p)$ is one of $f_{\mathbf{a}}$, with the same Hessian matrices (Definition~\ref{def:hessian-matrix}). If $M$ is compact, the critical points of a Morse function are finite in number (Corollary~\ref{cor:morse-compact}); $f$ attains a maximum and a minimum, both critical points, and they are distinct unless $f$ is constant, which a Morse function on a manifold of dimension $m \ge 1$ is not (every point would be critical, and critical points of a Morse function are isolated, Corollary~\ref{cor:morse-isolated}).
\end{proof}


% ============================================================================
% CHAPTER: INTEGRAL CURVES AND FLOWS (Lecture 23, Wed Oct 28, 2026)
% ============================================================================
\chapter{Integral Curves and Flows}

\textit{Lecture 23. This chapter follows Lee, Chapter~9. The chapter on vector fields (\ref{sec:fields}--\ref{sec:lie-morphisms}) treated vector fields \emph{as operators}: derivations, the commutator, the Lie algebra of a Lie group. Now comes the other side of vector fields, as velocities: vector fields as \emph{generators of dynamics}. Think of $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ as a section of $TM \to M$ (Definition~\ref{def:vector-field}), a velocity vector attached to each point.}

% ============================================================================
% SECTION: INTEGRAL CURVES
% ============================================================================
\section{Integral Curves}\label{sec:integral-curves}

\roadmark{Stage: dynamics}{Curves whose velocity is prescribed by a vector field; in coordinates, a first-order system of ODEs.}

The velocity of a curve at a time $t$, from \ref{sec:velocities}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Definition~\ref{def:velocity-at-t} (Velocity at Time $t$).} Let $\gamma : J \to M$ be a smooth curve and $t_0 \in J$. The \textbf{velocity} of $\gamma$ at time $t_0$ is
\[
\dot\gamma(t_0) = \frac{d\gamma}{dt}(t_0) := \gamma_{*t_0}\Big(\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t_0}\Big) \in T_{\gamma(t_0)}M, \qquad\text{explicitly}\qquad \dot\gamma(t_0)[f] = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=t_0} f\big(\gamma(t)\big)
\]
for a germ $f$ at $\gamma(t_0)$.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Corollary~\ref{cor:velocity-at-t-coords} (Velocity at Time $t$ in Coordinates).} Let $\gamma : J \to M$ be smooth, $t_0 \in J$, and $(U, \varphi)$ a chart at $\gamma(t_0)$ with coordinate functions $x^1, \ldots, x^n$. Then
\[
\dot\gamma(t_0) = \sum_{j=1}^n \big(x^j \circ \gamma\big)'(t_0)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_{\gamma(t_0)} .
\]
Writing $x^j(t) = x^j(\gamma(t))$, this is $\dot\gamma = \sum_j \dot x^j\, \partial/\partial x^j$.
\end{quote}

In this chapter curves are mostly called $c : I \to M$, with velocity $\dot c(t)$; the corollary is the board's $\dot c = \langle \dot x^1, \ldots, \dot x^m \rangle$.



\begin{defbox}[Integral Curve]\deflabel{def:integral-curve}
Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$. An \textbf{integral curve} of $\mathbf{X}$ is a smooth map $c : I \to M$, where $I = (a, b) \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is an open interval (possibly $a = -\infty$ or $b = +\infty$), such that
\[
\dot c(t) = \mathbf{X}_{c(t)} \qquad \text{for all } t \in I. \tag{$*$}
\]
The variable $t$ is called \textbf{time}. If $0 \in I$ and $c(0) = q$, the curve \textbf{starts at} $q$.
\leeref{Ch.~9, \emph{Integral Curves}}
\end{defbox}

This is the key notion of the chapter, familiar from ordinary differential equations (Proposition~\ref{prop:integral-curve-coords}).

\begin{propbox}[The Velocity Curve]\thmlabel{prop:velocity-curve}
Let $c : I \to M$ be a smooth curve. Then $\dot c : I \to TM$, $t \mapsto \dot c(t)$, is a smooth curve in $TM$ lying over $c$, that is, $\pi \circ \dot c = c$. A smooth curve $c$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ if and only if $\dot c = \mathbf{X} \circ c$ as maps $I \to TM$.
\leeref{Ch.~3, \emph{Velocity Vectors of Curves}; Ch.~9, \emph{Integral Curves}}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; added to answer how $\dot c$ is defined when $M$ is a general manifold.)} \emph{Over $c$.} $\dot c(t) \in T_{c(t)}M$ by Definition~\ref{def:velocity-at-t}, so $\pi(\dot c(t)) = c(t)$ (Definition~\ref{def:tb-projection}).

\emph{Smooth.} Let $t_0 \in I$ and $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$ a chart at $c(t_0)$; on the open set $I_0 = c^{-1}(U) \ni t_0$, $\dot c$ takes values in $TU$. In the chart $\tilde\varphi$ of $TM$ over $U$ (Definition~\ref{def:tb-chart}), whose last $m$ entries are the components in the coordinate basis, Corollary~\ref{cor:velocity-at-t-coords} gives
\[
\tilde\varphi\big(\dot c(t)\big) = \Big(x^1(c(t)), \ldots, x^m(c(t)),\ (x^1 \circ c)'(t), \ldots, (x^m \circ c)'(t)\Big), \qquad t \in I_0 ,
\]
smooth in $t$ because each $x^j \circ c$ is a smooth real function. So $\dot c$ is smooth near every $t_0$.

\emph{The integral-curve equation.} Both $\dot c(t)$ and $\mathbf{X}_{c(t)} = (\mathbf{X} \circ c)(t)$ lie in $T_{c(t)}M$, so $(\ast)$ compares two vectors in the same tangent space, for each $t$; and $(\ast)$ for all $t \in I$ says exactly that the maps $\dot c$ and $\mathbf{X} \circ c$ from $I$ to $TM$ are equal.
\end{proof}

So an integral curve is a curve whose velocity curve in $TM$ is the field read along the curve. For a curve in a regular level set $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$, the velocity $\dot c(t)$ is the ordinary derivative $c'(t)$, seen as the derivation $D_{c'(t)}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:velocity-at-t-level-set}).


\begin{propbox}[Integral Curves in Coordinates]\thmlabel{prop:integral-curve-coords}
Let $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ be open, with coordinates $x^1, \ldots, x^m$, and $\mathbf{X} = \sum_i f^i\, \partial/\partial x^i$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}). Write a smooth curve as $c(t) = (x^1(t), \ldots, x^m(t))$, with velocity $\dot c(t) = \langle \dot x^1(t), \ldots, \dot x^m(t) \rangle$. Then $c$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ if and only if
\[
\dot x^i(t) = f^i\big(x^1(t), \ldots, x^m(t)\big) \qquad \text{for all } i = 1, \ldots, m \text{ and all } t \in I .
\]
The same holds on any manifold, in any chart, with the $x^i(t)$ the coordinates of $c(t)$.
\leeref{Ch.~9, \emph{Integral Curves}, (9.1)}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
By Proposition~\ref{prop:velocity-coords}, applied at each time $t$ to the shifted curve $s \mapsto c(t + s)$, $\dot c(t) = \sum_i \dot x^i(t)\, \partial/\partial x^i|_{c(t)}$, while $\mathbf{X}_{c(t)} = \sum_i f^i(c(t))\, \partial/\partial x^i|_{c(t)}$. The $\partial/\partial x^i|_{c(t)}$ form a basis of $T_{c(t)}M$, so $(*)$ holds at $t$ exactly when the components agree. The argument uses only a chart, so it applies on any manifold.
\end{proof}

The angle brackets mark $\dot c$ as a vector, not a point, to keep vectors and points distinct. What the proposition shows is that $(*)$ is a \emph{system of first-order ODEs}, usually nonlinear. All the derivatives are on the left-hand side, solved for: the right-hand side involves no derivatives. And it is a genuine \emph{system}, because the equation for $\dot x^i$ involves, in principle, all of the $x$'s. (Lee: solving a system of ODEs is called ``integrating'' it, hence the name \emph{integral} curve.)

\begin{rembox}[Why an Integral Curve Is an ODE]\label{rem:integral-curve-is-ode}
\textit{(Not from lecture; added to answer how integral curves connect to ODEs.)} The definition is already an ODE, written without coordinates. In $(\ast)$ the unknown is the curve $c$; its derivative is set equal to something that depends on where $c$ currently is: the velocity at time $t$ is the arrow that $\mathbf{X}$ puts at the point where $c$ is at time $t$. The derivative of the unknown equals a known function of the unknown --- that is an ODE. Proposition~\ref{prop:integral-curve-coords} only unpacks it into components.
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
    \item \emph{The simplest example} is the field $x\, \frac{d}{dx}$ on $\mathbb{R}$, with the equation $\dot x = x$ (Example~\ref{ex:integral-curves-x-ddx} below).
    \item \emph{Conversely}, every autonomous system $\dot x^i = f^i(x)$ with smooth $f^i$ on an open $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ is the system of the field $\sum_i f^i\, \partial/\partial x^i$: autonomous first-order systems on $U$ and vector fields on $U$ are the same thing. (``Autonomous'': the right-hand side does not depend on $t$, as the field does not change in time.)
    \item \emph{Higher order.} A higher-order equation becomes a first-order system once the lower derivatives are taken as new unknowns; the harmonic oscillator $\ddot x = -x$ becomes ``follow this field in the phase plane'' (Example~\ref{ex:harmonic-oscillator-phase-field} below). Likewise Hamilton's equations, for a time-independent Hamiltonian, say that the motion follows the integral curves of one vector field on phase space.
    \item \emph{Local versus global.} On a manifold a chart turns $(\ast)$ into such a system, so the local questions --- existence, uniqueness, smooth dependence on the starting point --- reduce to ODE theory in $\mathbb{R}^m$; this is why Theorem~\ref{thm:ode-local} is quoted in its Euclidean form. What one chart cannot settle is how far a solution continues: solutions in different charts must be patched together, and a solution may escape in finite time, which already happens in $\mathbb{R}^2$ (Example~\ref{ex:finite-escape}). That is the content of Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-flow}.
\end{itemize}
\end{rembox}

\begin{exbox}[{The Field $x\,d/dx$ on the Line}]\exlabel{ex:integral-curves-x-ddx}
\textit{(Not from lecture.)} On $\mathbb{R}$, let $\mathbf{X} = x\, \frac{d}{dx}$. The integral curve starting at $x_0$ is $x(t) = x_0 e^t$, $t \in \mathbb{R}$. The point runs away from $0$ faster and faster, because the arrows get longer further out.

\emph{The equation.} By Proposition~\ref{prop:integral-curve-coords}, with $m = 1$ and $f^1(x) = x$, a curve $t \mapsto x(t)$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ if and only if $\dot x = x$.

\emph{A solution.} $x(t) = x_0e^t$ has $\dot x(t) = x_0e^t = x(t)$ and $x(0) = x_0$.

\emph{The only one.} If $x$ solves $\dot x = x$ on an interval containing $0$ with $x(0) = x_0$, then $\frac{d}{dt}\big(e^{-t}x(t)\big) = e^{-t}(\dot x(t) - x(t)) = 0$, so $e^{-t}x(t) = x_0$, that is, $x(t) = x_0e^t$.

\emph{Running away.} For $x_0 \neq 0$ the speed is $|\dot x(t)| = |x(t)| = |x_0|e^t$: it equals the distance from $0$, which grows exponentially. For $x_0 = 0$ the curve is constant, at the zero of $\mathbf{X}$.
\end{exbox}

\begin{exbox}[The Harmonic Oscillator as a Vector Field]\exlabel{ex:harmonic-oscillator-phase-field}
\textit{(Not from lecture.)} The equation $\ddot x = -x$ becomes, with $y = \dot x$, the first-order system $\dot x = y$, $\dot y = -x$, the system of the field $\mathbf{Y} = y\, \partial_x - x\, \partial_y$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$. Its integral curves are the circles about the origin, run clockwise, and the constant curve at the origin: $\mathbf{Y}$ is minus the rotation field of Example~\ref{ex:rotation-flow} (later), whose integral curves it runs backwards in time.

\emph{The reduction.} If $\ddot x = -x$, put $y = \dot x$; then $\dot x = y$ and $\dot y = \ddot x = -x$. Conversely, if $(x, y)$ solves the system, then $\ddot x = \dot y = -x$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:integral-curve-coords}, with $f^1(x, y) = y$ and $f^2(x, y) = -x$, the system says exactly that $t \mapsto (x(t), y(t))$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{Y}$.

\emph{The integral curves.} The curve $c(t) = \big(x_0\cos t + y_0\sin t,\ -x_0\sin t + y_0\cos t\big)$ starts at $(x_0, y_0)$, and $\dot x = -x_0\sin t + y_0\cos t = y$, $\dot y = -x_0\cos t - y_0\sin t = -x$; so it is the integral curve starting at $(x_0, y_0)$. It is the point $(x_0, y_0)$ rotated by the angle $-t$, so $x(t)^2 + y(t)^2 = x_0^2 + y_0^2$: for $(x_0, y_0) \neq 0$ it runs around the circle of that radius clockwise, and for $(x_0, y_0) = 0$ it is constant.

\emph{Minus the rotation field.} $\mathbf{Y} = -\big(-y\, \partial_x + x\, \partial_y\big)$, and $c(t)$ is the rotation of $(x_0, y_0)$ by $-t$, the integral curve of the rotation field through $(x_0, y_0)$ at time $-t$.
\end{exbox}

\textit{Lecture 24 recalled the definition with the velocity written as $\dot c(t) = c_{*t}(d/dt)$, the derivation at $c(t)$ defined by $c$ (Definition~\ref{def:velocity-at-t}), and gave the velocity curve a name: every curve $c : I \to M$ has a natural lift to the tangent bundle.}

\begin{defbox}[Lift of a Curve]\deflabel{def:curve-lift}
Let $c : I \to M$ be a smooth curve. Its \textbf{lift} to the tangent bundle is the curve
\[
\tilde c : I \to TM, \qquad \tilde c(t) = \big(c(t), \dot c(t)\big),
\]
the point $c(t)$ together with the velocity $\dot c(t) \in T_{c(t)}M$. It is the velocity curve $\dot c$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:velocity-curve}, so it is smooth and $\pi \circ \tilde c = c$.
\leeref{Ch.~3, \emph{Velocity Vectors of Curves}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
 & TM \arrow[d, "\pi"] \\
I \arrow[ur, "\tilde c"] \arrow[r, "c"'] & M
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

The lift exists for every smooth curve, injective or not. By Proposition~\ref{prop:velocity-curve}, $c$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ exactly when $\tilde c = \mathbf{X} \circ c$: the lift is the field along the curve.

\begin{propbox}[An Integral Curve Returns with the Same Velocity]\thmlabel{prop:same-point-same-velocity}
Let $c : I \to M$ be an integral curve of $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$. If $c(t_1) = c(t_2)$ for some $t_1, t_2 \in I$, then $\dot c(t_1) = \dot c(t_2)$. Hence a smooth curve that passes through a point twice with different velocities is an integral curve of no vector field.
\leeref{Ch.~9, \emph{Integral Curves}}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~24. The point is that the field has a single value at each point.)} By $(\ast)$ at the times $t_1$ and $t_2$, and since $c(t_1) = c(t_2)$,
\[
\dot c(t_1) = \mathbf{X}_{c(t_1)} = \mathbf{X}_{c(t_2)} = \dot c(t_2) .
\]
The second sentence is the contrapositive: if $c(t_1) = c(t_2)$ but $\dot c(t_1) \neq \dot c(t_2)$, no vector field $\mathbf{X}$ satisfies $(\ast)$ at both times.
\end{proof}

\textit{(Not from lecture; figure added.)} Proposition~\ref{prop:same-point-same-velocity} in the tangent bundle, for $M = \mathbb{R}$, where $TM = \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$ is a plane: the base point horizontally, and the fibre $T_xM$, the velocities at $x$, as the vertical line over $x$. A vector field is a section $x \mapsto (x, \mathbf{X}_x)$, so its image is a graph, which meets each fibre exactly once, and the lift of an integral curve lies on it ($\tilde c = \mathbf{X} \circ c$, Proposition~\ref{prop:velocity-curve}). The curve $c(t) = t^2 - 1$ passes through $0$ at $t = -1$, moving left, and at $t = 1$, moving right. Its lift $\tilde c(t) = (t^2 - 1, 2t)$ meets the fibre $T_0M$ in the two points $(0, -2)$ and $(0, 2)$, and no graph contains both. So $c$ is an integral curve of no vector field.

\begin{exbox}[A Curve with a Loop]\exlabel{ex:loop-curve}
Let $c : I \to M$ pass through the same point at two times, $c(t_1) = c(t_2)$, with different velocities $\dot c(t_1) \neq \dot c(t_2)$, as in the figure. Its lift $\tilde c$ is still a well-defined map: it records the time, not just the point. But $c$ is an integral curve of no vector field (Proposition~\ref{prop:same-point-same-velocity}).
\end{exbox}

\textit{(Not from lecture; figure added.)} A loop in the tangent bundle: $c(t) = (t^2 - 1, t^3 - t)$ in $M = \mathbb{R}^2$ passes through the origin at $t = -1$ and at $t = 1$, with velocities $\dot c(\mp 1) = (\mp 2, 2)$. Here $TM = \mathbb{R}^2 \times \mathbb{R}^2$ is four-dimensional; the figure keeps the point $c(t)$ (the grey floor) and, as height, only the direction of $\dot c(t)$, its angle, forgetting the speed (the angle is unrolled: $\theta$ and $\theta + 2\pi$ are the same direction). Over the crossing point the lift passes at two heights, $135^\circ$ and $45^\circ$. In $TM$ the two visits are different points of the same fibre, and the lift does not cross itself; a vector field would put only one point in that fibre.

\emph{Simple and useful lemmas} (Lecture~24), valid for any $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$.

\begin{lembox}[Translation and Rescaling]\thmlabel{lem:translation-rescaling}
Let $c : I \to M$ be an integral curve of $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$.
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item \emph{(Translation lemma.)} For $t_0 \in \mathbb{R}$, the curve $c_{t_0}(t) = c(t + t_0)$, defined on $I - t_0 = \{ t - t_0 : t \in I \}$, is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$.
\item \emph{(Rescaling.)} For $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, the curve $c_\lambda(t) = c(\lambda t)$, defined on $\{ t : \lambda t \in I \}$, is an integral curve of $\lambda\mathbf{X}$.
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Lemmas 9.3 and 9.4}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~24: immediate from the chain rule; filled in.)} Both domains are open intervals (for $\lambda = 0$ the second is all of $\mathbb{R}$ if $0 \in I$, and empty if $0 \notin I$, when there is nothing to prove). Fix $t$ in the domain and a germ $f$ at the point of the new curve at time $t$ (at $c_{t_0}(t)$ for (1), at $c_\lambda(t)$ for (2)); by Definition~\ref{def:velocity-at-t} and the chain rule for real functions of one variable:
\[
\dot c_{t_0}(t)[f] = \frac{d}{dt} f\big(c(t + t_0)\big) = (f \circ c)'(t + t_0) = \dot c(t + t_0)[f] = \mathbf{X}_{c(t + t_0)}[f] = \mathbf{X}_{c_{t_0}(t)}[f]
\]
for (1), and for (2)
\[
\dot c_\lambda(t)[f] = \frac{d}{dt} f\big(c(\lambda t)\big) = \lambda\, (f \circ c)'(\lambda t) = \lambda\, \dot c(\lambda t)[f] = \lambda\, \mathbf{X}_{c(\lambda t)}[f] = (\lambda\mathbf{X})_{c_\lambda(t)}[f] .
\]
Two tangent vectors at a point that agree on every germ are equal.
\end{proof}

Time can always be translated, and this is used often below. Rescaling a field pointwise by a fixed factor gives integral curves simply related to those of the original field. With $\lambda = -1$: the integral curves of $-\mathbf{X}$ are those of $\mathbf{X}$ run backwards.

\textit{(Not from lecture; figure added.)} Both operations keep the image of the curve and change only the clock. Translation relabels the times, so the point reached at time $t_0$ by $c$ is reached at time $0$ by $c_{t_0}$; the arrow (the velocity) is unchanged. Rescaling by $\lambda = -1$ reverses the arrow, which is why $c_\lambda$, $\lambda = -1$, follows $-\mathbf{X}$. (A general $\lambda$ also changes the speed by the factor $|\lambda|$.)

\begin{lembox}[Integral Curves Under a Diffeomorphism]\thmlabel{lem:integral-curves-diffeo}
Let $F : M \to N$ be a diffeomorphism, $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$, and $F_*\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(N)$ its pushforward (Definition~\ref{def:vf-pushforward}, Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-pushforward}). A smooth curve $c : I \to M$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ if and only if $F \circ c$ is an integral curve of $F_*\mathbf{X}$.
\leeref{Proposition 9.6}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~24: the verification step in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:ode-local-manifold}, there for a chart; written here for any diffeomorphism.)} $F \circ c$ is smooth, as a composite of smooth maps. Fix $t \in I$. By the chain rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}), the velocity of $F \circ c$ at $t$ is
\[
(F \circ c)_{*t}\Big(\frac{d}{dt}\Big) = dF_{c(t)}\Big(c_{*t}\Big(\frac{d}{dt}\Big)\Big) = dF_{c(t)}\big(\dot c(t)\big),
\]
and by Definition~\ref{def:vf-pushforward} at the point $F(c(t))$, whose preimage is $c(t)$,
\[
(F_*\mathbf{X})_{F(c(t))} = dF_{c(t)}\big(\mathbf{X}_{c(t)}\big) .
\]
The linear map $dF_{c(t)}$ is injective: by the chain rule, $d(F^{-1})_{F(c(t))} \circ dF_{c(t)} = d(F^{-1} \circ F)_{c(t)}$ is the identity. So the two vectors above agree exactly when $\dot c(t) = \mathbf{X}_{c(t)}$: $F \circ c$ satisfies the integral-curve equation of $F_*\mathbf{X}$ at $t$ if and only if $c$ satisfies that of $\mathbf{X}$ at $t$.
\end{proof}

This is a kind of naturality that recurs later in greater generality (Proposition~\ref{prop:naturality-integral-curves}; Lee, Proposition~9.6: a smooth $F$ takes integral curves of $\mathbf{X}$ to integral curves of $\mathbf{Y}$ for all integral curves exactly when $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ are $F$-related.)

% SECTION: LOCAL EXISTENCE AND UNIQUENESS
% ============================================================================
\section{Local Existence and Uniqueness}\label{sec:ode-existence}

\roadmark{Stage: dynamics}{Integral curves exist and are unique for short times: in $\mathbb{R}^m$ by ODE theory, on a manifold through a chart; two integral curves that meet agree on their whole common domain.}

The basic input is a theorem from ODE theory, quoted in the following form.

\begin{thmbox}[Local Existence and Uniqueness in Euclidean Space]\thmlabel{thm:ode-local}
Let $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ be open and $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$. Given any $p \in M$, there are $\varepsilon > 0$, an open neighbourhood $U \subseteq M$ of $p$, and a smooth map
\[
\varphi : (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times U \longrightarrow M
\]
such that
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item $\varphi(0, q) = q$ for every $q \in U$;
\item for every $q \in U$, the curve $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \to M$, $t \mapsto \varphi(t, q)$, is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$;
\item \emph{(uniqueness)} if $q \in U$ and $c : I \to M$ is any integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ with $0 \in I$ and $c(0) = q$, then
\[
c|_{I \cap (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)} = \varphi(\cdot, q)|_{I \cap (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)} .
\]
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Theorem D.1}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}[Proof (not given in this course)]
Taken from ODE theory, not proved in the course: this is the theorem on existence, uniqueness and smooth dependence on initial conditions, whose proof is long (Lee, Theorem~D.1, proved in Appendix~D). It contains everything that is quoted from the Euclidean case.
\end{proof}

Items~(1) and~(2) together are \emph{existence}: every $q \in U$ has an integral curve $\varphi(\cdot, q)$ starting at $q$, all defined on the same interval $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$; the smoothness of $\varphi$ in the pair $(t, q)$ is \emph{smooth dependence on the initial condition}. Item~(3) is \emph{uniqueness}, on a par with existence.

In the figure the field is drawn as arrows at sample points. The theorem gives a time interval $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$ and a neighbourhood $U$ of $p$ (drawn as a rectangle) such that from every point $q \in U$, $p$ included, there is an integral curve $t \mapsto \varphi(t, q)$ that starts at $q$ and is defined at least for $|t| < \varepsilon$.

\emph{What the theorem says beyond the existence of a path through $q$.} The time interval is \emph{uniform}: as long as $q \in U$, the curve is defined at least for $|t| < \varepsilon$. And $\varphi$ is smooth as a function of the pair $(t, q)$ on the product $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times U$: smooth in $t$, as an integral curve must be, but also, for fixed $t$, smooth in the initial condition $q$. The image of $\varphi$ need not be just a slightly bigger open set around $U$; many behaviours can occur, and the examples below show some of the possibilities.

\begin{defbox}[Notation: $\varphi_t$ and $\varphi^q$]\deflabel{def:flow-notation}
In the setting of Theorem~\ref{thm:ode-local}, and likewise of Theorem~\ref{thm:ode-local-manifold} below, for fixed $t \in (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$ and fixed $q \in U$ write
\[
\varphi_t(q) := \varphi(t, q), \qquad \varphi^q(t) := \varphi(t, q).
\]
Then $\varphi_t : U \to M$ is a smooth map, and $\varphi^q : (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \to M$ is the integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ with $\varphi^q(0) = q$: it ``starts at $q$''.
\leeref{Ch.~9, \emph{Flows}}
\end{defbox}

The notation $\varphi_t$ is useful when $t$ is held fixed, and $\varphi^q$ when the initial point is held fixed. In lecture the point was at first written as a subscript, $\varphi_q(t)$. From Lecture~25 on, the point is written as a superscript, $\varphi^q(t)$, as here: the variable pulled out as an index ($t$ in $\varphi_t$, the point in $\varphi^q$) is thought of as a parameter; logically the notation adds nothing new. The superscript also removes the clash between $\varphi_t$ and $\varphi_q$. Lee writes $\theta_t(p)$ and $\theta^{(p)}(t)$ for the two (Chapter~9). In these notes $\varphi$ also names charts $(U, \varphi)$; from here on it is the flow unless a chart is named.

\begin{exbox}[The Rotation Field]\exlabel{ex:rotation-flow}
On $\mathbb{R}^2$ let $\mathbf{X} = -y\, \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} + x\, \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}$, the classical rotation field. By Proposition~\ref{prop:integral-curve-coords} the integral curves solve
\[
\dot x = -y, \qquad \dot y = x .
\]
Then $\ddot x = -\dot y = -x$, so $x(t) = A\cos t + B\sin t$ and $y(t) = -\dot x(t) = A\sin t - B\cos t$. At $t = 0$, $(x_0, y_0) = (A, -B)$. So
\[
\varphi : \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}^2 \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^2, \qquad \big(t, (x_0, y_0)\big) \longmapsto \big(x_0\cos t - y_0\sin t,\ x_0\sin t + y_0\cos t\big).
\]
$\varphi_t$ is the rotation by the angle $t$. The integral curves are the circles centred at the origin, traversed counterclockwise, and the constant curve at the origin. They exist for all time.
\leeref{Example 9.1}
\end{exbox}

The same system is the harmonic oscillator. It is the benign case: in Theorem~\ref{thm:ode-local} one can take $U = \mathbb{R}^2$ and any $\varepsilon$, indeed $t \in \mathbb{R}$. Going back to the question about the image, $\varphi_t(U)$ is $U$ rotated about the origin, possibly far from $U$.

\textit{Lecture 24. The definition again, then the local theorem on a manifold, two simple and useful lemmas, and uniqueness on the whole common domain, the foundational theory of the subject. The definition and the lemmas are in \ref{sec:integral-curves}.}

The Euclidean theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:ode-local}) is Theorem~D.1 in Lee, proved there. Its manifold version follows immediately from the Euclidean version.

\begin{thmbox}[Local Existence and Uniqueness on a Manifold]\thmlabel{thm:ode-local-manifold}
Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ and $p \in M$. There are $\varepsilon > 0$, an open neighbourhood $U$ of $p$, and a map
\[
\varphi : (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times U \longrightarrow M
\]
such that
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item $\varphi(0, q) = q$ for every $q \in U$;
\item for every $q \in U$, the curve $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \to M$, $t \mapsto \varphi_t(q)$, is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$;
\item \emph{(local uniqueness)} if $c : I \to M$ is any integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ on an open interval $I \ni 0$ with $c(0) = q$ for some $q \in U$, then $c(t) = \varphi_t(q)$ for all $t \in I \cap (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$.
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, $\varphi$ is smooth.
\leeref{Proposition 9.2; Theorem D.1}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~24: use a chart at $p$ to push the field down to an open set in Euclidean space, apply the theorem there, and push the result back up. The chart is called $\psi$, since $\varphi$ is the flow; this clash of letters is why Lee writes $\theta$ for the flow. The details are filled in.)} When $M$ is an open set in $\mathbb{R}^m$ this is Theorem~\ref{thm:ode-local}. In general, take a chart $\psi : W \to \psi(W) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ at $p$. It is a diffeomorphism of the open submanifold $W$ onto the open set $\psi(W)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:chart-diffeo}), so the field $\mathbf{X}|_W$ has a pushforward $\mathbf{Y} = \psi_*\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(\psi(W))$ (Definition~\ref{def:vf-pushforward}, Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-pushforward}).

\emph{The check.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:integral-curves-diffeo}, applied to the diffeomorphism $\psi : W \to \psi(W)$, a curve $c : I \to W$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ if and only if $\psi \circ c$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{Y}$.

\emph{Push down, solve, push up.} Theorem~\ref{thm:ode-local}, for $\mathbf{Y}$ on $\psi(W)$ at $\psi(p)$, gives $\varepsilon > 0$, an open $U' \ni \psi(p)$ and a smooth $\varphi' : (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times U' \to \psi(W)$. Put $U = \psi^{-1}(U')$ and
\[
\varphi(t, q) = \psi^{-1}\big(\varphi'(t, \psi(q))\big) \in W .
\]
$\varphi$ is smooth, as a composite of smooth maps, and $\varphi(0, q) = \psi^{-1}(\psi(q)) = q$. For $q \in U$ the curve $t \mapsto \varphi'(t, \psi(q))$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{Y}$ in $\psi(W)$, so by the check, applied to $c = \varphi(\cdot, q)$ (for which $\psi \circ c = \varphi'(\cdot, \psi(q))$), $t \mapsto \varphi_t(q)$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$. This gives~(1) and~(2).

\emph{Uniqueness.} The one point beyond pushing down is that an integral curve $c$ of $\mathbf{X}$ might leave $W$, where the chart says nothing. Let $c : I \to M$ be an integral curve, $I \ni 0$ an open interval, $c(0) = q \in U$, and let $J = I \cap (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$. The set $c^{-1}(W) \cap J$ is open and contains $0$; let $J_0$ be the open interval that is its connected component containing $0$. On $J_0$, $\psi \circ c$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{Y}$ starting at $\psi(q)$ (the check), so Theorem~\ref{thm:ode-local}(3) gives $\psi(c(t)) = \varphi'(t, \psi(q))$, that is, $c(t) = \varphi(t, q)$, for $t \in J_0$. Suppose $J_0 \neq J$, say $b = \sup J_0 < \sup J$ (the left end is handled the same way). Then $b \in J$, and by continuity $c(b) = \lim_{t \to b^-} \varphi(t, q) = \varphi(b, q)$, which lies in $W$. So $b \in c^{-1}(W) \cap J$, an open set; an interval around $b$ lies in it, and the component $J_0$ would contain $b$ and points beyond it, contradicting $b = \sup J_0$. Hence $J_0 = J$, and $c(t) = \varphi_t(q)$ on all of $I \cap (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$: this is~(3).
\end{proof}

On the board, (3) was stated for $c : (-\delta, \delta) \to M$, with the conclusion on $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \cap (-\delta, \delta)$; the domains need not be symmetric, which gives the form of~(3) above. By~(3), there is only one map $\varphi$ with these properties.

The core technical result of this section is uniqueness on the common domain.

\begin{propbox}[Uniqueness on the Common Domain]\thmlabel{prop:global-uniqueness}
Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$, and let $c_i : I_i \to M$, $i = 1, 2$, be integral curves of $\mathbf{X}$. If there is $t_0 \in I_1 \cap I_2$ with $c_1(t_0) = c_2(t_0)$, then
\[
c_1|_{I_1 \cap I_2} = c_2|_{I_1 \cap I_2} .
\]
\leeref{Theorem 9.12 (proof)}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~24. Details from the discussion in class are added where noted.)} \emph{Reduction to $t_0 = 0$.} By the translation lemma (Lemma~\ref{lem:translation-rescaling}(1)), $t \mapsto c_i(t + t_0)$ are integral curves on $I_i - t_0$ that agree at $0$, and the conclusion for them is the conclusion for the $c_i$. So assume $t_0 = 0$, and let $q = c_1(0) = c_2(0)$.

\emph{Local uniqueness.} By Theorem~\ref{thm:ode-local-manifold}(3) at $q$, both $c_i$ equal $\varphi_\cdot(q)$ near $0$. So there is $\varepsilon > 0$ with $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \subseteq I_1 \cap I_2$ and
\[
c_1|_{(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)} = c_2|_{(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)} .
\]
It remains to extend this local uniqueness to global uniqueness.

\emph{Argue by contradiction.} Introduce
\[
\mathcal{T}_+ = \{ t \in I_1 \cap I_2 \cap (0, \infty) : c_1(t) \neq c_2(t) \} .
\]
We want to show $\mathcal{T}_+ = \varnothing$. Assume $\mathcal{T}_+ \neq \varnothing$. It is bounded below by $\varepsilon$; let $\tau = \inf \mathcal{T}_+ \ge \varepsilon > 0$. \textit{(Filled in: $\tau$ is in the domain.)} $I_1 \cap I_2$ is an interval containing $\varepsilon/2$ and some point of $\mathcal{T}_+ \ge \tau$, and $\varepsilon/2 < \tau$, so $\tau \in I_1 \cap I_2$. By the definition of the infimum, $c_1 = c_2$ on $(0, \tau)$.

\emph{Claim: $c_1(\tau) = c_2(\tau)$.} Again by contradiction. If $c_1(\tau) \neq c_2(\tau)$, since $M$ is Hausdorff (Definition~\ref{def:hausdorff-t2}) there are neighbourhoods $U_i$ of $c_i(\tau)$ with $U_1 \cap U_2 = \varnothing$. By continuity of $c_1$ and $c_2$ there is an open interval $J \ni \tau$, inside $I_1 \cap I_2$ (which is open), with $c_i(J) \subseteq U_i$. So there is $\tau_1 \in J$ with $0 < \tau_1 < \tau$, and $c_1(\tau_1) \in U_1$, $c_2(\tau_1) \in U_2$, so $c_1(\tau_1) \neq c_2(\tau_1)$ and $\tau_1 \in \mathcal{T}_+$. This contradicts $\tau = \inf \mathcal{T}_+$. Hence $c_1(\tau) = c_2(\tau)$.

\emph{Local uniqueness at $\tau$.} By the translation lemma, local uniqueness at $t = 0$ is equivalent to local uniqueness at any $\tau$: apply the local-uniqueness step to the integral curves $c_i(\cdot + \tau)$, which agree at $0$. So there is $\delta > 0$ such that the curves agree on $(\tau - \delta, \tau + \delta)$. Together with $c_1 = c_2$ on $(0, \tau]$, they agree on $(0, \tau + \delta) \cap I_1 \cap I_2$, so every point of $\mathcal{T}_+$ is $\ge \tau + \delta$, and $\inf \mathcal{T}_+ \ge \tau + \delta > \tau$: a contradiction. So $\mathcal{T}_+ = \varnothing$.

\emph{Negative times.} The same argument works from the other side, with a supremum in place of the infimum: take $\mathcal{T}_- = \{ t \in I_1 \cap I_2 \cap (-\infty, 0) : c_1(t) \neq c_2(t) \}$ and $\sup \mathcal{T}_-$, or apply the above to $t \mapsto c_i(-t)$, integral curves of $-\mathbf{X}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:translation-rescaling}(2)). With $c_1(0) = c_2(0)$, the curves agree on all of $I_1 \cap I_2$.
\end{proof}

In words: two integral curves that agree at some time $t_0$ agree wherever both are defined.

\textit{(Figure after the board.)} The situation the claim rules out: the curves agree on $(0, \tau)$ and differ at $\tau$, with disjoint neighbourhoods $U_1, U_2$; as with any picture in a proof by contradiction, it shows a situation that cannot occur. The argument is very similar to the Euclidean one. The interval $J$ can be taken inside $I_1 \cap I_2$ because the domains are open intervals.

\begin{rembox}[Where the Hausdorff Property Is Used]\label{rem:uniqueness-hausdorff}
\textit{(Filled in.)} The claim $c_1(\tau) = c_2(\tau)$ is the one step of the proof that uses that $M$ is Hausdorff ($T_2$): it says that the set of times where the two curves agree is closed in $I_1 \cap I_2$. Without the Hausdorff property the proposition fails (Example~\ref{ex:two-origins-integral-curves-split} below).
\end{rembox}

\begin{exbox}[Integral Curves on the Line with Two Origins]\exlabel{ex:two-origins-integral-curves-split}
\textit{(Filled in.)} The line with two origins $X$ (\ref{sec:ex-two-origins}), two copies $\mathbb{R} \times \{1\}$ and $\mathbb{R} \times \{2\}$ glued along $x \neq 0$, has smooth charts (each copy) but is not Hausdorff. The field $d/dx$, in either chart, is well defined, and $c_i(t) = (t, i)$, $t \in \mathbb{R}$, $i = 1, 2$, are integral curves of it. They agree at every $t \neq 0$ and differ at $t = 0$, where they pass through the two different origins. So the conclusion of Proposition~\ref{prop:global-uniqueness} fails on $X$.

\emph{The charts.} Write $[x, i]$ for the class of $(x, i)$, and $U_i = \{[x, i] : x \in \mathbb{R}\}$ for the image of the $i$-th copy. $U_i$ is open: its preimage in $\mathbb{R} \times \{1, 2\}$ is $\mathbb{R} \times \{i\}$ together with $(\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}) \times \{3 - i\}$. The map $\varphi_i : U_i \to \mathbb{R}$, $[x, i] \mapsto x$, is a bijection, continuous because its composite with the quotient map is the projection on $\mathbb{R} \times \{i\}$, and open because the quotient map is open (Example~\ref{ex:two-origins-criterion}); so it is a homeomorphism. On $U_1 \cap U_2 = \{[x, 1] : x \neq 0\}$ the transition map $\varphi_2 \circ \varphi_1^{-1}$ is the identity of $\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$, which is smooth. The definitions of tangent vectors, vector fields and integral curves make sense for this atlas; the Hausdorff property is not used in them.

\emph{The field.} On $U_i$ let $\mathbf{X}$ be the coordinate field $d/dx$ of the chart $\varphi_i$. On $U_1 \cap U_2$ the two coordinate fields agree, by the change of coordinates (Corollary~\ref{cor:change-coords}) with the identity as transition map, whose derivative is $1$. So $\mathbf{X}$ is a well-defined smooth vector field on $X$.

\emph{The curves.} In the chart $\varphi_i$, $c_i(t) = [t, i]$ reads $t \mapsto t$, with $\dot x = 1$, the coefficient of $\mathbf{X}$; so $c_i$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:integral-curve-coords}, in a chart).

\emph{Agreement and disagreement.} For $t \neq 0$, $(t, 1) \sim (t, 2)$, so $c_1(t) = c_2(t)$; but $c_1(0) = [0, 1] \neq [0, 2] = c_2(0)$. Thus $c_1(1) = c_2(1)$, while $c_1$ and $c_2$ differ on the common domain $\mathbb{R}$. In the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:global-uniqueness}, run backwards from $t_0 = 1$, the step that fails is the claim that the curves agree at the end time $\tau = 0$ of their agreement: the two origins have no disjoint neighbourhoods.
\end{exbox}

\begin{corbox}[Non-Injective Integral Curves Repeat]\thmlabel{cor:returning-curve-periodic}
Let $c : I \to M$ be an integral curve of $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$, and suppose $c(t_1) = c(t_2)$ for some $t_1 < t_2$ in $I$. Put $T = t_2 - t_1 > 0$. Then
\[
c(t + T) = c(t) \qquad \text{for every } t \in I \text{ with } t + T \in I .
\]
\leeref{Problem 9-1}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(From an email after Lecture~24, answering the question raised in that lecture whether integral curves must be injective: if an integral curve is not injective, then it must be periodic.)} By the translation lemma (Lemma~\ref{lem:translation-rescaling}(1)), the curve $g(t) = c(t + T)$, defined on $I - T$, is an integral curve of the same field. Both $c$ and $g$ are defined at $t_1$: $t_1 \in I$, and $t_1 \in I - T$ because $t_1 + T = t_2 \in I$. There they agree:
\[
g(t_1) = c(t_1 + T) = c(t_2) = c(t_1) .
\]
Therefore, by uniqueness (Proposition~\ref{prop:global-uniqueness}), $g = c$ on $I \cap (I - T)$, that is, $c(t + T) = c(t)$ for every $t \in I$ with $t + T \in I$.
\end{proof}

$T$ need not be the smallest period. For the rotation field (Example~\ref{ex:rotation-flow}), the integral curve $c(t) = (\cos t, \sin t)$ has $c(0) = c(4\pi)$, so $T = 4\pi$ is a period, while the smallest period is $2\pi$. A constant curve, at a zero of $\mathbf{X}$, is periodic with every $T > 0$. \textit{(Filled in.)} The email states $c(t + T) = c(t)$ for all $t$. For a curve on a bounded interval the corollary only covers the $t$ with both $t$ and $t + T$ in $I$; for the maximal integral curve the domain is then all of $\mathbb{R}$, and the identity holds for every $t$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:returning-maximal-periodic}).

\begin{rembox}[Must an Integral Curve Be Injective?]\label{rem:integral-curve-injective}
The question came up in Lecture~24, after Example~\ref{ex:loop-curve}; it is related to Proposition~\ref{prop:global-uniqueness}. An integral curve need not be injective (Example~\ref{ex:constant-integral-curve-at-zero} below), and constant curves are not the only exception (Example~\ref{ex:rotation-field-periodic-circles} below). The answer, sent by email after the lecture: if an integral curve is not injective, then it must be periodic (Corollary~\ref{cor:returning-curve-periodic}; for the maximal curve, Proposition~\ref{prop:returning-maximal-periodic}). Lee shows that a maximal integral curve is exactly one of: constant, injective, or periodic and nonconstant (Lee, Problem~9-1).
\end{rembox}

\begin{exbox}[Constant Integral Curves at Zeros]\exlabel{ex:constant-integral-curve-at-zero}
Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ and $p \in M$ with $\mathbf{X}_p = 0$. The constant curve $c : \mathbb{R} \to M$, $c(t) = p$, is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$, and it is not injective.

\emph{Integral curve.} For every $t$ and every germ $f$ at $p$, $\dot c(t)[f] = \frac{d}{dt} f(c(t)) = \frac{d}{dt} f(p) = 0$ (Definition~\ref{def:velocity-at-t}); so $\dot c(t) = 0 = \mathbf{X}_p = \mathbf{X}_{c(t)}$, which is $(\ast)$ of Definition~\ref{def:integral-curve}.

\emph{Not injective.} $c(0) = p = c(1)$.
\end{exbox}

\begin{exbox}[{The Circles of the Rotation Field Return Every $2\pi$}]\exlabel{ex:rotation-field-periodic-circles}
\textit{(Filled in.)} The circles of the rotation field $\mathbf{X} = -y\, \partial_x + x\, \partial_y$ (Example~\ref{ex:rotation-flow}) are integral curves that return to the same point with the same velocity, every $2\pi$: they are neither injective nor constant.

\emph{The curves.} For $(x_0, y_0) \neq 0$, $c(t) = \big(x_0\cos t - y_0\sin t,\ x_0\sin t + y_0\cos t\big)$ is the integral curve starting at $(x_0, y_0)$ (Example~\ref{ex:rotation-flow}), running around the circle of radius $|(x_0, y_0)|$.

\emph{Return every $2\pi$.} $\cos$ and $\sin$ have period $2\pi$, so $c(t + 2\pi) = c(t)$; and then $\dot c(t + 2\pi) = \mathbf{X}_{c(t + 2\pi)} = \mathbf{X}_{c(t)} = \dot c(t)$, the same velocity.

\emph{Neither injective nor constant.} $c(0) = c(2\pi)$; and $c(\pi) = -(x_0, y_0) \neq (x_0, y_0)$.
\end{exbox}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.95]
\foreach \a in {0,60,...,300} { \draw[->, black!55, thick] ({0.3*cos(\a)},{0.3*sin(\a)}) -- ({0.8*cos(\a)},{0.8*sin(\a)}); }
\fill[red!70!black] (0,0) circle (2pt);

\end{center}

\textit{(Not from lecture; figure added.)} The three kinds of maximal integral curve (Lee, Problem~9-1). An integral curve that comes back to a point comes back with the same velocity, the value of the field there; by Corollary~\ref{cor:returning-curve-periodic} it then repeats itself. The loop of Example~\ref{ex:loop-curve}, which comes back with a different velocity, is none of the three: it is not an integral curve.

\begin{exbox}[The Euler Field]\exlabel{ex:euler-field}
On $\mathbb{R}^2$ let $\mathbf{X} = x\, \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} + y\, \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}$. The integral curves solve $\dot x = x$, $\dot y = y$, so $\varphi_t(x_0, y_0) = e^t(x_0, y_0)$, $t \in \mathbb{R}$. For $(x_0, y_0) \neq 0$ the image is the open ray from the origin through $(x_0, y_0)$, since $e^t$ takes every value in $(0, \infty)$ and never $0$; at the origin the integral curve is constant.
\end{exbox}

Plotted, the integral curves of the Euler field on $\mathbb{R}^2$ are radial and seem to intersect at the origin, but they do not. The rays are open, and the origin is its own integral curve. The images of the integral curves $t \mapsto e^t(x_0, y_0)$, $t \in \mathbb{R}$, partition $\mathbb{R}^2$, as Proposition~\ref{prop:global-uniqueness} requires. \textit{(Filled in.)} If two of them pass through a common point, $c_1(t_1) = c_2(t_2)$, then $t \mapsto c_2(t + t_2 - t_1)$ is an integral curve (Lemma~\ref{lem:translation-rescaling}(1)) that agrees with $c_1$ at time $t_1$, so it equals $c_1$ on $\mathbb{R}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:global-uniqueness}), and the two images coincide.

% SECTION: MAXIMAL INTEGRAL CURVES AND FLOWS
% ============================================================================
\section{Maximal Integral Curves and Flows}\label{sec:flows}

\roadmark{Stage: dynamics}{The maximal integral curve through each point, and the flow: all maximal curves assembled into one smooth map on an open domain in $\mathbb{R} \times M$, which obeys the group law.}

\textit{Lecture 24. Uniqueness on the common domain, Proposition~\ref{prop:global-uniqueness}, allows one to define the maximal domain of an integral curve, given an initial condition.}

\begin{defbox}[Maximal Domain]\deflabel{def:maximal-domain}
Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ and $p \in M$. Define
\[
\big(\alpha(p), \beta(p)\big) = \bigcup_{I} I ,
\]
the union over the domains $I$ of all integral curves of $\mathbf{X}$ starting at $p$:
an open interval containing $0$, possibly infinite or semi-infinite. It is the \textbf{maximal domain} of integral curves of $\mathbf{X}$ starting at $p$.
\leeref{Theorem 9.12}
\end{defbox}

The union is nonempty, since an integral curve starting at $p$ exists (Theorem~\ref{thm:ode-local-manifold}). Each domain $I$ is an open interval containing $0$, because the curve starts at $p$, so the union is an open interval containing $0$.

\begin{propbox}[The Maximal Integral Curve]\thmlabel{prop:maximal-curve}
Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ and $p \in M$. There is an integral curve $\varphi^p : (\alpha(p), \beta(p)) \to M$ of $\mathbf{X}$ starting at $p$, and every integral curve $c : I \to M$ starting at $p$ satisfies $I \subseteq (\alpha(p), \beta(p))$ and $c = \varphi^p|_I$. So $(\alpha(p), \beta(p))$ is the largest possible domain of such a curve, and $\varphi^p$ is the unique maximal integral curve starting at $p$. This proves Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-flow}(1).
\leeref{Theorem 9.12}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~24: a point $t$ of the maximal domain lies in some $I$, so some integral curve is defined near $t$; define $\varphi^p(t)$ by it. By Proposition~\ref{prop:global-uniqueness} the choice of $I$ does not matter. Details filled in.)} For $t \in (\alpha(p), \beta(p))$, choose an integral curve $c : I \to M$ starting at $p$ with $t \in I$, and set $\varphi^p(t) = c(t)$. \emph{Well defined:} if $c' : I' \to M$ is another, then $c$ and $c'$ agree at time $0$, so by Proposition~\ref{prop:global-uniqueness} they agree on $I \cap I' \ni t$. \emph{An integral curve:} near each $t$, $\varphi^p$ equals the smooth curve $c$ on the open interval $I \ni t$, so $\varphi^p$ is smooth and $\dot\varphi^p(t) = \dot c(t) = \mathbf{X}_{c(t)} = \mathbf{X}_{\varphi^p(t)}$, since velocity at $t$ only depends on the curve near $t$. And $\varphi^p(0) = p$. \emph{Maximal:} if $c : I \to M$ starts at $p$, then $I$ is one of the domains in the union, so $I \subseteq (\alpha(p), \beta(p))$, and $c = \varphi^p|_I$ by the definition of $\varphi^p$.
\end{proof}

\begin{defbox}[Flow Domain and Flow]\deflabel{def:flow-domain}
\textit{(Lecture~23, inside the statement of Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-flow}(2), and the recap of Lecture~25; stated here as a definition.)} Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$, and for each $p \in M$ let $\varphi^p : (\alpha(p), \beta(p)) \to M$ be the maximal integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ starting at $p$ (Definition~\ref{def:maximal-domain}, Proposition~\ref{prop:maximal-curve}). The \textbf{flow domain} of $\mathbf{X}$ and the \textbf{flow} of $\mathbf{X}$ are
\[
\mathcal{D} = \bigcup_{p \in M} \big(\alpha(p), \beta(p)\big) \times \{p\} \ \subseteq\ \mathbb{R} \times M, \qquad \varphi : \mathcal{D} \longrightarrow M, \quad (t, p) \longmapsto \varphi^p(t).
\]
So $\mathcal{D} = \{ (t, p) \in \mathbb{R} \times M : t \in (\alpha(p), \beta(p)) \}$, and, in words, $\varphi(t, p)$ is the integral curve starting at $p$, evaluated at $t$. The notation of Definition~\ref{def:flow-notation} is kept: $\varphi_t(p) = \varphi(t, p) = \varphi^p(t)$.
\leeref{Theorem 9.12}
\end{defbox}

The maximal domains of the examples: $\mathbb{R}$ for the rotation and Euler fields (Examples~\ref{ex:rotation-flow} and~\ref{ex:euler-field}); $(-\infty, 1/(x_0y_0))$ and $(-\infty, -x_0)$ for the two examples that follow.

The next example is problematic: examples like it are what make the theory of flows necessarily elaborate.

\begin{exbox}[Escape in Finite Time]\exlabel{ex:finite-escape}
On $\mathbb{R}^2$ let $\mathbf{X} = y x^2\, \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} + 0 \cdot \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}$. The integral curves solve
\[
\dot x = y(t)\, x(t)^2, \qquad \dot y = 0 .
\]
So $y(t) = y(0) = y_0$ for all $t$, and $dx/dt = y_0 x^2$ separates, for $x_0 \neq 0$, as $dx/x^2 = y_0\, dt$: $-1/x(t) = y_0 t + C$ with $C = -1/x_0$. Hence
\[
x(t) = \frac{x_0}{1 - x_0 y_0\, t}, \qquad y(t) = y_0 .
\]
\emph{Observation:} the denominator is zero at $t = 1/(x_0y_0)$. Take $M$ to be the open first quadrant $\{x > 0,\ y > 0\}$ (otherwise there are sign issues, and nothing more interesting happens). Fix $T > 0$, and let $q = (x_0, y_0)$ lie on the hyperbola $xy = 1/T$. Then
\[
\lim_{t \to T^-} x(t) = +\infty .
\]
For negative $t$ nothing goes wrong: the denominator only grows, and $x(t) \to 0$ as $t \to -\infty$. So the maximal domain of an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ starting at $(x_0, y_0)$ is
\[
\Big( -\infty,\ \frac{1}{x_0 y_0} \Big).
\]
\leeref{Example 9.10}
\end{exbox}
