The integral curves lie on horizontal lines. Starting at $q$ the point moves to the right for $t > 0$, and the velocity $y_0x^2$ grows quadratically in $x$: the point gets to infinity in finite time. Backwards in time the point moves against the arrows, towards the $y$-axis, where the field vanishes: it creeps towards the axis, but there is no blowing up. The escape time $1/(x_0y_0)$ depends on the initial condition, through the hyperbola $xy = 1/T$ on which it lies. So, by inspection, not all integral curves are defined for all time. (The curve does not continue past $T$, even inside $\mathbb{R}^2$: its $x$-coordinate is unbounded. No other integral curve from $q$ does either, by uniqueness on the whole common domain: two integral curves starting at $q$ agree wherever both are defined (Proposition~\ref{prop:global-uniqueness}; Lee, Theorem~D.4). The uniqueness in Theorem~\ref{thm:ode-local} alone gives this only for $|t| < \varepsilon$.)

\begin{exbox}[Running Off the Edge]\exlabel{ex:half-line}
Let $M = (-\infty, 0)$ and $\mathbf{X} = \dfrac{d}{dx}$. The integral curves solve $\dot c(t) = 1$, so the integral curve starting at $x_0$ is
\[
\varphi_t(x_0) = x_0 + t ,
\]
translation by time $t$, with $\varphi_t(x_0)|_{t=0} = x_0$. It stays in $M$ exactly while $x_0 + t < 0$. So for every $x_0 \in (-\infty, 0)$ the maximal domain in $t$ is
\[
\{ t : x_0 + t < 0 \} = (-\infty, -x_0) .
\]
\end{exbox}

A much easier example than Example~\ref{ex:finite-escape} of integral curves not defined for all $t$. Here the curve does not run to infinity; it runs into the end of the manifold, and there is no manifold beyond it to continue in. Again the domain depends on the initial condition; this complication is what makes the theory much longer than it would be otherwise.

Compare the flow domain of Example~\ref{ex:finite-escape} above: there $\beta(p) = 1/(x_0y_0)$ blows up as $x_0 \to 0$, here $\beta(x_0) = -x_0$ shrinks to $0$ at the end of $M$. Neither field is complete (Definition~\ref{def:complete-field}).

\begin{propbox}[Non-Injective Maximal Integral Curves Are Periodic]\thmlabel{prop:returning-maximal-periodic}
Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$, $p \in M$, and let $\varphi^p : (\alpha(p), \beta(p)) \to M$ be the maximal integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ starting at $p$. If $\varphi^p$ is not injective, say $\varphi^p(t_1) = \varphi^p(t_2)$ with $T = t_2 - t_1 > 0$, then $(\alpha(p), \beta(p)) = \mathbb{R}$ and
\[
\varphi^p(t + T) = \varphi^p(t) \qquad \text{for all } t \in \mathbb{R} .
\]
\leeref{Problem 9-1}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture: the argument sent by email, Corollary~\ref{cor:returning-curve-periodic}, completed by maximality.)} Write $I = (\alpha, \beta) = (\alpha(p), \beta(p))$ and $c = \varphi^p$. By Corollary~\ref{cor:returning-curve-periodic},
\[
c(s + T) = c(s) \qquad \text{whenever } s \in I \text{ and } s + T \in I . \tag{$\dagger$}
\]
Since $\alpha < t_1 < t_2 < \beta$, we have $T < \beta - \alpha$.

\emph{$\beta = +\infty$.} Suppose $\beta < +\infty$. The intervals $I = (\alpha, \beta)$ and $I + T = (\alpha + T, \beta + T)$ overlap, because $\alpha + T < \beta$, and their union is $(\alpha, \beta + T)$. Define $\tilde c$ on it by
\[
\tilde c(t) = c(t) \ \ (t \in I), \qquad \tilde c(t) = c(t - T) \ \ (t \in I + T) .
\]
This is well defined: if $t \in I \cap (I + T)$, then $s = t - T$ has $s \in I$ and $s + T = t \in I$, so $c(t - T) = c(t)$ by $(\dagger)$. On the open interval $I$, $\tilde c$ is the integral curve $c$; on the open interval $I + T$, it is the integral curve $t \mapsto c(t - T)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:translation-rescaling}(1) with $t_0 = -T$). Smoothness and the equation $\dot{\tilde c}(t) = \mathbf{X}_{\tilde c(t)}$ only involve $\tilde c$ near $t$, so $\tilde c$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$. It starts at $p$, as $0 \in I$ and $\tilde c(0) = c(0) = p$. Its domain $(\alpha, \beta + T)$ is not contained in $(\alpha, \beta)$, which contradicts Proposition~\ref{prop:maximal-curve}. So $\beta = +\infty$.

\emph{$\alpha = -\infty$.} In the same way, if $\alpha > -\infty$, then $\tilde c(t) = c(t)$ on $I$ and $\tilde c(t) = c(t + T)$ on $I - T = (\alpha - T, \beta - T)$ define an integral curve starting at $p$ on $(\alpha - T, \beta)$: on the overlap $I \cap (I - T)$ the two agree by $(\dagger)$ with $s = t$. This again contradicts Proposition~\ref{prop:maximal-curve}.

\emph{Periodicity.} Now $I = \mathbb{R}$, so $(\dagger)$ holds for every $s \in \mathbb{R}$.
\end{proof}

So a maximal integral curve is either injective or periodic and defined for all time. Lee's Problem~9-1 separates out the constant curves, which are periodic with every period.

\textit{Lecture 25. A recap of the flow domain, with the cartoon redrawn.} Given $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$, every $p \in M$ has its maximal domain $(\alpha(p), \beta(p)) \ni 0$, which can be all of $\mathbb{R}$; when it is, things simplify. The flow domain and the flow (Definition~\ref{def:flow-domain}) are
\[
\mathcal{D} = \{ (t, p) \in \mathbb{R} \times M : t \in (\alpha(p), \beta(p)) \}, \qquad \varphi : \mathcal{D} \to M, \quad (t, p) \longmapsto \varphi(t, p),
\]
where, in words, $\varphi(t, p)$ is the integral curve starting at $p$, evaluated at $t$.

\textit{(Figure after the board.)} Time is horizontal and $M$ vertical here: over each $p$ the open segment $(\alpha(p), \beta(p)) \times \{p\}$, which always contains $(0, p)$; together they fill $\mathcal{D}$. The figure after Lemma~\ref{lem:uniform-time} in \ref{sec:complete-fields} is the same cartoon with the axes exchanged.

\emph{Careful.} The definition of integral curve allows any curve $c : I \to M$ with $\dot c(t) = \mathbf{X}_{c(t)}$ for all $t \in I$ (Definition~\ref{def:integral-curve}), so $I$ need not contain $0$: translating an integral curve (Lemma~\ref{lem:translation-rescaling}(1)) gives one whose domain misses $0$. The curve $t \mapsto \varphi^p(t)$, in the notation $\varphi_t(p) = \varphi(t, p) = \varphi^p(t)$ (Definition~\ref{def:flow-notation} and the paragraph after it), is an integral curve that is defined at $t = 0$, where it is $p$. The flow $\varphi$ is the local maps of Theorem~\ref{thm:ode-local-manifold} glued together; they fit together by uniqueness.

That $\mathcal{D}$ is open and $\varphi$ smooth (Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-flow}(2)) was not proved in class; the proof, from Lee, is filled in after the theorem.

\begin{defbox}[Flow Box]\deflabel{def:flow-box}
Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ with flow $\varphi : \mathcal{D} \to M$ (Definition~\ref{def:flow-domain}), and $p \in M$. A \textbf{flow box} (or \textbf{local domain}) at $p$ is a product $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times U \subseteq \mathcal{D}$, with $\varepsilon > 0$ and $U$ an open neighbourhood of $p$, on which $\varphi$ is smooth; together with the restriction $\varphi| : (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times U \to M$.
\leeref{Ch.~9, \emph{Flows}}
\end{defbox}

Both names are in use. Every point has such a box, by the next lemma.

\begin{lembox}[Flow Boxes Exist]\thmlabel{lem:flow-box}
Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$. Every $p \in M$ has a flow box $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times U$.
\leeref{Theorem 9.12 (proof)}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~25, recalled from Theorem~\ref{thm:ode-local-manifold}; the identification with the maximal flow is filled in.)} Theorem~\ref{thm:ode-local-manifold} gives $\varepsilon > 0$, an open $U \ni p$ and a smooth $\varphi' : (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times U \to M$ such that, for $q \in U$, $\varphi'(\cdot, q)$ is an integral curve starting at $q$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:maximal-curve}, $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \subseteq (\alpha(q), \beta(q))$ and $\varphi'(t, q) = \varphi^q(t) = \varphi(t, q)$. So $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times U \subseteq \mathcal{D}$, and $\varphi$ restricted to it is $\varphi'$, which is smooth.
\end{proof}

\textit{The flow. Lecture 23, the last minutes: the bigger picture, stated before it is proved; a large part of it is proved in Lecture~24.}

\begin{thmbox}[Maximal Integral Curves and the Flow]\thmlabel{thm:maximal-flow}
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$.
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item For every $p \in M$ there is a unique \emph{maximal} integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ starting at $p$, maximal with respect to its domain. Write it $\varphi^p$ and its domain $(\alpha(p), \beta(p))$, where $\alpha(p) \in [-\infty, 0)$ and $\beta(p) \in (0, +\infty]$, so either may be infinite.
\item The flow domain $\mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathbb{R} \times M$ of $\mathbf{X}$ is open in $\mathbb{R} \times M$, and the flow $\varphi : \mathcal{D} \to M$, $(t, p) \mapsto \varphi^p(t)$, is smooth (Definition~\ref{def:flow-domain}).
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Theorem 9.12}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\emph{(1)} is Proposition~\ref{prop:maximal-curve} above, proved in Lecture~24. The indication for (1) given in Lecture~23: by uniqueness and the translation lemma, which is easy, there is only one way to continue the curve forwards in time and then backwards in time until either it never stops or it runs into the edge of the manifold. Openness of $\mathcal{D}$ is surprisingly long to prove.

\emph{(2)} \textit{(Lecture~25: not proved in detail in class. That $\mathcal{D}$ is open is the hard part and takes quite a bit of work; once it is known, smoothness follows from local ODE theory. Filled in, following Lee's proof of Theorem~9.12; the argument gives openness and smoothness together.)} Let $W$ be the set of $(t, p) \in \mathcal{D}$ that have a neighbourhood of the form $J \times U \subseteq \mathcal{D}$, with $J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ an open interval containing $0$ and $t$ and $U \subseteq M$ open, on which $\varphi$ is smooth. Every point $(t', p')$ of such a $J \times U$ is again in $W$, with the same $J \times U$, since $J \ni 0, t'$. So $W$ is open in $\mathbb{R} \times M$, and $\varphi$ is smooth on $W$, smoothness being local. It suffices to show $W = \mathcal{D}$.

By the flow boxes of Lemma~\ref{lem:flow-box}, every $p \in M$ has $\varepsilon > 0$ and an open $U \ni p$ with $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times U \subseteq W$. Suppose $(\tau, p_0) \in \mathcal{D} \setminus W$. Then $\tau \neq 0$; say $\tau > 0$ (for $\tau < 0$ the argument is the same, with the supremum of the times $t \le 0$ where $(t, p_0) \notin W$). Let
\[
t_0 = \inf\{ t \ge 0 : (t, p_0) \notin W \} .
\]
The flow box at $p_0$ gives $t_0 > 0$; and $t_0 \le \tau$, so $t_0$ lies in the interval $(\alpha(p_0), \beta(p_0))$, which contains $0$ and $\tau$. By the definition of $t_0$, $(t, p_0) \in W$ for $0 \le t < t_0$.

Let $q_0 = \varphi(t_0, p_0)$, and take a flow box $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times U_0 \subseteq W$ at $q_0$. The curve $\varphi^{p_0}$ is continuous at $t_0$, so there is $t_1$ with $\max(0, t_0 - \varepsilon) < t_1 < t_0$ and $\varphi(t_1, p_0) \in U_0$. As $(t_1, p_0) \in W$, there is $J_1 \times U_1 \subseteq \mathcal{D}$ around it, with $J_1 \ni 0, t_1$, on which $\varphi$ is smooth; shrinking $U_1$, by continuity, $\varphi(\{t_1\} \times U_1) \subseteq U_0$.

Fix $p \in U_1$ and let $q = \varphi_{t_1}(p) \in U_0$. The curve $t \mapsto \varphi_{t - t_1}(q)$ is defined for $|t - t_1| < \varepsilon$ (flow box at $q_0$), it is an integral curve (translation lemma, Lemma~\ref{lem:translation-rescaling}(1)), and at $t = t_1$ it equals $q = \varphi^p(t_1)$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:global-uniqueness} it agrees with $\varphi^p$ on the common domain, and the two together form an integral curve starting at $p$ on the open interval $\tilde J = J_1 \cup (t_1 - \varepsilon, t_1 + \varepsilon)$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:maximal-curve}, $\tilde J \subseteq (\alpha(p), \beta(p))$ and this curve is $\varphi^p$. Hence $\tilde J \times U_1 \subseteq \mathcal{D}$, and
\[
\varphi(t, p) = \varphi\big(t - t_1, \varphi(t_1, p)\big) \qquad \text{for } (t, p) \in (t_1 - \varepsilon, t_1 + \varepsilon) \times U_1 ,
\]
a composite of smooth maps ($\varphi$ on $J_1 \times U_1$, then $\varphi$ on the flow box $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times U_0$). So $\varphi$ is smooth on the two open sets $J_1 \times U_1$ and $(t_1 - \varepsilon, t_1 + \varepsilon) \times U_1$, which cover $\tilde J \times U_1$. Now $\tilde J$ is an open interval containing $0$ and every $t \in [0, t_1 + \varepsilon)$, so $(t, p_0) \in W$ for all these $t$. As $t_1 + \varepsilon > t_0$, this contradicts the definition of $t_0$. Hence $W = \mathcal{D}$: $\mathcal{D}$ is open and $\varphi$ is smooth.
\end{proof}

$\varphi$ is just flowing along integral curves, as before, except that the domain of the time variable depends on the point, as in Example~\ref{ex:finite-escape}. The theorem is the local picture of Theorem~\ref{thm:ode-local}, with its rectangles $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times U$, put together on the whole manifold. In the two examples:
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
\item Rotation (Example~\ref{ex:rotation-flow}): $\alpha \equiv -\infty$, $\beta \equiv +\infty$, $\mathcal{D} = \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}^2$.
\item Escape (Example~\ref{ex:finite-escape}): $\alpha \equiv -\infty$, $\beta(x, y) = 1/(xy)$, so $\mathcal{D} = \{ (t, (x, y)) : x, y > 0,\ t\,xy < 1 \}$, open, and $\varphi(t, (x, y)) = \big(x/(1 - xyt),\ y\big)$, smooth on $\mathcal{D}$.
\end{itemize}

The first property of the flow is the group law, which is easy to prove.

\begin{propbox}[The Group Law]\thmlabel{prop:group-law}
Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$, $p \in M$ and $s \in (\alpha(p), \beta(p))$, and put $q = \varphi_s(p)$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item $(\alpha(q), \beta(q)) = (\alpha(p) - s, \beta(p) - s)$;
\item $\varphi_t(\varphi_s(p)) = \varphi_{t+s}(p)$ for every $t$ with $t + s \in (\alpha(p), \beta(p))$.
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Theorem 9.12(b)}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~25. On the board: fix $s$; $t \mapsto \varphi_t(\varphi_s(p))$ is an integral curve starting at $\varphi_s(p)$; so is $t \mapsto \varphi_{t+s}(p) = \varphi^p(t + s)$, by the translation lemma (the variable $t$ is translated by $s$); by uniqueness, these curves agree. The domains in (1) are filled in.)} Let
\[
c(t) = \varphi^p(t + s), \qquad t \in (\alpha(p) - s, \beta(p) - s).
\]
By the translation lemma (Lemma~\ref{lem:translation-rescaling}(1)), $c$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$, and $c(0) = \varphi^p(s) = q$. So $c$ starts at $q$, and by Proposition~\ref{prop:maximal-curve}
\[
(\alpha(p) - s, \beta(p) - s) \subseteq (\alpha(q), \beta(q)) \qquad\text{and}\qquad \varphi^q(t) = \varphi^p(t + s) \ \text{ for } t \in (\alpha(p) - s, \beta(p) - s). \tag{$\ast\ast$}
\]
In particular $-s \in (\alpha(q), \beta(q))$ and $\varphi_{-s}(q) = \varphi^p(0) = p$. The same argument with $q$ and $-s$ in place of $p$ and $s$ gives $(\alpha(q) + s, \beta(q) + s) \subseteq (\alpha(p), \beta(p))$, that is, $(\alpha(q), \beta(q)) \subseteq (\alpha(p) - s, \beta(p) - s)$. This proves~(1). Then~(2) is $(\ast\ast)$: if $t + s \in (\alpha(p), \beta(p))$, then $\varphi_t(\varphi_s(p)) = \varphi^q(t) = \varphi^p(t + s) = \varphi_{t+s}(p)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[Flows Commute with Themselves]\thmlabel{cor:flow-commute}
When $s$, $t$ and $s + t$ all lie in $(\alpha(p), \beta(p))$,
\[
\varphi_t\big(\varphi_s(p)\big) = \varphi_s\big(\varphi_t(p)\big) = \varphi_{t + s}(p) .
\]
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
Proposition~\ref{prop:group-law} for the pair $(s, t)$, and for the pair $(t, s)$, as $s + t = t + s$.
\end{proof}

The hypothesis that $s$, $t$ and $s + t$ lie in the domain is needed: with flows one always has to check where things are defined.

% ============================================================================
% SECTION: COMPLETE VECTOR FIELDS (Lectures 24, 25)
% ============================================================================
\section{Complete Vector Fields}\label{sec:complete-fields}

\roadmark{Stage: dynamics}{Vector fields whose integral curves exist for all time: the uniform time lemma, compact manifolds, actions of $\mathbb{R}$, and left-invariant fields on Lie groups.}

\textit{Lecture~24 (the definition and the uniform time lemma) and Lecture~25 (its proof and its consequences).}

\begin{defbox}[Complete Vector Field]\deflabel{def:complete-field}
$\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ is \textbf{complete} if $(\alpha(p), \beta(p)) = \mathbb{R}$ for every $p \in M$.
\leeref{Ch.~9, \emph{Complete Vector Fields}}
\end{defbox}

For a complete field there are no domain problems: every integral curve runs forever, forwards and backwards in time. The rotation field and the Euler field are complete; the fields of Examples~\ref{ex:finite-escape} and~\ref{ex:half-line} are not.

In general it is hard to tell whether a given vector field is complete, so results concluding that a field is complete are valuable. A short but powerful one:

\begin{lembox}[Uniform Time Lemma]\thmlabel{lem:uniform-time}
Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$. If there is $\varepsilon > 0$ such that $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \subseteq (\alpha(p), \beta(p))$ for every $p \in M$, then $\mathbf{X}$ is complete.
\leeref{Lemma 9.15}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~25, with the hypothesis written $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times M \subseteq \mathcal{D}$, Definition~\ref{def:flow-domain}.)} By contradiction. Suppose some $p \in M$ has $\alpha(p) \neq -\infty$ or $\beta(p) \neq +\infty$; take $\beta(p) < +\infty$; the other case is analogous. \textit{(Filled in: for $\alpha(p) > -\infty$, apply the argument to $-\mathbf{X}$, whose integral curves are those of $\mathbf{X}$ run backwards (Lemma~\ref{lem:translation-rescaling}(2)), whose maximal domains are the $(-\beta(p), -\alpha(p))$, and which satisfies the same hypothesis.)} Then $\beta(p)$ is a real number; choose $t_1 \in \mathbb{R}$ with
\[
\beta(p) - \varepsilon < t_1 < \beta(p) .
\]
\textit{(Filled in.)} $t_1 \in (\alpha(p), \beta(p))$: by hypothesis $\beta(p) \ge \varepsilon$, so $t_1 > 0 > \alpha(p)$. The time $\beta(p)$ is supposed to be the end of time for $\varphi^p$; the idea is to relaunch the flow at $\varphi_{t_1}(p)$, which by hypothesis can run for time $\varepsilon$ and so goes past $\beta(p)$. Define
\[
c(t) = \begin{cases} \varphi_t(p), & t \in (\alpha(p), \beta(p)), \\ \varphi_{t - t_1}\big(\varphi_{t_1}(p)\big), & |t - t_1| < \varepsilon, \text{ i.e. } t_1 - \varepsilon < t < t_1 + \varepsilon . \end{cases}
\]
The second line is defined, since $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \subseteq (\alpha(q), \beta(q))$ for $q = \varphi_{t_1}(p)$.

\emph{Claim: $c$ is an integral curve.} The first piece is $\varphi^p$. The second, $t \mapsto \varphi^{q}(t - t_1)$, is an integral curve by the translation lemma (Lemma~\ref{lem:translation-rescaling}(1)). Both pieces agree at $t = t_1$, where both equal $\varphi_{t_1}(p)$, so by Proposition~\ref{prop:global-uniqueness} they agree on their whole common domain: $c$ is well defined, and it is an integral curve on $(\alpha(p), t_1 + \varepsilon)$, since being one only involves $c$ near each time. It starts at $p$, and $t_1 + \varepsilon > \beta(p)$. This contradicts the maximality of $(\alpha(p), \beta(p))$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:maximal-curve}). So a uniform $\varepsilon$ is enough to keep every integral curve going forever.
\end{proof}

\textit{(Figure after the board.)} The horizontal line is $M$ and the vertical direction is $\mathbb{R}$: over each $p$, the maximal domain $(\alpha(p), \beta(p))$, between the graphs $t = \beta(p) > 0$ and $t = \alpha(p) < 0$. The lemma's hypothesis is that a uniform strip $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times M$ fits inside; its conclusion is that the whole of $\mathbb{R} \times M$ does.

Announced at the end of Lecture~24 and proved in Lecture~25 (Theorems~\ref{thm:compact-complete} and~\ref{thm:left-invariant-complete} below), as consequences of Lemma~\ref{lem:uniform-time}:
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
\item every vector field on a compact manifold is complete, since compactness gives a uniform time (Lee, Corollary~9.17);
\item every left-invariant vector field on a Lie group is complete, because solutions can be left-translated (Lee, Theorem~9.18).
\end{itemize}

The uniform time lemma (Lemma~\ref{lem:uniform-time}, proved in Lecture~25) says: if $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times M \subseteq \mathcal{D}$ for some $\varepsilon > 0$, that is, if a strip of constant width fits inside $\mathcal{D}$, then $\mathcal{D} = \mathbb{R} \times M$. The first corollary:

\begin{thmbox}[Vector Fields on Compact Manifolds Are Complete]\thmlabel{thm:compact-complete}
If $M$ is compact, every $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ is complete.
\leeref{Corollary 9.17}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~25.)} For every $p \in M$ there is a flow box $(-\varepsilon_p, \varepsilon_p) \times U_p$ with $p \in U_p$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:flow-box}). $\{U_p\}_{p \in M}$ is an open cover of $M$, so by compactness there are $p_1, \ldots, p_k \in M$ with
\[
M = \bigcup_{j=1}^k U_{p_j} .
\]
Let $\varepsilon = \min\{ \varepsilon_{p_j} : j = 1, \ldots, k \} > 0$. \emph{Claim: Lemma~\ref{lem:uniform-time} applies with this $\varepsilon$.} For $p \in M$ there is $j$ with $p \in U_{p_j}$, so $\varphi^p$ is defined on $(-\varepsilon_{p_j}, \varepsilon_{p_j}) \supseteq (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$. So $\mathbf{X}$ is complete.
\end{proof}

So on a compact manifold there is no need to check where the flow is defined.

Compactness is needed: the fields of Examples~\ref{ex:finite-escape} and~\ref{ex:half-line} live on noncompact manifolds and are not complete.

\textit{(Assignment~7, Problem~4.)} The argument of Theorem~\ref{thm:compact-complete} works on any compact subset, and it shows that an integral curve which stops in finite time must leave every compact set.

\begin{lembox}[Uniform Time on a Compact Set]\thmlabel{lem:uniform-time-compact}
Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ and $K \subseteq M$ compact. There is $\varepsilon > 0$ with $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \subseteq (\alpha(q), \beta(q))$ for every $q \in K$.
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~7, Problem~4: the submitted solution, the step ``a uniform time of existence on $K$''. For $K = M$ compact it is the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:compact-complete}.)} By Lemma~\ref{lem:flow-box}, for each $q \in K$ there are $\varepsilon_q > 0$ and an open neighbourhood $U_q$ of $q$ in $M$ with $(-\varepsilon_q, \varepsilon_q) \times U_q \subseteq \mathcal{D}$ (Definition~\ref{def:flow-box}); that is, $\alpha(q') \le -\varepsilon_q$ and $\beta(q') \ge \varepsilon_q$ for all $q' \in U_q$. Since $q \in U_q$ for each $q \in K$, $\{U_q\}_{q \in K}$ is a cover of $K$ by open subsets of $M$. Since $K$ is compact, there are $q_1, \ldots, q_m \in K$ with
\[
K \subseteq U_{q_1} \cup \cdots \cup U_{q_m} .
\]
Let $\varepsilon = \min\{\varepsilon_{q_1}, \ldots, \varepsilon_{q_m}\}$, positive as a minimum of finitely many positive numbers. For $q' \in K$ choose $j$ with $q' \in U_{q_j}$; then $\alpha(q') \le -\varepsilon_{q_j} \le -\varepsilon$ and $\beta(q') \ge \varepsilon_{q_j} \ge \varepsilon$.
\end{proof}

\begin{thmbox}[The Escape Lemma]\thmlabel{thm:escape-lemma}
Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ and $p \in M$ with $\beta(p) < +\infty$. Then the image $\varphi^p\big((\alpha(p), \beta(p))\big)$ of the maximal integral curve is not contained in any compact subset of $M$. The same holds if $\alpha(p) > -\infty$.
\leeref{Lemma 9.19}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~7, Problem~4: the submitted solution. The case $\alpha(p) > -\infty$ is filled in.)} Suppose, for contradiction, that $\varphi^p\big((\alpha(p), \beta(p))\big) \subseteq K$ for some compact $K \subseteq M$, and let $\varepsilon > 0$ be as in Lemma~\ref{lem:uniform-time-compact}: $\beta(q') \ge \varepsilon$ for all $q' \in K$. Since $\beta(p) < +\infty$, we may choose $s$ with
\[
\max\{0, \beta(p) - \varepsilon\} < s < \beta(p) .
\]
Then $\alpha(p) < 0 < s < \beta(p)$, so $q = \varphi^p(s)$ is defined. By assumption $q \in K$, so $\beta(q) \ge \varepsilon$. On the other hand, by the group law (Proposition~\ref{prop:group-law}(1)), $(\alpha(q), \beta(q)) = (\alpha(p) - s, \beta(p) - s)$, so
\[
\beta(q) = \beta(p) - s < \varepsilon ,
\]
a contradiction.

\emph{The case $\alpha(p) > -\infty$} \textit{(filled in)}: the maximal integral curve of $-\mathbf{X}$ starting at $p$ is $t \mapsto \varphi^p(-t)$ on $(-\beta(p), -\alpha(p))$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:translation-rescaling}(2), as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:uniform-time}); it has the same image and a finite right end $-\alpha(p)$, so the first case applies to it.
\end{proof}

In words: an incomplete integral curve has to escape every compact set --- to infinity, as in Example~\ref{ex:finite-escape}, or off an edge, as in Example~\ref{ex:half-line}.

\begin{corbox}[The Tail Escapes]\thmlabel{cor:escape-tail}
If $\beta(p) < +\infty$, then for every $t_0 \in (\alpha(p), \beta(p))$ the set $\varphi^p\big([t_0, \beta(p))\big)$ is not contained in any compact subset of $M$. Equivalently: if $\varphi^p\big([t_0, \beta(p))\big)$ lies in a compact set for some $t_0$, then $\beta(p) = +\infty$.
\leeref{Lemma 9.19}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Filled in. The proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:escape-lemma} uses the hypothesis only at the point $\varphi^p(s)$, for $s$ close to $\beta(p)$; so it proves this stronger statement, which is Lee's form.)} Suppose $\varphi^p\big([t_0, \beta(p))\big) \subseteq K$, $K$ compact, and take $\varepsilon$ for $K$ as in Lemma~\ref{lem:uniform-time-compact}. Choose $s$ with $\max\{t_0, 0, \beta(p) - \varepsilon\} < s < \beta(p)$. Then $s \in [t_0, \beta(p))$, so $q = \varphi^p(s) \in K$ and $\beta(q) \ge \varepsilon$, while $\beta(q) = \beta(p) - s < \varepsilon$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:group-law}(1): a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[Compactly Supported Vector Fields Are Complete]\thmlabel{cor:compact-support-complete}
Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ have compact support $\operatorname{supp}\mathbf{X} = \overline{\{q \in M : \mathbf{X}_q \neq 0\}}$. Then $\mathbf{X}$ is complete.
\leeref{Theorem 9.16}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from the assignment; filled in, from the escape lemma.)} Let $p \in M$ and suppose $\beta(p) < +\infty$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:escape-lemma}, the image of $\varphi^p$ is not contained in the compact set $K = \operatorname{supp}\mathbf{X}$: there is $t_0 \in (\alpha(p), \beta(p))$ with $q = \varphi^p(t_0) \notin K$, so $\mathbf{X}_q = 0$. Then the constant curve at $q$ is an integral curve defined on $\mathbb{R}$ (Example~\ref{ex:constant-integral-curve-at-zero}), so $\beta(q) = +\infty$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:maximal-curve}). But $\beta(q) = \beta(p) - t_0 < +\infty$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:group-law}(1), a contradiction. So $\beta(p) = +\infty$; and $\alpha(p) = -\infty$ by the same argument applied to $-\mathbf{X}$, which has the same support, as in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:escape-lemma}. Theorem~\ref{thm:compact-complete} is the case of a compact $M$, where every support is compact.
\end{proof}

\emph{Complete fields and actions of $\mathbb{R}$.} Suppose $\mathbf{X}$ is complete. Then $\mathcal{D} = \mathbb{R} \times M$, so for every $t \in \mathbb{R}$ there is a map $\varphi_t : M \to M$, and the group law holds for all $s, t$.

\begin{propbox}[The Flow of a Complete Field]\thmlabel{prop:complete-flow}
Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ be complete, with flow $\varphi : \mathbb{R} \times M \to M$. Then
\[
\varphi_0 = \mathrm{id}_M, \qquad \varphi_t \circ \varphi_s = \varphi_{t + s} \quad (s, t \in \mathbb{R}), \qquad \varphi_{-t} = (\varphi_t)^{-1},
\]
and every $\varphi_t$ is a diffeomorphism of $M$. Equivalently, $\varphi$ is a smooth action of the additive group $(\mathbb{R}, +)$ on $M$ (Definition~\ref{def:action}), written $t \cdot p = \varphi_t(p)$.
\leeref{Ch.~9, \emph{Flows}; Theorem 9.12(c)}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~25; details filled in.)} $\varphi_0(p) = \varphi^p(0) = p$. All maximal domains are $\mathbb{R}$, so Proposition~\ref{prop:group-law} applies for all $s, t \in \mathbb{R}$: $\varphi_t \circ \varphi_s = \varphi_{t + s}$. In particular $\varphi_{-t} \circ \varphi_t = \varphi_0 = \mathrm{id}_M = \varphi_t \circ \varphi_{-t}$, so $\varphi_t$ is a bijection with inverse $\varphi_{-t}$. Each $\varphi_t$ is smooth, as the smooth map $\varphi$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-flow}(2)) restricted to the slice $\{t\} \times M$; so is its inverse $\varphi_{-t}$. In the action notation, $0 \cdot p = p$ and the group law reads $t \cdot (s \cdot p) = (t + s) \cdot p$, the two conditions of Definition~\ref{def:action} for the group $(\mathbb{R}, +)$, whose identity is $0$ and whose product is $+$.
\end{proof}

There is a clash of notations: for an action, $(t, p) \mapsto t \cdot p$; for a flow, $(t, p) \mapsto \varphi_t(p)$. It is only a matter of notation; the two describe the same thing.

\begin{lembox}[A Complete Field Is Related to Itself by Its Flow]\thmlabel{lem:flow-related-to-itself}
Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ be complete, with flow $\varphi$. For every $t \in \mathbb{R}$, $\mathbf{X}$ is $\varphi_t$-related to itself: $d(\varphi_t)_p(\mathbf{X}_p) = \mathbf{X}_{\varphi_t(p)}$ for every $p \in M$.
\leeref{Ch.~9, \emph{Flows}}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~26, a warm-up; the lemma is a kind of infinitesimal version of the group law.)} Fix $t$ and $p$. To compute $d(\varphi_t)_p(\mathbf{X}_p)$ one needs a curve whose velocity is $\mathbf{X}_p$: $\mathbf{X}_p = \frac{d}{ds}\big|_{s=0} \varphi_s(p)$. By Corollary~\ref{cor:velocity-composite} (applied to the curve $s \mapsto \varphi_s(p)$ and the map $\varphi_t$) and the group law (Proposition~\ref{prop:complete-flow}),
\[
d(\varphi_t)_p(\mathbf{X}_p) = \frac{d}{ds}\Big|_{s=0} \varphi_t\big(\varphi_s(p)\big) = \frac{d}{ds}\Big|_{s=0} \varphi_{t+s}(p) = \mathbf{X}_{\varphi_t(p)} .
\]
The last step is the translation lemma: $s \mapsto \varphi_{t+s}(p) = \varphi^p(t + s)$ is an integral curve (Lemma~\ref{lem:translation-rescaling}(1)), so its velocity at $s = 0$ is the value of the field at $\varphi_t(p)$. So $\varphi_t$ pushes $\mathbf{X}$ forward to $\mathbf{X}$ itself, at the image point.
\end{proof}

\begin{defbox}[Infinitesimal Generator]\deflabel{def:infinitesimal-generator}
If $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ is complete, it is the \textbf{infinitesimal generator} of the $\mathbb{R}$-action $\varphi$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:complete-flow}.
\leeref{Ch.~9, \emph{Flows}}
\end{defbox}

This is half of a theorem: a complete vector field gives rise to an $\mathbb{R}$-action on $M$. The converse is also true.

\begin{thmbox}[Every Smooth $\mathbb{R}$-Action Has a Generator]\thmlabel{thm:action-generator}
Let $\varphi : \mathbb{R} \times M \to M$ be a smooth action of $(\mathbb{R}, +)$ on $M$, written $\varphi_t(p) = \varphi^p(t) = \varphi(t, p)$. Define
\[
\mathbf{X}_p = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} \varphi^p(t) = \dot\varphi^p(0) \in T_pM , \qquad p \in M .
\]
Then $\mathbf{X}$ is a smooth vector field, it is complete, and its flow is $\varphi$.
\leeref{Proposition 9.7}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~25. The smoothness of $\mathbf{X}$ and the last step, skipped in lecture, are filled in.)}

\emph{$\mathbf{X}$ is smooth.} The vectors $\mathbf{X}_p$ are defined because the action is smooth; $\mathbf{X}_p$ is a partial derivative in $t$, and these assemble into a vector field. In a chart $(U, x^1, \ldots, x^m)$ around $p_0$, for $p$ near $p_0$ and $t$ near $0$ the point $\varphi(t, p)$ stays in $U$ (continuity of $\varphi$, $\varphi(0, p_0) = p_0$), and by Corollary~\ref{cor:velocity-at-t-coords}
\[
\mathbf{X}_p = \sum_{i=1}^m \frac{\partial (x^i \circ \varphi)}{\partial t}(0, p)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p ,
\]
whose coefficients are smooth functions of $p$, since $x^i \circ \varphi$ is smooth near $(0, p_0)$. So $\mathbf{X}$ is smooth near $p_0$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}).

\emph{The curves $\varphi^p$ are integral curves of $\mathbf{X}$.} Let $\theta$ (script $\varphi$ on the board) be the flow of $\mathbf{X}$, defined on its maximal domain $\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{X}}$; we want $\theta = \varphi$, that is, $t \mapsto \varphi^p(t)$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$. By definition, the velocity of $\varphi^p$ equals $\mathbf{X}$ at time zero; at an arbitrary time this needs the group law. Fix $s$. The action gives $\varphi_t(\varphi_s(p)) = \varphi_{t + s}(p)$ for all $t$. Take $\frac{d}{dt}\big|_{t=0}$ of both sides: on the left, by the definition of $\mathbf{X}$ at the point $\varphi_s(p)$, $\mathbf{X}_{\varphi_s(p)}$; on the right, by the chain rule in the variable $t$, the velocity of $\varphi^p$ at time $s$:
\[
\mathbf{X}_{\varphi_s(p)} = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=s} \varphi_t(p) = \dot\varphi^p(s) .
\]
So $t \mapsto \varphi_t(p)$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ starting at $p$.

\emph{$\mathbf{X}$ is complete and $\theta = \varphi$.} Completeness of $\mathbf{X}$ cannot be assumed; it has to come out of the proof. In lecture it was to follow from the group law, a step that was skipped. \textit{(Filled in, by maximality instead.)} $\varphi^p$ is an integral curve starting at $p$ defined on all of $\mathbb{R}$, so by Proposition~\ref{prop:maximal-curve} the maximal domain of $p$ contains $\mathbb{R}$, and $\theta^p = \varphi^p$. This holds for every $p$: $\mathbf{X}$ is complete and $\theta = \varphi$ on $\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{X}} = \mathbb{R} \times M$.
\end{proof}

So complete vector fields on $M$ and smooth $\mathbb{R}$-actions on $M$ are the same thing, by $\mathbf{X} \mapsto$ its flow and $\varphi \mapsto$ its infinitesimal generator. In physics language: a time-independent dynamical law with solutions for all time is a one-parameter group of diffeomorphisms of the state space.

\emph{Naturality of integral curves.}

\begin{propbox}[Naturality of Integral Curves]\thmlabel{prop:naturality-integral-curves}
Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth, $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ and $\mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{X}(N)$. Then $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ are $F$-related (Definition~\ref{def:F-related}) if and only if, for every integral curve $c : I \to M$ of $\mathbf{X}$, $F \circ c : I \to N$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{Y}$.
\leeref{Proposition 9.6}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~25, $(\Rightarrow)$; $(\Leftarrow)$ filled in.)} Recall that $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ are $F$-related if and only if $dF_p(\mathbf{X}_p) = \mathbf{Y}_{F(p)}$ for every $p \in M$. For a smooth curve $c$, the chain rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}) gives the velocity of $F \circ c$:
\[
\frac{d}{dt}(F \circ c)(t) = (F \circ c)_{*t}\Big(\frac{d}{dt}\Big) = dF_{c(t)}\big(\dot c(t)\big) .
\]
$(\Rightarrow)$ If $\dot c(t) = \mathbf{X}_{c(t)}$, then with $p = c(t)$, relatedness gives $dF_{c(t)}(\dot c(t)) = dF_p(\mathbf{X}_p) = \mathbf{Y}_{F(c(t))}$, which by the display is the velocity of $F \circ c$ at $t$. The mechanism: $\mathbf{X}$ is the velocity of its integral curves, so integral curves can be used to compute the differential of $F$ applied to $\mathbf{X}$.

$(\Leftarrow)$ Given $p \in M$, let $c$ be an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ starting at $p$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:ode-local-manifold}). $F \circ c$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{Y}$, so at $t = 0$, by the display, $\mathbf{Y}_{F(p)} = dF_p(\dot c(0)) = dF_p(\mathbf{X}_p)$.
\end{proof}

In words: composing integral curves of $\mathbf{X}$ with $F$ gives integral curves of $\mathbf{Y}$ exactly when the two fields are $F$-related.

Lemma~\ref{lem:integral-curves-diffeo} is the case of a diffeomorphism $F$ and $\mathbf{Y} = F_*\mathbf{X}$, the unique field $F$-related to $\mathbf{X}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-pushforward}). A very important case of $F$-related fields is that of left-invariant fields on a Lie group.

\begin{thmbox}[Left-Invariant Fields Are Complete]\thmlabel{thm:left-invariant-complete}
Every left-invariant vector field $\mathbf{X}$ on a Lie group $G$ is complete. Moreover, $\varphi^g(t) = g\, \varphi^e(t)$ for all $g \in G$ and $t \in \mathbb{R}$.
\leeref{Theorem 9.18}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~25, by the uniform time lemma.)} Let $\varepsilon > 0$ be such that the integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ starting at $e \in G$ is defined for $|t| < \varepsilon$ (any $\varepsilon$ with $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \subseteq (\alpha(e), \beta(e))$). Pick $g \in G$. The left translation $L_g : G \to G$ is smooth and $\mathbf{X}$ is $L_g$-related to itself (Lemma~\ref{lem:left-invariant-related}), so by Proposition~\ref{prop:naturality-integral-curves}
\[
t \mapsto L_g\big(\varphi_t(e)\big) = g\, \varphi^e(t)
\]
is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$, defined for the same values of $t$, $|t| < \varepsilon$. It starts at $L_g(e) = g$, with velocity $dL_g(\mathbf{X}_e) = \mathbf{X}_g$. \textit{(On the board the starting point and the initial velocity were run together; the starting point is $g$, and $\mathbf{X}_g$ is the velocity there.)} So the integral curve starting at $g$ is defined at least for $|t| < \varepsilon$, with $\varepsilon$ independent of $g$, as $g$ was arbitrary; by Lemma~\ref{lem:uniform-time}, $\mathbf{X}$ is complete. \textit{(Filled in.)} For the last statement, now $\varphi^e$ is defined on $\mathbb{R}$, and the same argument shows that $t \mapsto g\varphi^e(t)$ is an integral curve on $\mathbb{R}$ starting at $g$, so it is $\varphi^g$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:maximal-curve}).
\end{proof}

The theorem says more: left-translating by $g$ the integral curve through the identity gives the integral curve through $g$, as in the figure. For $G = \GL(n, \mathbb{R})$ and the left-invariant field with $\mathbf{X}_I = A$, the curve $\varphi^I(t)$ is the matrix exponential $e^{tA}$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:exp-matrix}), and $\varphi^g(t) = g\, e^{tA}$.

\begin{exbox}[Left-Invariant Fields on the Affine Group of the Line]\exlabel{ex:affine-group-left-invariant}
\textit{(Not from lecture.)} A worked example: the group $G = \{(a, b) : a > 0\}$ of affine maps $x \mapsto ax + b$, an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^2$, with product $(a, b)(a', b') = (aa', ab' + b)$ and identity $e = (1, 0)$. Since $L_{(a,b)}(a', b') = (aa', ab' + b)$ has differential $a \cdot \mathrm{id}$, the left-invariant field with $\mathbf{X}_e = (u, v)$ is $\mathbf{X}_{(a,b)} = a(u, v)$. Its integral curve through $e$ is
\[
\varphi^e(t) = \big(e^{ut}, \tfrac{v}{u}(e^{ut} - 1)\big) \quad \text{if } u \neq 0, \qquad \varphi^e(t) = (1, vt) \quad \text{if } u = 0,
\]
defined for all $t$, as Theorem~\ref{thm:left-invariant-complete} requires: for $u > 0$, as $t \to -\infty$ it approaches the missing line $a = 0$ without reaching it. The curve through $g$ is $g\,\varphi^e(t)$.

\emph{The group.} \textit{(Filled in.)} The composite of $x \mapsto a'x + b'$ followed by $x \mapsto ax + b$ is $x \mapsto a(a'x + b') + b = aa'x + (ab' + b)$, which gives the product; $aa' > 0$, the identity map is $(1, 0)$, and the inverse of $(a, b)$ is $(1/a, -b/a)$. The product and the inverse are smooth on the open set $\{a > 0\}$ (polynomial, and rational with denominator $a \neq 0$), so $G$ is a Lie group (Definition~\ref{def:lie-group}).

\emph{The field.} $L_{(a,b)}$ is the restriction to $G$ of the affine map $(a', b') \mapsto (aa', ab' + b)$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$, whose Jacobian matrix is $a$ times the identity matrix. So $\mathbf{X}_{(a,b)} = d(L_{(a,b)})_e(u, v) = a(u, v)$ (Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant-extension}).

\emph{The integral curve through $e$.} By Proposition~\ref{prop:integral-curve-coords}, a curve $t \mapsto (a(t), b(t))$ in $G$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ if and only if $\dot a = ua$ and $\dot b = va$. With $a(0) = 1$ the first equation gives $a(t) = e^{ut}$ (the uniqueness argument of Example~\ref{ex:integral-curves-x-ddx}, applied to $e^{-ut}a(t)$). Then $\dot b = v e^{ut}$ and $b(0) = 0$ give $b(t) = \int_0^t v e^{us}\, ds$, which is $\tfrac{v}{u}(e^{ut} - 1)$ if $u \neq 0$ and $vt$ if $u = 0$. Since $a(t) = e^{ut} > 0$, the curve stays in $G$ for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$.

\emph{The curve through $g$.} For $g = (a_0, b_0)$, the product gives $g\,\varphi^e(t) = \big(a_0 a(t),\ a_0 b(t) + b_0\big)$, which is $\varphi^g(t)$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:left-invariant-complete}. Directly: its velocity is $\big(a_0 \dot a(t), a_0 \dot b(t)\big) = a_0 a(t)\,(u, v)$, the value of $\mathbf{X}$ at the point $g\,\varphi^e(t)$, whose first coordinate is $a_0 a(t)$; and at $t = 0$ it is $(a_0, b_0) = g$.
\end{exbox}

% SECTION: THE EXPONENTIAL MAP (Lecture 26, Wed Nov 4, 2026)

\section{The Exponential Map}\label{sec:exponential}

\roadmark{Stage: Lie groups}{The integral curve of a left-invariant field through the identity is a one-parameter subgroup; following it to time $1$ defines $\exp : \mathfrak{g} \to G$, the matrix exponential for linear groups, smooth and a local diffeomorphism at $0$.}

\textit{Lecture 26: the exponential map of Lie groups. Last time: every left-invariant field on $G$ is complete (Theorem~\ref{thm:left-invariant-complete}). The exponential map comes from the integral curve of a left-invariant field $\mathbf{X}$ starting at the identity, which is special.}

\emph{Notation.} The Lie algebra has two incarnations: the left-invariant fields with their bracket, and the tangent space at the identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:lie-algebra-TeG}; the remark \emph{Recap: $\mathfrak{g}$ Is $T_eG$} in \ref{sec:lie-morphisms}). Capital letters $A, B \in T_eG = \mathfrak{g}$ are vectors at the identity, and
\[
\mathbf{X}^A = \text{the corresponding left-invariant field, with } \mathbf{X}^A_e = A, \qquad \varphi^A = \text{the flow of } \mathbf{X}^A
\]
(Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant-extension}).
So $\varphi^A_t(e)$ is the integral curve of $\mathbf{X}^A$ starting at $e$, evaluated at $t$; here the superscript is the vector $A$, and the point is in parentheses. $A \mapsto \mathbf{X}^A$ is linear, since $\mathbf{X}^A_g = d(L_g)_e(A)$; in particular $\mathbf{X}^{cA} = c\,\mathbf{X}^A$.

\begin{propbox}[One-Parameter Subgroups]\thmlabel{prop:one-parameter-subgroup}
Let $\mathbf{X}$ be a left-invariant vector field on a Lie group $G$, with flow $\varphi$. Then for all $s, t \in \mathbb{R}$
\[
\varphi_{t+s}(e) = \varphi_s(e) \cdot \varphi_t(e),
\]
the product in $G$. So $t \mapsto \varphi_t(e)$ is a group morphism from the additive group $(\mathbb{R}, +)$ to $G$.
\leeref{Theorem 20.1}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~26.)} $\mathbf{X}$ is complete (Theorem~\ref{thm:left-invariant-complete}), so all these are defined. Fix $s$. $\mathbf{X}$ is $L_{\varphi_s(e)}$-related to itself, because being left-invariant means being $L_g$-related to itself for every $g$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:left-invariant-related}). So, by Proposition~\ref{prop:naturality-integral-curves},
\[
t \mapsto L_{\varphi_s(e)}\big(\varphi_t(e)\big)
\]
is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$, and it starts at $L_{\varphi_s(e)}(e) = \varphi_s(e)$: composing an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ with a map gives an integral curve of a related field, and here the related field is $\mathbf{X}$ itself. So is $t \mapsto \varphi_{t+s}(e)$, an integral curve by the translation lemma (Lemma~\ref{lem:translation-rescaling}(1)) with value $\varphi_s(e)$ at $t = 0$. Therefore, by uniqueness (Proposition~\ref{prop:global-uniqueness}), for all $t$,
\[
\varphi_{t+s}(e) = L_{\varphi_s(e)}\big(\varphi_t(e)\big) = \varphi_s(e) \cdot \varphi_t(e) .
\]
Writing out what $L$ is, the group multiplication appears explicitly for the first time.
\end{proof}

This is the case $g = \varphi^e(s)$ of $\varphi^g(t) = g\,\varphi^e(t)$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:left-invariant-complete}, combined with the group law $\varphi^{\varphi^e(s)}(t) = \varphi^e(t + s)$. Since $s + t = t + s$, the elements $\varphi_s(e)$ and $\varphi_t(e)$ commute: a one-parameter subgroup is abelian, even in a non-abelian $G$.

Conversely, every smooth group morphism $\mathbb{R} \to G$ arises this way (Proposition~\ref{prop:one-parameter-converse} below); this was not pursued in lecture.

The one-parameter subgroup is an orbit: the left-invariant field $\mathbf{X}^A$ is complete, so it generates an $\mathbb{R}$-action (Proposition~\ref{prop:complete-flow}), and $t \mapsto \varphi^A_t(e)$ is the orbit of the identity.

\begin{defbox}[The Exponential Map]\deflabel{def:exponential-map}
Let $G$ be a Lie group, with Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g} = T_eG$. The \textbf{exponential map} $\exp : \mathfrak{g} \to G$ is
\[
\exp(A) = \varphi^A_t(e)\big|_{t=1}, \qquad A \in \mathfrak{g} :
\]
make $A$ into the left-invariant field $\mathbf{X}^A$, take its flow, and follow the integral curve through $e$ up to time $1$.
\leeref{Ch.~20, \emph{The Exponential Map}}
\end{defbox}

\textit{(Figure after the board.)} The group is drawn like a sphere (think of a three-sphere). The vector $A$ in the tangent space $\mathfrak{g} = T_eG$ generates a one-parameter group; following it to time one gives a point $\exp(A)$ of the group.

The name is well motivated: for subgroups of the general linear group, $\exp$ is the matrix exponential (Theorem~\ref{thm:exp-matrix} below). The essential step is the following.

\begin{propbox}[Exponentials of Multiples]\thmlabel{prop:exp-tA}
For all $t \in \mathbb{R}$ and $A \in \mathfrak{g}$,
\[
\exp(tA) = \varphi^A_t(e) .
\]
So $t \mapsto \exp(tA)$ is the one-parameter subgroup of Proposition~\ref{prop:one-parameter-subgroup} for $\mathbf{X}^A$.
\leeref{Proposition 20.5}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~26.)} For $t = 1$ this is the definition. In general, by definition,
\[
\exp(tA) = \varphi^{tA}_s(e)\big|_{s=1} :
\]
take the field $\mathbf{X}^{tA} = t\,\mathbf{X}^A$ and flow $e$ up to $s = 1$. By the rescaling lemma (Lemma~\ref{lem:translation-rescaling}(2)), $s \mapsto \varphi^A_{ts}(e)$ is an integral curve of $t\,\mathbf{X}^A = \mathbf{X}^{tA}$, starting at $e$: the flow of $c\mathbf{X}$ is $\varphi_{ct}$, by the chain rule. By uniqueness (Proposition~\ref{prop:global-uniqueness}) it is $s \mapsto \varphi^{tA}_s(e)$, so
\[
\exp(tA) = \varphi^{tA}_s(e)\big|_{s=1} = \varphi^A_{ts}(e)\big|_{s=1} = \varphi^A_t(e) . \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[{Every Smooth One-Parameter Subgroup Is $t \mapsto \exp(tA)$}]\thmlabel{prop:one-parameter-converse}
Let $G$ be a Lie group and $\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to G$ a smooth group morphism from the additive group $(\mathbb{R}, +)$, and put $A = \dot\gamma(0) \in T_eG = \mathfrak{g}$. Then $\gamma$ is the integral curve of $\mathbf{X}^A$ starting at $e$:
\[
\gamma(t) = \varphi^A_t(e) = \exp(tA) \qquad \text{for all } t \in \mathbb{R} .
\]
\leeref{Theorem 20.1}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Filled in, for smooth morphisms; the converse was not pursued in lecture.)} $\gamma(0) = e$, because $\gamma$ is a group morphism; so $\dot\gamma(0) \in T_eG$. Fix $t \in \mathbb{R}$. Differentiating $\gamma(t + s) = \gamma(t)\gamma(s) = L_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma(s))$ in $s$ at $s = 0$ gives $\dot\gamma(t) = d(L_{\gamma(t)})_e(A) = \mathbf{X}^A_{\gamma(t)}$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:velocity-composite}). In detail: on the left, the derivative of $s \mapsto \gamma(t + s)$ at $s = 0$ is $\dot\gamma(t)$ (Definition~\ref{def:velocity-at-t} and the chain rule for real functions, as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:translation-rescaling}); on the right, the curve $s \mapsto \gamma(s)$ passes through $e$ at $s = 0$ with velocity $A$, so by Corollary~\ref{cor:velocity-composite} the velocity of $s \mapsto L_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma(s))$ at $s = 0$ is $d(L_{\gamma(t)})_e(A)$, which is $\mathbf{X}^A_{\gamma(t)}$ by Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant-extension}. So $\gamma$ is the integral curve of $\mathbf{X}^A$ starting at $\gamma(0) = e$, defined on $\mathbb{R}$, and $\gamma(t) = \varphi^A_t(e)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:maximal-curve}); this is $\exp(tA)$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:exp-tA}.
\end{proof}

Continuous group morphisms $\mathbb{R} \to G$ are automatically smooth (Lee, Problem~20-11(a); not proved in these notes), so the same holds for them.

\begin{corbox}[The Exponential Law on a Line]\thmlabel{cor:exp-law}
For all $s, t \in \mathbb{R}$ and $A \in \mathfrak{g}$,
\[
\exp\big((s + t)A\big) = \exp(sA) \cdot \exp(tA) .
\]
\leeref{Proposition 20.8}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~26.)} By Proposition~\ref{prop:exp-tA}, then Proposition~\ref{prop:one-parameter-subgroup}, then Proposition~\ref{prop:exp-tA} twice:
\[
\exp\big((s + t)A\big) = \varphi^A_{s+t}(e) = \varphi^A_s(e) \cdot \varphi^A_t(e) = \exp(sA) \cdot \exp(tA) . \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

This explains the name: it is an exponential law. In particular $\exp(0) = e$ and $\exp(-A) = \exp(A)^{-1}$.

\begin{rembox}[Warning: $\exp(A + B) \neq \exp(A)\exp(B)$ in General]\label{rem:exp-not-additive}
It is \emph{not} true in general that
\[
\exp(A + B) = \exp(A) \cdot \exp(B) .
\]
The reason: many Lie groups are non-abelian. The plus on the left is the addition in the tangent space at the identity, which is commutative, while the group law is not; so the identity cannot hold in general. There is a famous formula for $\exp(A)\exp(B)$, the Baker--Campbell--Hausdorff formula, a complicated series of iterated brackets of $A$ and $B$. For a single direction, $A$ and $B = cA$, the identity holds (Corollary~\ref{cor:exp-law}); more generally, it holds if $A$ and $B$ commute, which is not easy to show and is not proved in the course. (Lee, Problem~20-8, characterizes the groups where it holds for all $A$, $B$.)

\textit{(Not from lecture.)} A concrete failure in $\GL(2, \mathbb{R})$, using the matrix exponential of Theorem~\ref{thm:exp-matrix}, is Example~\ref{ex:exp-not-additive-nilpotent-pair} below.
\end{rembox}

\textit{(Assignment~7, Problem~5.)} The exponential map of a subgroup is the restriction of that of the larger group, because the integral curves are; for a linear group this identifies $\exp$ with the matrix exponential series, completing the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:exp-matrix} below. The series facts are Lemma~\ref{lem:matrix-exp-series}: $e^{tA} = \sum_{\ell \ge 0} \frac{t^\ell}{\ell!} A^\ell$ converges and may be differentiated term by term, $\frac{d}{dt} e^{tA} = A\, e^{tA} = e^{tA} A$.

\begin{lembox}[The Matrix Exponential Series]\thmlabel{lem:matrix-exp-series}
Let $A \in \Mat(n, \mathbb{R})$.
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item For every $t \in \mathbb{R}$ the series
\[
e^{tA} = \sum_{\ell=0}^\infty \frac{t^\ell}{\ell!} A^\ell
\]
converges in $\Mat(n, \mathbb{R})$, in any norm: each entry of $e^{tA}$ is a real power series in $t$ that converges absolutely for every $t \in \mathbb{R}$. In particular $e^{0 \cdot A} = I$.
\item The curve $\mathbb{R} \to \Mat(n, \mathbb{R})$, $t \mapsto e^{tA}$, is smooth, the series may be differentiated term by term, and
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\, e^{tA} = A\, e^{tA} = e^{tA} A .
\]
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Proposition 20.2}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in. Lecture~26 left the series facts as an exercise. Three facts are quoted from analysis: the comparison test for series; that a real power series $\sum_\ell c_\ell t^\ell$ which converges for every $t \in \mathbb{R}$ is a smooth function of $t$, whose derivative is the series $\sum_{\ell \ge 1} \ell c_\ell t^{\ell - 1}$ of the derivatives of its terms, again convergent for every $t$; and that all norms on a finite-dimensional real vector space are equivalent.)}

\emph{A bound on the powers.} For $B \in \Mat(n, \mathbb{R})$ write $|B| = \max_{i,j} |B_{ij}|$, a norm on $\Mat(n, \mathbb{R})$. For $B, C \in \Mat(n, \mathbb{R})$ each entry $(BC)_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^n B_{ik} C_{kj}$ is a sum of $n$ products, so $|BC| \le n\, |B|\, |C|$. Put $a = n|A|$. Then $|A^\ell| \le a^\ell$ for every $\ell \ge 0$, by induction: $|A^0| = |I| = 1$, and if $|A^\ell| \le a^\ell$, then $|A^{\ell + 1}| = |A^\ell A| \le n\, |A^\ell|\, |A| \le a^\ell \cdot a$.

\emph{(1)} Fix $i, j$. The $(i, j)$ entry of the $\ell$-th term of the series is $c_\ell t^\ell$ with $c_\ell = (A^\ell)_{ij}/\ell!$, and by the bound $|c_\ell t^\ell| \le (a|t|)^\ell/\ell!$. The series $\sum_\ell (a|t|)^\ell/\ell!$ converges, to $e^{a|t|}$; so by the comparison test $\sum_\ell c_\ell t^\ell$ converges absolutely, for every $t \in \mathbb{R}$. Hence the partial sums of the matrix series converge in every entry, which is convergence in the norm $|\cdot|$, and so in any norm on $\Mat(n, \mathbb{R})$, since all norms on this finite-dimensional space are equivalent. At $t = 0$ only the term $\ell = 0$ is nonzero, and it is $A^0 = I$.

\emph{(2)} A curve in $\Mat(n, \mathbb{R}) = \mathbb{R}^{n^2}$ is smooth exactly when its entries are, and its derivative is taken entry by entry. By the quoted fact on power series, each entry $t \mapsto \sum_\ell c_\ell t^\ell$ of $e^{tA}$ is smooth, with derivative
\[
\sum_{\ell \ge 1} \ell\, c_\ell\, t^{\ell - 1} = \sum_{\ell \ge 1} \frac{t^{\ell - 1}}{(\ell - 1)!}\, (A^\ell)_{ij} = \sum_{m \ge 0} \frac{t^m}{m!}\, (A^{m+1})_{ij} \qquad (m = \ell - 1) :
\]
differentiating $t^\ell$ brings out a factor $\ell$, which cancels against $\ell!$, and the index is shifted. So $t \mapsto e^{tA}$ is smooth and
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\, e^{tA} = \sum_{m=0}^\infty \frac{t^m}{m!}\, A^{m+1} .
\]
Now $A^{m+1} = A\, A^m = A^m A$. For a fixed matrix $B$, each entry of $BC$ and of $CB$ is a finite sum of entries of $C$ multiplied by entries of $B$; so if a series of matrices $\sum_m C_m$ converges in every entry, then $\sum_m B C_m = B \sum_m C_m$ and $\sum_m C_m B = \big(\sum_m C_m\big) B$, by the linearity of limits. With $B = A$ and $C_m = \frac{t^m}{m!} A^m$:
\[
\sum_{m=0}^\infty \frac{t^m}{m!}\, A\, A^m = A\, e^{tA}, \qquad \sum_{m=0}^\infty \frac{t^m}{m!}\, A^m A = e^{tA} A .
\]
The extra factor $A$ can be put on the left or on the right.
\end{proof}

\begin{lembox}[The Matrix Exponential Is Invertible]\thmlabel{lem:matrix-exp-invertible}
For $A \in \Mat(n, \mathbb{R})$ and $t \in \mathbb{R}$, $e^{tA}\, e^{-tA} = I$. So $e^{tA} \in \GL(n, \mathbb{R})$, with inverse $e^{-tA}$.
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in. The outline of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:exp-matrix} and the submitted solution of Assignment~7, Problem~5(b), use that $e^{tA}$ is invertible without proof.)} Each entry of a product of matrix-valued curves is a sum of products of entries, so the product rule holds: $\frac{d}{dt}(B(t)C(t)) = B'(t)C(t) + B(t)C'(t)$. With $\frac{d}{dt} e^{tA} = A e^{tA} = e^{tA} A$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:matrix-exp-series}(2)) and, by the chain rule, $\frac{d}{dt} e^{-tA} = -A\, e^{-tA}$,
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\big(e^{tA} e^{-tA}\big) = \big(e^{tA} A\big) e^{-tA} + e^{tA}\big(-A\, e^{-tA}\big) = 0 .
\]
So every entry of $e^{tA} e^{-tA}$ is a function on $\mathbb{R}$ with zero derivative, hence constant, and at $t = 0$ the product is $I \cdot I = I$. Thus $e^{tA} e^{-tA} = I$ for all $t$; then $\det(e^{tA}) \det(e^{-tA}) = 1$, so $e^{tA}$ is invertible, and its inverse is $e^{-tA}$, since a one-sided inverse of a square matrix is the inverse.
\end{proof}

\begin{lembox}[Integral Curves of a Left-Invariant Field on a Lie Subgroup]\thmlabel{lem:subgroup-integral-curves}
Let $H$ be a Lie group and $G \subseteq H$ a subgroup that is a Lie group with the inclusion $\iota : G \hookrightarrow H$ smooth and $d\iota_e$ injective --- a Lie subgroup, as in Theorem~\ref{thm:linear-group-bracket} --- so that $\mathfrak{g} = T_eG$ is identified with $d\iota_e(\mathfrak{g}) \subseteq \mathfrak{h} = T_eH$. For $A \in \mathfrak{g}$ let $\mathbf{A}^G \in \mathfrak{X}(G)$ and $\mathbf{A}^H \in \mathfrak{X}(H)$ be the left-invariant fields with $\mathbf{A}^G_e = A$ and $\mathbf{A}^H_e = d\iota_e(A)$ (the fields written $\mathbf{X}^A$ in the notation of this section, one on each group). Then $\mathbf{A}^G$ is $\iota$-related to $\mathbf{A}^H$, and for every integral curve $\gamma$ of $\mathbf{A}^G$, $\iota \circ \gamma$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{A}^H$.
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~7, Problem~5(a): the submitted solution. The relatedness is also Lemma~\ref{lem:morphism-related} for the morphism $\iota$, and the second statement Proposition~\ref{prop:naturality-integral-curves}; the solution proves both directly.)} $\iota$ is a Lie group morphism (Definition~\ref{def:lie-group-morphism}), and by Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant-extension}
\[
\mathbf{A}^G_g = d(L_g)_e(A) \quad (g \in G), \qquad \mathbf{A}^H_h = d(L_h)_e\big(d\iota_e(A)\big) \quad (h \in H),
\]
where $L_g$ and $L_h$ are left translations in $G$ and in $H$.

\emph{$\mathbf{A}^G$ is $\iota$-related to $\mathbf{A}^H$.} Let $g \in G$. For $k \in G$, since $\iota$ is a homomorphism, $\iota \circ L_g(k) = \iota(gk) = \iota(g)\iota(k) = L_{\iota(g)} \circ \iota(k)$; so $\iota \circ L_g = L_{\iota(g)} \circ \iota$ as maps $G \to H$. Differentiating at $e$ by the chain rule, with $L_g(e) = g$ and $\iota(e) = e$,
\[
d\iota_g \circ d(L_g)_e = d(L_{\iota(g)})_e \circ d\iota_e : T_eG \to T_{\iota(g)}H .
\]
Applying both sides to $A$,
\[
d\iota_g\big(\mathbf{A}^G_g\big) = d\iota_g\big(d(L_g)_e(A)\big) = d(L_{\iota(g)})_e\big(d\iota_e(A)\big) = \mathbf{A}^H_{\iota(g)} \qquad \text{for all } g \in G .
\]

\emph{Integral curves.} Let $\gamma : J \to G$ be an integral curve of $\mathbf{A}^G$, so $\gamma'(t) = \mathbf{A}^G_{\gamma(t)}$ for $t \in J$. The curve $\iota \circ \gamma : J \to H$ is smooth, and by the chain rule and the relatedness,
\[
(\iota \circ \gamma)'(t) = d\iota_{\gamma(t)}\big(\gamma'(t)\big) = d\iota_{\gamma(t)}\big(\mathbf{A}^G_{\gamma(t)}\big) = \mathbf{A}^H_{\iota(\gamma(t))} \qquad \text{for all } t \in J .
\]
So $\iota \circ \gamma$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{A}^H$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[The Exponential Map of a Lie Subgroup]\thmlabel{cor:exp-subgroup}
In the setting of Lemma~\ref{lem:subgroup-integral-curves}, for $A \in \mathfrak{g}$ and $t \in \mathbb{R}$,
\[
\iota\big(\exp_G(tA)\big) = \exp_H\big(t\, d\iota_e(A)\big) .
\]
So the exponential map of $G$ is the restriction of that of $H$ to $\mathfrak{g} \subseteq \mathfrak{h}$, and $\exp_H(tA) \in G$ for all $t$.
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Filled in.)} $\mathbf{A}^G$ is complete (Theorem~\ref{thm:left-invariant-complete}), and its integral curve starting at $e$ is $\gamma(t) = \exp_G(tA)$, $t \in \mathbb{R}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:exp-tA}). By Lemma~\ref{lem:subgroup-integral-curves}, $\iota \circ \gamma$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{A}^H$ defined on $\mathbb{R}$ and starting at $\iota(e) = e$; so it is the maximal integral curve of $\mathbf{A}^H$ starting at $e$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:maximal-curve}), which is $t \mapsto \exp_H(t\, d\iota_e(A))$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:exp-tA}).
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[Lie Group Morphisms Commute with the Exponential Map]\thmlabel{cor:exp-natural}
Let $F : H \to G$ be a Lie group morphism. Then $F(\exp_H A) = \exp_G\big(dF_e(A)\big)$ for every $A \in \mathfrak{h}$.
\leeref{Proposition 20.8(g)}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from the assignment; filled in: the proof of Corollary~\ref{cor:exp-subgroup} with $F$ in place of $\iota$.)} Let $\mathbf{X}^A \in \mathfrak{X}(H)$ and $\mathbf{Y}^{\tilde A} \in \mathfrak{X}(G)$, $\tilde A = dF_e(A)$, be the left-invariant extensions; they are $F$-related (Lemma~\ref{lem:morphism-related}). The integral curve $t \mapsto \exp_H(tA)$ of $\mathbf{X}^A$ starting at $e$ is defined on $\mathbb{R}$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:left-invariant-complete}, Proposition~\ref{prop:exp-tA}), so $t \mapsto F(\exp_H(tA))$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{Y}^{\tilde A}$ on $\mathbb{R}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:naturality-integral-curves}) starting at $F(e) = e$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:maximal-curve} it is $t \mapsto \exp_G(t\tilde A)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:exp-tA}); take $t = 1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[Integral Curves of Left-Invariant Fields on a Linear Group]\thmlabel{prop:linear-group-integral-curves}
Let $G \subseteq \GL(n, \mathbb{R})$ be a linear group that is a Lie subgroup (Theorem~\ref{thm:linear-group-bracket}), with $\mathfrak{g}$ identified with a subspace of $\Mat(n, \mathbb{R})$, and $A \in \mathfrak{g}$. For every $g \in G$ the integral curve of the left-invariant field $\mathbf{A}^G$ (with $\mathbf{A}^G_e = A$, as in Lemma~\ref{lem:subgroup-integral-curves}) starting at $g$ is
\[
t \longmapsto g\, e^{tA} = g \Big(\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty \frac{t^\ell}{\ell!} A^\ell\Big), \qquad t \in \mathbb{R} .
\]
In particular $g\, e^{tA} \in G$ for all $t$.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~7, Problem~5(b): the submitted solution, with the invertibility of $e^{tA}$ supplied by Lemma~\ref{lem:matrix-exp-invertible} and the convergence and term-by-term differentiation of the series by Lemma~\ref{lem:matrix-exp-series}; the solution takes $c(t) \in \GL(n, \mathbb{R})$ for granted.)} Let $\iota : G \hookrightarrow \GL(n, \mathbb{R})$ be the inclusion. Since $\GL(n, \mathbb{R})$ is open in $\Mat(n, \mathbb{R})$, $T_X \GL(n, \mathbb{R}) = \Mat(n, \mathbb{R})$ for each $X$ (Example~\ref{ex:left-invariant-GL}); the velocity of a matrix-valued curve is its entrywise derivative, and $A \in \mathfrak{g}$ is identified with the matrix $d\iota_e(A)$. Let $\mathbf{A}^{\GL}$ be the left-invariant field on $\GL(n, \mathbb{R})$ with $\mathbf{A}^{\GL}_I = A$.

\emph{The field $\mathbf{A}^{\GL}$.} For $h \in \GL(n, \mathbb{R})$, $L_h(X) = hX$ is the restriction of the linear map $X \mapsto hX$ of $\Mat(n, \mathbb{R})$. Computing its differential along the curve $t \mapsto I + tA$, which passes through $I$ with velocity $A$,
\[
\mathbf{A}^{\GL}_h = d(L_h)_I(A) = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} h(I + tA) = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} (h + t\, hA) = hA ,
\]
as in Example~\ref{ex:left-invariant-GL}.

\emph{$t \mapsto g\,e^{tA}$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{A}^{\GL}$.} Let $g \in G$ and $c(t) = g \sum_{\ell \ge 0} \frac{t^\ell}{\ell!} A^\ell$, $t \in \mathbb{R}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:matrix-exp-invertible}, $c(t) = g\, e^{tA}$ is a product of invertible matrices, so $c : \mathbb{R} \to \GL(n, \mathbb{R})$; and $c(0) = gI = g$. Differentiating term by term, the $\ell = 0$ term $I$ is constant, and for $\ell \ge 1$, $\frac{d}{dt}\frac{t^\ell}{\ell!} A^\ell = \frac{t^{\ell-1}}{(\ell-1)!} A^\ell$. Since left multiplication by $g$ and right multiplication by $A$ are linear and continuous, reindexing with $m = \ell - 1$ gives
\[
c'(t) = g \sum_{m=0}^\infty \frac{t^m}{m!} A^{m+1} = \Big(g \sum_{m=0}^\infty \frac{t^m}{m!} A^m\Big) A = c(t)\, A = \mathbf{A}^{\GL}_{c(t)} \qquad \text{for all } t \in \mathbb{R} .
\]

\emph{Comparison with $\mathbf{A}^G$.} Left-invariant fields are complete (Theorem~\ref{thm:left-invariant-complete}), so the integral curve $\gamma$ of $\mathbf{A}^G$ starting at $g$ is defined on $\mathbb{R}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:subgroup-integral-curves} with $H = \GL(n, \mathbb{R})$, $\iota \circ \gamma : \mathbb{R} \to \GL(n, \mathbb{R})$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{A}^{\GL}$ with $\iota \circ \gamma(0) = g$. So $c$ and $\iota \circ \gamma$ are integral curves of $\mathbf{A}^{\GL}$ on $\mathbb{R}$ with the same starting point, and by uniqueness (Proposition~\ref{prop:global-uniqueness})
\[
c(t) = \iota(\gamma(t)) \qquad \text{for all } t \in \mathbb{R} .
\]
Hence $c(t) \in G$ for all $t$, and $c$ is the integral curve of $\mathbf{A}^G$ starting at $g$.
\end{proof}

\begin{thmbox}[The Exponential Map of a Linear Group]\thmlabel{thm:exp-matrix}
Let $G \subseteq \GL(n, \mathbb{R})$ be a linear group (Definition~\ref{def:linear-group}) that is a Lie subgroup (Theorem~\ref{thm:linear-group-bracket}), and $A \in \mathfrak{g}$, a matrix. Then
\[
\exp(A) = \sum_{\ell=0}^\infty \frac{1}{\ell!} A^\ell ,
\]
the series converging in any norm on $\Mat(n, \mathbb{R})$.
\leeref{Proposition 20.2, Example 20.4}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}[Proof (outline from Lecture~26; the general case from Assignment~7, Problem~5)]
\textit{(The lecture gave the case $G = \GL(n, \mathbb{R})$ in outline; the series facts are an exercise, worked out in Lemma~\ref{lem:matrix-exp-series}, and the case of a general $G \subseteq \GL(n, \mathbb{R})$ needs an extra argument, which is part of the homework: Proposition~\ref{prop:linear-group-integral-curves}, Assignment~7, Problem~5(b).)} The method is once again uniqueness. Show it first for $G = \GL(n, \mathbb{R})$. Define $e^A = \sum_{\ell \ge 0} A^\ell / \ell!$. Then
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\, e^{tA} = A\, e^{tA} = e^{tA} A ,
\]
by manipulating the series (Lemma~\ref{lem:matrix-exp-series}): it converges strongly enough in norm to be differentiated term by term; differentiating $t^\ell$ brings out a factor $\ell$, which cancels against $\ell!$, and the resulting shift of index produces the extra factor $A$, which can be put on the left or on the right. So $\gamma(t) = e^{tA}$ is a curve in $\GL(n, \mathbb{R})$ (it is invertible, Lemma~\ref{lem:matrix-exp-invertible}), and
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\gamma(t) = e^{tA} A = d\big(L_{e^{tA}}\big)_e(A) = \mathbf{X}^A_{e^{tA}} ,
\]
because $L_{e^{tA}} : g \mapsto e^{tA} g$ is the restriction to $\GL(n, \mathbb{R})$ of a linear map, so it is its own differential (Example~\ref{ex:left-invariant-GL}). With $\gamma(0) = e$, $\gamma$ is the integral curve of $\mathbf{X}^A$ starting at $e$:
\[
\left\{ \begin{aligned} \tfrac{d}{dt}\gamma(t) &= \mathbf{X}^A_{\gamma(t)} \\ \gamma(0) &= e \end{aligned} \right.
\qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad e^{tA} = \varphi^A_t(e) ,
\]
and at $t = 1$, $e^A = \exp(A)$ by Definition~\ref{def:exponential-map}. For a general $G \subseteq \GL(n, \mathbb{R})$: by Proposition~\ref{prop:linear-group-integral-curves} with $g = e = I$, the integral curve of the left-invariant field $\mathbf{X}^A$ on $G$ starting at $e$ is $t \mapsto e^{tA}$, and at $t = 1$, $\exp(A) = e^A$ by Definition~\ref{def:exponential-map}. \textit{(Completed with Assignment~7, Problem~5.)}
\end{proof}

\begin{exbox}[{$\exp(A + B) \neq \exp(A)\exp(B)$ for Two Nilpotent Matrices}]\exlabel{ex:exp-not-additive-nilpotent-pair}
\textit{(Not from lecture.)} In $\GL(2, \mathbb{R})$, for $A = \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}$,
\[
\exp(A)\exp(B) = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \neq \begin{pmatrix} \cosh 1 & \sinh 1 \\ \sinh 1 & \cosh 1 \end{pmatrix} = \exp(A + B) ,
\]
a concrete failure of the identity of the remark \emph{Warning: $\exp(A + B) \neq \exp(A)\exp(B)$ in General} above. Here $[A, B] = AB - BA = \begin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{psmallmatrix} \neq 0$.

\emph{The exponential is the series.} For $G = \GL(2, \mathbb{R})$, $\mathfrak{g} = \Mat(2, \mathbb{R})$ (Example~\ref{ex:left-invariant-GL}), and Theorem~\ref{thm:exp-matrix} gives $\exp(C) = \sum_{\ell \ge 0} C^\ell/\ell!$.

\emph{$\exp(A)\exp(B)$.} $A^2 = B^2 = 0$, so all higher powers vanish and $\exp(A) = I + A$, $\exp(B) = I + B$:
\[
\exp(A)\exp(B) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}.
\]

\emph{$\exp(A + B)$.} $A + B = \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}$ has $(A + B)^2 = I$, so $(A + B)^{2k} = I$ and $(A + B)^{2k+1} = A + B$. Splitting the series into even and odd terms,
\[
\exp(A + B) = \Big(\sum_{k \ge 0} \frac{1}{(2k)!}\Big) I + \Big(\sum_{k \ge 0} \frac{1}{(2k+1)!}\Big)(A + B) = \cosh 1\; I + \sinh 1\; (A + B) = \begin{pmatrix} \cosh 1 & \sinh 1 \\ \sinh 1 & \cosh 1 \end{pmatrix}.
\]

\emph{They differ.} The top-left entries are $2$ and $\cosh 1 = (e + e^{-1})/2 < (3 + 1)/2 = 2$.

\emph{The bracket.} $AB = \begin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}$ and $BA = \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix}$, so $[A, B] = \begin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{psmallmatrix} \neq 0$: $A$ and $B$ do not commute.
\end{exbox}

\begin{rembox}[{Surjectivity and Injectivity of $\exp$}]\label{rem:exp-surjectivity}
For many groups, but not for all groups, $\exp$ is surjective: for instance for all unitary groups, and more generally for compact connected groups, a fact that needs proof \textit{(not proved here)}. But globally it is not one-to-one for a compact group: the exponential wraps the tangent space around the group, as $t \mapsto e^{it}$ wraps $\mathfrak{u}(1) = i\mathbb{R}$ around $\Ugp(1)$ (the figure below). \textit{(Not from lecture.)} Surjectivity can fail: $\exp$ takes values in the identity component, so it misses $\Ogp(n) \setminus \SO(n)$; and even for the connected group $\SL(2, \mathbb{R})$ the matrix $\begin{psmallmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 \end{psmallmatrix}$ is not an exponential (Example~\ref{ex:exp-not-surjective} below).
\end{rembox}

\begin{exbox}[{Two Groups Where $\exp$ Is Not Surjective}]\exlabel{ex:exp-not-surjective}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)}
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item For $G = \Ogp(n)$, $\exp(A) \in \SO(n)$ for every $A \in T_I\Ogp(n)$; so no element of $\Ogp(n) \setminus \SO(n)$, for instance $\mathrm{diag}(-1, 1, \ldots, 1)$, is an exponential.
\item For $G = \SL(2, \mathbb{R})$, the matrix $B = \begin{psmallmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 \end{psmallmatrix}$, which has $\det B = 1$, is not $\exp(A)$ for any $A \in \mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{R})$. ($\SL(2, \mathbb{R})$ is connected, a fact not proved in these notes; so here the failure is not a matter of components.)
\end{enumerate}

\emph{(1).} Let $A \in T_I\Ogp(n)$. The curve $t \mapsto \exp(tA)$ is an integral curve in $\Ogp(n)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:exp-tA}), so it is continuous. Every $g \in \Ogp(n)$ has $\det(g)^2 = \det(g)\det(g^{\mathsf T}) = \det I = 1$, so $\det g = \pm 1$. Hence $t \mapsto \det \exp(tA)$ is a continuous function $\mathbb{R} \to \{1, -1\}$ with the value $\det I = 1$ at $t = 0$; by the intermediate value theorem it is constant, and $\det \exp(A) = 1$: $\exp(A) \in \SO(n)$ (Definition~\ref{def:special-orthogonal-group}). The matrix $\mathrm{diag}(-1, 1, \ldots, 1)$ is orthogonal with determinant $-1$, so $\Ogp(n) \setminus \SO(n)$ is not empty.

\emph{(2), the exponential.} $\SL(2, \mathbb{R})$ is a linear group that is a Lie subgroup of $\GL(2, \mathbb{R})$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:linear-group-bracket}), with $\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{R}) = \{ A \in \Mat(2, \mathbb{R}) : \tr A = 0 \}$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:classical-summary}); so $\exp(A) = \sum_{\ell \ge 0} A^\ell/\ell!$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:exp-matrix}).

\emph{(2), the series for a traceless matrix.} Let $A = \begin{psmallmatrix} a & b \\ c & -a \end{psmallmatrix}$ and $d = \det A = -a^2 - bc$. Then
\[
A^2 = \begin{pmatrix} a^2 + bc & ab - ba \\ ca - ac & cb + a^2 \end{pmatrix} = -d\, I ,
\]
so $A^{2k} = (-d)^k I$ and $A^{2k+1} = (-d)^k A$. Splitting the series, which converges absolutely in every entry (Lemma~\ref{lem:matrix-exp-series}), into even and odd terms,
\[
\exp(A) = \alpha\, I + \beta\, A, \qquad \alpha = \sum_{k \ge 0} \frac{(-d)^k}{(2k)!}, \quad \beta = \sum_{k \ge 0} \frac{(-d)^k}{(2k+1)!} ,
\]
and $\tr \exp(A) = 2\alpha$, because $\tr I = 2$ and $\tr A = 0$.

\emph{(2), $\exp(A) \neq B$.} Suppose $\exp(A) = B$. Then $2\alpha = \tr B = -2$, so $\alpha = -1$. If $d = 0$, then $\alpha = 1$. If $d < 0$, put $\omega = \sqrt{-d}$; then $\alpha = \sum_k \omega^{2k}/(2k)! = \cosh\omega \ge 1$. So $d > 0$; put $\omega = \sqrt{d} > 0$. Then $\alpha = \sum_k (-1)^k \omega^{2k}/(2k)! = \cos\omega$ and $\beta = \sum_k (-1)^k \omega^{2k}/(2k+1)! = \sin\omega/\omega$. From $\cos\omega = -1$ and $\cos^2\omega + \sin^2\omega = 1$, $\sin\omega = 0$, so $\beta = 0$ and $\exp(A) = -I$. But $-I \neq B$: their upper right entries are $0$ and $1$. So $B$ is not an exponential.
\end{exbox}

What is always true is the following local statement.

\begin{propbox}[Smoothness and the Differential at $0$]\thmlabel{prop:exp-smooth}
$\exp : \mathfrak{g} \to G$ is smooth, and $d(\exp)_0 = \mathrm{Id}_{\mathfrak{g}}$, under the identifications $T_0\mathfrak{g} = \mathfrak{g}$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs}) and $T_eG = \mathfrak{g}$. Hence $\exp$ is a local diffeomorphism at $0 \in \mathfrak{g} = T_eG$: it maps some open neighbourhood of $0$ diffeomorphically onto an open neighbourhood of $e$.
\leeref{Proposition 20.8}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~26. Smoothness is awkward to prove directly, but there is a neat trick. The smoothness of the field $\mathbf{V}$, not gone into in lecture, is filled in.)}

\emph{1. Smoothness.} The flow evaluated at time one has to be considered as a function of $A$, which is new: so far only one vector field at a time has been considered. The trick, also used for variations, is to put together all the $\mathbf{X}^A$ as a single field over a larger space that includes the parameters, $G \times \mathfrak{g}$. Define
\[
\mathbf{V}_{(g, A)} = \big(\mathbf{X}^A_g, 0\big) \in T_gG \oplus T_A\mathfrak{g} = T_{(g, A)}(G \times \mathfrak{g}) ,
\]
using Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-product}, and $T_A\mathfrak{g} = \mathfrak{g}$, by the vector space structure. In the second slot one simply puts zero.

\textit{Claim: $\mathbf{V}$ is smooth} (this is where the smoothness of left multiplication is used). \textit{(Filled in.)} By Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-smooth-criterion} it suffices that $\mathbf{V}h$ is smooth for every $h \in C^\infty(G \times \mathfrak{g})$. With $\iota_A : G \to G \times \mathfrak{g}$, $x \mapsto (x, A)$, Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-product} gives $\mathbf{V}_{(g,A)} = (\iota_A)_{*}\mathbf{X}^A_g$, so
\[
(\mathbf{V}h)(g, A) = \mathbf{X}^A_g\big[h(\cdot, A)\big] = d(L_g)_e(A)\big[h(\cdot, A)\big] = A\big[x \mapsto h(gx, A)\big] .
\]
Let $\psi(g, x, A) = h(gx, A)$, smooth on $G \times G \times \mathfrak{g}$ because multiplication is smooth (Definition~\ref{def:lie-group}). Take a chart $(W, y^1, \ldots, y^m)$ of $G$ at $e$ and write $A = \sum_j A^j\, \partial/\partial y^j|_e$; the coefficients $A^j$ are linear, hence smooth, functions of $A \in \mathfrak{g}$. Then
\[
(\mathbf{V}h)(g, A) = \sum_{j=1}^m A^j\, \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial y^j}(g, e, A) ,
\]
the partial derivatives of $\psi$ in the coordinates $y^j$ of the middle factor, which are smooth on $G \times W \times \mathfrak{g}$. So $\mathbf{V}h$ is smooth. (This is the trick of Proposition~\ref{prop:left-invariant-extension-smooth}, now with $A$ varying too.)

\textit{$\mathbf{V}$ is complete} --- because each $\mathbf{X}^A$ is, and the integration only takes place in the $G$ variable; the $\mathfrak{g}$ variable plays no role. For $(g, A) \in G \times \mathfrak{g}$, the curve $t \mapsto \big(\varphi^A_t(g), A\big)$ has velocity $\big(\mathbf{X}^A_{\varphi^A_t(g)}, 0\big) = \mathbf{V}_{(\varphi^A_t(g), A)}$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-product}: the components of a velocity are the velocities of the components), it starts at $(g, A)$, and it is defined for all $t$, since $\mathbf{X}^A$ is complete. So the flow of $\mathbf{V}$ is
\[
\Phi : \mathbb{R} \times G \times \mathfrak{g} \longrightarrow G \times \mathfrak{g}, \qquad (t, g, A) \longmapsto \big(\varphi^A_t(g), A\big),
\]
which is smooth (Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-flow}(2)). Now put $t = 1$, $g = e$, and project:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
\mathfrak{g} \cong \{(1, e)\} \times \mathfrak{g} \arrow[r, hook] & \mathbb{R} \times G \times \mathfrak{g} \arrow[r, "\Phi"] & G \times \mathfrak{g} \arrow[r, "\mathrm{pr}_1"] & G ,
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad A \longmapsto \varphi^A_1(e) = \exp(A) .
\]
The composite is $\exp$, so $\exp$ is smooth.

\emph{2. The differential at $0$.} We want $d(\exp)_0 : T_0\mathfrak{g} = \mathfrak{g} \to T_eG = \mathfrak{g}$ invertible; in fact it is the identity. The differential of a map is computed with curves (Corollary~\ref{cor:velocity-composite}). The straight line $t \mapsto tA$ in $\mathfrak{g}$ is at $0$ when $t = 0$, with velocity $A$; so, with Proposition~\ref{prop:exp-tA},
\[
d(\exp)_0(A) = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} \exp(tA) = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} \varphi^A_t(e) = \mathbf{X}^A_e = A .
\]
\emph{3. Local diffeomorphism.} $d(\exp)_0$ is bijective, so by the inverse function theorem, in the form of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:local-diffeo-criterion} ($\Leftarrow$) at the single point $0$, $\exp$ restricts to a diffeomorphism from an open neighbourhood of $0$ onto an open neighbourhood of $e$.
\end{proof}

\textbf{Transcription note (board 11/4).} The board writes $\exp : \mathfrak{g} \to A$ in the statement (for $G$), $\mathbf{V}_{(g,A)} \in (T_gG) \times \mathfrak{g} = T_A\mathfrak{g}$ (the space is $T_{(g,A)}(G \times \mathfrak{g})$), and the flow as $(t, g, A) \mapsto (\varphi^A_t(g), 0)$; the second component of the flow is $A$, which the field leaves unchanged, as above.

\textit{(Not from lecture; figure added.)} $\exp$ for the group $G = \{(a, b) : a > 0\}$ of affine maps $x \mapsto ax + b$ of Example~\ref{ex:affine-group-left-invariant}. With $A = (u, v) \in \mathfrak{g}$ (meaning $\mathbf{X}^A_e = (u, v)$ in the coordinates $(a, b)$), the one-parameter subgroup is $\varphi^A_t(e) = \big(e^{ut}, \tfrac{v}{u}(e^{ut} - 1)\big)$, so $\exp(u, v) = \big(e^u, \tfrac{v}{u}(e^u - 1)\big)$ ($= (1, v)$ if $u = 0$). Lines $u = \text{const}$ (blue) go to the horizontal lines $a = e^u$, lines $v = \text{const}$ (red) to curves crossing the row $a = 1$ at $b = v$, and each one-parameter subgroup is a straight ray $b = \tfrac{v}{u}(a - 1)$ through $e$, run at exponential speed; near $0$ the grid is barely distorted, which is $d(\exp)_0 = \mathrm{Id}$. Here $\exp$ is even a diffeomorphism of $\mathfrak{g}$ onto $G$: given $(a, b)$, $u = \log a$ and $v = bu/(a - 1)$.
%% <<< END ADDED

The term exponential map comes up again in Riemannian geometry (MATH 635), for any manifold with a Riemannian structure. There, a tangent vector is the initial data of a geodesic, which one follows to time $1$. To exponentiate geometrically one needs a way of launching a curve from a tangent vector: here the one-parameter subgroups do this, in Riemannian geometry the geodesics. Next topic: Lie derivatives.
