% SECTION: LIE DERIVATIVES (Lecture 27, Fri Nov 6)
% ============================================================================
\section{Lie Derivatives}\label{sec:lie-derivative}

\roadmark{Stage: dynamics}{Differentiating along a flow: on functions the Lie derivative is the field itself, on vector fields it is the bracket; commuting fields are those invariant under each other's flows.}

\textit{(Lecture 27.)} The Lie derivative is a general construction; it returns with differential forms, the next chapter.

\emph{Motivation.} Go back to the definition of $\partial/\partial x^1$ on functions $f : \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}$ (or on an open subset; the definition is local). If $p = (a^1, \ldots, a^m)$,
\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x^1}(p) = \lim_{t \to 0} \frac{1}{t}\Big( f(a^1 + t, a^2, \ldots, a^m) - f(a^1, \ldots, a^m) \Big) .
\]
\emph{Observation:} the integral curve of $\mathbf{X} = \partial/\partial x^1$ starting at $p$ is $\varphi_t(p) = (a^1 + t, a^2, \ldots, a^m)$, exactly what sits inside the first $f$. So, with the pullback $(\varphi_t^*f)(p) = f(\varphi_t(p))$ (Definition~\ref{def:pullback-function}),
\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x^1}(p) = \lim_{t \to 0} \frac{1}{t}\Big( (\varphi_t^*f)(p) - f(p) \Big) ,
\]
and the right-hand side now makes sense on a manifold.

\begin{defbox}[Lie Derivative of a Function]\deflabel{def:lie-derivative-function}
Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$, with flow $\varphi$, and $p \in M$. For $f \in C^\infty(M)$, the \textbf{Lie derivative} of $f$ with respect to $\mathbf{X}$ at $p$ is
\[
(\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{X}} f)(p) = \lim_{t \to 0} \frac{1}{t}\Big( (\varphi_t^*f)(p) - f(p) \Big) .
\]
The field differentiated along is the subscript. Only small $t$ enter, and $\varphi_t(p)$ is defined for $|t|$ small (Lemma~\ref{lem:flow-box}), so $\mathbf{X}$ need not be complete.
\leeref{Ch.~9, \emph{Lie Derivatives}}
\end{defbox}


\begin{propbox}[On Functions $\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{X}}$ Is $\mathbf{X}$]\thmlabel{prop:lie-derivative-function}
For $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ and $f \in C^\infty(M)$, $\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{X}} f = \mathbf{X}f$. So $\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{X}}$, as an operator on $C^\infty(M)$, is $\mathbf{X}$ itself.
\leeref{Ch.~9, \emph{Lie Derivatives}}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~27.)} The limit is the derivative at $t = 0$ of the real function $t \mapsto f(\varphi_t(p))$:
\[
(\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{X}} f)(p) = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} f\big(\varphi_t(p)\big) = (\mathbf{X}f)(p),
\]
because $t \mapsto \varphi_t(p)$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ starting at $p$, so its velocity at $0$, which acts on $f$ by this derivative (Definition~\ref{def:velocity-at-t}), is $\mathbf{X}_p$.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[The Flow and the Operator]\label{rem:lie-derivative-function-meaning}
Proposition~\ref{prop:lie-derivative-function} gives no new operator, but it connects the two descriptions of a vector field: the dynamical one, by its flow, and the algebraic one, as a derivation of $C^\infty(M)$. The Lie derivative of other objects is defined by the same formula.
\end{rembox}

\begin{rembox}[Lie Derivatives of Other Objects]\label{rem:lie-derivative-other-objects}
In the definition, $f$ can be replaced by any object that can be pulled back by $\varphi_t$ (a tensor field; tensors are not yet defined in these notes). In this course these are differential forms, which pull back naturally (for one-forms, Definition~\ref{def:pullback-one-form}), and vector fields. A vector field cannot be pulled back by a general map, but each $\varphi_t$ is a diffeomorphism onto its image, so $d\varphi_t$ is invertible and its inverse carries the field back; this is Definition~\ref{def:lie-derivative-field} below.
\end{rembox}

\begin{rembox}[Where $\varphi_t$ Is Defined]\label{rem:lie-derivative-domain}
If $\mathbf{X}$ is incomplete, $\varphi_t$ is not defined on all of $M$. By the existence of flow boxes (Lemma~\ref{lem:flow-box}), every $p$ has a neighbourhood $U$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ such that $\varphi_t$ is defined on $U$ for $|t| < \varepsilon$; $\varphi_t(U)$ need not lie in $U$, and $\varphi_{-t} : \varphi_t(U) \to U$ brings it back, by the group law (Proposition~\ref{prop:group-law}); moreover $\varphi_{-t}$ is defined and smooth on an open set containing $\varphi_t(U)$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:flow-inverse-open-domain} below, from Lemma~\ref{lem:flow-diffeo-Mt}). An open domain is needed: the definition below takes the differential of $\varphi_{-t}$, which requires the map on a neighbourhood, not only along one trajectory.
\end{rembox}

\begin{lembox}[{$\varphi_t$ Is a Diffeomorphism from $M_t$ onto $M_{-t}$}]\thmlabel{lem:flow-diffeo-Mt}
Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ with flow $\varphi : \mathcal{D} \to M$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-flow}). For $t \in \mathbb{R}$ let $M_t = \{ p \in M : (t, p) \in \mathcal{D} \}$. Then $M_t$ is open, and $\varphi_t$ maps $M_t$ diffeomorphically onto $M_{-t}$, with inverse $\varphi_{-t}$.
\leeref{Theorem 9.12(c)}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; Lee's argument, used below for every time $t$; Corollary~\ref{cor:flow-inverse-open-domain} is the case of a flow box, where $|t|$ is small.)} \emph{Open and smooth.} The map $j_t : M \to \mathbb{R} \times M$, $j_t(p) = (t, p)$, is smooth, its components being a constant and the identity (Proposition~\ref{prop:product-maps}); in particular it is continuous, and $M_t = j_t^{-1}(\mathcal{D})$ is open because $\mathcal{D}$ is (Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-flow}(2)); $\varphi_t = \varphi \circ j_t$ is smooth on $M_t$, a composite of smooth maps, $\varphi$ being smooth on $\mathcal{D}$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-flow}(2)).

\emph{$\varphi_t(M_t) \subseteq M_{-t}$.} Let $p \in M_t$, i.e.\ $t \in (\alpha(p), \beta(p))$, and $q = \varphi_t(p)$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:group-law}(1), $(\alpha(q), \beta(q)) = (\alpha(p) - t, \beta(p) - t)$, which contains $-t$ because $0 \in (\alpha(p), \beta(p))$. So $q \in M_{-t}$.

\emph{Inverse.} For $p \in M_t$, Proposition~\ref{prop:group-law}(2) with $s = t$ and time $-t$ (allowed, since $-t + t = 0 \in (\alpha(p), \beta(p))$) gives $\varphi_{-t}(\varphi_t(p)) = \varphi_0(p) = p$, the maximal integral curve starting at $p$ being at $p$ at time $0$. The same argument with $-t$ in place of $t$ shows that $\varphi_{-t}$ maps $M_{-t}$ into $M_t$ and $\varphi_t(\varphi_{-t}(q)) = q$ for $q \in M_{-t}$. So $\varphi_t : M_t \to M_{-t}$ and $\varphi_{-t} : M_{-t} \to M_t$ are smooth and inverse to each other.
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[{The Inverse Flow Map $\varphi_{-t}$ Has an Open Domain}]\thmlabel{cor:flow-inverse-open-domain}
Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ with flow $\varphi : \mathcal{D} \to M$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-flow}), and let $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times U$ be a flow box (Definition~\ref{def:flow-box}). For $|t| < \varepsilon$:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $M_{-t} = \{ q \in M : (-t, q) \in \mathcal{D} \}$ is open in $M$, and $\varphi_{-t} : M_{-t} \to M$ is smooth;
    \item $\varphi_t(U) \subseteq M_{-t}$, and $\varphi_{-t}(\varphi_t(q)) = q$ for every $q \in U$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Filled in.)} \emph{(1)} is Lemma~\ref{lem:flow-diffeo-Mt} at the time $-t$: $M_{-t}$ is open and $\varphi_{-t}$ is smooth on it.

\emph{(2)} Let $q \in U$. Since $(t, q) \in (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times U \subseteq \mathcal{D}$, $q \in M_t$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:flow-diffeo-Mt}, $\varphi_t$ maps $M_t$ into $M_{-t}$, with inverse $\varphi_{-t}$; so $\varphi_t(q) \in M_{-t}$ and $\varphi_{-t}(\varphi_t(q)) = q$.
\end{proof}

\begin{defbox}[Lie Derivative of a Vector Field]\deflabel{def:lie-derivative-field}
Let $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$, let $\varphi$ be the flow of $\mathbf{X}$, and $p \in M$. The \textbf{Lie derivative} of $\mathbf{Y}$ with respect to $\mathbf{X}$ at $p$ is
\[
(\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{Y})_p = \lim_{t \to 0} \frac{1}{t}\Big( d(\varphi_{-t})_{\varphi_t(p)}\big(\mathbf{Y}_{\varphi_t(p)}\big) - \mathbf{Y}_p \Big) \in T_pM .
\]
\leeref{Ch.~9, \emph{Lie Derivatives}}
\end{defbox}

The two fields play different roles: $\mathbf{Y}$ is differentiated, along the flow of $\mathbf{X}$. Along the integral curve $t \mapsto \varphi_t(p)$, take the value of $\mathbf{Y}$ at $\varphi_t(p)$ and carry it back to $T_pM$ by $d(\varphi_{-t})_{\varphi_t(p)} : T_{\varphi_t(p)}M \to T_pM$; this uses $\varphi_{-t}$ near $\varphi_t(p)$, which it sends back to $p$ by the group law.

\textit{(Figure after the board.)} The value of $\mathbf{Y}$ along the trajectory, carried back to $T_pM$ by the flow.

\emph{Observation.} The limit is the limit of a curve of vectors
\[
V_t = d(\varphi_{-t})_{\varphi_t(p)}\big(\mathbf{Y}_{\varphi_t(p)}\big) \in T_pM
\]
in the fixed vector space $T_pM$, so it is taken in any linear coordinates on $T_pM$: $(\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{Y})_p = \dot V_0$. Note that $V_t \to V_0 = \mathbf{Y}_p$ as $t \to 0$, by continuity, just as $\mathbf{Y}_{\varphi_t(p)} \to \mathbf{Y}_p$; the Lie derivative is not where $V_t$ goes but how fast it gets there: $V_t - \mathbf{Y}_p = t\,(\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{Y})_p + o(t)$. Letting $p$ vary, this defines $\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{Y}$, a vector field on $M$. (For differential forms no such construction is needed, since forms pull back.)

That the limit exists is not obvious; it is the content of the next lemma.

\begin{lembox}[The Lie Derivative Exists and Is Smooth]\thmlabel{lem:lie-derivative-smooth}
For $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$, the limit in Definition~\ref{def:lie-derivative-field} exists at every $p \in M$, and $\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{Y}$ is a smooth vector field.
\leeref{Lemma 9.36}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Stated without proof in Lecture~27; Lee's proof, filled in.)} Fix $p \in M$ and a chart $(U, (x^i))$ at $p$. Since $\mathcal{D}$ is open and $\varphi$ is continuous (Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-flow}(2)), with $(0, p) \in \mathcal{D}$ and $\varphi(0, p) = p$, there are $\delta > 0$ and open sets $U_1 \subseteq U_0 \subseteq U$ containing $p$ with $(-\delta, \delta) \times U_0 \subseteq \mathcal{D}$, $\varphi\big((-\delta, \delta) \times U_0\big) \subseteq U$ and $\varphi\big((-\delta, \delta) \times U_1\big) \subseteq U_0$. Write $\varphi^i(t, x)$ for the components of $\varphi$ on $(-\delta, \delta) \times U_0$ in the chart.

Let $|t| < \delta$ and $x \in U_1$. Then $\varphi_t(x) \in U_0$, and on the open set $U_0$ the map $\varphi_{-t} = \varphi(-t, \cdot\,)$ is defined with values in $U$; the Jacobian of its coordinate representation at $\varphi_t(x)$ is the matrix $\big(\frac{\partial \varphi^i}{\partial x^j}(-t, \varphi(t, x))\big)$. Hence, by Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix} (the matrix of a differential in coordinates is the Jacobian of the coordinate representation),
\[
V_t(x) := d(\varphi_{-t})_{\varphi_t(x)}\big(\mathbf{Y}_{\varphi_t(x)}\big) = \sum_{i,j} \frac{\partial \varphi^i}{\partial x^j}\big(-t, \varphi(t, x)\big)\, Y^j\big(\varphi(t, x)\big)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_x ,
\]
where $Y^j$ are the components of $\mathbf{Y}$. The coefficient of $\partial/\partial x^i|_x$ is a smooth function of $(t, x) \in (-\delta, \delta) \times U_1$, a composite of smooth functions. Therefore $(\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{Y})_x$, the $t$-derivative at $t = 0$ of this expression (Definition~\ref{def:lie-derivative-field}), exists for each $x \in U_1$, and its coefficients $\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\big|_{t=0}$ of smooth functions of $(t, x)$ are smooth in $x$. As $p$ was arbitrary, $\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{Y}$ is defined everywhere and is a smooth vector field. The same formula shows that $t \mapsto V_t(x)$ is a smooth curve in $T_xM$ for $|t| < \delta$.
\end{proof}

\begin{exbox}[The Lie Derivative along $\partial/\partial x^1$]\exlabel{ex:lie-derivative-d1}
On $\mathbb{R}^m$ let $\mathbf{X} = \partial/\partial x^1$ and $\mathbf{Y} = \sum_i g^i\, \partial/\partial x^i$. The flow is translation in the first variable,
\[
\varphi_t(x^1, \ldots, x^m) = (x^1 + t, x^2, \ldots, x^m), \qquad \text{i.e. } \varphi_t(x) = x + te_1, \quad e_1 = (1, 0, \ldots, 0) .
\]
Its differential is the identity everywhere, in the coordinate bases: $d(\varphi_{-t})_{x}(\partial/\partial x^i|_x) = \partial/\partial x^i|_{x - te_1}$. So
\[
(\mathcal{L}_{\partial/\partial x^1}\mathbf{Y})_p = \lim_{t \to 0} \frac{1}{t}\big( \mathbf{Y}_{p + te_1} - \mathbf{Y}_p \big) = \lim_{t \to 0} \frac{1}{t} \sum_{i=1}^m \big( g^i(p + te_1) - g^i(p) \big) \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p = \sum_{i=1}^m \frac{\partial g^i}{\partial x^1}(p)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p .
\]
The flow is written down at every point $x$, not only along the trajectory of $p$, because the definition takes the differential of the time-$t$ map. Here the Lie derivative is componentwise differentiation of $\mathbf{Y}$ in the direction $x^1$; this case is the core of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:lie-derivative-bracket}.
\end{exbox}

The Lie derivative of a vector field turns out to be a known operation, the bracket. The proof uses a normal form for a vector field near a point where it does not vanish; its proof, by the flow, was postponed to Lecture~28 and is given after the lemma.

\begin{lembox}[Canonical Form Near a Regular Point]\thmlabel{lem:straightening}
Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ and $p \in M$ with $\mathbf{X}_p \neq 0$. There is a coordinate chart $(U, x^1, \ldots, x^m)$ with $p \in U$ such that
\[
\mathbf{X}|_U = \frac{\partial}{\partial x^1} .
\]
\leeref{Theorem 9.22}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~28, the last proof on vector fields in the course. Here $\varphi$ is the flow of $\mathbf{X}$, so the charts are called $\psi$ and $y$ along the way. Details marked are filled in.)} Start with any coordinates $\psi = (u^1, \ldots, u^m)$ at $p$, centred: $\psi(p) = 0$.

\emph{Step 1: a linear change of coordinates.} Find an invertible linear map $L : \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^m$ such that, for the new coordinates $(y^1, \ldots, y^m) = L(u^1, \ldots, u^m)$, i.e.\ $y^i = \sum_j a_{ij} u^j$,
\[
\mathbf{X}_p = \frac{\partial}{\partial y^1}\Big|_p \qquad (\text{at } p \text{ only}).
\]
This is possible because $\mathbf{X}_p \neq 0$: in the $u$-coordinates $\mathbf{X}_p$ is a nonzero vector of $\mathbb{R}^m$, and $L$ only has to send it to $e_1$; $L$ need not be a rotation, and may have to rescale.

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.95]
\draw[->, gray!60] (-0.3,0) -- (2.2,0) node[right, font=\scriptsize, text=black] {$u^1$};
\draw[->, gray!60] (0,-0.3) -- (0,1.8) node[above, font=\scriptsize, text=black] {$u^2$};
\draw[->, very thick, orange!85!black] (0,0) -- (1.4,1.1) node[above right, font=\scriptsize] {$\mathbf{X}_p$};
\fill (0,0) circle (1.2pt) node[below left, font=\scriptsize] {$p$};
\draw[->, thick] (2.6,0.8) -- node[above, font=\scriptsize] {$L$} (3.6,0.8);
\begin{scope}[xshift=4.3cm]
\draw[->, gray!60] (-0.3,0) -- (2.2,0) node[right, font=\scriptsize, text=black] {$y^1$};
\draw[->, gray!60] (0,-0.3) -- (0,1.8) node[above, font=\scriptsize, text=black] {$y^2$};
\draw[->, very thick, orange!85!black] (0,0) -- (1.0,0) node[below=2pt, font=\scriptsize] {$\mathbf{X}_p = e_1$};
\fill (0,0) circle (1.2pt) node[below left, font=\scriptsize] {$p$};
\node[font=\scriptsize, orange!70!black] at (1.2,1.2) {in the new coordinates};
\end{scope}
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

Let $V \subseteq M$ be the domain of $(y^1, \ldots, y^m)$, and introduce the hypersurface
\[
S = \{ y^1 = 0 \} \subseteq V , \qquad \dim S = m - 1 ,
\]
with coordinates $(y^2, \ldots, y^m)$. On $V$, $\mathbf{X}|_V = \sum_i f^i\, \partial/\partial y^i$ with $f^1(p) = 1$ and $f^i(p) = 0$ for $i = 2, \ldots, m$. Shrinking $V$, we may assume $f^1 \neq 0$ on $S$: then $\mathbf{X}$ is transverse to $S$ at every point of $S$. (The assumption is geometric, a field crossing $S$ everywhere; the argument below only uses $f^1(p) \neq 0$.)

\emph{Step 2: flow out $S$.} Flow out $S$ by the flow of $\mathbf{X}$: the integral curves through all the points of $S$ fill a neighbourhood of $p$. By a flow box at $p$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:flow-box}), shrinking $S$ around $p$, there is $\varepsilon > 0$ such that
\[
\theta : (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times S \longrightarrow M, \qquad (t, q) \longmapsto \varphi_t(q)
\]
is defined; it is smooth, as the restriction of the flow (Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-flow}(2)).

\emph{Claim: $d\theta_{(0,p)} = \mathrm{Id}$,} in the coordinates $(t, y^2, \ldots, y^m)$ on $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times S$ and $(y^1, \ldots, y^m)$ on $V$. Since $\theta(0, q) = q$, the curves $t \mapsto \theta(0, y^2, \ldots, y^i + t, \ldots, y^m)$, $i = 2, \ldots, m$, are the coordinate curves of $S$, so in the $S$ directions $d\theta_{(0,p)}$ is the identity block. And $t \mapsto \theta(t, 0, \ldots, 0) = \varphi_t(p)$ is the integral curve through $p$, whose velocity at $t = 0$ is $\mathbf{X}_p = \partial/\partial y^1|_p$, by the choice of the $y$-coordinates. So $d\theta_{(0,p)}$ sends each coordinate vector to the coordinate vector of the same index. The dimensions match, $1 + (m - 1) = m$, so by the inverse function theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:inverse-function} in charts, as in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:local-diffeo-criterion}, at the single point $(0, p)$), $\theta$ is a local diffeomorphism near $(0, p)$: there are a neighbourhood $U$ of $p$ and an inverse
\[
\theta^{-1} : U \longrightarrow (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times S
\]
(onto an open neighbourhood of $(0, p)$, shrinking $\varepsilon$ and $S$ again).

\emph{Step 3: the coordinates.} Define
\[
(x^1, \ldots, x^m) = (t, y^2, \ldots, y^m) \circ \theta^{-1} \qquad \text{on } U .
\]
\textit{(Filled in.)} This is a chart: a composite of the diffeomorphism $\theta^{-1}$ onto an open set and the coordinates $(t, y^2, \ldots, y^m)$, so a diffeomorphism of $U$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^m$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:chart-diffeo}). Geometrically: given $q \in U$, there is $(t, r) \in (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times S$ with $q = \theta(t, r)$: the integral curve starting at $r \in S$ passes through $q$ at time $t$. So $x^1(q) = t$ is the time it takes to flow from $S$ to $q$, and $(x^2, \ldots, x^m)(q)$ are the $y$-coordinates of the point $r$ where the curve through $q$, traced back, meets $S$.

\emph{In these coordinates, $\mathbf{X} = \partial/\partial x^1$.} $\partial/\partial x^1|_q$ is the velocity of the curve that fixes all other coordinates and translates $x^1$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:velocity-coords}). That curve is $s \mapsto \theta(t + s, r) = \varphi_{t+s}(r)$, which equals $\varphi_s(q)$ by the group law (Proposition~\ref{prop:group-law}): the integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ through $q$. Its velocity at $s = 0$ is $\mathbf{X}_q$. So the $x^1$-coordinate curves are exactly the integral curves of $\mathbf{X}$.
\end{proof}

\textit{(Figure after the board, redrawn from a computed field.)} The \emph{flowout} of the transverse slice $S$, for the field $\mathbf{X} = \big(1 - 0.15 (y^2)^2\big)\, \partial/\partial y^1 + (0.5\, y^1 + 0.2\, y^2)\, \partial/\partial y^2$ on the plane, with $\mathbf{X}_p = \partial/\partial y^1|_p$ at $p = 0$. Left: the domain $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times S$ of $\theta$, with the lines $\{t\} \times S$ (grey) and $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times \{r\}$ (blue). Right: their images in $V$, the slices $\varphi_t(S)$ (grey, $t = \pm 0.5, \pm 1$) and the integral curves of $\mathbf{X}$ through points of $S$ (blue); the shaded region is $U = \theta\big((-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times S\big)$. Each point $q$ near $p$ is reached by exactly one integral curve from $S$, after a time $t$: here $q = \theta(t, r)$ with $t = 0.8$ (red). The chart $\theta^{-1}$ gives $q$ the coordinates $x^1(q) = t$, the time from $S$ to $q$, and $(x^2, \ldots, x^m)(q) = (y^2, \ldots, y^m)(r)$, the coordinates of the starting point. The construction reappears in classical mechanics, where $t$ is physical time. Lee proves the theorem with his flowout theorem (Theorem~9.20); the inverse function theorem above does the same job locally.

Lemma~\ref{lem:straightening} in a picture. Left: integral curves of $\mathbf{X}$ in $M$ near $p$ (continuing outside $U$), and the chart domain $U$. Right: in the chart $(x^1, \ldots, x^m)$, the same curves are the parallel lines on which $x^2, \ldots, x^m$ are constant, run at unit speed in $x^1$.

A field that is nonzero at $p$ is nonzero on a neighbourhood of $p$, by continuity, and in suitable coordinates there it is the constant field $\partial_1$: its integral curves are straightened into parallel lines.

\begin{thmbox}[The Lie Derivative Is the Bracket]\thmlabel{thm:lie-derivative-bracket}
For $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$,
\[
\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{Y} = [\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}] .
\]
\leeref{Theorem 9.38}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~27, modulo Lemmas~\ref{lem:lie-derivative-smooth} and~\ref{lem:straightening}. The locality in Case~2 and the continuity argument in Case~3 are filled in.)} Take $p \in M$.

\emph{Case 1: $\mathbf{X}$ is zero in a neighbourhood $W$ of $p$.} Then $\varphi_t(q) = q$ for all $q \in W$, since $\mathbf{X} = 0$ there and so the constant curve is an integral curve there. So $\varphi_{-t}$ is the identity on the open set $W$, $d(\varphi_{-t})_p = \mathrm{id}$, $V_t = \mathbf{Y}_p$, and $(\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{Y})_p = 0 \in T_pM$. Also $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]_p f = \mathbf{X}_p(\mathbf{Y}f) - \mathbf{Y}_p(\mathbf{X}f) = 0$, as $\mathbf{X}_p = 0$ and $\mathbf{X}f$ vanishes on $W$, so its germ at $p$ is $0$.

\emph{Case 2: $\mathbf{X}_p \neq 0$.} Take the chart $(U, x^1, \ldots, x^m)$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:straightening}, with $\mathbf{X}|_U = \partial/\partial x^1$, and write $\mathbf{Y} = \sum_i g^i\, \partial/\partial x^i$ on $U$. \textit{(Filled in.)} The Lie derivative at $p$ only involves $\varphi_t$ near $p$ and $\varphi_{-t}$ near $\varphi_t(p)$, for small $t$. Choose a neighbourhood $U' \subseteq U$ of $p$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ with $\varphi_t(U') \subseteq U$ for $|t| < \varepsilon$. For $q \in U'$, the curve $t \mapsto \varphi_t(q)$, $|t| < \varepsilon$, is an integral curve of $\partial/\partial x^1$ inside $U$, so in coordinates it is $x(q) + te_1$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:integral-curves-diffeo} and uniqueness). So in the chart the flow is the translation of Example~\ref{ex:lie-derivative-d1}, and the problem reduces to that Euclidean computation:
\[
\mathcal{L}_{\partial/\partial x^1}\mathbf{Y} = \sum_i \frac{\partial g^i}{\partial x^1}\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i} \qquad \text{at } p ,
\]
the left-hand side of the identity. The right-hand side, by Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket-coords}:
\[
\Big[ \frac{\partial}{\partial x^1}, \sum_i g^i \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i} \Big] = \sum_i \frac{\partial g^i}{\partial x^1}\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i} ,
\]
since the other term, $\mathbf{Y}$ applied to the coefficients of $\partial/\partial x^1$, vanishes: they are constant. The two sides agree.

\emph{Case 3: $\mathbf{X}_p = 0$, but $\mathbf{X}$ is not zero on any neighbourhood of $p$.} Cases~1 and~2 do not cover every point: $p$ may lie on the boundary of the support of $\mathbf{X}$. This case follows by continuity, given that the Lie derivative is smooth. \textit{(Filled in.)} Every neighbourhood of $p$ contains points $q$ with $\mathbf{X}_q \neq 0$, so $p$ is a limit of such points. At those points the two sides agree by Case~2, and both $\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{Y}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:lie-derivative-smooth}) and $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:bracket-field}) are continuous. In a chart around $p$ their components are continuous functions agreeing at the points $q$, hence at $p$.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[The Bracket Has a Dynamical Meaning]\label{rem:bracket-dynamical}
The bracket was defined algebraically, as the commutator of two derivations (Lemma~\ref{lem:bracket-field}). Theorem~\ref{thm:lie-derivative-bracket} reaches it from the flow: $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]_p$ is the rate at which $\mathbf{Y}$, carried back along the flow of $\mathbf{X}$, changes at $p$. This has dynamical consequences, the first being Theorem~\ref{thm:commuting-flows} below.
\end{rembox}

\textit{(Not from lecture; figure added.)} A check of Theorem~\ref{thm:lie-derivative-bracket} on $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the rotation field $\mathbf{X} = -y\,\partial/\partial x + x\,\partial/\partial y$, whose flow $\varphi_t$ is rotation by the angle $t$ (Example~\ref{ex:rotation-flow}), and the constant field $\mathbf{Y} = \partial/\partial x$ (blue). Since $\varphi_{-t}$ is the linear rotation by $-t$, $d(\varphi_{-t})$ is that rotation too, so the value $\mathbf{Y}_{\varphi_t(p)} = (1, 0)$ carried back to $p$ is $V_t = (\cos t, -\sin t)$ (orange): the carried-back vectors turn clockwise. Their derivative at $t = 0$ is $(0, -1)$, so $\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{Y} = -\partial/\partial y$ (red). By Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket-coords}, $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}] = \big(\mathbf{X}(1) - \mathbf{Y}(-y)\big)\partial/\partial x + \big(\mathbf{X}(0) - \mathbf{Y}(x)\big)\partial/\partial y = -\partial/\partial y$ as well. Here $\mathbf{X}_0 = 0$ while $\mathbf{X}$ vanishes on no neighbourhood of $0$: the origin is a point of Case~3 of the proof.

\begin{corbox}[Properties of the Lie Derivative]\thmlabel{cor:lie-derivative-properties}
For $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{Z} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item $\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{Y} = -\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{Y}}\mathbf{X}$;
\item $\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{X}}[\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{Z}] = [\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{Z}] + [\mathbf{Y}, \mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{Z}]$.
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Corollary 9.39}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}[Proof (to be filled after the homework)]
From Theorem~\ref{thm:lie-derivative-bracket}. For (2), the left-hand side is $[\mathbf{X}, [\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{Z}]]$, and the tool is the Jacobi identity (Corollary~\ref{cor:vf-lie-algebra}). One of these entries is a problem on the next homework.
\end{proof}

\textbf{Transcription note (board 11/6 and Lecture 27).} On the board, the definition of $(\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{X}} f)(p)$ repeats the left-hand side of the motivating formula, ``$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x^1}(p) = \lim_{t \to 0} \ldots$''; the definition is the limit, as above. The board's single definition box of commuting fields and invariance is split here into Definitions~\ref{def:commuting-fields} and~\ref{def:invariant-under-flow}. Uribe cited this as Lee's Corollary~3.9, then 9.3, with a question mark; it is Lee's Corollary~9.39 (Lee's list also has $\mathcal{L}_{[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]} = \mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{Y}} - \mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{Y}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{X}}$ and a product rule).

The derivative of the curve $V_t$ at $t = 0$ is $(\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{Y})_p$ by definition. The next proposition computes it at every time; it is the key step in Theorem~\ref{thm:commuting-flows}.

\begin{propbox}[The Derivative of the Pulled-Back Field at Any Time]\thmlabel{prop:pulled-back-derivative}
Let $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$, let $\varphi$ be the flow of $\mathbf{X}$, and $p \in M$. For $t \in (\alpha(p), \beta(p))$ put
\[
V_t = d(\varphi_{-t})_{\varphi_t(p)}\big(\mathbf{Y}_{\varphi_t(p)}\big) \in T_pM .
\]
Then $t \mapsto V_t$ is a smooth curve in $T_pM$, and for every $t_0 \in (\alpha(p), \beta(p))$
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t = t_0} V_t = d(\varphi_{-t_0})_{\varphi_{t_0}(p)}\Big( (\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{Y})_{\varphi_{t_0}(p)} \Big) .
\]
\leeref{Proposition 9.41}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Reading assigned by email after Lecture~27: Lee, Proposition~9.41 and Theorems~9.42 and~9.44; not presented in lecture. Lee's proof.)} $V_t$ is defined: $\varphi_t(p) \in M_{-t}$, where $\varphi_{-t}$ is defined and smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:flow-diffeo-Mt}). Fix $t_0$ and put $q = \varphi_{t_0}(p)$. For small $|s|$, write $W_s = d(\varphi_{-s})_{\varphi_s(q)}\big(\mathbf{Y}_{\varphi_s(q)}\big) \in T_qM$, the curve of Definition~\ref{def:lie-derivative-field} at the point $q$.

\emph{Step 1: $V_{t_0 + s} = d(\varphi_{-t_0})_q (W_s)$ for small $|s|$.} By Proposition~\ref{prop:group-law}(2), $\varphi_{t_0 + s}(p) = \varphi_s(q)$, for $|s|$ small enough that $t_0 + s \in (\alpha(p), \beta(p))$ and $s \in (\alpha(q), \beta(q))$. Near $\varphi_s(q)$ the two maps $\varphi_{-t_0 - s}$ and $\varphi_{-t_0} \circ \varphi_{-s}$ agree: both are defined on the open set of points $x$ with $\varphi_{-s}(x) \in M_{-t_0}$, which contains $\varphi_s(q)$ (since $\varphi_{-s}(\varphi_s(q)) = q \in M_{-t_0}$, Lemma~\ref{lem:flow-diffeo-Mt}), and there $\varphi_{-t_0}(\varphi_{-s}(x)) = \varphi_{-t_0 - s}(x)$ by the group law. By the chain rule, and because $\varphi_{-s}(\varphi_s(q)) = q$,
\[
d(\varphi_{-t_0 - s})_{\varphi_s(q)} = d(\varphi_{-t_0})_q \circ d(\varphi_{-s})_{\varphi_s(q)} .
\]
Applying this to $\mathbf{Y}_{\varphi_s(q)} = \mathbf{Y}_{\varphi_{t_0 + s}(p)}$ gives $V_{t_0 + s} = d(\varphi_{-t_0})_q(W_s)$.

\emph{Step 2: differentiate.} By the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:lie-derivative-smooth} at the point $q$, $s \mapsto W_s$ is a smooth curve in $T_qM$ near $s = 0$, with derivative $(\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{Y})_q$ at $s = 0$. The map $d(\varphi_{-t_0})_q : T_qM \to T_pM$ is linear and does not depend on $s$, so $s \mapsto V_{t_0 + s}$ is smooth near $0$ and
\[
\frac{d}{ds}\Big|_{s = 0} V_{t_0 + s} = d(\varphi_{-t_0})_q\Big( \frac{d}{ds}\Big|_{s = 0} W_s \Big) = d(\varphi_{-t_0})_q\big( (\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{Y})_q \big) .
\]
As $t_0$ was arbitrary, $V_t$ is smooth on $(\alpha(p), \beta(p))$, with the stated derivative.
\end{proof}

\emph{Commuting vector fields.} The main application of Theorem~\ref{thm:lie-derivative-bracket} is to the case $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}] = 0$.

\begin{defbox}[Commuting Vector Fields]\deflabel{def:commuting-fields}
Vector fields $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ \textbf{commute} if $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}] = 0$.
\leeref{Ch.~9, \emph{Commuting Vector Fields}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[Invariance under a Flow]\deflabel{def:invariant-under-flow}
Let $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$, and let $\varphi$ be the flow of $\mathbf{X}$. Then $\mathbf{Y}$ is \textbf{invariant under the flow} $\varphi$ of $\mathbf{X}$ if for every $t$, $\mathbf{Y}$ is $\varphi_t$-related to itself (Definition~\ref{def:F-related}): $d(\varphi_t)_p(\mathbf{Y}_p) = \mathbf{Y}_{\varphi_t(p)}$ for all $(t, p)$ in the flow domain $\mathcal{D}$. For incomplete $\mathbf{X}$ the condition is read where $\varphi_t$ is defined, on the open sets $M_t$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:flow-diffeo-Mt} above. A complete field is invariant under its own flow (Lemma~\ref{lem:flow-related-to-itself}); without completeness this is Corollary~\ref{cor:invariant-own-flow} below (Lee, Corollary~9.43).
\leeref{Ch.~9, \emph{Commuting Vector Fields}}
\end{defbox}


\begin{thmbox}[Commuting Fields: Invariance and Commuting Flows]\thmlabel{thm:commuting-flows}
Let $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$, with flows $\varphi$ and $\psi$. The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}] = 0$;
\item $\mathbf{Y}$ is invariant under the flow of $\mathbf{X}$;
\item the flows commute: $\varphi_s \circ \psi_t = \psi_t \circ \varphi_s$. Precisely: for all open intervals $I, J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ containing $0$ and every $p \in M$, if $\varphi_s \circ \psi_t(p)$ or $\psi_t \circ \varphi_s(p)$ exists for all $(s, t) \in I \times J$, then the other exists too, and they are equal.
\end{enumerate}
If $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ are complete, (3) just says $\varphi_s \circ \psi_t = \psi_t \circ \varphi_s$ for all $s, t \in \mathbb{R}$. Since $[\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}] = -[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]$, (1)--(3) are also equivalent to: $\mathbf{X}$ is invariant under the flow $\psi$ of $\mathbf{Y}$ (Lee, Theorem~9.42(c)).
\leeref{Theorems 9.42 and 9.44}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~27's indication for (1)$\Rightarrow$(2).)} $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}] = 0$ means, by Theorem~\ref{thm:lie-derivative-bracket}, that the derivative at $t = 0$ of the curve $V_t$ of pulled-back values of $\mathbf{Y}$ is zero, at every point; by the group law, the derivative of $V_t$ at any time $t$ is the derivative at time $0$ at the point $\varphi_t(p)$, carried back to $p$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:pulled-back-derivative}); so it vanishes for every $t$, $V_t$ is constant, and $\mathbf{Y}$ is invariant under the flow.

\textit{(Reading assigned by email after Lecture~27: Lee, Proposition~9.41 and Theorems~9.42 and~9.44; not presented in lecture. Lee's proof.)} Throughout, for $p \in M$ let $V_t = d(\varphi_{-t})_{\varphi_t(p)}\big(\mathbf{Y}_{\varphi_t(p)}\big)$, $t \in (\alpha(p), \beta(p))$, as in Proposition~\ref{prop:pulled-back-derivative}; $V_0 = \mathbf{Y}_p$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:flow-diffeo-Mt}, $d(\varphi_{-t})_{\varphi_t(p)}$ and $d(\varphi_t)_p$ are inverse linear isomorphisms, so
\[
\mathbf{Y} \text{ is invariant at } (t, p), \text{ i.e. } d(\varphi_t)_p(\mathbf{Y}_p) = \mathbf{Y}_{\varphi_t(p)} \iff V_t = \mathbf{Y}_p . \tag{$\dagger$}
\]

\emph{(1)$\Rightarrow$(2)} (Lee 9.42). Let $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}] = 0$. Then $\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{Y} = 0$ everywhere (Theorem~\ref{thm:lie-derivative-bracket}), so by Proposition~\ref{prop:pulled-back-derivative} the derivative of $V_t$ vanishes at every $t \in (\alpha(p), \beta(p))$. A curve in the vector space $T_pM$ with zero derivative on an interval is constant (apply the mean value theorem to each component in a basis), so $V_t = V_0 = \mathbf{Y}_p$ for all $t$, and by ($\dagger$) $\mathbf{Y}$ is invariant under $\varphi$.

\emph{(2)$\Rightarrow$(1)} (Lee 9.42). If $\mathbf{Y}$ is invariant under $\varphi$, then by ($\dagger$) $V_t = \mathbf{Y}_p$ for all $t$, so $(\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{Y})_p = \frac{d}{dt}\big|_{t=0} V_t = 0$ (Definition~\ref{def:lie-derivative-field}), and $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]_p = 0$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:lie-derivative-bracket}. As $p$ was arbitrary, $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}] = 0$.

\emph{The symmetric statement.} $[\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{X}] = -[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]$, so the same two arguments with the roles of $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ exchanged show: $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}] = 0$ if and only if $\mathbf{X}$ is invariant under $\psi$.

\emph{(1)$\Rightarrow$(3)} (Lee 9.44). Let $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}] = 0$, $p \in M$, and $I, J$ open intervals containing $0$ such that $\psi_t \circ \varphi_s(p)$ is defined for all $(s, t) \in I \times J$. (If instead $\varphi_s \circ \psi_t(p)$ is defined on $I \times J$, exchange the roles of $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$.) By the symmetric statement, $\mathbf{X}$ is invariant under $\psi$. Fix $t \in J$ and let $\gamma(s) = \psi_t(\varphi_s(p))$, $s \in I$. Then $\gamma(0) = \psi_t(p)$, and by the chain rule (Corollary~\ref{cor:velocity-composite}), the fact that $s \mapsto \varphi_s(p)$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$, and invariance of $\mathbf{X}$ under $\psi$ at the point $\varphi_s(p)$ (where $\psi_t$ is defined),
\[
\dot\gamma(s) = d(\psi_t)_{\varphi_s(p)}\big(\mathbf{X}_{\varphi_s(p)}\big) = \mathbf{X}_{\psi_t(\varphi_s(p))} = \mathbf{X}_{\gamma(s)} .
\]
So $\gamma : I \to M$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ starting at $\psi_t(p)$. The maximal integral curve $\varphi^{\psi_t(p)}$ extends every integral curve starting at $\psi_t(p)$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-flow}(1), Proposition~\ref{prop:global-uniqueness}), so its domain contains $I$ and $\varphi_s(\psi_t(p)) = \gamma(s) = \psi_t(\varphi_s(p))$ for all $s \in I$. Hence both compositions are defined on $I \times J$ and agree.

\emph{(3)$\Rightarrow$(1)} (Lee 9.44). Assume the flows commute in the sense of (3), and let $p \in M$. The map $(s, t) \mapsto \psi_t(\varphi_s(p))$ is defined near $(0, 0)$: $\psi$ is defined on an open set $(-\varepsilon_2, \varepsilon_2) \times U$ around $(0, p)$ in its domain, and $\varphi_s(p) \in U$ for $|s| < \varepsilon_1$ by continuity. With $\varepsilon = \min(\varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2)$ and $I = J = (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$, (3) gives $\varphi_s(\psi_t(p)) = \psi_t(\varphi_s(p))$ for $|s|, |t| < \varepsilon$. Fix $|s| < \varepsilon$ and differentiate in $t$ at $t = 0$. On the left, $t \mapsto \psi_t(p)$ has velocity $\mathbf{Y}_p$ at $t = 0$, so the chain rule (Corollary~\ref{cor:velocity-composite}) gives $d(\varphi_s)_p(\mathbf{Y}_p)$; on the right, $t \mapsto \psi_t(\varphi_s(p))$ is the integral curve of $\mathbf{Y}$ through $\varphi_s(p)$, with velocity $\mathbf{Y}_{\varphi_s(p)}$ at $t = 0$. So $d(\varphi_s)_p(\mathbf{Y}_p) = \mathbf{Y}_{\varphi_s(p)}$, that is, $V_s = \mathbf{Y}_p$ for $|s| < \varepsilon$ by ($\dagger$). Hence $(\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{Y})_p = \frac{d}{ds}\big|_{s=0} V_s = 0$ and $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]_p = 0$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:lie-derivative-bracket}).
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[Every Vector Field Is Invariant under Its Own Flow]\thmlabel{cor:invariant-own-flow}
Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ with flow $\varphi$. Then $d(\varphi_t)_p(\mathbf{X}_p) = \mathbf{X}_{\varphi_t(p)}$ for all $(t, p) \in \mathcal{D}$.
\leeref{Corollary 9.43}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lee's proof; not presented in lecture.)} $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{X}] = 0$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:commuting-flows} (1)$\Rightarrow$(2) with $\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X}$ gives the invariance. For complete $\mathbf{X}$ this is Lemma~\ref{lem:flow-related-to-itself}.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[Commuting Flows of Incomplete Fields]\label{rem:commuting-flows-incomplete}
For incomplete fields, condition~(3) is delicate: $\varphi_s \circ \psi_t(p)$ need not be defined for all $s, t$, which is why it is stated with intervals $I$, $J$ on which one of the two compositions exists. A problem on the next homework shows why this care is needed.
\end{rembox}

Left: the flows of $\partial_x$ and $\partial_y$ are translations, and the two routes around the rectangle end at the same point. Right: $\mathbf{Y} = x\,\partial_y$ has the flow $\psi_t(x, y) = (x, y + tx)$, a shear, so it lifts a point by $t$ times its distance from the axis $x = 0$. Moving out first (blue) gives $\psi_t \circ \varphi_s(p) = (x + s, y + t(x + s))$, moving up first (red) gives $\varphi_s \circ \psi_t(p) = (x + s, y + tx)$: they differ by $st$ in the $y$-direction. By Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket-coords}, $[\partial_x, x\,\partial_y] = \partial_y \neq 0$, and the gap is exactly $st\,[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]$ here.
%% <<< END ADDED

\textit{(Assignment~7, Problems~2 and~3.)} Condition~(3) of Theorem~\ref{thm:commuting-flows} has an infinitesimal version: the bracket is the mixed second derivative of the difference of the two compositions of the flows.

\begin{lembox}[The Mixed Derivative of Two Flows]\thmlabel{lem:mixed-derivative-flows}
Let $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be open, $\mathbf{X} = \sum_i f^i\, \partial/\partial x^i$ and $\mathbf{Y} = \sum_i g^i\, \partial/\partial x^i$ in $\mathfrak{X}(U)$, with flows $\varphi$ and $\psi$, and $p \in U$. Then $(s, t) \mapsto \psi_s \circ \varphi_t(p)$ is defined and smooth on a neighbourhood of $(0, 0)$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$, and
\[
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial t\, \partial s}\big(\psi_s \circ \varphi_t(p)\big)\Big|_{(s, t) = (0, 0)} = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{X}(g^i)(p)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p ,
\]
the second derivative of a map into $\mathbb{R}^n$ being read as a vector at $\psi_0 \circ \varphi_0(p) = p$ through $\mathbb{R}^n \cong T_p\mathbb{R}^n$, $e_i \mapsto \partial/\partial x^i|_p$.
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~7, Problem~2(a): the submitted solution. The domain of definition is filled in.)} Write $\varphi(t, q) = \varphi_t(q)$ and $\psi(s, q) = \psi_s(q)$, with components $\varphi^j$ and $\psi^i$; they are smooth on the flow domains $\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{X}}, \mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{Y}}$, open subsets of $\mathbb{R} \times U$ containing $\{0\} \times U$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-flow}). \emph{Domain} \textit{(filled in)}: the set of $(s, t)$ with $(t, p) \in \mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{X}}$ and $(s, \varphi(t, p)) \in \mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{Y}}$ is open, as the preimage of the open set $\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{Y}}$ under the continuous map $(s, t) \mapsto (s, \varphi(t, p))$ on the open set $\mathbb{R} \times \{t : (t, p) \in \mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{X}}\}$; it contains $(0, 0)$, and on it $F(s, t) = \psi_s \circ \varphi_t(p)$ is a composite of smooth maps. We write $\partial/\partial x^j$ for the partial derivative in the $j$-th coordinate of $\mathbb{R}^n$; for $\psi^i(s, q)$ it acts on the variable $q$. Let $f = (f^1, \ldots, f^n)$ and $g = (g^1, \ldots, g^n) : U \to \mathbb{R}^n$. Since $\varphi$ and $\psi$ are the flows of $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$, $\varphi(0, q) = \psi(0, q) = q$ and
\[
\frac{\partial \varphi^j}{\partial t}(t, q) = f^j(\varphi(t, q)), \qquad \frac{\partial \psi^i}{\partial s}(s, q) = g^i(\psi(s, q)) .
\]
By Clairaut's theorem the mixed partials of $F$ agree, so it suffices to compute $\frac{d}{ds}\big[\partial_t F(s, 0)\big]_{s=0}$. By the chain rule, using $\varphi(0, p) = p$ and $\frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial t}(0, p) = \mathbf{X}_p$,
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\, \psi_s(\varphi_t(p))\Big|_{t=0} = d(\psi_s)_p(\mathbf{X}_p) \in T_{\psi_s(p)}\mathbb{R}^n .
\]
As $s$ varies these vectors lie in different tangent spaces; to differentiate in $s$ we use $T_q\mathbb{R}^n \cong \mathbb{R}^n$ and compute in components. The matrix of $d(\psi_s)_p$ is $\big(\frac{\partial \psi^i}{\partial x^j}(s, p)\big)_{i, j}$, so
\[
d(\psi_s)_p(\mathbf{X}_p) = \sum_{i=1}^n \Big(\sum_{j=1}^n \frac{\partial \psi^i}{\partial x^j}(s, p)\, f^j(p)\Big)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_{\psi_s(p)} .
\]
Fix $i$. The factors $f^j(p)$ do not depend on $s$. By Clairaut's theorem for $\psi^i$, $\partial_s$ and $\partial/\partial x^j$ commute; and since $\frac{\partial \psi^i}{\partial s}(0, q) = g^i(q)$ for all $q \in U$, $\frac{\partial^2 \psi^i}{\partial x^j\, \partial s}(0, p) = \frac{\partial g^i}{\partial x^j}(p)$. Hence the $i$-th component of the mixed partial is
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial s}\Big[\sum_{j=1}^n \frac{\partial \psi^i}{\partial x^j}(s, p)\, f^j(p)\Big]_{s=0} = \sum_{j=1}^n f^j(p)\, \frac{\partial g^i}{\partial x^j}(p) = \mathbf{X}_p(g^i) = \mathbf{X}(g^i)(p) .
\]
Since $\psi_0(p) = p$, identifying $e_i$ with $\partial/\partial x^i|_p$ gives the formula.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[The Bracket Measures the Failure of Flows to Commute]\thmlabel{prop:bracket-flows}
In the setting of Lemma~\ref{lem:mixed-derivative-flows},
\[
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial t\, \partial s}\big(\psi_s \circ \varphi_t(p) - \varphi_t \circ \psi_s(p)\big)\Big|_{(s, t) = (0, 0)} = [\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]_p .
\]
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~7, Problem~2(b): the submitted solution. Its last step recomputes Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket-coords}.)} Both maps are smooth near $(0, 0)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:mixed-derivative-flows}, and the same with the roles exchanged), so by linearity the left side is the difference of the two mixed partials. By Clairaut's theorem, $\frac{\partial^2}{\partial t\, \partial s}$ and $\frac{\partial^2}{\partial s\, \partial t}$ agree on $(s, t) \mapsto \varphi_t \circ \psi_s(p)$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:mixed-derivative-flows} with the roles of $(\mathbf{X}, f, \varphi, t)$ and $(\mathbf{Y}, g, \psi, s)$ interchanged gives
\[
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial s\, \partial t}\big(\varphi_t \circ \psi_s(p)\big)\Big|_{(0, 0)} = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{Y}(f^i)(p)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p .
\]
Together with the lemma, the left side is $\sum_i \big(\mathbf{X}(g^i)(p) - \mathbf{Y}(f^i)(p)\big)\, \partial/\partial x^i|_p$.

It remains to identify this with $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]_p$. Let $h \in C^\infty(U)$. Then $\mathbf{Y}h = \sum_i g^i\, \frac{\partial h}{\partial x^i}$ and $\mathbf{X}h = \sum_j f^j\, \frac{\partial h}{\partial x^j}$, so by the product rule
\[
\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{Y}h) = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{X}(g^i)\, \frac{\partial h}{\partial x^i} + \sum_{i, j=1}^n f^j g^i\, \frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x^j\, \partial x^i}, \qquad \mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{X}h) = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{Y}(f^i)\, \frac{\partial h}{\partial x^i} + \sum_{i, j=1}^n g^j f^i\, \frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x^j\, \partial x^i} .
\]
Relabelling $i \leftrightarrow j$ in the last sum and using Clairaut's theorem for $h$, the second-order sums are equal and cancel in $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]h = \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{Y}h) - \mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{X}h)$:
\[
[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]h = \sum_{i=1}^n \big(\mathbf{X}(g^i) - \mathbf{Y}(f^i)\big)\, \frac{\partial h}{\partial x^i} .
\]
Evaluating at $p$ for every $h$ gives $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]_p = \sum_i \big(\mathbf{X}(g^i)(p) - \mathbf{Y}(f^i)(p)\big)\, \partial/\partial x^i|_p$, the left side.
\end{proof}

The statement is local, so on a manifold it holds in any chart at $p$, with the difference taken in the chart (the remark of the assignment); since the right side does not depend on the chart, neither does the left. In the second example of the figure above, $\psi_t \circ \varphi_s(p) - \varphi_s \circ \psi_t(p) = (0, st)$, whose mixed derivative is $(0, 1)$, that is $\partial_y = [\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]$.

\begin{corbox}[Commuting Flows Have Zero Bracket]\thmlabel{cor:commuting-flows-bracket}
Let $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ with flows $\varphi$ and $\psi$. If for every $p \in M$ there is a neighbourhood $N$ of $(0, 0)$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with $\psi_s \circ \varphi_t(p) = \varphi_t \circ \psi_s(p)$ for all $(s, t) \in N$, then $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}] = 0$.
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Filled in; a second proof of (3)~$\Rightarrow$~(1) in Theorem~\ref{thm:commuting-flows}.)} Fix $p$ and a chart $(U, \chi)$ at $p$. The pushforwards of $\mathbf{X}|_U$ and $\mathbf{Y}|_U$ by the diffeomorphism $\chi : U \to \chi(U)$ are fields on $\chi(U) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ whose integral curves are the images under $\chi$ of those of $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ in $U$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:naturality-integral-curves}); for $(s, t)$ near $(0, 0)$ all the points involved stay in $U$, so near $(0, 0)$ the compositions of their flows at $\chi(p)$ are $\chi(\psi_s \circ \varphi_t(p))$ and $\chi(\varphi_t \circ \psi_s(p))$, which agree by hypothesis. By Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket-flows} the bracket of the pushed-forward fields vanishes at $\chi(p)$, and it is the pushforward of $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:diffeo-bracket}); so $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]_p = 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{exbox}[Two Linear Fields with Non-Commuting Flows]\exlabel{ex:noncommuting-linear-flows}
On $\mathbb{R}^2$ let $\mathbf{X} = x\, \partial/\partial x - y\, \partial/\partial y$ and $\mathbf{Y} = y\, \partial/\partial x + x\, \partial/\partial y$. Both are complete, and their flows are the linear maps
\[
\varphi_s = \begin{pmatrix} e^{s} & 0 \\ 0 & e^{-s} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \psi_t = \begin{pmatrix} \cosh t & \sinh t \\ \sinh t & \cosh t \end{pmatrix} .
\]
They do not commute: for all $(s, t) \in J \times K = \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$ both compositions are defined, and
\[
\varphi_s \circ \psi_t - \psi_t \circ \varphi_s = 2 \sinh s\, \sinh t \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix},
\]
which is nonzero whenever $s \neq 0$ and $t \neq 0$.
\leeref{Problem 9-18}
\end{exbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~7, Problem~3: the submitted solution. The check against Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket-flows} is filled in.)} Let $c(t) = (c_1(t), c_2(t))$ be a smooth curve with $c(0) = (x_0, y_0)$.

\emph{The flow of $\mathbf{X}$.} Since $\mathbf{X}_{c(t)} = c_1(t)\, \partial_x|_{c(t)} - c_2(t)\, \partial_y|_{c(t)}$, $c$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ if and only if $\dot c_1 = c_1$, $\dot c_2 = -c_2$, whose solution with $c(0) = (x_0, y_0)$ is $c(t) = (x_0 e^{t}, y_0 e^{-t})$, defined for all $t$.

\emph{The flow of $\mathbf{Y}$.} Since $\mathbf{Y}_{c(t)} = c_2(t)\, \partial_x|_{c(t)} + c_1(t)\, \partial_y|_{c(t)}$, $c$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{Y}$ if and only if $\dot c_1 = c_2$, $\dot c_2 = c_1$. Differentiating, $\ddot c_1 = c_1$ and $\ddot c_2 = c_2$, with $c_1(0) = x_0$, $\dot c_1(0) = y_0$, $c_2(0) = y_0$, $\dot c_2(0) = x_0$. The solutions of $u'' = u$ are $u = A \cosh t + B \sinh t$, so
\[
c(t) = (x_0 \cosh t + y_0 \sinh t,\ x_0 \sinh t + y_0 \cosh t), \qquad t \in \mathbb{R} ;
\]
indeed $\dot c_1 = c_2$ and $\dot c_2 = c_1$.

Both integral curves are defined on $\mathbb{R}$, so they are the maximal ones (Proposition~\ref{prop:maximal-curve}), $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ are complete, and the flows are the linear maps of the statement.

\emph{The flows do not commute.} Take $J = K = \mathbb{R}$. The compositions are the linear maps with matrices
\[
\varphi_s \circ \psi_t = \begin{pmatrix} e^{s} \cosh t & e^{s} \sinh t \\ e^{-s} \sinh t & e^{-s} \cosh t \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \psi_t \circ \varphi_s = \begin{pmatrix} e^{s} \cosh t & e^{-s} \sinh t \\ e^{s} \sinh t & e^{-s} \cosh t \end{pmatrix},
\]
whose difference is $\begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & (e^s - e^{-s}) \sinh t \\ (e^{-s} - e^s) \sinh t & 0 \end{psmallmatrix} = 2 \sinh s\, \sinh t \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}$. For instance, at $(s, t) = (1, 1)$ and the point $(0, 1)$,
\[
\varphi_1 \circ \psi_1(0, 1) = (e \sinh 1,\ e^{-1} \cosh 1) \neq (e^{-1} \sinh 1,\ e^{-1} \cosh 1) = \psi_1 \circ \varphi_1(0, 1) .
\]

\emph{Check against Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket-flows}} \textit{(filled in)}. By Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket-coords}, with components $(x, -y)$ and $(y, x)$, $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}] = (\mathbf{X}(y) - \mathbf{Y}(x))\, \partial_x + (\mathbf{X}(x) - \mathbf{Y}(-y))\, \partial_y = -2y\, \partial_x + 2x\, \partial_y$. In the proposition the flow of $\mathbf{Y}$ is applied last in the first term; here that is $\psi_t \circ \varphi_s - \varphi_s \circ \psi_t = -2 \sinh s\, \sinh t \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}$, whose mixed derivative at $(0, 0)$, applied to $p = (x, y)$, is $-2(y, -x) = (-2y, 2x) = [\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]_p$.
\end{proof}

\chapter{Differential Forms}

\textit{Lecture 28. This chapter, planned to run until Thanksgiving, is differential forms and Stokes' theorem. It will need manifolds with boundary, orientations, integrals of forms, and the general Stokes theorem. It opens with the theorem to be generalized, recalled from Calculus~III (\ref{sec:stokes-calc3}); the next section reads its integrand as a two-form (\ref{sec:two-form-integrand}), and the multilinear algebra behind that reading starts in \ref{sec:multilinear}.}

% ============================================================================
% SECTION: STOKES' THEOREM IN CALCULUS III
% ============================================================================
\section{Stokes' Theorem in Calculus III}\label{sec:stokes-calc3}

\roadmark{Stage: forms}{The theorem to be generalized, recalled from Calculus~III: parametrized surfaces, orientation by a unit normal, surface integrals, the induced orientation of the boundary, and Stokes' theorem in $\mathbb{R}^3$.}

\textit{(Lecture 28.)} The course reviews Stokes' theorem of Calculus~III because it is the theorem to be generalized. The definitions of this section are recalled from Calculus~III (Stewart, Sections~16.6--16.8, in MATH 233) and from MATH 452 (\S\S31--34), where the theorem is proved. They are restated in the notation of the lecture, which differs from both:

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{llll}
\toprule
 & these notes & Calculus~III (Stewart) & MATH 452 \\ \midrule
vector field & $\mathbf{X} = (f^1, f^2, f^3)$, $\vec G = (g^1, g^2, g^3)$ & $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j} + R\,\mathbf{k}$ & $\mathbf{F} = (P, Q, R)$ \\
coordinates on $\mathbb{R}^3$ & $x^1, x^2, x^3$ & $x, y, z$ & $x, y, z$ \\
parametrization & $\vec r(s, t)$, $(s, t) \in D$ & $\mathbf{r}(u, v)$ & $\mathbf{X}(u, v)$ \\
tangent vectors & $\vec r_s$, $\vec r_t$ & $\mathbf{r}_u$, $\mathbf{r}_v$ & $\mathbf{X}_u$, $\mathbf{X}_v$ \\
unit normal & $\mathbf{n}$ & $\mathbf{n}$ & $\hat n$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
In these notes a bold $\mathbf{X}$ is always a vector field; in MATH 452 the same letter is the parametrization of the surface.

\begin{defbox}[Parametrized Surface]\deflabel{def:parametrized-surface}
Let $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ be a compact region of the $(s, t)$-plane bounded by a piecewise smooth closed curve, and let $\vec r : D \to \mathbb{R}^3$ be the restriction of a smooth map defined on an open set containing $D$,
\[
\vec r(s, t) = \big( x^1(s, t), x^2(s, t), x^3(s, t) \big) .
\]
The image $S = \vec r(D)$ is a \textbf{parametrized surface}, and $\vec r$ is a \textbf{parametrization} of $S$.
\end{defbox}

\textit{(Recalled from Calculus~III: Stewart, Section~16.6; MATH 452, \S31.)} The partial derivatives
\[
\vec r_s = \frac{\partial \vec r}{\partial s} = (x^1_s, x^2_s, x^3_s), \qquad \vec r_t = \frac{\partial \vec r}{\partial t} = (x^1_t, x^2_t, x^3_t)
\]
are two fields of vectors along $S$, tangent to $S$: $\vec r_s$ is the velocity of the curve $s \mapsto \vec r(s, t)$ with $t$ fixed, $\vec r_t$ that of $t \mapsto \vec r(s, t)$. The standard grid of $D$ goes to a mesh of these curves on $S$ (figure below).

\begin{defbox}[Regular Parametrization]\deflabel{def:regular-parametrization}
A parametrization $\vec r : D \to \mathbb{R}^3$ (Definition~\ref{def:parametrized-surface}) is \textbf{regular} if $\vec r_s \times \vec r_t \neq 0$ at every point of $D$, that is, if $\vec r_s$ and $\vec r_t$ are linearly independent everywhere.
\end{defbox}

\textit{(Recalled from Calculus~III: Stewart, Section~16.6, a smooth surface; MATH 452, \S31.)} Regular means that the Jacobian $d\vec r$, the $3 \times 2$ matrix with columns $\vec r_s, \vec r_t$, has rank~$2$: on the interior of $D$, $\vec r$ is an immersion (Definition~\ref{def:immersion}). In most examples of Calculus~III a single injective regular parametrization covers $S$; when $\vec r$ restricted to the interior of $D$ is moreover a homeomorphism onto its image, it is an embedding (Definition~\ref{def:embedding}), its image is a regular submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^3$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image}), and the inverse of $\vec r$ is a chart of that submanifold.

\begin{defbox}[Orientation of a Surface by a Unit Normal]\deflabel{def:surface-orientation}
Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ be a $2$-dimensional regular submanifold (Definition~\ref{def:submanifold}). A \textbf{unit normal field} on $S$ is a continuous map $\mathbf{n} : S \to \mathbb{R}^3$ such that for every $q \in S$, $\mathbf{n}(q)$ is a unit vector perpendicular to the tangent plane $T_qS \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$. A choice of unit normal field is an \textbf{orientation} of $S$, and $S$ with this choice is an \textbf{oriented surface}.
\end{defbox}

\textit{(Recalled from Calculus~III: Stewart, Section~16.7; MATH 452, \S32.)} At each point there are two unit normals, $\mathbf{n}(q)$ and $-\mathbf{n}(q)$; the orientation is a continuous choice of one of them. The continuity is part of the definition. If $\mathbf{n}$ is an orientation, so is $-\mathbf{n}$.

\begin{defbox}[Positive Parametrization]\deflabel{def:positive-parametrization}
Let $S$ be oriented by $\mathbf{n}$ (Definition~\ref{def:surface-orientation}). A regular parametrization $\vec r : D \to S$ (Definition~\ref{def:regular-parametrization}) is \textbf{positive} if the normal $\vec r_s \times \vec r_t$ points in the direction of $\mathbf{n}$:
\[
\vec r_s \times \vec r_t = |\vec r_s \times \vec r_t|\; \mathbf{n}\big(\vec r(s, t)\big) \qquad \text{for all } (s, t) \in D .
\]
\end{defbox}

\textit{(Lecture~28; Stewart, Section~16.7, calls $\mathbf{n} = \vec r_s \times \vec r_t / |\vec r_s \times \vec r_t|$ the orientation that a parametrization ``supplies''.)} Exchanging $s$ and $t$ turns a positive parametrization into a negative one, since $\vec r_t \times \vec r_s = -\vec r_s \times \vec r_t$. The inverse of a positive parametrization will be a positively oriented chart, once orientations of manifolds are defined.

\textit{(Figure after the board, redrawn from a computed surface.)} A positive parametrization. Left: the parameter domain $D$ with its grid, the lines $t = \text{const}$ (orange) and $s = \text{const}$ (blue), and the unit vectors $e_s, e_t$ at a point $(s_0, t_0)$. Right: the image $S = \vec r(D)$; the grid goes to the mesh of the two families of curves on $S$, and $e_s, e_t$ go to the tangent vectors $\vec r_s, \vec r_t$ at $\vec r(s_0, t_0)$, the velocities of the orange and the blue curve through that point. The normal $\vec r_s \times \vec r_t$ (red) points to the side from which the mesh is seen here; orienting $S$ by that side makes $\vec r$ positive (Definition~\ref{def:positive-parametrization}). The surface drawn is $\vec r(s, t) = \big(1.7s + 0.3,\ 1.5t + 0.3,\ 0.75 + 0.25 \sin 2.4s - 0.3t^2 + 0.1st\big)$ on $D = [0, 1]^2$.

\begin{defbox}[Surface Integral of a Vector Field]\deflabel{def:flux-integral}
Let $S$ be oriented by $\mathbf{n}$, let $\vec r : D \to S$ be a positive parametrization (Definition~\ref{def:positive-parametrization}) that is injective on the interior of $D$, and let $\vec G = (g^1, g^2, g^3)$ be a continuous vector field on $S$. The \textbf{surface integral} (or \textbf{flux}) of $\vec G$ through $S$ is
\[
\iint_S \vec G \cdot d\vec S = \iint_S (\vec G \cdot \mathbf{n})\, dS = \iint_D \vec G\big(\vec r(s, t)\big) \cdot \mathbf{n}\big(\vec r(s, t)\big)\, |\vec r_s \times \vec r_t|\; ds\, dt ,
\]
where $dS = |\vec r_s \times \vec r_t|\, ds\, dt$ is the element of surface area and $d\vec S = \mathbf{n}\, dS$.
\leeref{Ch.~16, \emph{Surface Integrals}}
\end{defbox}

\textit{(Recalled from Calculus~III: Stewart, Section~16.7; MATH 452, Definition~32.1.)} The factor $|\vec r_s \times \vec r_t|\, ds\, dt$ is the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\vec r_s\, ds$ and $\vec r_t\, dt$, the image of a small rectangle of $D$ to first order. That the integral does not depend on the positive parametrization is the change of variables formula (MATH 452, \S\S24 and~32); for integrals of forms it will be proved in this course.

\begin{defbox}[Induced Orientation of the Boundary Curve]\deflabel{def:induced-boundary-orientation}
Let $S$ be a compact oriented surface with boundary in $\mathbb{R}^3$, oriented by $\mathbf{n}$, whose boundary $\partial S$ is a piecewise smooth closed curve (or a finite union of such curves). The \textbf{induced orientation} of $\partial S$ is the direction of travel along $\partial S$ in which a walker with $\mathbf{n}$ pointing from his feet to his head has the surface on his left. With this orientation, $\partial S$ is \textbf{positively oriented}.
\end{defbox}

\textit{(Lecture~28: the right-hand rule, or ``Amp\`ere's little guy''; Stewart, Section~16.8; MATH 452, Theorem~34.1.)} Surfaces with boundary are taken here in the sense of Calculus~III; manifolds with boundary come later in the chapter. The walker can be traded for a formula of the kind that will generalize: put the outward direction first.

\begin{lembox}[The Induced Orientation Puts the Outward Direction First]\thmlabel{lem:outward-first}
In the setting of Definition~\ref{def:induced-boundary-orientation}, let $q \in \partial S$ be a point where $\partial S$ is smooth, let $T$ be the unit tangent vector of $\partial S$ at $q$ in the direction of travel, and let $\nu$ be the unit vector tangent to $S$ at $q$, perpendicular to $T$ and pointing out of $S$. Then $\partial S$ is positively oriented at $q$ if and only if
\[
\nu \times T = \mathbf{n}(q) .
\]
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Filled in.)} The vectors $\nu, T$ are orthonormal and span $T_qS$, and $\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{n}(q)$ is a unit vector perpendicular to both. So $\nu \times T$, a unit vector perpendicular to $\nu$ and $T$, is $\pm\mathbf{n}$; we show that it is $+\mathbf{n}$ exactly when the surface is on the walker's left.

\emph{The walker's left.} A walker facing the unit vector $T$ with his head along the unit vector $\mathbf{n} \perp T$ has his left along $\mathbf{n} \times T$: for $T = e_1$ and $\mathbf{n} = e_3$ his left is $e_2 = e_3 \times e_1$, and every such pair $(T, \mathbf{n})$ is carried to $(e_1, e_3)$ by a rotation, which preserves cross products. The surface lies on his left exactly when the inward vector $-\nu$ is his left, $\mathbf{n} \times T = -\nu$.

\emph{The two conditions agree.} If $\nu \times T = \mathbf{n}$, then $(\nu, T, \mathbf{n})$ is a positively oriented orthonormal basis, so its cross products are cyclic: $T \times \mathbf{n} = \nu$, and $\mathbf{n} \times T = -T \times \mathbf{n} = -\nu$. If instead $\nu \times T = -\mathbf{n}$, the same argument with $-\mathbf{n}$ in place of $\mathbf{n}$ gives $(-\mathbf{n}) \times T = -\nu$, so $\mathbf{n} \times T = \nu \neq -\nu$. Hence the surface is on the walker's left if and only if $\nu \times T = \mathbf{n}$.
\end{proof}

For a region of the $(x^1, x^2)$-plane oriented by $\mathbf{n} = e_3$, the lemma says that the boundary is traversed counterclockwise: on the right edge of a disk, $\nu = e_1$ and $T = e_2$, and $e_1 \times e_2 = e_3$. This is the orientation of Green's theorem.

\begin{thmbox}[Stokes' Theorem in $\mathbb{R}^3$]\thmlabel{thm:stokes-calc3}
Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ be a compact oriented surface with boundary, oriented by $\mathbf{n}$ (Definition~\ref{def:surface-orientation}), with $\partial S$ carrying the induced orientation (Definition~\ref{def:induced-boundary-orientation}), and let $\mathbf{X} = (f^1, f^2, f^3)$ be a smooth vector field on a neighbourhood of $S$. Then
\[
\oint_{\partial S} \mathbf{X} \cdot d\vec r = \iint_S (\nabla \times \mathbf{X}) \cdot d\vec S ,
\]
where the right-hand side is the surface integral of Definition~\ref{def:flux-integral}, $d\vec S = \mathbf{n}\, dS$.
\leeref{Theorem 16.34}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}[Proof (not given in this course)]
The theorem is proved in MATH 452 (Theorem~34.1: first for graphs, then for parametrized surfaces, by pulling both sides back to the parameter domain and applying Green's theorem there); Stewart (Section~16.8) proves the case of a graph. In this course it will be a special case of the general Stokes theorem, which is how Lee deduces it (Theorem~16.34).
\end{proof}

The ingredients, all to be generalized:
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
\item a \emph{surface with boundary}: manifolds with boundary will be needed;
\item an \emph{orientation}: in Calculus~III a unit normal field $\mathbf{n}$ (Definition~\ref{def:surface-orientation});
\item the \emph{induced orientation} on $\partial S$, by the right-hand rule (Definition~\ref{def:induced-boundary-orientation}, Lemma~\ref{lem:outward-first});
\item the \emph{integrals} on the two sides: a line integral of $\mathbf{X}$ and a surface integral of $\nabla \times \mathbf{X}$ (Definition~\ref{def:flux-integral});
\item the operation $\mathbf{X} \mapsto \nabla \times \mathbf{X}$.
\end{itemize}
All of them have to be understood and generalized to manifolds.

\textit{(Figure after the board, redrawn from a computed surface.)} The cap $x^3 = 0.4\,\big(1 - (x^1)^2 - (x^2)^2\big)$ over the unit disk, oriented by the upward unit normal $\mathbf{n}$ (orange, drawn at a few points). Its boundary $\partial S$ is the unit circle in the $(x^1, x^2)$-plane, with the induced orientation (red): counterclockwise seen from above, dashed where the cap hides it. ``Amp\`ere's little guy'' stands on $\partial S$ with $\mathbf{n}$ from his feet to his head; at the rim the normal leans outward, so he leans too. Walking in the direction of $\partial S$ he has the surface on his left (Definition~\ref{def:induced-boundary-orientation}); at his position the outward direction $\nu$ points towards the viewer and $T$ to the right, and $\nu \times T = \mathbf{n}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:outward-first}).

\emph{The surface integral, computed.} The right-hand side of Stokes' theorem is the surface integral of a field, $\nabla \times \mathbf{X}$. For any field $\vec G = (g^1, g^2, g^3)$, how is $\iint_S \vec G \cdot d\vec S$ computed? Parametrize $S$ positively; then the integrand is a $3 \times 3$ determinant, the ``magic formula'' of the lecture.

\begin{lembox}[The Surface Integrand as a Determinant]\thmlabel{lem:flux-determinant}
Let $\vec r : D \to S$ be a positive parametrization of the surface $S$ oriented by $\mathbf{n}$ (Definition~\ref{def:positive-parametrization}), and $\vec G = (g^1, g^2, g^3)$ a continuous field on $S$. At every point of $D$, with $\vec G$ evaluated at $\vec r(s, t)$,
\[
\det \begin{pmatrix} g^1 & g^2 & g^3 \\ x^1_s & x^2_s & x^3_s \\ x^1_t & x^2_t & x^3_t \end{pmatrix} = \vec G \cdot (\vec r_s \times \vec r_t) = (\vec G \cdot \mathbf{n})\, |\vec r_s \times \vec r_t| .
\]
Consequently
\[
\iint_S \vec G \cdot d\vec S = \iint_D \det \begin{pmatrix} g^1 & g^2 & g^3 \\ x^1_s & x^2_s & x^3_s \\ x^1_t & x^2_t & x^3_t \end{pmatrix} ds\, dt .
\]
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~28 states the formula, ``$\vec G \cdot d\vec S = \det(\ldots)\, ds\, dt = (\vec G \cdot \mathbf{n})\, dS$''; the proof is filled in.)} \emph{The first equality.} Expand the determinant along the first row:
\[
\det(\ldots) = g^1 \big(x^2_s x^3_t - x^3_s x^2_t\big) - g^2 \big(x^1_s x^3_t - x^3_s x^1_t\big) + g^3 \big(x^1_s x^2_t - x^2_s x^1_t\big) .
\]
The three brackets, with the sign of the middle one moved inside, are the components of the cross product,
\[
\vec r_s \times \vec r_t = \big( x^2_s x^3_t - x^3_s x^2_t,\ \ x^3_s x^1_t - x^1_s x^3_t,\ \ x^1_s x^2_t - x^2_s x^1_t \big) ,
\]
so the determinant is $g^1 (\vec r_s \times \vec r_t)^1 + g^2 (\vec r_s \times \vec r_t)^2 + g^3 (\vec r_s \times \vec r_t)^3 = \vec G \cdot (\vec r_s \times \vec r_t)$, the triple product.

\emph{The second equality.} Since $\vec r$ is positive, $\vec r_s \times \vec r_t = |\vec r_s \times \vec r_t|\, \mathbf{n}$ (Definition~\ref{def:positive-parametrization}); taking the dot product with $\vec G$ gives $\vec G \cdot (\vec r_s \times \vec r_t) = (\vec G \cdot \mathbf{n})\, |\vec r_s \times \vec r_t|$.

\emph{The integral.} By Definition~\ref{def:flux-integral}, $\iint_S \vec G \cdot d\vec S$ is the integral over $D$ of $(\vec G \cdot \mathbf{n})\, |\vec r_s \times \vec r_t|$, which by the two equalities is the integral of the determinant.
\end{proof}

\textit{(Not from lecture; figure added.)} Lemma~\ref{lem:flux-determinant} in one picture. A small rectangle $\Delta s \times \Delta t$ of $D$ goes, to first order, to the parallelogram spanned by $\vec r_s\, \Delta s$ and $\vec r_t\, \Delta t$ (blue), of area $|\vec r_s \times \vec r_t|\, \Delta s\, \Delta t$. The field $\vec G$ (orange) sweeps it out into a slanted box, whose volume is the absolute value of the determinant with rows $\vec G$, $\vec r_s\, \Delta s$, $\vec r_t\, \Delta t$. The volume is also base times height, and the height is the component $\vec G \cdot \mathbf{n}$ of $\vec G$ along the unit normal (red, dashed from the centre of the top face down to the plane of the base). If $\vec G$ is the velocity of a fluid, the box is the fluid crossing the patch in unit time: this is why $\iint_S \vec G \cdot d\vec S$ is called a flux. The sign of the determinant records on which side of the patch $\vec G$ points.

% SECTION: THE INTEGRAND IS A TWO-FORM
% ============================================================================
\section{The Integrand Is a Two-Form}\label{sec:two-form-integrand}

\roadmark{Stage: forms}{Reading the Calculus~III surface integrand as a two-form: the $2 \times 2$ minors $dx^i \wedge dx^j$ fed the two tangent vectors; and the shape of the general Stokes theorem.}

\textit{(Lecture 28.)} Back to manifolds, thinking geometrically: what kind of object is integrated in the surface integral of \ref{sec:stokes-calc3}? Expand the determinant of Lemma~\ref{lem:flux-determinant} along its top row:
\[
g^1\big(x^2_s x^3_t - x^2_t x^3_s\big) + g^2\big(x^3_s x^1_t - x^3_t x^1_s\big) + g^3\big(x^1_s x^2_t - x^1_t x^2_s\big) .
\]
\textit{(The lecture wrote the first term; the other two are filled in.)} Each bracket is a $2 \times 2$ minor of the matrix with rows $\vec r_s, \vec r_t$: a scalar extracted from the two vectors $\vec r_s, \vec r_t$, linearly in each of them. A function that is fed two vectors and returns a scalar in this way is a two-form.

\begin{defbox}[The Two-Forms $dx^i \wedge dx^j$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$]\deflabel{def:dx-wedge-dx}
For $i, j \in \{1, 2, 3\}$, define the bilinear map
\[
dx^i \wedge dx^j : \mathbb{R}^3 \times \mathbb{R}^3 \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}, \qquad (u, v) \longmapsto \det \begin{pmatrix} u^i & u^j \\ v^i & v^j \end{pmatrix} = u^i v^j - u^j v^i .
\]
\leeref{Ch.~14, \emph{The Wedge Product}}
\end{defbox}

\textit{(Lecture~28, on the board for $(i, j) = (2, 3)$, named $dx^2 \wedge dx^3$ after the two indices involved; the other pairs are filled in the same way.)} The name is explained by the wedge product of covectors: $dx^i$ is the covector $u \mapsto u^i$ (Definition~\ref{def:dual}), and $dx^i \wedge dx^j$ is the wedge product of $dx^i$ and $dx^j$ (Example~\ref{ex:wedge-one-forms}).

\begin{lembox}[Properties of $dx^i \wedge dx^j$]\thmlabel{lem:dx-wedge-properties}
For $i, j \in \{1, 2, 3\}$ and $u, v \in \mathbb{R}^3$:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item $dx^i \wedge dx^j$ is bilinear, and alternating: $(dx^i \wedge dx^j)(v, u) = -(dx^i \wedge dx^j)(u, v)$; in particular $(dx^i \wedge dx^j)(u, u) = 0$;
\item $dx^j \wedge dx^i = -\,dx^i \wedge dx^j$, and $dx^i \wedge dx^i = 0$;
\item the values of the three forms $dx^2 \wedge dx^3$, $dx^3 \wedge dx^1$, $dx^1 \wedge dx^2$ on $(u, v)$ are the three components of the cross product:
\[
u \times v = \big( (dx^2 \wedge dx^3)(u, v),\ (dx^3 \wedge dx^1)(u, v),\ (dx^1 \wedge dx^2)(u, v) \big) ;
\]
\item $(dx^i \wedge dx^j)(u, v)$ is the signed area of the parallelogram spanned by the projections of $u$ and $v$ to the $(x^i, x^j)$-plane, positive when the projection of $u$ turns to the projection of $v$ counterclockwise as seen with the $x^i$-axis pointing right and the $x^j$-axis up.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} All four are properties of $2 \times 2$ determinants.

(1) For fixed $v$, $u \mapsto u^i v^j - u^j v^i$ is linear, since $u \mapsto u^i$ and $u \mapsto u^j$ are; likewise in $v$. Exchanging $u$ and $v$ gives $v^i u^j - v^j u^i = -(u^i v^j - u^j v^i)$. With $v = u$ this says $(dx^i \wedge dx^j)(u, u) = -(dx^i \wedge dx^j)(u, u)$, so it is $0$.

(2) $(dx^j \wedge dx^i)(u, v) = u^j v^i - u^i v^j = -(u^i v^j - u^j v^i)$ for all $u, v$; and $(dx^i \wedge dx^i)(u, v) = u^i v^i - u^i v^i = 0$.

(3) By definition of the cross product, $u \times v = (u^2 v^3 - u^3 v^2,\ u^3 v^1 - u^1 v^3,\ u^1 v^2 - u^2 v^1)$, and the three components are, by Definition~\ref{def:dx-wedge-dx}, the values of $dx^2 \wedge dx^3$, $dx^3 \wedge dx^1$ and $dx^1 \wedge dx^2$ on $(u, v)$.

(4) The projection to the $(x^i, x^j)$-plane sends $u$ to the plane vector $(u^i, u^j)$ and $v$ to $(v^i, v^j)$. The determinant of two plane vectors $a, b$ is $|a|\,|b| \sin\phi$, with $\phi$ the counterclockwise angle from $a$ to $b$; this is the area of the parallelogram they span, with the sign of $\sin \phi$. Applied to $a = (u^i, u^j)$, $b = (v^i, v^j)$, it gives the claim.
\end{proof}

The signed areas of the shadows are the values of $dx^2 \wedge dx^3$, $dx^3 \wedge dx^1$, $dx^1 \wedge dx^2$ on $(u, v)$, and together they are $u \times v$. A shadow whose orientation is reversed gives a negative value, and a parallelogram seen edge-on from a coordinate axis has a shadow of area $0$ there.

\begin{propbox}[The Surface Integrand Is a Two-Form]\thmlabel{prop:flux-two-form}
Let $\vec r : D \to S$ be a positive parametrization of the oriented surface $S$ and $\vec G = (g^1, g^2, g^3)$ a continuous field on $S$. Put
\[
\omega_{\vec G} = g^1\, dx^2 \wedge dx^3 + g^2\, dx^3 \wedge dx^1 + g^3\, dx^1 \wedge dx^2 ,
\]
a two-form with variable coefficients: at each point $q \in S$ the bilinear map $(u, v) \mapsto g^1(q)\, (dx^2 \wedge dx^3)(u, v) + g^2(q)\, (dx^3 \wedge dx^1)(u, v) + g^3(q)\, (dx^1 \wedge dx^2)(u, v)$. Then at every point of $D$, with the coefficients evaluated at $\vec r(s, t)$,
\[
\vec G \cdot (\vec r_s \times \vec r_t) = \omega_{\vec G}(\vec r_s, \vec r_t), \qquad \text{so} \qquad \iint_S \vec G \cdot d\vec S = \iint_D \omega_{\vec G}(\vec r_s, \vec r_t)\, ds\, dt .
\]
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~28: ``$\vec G \cdot d\vec S = (g^1\, dx^2 \wedge dx^3 + \cdots)(\vec r_s, \vec r_t)\, ds\, dt$''; the details are filled in.)} By Lemma~\ref{lem:dx-wedge-properties}(3) with $u = \vec r_s$, $v = \vec r_t$, the components of $\vec r_s \times \vec r_t$ are $(dx^2 \wedge dx^3)(\vec r_s, \vec r_t)$, $(dx^3 \wedge dx^1)(\vec r_s, \vec r_t)$ and $(dx^1 \wedge dx^2)(\vec r_s, \vec r_t)$. So
\[
\vec G \cdot (\vec r_s \times \vec r_t) = g^1 (dx^2 \wedge dx^3)(\vec r_s, \vec r_t) + g^2 (dx^3 \wedge dx^1)(\vec r_s, \vec r_t) + g^3 (dx^1 \wedge dx^2)(\vec r_s, \vec r_t) = \omega_{\vec G}(\vec r_s, \vec r_t) .
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:flux-determinant}, $\iint_S \vec G \cdot d\vec S$ is the integral over $D$ of $\vec G \cdot (\vec r_s \times \vec r_t)$, hence of $\omega_{\vec G}(\vec r_s, \vec r_t)$.
\end{proof}

So the thing integrated in a surface integral is a two-form: at every point, evaluate the coefficients $g^i$ to get scalars and combine the three basic forms; then feed it the two tangent vectors $\vec r_s, \vec r_t$, and integrate the result over $D$. In Calculus~III one does exactly this in Stokes' theorem without saying so. By Lemma~\ref{lem:dx-wedge-properties}(4), $\omega_{\vec G}(\vec r_s, \vec r_t)\, ds\, dt$ weighs the shadows of the small parallelogram on the three coordinate planes by the components of $\vec G$.

\emph{Where this is going: the general Stokes theorem.} \textit{(In the lecture this came right after Stokes' theorem in $\mathbb{R}^3$.)} The theorem of this chapter will read
\[
\int_{\partial S} \alpha = \int_S d\alpha .
\]
Here $S$ is an oriented manifold with boundary of dimension $m$, its boundary $\partial S$ has dimension $m - 1$, $\alpha$ is a \emph{differential form} of degree $m - 1$, and $d\alpha$, the \emph{exterior derivative} of $\alpha$, has degree $m$: to integrate a form over a manifold, the degree of the form has to match the dimension of the manifold. Matching the ingredients with Theorem~\ref{thm:stokes-calc3} ($m = 2$):
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
\item the field $\mathbf{X}$ on the left becomes a one-form, a section of the cotangent bundle (Definition~\ref{def:one-form}), the kind of form already known;
\item the integrand on the right becomes a two-form, as in Proposition~\ref{prop:flux-two-form};
\item $\mathbf{X} \mapsto \nabla \times \mathbf{X}$ is an instance of $d$.
\end{itemize}
Green's theorem, the divergence theorem, the fundamental theorem of calculus for line integrals, and also Cauchy's theorem in complex analysis are instances of the same formula. For Cauchy's theorem, $d\alpha$ is zero. \textit{(Filled in: with $\alpha = f\, dz$ for holomorphic $f$, $d\alpha = \frac{\partial f}{\partial \bar z}\, d\bar z \wedge dz = 0$.)}
