\section{Multilinear Algebra}\label{sec:multilinear}

\roadmark{Stage: forms}{Alternating multilinear forms on a vector space: the pointwise objects that differential forms are made of.}

\textit{(Lecture 28.)} Forms are needed in every degree, not just two: this takes some multilinear algebra. A useful way to think of these objects is as minors of large determinants (Example~\ref{ex:linear-k-forms}(3)).

\begin{defbox}[Linear $k$-Form]\deflabel{def:linear-k-form}
Let $V$ be an $m$-dimensional real vector space and $k \in \{0, 1, 2, \ldots\}$. A \textbf{linear $k$-form} on $V$ is a multilinear map
\[
\alpha : \underbrace{V \times \cdots \times V}_{k} \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}
\]
(linear in each entry with the others fixed) that is \textbf{alternating}: exchanging two entries changes the sign,
\[
\alpha(v^1, \ldots, v^i, \ldots, v^j, \ldots, v^k) = -\alpha(v^1, \ldots, v^j, \ldots, v^i, \ldots, v^k) \qquad (i \neq j) .
\]
\leeref{Ch.~12, \emph{Symmetric and Alternating Tensors}; Ch.~14, \emph{The Algebra of Alternating Tensors}}
\end{defbox}

The definition copies the determinant, which changes sign when two columns are exchanged. For $k = 1$ the alternating condition is empty and the linear $1$-forms are the covectors, $V^*$ (Definition~\ref{def:dual}); for $k = 0$ the linear $0$-forms are, by convention, the scalars. On a manifold there will be one of these at each point, with $V$ the tangent space.

\begin{exbox}[Linear $k$-Forms]\exlabel{ex:linear-k-forms}
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item On $\mathbb{R}^3$, each $dx^i \wedge dx^j$ (Definition~\ref{def:dx-wedge-dx}) is a linear $2$-form, by Lemma~\ref{lem:dx-wedge-properties}(1).
\item On $\mathbb{R}^m$, the determinant $\alpha(v^1, \ldots, v^m) = \det(v^1 \cdots v^m)$ of the matrix with columns $v^1, \ldots, v^m$ is a linear $m$-form: it is linear in each column, and exchanging two columns changes its sign. For $m = 2$, $\det(v, w)$ is the signed area of the parallelogram spanned by $v$ and $w$ (figure below).
\item On $\mathbb{R}^m$, fix rows $1 \le i_1, \ldots, i_k \le m$. Let $\alpha(v^1, \ldots, v^k)$ be the $k \times k$ minor in the rows $i_1, \ldots, i_k$ of the $m \times k$ matrix with columns $v^1, \ldots, v^k$. Then $\alpha$ is a linear $k$-form, by the same two properties of the $k \times k$ determinant. This generalizes item~1, where $m = 3$, $k = 2$ and the rows are $i, j$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{exbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} (2) Multilinearity: expanding along the $j$-th column, $\det$ is a linear function of $v^j$ with the other columns fixed. Exchanging two columns changes the sign of a determinant. (3) The minor is the determinant of the $k \times k$ matrix whose $a$-th column is $(v^a_{i_1}, \ldots, v^a_{i_k})$; this column depends linearly on $v^a$, and exchanging $v^a$ and $v^{a'}$ exchanges two columns. So (2) applies. (1) is (3) with $m = 3$, $k = 2$, $(i_1, i_2) = (i, j)$, written with rows and columns exchanged, which does not change a determinant.
\end{proof}

\begin{lembox}[Permuting the Entries of a $k$-Form]\thmlabel{lem:k-form-permutation}
Let $\alpha$ be a linear $k$-form on $V$ (Definition~\ref{def:linear-k-form}) and $v^1, \ldots, v^k \in V$. For every permutation $\sigma \in S_k$,
\[
\alpha\big(v^{\sigma(1)}, \ldots, v^{\sigma(k)}\big) = \sgn(\sigma)\, \alpha(v^1, \ldots, v^k) ,
\]
with $\sgn$ the sign of a permutation (Definition~\ref{def:sgn}). Conversely, a multilinear map $V \times \cdots \times V \to \mathbb{R}$ with this property for every $\sigma \in S_k$ is alternating.
\leeref{Exercise 12.17}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Discussed with Uribe after Lecture~28; the proof is written out here.)} For $\rho \in S_k$ write $\alpha_\rho = \alpha\big(v^{\rho(1)}, \ldots, v^{\rho(k)}\big)$, the value on the list rearranged by $\rho$; products of permutations are composites, $(\rho\tau)(i) = \rho(\tau(i))$.

\emph{Step 1: one more transposition changes the sign.} Let $\rho \in S_k$ and let $\tau = (a\ b)$ be a transposition, $a \neq b$. Put $u^i = v^{\rho(i)}$, so that $\alpha_\rho = \alpha(u^1, \ldots, u^k)$. Then $v^{(\rho\tau)(i)} = u^{\tau(i)}$, and since $\tau(a) = b$, $\tau(b) = a$ and $\tau(i) = i$ otherwise, the list $\big(u^{\tau(1)}, \ldots, u^{\tau(k)}\big)$ is the list $(u^1, \ldots, u^k)$ with the entries in places $a$ and $b$ exchanged. By the alternating property (Definition~\ref{def:linear-k-form}),
\[
\alpha_{\rho\tau} = \alpha\big(u^{\tau(1)}, \ldots, u^{\tau(k)}\big) = -\alpha(u^1, \ldots, u^k) = -\alpha_\rho .
\]

\emph{Step 2: induction along a factorization.} By Proposition~\ref{prop:sgn}(3), $\sigma = \tau_1 \tau_2 \cdots \tau_r$ for some transpositions $\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_r$, and $\sgn(\sigma) = (-1)^r$ (for $\sigma = \mathrm{id}$ take $r = 0$). Put $\rho_0 = \mathrm{id}$ and $\rho_j = \tau_1 \cdots \tau_j$, so $\rho_j = \rho_{j-1}\tau_j$ and $\rho_r = \sigma$. Step~1 with $\rho = \rho_{j-1}$ and $\tau = \tau_j$ gives $\alpha_{\rho_j} = -\alpha_{\rho_{j-1}}$ for $j = 1, \ldots, r$, hence
\[
\alpha\big(v^{\sigma(1)}, \ldots, v^{\sigma(k)}\big) = \alpha_{\rho_r} = (-1)^r \alpha_{\rho_0} = \sgn(\sigma)\, \alpha(v^1, \ldots, v^k) .
\]

\emph{The converse.} If the identity holds for every $\sigma$, take $\sigma = (i\ j)$ with $i \neq j$: its sign is $-1$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:sgn}(2)), and the rearranged list is $(v^1, \ldots, v^k)$ with the entries $i$ and $j$ exchanged. So exchanging two entries changes the sign: the map is alternating.
\end{proof}

For $k = 2$ the lemma is the definition. For the determinant (Example~\ref{ex:linear-k-forms}(2)) it says that permuting the columns multiplies the determinant by the sign of the permutation, the fact behind the Leibniz formula. The sign does not depend on how $\sigma$ is written as a product of transpositions (Proposition~\ref{prop:sgn}(3)); without that, Step~2 would give two different values for one number. Lee uses the lemma to find a basis of $\Lambda^k(V^*)$ (Lemma~14.7 and Proposition~14.8); it is used in the same way in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:dim-k-forms}.

The same box, spanned by $v^1$ (blue), $v^2$ (orange) and $v^3$ (red), is read in three orders; the circled numbers give each vector's place in the order. Curl the fingers of the right hand from the first entry to the second (black arc): if the third entry lies on the side of the thumb the order is right-handed and the value is $+\mathrm{vol}$, otherwise $-\mathrm{vol}$. Left: $(v^1, v^2, v^3)$, right-handed. Middle: the cyclic order $(v^2, v^3, v^1)$ is a product of two transpositions, $\sgn = +1$, and is right-handed again. \begin{lembox}[Alternating Forms Vanish on Dependent Vectors]\thmlabel{lem:alternating-dependent}
Let $\alpha$ be a linear $k$-form on $V$ (Definition~\ref{def:linear-k-form}).
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item If two of the entries are equal, $v^i = v^j$ for some $i \neq j$, then $\alpha(v^1, \ldots, v^k) = 0$.
\item If $v^1, \ldots, v^k$ are linearly dependent, then $\alpha(v^1, \ldots, v^k) = 0$.
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Lemma 14.1}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in, as in LADR, 9.28.)} (1) Exchanging the two equal entries does not change the list, but changes the sign of $\alpha$: $\alpha(v^1, \ldots, v^k) = -\alpha(v^1, \ldots, v^k)$, so the value is $0$.

(2) Some $v^j$ is a linear combination of the others, $v^j = \sum_{i \neq j} c_i v^i$. By linearity of $\alpha$ in the $j$-th entry,
\[
\alpha(v^1, \ldots, v^j, \ldots, v^k) = \sum_{i \neq j} c_i\, \alpha(v^1, \ldots, \underbrace{v^i}_{j\text{-th entry}}, \ldots, v^k) ,
\]
and in the $i$-th term the vector $v^i$ appears twice, in the entries $i$ and $j$; by~(1) every term is $0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[No Nonzero $k$-Forms of Degree above the Dimension]\thmlabel{cor:forms-above-dimension}
If $k > m = \dim V$, the only linear $k$-form on $V$ is $0$.
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} Any $k > m$ vectors in the $m$-dimensional space $V$ are linearly dependent, so every value of a linear $k$-form is $0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:alternating-dependent}(2).
\end{proof}

% ============================================================================
% Lecture 29 (Wed Nov 11, 2026): a basis of Lambda^k V^*
% ============================================================================

\textit{(Lecture 29.)} The linear algebra continues, with $V$ an $m$-dimensional real vector space (to be thought of as a tangent space, $V = T_pM$) and $k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$. The lecture restated the definition of a $k$-form with all permutations at once: a multilinear map $\alpha : V \times \cdots \times V \to \mathbb{R}$ of $k$ entries is a $k$-form when, for every $\sigma \in S_k$ and all $v^1, \ldots, v^k \in V$,
\[
\alpha\big(v^{\sigma(1)}, \ldots, v^{\sigma(k)}\big) = \sgn(\sigma)\, \alpha(v^1, \ldots, v^k) .
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:k-form-permutation} this is equivalent to Definition~\ref{def:linear-k-form}, which is the case of a transposition. Here $S_k$ is the group of permutations of $\{1, \ldots, k\}$ (Definition~\ref{def:symmetric-group}) and $\sgn(\sigma)$ is the sign of $\sigma$ (Definition~\ref{def:sgn}): every permutation is a composition of transpositions; the decomposition is not unique, but the parity of the number of transpositions is, and $\sgn(\sigma)$ is $+1$ when that number is even and $-1$ when it is odd (Proposition~\ref{prop:sgn}(3)).

\begin{defbox}[The Space $\Lambda^k V^*$]\deflabel{def:lambda-k}
$\Lambda^k V^*$ is the set of all linear $k$-forms on $V$ (Definition~\ref{def:linear-k-form}), with the pointwise operations
\[
(\alpha + \beta)(v^1, \ldots, v^k) = \alpha(v^1, \ldots, v^k) + \beta(v^1, \ldots, v^k), \qquad (c\, \alpha)(v^1, \ldots, v^k) = c\, \alpha(v^1, \ldots, v^k) .
\]
In particular $\Lambda^1 V^* = V^*$, the dual space of all linear maps $V \to \mathbb{R}$ (Definition~\ref{def:dual}), and by convention $\Lambda^0 V^* = \mathbb{R}$.
\leeref{Ch.~14, \emph{The Algebra of Alternating Tensors}}
\end{defbox}

Sums and scalar multiples of alternating multilinear maps are again alternating and multilinear, so $\Lambda^k V^*$ is a vector space, a subspace of the space of all functions $V^k \to \mathbb{R}$ \textit{(Lecture~28)}. For $k = 1$ the group $S_1$ has one element and the alternating condition is empty, which is why $\Lambda^1 V^* = V^*$. The convention $\Lambda^0 V^* = \mathbb{R}$ is a useful one: with it the dimension formula of Proposition~\ref{prop:dim-k-forms} and the wedge product of \ref{sec:wedge-product} also hold in degree $0$. For $k > m$, $\Lambda^k V^* = \{0\}$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:forms-above-dimension}); this comes out again from the basis constructed below.

\begin{rembox}[Notation in This Section]\label{rem:notation-forms}
The board's notation and the notation of these notes differ in a few places.
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
\item \emph{The space of $k$-forms.} Lecture~28 wrote $\Lambda^k V$; Lecture~29 corrected this to $\Lambda^k V^*$, which is Lee's $\Lambda^k(V^*)$. These notes write $\Lambda^k V^*$ (Definition~\ref{def:lambda-k}).
\item \emph{The symmetric group.} The permutations are those of $\{1, \ldots, k\}$, the group $S_k$ (the board first wrote $S_n$). The board's $(-1)^\sigma$ is $\sgn(\sigma)$.
\item \emph{Vectors and components.} The board writes the vectors as $v_1, \ldots, v_k$ and expands $v_i = \sum_a v_i^a e_a$. These notes keep the convention of Definition~\ref{def:linear-k-form} and Example~\ref{ex:linear-k-forms}(3): the vectors are $v^1, \ldots, v^k$ (label up), and $v^j = \sum_{c=1}^m v^j_c\, e_c$ (component index down), so that $\varepsilon^i(v^j) = v^j_i$.
\item \emph{Index sets.} A $k$-element subset $A \subseteq \{1, \ldots, m\}$ is always listed increasingly, $A = \{a_1 < \cdots < a_k\}$. On the board the letters $a_1, \ldots, a_k$ also served as summation indices running over all of $\{1, \ldots, m\}$ in any order; these notes call those $c_1, \ldots, c_k$. Lee indexes the basis by increasing multi-indices $I = (i_1 < \cdots < i_k)$ and writes $\sum'_I$ for a sum over them.
\end{itemize}
\end{rembox}

\emph{The building blocks.} The $k$-forms are built from a basis $(\varepsilon^i)_{i = 1, \ldots, m}$ of $V^*$, as determinants.

\begin{defbox}[The Elementary $k$-Forms $\varepsilon^A$]\deflabel{def:epsilon-A}
Let $(\varepsilon^1, \ldots, \varepsilon^m)$ be a basis of $V^*$, let $1 \le k \le m$, and let $A \subseteq \{1, \ldots, m\}$ be a subset with exactly $k$ elements, listed increasingly: $A = \{a_1 < a_2 < \cdots < a_k\}$. For $v^1, \ldots, v^k \in V$ define
\[
\varepsilon^A(v^1, \ldots, v^k) = \det\big( \varepsilon^{a_i}(v^j) \big)_{i, j = 1, \ldots, k} = \det \begin{pmatrix} \varepsilon^{a_1}(v^1) & \cdots & \varepsilon^{a_1}(v^k) \\ \vdots & & \vdots \\ \varepsilon^{a_k}(v^1) & \cdots & \varepsilon^{a_k}(v^k) \end{pmatrix} ,
\]
the $k \times k$ determinant with row index $i$ and column index $j$. For $k = 0$ the only subset is $A = \varnothing$, and $\varepsilon^{\varnothing} = 1 \in \mathbb{R} = \Lambda^0 V^*$.
\leeref{Ch.~14, \emph{Elementary Alternating Tensors}}
\end{defbox}

The order of the elements of $A$ has to be fixed: with the elements listed in another order the rows of the determinant are permuted, and it changes by the sign of the reordering. The convention is the increasing order. That $i$ is the row index is also only a convention, since transposing a matrix does not change its determinant. Lee calls $\varepsilon^A$ an \emph{elementary $k$-covector} and indexes it by the increasing multi-index $(a_1, \ldots, a_k)$.

\begin{lembox}[The Basis of $V$ Dual to a Basis of $V^*$]\thmlabel{lem:predual-basis}
Let $(\varepsilon^1, \ldots, \varepsilon^m)$ be a basis of $V^*$. There is exactly one basis $(e_1, \ldots, e_m)$ of $V$ with
\[
\varepsilon^i(e_j) = \delta^i_j ,
\]
that is, with dual basis $(\varepsilon^i)$ (Definition~\ref{def:dual-basis}). It is called the basis of $V$ \textbf{dual to} $(\varepsilon^i)$.
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Used in Lecture~29 without comment; filled in.)} Let $(\eta_1, \ldots, \eta_m)$ be the basis of $V^{**} = (V^*)^*$ dual to the basis $(\varepsilon^i)$ of $V^*$: $\eta_j(\varepsilon^i) = \delta^i_j$ (Definition~\ref{def:dual-basis} and Proposition~\ref{prop:dual-basis}, applied to the vector space $V^*$). The map $\iota : V \to V^{**}$, $\iota(v)(\lambda) = \lambda(v)$, is a linear isomorphism (Proposition~\ref{prop:double-dual}). Put $e_j = \iota^{-1}(\eta_j)$. An isomorphism carries a basis to a basis, so $(e_j)$ is a basis of $V$, and
\[
\varepsilon^i(e_j) = \iota(e_j)(\varepsilon^i) = \eta_j(\varepsilon^i) = \delta^i_j .
\]
\emph{Uniqueness.} If $(e'_j)$ is another basis with $\varepsilon^i(e'_j) = \delta^i_j$, then the linear maps $\iota(e'_j)$ and $\eta_j$ on $V^*$ agree on the basis $(\varepsilon^i)$, so they are equal (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(2)), and $e'_j = \iota^{-1}(\eta_j) = e_j$.
\end{proof}

In the coordinates of this basis, $v^j = \sum_{c=1}^m v^j_c\, e_c$ gives $\varepsilon^{a_i}(v^j) = v^j_{a_i}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:dual-basis}), so $\varepsilon^A(v^1, \ldots, v^k)$ is the minor in the rows $a_1, \ldots, a_k$ of the $m \times k$ matrix of components whose columns are $v^1, \ldots, v^k$: the form of Example~\ref{ex:linear-k-forms}(3).

\begin{lembox}[The Elementary $k$-Forms on the Dual Basis]\thmlabel{lem:epsilon-A-dual}
Let $(\varepsilon^i)$ be a basis of $V^*$ and $(e_j)$ the basis of $V$ dual to it (Lemma~\ref{lem:predual-basis}). Let $A = \{a_1 < \cdots < a_k\}$ and $B = \{b_1 < \cdots < b_k\}$ be $k$-element subsets of $\{1, \ldots, m\}$.
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item $\varepsilon^A$ (Definition~\ref{def:epsilon-A}) is a linear $k$-form: $\varepsilon^A \in \Lambda^k V^*$.
\item The value of $\varepsilon^A$ on the basis vectors singled out by $B$ is
\[
\varepsilon^A(e_{b_1}, \ldots, e_{b_k}) = \delta_{AB} = \begin{cases} 1, & A = B, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases}
\]
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Lemma 14.7}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~29.)} (1) By the properties of the determinant. The $j$-th column of the matrix $\big(\varepsilon^{a_i}(v^j)\big)$ is $\big(\varepsilon^{a_1}(v^j), \ldots, \varepsilon^{a_k}(v^j)\big)$; it depends linearly on $v^j$, and on no other vector. The determinant is linear in each column, so $\varepsilon^A$ is multilinear. Exchanging $v^j$ and $v^{j'}$ exchanges two columns, which changes the sign of the determinant, so $\varepsilon^A$ is alternating.

(2) The matrix is $\big(\varepsilon^{a_i}(e_{b_j})\big)_{i, j} = \big(\delta^{a_i}_{b_j}\big)_{i, j}$. If $A = B$, then $a_i = b_i$ for all $i$, because both sets are listed increasingly; the matrix is the identity matrix, with determinant $1$. If $A \neq B$, some $b_j$ is not in $A$, because $A$ and $B$ have the same number of elements; then $\delta^{a_i}_{b_j} = 0$ for every $i$, the $j$-th column is zero, and the determinant is $0$.
\end{proof}

By~(2), the forms $\varepsilon^A$ behave like a dual basis: each is $1$ on its own $k$-tuple of basis vectors and $0$ on the others.

\begin{propbox}[A Basis of $\Lambda^k V^*$]\thmlabel{prop:dim-k-forms}
The set $\Lambda^k V^*$ of all linear $k$-forms on the $m$-dimensional space $V$ is a vector space, of dimension $\binom{m}{k}$. More precisely, for any basis $(\varepsilon^i)$ of $V^*$,
\[
\big\{ \varepsilon^A : A \subseteq \{1, \ldots, m\},\ |A| = k \big\}
\]
is a basis of $\Lambda^k V^*$, and if $(e_j)$ is the basis of $V$ dual to $(\varepsilon^i)$, every $\alpha \in \Lambda^k V^*$ is
\[
\alpha = \sum_{|A| = k} \alpha(e_{a_1}, \ldots, e_{a_k})\, \varepsilon^A ,
\]
the sum over all $k$-element subsets $A = \{a_1 < \cdots < a_k\}$ of $\{1, \ldots, m\}$.
\leeref{Proposition 14.8}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~28 for the vector space; Lecture~29 for the basis, which is constructed in the course of the proof. The notation follows the remark \emph{Notation in This Section} above.)} That $\Lambda^k V^*$ is a vector space was noted after Definition~\ref{def:lambda-k}. There are exactly $\binom{m}{k}$ subsets $A$ of $\{1, \ldots, m\}$ with $k$ elements, by the definition of the binomial coefficient, so it is enough to show that the forms $\varepsilon^A$, which lie in $\Lambda^k V^*$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:epsilon-A-dual}(1), are linearly independent and span. Let $(e_j)$ be the basis of $V$ dual to $(\varepsilon^i)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:predual-basis}).

\emph{Linear independence.} Suppose $\sum_A c_A\, \varepsilon^A = 0$ with $c_A \in \mathbb{R}$. Fix a $k$-element subset $B = \{b_1 < \cdots < b_k\}$ and evaluate both sides on $(e_{b_1}, \ldots, e_{b_k})$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:epsilon-A-dual}(2),
\[
0 = \sum_A c_A\, \varepsilon^A(e_{b_1}, \ldots, e_{b_k}) = \sum_A c_A\, \delta_{AB} = c_B .
\]
So $c_B = 0$ for every $B$.

\emph{Span.} Let $\alpha \in \Lambda^k V^*$ and $v^1, \ldots, v^k \in V$, and expand each vector in the basis, $v^j = \sum_{c=1}^m v^j_c\, e_c$. Each of the $k$ entries needs its own summation index, $c_1, \ldots, c_k$. By multilinearity,
\[
\alpha(v^1, \ldots, v^k) = \alpha\Big( \sum_{c_1=1}^m v^1_{c_1} e_{c_1}, \ldots, \sum_{c_k=1}^m v^k_{c_k} e_{c_k} \Big) = \sum_{c_1, \ldots, c_k = 1}^m \Big( \prod_{j=1}^k v^j_{c_j} \Big)\, \alpha(e_{c_1}, \ldots, e_{c_k}) .
\]
Here $c_1, \ldots, c_k$ run independently over $\{1, \ldots, m\}$, in no particular order. If two of them are equal, two entries of $\alpha(e_{c_1}, \ldots, e_{c_k})$ are equal and the term is $0$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:alternating-dependent}(1). If they are all different, $\{c_1, \ldots, c_k\}$ is a $k$-element set $A$; list it increasingly, $A = \{a_1 < \cdots < a_k\}$. Then $c_j = a_{\sigma(j)}$ for exactly one $\sigma \in S_k$, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:k-form-permutation}, applied to the vectors $e_{a_1}, \ldots, e_{a_k}$,
\[
\alpha(e_{c_1}, \ldots, e_{c_k}) = \alpha\big(e_{a_{\sigma(1)}}, \ldots, e_{a_{\sigma(k)}}\big) = \sgn(\sigma)\, \alpha(e_{a_1}, \ldots, e_{a_k}) .
\]
So in each term with all indices different, the indices are rearranged into increasing order at the price of the factor $\sgn(\sigma)$. Conversely, each pair of a $k$-element set $A$ and a permutation $\sigma \in S_k$ gives one such term, the one with $c_j = a_{\sigma(j)}$. Gathering the terms with the same set $A$:
\[
\alpha(v^1, \ldots, v^k) = \sum_{|A| = k} \Big( \sum_{\sigma \in S_k} \sgn(\sigma) \prod_{j=1}^k v^j_{a_{\sigma(j)}} \Big)\, \alpha(e_{a_1}, \ldots, e_{a_k}) .
\]
The inner sum is a determinant. Let $M$ be the $k \times k$ matrix with entries $M_{ij} = v^j_{a_i} = \varepsilon^{a_i}(v^j)$, so that $\prod_j v^j_{a_{\sigma(j)}} = \prod_j M_{\sigma(j), j}$. The Leibniz formula (stated in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:det-cont}), applied to the transpose $M^{\mathsf T}$, whose $(j, i)$ entry is $M_{ij}$, reads $\det M^{\mathsf T} = \sum_{\sigma} \sgn(\sigma) \prod_j M_{\sigma(j), j}$, and $\det M^{\mathsf T} = \det M$. Hence the inner sum is
\[
\det\big( v^j_{a_i} \big)_{i, j} = \det\big( \varepsilon^{a_i}(v^j) \big)_{i, j} = \varepsilon^A(v^1, \ldots, v^k) ,
\]
by Definition~\ref{def:epsilon-A}. Therefore
\[
\alpha(v^1, \ldots, v^k) = \sum_{|A| = k} \alpha(e_{a_1}, \ldots, e_{a_k})\, \varepsilon^A(v^1, \ldots, v^k)
\]
for all $v^1, \ldots, v^k$. This is the formula of the proposition; in particular the $\varepsilon^A$ span. The coefficients are the ones forced by Lemma~\ref{lem:epsilon-A-dual}(2): evaluating $\alpha = \sum_A c_A \varepsilon^A$ on $(e_{b_1}, \ldots, e_{b_k})$ gives $c_B = \alpha(e_{b_1}, \ldots, e_{b_k})$.

\emph{The edge cases.} For $k = 0$ the only subset is $\varnothing$, with $\varepsilon^\varnothing = 1$, a basis of $\Lambda^0 V^* = \mathbb{R}$, and $\binom{m}{0} = 1$. For $k > m$ there are no subsets, $\binom{m}{k} = 0$, and $\Lambda^k V^* = \{0\}$ by Corollary~\ref{cor:forms-above-dimension}.
\end{proof}

The proof gives more than the dimension: every $k$-form is a linear combination of determinants of size $k$, the forms $\varepsilon^A$.

\textbf{Transcription note (Lecture 29).} In the span step the board wrote the coefficient as $v_j^{\sigma(a_j)}$, letting $\sigma$ act on the elements of $A$; with $\sigma \in S_k$ acting on the positions it is $v^j_{a_{\sigma(j)}}$ in the convention of these notes (remark \emph{Notation in This Section}). The step was corrected during the lecture; the version above is the one settled on in class.

\begin{corbox}[The Top Degree]\thmlabel{cor:top-degree-forms}
Let $\dim V = m$. The space $\Lambda^m V^*$ is one-dimensional. For any basis $(\varepsilon^i)$ of $V^*$, with $(e_j)$ the basis of $V$ dual to it, it is spanned by
\[
\varepsilon^{\{1, \ldots, m\}}(v^1, \ldots, v^m) = \det\big( \varepsilon^i(v^j) \big)_{i, j = 1, \ldots, m} ,
\]
and every $\alpha \in \Lambda^m V^*$ is $\alpha = \alpha(e_1, \ldots, e_m)\, \varepsilon^{\{1, \ldots, m\}}$.
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Stated in Lecture~28; it follows from the basis of Lecture~29.)} This is Proposition~\ref{prop:dim-k-forms} for $k = m$: the only $m$-element subset of $\{1, \ldots, m\}$ is $A = \{1, \ldots, m\}$, and $\binom{m}{m} = 1$.
\end{proof}

On $V = \mathbb{R}^m$ with the standard basis this says that every linear $m$-form is a constant multiple of the determinant of Example~\ref{ex:linear-k-forms}(2).

\begin{exbox}[The Euclidean Case]\exlabel{ex:basis-euclidean-forms}
On $V = \mathbb{R}^m$ take $\varepsilon^i = dx^i : \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}$, the differential of the $i$-th coordinate function, which extracts the $i$-th coordinate: $dx^i(u) = u^i$. The basis of $\mathbb{R}^m$ dual to $(dx^i)$ is the standard basis. For $i < j$,
\[
\varepsilon^{\{i, j\}}(u, v) = \det \begin{pmatrix} u^i & v^i \\ u^j & v^j \end{pmatrix} = u^i v^j - u^j v^i ,
\]
which is the form $dx^i \wedge dx^j$ of Definition~\ref{def:dx-wedge-dx} (there for $m = 3$; the formula is the same for every $m$). For example, $\Lambda^2 (\mathbb{R}^4)^*$, written $\Lambda^2 \mathbb{R}^4$ on the board, has dimension $\binom{4}{2} = 6$, with basis
\[
dx^1 \wedge dx^2, \quad dx^1 \wedge dx^3, \quad dx^1 \wedge dx^4, \quad dx^2 \wedge dx^3, \quad dx^2 \wedge dx^4, \quad dx^3 \wedge dx^4 .
\]
\end{exbox}

\textit{(Not from lecture; figure added.)} The six basis forms of $\Lambda^2 (\mathbb{R}^4)^*$ in Example~\ref{ex:basis-euclidean-forms}. The two vectors $u, v \in \mathbb{R}^4$ are the columns of a $4 \times 2$ matrix. Each two-element subset $A = \{i < j\}$ of $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ selects two rows (shaded), and $\varepsilon^A(u, v) = (dx^i \wedge dx^j)(u, v)$ is the $2 \times 2$ minor in those rows. There are $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ ways to choose the rows, which is the dimension. In general $\varepsilon^A(v^1, \ldots, v^k)$ is the minor in the rows $a_1 < \cdots < a_k$ of the $m \times k$ matrix with columns $v^1, \ldots, v^k$, and Proposition~\ref{prop:dim-k-forms} says that every $k$-form is a combination of these $\binom{m}{k}$ minors.
%% <<< END ADDED

The six-dimensional space $\Lambda^2 (\mathbb{R}^4)^*$ is the one that appears in Yang--Mills theory: two-forms in four variables. \textit{(Not from lecture.)} The first instance is electromagnetism: the field strength is a two-form on spacetime $\mathbb{R}^4$, and its six components are the three components of the electric field and the three of the magnetic field.

% SECTION: THE WEDGE PRODUCT
% ============================================================================
\section{The Wedge Product}\label{sec:wedge-product}

\roadmark{Stage: forms}{Multiplying a $k$-form and an $l$-form into a $(k + l)$-form, by signed shuffles; bilinear, associative, graded anticommutative.}

\textit{(Lecture 29.)} The wedge in $dx^i \wedge dx^j$ has been written many times (Definition~\ref{def:dx-wedge-dx}), but as an operation it has not been defined. This section defines it: a product that takes a $k$-form $\alpha$ and an $l$-form $\beta$ on $V$ (Definition~\ref{def:lambda-k}) to a $(k + l)$-form $\alpha \wedge \beta$. The forms of all degrees with this product make up the \emph{Grassmann algebra} of $V$ (Lee: the exterior algebra). It was developed in the 19th century, and brought into its present form, for differential forms, by \'Elie Cartan in the first half of the 20th century. Throughout, $V$ is an $m$-dimensional real vector space and $k, l \ge 0$.

\begin{defbox}[Shuffles]\deflabel{def:shuffle}
For $k, l \ge 0$, a \textbf{$(k, l)$-shuffle} is a permutation $\sigma \in S_{k+l}$ (Definition~\ref{def:symmetric-group}) with
\[
\sigma(1) < \sigma(2) < \cdots < \sigma(k) \qquad \text{and} \qquad \sigma(k+1) < \sigma(k+2) < \cdots < \sigma(k+l) .
\]
$\mathrm{Sh}(k, l)$ denotes the set of $(k, l)$-shuffles.
\end{defbox}

The name comes from shuffling a deck of cards. Put $k$ cards on the left and $l$ cards on the right and interleave the two piles: the cards mix, but the internal order of each pile does not change. The card in place $i$ before the shuffle lands in place $\sigma(i)$ of the deck; the first pile is the cards $1, \ldots, k$ and the second the cards $k + 1, \ldots, k + l$. A shuffle is determined by the set $\{\sigma(1), \ldots, \sigma(k)\}$ of places taken by the first pile (Lemma~\ref{lem:shuffle-factorization}(2)).

\textit{(Not from lecture; figure added.)} One $(2, 3)$-shuffle, $\sigma = (2, 4, 1, 3, 5)$ in one-line notation ($\sigma(1) = 2$, $\sigma(2) = 4$, $\sigma(3) = 1$, $\sigma(4) = 3$, $\sigma(5) = 5$): the cards $1, 2$ of the first pile land in places $2, 4$, the cards $3, 4, 5$ of the second pile in places $1, 3, 5$, each pile keeping its order. It has three inversions (Definition~\ref{def:sgn}), the pairs $(1, 3)$, $(2, 3)$ and $(2, 4)$, so $\sgn(\sigma) = -1$. In the picture the inversions are the crossings: two arrows cross exactly when the card that starts further left lands further right, and for a shuffle only a red arrow and a blue arrow can cross.

\begin{lembox}[Shuffles and the Subgroup $S_k \times S_l$]\thmlabel{lem:shuffle-factorization}
Let $S_k \times S_l \subseteq S_{k+l}$ denote the set of permutations $\rho$ with $\rho(\{1, \ldots, k\}) = \{1, \ldots, k\}$. Such a $\rho$ permutes $\{1, \ldots, k\}$ by some $\tau \in S_k$ and $\{k+1, \ldots, k+l\}$ by $\rho(k + j) = k + \tau'(j)$ for some $\tau' \in S_l$.
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item $S_k \times S_l$ is a subgroup of $S_{k+l}$ with $k!\, l!$ elements, and $\sgn(\rho) = \sgn(\tau)\, \sgn(\tau')$.
\item A $(k, l)$-shuffle $\sigma$ is determined by the set $\sigma(\{1, \ldots, k\})$, and every $k$-element subset of $\{1, \ldots, k+l\}$ is $\sigma(\{1, \ldots, k\})$ for a shuffle $\sigma$. Hence $|\mathrm{Sh}(k, l)| = \binom{k+l}{k}$.
\item Every $\pi \in S_{k+l}$ factors in exactly one way as
\[
\pi = \sigma \circ \rho, \qquad \sigma \in \mathrm{Sh}(k, l), \quad \rho \in S_k \times S_l .
\]
\end{enumerate}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} Write $n = k + l$, $I = \{1, \ldots, k\}$ and $J = \{k+1, \ldots, n\}$.

(1) If $\rho(I) = I$ then also $\rho(J) = J$, because $\rho$ is a bijection of $I \cup J$. If $\rho$ and $\rho'$ map $I$ onto $I$, so do $\rho \circ \rho'$ and $\rho^{-1}$, and so does the identity: $S_k \times S_l$ is a subgroup. The element $\rho$ is determined by the pair $(\tau, \tau')$, and every pair occurs, so there are $k!\, l!$ elements. For the sign, count inversions (Definition~\ref{def:sgn}). A pair $i < j$ with $i \in I$ and $j \in J$ is not an inversion of $\rho$, since $\rho(i) \le k < \rho(j)$. The inversions with $i, j \in I$ are the inversions of $\tau$, and those with $i, j \in J$ correspond to the inversions of $\tau'$. So the number of inversions of $\rho$ is the sum of those of $\tau$ and $\tau'$, and $\sgn(\rho) = \sgn(\tau)\sgn(\tau')$.

(2) Let $\sigma$ be a shuffle and $P = \sigma(I)$. Since $\sigma(1) < \cdots < \sigma(k)$, these values are the elements of $P$ in increasing order; since $\sigma(k+1) < \cdots < \sigma(n)$, those values are the elements of the complement of $P$ in increasing order. So $P$ determines $\sigma$. Conversely, for any $k$-element subset $P = \{p_1 < \cdots < p_k\}$ of $\{1, \ldots, n\}$, with complement $\{q_1 < \cdots < q_l\}$, the permutation $\sigma(i) = p_i$ for $i \le k$, $\sigma(k + j) = q_j$ for $j \le l$, is a shuffle with $\sigma(I) = P$. So $\sigma \mapsto \sigma(I)$ is a bijection from $\mathrm{Sh}(k, l)$ to the set of $k$-element subsets of $\{1, \ldots, n\}$, which has $\binom{n}{k}$ elements.

(3) \emph{Existence.} Given $\pi$, let $\sigma$ be the shuffle with $\sigma(I) = \pi(I)$, from~(2), and put $\rho = \sigma^{-1} \circ \pi$. Then $\rho(I) = \sigma^{-1}(\pi(I)) = \sigma^{-1}(\sigma(I)) = I$, so $\rho \in S_k \times S_l$, and $\pi = \sigma \circ \rho$. \emph{Uniqueness.} If $\pi = \sigma \circ \rho$ with $\sigma$ a shuffle and $\rho(I) = I$, then $\sigma(I) = \sigma(\rho(I)) = \pi(I)$, which determines $\sigma$ by~(2), and then $\rho = \sigma^{-1} \circ \pi$.
\end{proof}

By~(3) the shuffles are a set of representatives for the left cosets $\sigma \circ (S_k \times S_l)$ of the subgroup $S_k \times S_l$, one in each coset. The count agrees: $(k+l)! = \binom{k+l}{k} \cdot k!\, l!$.

\begin{exbox}[Shuffles Do Not Form a Subgroup]\exlabel{ex:shuffles-not-subgroup}
\textit{(Lecture~29: a student asked whether $\mathrm{Sh}(k, l)$ is a subgroup of $S_{k+l}$ isomorphic to $S_k \times S_l$. It is not; the example is filled in.)} Take $k = 1$ and $l = 2$. The only condition on a $(1, 2)$-shuffle is $\sigma(2) < \sigma(3)$, and in one-line notation $(\sigma(1), \sigma(2), \sigma(3))$,
\[
\mathrm{Sh}(1, 2) = \{ (1, 2, 3),\ (2, 1, 3),\ (3, 1, 2) \} ,
\]
three elements, in agreement with $\binom{3}{1} = 3$. Let $\sigma = (2, 1, 3)$ and $\sigma' = (3, 1, 2)$. Then
\[
(\sigma' \circ \sigma)(1) = \sigma'(2) = 1, \qquad (\sigma' \circ \sigma)(2) = \sigma'(1) = 3, \qquad (\sigma' \circ \sigma)(3) = \sigma'(3) = 2 ,
\]
so $\sigma' \circ \sigma = (1, 3, 2)$, which is not a shuffle: its values at $2$ and $3$ are $3 > 2$. So $\mathrm{Sh}(1, 2)$ is not closed under composition. The subgroup in the picture is $S_1 \times S_2 = \{(1, 2, 3), (1, 3, 2)\}$, with two elements, and the three shuffles represent its three left cosets (Lemma~\ref{lem:shuffle-factorization}(3)).
\end{exbox}

\begin{defbox}[Wedge Product]\deflabel{def:wedge-product}
Given $\alpha \in \Lambda^k V^*$ and $\beta \in \Lambda^l V^*$ (Definition~\ref{def:lambda-k}), their \textbf{wedge product} is the function $\alpha \wedge \beta : V^{k+l} \to \mathbb{R}$,
\[
(\alpha \wedge \beta)(v^1, \ldots, v^{k+l}) = \sum_{\sigma \in \mathrm{Sh}(k, l)} \sgn(\sigma)\, \alpha\big(v^{\sigma(1)}, \ldots, v^{\sigma(k)}\big)\, \beta\big(v^{\sigma(k+1)}, \ldots, v^{\sigma(k+l)}\big) ,
\]
the sum over all $(k, l)$-shuffles (Definition~\ref{def:shuffle}). It is a linear $(k + l)$-form, $\alpha \wedge \beta \in \Lambda^{k+l} V^*$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:wedge-all-permutations}(3)).
\leeref{Ch.~14, \emph{The Wedge Product}}
\end{defbox}

Degrees add under multiplication, as a degree should. Each term of the sum hands $k$ of the $k + l$ vectors to $\alpha$ and the remaining $l$ to $\beta$, both in increasing order of their labels; by Lemma~\ref{lem:shuffle-factorization}(2) there is one term for each way of choosing which $k$ vectors go to $\alpha$, and its sign is the sign of the shuffle. For $k = 0$, $\alpha$ is a number $c$, the only $(0, l)$-shuffle is the identity, and $c \wedge \beta = c\, \beta$. In practice the formula is used directly only in low degrees.

\textbf{Transcription note (Lecture 29).} The board wrote $(-1)^\sigma$ for $\sgn(\sigma)$, lower labels $v_{\sigma(1)}, \ldots$ for the vectors, and $r_{\sigma(1)}, \ldots, r_{\sigma(k)}$ in the entries of $\alpha$, which are $v^{\sigma(1)}, \ldots, v^{\sigma(k)}$.

One can also sum over all permutations of $\{1, \ldots, k+l\}$ instead of the shuffles, but then there are many repetitions: in each term the entries of $\alpha$, and those of $\beta$, can be put into increasing order at the price of a sign. This, and the algebraic meaning of the formula, are made precise next. The lecture presented the algebraic description for conceptual understanding only; it is not used in computations.

\begin{defbox}[Tensor Product of Multilinear Maps]\deflabel{def:tensor-product-multilinear}
Let $S : V^k \to \mathbb{R}$ and $T : V^l \to \mathbb{R}$ be multilinear. Their \textbf{tensor product} is the map $S \otimes T : V^{k+l} \to \mathbb{R}$,
\[
(S \otimes T)(v^1, \ldots, v^{k+l}) = S(v^1, \ldots, v^k)\, T(v^{k+1}, \ldots, v^{k+l}) .
\]
It is multilinear.
\leeref{Ch.~12, \emph{Multilinear Algebra}}
\end{defbox}

$S \otimes T$ is linear in each of the first $k$ entries because $S$ is, and in each of the last $l$ entries because $T$ is. For forms $\alpha \in \Lambda^k V^*$ and $\beta \in \Lambda^l V^*$ the tensor product $\alpha \otimes \beta$ is multilinear but in general not alternating: for $k = l = 1$, $(\alpha \otimes \beta)(v, v) = \alpha(v)\beta(v)$, which is not $0$ when $\alpha(v) \neq 0 \neq \beta(v)$ (compare Lemma~\ref{lem:alternating-dependent}(1)). The board writes $V^* \otimes \cdots \otimes V^*$ ($n$ factors) for the vector space of all multilinear maps $V^n \to \mathbb{R}$.

\begin{defbox}[The Skew-Symmetrizer]\deflabel{def:skew-symmetrizer}
Let $T : V^n \to \mathbb{R}$ be multilinear. For $\pi \in S_n$ let $T^\pi$ be $T$ with its entries rearranged by $\pi$,
\[
T^\pi(v^1, \ldots, v^n) = T\big(v^{\pi(1)}, \ldots, v^{\pi(n)}\big) .
\]
The \textbf{skew-symmetrizer} is the map $\mathcal{A}$ that sends $T$ to
\[
\mathcal{A}(T) = \frac{1}{n!} \sum_{\pi \in S_n} \sgn(\pi)\, T^\pi .
\]
\leeref{Ch.~14, \emph{The Algebra of Alternating Tensors}}
\end{defbox}

\textit{(Lecture~29 named the map and described it as the natural projection onto the completely antisymmetric maps, without writing the formula; the formula is filled in. Lee calls it alternation and writes $\operatorname{Alt}$.)} Each $T^\pi$ is multilinear, so $\mathcal{A}(T)$ is multilinear, and $\mathcal{A}$ is a linear map from the space of multilinear maps $V^n \to \mathbb{R}$ to itself.

\begin{lembox}[The Skew-Symmetrizer Projects onto the Forms]\thmlabel{lem:skew-symmetrizer}
Let $T : V^n \to \mathbb{R}$ be multilinear and $\mathcal{A}$ the skew-symmetrizer (Definition~\ref{def:skew-symmetrizer}).
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item $\mathcal{A}(T)$ is alternating: $\mathcal{A}(T) \in \Lambda^n V^*$.
\item If $T$ is alternating, then $\mathcal{A}(T) = T$.
\end{enumerate}
So $\mathcal{A}$ is a linear projection of the space of multilinear maps $V^n \to \mathbb{R}$ onto $\Lambda^n V^*$: its image is $\Lambda^n V^*$, and $\mathcal{A} \circ \mathcal{A} = \mathcal{A}$.
\leeref{Proposition 14.3}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not proved in lecture; filled in.)} \emph{A rule for rearranging twice.} For $\pi, \mu \in S_n$, $(T^\pi)^\mu = T^{\mu \circ \pi}$. Indeed, put $w^i = v^{\mu(i)}$; then
\[
\begin{aligned}
(T^\pi)^\mu(v^1, \ldots, v^n) &= T^\pi(w^1, \ldots, w^n) = T\big(w^{\pi(1)}, \ldots, w^{\pi(n)}\big) \\
&= T\big(v^{\mu(\pi(1))}, \ldots, v^{\mu(\pi(n))}\big) = T^{\mu \circ \pi}(v^1, \ldots, v^n) .
\end{aligned}
\]

(1) Let $\mu \in S_n$. By the rule, and since $\sgn(\pi) = \sgn(\mu)\, \sgn(\mu \circ \pi)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:sgn}(1), with $\sgn(\mu)^2 = 1$),
\[
\mathcal{A}(T)^\mu = \frac{1}{n!} \sum_{\pi \in S_n} \sgn(\pi)\, T^{\mu \circ \pi} = \sgn(\mu)\, \frac{1}{n!} \sum_{\pi \in S_n} \sgn(\mu \circ \pi)\, T^{\mu \circ \pi} = \sgn(\mu)\, \mathcal{A}(T) ;
\]
the last step holds because $\pi \mapsto \mu \circ \pi$ is a bijection of $S_n$, so the sum runs over all of $S_n$ again. Thus $\mathcal{A}(T)\big(v^{\mu(1)}, \ldots, v^{\mu(n)}\big) = \sgn(\mu)\, \mathcal{A}(T)(v^1, \ldots, v^n)$ for every $\mu$, and $\mathcal{A}(T)$ is multilinear. By the converse in Lemma~\ref{lem:k-form-permutation}, $\mathcal{A}(T)$ is alternating.

(2) If $T$ is alternating, $T^\pi = \sgn(\pi)\, T$ for every $\pi$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:k-form-permutation}. Then $\mathcal{A}(T) = \frac{1}{n!} \sum_\pi \sgn(\pi)^2\, T = T$, as $S_n$ has $n!$ elements.

\emph{The projection.} By~(1) the image of $\mathcal{A}$ lies in $\Lambda^n V^*$, and by~(2) every element of $\Lambda^n V^*$ is its own image. Applying~(2) to the alternating map $\mathcal{A}(T)$ gives $\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{A}(T)) = \mathcal{A}(T)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[The Wedge Product as a Skew-Symmetrized Tensor Product]\thmlabel{prop:wedge-all-permutations}
Let $\alpha \in \Lambda^k V^*$ and $\beta \in \Lambda^l V^*$.
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item The wedge product (Definition~\ref{def:wedge-product}) is also the sum over all permutations, divided by $k!\, l!$:
\[
(\alpha \wedge \beta)(v^1, \ldots, v^{k+l}) = \frac{1}{k!\, l!} \sum_{\pi \in S_{k+l}} \sgn(\pi)\, \alpha\big(v^{\pi(1)}, \ldots, v^{\pi(k)}\big)\, \beta\big(v^{\pi(k+1)}, \ldots, v^{\pi(k+l)}\big) .
\]
\item In terms of the tensor product (Definition~\ref{def:tensor-product-multilinear}) and the skew-symmetrizer (Definition~\ref{def:skew-symmetrizer}),
\[
\alpha \wedge \beta = \frac{(k + l)!}{k!\, l!}\, \mathcal{A}(\alpha \otimes \beta) .
\]
\item $\alpha \wedge \beta$ is a linear $(k + l)$-form: $\alpha \wedge \beta \in \Lambda^{k+l} V^*$.
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Ch.~14, \emph{The Wedge Product}}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{((1) was stated in Lecture~29, and (2) in the form $\alpha \wedge \beta = \mathcal{A}(\alpha \otimes \beta)$; the proofs and the factor in (2) are filled in.)} Write $n = k + l$.

(1) Let $\pi \in S_n$ and factor it as $\pi = \sigma \circ \rho$ with $\sigma \in \mathrm{Sh}(k, l)$ and $\rho \in S_k \times S_l$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:shuffle-factorization}(3)), where $\rho$ acts by $\tau \in S_k$ on $\{1, \ldots, k\}$ and by $\rho(k + j) = k + \tau'(j)$, $\tau' \in S_l$. Put $u^i = v^{\sigma(i)}$ for $i \le k$ and $w^j = v^{\sigma(k + j)}$ for $j \le l$. Then $v^{\pi(i)} = v^{\sigma(\tau(i))} = u^{\tau(i)}$ and $v^{\pi(k + j)} = v^{\sigma(k + \tau'(j))} = w^{\tau'(j)}$, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:k-form-permutation}, applied to $\alpha$ and to $\beta$,
\[
\alpha\big(v^{\pi(1)}, \ldots, v^{\pi(k)}\big) = \alpha\big(u^{\tau(1)}, \ldots, u^{\tau(k)}\big) = \sgn(\tau)\, \alpha\big(v^{\sigma(1)}, \ldots, v^{\sigma(k)}\big) ,
\]
\[
\beta\big(v^{\pi(k+1)}, \ldots, v^{\pi(k+l)}\big) = \beta\big(w^{\tau'(1)}, \ldots, w^{\tau'(l)}\big) = \sgn(\tau')\, \beta\big(v^{\sigma(k+1)}, \ldots, v^{\sigma(k+l)}\big) .
\]
Also $\sgn(\pi) = \sgn(\sigma)\, \sgn(\rho) = \sgn(\sigma)\, \sgn(\tau)\, \sgn(\tau')$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:sgn}(1) and Lemma~\ref{lem:shuffle-factorization}(1)). Multiplying the three equations, the signs of $\tau$ and $\tau'$ appear squared, and the term of $\pi$ in the sum over $S_n$ equals the term of $\sigma$ in the sum over shuffles:
\[
\sgn(\pi)\, \alpha\big(v^{\pi(1)}, \ldots\big)\, \beta\big(v^{\pi(k+1)}, \ldots\big) = \sgn(\sigma)\, \alpha\big(v^{\sigma(1)}, \ldots\big)\, \beta\big(v^{\sigma(k+1)}, \ldots\big) .
\]
By the uniqueness of the factorization, the permutations $\pi$ with a given shuffle $\sigma$ are the $\sigma \circ \rho$ with $\rho \in S_k \times S_l$, and there are $k!\, l!$ of them. So the sum over $S_n$ is $k!\, l!$ times the sum over $\mathrm{Sh}(k, l)$.

(2) By Definitions~\ref{def:tensor-product-multilinear} and~\ref{def:skew-symmetrizer}, $(\alpha \otimes \beta)^\pi(v^1, \ldots, v^n) = \alpha\big(v^{\pi(1)}, \ldots, v^{\pi(k)}\big)\, \beta\big(v^{\pi(k+1)}, \ldots, v^{\pi(n)}\big)$, so the sum in~(1) is $\sum_\pi \sgn(\pi)\, (\alpha \otimes \beta)^\pi = n!\, \mathcal{A}(\alpha \otimes \beta)$. Dividing by $k!\, l!$ gives~(2).

(3) $\mathcal{A}(\alpha \otimes \beta) \in \Lambda^n V^*$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:skew-symmetrizer}(1), and $\Lambda^n V^*$ is a vector space; so~(3) follows from~(2).
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[Two Conventions for the Wedge Product]\label{rem:wedge-conventions}
The board wrote $\alpha \wedge \beta = \mathcal{A}(\alpha \otimes \beta)$: take the tensor product, then its skew-symmetric part. With $\mathcal{A}$ normalized as a projection (Lemma~\ref{lem:skew-symmetrizer}), this holds up to the factor $\binom{k+l}{k}$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:wedge-all-permutations}(2). Lee defines the wedge product by the formula with the factor and calls this the \emph{determinant convention}: the factor is what makes $\varepsilon^{a_1} \wedge \cdots \wedge \varepsilon^{a_k}$ equal to the determinant $\varepsilon^A$ with no factorials (Proposition~\ref{prop:wedge-properties}(4)), and it is the convention of the shuffle formula of Definition~\ref{def:wedge-product}, which has no factorials at all. Some books, for example Kobayashi--Nomizu, define the product as $\mathcal{A}(\alpha \otimes \beta)$ without the factor (the \emph{Alt convention}); their wedge product differs from this one by the constant $\binom{k+l}{k}$.
\end{rembox}

\begin{exbox}[The Wedge of Two One-Forms]\exlabel{ex:wedge-one-forms}
Let $k = l = 1$, so $\alpha, \beta \in V^*$. The group $S_2$ has two elements, the identity $(1, 2)$ and the transposition $(2, 1)$ in one-line notation, and both are shuffles: $\mathrm{Sh}(1, 1) = S_2$, because with $k = l = 1$ there are no two values to compare. The identity has sign $+1$ and the transposition $-1$, so
\[
(\alpha \wedge \beta)(v^1, v^2) = \alpha(v^1)\beta(v^2) - \alpha(v^2)\beta(v^1) = \det \begin{pmatrix} \alpha(v^1) & \alpha(v^2) \\ \beta(v^1) & \beta(v^2) \end{pmatrix} .
\]
\leeref{Ch.~14, \emph{The Wedge Product}}
\end{exbox}

This is the formula of Lecture~28: for $\alpha = dx^i$ and $\beta = dx^j$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$ it gives $(dx^i \wedge dx^j)(u, v) = u^i v^j - u^j v^i$, which is Definition~\ref{def:dx-wedge-dx}. So the two-form named $dx^i \wedge dx^j$ there is the wedge product of the one-forms $dx^i$ and $dx^j$. This case of the wedge product is the one used most often. The next case, $k = 1$ and $l = 2$, is left for Lecture~30.

\begin{exbox}[The Wedge of Two Two-Forms]\exlabel{ex:wedge-two-forms}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} Let $k = l = 2$. A $(2, 2)$-shuffle is determined by the two places $\sigma(1) < \sigma(2)$, so there are $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ of them (Lemma~\ref{lem:shuffle-factorization}(2)); in one-line notation, with their signs, they are
\[
(1, 2, 3, 4)\ {+}, \quad (1, 3, 2, 4)\ {-}, \quad (1, 4, 2, 3)\ {+}, \quad (2, 3, 1, 4)\ {+}, \quad (2, 4, 1, 3)\ {-}, \quad (3, 4, 1, 2)\ {+} ,
\]
with $0, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4$ inversions. For $\alpha, \beta \in \Lambda^2 V^*$, Definition~\ref{def:wedge-product} gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
(\alpha \wedge \beta)(v^1, v^2, v^3, v^4) ={}& \alpha(v^1, v^2)\beta(v^3, v^4) - \alpha(v^1, v^3)\beta(v^2, v^4) + \alpha(v^1, v^4)\beta(v^2, v^3) \\
&+ \alpha(v^2, v^3)\beta(v^1, v^4) - \alpha(v^2, v^4)\beta(v^1, v^3) + \alpha(v^3, v^4)\beta(v^1, v^2) .
\end{aligned}
\]
\end{exbox}

\textit{(Not from lecture; figure added.)} The six $(2, 2)$-shuffles of Example~\ref{ex:wedge-two-forms}. In each diagram the top row is the entries $1, 2$ of $\alpha$ (red) and $3, 4$ of $\beta$ (blue), and the strand from $i$ ends at the vector $v^{\sigma(i)}$ that this entry receives. Strands of the same colour never cross, which is the shuffle condition. Each crossing of a red strand with a blue one (black dot) is an inversion of $\sigma$, so the sign of the term is $+$ for an even number of crossings (green) and $-$ for an odd number (red).
%% <<< END ADDED

\begin{propbox}[Properties of the Wedge Product]\thmlabel{prop:wedge-properties}
For $\alpha, \alpha_1, \alpha_2 \in \Lambda^k V^*$, $\beta \in \Lambda^l V^*$, $\gamma \in \Lambda^r V^*$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item \emph{bilinear}: $(\alpha_1 + \lambda\alpha_2) \wedge \beta = \alpha_1 \wedge \beta + \lambda\, \alpha_2 \wedge \beta$, and likewise in $\beta$;
\item \emph{associative}: $\alpha \wedge (\beta \wedge \gamma) = (\alpha \wedge \beta) \wedge \gamma$;
\item \emph{graded anticommutative}: $\beta \wedge \alpha = (-1)^{kl}\, \alpha \wedge \beta$; in particular, forms of even degree commute with all forms;
\item for a basis $(\varepsilon^i)$ of $V^*$ and $A = \{a_1 < \cdots < a_k\}$: $\varepsilon^A = \varepsilon^{a_1} \wedge \cdots \wedge \varepsilon^{a_k}$ (Definition~\ref{def:epsilon-A}).
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Proposition 14.11}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}[Proof (to be filled)]
Lecture~29 stated the four properties without proof. (1) is immediate from Definition~\ref{def:wedge-product}, each term of the sum being linear in $\alpha$ and in $\beta$. In~(3), forms of even degree commute with all forms because $(-1)^{kl} = 1$ when $k$ or $l$ is even. (4) is a nontrivial computation: the shuffle formula is, in disguise, an expansion of a determinant. (2)--(4) are to be filled.
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[Forms of Odd Degree Square to Zero]\thmlabel{cor:odd-forms-square-zero}
If $\alpha \in \Lambda^k V^*$ with $k$ odd, then $\alpha \wedge \alpha = 0$. In particular $\varepsilon \wedge \varepsilon = 0$ for every covector $\varepsilon \in V^*$.
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} By Proposition~\ref{prop:wedge-properties}(3) with $\beta = \alpha$ and $l = k$: $\alpha \wedge \alpha = (-1)^{k^2}\, \alpha \wedge \alpha = -\alpha \wedge \alpha$, since $k^2$ is odd. So $2\, \alpha \wedge \alpha = 0$. For a covector, $k = 1$; this can also be read off Example~\ref{ex:wedge-one-forms}: $(\varepsilon \wedge \varepsilon)(v^1, v^2) = \varepsilon(v^1)\varepsilon(v^2) - \varepsilon(v^2)\varepsilon(v^1) = 0$.
\end{proof}

For $\varepsilon = dx^i$ this is $dx^i \wedge dx^i = 0$, as in Lemma~\ref{lem:dx-wedge-properties}(2).

\begin{exbox}[A Form of Even Degree with Nonzero Square]\exlabel{ex:even-form-nonzero-square}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} For even degree the corollary fails. On $\mathbb{R}^4$ let
\[
\omega = dx^1 \wedge dx^2 + dx^3 \wedge dx^4 \in \Lambda^2 (\mathbb{R}^4)^* , \qquad \omega(u, v) = u^1 v^2 - u^2 v^1 + u^3 v^4 - u^4 v^3
\]
(Example~\ref{ex:basis-euclidean-forms}). On the standard basis, $\omega(e_1, e_2) = \omega(e_3, e_4) = 1$, and $\omega(e_i, e_j) = 0$ for the other pairs $i < j$. By the six-term formula of Example~\ref{ex:wedge-two-forms} with $\alpha = \beta = \omega$, only the first and the last term are not zero:
\[
(\omega \wedge \omega)(e_1, e_2, e_3, e_4) = \omega(e_1, e_2)\,\omega(e_3, e_4) + \omega(e_3, e_4)\,\omega(e_1, e_2) = 2 .
\]
So $\omega \wedge \omega \neq 0$. By Corollary~\ref{cor:top-degree-forms}, $\omega \wedge \omega = 2\, \varepsilon^{\{1, 2, 3, 4\}}$, twice the determinant; with Proposition~\ref{prop:wedge-properties}(4) this reads $\omega \wedge \omega = 2\, dx^1 \wedge dx^2 \wedge dx^3 \wedge dx^4$.
\end{exbox}

Next (Lecture~30): more computations in low degree; then $V$ becomes the tangent space $T_pM$ again, and the point $p$ varies over a manifold, so that the forms become functions of the point.

\appendix
\chapter{Concordance with Lee}\label{app:lee}

These notes follow the course, and Lee's \emph{Introduction to Smooth Manifolds} (2nd ed.) is the course text. The two cover the same mathematics by different routes. The course is more algebraic --- germs, derivations of germs, the ideal $I_p$ --- and it builds tangent spaces from the geometric picture towards the abstract one, where Lee starts abstract. This appendix is for reading the two side by side. It records where the notation differs, where the routes diverge, which parts of Lee each section corresponds to, and, for every result of Lee's cited in these notes, where its counterpart is. Throughout the notes, the line \textsc{Lee}: at the foot of a box gives the same information locally.

\section*{A.1\quad Notation}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{A.1\quad Notation}

$T^{\geo}_pM$, the geometric tangent space & $\mathbb{R}^n_a$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$; $T_pS \subseteq T_pM$ for embedded $S$ & Theorem~\ref{thm:ambient-abstract}; Lee, Propositions 3.2 and 5.38. \\

$\Gamma = \{(x, g \cdot x)\}$, the orbit relation & $\mathcal{O} = \{(g \cdot p, p)\}$ & The same set with the factors swapped (proof of Lee, Proposition 21.4). \\
$H_{x_0}$, the isotropy group & $G_p$ & Definition~\ref{def:isotropy}. \\
$\Phi : G/H \to X$, $gH \mapsto g \cdot x_0$ & $F : G/G_p \to M$ & Theorem~\ref{thm:GH-homeo}; Lee, Theorem 21.18. \\

$\varphi_t(q) = \varphi^q(t) = \varphi(t, q)$ (Lectures~23--24: $\varphi_q(t)$); $\dot c(t)$ & $\theta_t(p) = \theta^{(p)}(t) = \theta(t, p)$; $\gamma'(t)$ & The flow and its integral curves (Definition~\ref{def:flow-notation}); the subscript is a time for $\varphi_t$, a point for $\varphi_q$. \\

\section*{A.2\quad Where the routes diverge}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{A.2\quad Where the routes diverge}

Each row is expanded in a \textbf{Comparison with Lee} paragraph at the place indicated.

\begin{longtable}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3.2cm} >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{5.9cm} >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{5.7cm}}
\toprule
\textbf{Topic} & \textbf{These notes} & \textbf{Lee} \\ \midrule \endhead
Hausdorff quotients & One criterion for all open quotients (Theorems~\ref{thm:hausdorff-criterion} and~\ref{thm:2c-quotient}), reused for orbit and coset spaces & Checked example by example (Example 1.5, Problem 1-9) \\
Regular level sets & Implicit function theorem, topological first (Theorem~\ref{thm:regular-value}), smooth afterwards (Proposition~\ref{prop:level-set-smooth}) & Example 1.32 for one function; Corollary 5.14 via the constant-rank theorem \\
Hausdorff orbit spaces & Compact group on a Hausdorff space, purely topological (Theorem~\ref{thm:orbit-T2-strong}) & Proper actions of Lie groups (Proposition 21.4, Corollary 21.6) \\
Homogeneous spaces & $G/H$ compact and $X$ Hausdorff (Theorem~\ref{thm:GH-homeo}); the hypothesis is needed (Example~\ref{ex:GH-not-homeo}) & Smooth version, no compactness (Theorem 21.18) \\
Tangent vectors & Derivations of germs; locality is built in, and no bump functions are needed & Derivations of $C^\infty(M)$; locality from bump functions (Proposition 3.8) \\
Order of ideas & Geometric first, $T^{\geo}_pM = \ker F'(p)$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel}), then derivations & Derivations first; $T_pS = \ker d\Phi_p$ later (Proposition 5.38) \\
Cotangent space & The dual, and also $I_p/I_p^2$ of germs, via a non-degenerate pairing (Theorem~\ref{thm:cotangent-ideal}) & The dual in the text (Chapter~11); $I_p/I_p^2$ of global functions, via $f \mapsto df_p$, as Problem 11-4 \\
Transversality & Level sets in Euclidean space (Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-preimage}) & Embedded submanifolds (Theorem 6.30) \\
Linear algebra & The toolkit of \ref{sec:vector-spaces}, including the pairing theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:pairing}) & Appendix B; dual spaces in Chapter~11 \\
